A Yemeni government military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said more than 20 government soldiers and nearly 10 allied local fighters had been killed and dozens of others wounded in fighting in Taiz over the past 24 hours.
The official described fierce battles across several fronts, with opposing forces engaging in close-range combat for key positions in the province.
The most intense confrontations were concentrated in rural areas stretching toward Yemen's Red Sea coast, where government forces were seeking to halt Houthi advances and prevent the group from consolidating its recent gains near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, according to the official.
In the southern port city of Aden, government forces' air defenses intercepted several Houthi drones as they approached vital facilities and public service sites in the city, according to a statement posted on social media platform X.
Majid al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for the government forces, said on X that government forces had carried out 474 strikes and targeting operations against the Houthis using fighter jets, drones, and other weapons. He claimed the strikes had killed or wounded 1,540 Houthi fighters, most of them in Taiz, and destroyed or disabled 216 pieces of military equipment.
On the other hand, a medical source affiliated with the Houthis, also speaking on condition of anonymity, told Xinhua that more than 40 Houthi fighters had been killed and dozens of others wounded over the past 24 hours.
"Many of the deaths resulted from airstrikes on vehicles transporting reinforcements to active combat areas in rural Taiz," the source said.
In a separate statement posted on X, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said 94 Saudi air and missile strikes had hit areas across the provinces of Sanaa, Saada, Taiz, Hajjah, Amran and Ibb over the previous 24 hours. He claimed civilian sites were among the targets and that the attacks had caused casualties, without providing a detailed toll.
He said the latest attacks brought the total number of air and missile strikes recorded by the group since the current escalation began to 1,350.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Turki Al-Maliki said on X that three ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi group toward Khamis Mushait were intercepted and destroyed.
The latest fighting is part of a broader escalation around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the strategic waterway linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and a major route for international shipping.
Clashes have intensified in Taiz and neighboring Lahj since the Houthis captured the Red Sea port city of Mocha on Sept. 10 and Mayyun Island, also known as Perim, on Sept. 11, expanding their presence around the strait and pushing some of the heaviest ground fighting into nearby mountainous areas.
The escalation has also been accompanied by renewed Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and what the group says are Saudi air and missile strikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen, reviving cross-border hostilities that had largely subsided after a UN-brokered truce in 2022.
Yemen's conflict began in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government. ■

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- South Africa is stepping up efforts to root out corruption and fraud at its borders and ports of entry, with officials implicated in misconduct facing disciplinary action, dismissal and criminal charges, an official said Friday.
The Border Management Authority (BMA) handled 57 labor and disciplinary cases involving breaches of internal controls, fraud, corruption and other misconduct in the last quarter, while 33 cases remain under disciplinary proceedings, BMA Commissioner Michael Masiapato said during a quarterly anti-corruption campaign at O.R. Tambo International Airport in Johannesburg.
The campaign brought together government and law-enforcement bodies including the Special Investigating Unit (SIU), the Department of Home Affairs and the National Prosecuting Authority.
Masiapato said corruption at ports of entry could involve border guards, immigration and customs officials, port operators and others exercising discretionary powers.
Such misconduct includes colluding with travelers or third parties to evade duties and taxes, facilitating the movement of illicit goods, soliciting bribes for routine services and fraudulently issuing travel or immigration documents, he said.
In February, the SIU said South Africa's immigration system had been treated as "a marketplace," where permits and visas were sold to the highest bidder through corrupt networks involving officials and external actors.
The Department of Home Affairs said at the time that it had identified more than 2,000 study visas fraudulently issued through such syndicates and that administrative processes were underway to cancel them.
Rooting out corruption in the immigration system is also part of the government's comprehensive approach to migration management adopted in June. President Cyril Ramaphosa said when announcing the measures that the government would strengthen border security, crack down on violations of immigration laws and continue efforts to eliminate corruption in the immigration system. ■

Trump visa policies weigh on Columbia University’s journalism programme as admissions pause
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:38:18 UTC
06:38:18 KST

Trump visa policies weigh on Columbia University’s journalism programme as admissions pause
The Trump administration’s changing visa policies caused a sharp drop in international applications to Columbia University and contributed to the university pausing admissions to one of its journalism programmes, four people familiar with the matter said.
The journalism school announced on Oct 1 that it was pausing admissions to its Master of Arts offering to conduct a “critical evaluation”, without giving further details about the reasons.
Jelani Cobb, the journalism school’s dean, said admissions to its Master of Arts programme would pause for one year while the school reworked a degree created in 2005, when the “journalism marketplace looked different”.
“The dynamics of visas and all those other kinds of things were part of the consideration,” Cobb told Reuters. Additionally, the department needs time to think through changes to the programme, he added.
The connection between the admissions pause and US visa policies has not been previously reported, nor has the length of the admissions pause.
The drop in international applications shows how uncertainty over US President Donald Trump’s visa policies is affecting one of the preeminent US journalism institutions, which also administers the profession’s highest US honour, the Pulitzer Prize. The people did not disclose the exact size of the drop in applications.
Last year, the Trump administration temporarily halted new student-visa appointments, then resumed them with expanded screening of applicants’ online activity, saying the checks were needed to identify potential threats to US national security.
Columbia was among the universities targeted by his administration over pro-Palestinian campus protests in 2024. Last year, it agreed to pay over US$200 million to settle federal investigations and regain most of its suspended federal funding.
A new rule this year also sought to limit how long foreign students and journalists could stay in the US without seeking extensions, but a federal judge blocked it before it took effect last month, calling its rationale “exceptionally weak”.
Reliance on international students
Visa difficulties and immigration policy uncertainty have deterred prospective Columbia journalism students from abroad, the four people said, requesting anonymity to discuss its admissions. International students make up roughly half of the MA programme’s enrollment, the people said.
Kaushik Raj, an Indian journalist admitted to Columbia’s separate Master of Science (MS) programme in data journalism, was denied a US student visa last year, the Intercept reported. His rejection letter said he had not shown sufficient ties to India to establish he would return after his studies, according to the report.
Geared toward mid-career journalists seeking expertise in subjects such as politics, business and science, the MA programme is smaller than the MS programme aimed at students with less journalism experience. The school is not pausing the MS programme.
Lower enrollment has prompted changes to the MA programme, including the combination of science and politics seminars in the 2024-25 academic year, two of the people familiar with the matter said.
On Oct 1, the school also announced a two-year, part-time online MS programme. The move could allow Columbia to enroll international students without visas, but Cobb said it was unrelated to the MA admissions pause because the programmes serve different students.
Changing dynamics of journalism
The MA pause comes as news organisations grapple with AI’s potential to reshape how stories are produced and found, while falling search traffic piles pressure on their business.
Last year, at least 3,434 journalism jobs were cut in Britain and the United States, according to a Press Gazette tracker. The British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) and American news outlet CBS News have announced layoffs this year.
Some journalists took to social media on Oct 1 to criticise the MA programme as too short and too expensive. The course spans nine months and Columbia estimates the cost of attendance at US$120,000 before financial aid.
The year-long MS in data journalism costs about US$180,000.
Two of the people familiar with the matter said the financial assistance made tuition less of a deterrent because most students receive financial aid.
About 80 per cent of the students receive financial aid, including grants, loans, or scholarships from institutional, federal and private funds, according to its website.
Cobb said the journalism school wants to create a new fundraising strategy for the MA programme and is considering starting a part-time version. REUTERS

Rais-Ali Delvari Museum reopens after major redesign in southern Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

06:32:00 KST

Rais-Ali Delvari Museum reopens after major redesign in southern Iran
TEHRAN - Rais-Ali Delvari Museum has reopened in the southern city of Delvar following extensive physical and content redesign, with officials describing the museum as a venue for documenting the resistance of local communities against British forces during World War I.
Speaking at the reopening ceremony on Thursday evening, Minister of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri said museums serve as part of a nation’s collective memory and provide a platform for revisiting its historical and cultural identity.
Salehi-Amiri stressed the importance of presenting historical narratives accurately and professionally to younger generations as well as domestic and international visitors.
He said the Rais-Ali Delvari Museum had undergone comprehensive renovation and redesign, including the refurbishment of its rooms, revision and translation of exhibition content, landscaping and preparation of its central courtyard.
A newly designed relief wall in the courtyard depicts the history of resistance by Iranians, particularly the people of Tangestan, against British colonial forces. According to the minister, efforts have been made to present the historical narrative in a way suited to contemporary audiences.
Four books focusing on Rais-Ali Delvari, the history of resistance in Delvar and the struggles of the people of Tangestan against British forces were also unveiled during the ceremony.
Salehi-Amiri said museums need knowledgeable and capable narrators who can communicate historical subjects clearly and engagingly.
“Rais-Ali Delvari” has become part of the popular cultural memory of people in southern Iran and Tangestan, he said, adding that the museum could serve as a center for revisiting this historical identity and passing it on to future generations.
The minister also highlighted Bushehr’s historical significance as a center of resistance in modern Iranian history, saying the region’s heritage could be incorporated into new cultural tourism products.
He suggested turning the history of southern Iran’s resistance to foreign powers into a subject for research and tourism, using museums, storytelling, cultural tourism and specialized programs to present it to different audiences.
Salehi-Amiri also outlined the ministry’s plan to expand coastal and maritime tourism, saying Iran’s southern coastline, from Chabahar and Makran (or Makkoran) to Hormozgan, the Persian Gulf islands, Bushehr and Khuzestan, could be developed as an interconnected tourism corridor.
He said investment in accommodation facilities, piers and tourism services, along with the expansion of maritime tours, could help local communities and the economy of Bushehr benefit from the region’s coastal potential.
Rais-Ali Delvari (1882–1915) was a military leader and a prominent figure in Iran’s resistance to British forces following the occupation of Bushehr in 1915, during World War I. Iran had declared neutrality in the war.
Born in the port city of Bushehr, Delvari organized resistance in Tangestan after British forces occupied Bushehr and Delvar. He was killed on Sept. 2, 1915, aged 33.
His former house in Delvar, near Bushehr, was previously converted into an ethnological museum. The collection includes some of his personal belongings and historical documents, as well as firearms and horse equipment.

The war with Iran derailed OPEC+’s oil plans — a review of future quotas has been postponed
Kyiv • UNN
OPEC+ postponed its assessment of countries’ production capacities from September to November 2026 due to projects disrupted by the war. The results will determine quotas for 2027.
OPEC+ has postponed its review of the member countries’ production capacities, which is to serve as the basis for determining oil production quotas in 2027. The reason was the consequences of the US and Israeli war against Iran, which disrupted some projects to expand oil production capacity in the Middle East, Reuters reports, citing two sources, writes UNN.
Details
The assessment of the maximum sustainable production capacity of OPEC+ countries was initially planned to be completed by the end of September 2026. Now, according to the agency’s sources, the deadline has been moved to mid-November.
The war in the Middle East delayed the implementation of projects that were intended to increase the production capacity of several countries. As a result, it has become more difficult to assess how much oil they will actually be able to produce steadily in the future. In addition, not all OPEC+ participants have managed to provide the necessary data.
Oil quotas will depend on the assessment
An independent assessment of the capacities of most OPEC+ members is being conducted by the US consulting company DeGolyer and MacNaughton. Its report is now expected by mid-November—shortly before the next OPEC+ meeting at the end of the month.
Oil prices fell by 1% — what is the price forecast01.10.26, 08:40 • 8150 views
The results are expected to become one of the key benchmarks during negotiations on quotas for 2027. Countries whose production capabilities are assessed as lower may face pressure to reduce their quotas, while states that have increased their capacities may demand permission to produce more.
The situation has already caused disputes within the oil alliance. The United Arab Emirates, which sought a higher quota due to an increase in its own production capacity, left OPEC+ in May. Iraq is also seeking an increased quota and, according to Reuters, considered the possibility of leaving the organization.

Saudi Arabia is preparing a large-scale offensive against the Houthis involving more than 100,000 troops
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
00:28:00 EEST
06:28:00 KST

Saudi Arabia is preparing a large-scale offensive against the Houthis involving more than 100,000 troops
Kyiv • UNN
Riyadh may launch an offensive in Yemen in the coming weeks to retake Bab el-Mandeb. More than 100,000 troops are planned to be involved in the operation.
Saudi Arabia is preparing a new offensive against the Houthis in Yemen, the main objective of which could be to regain control over the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea coast. More than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be involved in the operation, Reuters reports, citing regional and Western officials, writes UNN.
Details
According to six agency sources, the operation could begin as early as in the coming weeks. The ground offensive is to be carried out by Yemeni forces under Riyadh's leadership and with the support of Saudi aviation.
Saudi Arabia is considering two main scenarios. The first involves a limited offensive in the area of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait; the second is a larger-scale operation with simultaneous strikes along several fronts in the provinces of Al-Bayda, Marib, Taiz, and Al-Jawf.
One of the world's key sea routes is under threat
Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit from the Red Sea and part of one of the most important trade routes between Asia and the Mediterranean. According to Reuters, last month the Houthis advanced along the coast and established control over the strait.
The agency's sources claim that Riyadh sees no possibility of returning to peace talks while the Houthis control Bab el-Mandeb. Regaining the coastal areas is considered one of the key objectives of the future operation.
International assistance
The United States is already providing Saudi Arabia with intelligence and military advisers, but direct participation by American forces in combat operations is not expected. Reuters previously reported that Donald Trump rejected Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's request for direct military support, including U.S. airstrikes.
Pakistan and Turkey are also providing military support to Riyadh. According to Reuters sources, Pakistan has supplied air defense systems, artillery, drones, and counter-drone equipment, while between 30,000 and 40,000 Pakistani troops are stationed in Saudi Arabia to protect its territory and intercept missiles and UAVs.
The sources do not name the exact date when the operation will begin. According to various estimates, the offensive could begin sometime between next week and early November. Officially, Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government, and the Houthis have not yet commented on reports of preparations for the operation.

Iran, UNESCO discuss stronger intl. cooperation to protect World Heritage sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:26:36 UTC
06:26:36 KST

Iran, UNESCO discuss stronger intl. cooperation to protect World Heritage sites
TEHRAN - Iran and UNESCO have discussed expanding technical and international cooperation to assess, document, restore and protect Iran’s World Heritage sites, including properties reportedly damaged during the recent war.
Farhad Azizi Zelani, director general of Iran’s World Heritage sites under the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts, on Wednesday met with Lazare Eloundou Assomo, director of UNESCO’s World Heritage Centre, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Dialogue on Heritage and Authenticity in Hanoi, Vietnam.
During the meeting, Azizi Zelani presented an update on the condition of Iran’s cultural heritage sites and properties, with particular focus on World Heritage sites that were damaged during the recent conflict with the combined forces of the US and the Israeli regime. He outlined the reported extent of the damage as well as ongoing expert assessments, documentation and emergency measures aimed at protecting and restoring the affected sites.
The Iranian official also outlined the ministry’s expectations from UNESCO’s World Heritage Centre, emphasizing the need to make greater use of its technical, professional and international capacities.
The two sides discussed expanding expert cooperation, exchanging technical knowledge and experience, supporting conservation programs and facilitating the participation of international experts in assessing damaged heritage sites.
Assomo said the World Heritage Centre supports Iran’s cultural heritage and properties inscribed on the World Heritage List. He also said UNESCO was planning to send representatives to conduct field assessments, examine the extent of damage and identify possible forms of support and cooperation.
He stressed the importance of maintaining professional communication and coordination among the relevant institutions, saying continued technical engagement could contribute to stronger conservation efforts and more effective approaches to safeguarding Iran’s World Heritage.
They also stressed the historical, civilizational and international importance of Iran’s cultural heritage and called for stronger cooperation between Iran and the World Heritage Centre to make targeted use of available capacities to protect heritage of importance to humanity.
 
Among the sites cited were Golestan Palace in Tehran and Imam Mosque in Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan.

Finnish Police Investigate Suspected Break-Ins Targeting Nearly 20 MPs Amid Foreign Interference Concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:24:11 UTC
06:24:11 KST

- Category
- World
Finnish Police Investigate Suspected Break-Ins Targeting Nearly 20 MPs Amid Foreign Interference Concerns
Several Finnish MPs are believed to have been targeted in a series of unexplained home intrusions over the past year, Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported on October 1.
The Helsinki Police Department has opened a preliminary investigation with support from Finland’s National Bureau of Investigation. Fewer than 20 MPs are believed to have been affected, although the exact number remains unclear.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Finland had already warned citizens to prepare for possible Russian hybrid attacks, including sabotage and unauthorized drone incidents. Finnish President Alexander Stubb stated in September that Russia was waging a hybrid war against Europe and urged the public to remain alert without panicking.
No signs of forced entry were found, and nothing was reported stolen or damaged. Instead, lawmakers noticed small unexplained changes inside their homes, including open doors or lights left on.
Parliamentary Speaker Jussi Halla-aho stated that some of those signs may have been deliberately left to show that someone had entered the properties.
“There may be certain general signs that recur in these suspected intrusions,” Halla-aho stated. “From the point of view of the investigation, it would not be sensible to specify what they are.”
Yle noted that the affected MPs do not appear to share a common political or demographic background. The cases only became apparent after First Deputy Speaker Paula Risikko learned of a suspected intrusion on September 23.
Parliament subsequently asked political group leaders to determine whether other MPs had experienced similar incidents, after which more cases emerged. Lawmakers were also instructed to report suspicious signs to parliamentary security and police.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo stated that foreign interference could be behind the incidents, although authorities have not identified who was responsible or established a motive, Yle wrote.
“It is quite possible in this day and age,” Orpo stated.
He also warned that election interference should be taken seriously as future votes approach, noting that Russia has previously sought to influence elections in European countries.
Alexander Stubb also commented on the incidents, describing attacks on elected lawmakers as attacks on democratic institutions.
“An attack on a member of parliament is an attack on democracy,” Stubb stated, according to Yle. “It should not be allowed or accepted in any form.”
NATO had previously emphasized that its Article 5 mutual defense clause remains deliberately ambiguous when it comes to hybrid attacks. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated that the alliance would not define a fixed threshold for collective defense, while noting that NATO could respond asymmetrically to sabotage, cyberattacks, and other gray-zone operations.

Israel's 'arbitrary' checkpoints 'choking' Palestinian life in West Bank: UN special rapporteur
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:23:52 UTC
06:23:52 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
03 October 2026•Update: 03 October 2026
Israel's growing network of checkpoints and road barriers in the occupied West Bank is increasingly restricting the daily lives of Palestinians and dividing the territory, a UN special rapporteur said on Friday.
“Arbitrariness itself becomes a form of torment when every journey, every appointment and every family visit depends on whether a gate is open or a soldier allows passage,” Francesca Albanese, special rapporteur on the situation of occupied Palestinian territories, said in a statement.
UN figures cited in the statement found that 925 checkpoints and other movement obstacles were in place in West Bank, including East Jerusalem, as of December 2025, affecting the movement of 3.4 million Palestinians.
That was the highest number documented in two decades, and 43% above the average recorded in the previous 20 years, according to the UN.
Albanese stressed that movement restrictions have worsened since October 2023. Around Nablus, delays have risen sharply, while in Beit Furik, home to nearly 16,000 and served by a single gate, a journey that normally takes a 15-minute drive has at times stretched to between five and 10 hours.
She also cited the case of four-month-old Ahmed Zaid, who died in July after Israeli soldiers held his family at a checkpoint for more than an hour as they tried to reach an ambulance waiting on the other side.
“Ahmed's death is a devastating illustration of what this system means in human terms,” she said.
Albanese said the growing number of checkpoints comes amid increasing settler "terror," settlement expansion, demolitions, displacement and damage to Palestinian agriculture in the West Bank.

Brazil’s Lula says only he can stop rise of fascism under Bolsonaro’s son
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:12:29 UTC
06:12:29 KST

The Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has claimed he is the only thing standing in the way of far-right “fascists” reclaiming power, as he led a huge rally through the streets of Rio ahead of Sunday’s crunch election.
Speaking on the eve of the demonstration, the 80-year-old leftwinger said he had decided to seek a historic fourth term because he believed only he could prevent the family of his rightwing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, returning to government.
“If it weren’t for me standing up to these fascists they’d easily win another election. I’m the one standing in their way,” Lula told a popular podcast called Flow, before adding: “It’s either me, or it’s barbarism.”
Hours later, Lula flew to Rio, staging what his team called a “victory march” between two highly symbolic downtown locations that played an important role in Brazil’s fight for democracy during the 1964-1985 military dictatorship.
“What’s at stake is not the victory of one man, it is the victory of an idea, it’s the victory of democracy,” Brazil’s president said after the parade set off from the Candelária church. The church is the location where more than a million people, including Lula, famously gathered in 1984 to demand direct presidential elections.
Lula, who was among those who spoke at that historic demo when he was an up-and-coming politician in his 30s, added: “Either we consolidate democracy, or we will lose it.”
From Candelária, a sea of red-clad Lula supporters marched a mile south towards Cinelândia, the scene of an equally well-known pro-democracy protest in 1968 called the March of the Hundred Thousand.
“No gringo is going to lay a finger on Brazil’s things,” vowed Lula, in an indirect reference to claims Donald Trump’s administration is seeking to sway the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour with a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure.
The decision to hold Friday’s rally between two such politically charged places spoke to how this year’s election has stirred up renewed fears over the future of Latin America’s biggest democracy.
Election-eve polls suggest Lula holds only a slender lead over his adversary, whose father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after Lula beat him in the 2022 election.
Many Brazilian democrats fear that if 45-year-old Bolsonaro wins this year’s election, he will move quickly to free his father and his fellow coup-plotters from jail – and then set about dismantling and co-opting the country’s democratic institutions, such as the supreme court.
“This is the most important election of our lives – and we have to do everything we can to win,” said Marcelo Freixo, a politician from Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) who is running for a seat in congress.
Freixo warned: “We spent 21 years living under a really harsh dictatorship. We fought so hard to attain our democratic institutions. And a victory for the Bolsonaro family – a family that always … openly defended the dictatorship and tried to stage a coup … would spell the end for our democratic process and institutions.”
Valmir Aleixo, a 55-year-old history teacher who was one of thousands of people who joined Friday’s pro-Lula demo, said: “This is [a choice] between democracy and the savagery of far-right fascism. This is perhaps the most important election since the return of democracy in the 80s.”
Noni Ostrower, 74, came to what was Rio’s largest leftwing protest in years carrying a homemade banner that read: “Democracy Is Valuable”.
“I’m the daughter of two refugees from nazism. They came to Brazil from Germany because of this,” Ostrower said. “I was born here in Brazil … and today I have grandchildren and I absolutely do not want to see fascism return to Brazil – it would be a tragedy for the country. That’s why I’m here today.”
During the campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his 71-year-old father if elected, with some speculating Jair Bolsonaro could even become a minister. His brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, a radical former congressman with ties to Trump’s Maga movement, reputedly hopes to become foreign minister. Flávio Bolsonaro has announced plans to appoint five firmly conservative supreme court judges.
Luiz Eduardo Soares, a prominent anthropologist and writer, said he feared what might happen if the Bolsonaro clan managed to reclaim power.
“I think these elections could be the last ones in my life, for my generation … What was done over the course of 10 years in Hungary, [Bolsonaro] will do in two,” Soares predicted in reference to the European country’s transformation into an “electoral autocracy” under its former prime minister, Viktor Orbán.
Diogo Nogueira, a famous samba singer who came to the rally wearing his trademark panama hat, said: “We need to win in the first round so we don’t allow this type of people to get back into government. If they do get back in, it won’t just be a problem for four years, but for 10 or 20.”
Polls suggest the election is likely to go to a second round runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro on 25 October, with Lula expected to secure about 45% of votes on Sunday and Bolsonaro 40%, according to the Datafolha pollster. But at Friday’s rally Lula claimed he could pull off a shock first-round win by claiming more than 50% of the vote.
In an online broadcast, Bolsonaro insisted his campaign would prevail. “Brazil is a few hours from deciding its future … for the next 30, 40, 50 years. It’s the end of an era. It’s the end of the Worker’s party era,” he claimed, asking undecided voters to back him to achieve that aim, even if they didn’t like him.

Houthis condemn Saudi claims of attack on Medina
Yemen’s Houthis have denied targeting a power station in the city of Medina. A Saudi-led coalition earlier accused the militant group of targeting the facility supplying power to the Prophet’s Mosque – one of the holiest sites in the Muslim world.
A senior Houthi official branded the accusation a “lie” aimed at tarnishing the group’s image and reinforcing similar claims made by the coalition in the past.
On Thursday, the Saudi coalition’s spokesman, Major General Turki al-Maliki, accused the Yemeni militants of striking the Taibah electricity distribution station in Medina earlier this week in what he called a “cowardly terrorist act” and a part of an alleged broader campaign by the Houthis to “target the Two Holy Mosques.”
In mid-September, Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of launching a drone towards the holy city of Mecca. The unmanned aerial vehicle was intercepted and destroyed, it added. The Yemeni movement’s leader, Abdel-Malik al-Houthi, dismissed that claim as a “heinous lie” in a televised address at the time, claiming Riyadh was “weaponizing lies” to advance its own agenda.
The developments have sparked concerns in Türkiye and Pakistan, which signed a joint defense agreement with Saudi Arabia in August. Speaking to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called any “threat to the sanctity” of the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina a “red line that must never be crossed.”
Ankara denounced this week’s alleged Medina attack. “Any attack targeting the sanctity, peace, and security of the Two Holy Mosques is an unacceptable affront directed at the shared sensitivities of the entire Islamic world,” the Turkish government spokesman, Burhanettin Duran, said on X on Friday. He vowed that Türkiye “will continue to stand by Saudi Arabia.”
The developments come amid the continued escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition. Riyadh has backed Yemen’s internationally recognized government against the Houthis since intervening in the country’s civil war in 2015.
Large-scale fighting largely subsided after a UN-brokered truce in 2022, but the conflict erupted again this summer after an airport in the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital of Sanaa was bombed to prevent a returning Houthi delegation that had flown to Iran from landing.

Trump strikes positive tone on lifting Türkiye CAATSA sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:04:50 UTC
06:04:50 KST

US President Donald Trump has responded positively when asked about lifting US sanctions on Türkiye under the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA), without announcing a decision.
“I’ll always speak to President Erdogan. He is a friend of mine, as you know. And I’ll always make him happy,” Trump said when asked what was holding up the removal of the sanctions.
Trump said during a meeting with Erdogan on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Türkiye in July that he wanted to lift the CAATSA sanctions and would “certainly” consider allowing Ankara to purchase F-35 fighter jets.
The US removed Türkiye from the F-35 programme in 2019 after Ankara acquired the Russian S-400 air defence system.
Washington said the system posed a security risk to the F-35 and was incompatible with NATO systems.
In December 2020, the US imposed CAATSA sanctions on Türkiye’s defence industry and several senior officials over the S-400 purchase.
Türkiye says it purchased the Russian system to meet urgent air defence needs after being denied US-made Patriot missiles and has repeatedly rejected Washington’s concerns over the S-400 and F-35.
The dispute has remained a major issue in US-Türkiye defence ties, with Ankara seeking the removal of the sanctions and its return to the F-35 programme.
Trump pledged to lift the sanctions earlier this year
“We’re going to be taking the sanctions off. It’s time to do that… we don't want to sanction friends. It's very simple,” Trump said.

US FAA says Boeing 737 Max software glitch poses no safety issue
- The FAA expert panel found the Boeing 737 Max software glitch poses no safety risk, allowing certification of the larger Max 10 variant to proceed.
- The software issue affects automated flight guidance during unusual landings but pilots retain full control and clear indicators.
- Boeing is working on a software update and pilot procedures, with Max 10 certification expected soon, benefiting airlines like Southwest and United Airlines.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said on Oct 2 that a panel of experts had determined a software glitch in some Boeing 737 Max flight computers poses no safety concern, clearing the way for approval of a larger version of the best-selling narrow-body jet.
The decision removes a late obstacle to certification of the Max 10, the largest variant of the 737 Max family, which has been delayed for years. It should also ease concerns at airlines that fly the Max 7, which uses the same software and was certified by the FAA in August.
The FAA said the determination by the Corrective Action Review Board that met in Seattle on Oct 2 was based on the fact that “pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous.”
The FAA said earlier this week it was delaying certification of the Max 10 until it completed an analysis of the software issue, which could prevent pilots from accessing automated flight guidance during an unusual landing scenario.
Boeing said it “will continue to follow the lead of the FAA as our engineers work on the next software update.”
Boeing added it is working directly with airlines to formalise a procedure that will allow pilots “to re-enable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur.”
Aviation officials now believe the Max 10 could be certified as soon as later this month.
The issue could also have affected Southwest Airlines because the same software is used on the newly certified Max 7 plane.
Other large airlines, including Alaska Airlines and United Airlines, that have ordered the Max 10 could also have been impacted by a lengthy delay.
Jefferies said in a research note the decision allows the Max 10 to be certified before the end of the year and estimated Boeing has nearly 1,500 Max 10s on order from airlines.
The FAA said one software version can increase pilot workload during a go-around, when a pilot aborts a landing attempt, applies power, and climbs to make another landing attempt.
An FAA official said Boeing will issue a bulletin to airlines on how to recognise and respond to the situation should it occur, and the FAA will issue a Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin to US airlines and foreign regulators to ensure they’re aware of Boeing’s bulletin.
Major US airlines had opted not to use that version of the software while the analysis was under way. REUTERS

Space Development Agency to Launch 21 More Data Transport Satellites Next Week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:01:00 UTC
06:01:00 KST

The Space Development Agency is set to launch 21 Tranche 1 data transport satellites on Oct. 5—its fourth Tranche 1 mission since last fall and the first to carry Northrop Grumman-built satellites.
The launch is scheduled for 1:15 a.m. local time from Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Once in orbit, the 21 spacecraft will join 63 Tranche 1 satellites built by York Space Systems and Lockheed Martin.
The mission represents a few firsts for Northrop. It’s not only the contractor’s inaugural Tranche 1 launch—the company is on the hook for another batch of 21 Tranche 1 Transport satellites and 14 missile tracking spacecraft—but it’s also the firm’s first time delivering and operating such a large quantity of satellites. SDA Director Gurpartap Sandhoo told reporters during an Oct. 1 prelaunch call that based on some of the challenges other providers have had with scaling, he expects there will be some challenges.
“It’s one thing to go through launch and early ops of one, two, maybe even three or four satellites. Twenty-one is a completely different ball of wax,” said Sandhoo, who is also the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for missile warning, tracking, and defense. “We’ll see some issues, but I’m confident the team at Northrop … the issues that pop up, any patches, any updates we have to do, they’re ready to go.”
Since SDA started in 2019 to build out a proliferated constellation of data transport and missile warning satellites in low Earth orbit, the agency has faced setbacks that have delayed launches and fielding timelines. While it had hoped to have all 154 of its Tranche 1 satellites in low-Earth orbit by this summer, supply chain issues and technical challenges on the ground and in orbit disrupted those plans. Sandhoo has attributed many of those slowdowns to the challenges that come with building and launching satellites in large numbers.
“The issue has not been the capability of the system,” Sandhoo told reporters. “The issue has been building them at scale, getting them tested at scale, launching them at scale, doing the launch and early ops at scale. It’s the volume of these things that has been a challenge.”
Following the launch of York and Lockheed’s first spacecraft last year, initial on-orbit checkout and testing took much longer than the four to six months SDA expected. The agency ended up taking a nine-month pause to sort out issues on orbit and make changes on the ground to ensure its next satellites didn’t run into the same hiccups.
In July, SDA resumed Tranche 1 launches, flying York’s last 21 transport satellites. Checkout of those spacecraft went much smoother, Sandhoo said. Since then, the agency has moved control of York’s satellites into its operations center and started doing some limited experimentation. SDA has had some issues transferring Lockheed’s spacecraft to the operations center. To date, it’s only been able to move four, and Sandhoo said the company and SDA are working through the engineering issues to understand the cause and make sure it’s addressed before Lockheed launches more satellites.
“As we get the rest of the architecture, the rest of the planes up, it’s going to get more complicated,” he said. “We need to make sure the understanding is there, the behavior, and the dependability. Being able to get them in the ops and working properly is critical.”
A spokesperson for Lockheed told Air & Space Forces Magazine the company is working closely with SDA to transition the satellites to the agency’s control centers.
“These experiences are an important part of developing new, integrated space systems and we’re focused on ensuring reliability and mission success during this transition, while still moving quickly as a team,” Lockheed said. “We will apply lessons learned from each plane into future efforts.”
While the agency isn’t out of the woods yet in terms of schedule and scaling woes, Sandhoo told reporters he expects that as companies and their suppliers get used to building and flying larger numbers of satellites, their performance will improve. But for now, he said, he’s not satisfied with the time it’s taken to get to this point.
Asked what SDA could have done differently to avoid these setbacks, Sandhoo said it’s possible that for the early tranches of satellites, the agency could have required more insight into the companies’ processes rather than opt for the more hands-off approach it took in its contracting strategy.
“We are trying to get to a place where we can have a capability-driven architecture. We tell them what the system needs to do, and our vendors and our industrial base builds that out to that spec with minimal oversight,” he said. “Maybe we should have, for the first tranche, been probably more intrusive in that process than we were.”
Following the Oct. 5 launch, SDA is eyeing its first Tranche 1 tracking layer mission either in December or early next year. Beyond that flight, it’s hoping to finish the last four launches and have all Tranche 1 satellites in orbit by late spring 2027.

UK plays the blame game, terror in the skies, Russia’s red lines: RT stories that shaped the week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:00:05 UTC
06:00:05 KST

UK plays the blame game, terror in the skies, Russia’s red lines: RT stories that shaped the week
The terror plot that wasn’t
The arrest of five men at RAF Fairford in the UK on Sunday sparked a terror panic whose consequences are still playing out almost a week later. Shortly after the arrests, British Foreign Secretary Ed Milliband described the incident as an example of “the threats our country faces,” while the British media’s ‘security experts’ pinned the blame on Iran – or in some cases Russia.
The men – all British nationals aged between 21 and 25 – were released on bail on Monday, and no explosives were found in their vehicles. Nevertheless, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced on Thursday that “we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part.”
“Our belief that we believe” is not the most confident assertion, and this was immediately picked up in Tehran. “I can confirm Iran’s belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You’re barking up the wrong tree,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X.
Counterterror police arrested a British-Iranian dual national in connection with the supposed plot on Thursday, but it’s still unclear whether he’ll be charged.
Russia reveals its red lines
It is unsurprising that the British media immediately used the incident to escalate tensions with Iran and Russia. After days of intensifying war rhetoric from Ukraine’s British and European backers – which RT is tracking in our ‘Escalation Watch’ special – Russia definitively restated its red lines this week.
In a statement released by three of its embassies on Wednesday, the Russian Foreign Ministry said that Moscow “would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country.”
⚡️ Statement by the Embassy of Russia in Ireland (September 29, 2026)
There has been an abundance of talk, recently, from the European political circles that Russia somehow is planning to launch a military invasion of Europe, escalate its alleged hybrid campaign against… pic.twitter.com/eQsrIUFwmL
— Russia in Ireland (@Rus_Emb_Ireland) September 30, 2026
NATO has carried out several military exercises near Kaliningrad this year, and Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski recently called on the bloc’s military chiefs to surge troops to the Kaliningrad border so that Moscow would be “uncertain of what we will do.”
However, Moscow’s statement – the second of its kind this week – was intended to “remind those hotheads in Europe” of Russia’s long-established conditions for the use of nuclear weapons, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained on Wednesday. In his speech at the Valdai Discussion Club’s annual forum on Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin reiterated that any military action against Kaliningrad would “inevitably” trigger nuclear retaliation.
Western “hotheads,” however, would do well to consider that NATO’s Article 5 – the bloc’s mutual-defense clause – isn’t as clear-cut as it’s sometimes portrayed. As Russian International Affairs Council President Dmitry Trenin wrote for RT this week, it’s “deliberately ambiguous,” heavily mythologized, and doesn’t guarantee US intervention.
Meanwhile, Russia has continued to intensify its strikes on Ukrainian military and dual-use targets, hitting data centers and logistics hubs in Kiev, and ports and warehouses on Ukraine’s Black Sea coast.
Speaking at Valdai, Putin ruled out any kind of ‘energy ceasefire’. With Ukraine striking Russian refineries and sanctions impairing Russia’s ability to export oil, the idea that Moscow “is supposed to stop hitting things that are important to their economy” is “absurd,” the Russian president stated.
The FlyDubai emergency
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s warnings of an imminent attack against the Jewish state were almost realized on Wednesday, when the first officer of a FlyDubai Boeing 737 en route to Tel Aviv allegedly stabbed his captain and attempted to crash the airliner.
Little is known about the incident beyond what the Israeli government and media has shared, but it appears that a group of passengers overpowered the first officer and pulled the jet out of its dive, before two pilots on board took control and landed in Tabuk, in northern Saudi Arabia.
The pilot, Captain Smit Machchhar, has become a national hero in his native India, while the passengers who reportedly stormed the cockpit were lauded by Netanyahu upon arrival in Tel Aviv. Netanyahu has claimed that the first officer had acted based on “Islamist radical indoctrination,” while his government considers the incident an attempted “terrorist attack.”
Although Netanyahu’s ministers have already used the incident to justify – in the words of National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir – taking their war against “Iran, Lebanon, Gaza and Judea and Samaria [the West Bank]... to the next level”, the unanswered questions are piling up, as Middle East analyst Farhad Ibragimov wrote for RT.
Lavrov shuts down the propaganda
Another unanswered question: what exactly do Western leaders mean when they accuse Russia of waging “hybrid war?” The accusation, typically leveled at Russia after drone sightings, fires and accidents at weapons factories, and even natural disasters, is almost never substantiated, yet serves to justify the West’s rearmament and escalating war rhetoric against Moscow.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov refused to play into the narrative when he was questioned by the BBC’s Steve Rosenberg on Tuesday. The British state journalist asked Lavrov if he would admit “that Russia is waging a covert hybrid war against European countries,” but Lavrov flipped the questioning.
“Are you referring to when we destroy the drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe supply to Ukraine, which are then fired at us?” the Russian foreign minister retorted. “Is that what you mean by hybrid war?”
Rosenberg wasn’t the only Western antagonist humiliated this week. On Tuesday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz suffered the indignity of having to stand beside Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in Berlin, as Tokayev described Putin as “an outstanding statesman” possessing “the qualities that are most essential for the leader of a great country.”
Merz, fresh from his party’s back-to-back election losses last month, then traveled to Munster on Thursday, where NATO had inexplicably been awarded the ‘Westphalian Peace Prize’. After NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte accepted the award, he and Merz were met with boos, whistles, and chants of “murderers” and “blood on your hands” when they stepped outside to greet the public.
Russia expands its Arctic footprint
Finally, while it’s easy to assume that the world’s great powers have traversed, mapped, and tamed every inch of the Earth’s surface, that’s not the case, and new milestones are still being reached. On Tuesday, the Russian Navy’s Northern Fleet announced that it had traversed the iceberg-filled Shokalsky Strait for the first time in history.
The strait runs between October Revolution Island and Bolshevik Island in the Severnaya Zemlya archipelago, deep inside the Arctic Circle along the strategically important Northern Sea Route.
The Russian Navy group, consisting of the ice-class patrol ship Ivan Papanin, the large landing ship Kondopoga, the salvage tug Pamir, and the naval tanker Sergey Osipov, successfully passed from the Laptev Sea into the Kara Sea, after repeatedly changing course and speed at short notice to avoid icebergs in the treacherous strait.
Russia is invested in the development of the Northern Sea Route, which is the shortest maritime passage between the Asia-Pacific region and northern Europe. Moscow has also renovated some of its Soviet-era military bases along its northern coast, and stepped up military exercises in the Arctic. As the Northern Fleet passed through the Shokalsky Strait this week, its reconnaissance teams practiced amphibious assault maneuvers on the western side of October Revolution Island.

But what surprised me the most about the statistics is the extent to which females are outliving males, and in far greater numbers.
Among Australians who lived to 100 or older, women far outnumbered men: 2,392 women died last year, compared with 724 men.
That’s more than three women for every man.

AI makes games more expensive
The Reserve Bank lifted interest rates this week to a 15-year high because it’s worried about rising inflation.
A key factor is how much businesses are passing on higher costs from the war in the Middle East to consumers.
In its official inflation report this week, the ABS said builders are passing on rising labour and material costs to customers via higher project home prices.
But it’s not the only industry passing on rising costs, and not all are related to the conflict.

“Upon arrival, both of her arms were swollen, burned, and blistered,” Pike’s lawyers wrote about the drug’s effects on her body.
The filing, which was part of an emergency request by Pike’s lawyers to preserve state records related to her execution, marks the most detailed update on Pike’s condition after she was transported by ambulance to hospital from a Tennessee prison on Wednesday, following the botched attempt.
Pike’s lawyers argued that problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike’s body,” they wrote.
The lawyers allege prison staff prepared “a backup set of syringes” and “administered another lethal dose of pentobarbital”.
Pike, who was sentenced to death at 18 after she was found guilty of torturing and murdering another young woman in 1995, would have been the first woman in more than 200 years to be executed in Tennessee. She was also the only woman on the state’s death row.
Pike’s lawyers have called for her sentence to be commuted to life in prison after she endured what they called “chemical torture”.
Tennessee’s Governor Bill Lee has suspended all executions for the rest of the year while the state investigates what happened.

War and diplomatic crisis in the Horn of Africa: Why Ethiopia is at odds with its neighbors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:57:29 UTC
05:57:29 KST

War and diplomatic crisis in the Horn of Africa: Why Ethiopia is at odds with its neighbors
Renewed fighting between Ethiopia’s federal government and regional armed groups has escalated into a diplomatic rupture with former wartime ally Eritrea. What was an internal conflict has become a wider regional confrontation over ports, water, and alleged foreign interference. The violence threatens a fragile 2022 peace deal that ended Ethiopia’s two-year Tigray war, raising fears of a return to full-scale conflict.
What triggered the diplomatic rupture?
Ethiopia announced on Thursday the closure of its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered ten Eritrean diplomats stationed in Addis Ababa to leave Ethiopia within 48 hours. Its Foreign Ministry accused them of threatening national security and blamed Eritrea for “direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia.”
Eritrea reciprocated the measure and severed “all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia with all the negative corollaries that this entails.” It rejected the allegations and accused Addis Ababa of planning to take Eritrean ports and of training and arming Eritrean opposition groups to pursue regime change. Addis Ababa said it remained committed to peaceful coexistence and resolving disputes through dialogue.
The breakdown in relations came days after Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of financing armed groups seeking to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. Asmara denies the accusations.
What are they fighting over?
The conflict grew out of a struggle over federal power and regional autonomy. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the political party governing Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, dominated national politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018. Tigrayan leaders accused his government of seeking to centralize power at the region’s expense. Their confrontation erupted into war in November 2020.
Eritrean troops and Amhara forces fought alongside the federal army. Hundreds of thousands died before an African Union-mediated agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in November 2022 halted the large-scale fighting. But disputes over territory claimed by both Amhara and Tigray, the return of displaced people, and the disarmament of Tigrayan forces remained unresolved. Addis Ababa accuses the TPLF of failing to disarm; Tigrayan leaders accuse the government of failing to honor the settlement.
The TPLF further strained the settlement in May by restoring Tigray’s prewar regional council, displacing the interim administration established under the agreement. Amhara militia fighters known as Fano, meanwhile, had turned against Addis Ababa in 2023 after the government moved to dismantle regional security forces.
Separate disputes have widened the confrontation. Landlocked Ethiopia wants sovereign access to the Red Sea, particularly through Eritrea’s Assab port, which it calls vital to its economy and security. Asmara fears an attempt to take its coastline by force. Egypt and Sudan also dispute Ethiopia’s operation of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile, fearing threats to their water supplies and demanding a binding agreement governing its filling and operation.
Why has fighting resumed in Ethiopia?
On September 20, seven armed groups, including the TPLF and its former battlefield enemies, announced an alliance pledging to oust Abiy’s government and establish a transitional administration. The coalition, known as the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, accused the ruling Prosperity Party of imposing “dictatorial” rule and pushing the East African country toward disintegration.
Clashes erupted two days later. TPLF forces took control of airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire, prompting state-owned Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to all three cities. Flights were also suspended to the Amhara town of Lalibela, home to UNESCO-listed rock-hewn churches, as fighting spread.
On September 23, Addis Ababa accused the TPLF of launching an “all-out offensive” against government positions in Amhara and Afar. Tigray’s regional authorities said their troops entered a “defensive battle” after federal forces attacked them with aircraft, drones, and artillery. The federal army said it had repelled attacks in Amhara’s North Wollo Zone and killed 272 Tigrayan fighters and wounded 260 others in a counteroffensive.
The army and its allied Tigray Peace Forces subsequently reported capturing Alamata and Korem and retaking Erebti in Afar. Explosions were also heard in Addis Ababa overnight Wednesday to Thursday of this week, although opposition claims of drone attacks remain unverified.
What is the impact on civilians?
Doctors Without Borders reported more than 420 war-wounded patients at Korem and Alamata hospitals between September 22 and 25, and over 300 at Suhul hospital in Shire during the latest fighting. Insecurity forced the organization to suspend activities at Alamata hospital.
On September 25, UN human rights chief Volker Turk condemned forced recruitment by the TPLF, including of children, and reprisals against those resisting recruitment and their families. He also raised reports of arbitrary conscription by government forces.
Why did Ethiopia and Eritrea fall out?
Eritrea was once part of Ethiopia but gained independence in 1993 after a decades-long liberation war, leaving Ethiopia landlocked. The neighbors fought a border war in 1998–2000, followed by years of hostility until Abiy and Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki reconciled in 2018. The rapprochement helped earn Abiy the 2019 Nobel Peace Prize.
Their partnership fractured after the Tigray war. Eritrea was not a party to the Pretoria agreement despite its military involvement. According to the International Crisis Group, Asmara resented being sidelined and wanted Addis Ababa to pursue a complete battlefield victory over the TPLF rather than a negotiated settlement.
Who else is accused of backing the armed groups?
Ethiopia’s accusations extend beyond Eritrea. Army chief Birhanu Jula also accused Egypt and Sudan of supporting the rebels. Both countries denied the allegations. On Thursday, Ethiopia ordered an Egyptian diplomat to leave within 48 hours. Egypt retaliated by giving an Ethiopian Embassy counselor the same deadline, calling Addis Ababa’s decision unjustified.
Sudan’s army has also accused Ethiopia of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, its opponent in a civil war that began in April 2023.
How are regional and international bodies responding?
The AU has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Egypt to exercise “maximum restraint and refrain from actions or statements that could further escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability.” It asked the three countries to resolve their differences through diplomatic channels.
The UN and EU also urged de-escalation. Russia called for a ceasefire on September 25. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova urged compliance with peace commitments and noninterference, stressing Ethiopia’s unity and territorial integrity.

The cockatoo-inspired emblems for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics and Paralympics have been accidentally leaked by the Games' official YouTube channel.

What's next?
The emblems will be officially revealed on Monday in Brisbane.
The emblems for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics and Paralympics have been accidentally leaked by the Games' official YouTube channel, ruining its own grand unveiling.
Pieces of the emblem had been revealed during a Queensland tour over the past week, with the full picture slated to come together on Monday.
But the cockatoo-inspired emblem was entirely revealed last night in a preview image for an "Emblem Explainer" video set to go live on Monday morning.
An explanation of the emblem was also visible in the video's description.
"The Brisbane 2032 emblems are inspired by the spirited cockatoo — a symbol of Australia's unique wildlife and playful heart! The cockatoo's crest is a living torch, reminiscent of the iconic Olympic and Paralympic flame," the description reportedly read.
"Shaped like Queensland, with its eye on Brisbane, the emblem is a universal symbol to unite Brisbane, Australia and the world in 2032."
The image has subsequently been removed from YouTube.
Olympics Minister Tim Mander told the Today show he was "excited" the emblem was "finally out".
"The emblem is something that will make us known around the world with regard to the Games in 2032," he said.
"We just want to celebrate it."
Mr Mander would not comment when questioned if the leak was planned.
"Obviously there were people so enthusiastic about looking for the emblem that they'd been scanning the internet,"
he said.
"It's appeared for a short time, and it's out there."
Brisbane 2032 chief marketing officer Brent Hill said the leak had generated "incredible" publicity for the Games.
"If we had our time over, maybe there's different ways that we could have done it,"
Mr Hill said.
"The overarching piece from our side is still the fact that we wanted people to guess, we wanted the clues to be out there, and now it's out there.
"The reaction to it has been really positive."
Opposition leader Steven Miles welcomed the cockatoo-inspired emblems, but said Brisbane 2032 organisers should own up to the blunder.
"No doubt there will be a lot of questions asked about how this mistake was made so that they can avoid it again in the future," he said.
"I know there was a lot of interest though, so Queenslanders will be excited that they got to see it sooner than they were meant to."
The emblem unveiling tour is set to continue in Brisbane this weekend after stops in Cairns, Townsville, Rockhampton and the Sunshine Coast last week.
There will be a community unveiling of the emblem on Monday night in Brisbane.

Can't invoke anti-slaughter law in case of mere illegal cattle transportation: SC

Acquitting a person convicted by a trial court and Chhattisgarh HC for illegally transporting 32 bulls under Chhattisgarh Agricultural Cattle Preservation Act, 2004, a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said police have failed to establish the intention of the accused.
NEW DELHI: At a time when vigilante groups are active in stopping cattle smuggling purportedly to prevent slaughter, the Supreme Court has ruled that the police cannot presumptively invoke stringent provisions of anti-cattle slaughter laws against people for mere illegal transportation of bovine animals.Acquitting a person convicted by a trial court and Chhattisgarh HC for illegally transporting 32 bulls under Chhattisgarh Agricultural Cattle Preservation Act, 2004, a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said police have failed to establish the intention of the accused that cattle were being transported for slaughter. The prosecution said the intercepted truck did not have any document that authorised the driver and cleaner to transport cattle from Chhattisgarh to Odisha.
"The mere fact that the transport was not accompanied by any documents cannot lead to a presumption that it was for slaughter," SC said. "We find no reason to uphold the conviction, especially when a veterinary doctor and the 'Gaushala Committee' chief said before the court that the seized cattle were fit for use in agriculture."

Tykhyi's comments came after comments from an unnamed diplomat reported by the Guardian sparked concerns that embassies were planning to evacuate from Kyiv due to escalating Russian attacks.

However, these measures would only take effect if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign diplomatic missions.
Otherwise, even as Russia attacks Kyiv's schools, homes, bridges, and energy facilities, embassies intend to stay.

read also

The CJI could not be contacted, as he is abroad.The SC registry, from which an explanation was sought, filed a report on clubbing of the two cases. The bench of Justices Misra and Bhuyan said in its order, "The explanation tendered by the registry is accepted and taken on record. The same shall be kept in a sealed cover by the concerned section." It posted both the contempt petition and the writ petition for hearing together on Oct 15.

In January, an F-16V of the Republic of China Air Force crashed during a training flight from Hualien Air Base.

After Russian strikes, Kyiv is covered in smoke and soot: the air is becoming dangerous for residents – BILD
Kyiv • UNN
Smoke and soot from the fires have lingered over Kyiv due to a high-pressure system and calm winds. Residents are advised to keep their windows closed and purify the air.
After a series of Russian attacks, Kyiv was shrouded in dense smog formed, among other things, by residual smoke and soot from fires. Due to weather conditions, the polluted air lingered over the city, which may pose a health hazard to people. BILD reports, according to UNN.
Details
In the morning, the capital was covered by such dense gray fog that visibility sharply deteriorated in some areas. Drivers had to turn on their fog lights, while residents were advised to keep their windows closed.
The unusual phenomenon was caused by a combination of the aftermath of Russian strikes and the weather. Smoke and soot particles entered the air after the fires, while an anticyclone and the almost complete absence of wind prevented them from dispersing quickly.
Why smog is dangerous
The State Emergency Service explained that residual smoke and soot had risen into the atmosphere, but the anticyclone was temporarily keeping them close to the ground. The highest levels of pollution were recorded in the Podil, Lukianivka, Shevchenkivskyi District, and Borshchahivka areas.
Residents were advised not to ventilate their premises, to keep windows and vents closed, to use air purifiers, and to carry out wet cleaning. People with respiratory and cardiovascular diseases should be especially careful during periods of severe air pollution.
Given that Russia continues to regularly strike the capital of Ukraine, the situation with air pollution remains an extremely serious problem for Kyiv residents.

Latin America sees China as more positive global influence than US: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:52:29 UTC
05:52:29 KST

Latin America sees China as more positive global influence than US: Poll
Annual Latinobarometro survey finds views of China’s influence improving as perceptions of US influence worsen.
China is perceived more positively as a global influence than the United States in Latin America, according to a new regional survey, in a first since the poll began in 1995.
The 2026 Latinobarometro survey published on Friday found that 65 percent of respondents in 17 countries saw China as a positive influence. That was compared with 57 percent who said the same of the US.
Support for China has risen sharply since 2020, when 48 percent of respondents viewed its influence positively. The figure for the US has fallen from 60 percent over the same period.
Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic were the only countries surveyed where respondents viewed US influence more positively than China’s.
Latinobarometro, a Chile-based nonprofit organisation, conducts annual surveys across the region on issues including democracy, the economy, security and migration.
The findings come during US President Donald Trump’s second term, as his administration has sought to strengthen Washington’s influence in Latin America, particularly through exercising more military might.
That has included conducting strikes on alleged drug smuggling boats in the region, which rights groups have decried as extrajudicial killings, and abducting Venezuela’s then-leader Nicolas Maduro in Brazil.
Trump has described his approach as the “Donroe Doctrine”.
Despite the findings on global influence, the US remained more popular than China when respondents were asked about their overall views of the two countries.
Some 63 percent of respondents said they had a favourable opinion of the US, compared with 58 percent for China. The US figure was down from 73 percent in 2024.
The survey also asked respondents about the US military capture of Maduro.
A majority in all but one country, Argentina, approved of Maduro’s capture by US forces.
Views were more divided over what the operation meant for Venezuela, with 35 percent saying removing Maduro had benefitted the country and 28 percent saying it had harmed it.
Venezuelans were among the populations most likely to view US influence positively, according to the survey.
The 2026 survey was based on about 19,200 face-to-face interviews conducted in 17 countries between May 7 and June 17, with a margin of error of 1 percent.
