Why Are Students Protesting Across France? Escalating Unrest Closes Schools, Leaves Hundreds Injured
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:23:50 UTC
05:23:50 KST

High schools across France have closed, thousands of teenagers have been arrested, and hundreds of people have suffered injuries as unrest over conditions in the lycée system has spread and erupted into violence in recent days.
Roughly 3,000 people have been arrested since the protests began nearly two weeks ago outside of Paris, with nearly 2,000 being detained on Thursday alone, the French interior ministry announced.
As demonstrations have at times escalated into violent clashes, 170 students and 65 school staff members have been injured, according to education minister Édouard Geffray. Nearly 400 police officers have also reportedly suffered injuries.
And the protests showed no signs of abating on Friday, when roughly 900 demonstrations took place around France, according to police. More than 500 French schools remained closed as students set fires, blockaded schools, and clashed with riot police around the country.
Geffray met with education unions, student organizations, and parent associations on Friday morning in an attempt to temper the protests through dialogue.
“High school students must be listened to. Their difficulties call for concrete responses, both in their schools and at the national level,” Geffray wrote on X. “This is the purpose of the dialogue initiated in high schools and academies, which I am continuing today with representatives of staff, parents, and high school students.”
He announced a platform students can use to submit proposals for education reform, which he said will be evaluated and used for a “national report.”
High school student organizations, however, have called for continued demonstrations following their meetings with Geffray, citing a lack of “concrete measures” from the French government to address their complaints.
Here’s what you should know about the ongoing protests.
Why are students protesting?
The protests have been driven by anger over a variety of issues impacting French high schools.
A main complaint among demonstrators is the shortage of teachers and support staff in the country’s schools.
The education ministry found that during the 2024-2025 school year, nearly 10% of teaching hours went untaught in public secondary schools. About 7.5% of those lost hours were due to a failure to find substitutes.
"Today our school is paralyzed due to a lack of resources, teachers, and not enough desks,” one student told the French outlet Agence France Presse (AFP). “We don't have nurses or supervisors, and all they do for us is take away our phones.”
Complaints about insufficient resources and funding and poor infrastructure in schools have also been raised in the student protests.
"We are 35 per class, we don’t have enough chairs in classrooms,” a 15-year-old student told Reuters in the Paris suburb of Pantin as demonstrators clashed with police deploying tear gas in an effort to quell the protest.
“There are 35 of us per classroom. With 35 degrees Celsius [95 degrees Fahrenheit] in summer, it’s unbearable. There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms,” a 17-year-old said while speaking to AFP at a protest in Strasbourg in the northeast of France. “The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors.”
Another student also raised concerns about a lack of resources to address high supper temperatures when talking to The Guardian.
“We’re also protesting about the conditions in the heatwave,” the 19-year-old said. “Young people just want to study and learn in decent conditions. The French state seems surprised about worsening school results, but they’re doing nothing to remedy that.”
A series of deadly heatwaves hit Europe over the summer, with Western Europe experiencing its hottest summer ever. In France, nearly 8,000 people died over the course of the summer as a result of the high temperatures.
Student protesters have also expressed grievances with the country’s online university application system, Parcoursup, which they have described as a source of stress and mistrust in the education system.
The particular complaints being raised by demonstrators have varied somewhat across different parts of the country, however.
Geffray characterized this as a complicating factor in addressing the roots of the unrest. "One of the difficulties of this movement is that there are no national demands. It all started with local demands,” the Education Minister said Friday morning.
Where did the protests begin, and how have they expanded?
The protests began with r students at Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil outside Paris mobilizing to protest teacher shortages and a lack of adequate resources in late September.
In the days that followed, protests spread throughout the Île-de-France region, which includes Paris and its surrounding metropolitan areas, as students attempted to set up blockades at dozens of schools.
The demonstrations have escalated still further this week, spreading outside of Paris’ surrounding area and into regions around the country. Tracking from Reuters also showed that protests have sprouted across western France in Rennes, Nantes, Quimper, and Brest; around the southern part of the country in Bordeaux, Toulouse, Toulon, Marseilles and Grenoble; as far east as Strasbourg; and as far north as Lille.
By Monday, 180 schools were disrupted by the expanded demonstrations, according to the interior ministry. That number had risen to over 500 at week’s end.
Thursday marked the largest escalation of protests.
Fires were started at at least two French schools that day. Several teachers were accidentally splashed with gasoline at Marseille's Victor Hugo high school. At Saint-Exupery high school, also in Marseilles, hundreds of students set ablaze a fire truck that had arrived to put out a previous fire from the morning. Firefighters were forced by students to exit their vehicle before it was burned. In protests around the country, confrontations broke out between students and police, who fired projectiles in attempts to control crowds of demonstrators.
As of Friday night, the protests show no signs of stopping. Two student unions, the Student Union and the High School Trade Union, have jointly called for continued protests next week.
“Students and high school students, while the authorities seek to drive us out of our places of study through budget cuts, the closure of places, dilapidated buildings, selection, or repression, let's not let them: let's block and retake the universities and high schools!” the unions wrote in a press release.
What French officials are saying
Several French officials have weighed in the student demonstrations as they have continued to escalate and expand around the country. Some have specifically addressed remarks toward protesters’ parents.
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin told RTL radio on Thursday that parents whose children have caused damage to property should pay reparations.
Meanwhile, Geffray cautioned against the dangers he said the increasingly violent protests pose to students.
"Parents clearly need to mobilize and tell their children not to go" to the blockades, Geffray said on Friday. "Now, what matters is ensuring that our children are no longer in the streets because they are in danger.”
As the protests intensified this week, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu called a crisis meeting on Thursday and canceled ministers’ travel plans to work on quelling the demonstrations.
"I hear and understand the anxieties and anger that our youth may have,” French President Emmanuel Macron said on Wednesday while speaking in Madrid. “However, none of these debates, none of these fears legitimizes violence.”

After the New York Times’ Anthropic Report: What Should AI Consciousness Uncertainty Justify?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:18:53 UTC
05:18:53 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Many of us have probably read the recent New York Times article which describes a series of private meetings that Anthropic has held with religious scholars on the prospect of Claude being conscious, on moral formation, and Claude’s possible moral status.
According to the report, Anthropic has spent months bringing religious scholars from a variety of religions and backgrounds to San Francisco to have discussions with company researchers in Anthropic on Claudes status as a potentially conscious entity.
Per the report, the meetings included presentations about the research that has been conduced by Anthropic on the mechanisms of Claude models, and whether AI systems could be conscious or entities deserving of moral consideration.
At a minimum, it seems reasonable to conclude that Anthropic are taking the possibility of Claude’s consciousness very seriously. And the internet has responded:
Neuroscientist Anil Seth, for instance, describes the events as ‘disturbing’, directs us to his article on the ‘mythology of consciousness’ —a read that I highly recommend — and states that there is a ‘vanishingly unlikely’ possibility that AI is conscious.
Theologian and Philosopher David Decosimo equally writes that:
I am also disturbed by these events, and it forces us to ask uncomfortable questions about the current state of AI consciousness research, the power dynamics that exist in this domain, and how future research into AI consciousness should be conducted.
Are we really going to live in a world where the science of a subject matter is blended with wining and dining prominent thinkers behind closed doors to discuss these kinds of topics? If Anthropic are themselves so uncertain about the moral status of Claude or of its status as a conscious entity, why are we seeing such extensive institutional responses on Anthropic’s part to this possibility?
I think there is a repeated pattern coming out of AI consciousness research in Anthropic in particular, but in AI consciousness research generally: stated uncertainty about the status of AI consciousness being invoked as justification for potentially significant changes in how we view and govern AI models.
But there is a sharp disconnect between the claim of uncertainty and the behavioral actions and institutional responses that come with them. Why do we need private meetings, welfare discussions, moral status discussions and fine dining in the face of such uncertainty? How are we to make sense of what is being said, and what is being done? The degree of uncertainty being expressed and the scale of institutional response strikes me as difficult to reconcile.
We cannot simply hand-wring about the behaviors of companies like Anthropic. We need to ask hard questions so that we can hold such companies accountable when necessary, and make sure research is transparent and governed in appropriate ways.
What kinds of actions, for example, should claims to uncertainty about AI consciousness actually justify? How should AI consciousness and AI welfare proceed, when much of the research is conducted by the institutions building the machines? Who should determine the answer to these questions, and how? What democratic mechanisms, external input, and transparency requirements should be involved?
We cannot live in a world where uncertainty-claims about AI consciousness becomes an open-ended mechanism or justification for whatever institutional responses AI companies see fit to pursue.
Not for a second do I believe Claude is conscious —and I will continue to offer arguments for my views —but in the meantime, if uncertainty-claims coming out of AI labs are going to justifying changes to how LLMs are treated, trained, governed, or conceived of (something that has already happened with Anthropic committed to preserving model weights), we need to develop standards for determining what responses are appropriate to the claimed evidence bearing on the claimed uncertainty.
This New York Times article makes it very difficult to postpone these questions any longer than we already have. The questions need answering, and the time to answer them is now.

Hawaii’s centuries-old sea arch collapses into Pacific after series of rough storms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:16:35 UTC
05:16:35 KST

A famed centuries-old sea arch on Hawaii’s remote and rugged coastline has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean, the National Park Service confirmed on Friday, following a stretch of rough storms in the region in recent weeks.
The beloved landmark, Hōlei sea arch, stood at around 90ft high for over half a millennium in Hawaii’s Volcanoes national park, located on the dramatic southern coast of the Big Island. It was naturally formed around 550 years ago due to differential erosion by ocean waves.
The exact timing of the collapse is unknown. The National Park Service (NPS) said the arch was still standing on Wednesday 23 September, when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo, but had collapsed by Sunday night, on 27 September.
“The arch formed in ancient lava flows by removing rock along cracks and weaker rocks,” the US Geological Survey said in a description of the arch in 2014. “It will not be here for ever. Every day the ocean crashes against the pillar of the arch, eroding it a little more. One day, it will be gone.”
Indeed, the cliffs on either side of the sea arch had shown signs of instability for years amid tropical systems and volcanic activity, the NPS said, meaning the arch’s collapse had long been expected.
Earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea volcanic eruption and summit collapse damaged the cliffs around the arch. Then, in January 2020, new cracks and instability prompted the park to close the original viewing area and open a safer one further from the cliff edge three months later. Later that year, huge surf from Tropical Storm Darby broke off a chunk of rock from the arch’s lower portion.
The Hawaiian islands have seen an unusually high number of severe storms this year, with storm activity in the Pacific running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. Experts say the pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes.
Nolo, which rapidly intensified into a hurricane on 24 September – causing Volcanoes national park to shutter - was the third major storm to devastate the islands of Hawaii in recent months. Residents were still recovering from hurricanes Lala in August and Lowell in early September, which had flooded homes and roads, toppled trees and caused power outages, when Nolo then battered the islands with heavy rain and high surf.
Forecasters have warned there is a high probability that this “supercharged” El Niño will reach a historic intensity, with its effects in strengthening the storms compounded by the broader overheating of the planet caused by the burning of fossil fuels.

Under fire, EC orders special drive to add genuine electors 'left out' during SIR
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:11:37 UTC
05:11:37 KST

An EC official said an average 10% of 800-900 electors per booth were deleted through SIR. Thus, each BLO will have to verify enrolment eligibility of less than 100 'deleted' voters.
NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Thursday ordered a special drive to identify and add back genuine electors who may have been "left out" during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) drive completed in 20 states, besides facilitating first-time or young electors.As part of the drive - meant to percolate to the grassroots the message that the deletions made during SIR, if erroneous, can be undone at any time by simply filling up Form 6 (for fresh enrolment) - booth level officers (BLOs) will visit homes of electors who were there in the pre-SIR electoral roll but were not included in the current electoral roll. They will, during these visits, ascertain the present status of such electors and facilitate their enrolment through Form 6, wherever a person is found to be eligible. This could be due to a valid eligibility proof not submitted earlier, corrected mapping to roll from last SIR, return of a shifted voter at registered address, or a young voter who has turned 18 since SIR, etc, said an official.
"Voter enrolment is a continuous process and any person not yet enrolled in the electoral roll or whose name has got deleted can apply for enrolment at any point of time. The objective of the special drive is to identify and facilitate such electors," EC said in a letter to state chief electoral officers (CEOs) Thursday.
This followed a meeting held by EC with state/UT CEOs on Tuesday.As per the decision taken by the full commission on Sept 26, no declaration will need to be attached with Form 6 during the special drive.Nearly 7.7 crore voters were deleted across 13 states covered in SIR's first two phases, though net deletions came to around 5.6 crore. In Phase 3, completed in seven states, net deletions total nearly 24 lakh.The special drive's timing is significant as it comes days after a report in The Indian Express report alleged that election commissioners S S Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised questions over the SIR process in internal notes. However, the EC, in a statement released after a full commission meeting on Sept 26, placed it on record that all decisions related to SIR were unanimously approved by the CEC and the commissioners.The opposition, however, continues to amplify the issue, "unilaterally" blaming CEC Gyanesh Kumar for a "flawed" SIR, "unauthorised" changes to Form 6 and allegedly limited access of field officers to ECINet for making changes.Sources in the EC, however, told TOI Friday that the special drive is only in furtherance of the repeated directions by CEC to BLOs that "not a single Indian citizen who has completed 18 years of age should be left out of electoral roll".An EC official said an average 10% of 800-900 electors per booth were deleted through SIR. Thus, each BLO will have to verify enrolment eligibility of less than 100 "deleted" voters. With the EC instructing BLOs on Friday to visit the homes of 20-25 electors per week, house-to-house outreach and verification is expected to last a month.BLOs who visit the houses of deleted electors shall indicate the present status of each such elector in a list of absent, permanently shifted, deceased, duplicate and foreigner electors prepared by them. Electors for whom Form 6 has been filled up will also be indicated.They will share this list with booth level agents (BLAs) of recognised political parties and with electoral registration officers (EROs), along with the filled-up Form 6 and their field verification report. ERO is the competent authority to decide on addition or deletion.At the end of this exercise, the booth-wise lists prepared as above will also be shared by the EROs with the representatives of the political parties, giving them a further opportunity to enable enrolment of any left-out electors.
Booth-level camps shall be organised to facilitate submission of applications for enrolment. Special camps may also be organised for enrolment of people living in night shelters, labour colonies and also for homeless & marginalised persons.As part of SIR completed in 20 states, a list of ASDD voters was prepared by each BLO with the probable reason for non-inclusion of their names. This list was displayed at the notice board of respective panchayat bhawans/urban local bodies and offices of the BDOs/panchayat, shared with the BLAs and with the political parties and also uploaded on the CEO website.Thereafter, the draft was published and shared with the political parties and uploaded on the CEO website. The final electoral roll was published after decisions on the claims and objections by the EROs and includes the list of electors that were added or deleted after the draft publication.
Bharti Jain is senior editor with The Times of India, New Delhi. She has been writing on security matters since 1996. Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the ‘prime’ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012. Her repertoire of news stories delves into the whole gamut of issues related to terrorism and internal strife, besides probing strategic affairs in India’s neighbourhood.

B-52s Get Prototype System for Beyond-Line-of-Sight Communications
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:01:02 UTC
05:01:02 KST

Air Force Global Strike Command has fielded a new prototype system for beyond-line-of-sight communications on the B-52H Stratofortress in a step forward for modernizing the Cold War-era heavy bomber.
IRIS, a communications system developed by Outerlink Global Solutions, integrates a satellite communication terminal with other components both on the bomber itself and on the ground, the command said in an Oct. 1 statement. IRIS is meant to make it easier for B-52 crews to carry out their missions and increase their flexibility when carrying out long-range strike missions, Global Strike said.
“The ability to communicate reliably across vast distances is foundational to our global operations,” Maj. Gen. Ty Neuman, commander of the 8th Air Force and the Joint-Global Strike Operations Center, said in a statement. “Fielding IRIS gives our crews a modern tool to stay connected, share information, and execute the mission in dynamic and contested environments.”
The name IRIS is not an acronym, Global Strike said. A 2022 U.S. Strategic Command release on an early demonstration of the IRIS system said it uses Iridium’s high-bandwidth CERTUS broadband service, which is powered by Iridium Next satellites in low-Earth orbit.
The Air Force is now working on a sweeping array of programs to modernize its fleet of 75 B-52s, which are more than six decades old. The bombers still fly with their original 1960s-era Pratt & Whitney-made TF33 engines, which will be replaced with new Rolls-Royce F130 engines under the Commercial Engine Replacement Program. B-52s will also receive a new radar, upgraded avionics, new cockpit displays, and other systems intended to keep it flying at least into the 2050s.
Modern communication capabilities are essential for the B-52 to continue to support global operations and joint force requirements in increasingly contested airspaces, Global Strike said.
“This is about readiness,” Jackie Ford, chief of Global Strike’s rapid capabilities division, said in the statement. “Rapidly fielding capabilities into our operators hands will ensure the B-52 remains ready not just for today’s mission, but for the missions of tomorrow as well.”
The Air Force first showed an earlier version of IRIS could work on a B-52 in June 2022, when the 49th Test and Evaluation Squadron at Barksdale Air Force Base, La., carried out an aerial demonstration on a Stratofortress. Global Strike said a team from the 608th Air Operations Center, also at Barksdale, studied how well voice and data, including images and videos, transferred from the B-52.
After IRIS’s successful demonstration, the command kept working with other Air Force innovation and acquisition units to evolve it from a test case to operational use, including using a Small Business Innovation Research Phase II contract from AFWERX to integrate the system onto the B-52.
The IRIS work transitioned to a formal program in 2023 into a $26 million Strategic Funding Increase contract, which represented Global Strike’s first such deal, the command said.
The command’s rapid capabilities and bomber requirements divisions took the lead on defining what the program’s requirements should be.
The 49th worked with the B-52 System Program Office and Airmen with operational expertise from the 307th Bomb Wing at Barksdale to make sure IRIS developed into a useful system on the bomber. Global Strike said leaders prioritized the program and ensured it moved forward quickly.
By March 2026, IRIS was ready for ground and flight testing which showed it could reliably stay connected while a B-52 was airborne and was technically mature enough to support operational use.
Testing continued, and by the time April began, Global Strike Command had installed multiple IRIS kits on B-52s and delivered them to the 49th to help support training and operational employment.
While IRIS is fielded operationally, Global Strike said, it remains a prototype, and more testing and evaluation will come as the system matures.
“Partnership is what made this possible,” Maj. Gen. Peter Bonetti, director of Global Strike’s strategic plans, programs, and requirements directorate. “We had a clear operational need, the right partner capabilities, and engaged stakeholders working together to deliver capability operators needed and are using today.”

Thousands of 'cockroaches' join India protests demanding resignation of Modi's election chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:00:10 UTC
05:00:10 KST

Indian protesters have rallied in New Delhi and Mumbai, including members of the popular youth-led "cockroach" party, demanding the resignation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s chief election commissioner over alleged voter-roll irregularities.
Police deployed in large numbers on Friday as protesters waved the national flag and chanted slogans against the Election Commission of India (ECI), demanding its chief Gyanesh Kumar step down.
A newspaper investigation by The Indian Express last month alleged impropriety during a large-scale voter-roll revision that has struck roughly 130 million to 133 million names from lists.
The ECI, India's constitutional body responsible for conducting elections, has rejected allegations of wrongdoing, while Kumar has not commented.
Hundreds of people gathered on roads around Jantar Mantar, a government-designated protest site in the heart of New Delhi, which was sealed off behind police barricades.
"My motivation is our future," 19-year-old protester Nidhi Sharma, a Delhi University student, told AFP news agency. "I have to vote."
Supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party or CJP — which began in May as a satirical online movement — meanwhile rallied in Mumbai's Shivaji Park, in their first protests since July, when their nationwide campaign helped oust the education minister.
"One Nation One Election is just a slogan. BJP wants One Nation One Party," said Abhijeet Dipke, founder of CJP, during a protest in Mumbai.
"After vote deletion, BJP won states it had not won even during the peak Modi wave," he said, adding the Modi government is "so incompetent that we have to protest again in two months."
Dipke was joined by prominent Indian cinema figures, including actors Naseeruddin Shah and Shabana Azmi, musician Vishal Dadlani, and filmmaker Vishal Bharadwaj.
Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was also in attendance.
Opposition politicians have accused the ECI of acting at the behest of Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
'Right to vote'
At the Delhi protest, Mina Giri, 38, said her name had been removed from the rolls even though she has lived in the capital for 15 years and voted in previous elections.
"How could my fundamental right be taken away from me?" she said.
Another protester, Imran, 18, said his family had been left off the list.
"Because of this, we are struggling to get our other official documents," preventing them from receiving government benefits, he said.
"We are poor, don't have a lot and are dependent on it."
Police detained multiple protesters in Delhi, put them on buses and dropped them off elsewhere, but some returned to the Jantar Mantar site on foot.
"No matter how many times they do this, we are going to return and protest," said Sahana, an advocate who was picked up by police but then walked back two kilometres (a mile) to rejoin the demonstration.
"You cannot take away our right to walk, can you?" she said.
Mobile internet services were also suspended in the area.
Some opposition politicians who joined the protest were briefly detained by police.
Opposition parties have also announced plans for more protests, including a march to the Election Commission in New Delhi on Tuesday and "Save Democracy" rallies countrywide in the days following.
Activist Vijeta Dahiya, who was involved in the previous "cockroach" campaign against the education minister, said that "no one wants to protest, but are forced to raise their voice when the government makes mistakes".
"Protest anywhere in the country," he said. "It is a matter of a right to vote."
Indian police in New Delhi detained more than 700 protesters, including former Delhi Chief Minister Atishi, from Jantar Mantar and several locations nearby, Indian media reported.

Scientists reveal the brain’s hidden role in building exercise endurance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

Repeated physical activity builds endurance by triggering widespread adaptations throughout the human body, but a new study reveals that the brain actually directs these physiological changes. Researchers found that activating a specific cluster of brain cells immediately after a workout is required for mice to increase their physical stamina over time. This discovery flips the traditional view of exercise physiology by showing that structural changes in the brain drive muscle adaptations, rather than just reflecting them. The findings were published in the journal Neuron.
Physiology research on exercise adaptations often focuses on the periphery of the body. When an animal or a human engages in a workout routine, skeletal muscles, the cardiovascular system, and immune function all undergo structural and chemical changes. For years, researchers viewed the brain’s structural changes during exercise as a reflection of these peripheral adaptations. Under this model, muscle tissues release chemical signals into the bloodstream, and the rest of the body responds to that muscular stress.
However, the central nervous system maintains an expansive network for sensing and regulating the body’s daily energy demands. The ventromedial hypothalamus is a region deep in the brain that manages energy expenditure, feeding behavior, and blood sugar levels. Within this neural region sits a specific population of neurons that express a protein known as steroidogenic factor-1, or SF1. Because these cells regulate metabolism, researchers suspected they might play an active role in how the body handles the physical stress of a demanding workout.
University of Pennsylvania researcher Morgan Kindel, Providence College researcher Ryan J. Post, and a team of colleagues investigated whether these SF1 neurons respond to physical exertion. The scientists hypothesized that the brain actively coordinates the metabolic remodeling that leads to increased athletic stamina. They designed a series of small studies using mice to test how manipulating this tiny cluster of brain cells would affect overall physical endurance. The resulting data established a feed-forward loop between physical movement and brain plasticity.
The researchers first exposed a small group of mice to a single session of treadmill running and analyzed their brain tissue. They stained the tissue to measure the expression of a gene called Bdnf, which becomes more active when neurons fire. The analysis showed an increase in both the number of SF1 neurons expressing this gene and the total amount of the gene’s transcripts per cell. This initial test indicated that the exercise session successfully stimulated the neural population.
To see what happens when this neural activity is blocked, the team injected a specialized genetic tool into the brains of a small group of mice. This tool produced a tetanus toxin that prevented the SF1 neurons from releasing chemical signals to other cells. When placed on a treadmill stress test that gradually increased in speed, the mice with silenced SF1 neurons reached exhaustion faster than unmodified control mice. The researchers used indirect calorimetry, which measures oxygen intake and carbon dioxide output to track metabolism, and found that the modified mice burned through their carbohydrate stores prematurely rather than relying on fat reserves.
Next, the researchers put the mice through a three-week treadmill training program to see if they could build endurance. The control mice steadily improved their running times and maximum distances over the three weeks. The mice with silenced SF1 neurons failed to build this endurance capacity. An analysis of their leg muscles showed an absence of the genetic changes that typically optimize energy use after regular training, showing that silencing the brain cells halted the muscles’ ability to adapt.
To track how the neurons behaved in real time, the team used tiny head-mounted microscopes to monitor calcium levels in the brains of active mice. Calcium flows into neurons when they fire, providing a visual proxy for cellular activity. During a week of daily training, the researchers observed a specific subset of SF1 neurons that consistently became active right after the exercise ended. Over the course of the week, the repeated training increased both the number of these post-workout neurons and the intensity of their firing.
The researchers then extracted brain tissue from mice that had exercised for three weeks and measured the electrical properties of individual SF1 neurons. Compared to tissue from sedentary mice, the cells from the trained animals were more electrically excitable and fired spontaneous action potentials at a higher rate. High-resolution imaging of the cells’ branches, or dendrites, revealed that the exercised mice had twice as many tiny protrusions called dendritic spines. This structural growth means the neurons had physically adapted to accommodate more synaptic connections.
Because the live imaging showed peak activity right after running, the team tested whether post-workout firing is the primary driver of endurance. They used optogenetics, a technique that allows researchers to turn specific neurons off using targeted light. By delivering light through fiber optic implants, they inhibited SF1 neurons for exactly 15 minutes immediately following each daily treadmill session. This brief post-workout suppression blunted the endurance gains that the mice would normally achieve.
In a final test, the researchers used a different optogenetic setup to artificially stimulate the SF1 neurons for one hour immediately after daily exercise. Activating the cells during this recovery window enhanced the animals’ endurance gains beyond their normal physiological plateau. The artificial stimulation triggered an increase in blood sugar and overall energy expenditure, which the researchers suggest may help initiate the metabolic recovery signals that prepare muscles for future physical stress.
These experiments rely on mouse models running on treadmills, and rodent metabolism does not perfectly map onto human physiology. Human endurance adaptations take place over longer time scales and involve more varied types of physical training. The results show that activating these brain cells is necessary for building stamina in mice, but they do not establish exactly how the brain receives the message that the exercise has stopped.
Identifying the physical pathways that carry signals from fatigued muscles back up to the ventromedial hypothalamus remains a goal for future studies. Researchers will also need to determine if different types of exercise, such as weightlifting or high-intensity interval training, recruit these exact same neural pathways. Mapping out this brain-to-body loop could eventually inform the development of therapeutics for individuals who cannot safely engage in rigorous physical activity.
The study, “Exercise-induced activation of ventromedial hypothalamic steroidogenic factor-1 neurons mediates improvements in endurance,” was published in May 2026. It was authored by Morgan Kindel, Ryan J. Post, Kyle Grose, Louise Lantier, Eunsang Hwang, Jamie R.E. Carty, Lenka Dohnalova´, Lauren Lepeak, Hallie C. Kern, Rachael Villari, Nitsan Goldstein, Emily Lo, Albert Yeung, Lukas Richie, Bridget Skelly, Jenna Golub, Manmeet Rai, Teppei Fujikawa, Julio E. Ayala, Joel K. Elmquist, Christoph A. Thaiss, David H. Wasserman, Kevin W. Williams, Erik B. Bloss, and J. Nicholas Betley.

How accurate is the climate disaster in Tom Cruise’s new movie
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:59:43 UTC
04:59:43 KST

In Tom Cruise’s new movie Digger, the actor plays a crazed oil baron whose irresponsible drilling causes a massive iceberg to split off Greenland. Named Judy by climate scientists in the movie, the marauding ice barrels toward Europe, imperiling lives—but real climate scientists say this may be a little more fantastical than what we’d see if such an event really happened.
In the movie, Judy threatens to bring a tsunami to Norway. The plot point is dramatic, but it misunderstands how ice shelves work, says Nils Bochow, a climate scientist at the Alfred Wegener Institute in Potsdam, Germany. Ice shelves are already floating on the water, so “if [icebergs] break off, nothing much happens because they don't cause any change in sea level.”
Icebergs can make waves if they break off ice shelves or glaciers, but these are typically confined to a range of a few kilometers (one km is 0.6 mile), Borchow says. “And they’re also moving very, very slowly. It’s not very spectacular.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Judy’s size is about 400 square miles—that’s likely much larger than any possible Greenland iceberg, Borchow says. For example, a recent large iceberg that broke free of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier was 29 square miles; it eventually collided with the country’s Joe Island. The largest Greenland iceberg in recent history broke off Petermann Glacier in 2010, and it was only a quarter the size of Judy.
In Antarctica, however, icebergs much larger than Judy break off ice shelves regularly. But again, these aren’t known to cause havoc to humans on land. (They have been known to trouble penguins, though.) In fact, many of these events are a natural part of an ice shelf's life cycle rather than the result of climate change or human activity. For instance, in 2023 an iceberg 1.5 times as big as Judy broke off of Antarctica's Brunt Ice Shelf. It was the fourth in a succession of large calving events off Antarctica—and it wasn’t even the largest: one iceberg that broke off another Antarctic ice shelf in 2017 was about 2,240 square miles.
“It’s unlikely that an iceberg would make its way to a major populated area [because icebergs] usually melt as they enter the warmer waters away from the ice sheet,” says Chris Stokes, who studies glaciers at the Durham University in England.
“However, they pose a serious hazard to shipping and other maritime human activities and there may be some local impacts on coastal settlements or tourist activities near the ice sheets,” he adds.
Icebergs aside, what is true is that human-driven climate change is causing ice at the planet’s poles to melt. The resulting destruction of critical ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica will raise global sea levels.
Digger is, first and foremost, a parable—without spoiling the plot, its events are intentionally exaggerated to make a point about humans and climate change. But Borchow says that the movie misses one of the least recognized truths about climate change.
“I think a lot of people think that [climate change] is happening very fast, but these ice sheets are very, very slow,” he says. “We see this change, but it doesn’t seem urgent to most people… But everything that we do today has an influence on the future. It’s really hard to put that in a movie.”

In the Netherlands and Belgium, one of the chains suspended sales of Meta smart glasses — what they fear
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:56:36 EEST
04:56:36 KST

In the Netherlands and Belgium, one of the chains suspended sales of Meta smart glasses — what they fear
Kyiv • UNN
The Hans Anders chain stopped selling Ray-Ban Meta in the Netherlands and Belgium over privacy concerns. Meta denies the risks of covert recording.
One of the largest Dutch optical retail chains announced on Friday that it was suspending sales of Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses in the Netherlands and Belgium amid growing privacy concerns. This is one of the first such moves by a retailer, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
"This decision is driven by ongoing public and political discussions surrounding smart glasses, as well as questions about the conditions for using this technology," a representative of the Hans Anders chain said.
The wave of discontent in the Netherlands over these glasses reflects a broader negative reaction to camera-equipped smart glasses.
In the United Kingdom, pub chain Wetherspoon restricted the use of Meta glasses over concerns about covert recording, while in the United States a lawsuit was filed against Meta and Luxottica alleging that videos recorded with the glasses were viewed by human annotators without the knowledge of those filmed.
A Meta representative said the company continues to develop these popular glasses. "Every camera-equipped pair has a bright indicator on the front that flashes when photos or videos are being recorded; it cannot be disabled, and the camera switches off if someone covers it or interferes with its operation," the company said.
In the Netherlands, the data protection regulator (AP) warned last month that videos recorded with smart glasses in which people can be identified generally may not be shared or published without their permission — obtaining which is quite difficult in a public place.
Consumer rights organization Consumentenbond said this week that it would sue Meta if the company did not redesign the glasses in accordance with privacy protection legislation.
The anti-cyberbullying organization Offlimits also called on Meta and Ray-Ban brand owner EssilorLuxottica on Friday to voluntarily withdraw the glasses from sale until a way is found to prevent covert recording.
Hans Anders is a subsidiary of Nexeye, which is owned by investment firm KKR. Nexeye operates 776 stores in the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, Austria and Sweden. The company does not sell the glasses in the last three countries.

Unknown Publisher

19:54:13 UTC
04:54:13 KST

Ukraine’s industrial partners have accelerated the repair of Ukrainian F-16 fighter jets following intensive use.
This was reported by a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Heorhiy Tykhyi.
“Our industrial partners providing technical support are not only continuing to deliver the aircraft after major overhauls, but are also doing so increasingly quickly. The turnaround times are getting shorter, not longer,” the spokesperson said.
Problems with maintaining these aircraft stem, in particular, from the fact that some components for early F-16 models are no longer manufactured, and they are becoming increasingly difficult to procure.
“However, recent reports about an allegedly catastrophically low level of aircraft readiness and excessively long maintenance times simply do not correspond to reality,” Tykhyi noted.
Recently, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that about half of the F-16 fighter jets have been in Europe for repairs and maintenance for a long time.
According to him, the return of some aircraft is being delayed to such an extent that Ukraine is losing precious time when the fighter jets are most needed to defend its airspace.
Zelensky noted that Kyiv is seeking assistance from Western partners to shift most of the maintenance work to Ukrainian territory. He said that keeping the aircraft closer to the theater of operations will allow them to be returned to service more quickly.
As of the end of September, Ukrainian pilots flying F-16 fighter jets had already shot down more than 3,150 enemy aerial targets.
Due to a shortage of AIM-120 and AIM-9 air-to-air missiles, Ukrainian F-16 pilots are increasingly firing at drones with 20-mm cannons. To address this, Ukraine is working on a large-scale procurement of 20-mm ammunition for the F-16s.
Last year, to support pre-flight training for F-16 fighter jets, the Come Back Alive Foundation provided the military with mobile maintenance systems.

ICE Has Been Dumping Protester Photos Into a Palantir Database
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:52:36 UTC
04:52:36 KST

An explosive and newly partially unsealed court filing alleges that the US Department of Homeland Security built up dossiers on ICE observers—including their photos, license plate numbers, and other information—and stored them in a system called the Investigative Case Management database, which was built by Palantir.
Palantir did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for DHS calls the case “meritless” and says that “the underlying lawsuit is based on the lie that there is a database of ‘domestic terrorists’ run by DHS.”
Plaintiffs allege in the filing, which is heavily based on documents produced by the government and depositions of DHS agents, that agents had a practice of intimidating protesters and observers. They did this, the filing says, by doing drive-bys of the observers’ homes and, in the case of at least one observer, requiring that she be referred to secondary inspection any time she tries to cross the border until at least January 2027.
"The government is treating people who exercise their First Amendment rights and seek to hold it accountable as criminal suspects, and that's what we're asking the court to stop,” says JoAnna Suriani, an attorney at Protect Democracy who is representing ICE observers in the case.
The filing focuses on agents’ conduct during “Operation Catch of the Day,” an immigration enforcement surge in Maine this past January. It is part of a proposed class action brought in federal court in Maine by four observers: Elinor Hilton, Colleen Fagan, Polyxenia Pantos, and Carlyn Williams. It was filed under seal in September, and a redacted version was made public Friday.
In particular, it describes how one DHS agent, referred to as “Agent J.C.” in the filing, used the Investigative Case Management (ICM) database, which the government describes as the case management system the ICE component Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) uses to document its investigations, to flag observers.
According to the filings, J.C. created ICM records on at least six observers; the government puts the number of people at eight. He labeled two people he filmed at a Home Depot parking lot with “Threat to Law Enforcement, Professional Protestor,” according to the filing, and sent photos of them and others to a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer so he could run a facial recognition search on them using an app called Mobile Query.
On January 20, Pantos briefly watched and photographed an arrest in Portland, Maine, standing a few car lengths away beside their spouse's car. Hours later, per the filing, J.C. ran the car's plate and pulled a report on the owner—Williams—from Accurint, a LexisNexis database for law enforcement, which listed her address, phone numbers, and cohabitants. J.C. then allegedly circulated her photo to his team, asking, “Was this the protestor.” Another agent, per the filing, replied that it didn’t match the woman he had dealt with at the scene; J.C. then told colleagues he was "adding them in ICM now."
According to the legal filing, that afternoon, J.C. called Williams on her cell phone, identifying himself only as "the Department of Homeland Security." According to Williams, he told her she "should encourage" her spouse, Pantos, "not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist." J.C. testified in a deposition that he warned Williams she would be arrested if she “continue[d] to do this.” Government attorneys asserted in a court filing that he denied referencing a “domestic terrorism watchlist.”
According to documents produced by the government, Williams’ ICM record says that she was the registered owner of a vehicle used to “interrupt ICE arrests” and that her driver’s license photo matched a video of "aggressive woman [who] interject[ed] herself into an arrest." According to a 2016 DHS privacy assessment, ICM automatically shares the subject records agents create with CBP’s TECS system, where they act as "lookout records" for screening travelers at the border.
ICM is the system used by HSI agents to create and track case files. ICE awarded Palantir the contract to build ICM in 2014, and the system is built on the company’s Gotham software, which ICE says was customized specifically for operational needs. In 2022, ICE awarded Palantir a new five-year ICM support contract initially valued at up to about $96 million. In 2025, the agency added nearly $30 million to that contract to develop a new platform called “ImmigrationOS.”
Todd Lyons, the former acting director of ICE, wrote in an April letter to Rep. Maxwell Frost, the Florida Democrat, that ICE “does not maintain any kind of database of U.S. citizens protesting ICE activities.” He also said DHS isn’t keeping a “separate, standalone database” of people it hasn’t arrested or detained.
The government’s motion to dismiss argues that these were isolated incidents and that DHS policy prohibits this conduct. It says J.C. made records on people he believed were “potential threats to law enforcement” and “did not attempt to nominate any individuals to the terrorist watchlist.”
Attorneys for the observers say that DHS’s efforts have had a chilling effect on their First Amendment rights. According to the motion, Pantos stopped all ICE observation work after J.C.’s phone call to Williams, who briefly continued to observe ICE activity and then stopped all together too.
The observers are asking the court to order that Williams’ records be archived, to bar DHS from using the information it collected about the plaintiffs against them, and to prohibit agents in Maine from threatening observers with watchlists or following them to their homes.

Tennessee execution survivor Christa Pike on ventilator, attorneys say

Death row execution survivor Christa Pike on ventilator, US attorneys say
- Convicted murderer Christa Pike is unconscious and on a ventilator after Tennessee's failed execution attempt using pentobarbital.
- Pike suffered serious injuries to both arms due to improperly placed IV lines during the botched lethal injection.
- Governor Bill Lee halted executions for 2026 and ordered an independent review following Tennessee's second failed execution this year.
AI generated
NASHVILLE, Tennessee - Convicted murderer Christa Pike is unconscious, intubated and receiving breathing assistance from a ventilator after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her, her attorneys said on Oct 2, providing the first detailed account of the extent of injuries she suffered during the lethal injection.
Hospital staff are working to save Pike’s life and clear the lethal drug pentobarbital from her system, her attorneys said, in an emergency court filing seeking an order requiring Tennessee’s Department of Correction to preserve evidence from the Sept 30 botched execution.
Pike remains in critical condition, her lawyers said, two days after the state administered two doses of pentobarbital but failed to kill her.
She has suffered significant injuries to both arms, they added.
“At no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike’s body,” Pike’s lawyers said, in a filing in the Chancery Court for the State of Tennessee Twentieth Judicial District.
The filing provides the fullest picture yet of the medical consequences of an attempted execution that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee said followed the state’s established protocol.
It was the state’s second botched execution this year and Lee has halted any further state killings for the rest of 2026 and ordered an independent review of what happened.
Pike’s attorneys have said the execution team’s difficulties administering the drug were related to intravenous access, an issue they had warned the state and courts about before the execution.
Pike, 50, was convicted of killing her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, when Pike was 18.
She had been scheduled to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than two centuries. REUTERS

Two Iranian nationals charged over alleged terrorism plot targeting Jewish community

Two Iranians charged in UK with planning attack on Manchester Jews

Sánchez begins reflection on early election as protesters call for general strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:46:10 UTC
04:46:10 KST

Spanish Prime Minister will decide this weekend whether to call early elections after his two housing decrees were rejected, as housing activists prepare fresh protests and consider a general strike as the next step.
Pedro Sánchez enters a period of reflection. The Prime Minister will use this weekend to decide whether to bring forward the general election after Congress on Friday threw out two housing decrees put forward by his Socialist government.
The parliamentary defeat leaves the government facing a new scenario and Sánchez having to decide on the future of the legislature. According to government sources cited by several national media outlets, the prime minister will, over the coming days, consider whether to call elections before the end of the year.
Hours before the votes, the government had played down that possibility and insisted that an early election was not on the table because "hoy no toca" (today is not the day). After the result unfolded, the executive said it would analyse the situation without ruling out any option.
The two decrees were rejected after more than four hours of debate. The first fell by 178 votes to 172, with the Popular Party, Vox, Junts, and UPN all voting against. The second was defeated by 184 votes to 166, after the PNV and Canary Islands Coalition joined the 'no' camp.
Sánchez's political future hanging
While Sánchez's political future hangs in the balance, the reaction outside Congress has been immediate. Protesters who had been camped out for days in Puerta del Sol marched to Congress on Friday to follow a vote they regarded as crucial to their demands.
Once the rejection of the first decree was confirmed, some of the protesters headed back to Sol chanting "general strike". A general assembly was scheduled for the afternoon to decide the next steps in the movement and the future of the camp itself.
The Confederation of Tenants' Unions has also called demonstrations this Saturday in more than 50 Spanish cities and is already signalling an escalation in protest: "the next step is a general strike", the organisation said.
The spokesperson for the Tenants' Union, Alicia del Río, had already on Friday called for a general strike over housing and warned that the mobilisation would not end with the vote in Congress.
A weekend with two unknowns
The fall of the decrees opens a weekend marked by two key questions. The first will be answered in the political arena: whether Sánchez chooses to continue the legislature or bring forward the general election.
The second lies on the streets. Protests will continue this Saturday in dozens of cities, and housing campaign groups will have to decide how far to step up their mobilisation and how to put into practice their call for a general strike.
Two very different responses to the same vote, which has put on hold both the government's next move and that of a housing protest which, for now, shows no sign of ending.

7th Air Force Ends ‘Super Squadron’ Test, Returns F-16s to Kunsan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:38:54 UTC
04:38:54 KST

After a two-year experiment that created F-16 “Super Squadrons” at Osan Air Base just 50 miles away from North Korea, the U.S. Air Force has returned some of the fighters to its other base on the peninsula.
The 7th Air Force, which oversees USAF forces in Korea, announced the phased return of F-16s to Kunsan Air Base on Sept. 28. But captions for images released by the 7th state some of the jets returned in May and August.
After the return is complete, there will be two fighter squadrons at Kunsan and one at Osan. Kunsan is about 150 miles from the to the Demilitarized Zone that splits North and South Korea
“The decision to return the F-16s on the Korean Peninsula to a three-squadron structure leverages the strategic advantages of both Osan and Kunsan Air Bases while increasing operational flexibility,” Won Hee Kim, a spokesperson for the 7th Air Force, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.
The Air Force launched its Super Squadron experiment in 2024, shifting F-16s and the associated personnel from the 8th Fighter Wing at Kunsan to the 51st Fighter Wing at Osan. As the experiment began, Osan was divesting its A-10 Warthogs and would have had only a single F-16 squadron left.
The experiment unfolded in two phases, each creating a jumbo squadron of 31 jets instead of the usual 24. It was slated to run through October 2026, but Pacific Air Forces commander Gen. Kevin Schneider announced in April that the test “was successfully completed” and the forces would “reset” to their bases.
Officials did not provide specific reasons for the experiment’s conclusion when they announced it in April.
Super Squadron Background
Under the three-squadron structure, the 7th Air Force has the 36th Fighter Squadron and the 80th Fighter Squadron at Kunsan, and 35th Fighter Squadron at Osan, with an estimated 72 F-16s spread between the two locations—F-16s from Misawa Air Base in Japan began transferring to Osan in a move separate from the Super Squadron experiment.
Those 72 Fighting Falcons represent a sizable chunk of the U.S. Air Force’s 826 or so F-16s: nearly 9 percent.
The fighter wings at Kunsan and Osan both operate F-16Cs and F-16Ds, primarily Block 40 Vipers, an aircraft with modernized features for Suppression of Enemy Air Defense, night operation, and precision strike capabilities.
The Super Squadron aimed to measure maintenance and combat generation efficiencies, commanders said at the time. Lt. Col. Karl Wiest, spokesperson for then-Chief of Staff Gen. David W. Allvin, said in 2025 that the move sought to improve readiness and training while “reducing manpower and logistical support requirements.”
Allvin also sought to reduce excess infrastructure and logistical requirements across the Air Force.
“The Super Squadron test provided valuable data and critical insights for F-16 operations across the U.S. Air Force,” according to an April release.
Neither the 7th Air Force nor the 8th Fighter Wing provided details on the lessons learned from the Super Squadron experiments.
“The Airmen involved in this effort demonstrated a culture of adaptability, innovation, and complemented the Agile Combat Employment model by enhancing flexibility within the force,” Kim wrote.

The US military is planning a potential increase of thousands of naval forces in the Middle East in the coming weeks, the Washington Post reported on Friday.
The Pentagon intends to move up three aircraft carriers and escort ships into the region to create flexibility in overseeing the war, according to the report.
Administration deliberates next move on Iran
The planning comes as US President Donald Trump’s administration deliberates on how to approach the Iran war, which has now entered its eighth month, causing dissatisfaction among the American public and roiling the global economy, according to the WP.
Additional forces deployed to the region will include 20,000 troops, up to 150 fighter jets, and numerous destroyers to launch and fend off missile attacks, it added.
The USS George Washington, last deployed to the Arabian Sea, the USS George H.W. Bush, currently in the Indian Ocean, and the USS Theodore Roosevelt are among the carriers involved in the discussions, the WP said, citing an earlier report by the Wall Street Journal.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt was deployed recently to San Diego and must make its way across the Pacific Ocean, it added.
The plans come as Trump considers renewing strikes on Iran following November’s midterm elections, the WP said, citing US officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity. 
In an interview published by Time magazine on Thursday, the US President said that it’s  “possible” he will ramp up bombing after the midterms, according to the WP’s report. 
50,000 troops are currently deployed
Around 50,000 US troops are currently deployed in the Middle East, the WP cited US officials as saying.
The Navy, according to the report, recently deployed the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, a three-ship task force of Marines and sailors from California.
The Boxer Amphibious Ready Group, a similar unit, has already been in the Middle East for months and includes more than 4,000 sailors and Marines, the report added, citing officials.
If Trump decides against expanding the conflict with Iran, the recently deployed vessels would likely replace those that have been there for months, the WP cited officials as saying.
The war, according to the report, has challenged the Pentagon as troop morale declines and ships require additional maintenance.
The war with Iran has cost the US billions of dollars, it added, left more than 800 troops wounded, and killed at least 19 others.

Saudi Arabia has carried out 94 airstrikes in Yemen over the past 24 hours, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarie claimed, according to a Friday Ynet report.

Sarie alleged the strikes caused civilian deaths and injuries, according to the report.
He also claimed that the total number of Saudi strikes on Yemen since the beginning of the escalation has reached 1,350.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Friday that it had intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Reuters reported on Friday.
Tensions between Saudi Arabia, Houthis remain high
The Houthis threatened to target bridges in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for airstrikes the group claims were carried out by the Saudi military, a Sana'a military source told Lebanese outlet Al Akhbar on Monday.
According to the source, Saudi Arabian airstrikes have targeted Yemeni bridges and other civilian infrastructure while claiming they were missile launch platforms.
"Civilian bridges are not used for military purposes," the source said, calling the Saudi practice "utter bankruptcy."
Saudi Arabia prepares offensive against Houthis
Reuters also reported Friday that Saudi Arabia is preparing an offensive against the Houthis aimed at breaking the group's grip on the coast and securing Red Sea shipping routes.
According to six people familiar with the preparations, the operation is expected to begin in the coming weeks. It would be led on the ground by Yemeni forces overseen by Riyadh and supported by Saudi airstrikes.
The objective of the offensive is to reverse gains made by the Houthis last month, when they seized control of parts of the coast, particularly around the Bab al Mandab Strait, according to the report.
Saudi officials are considering two possible options for the assault, according to Gulf and Yemeni officials. One would involve a narrowly focused attack around Bab al Mandab, while the other would involve a broader offensive with synchronized attacks on multiple fronts across Yemen, including in Al Bayda, Marib, Taiz, and Al Jawf.
More than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilized in the offensive, depending on the scale, the officials all said.
Spokespeople for the Saudi and Yemeni governments, the Houthi group and the US military didn't immediately respond to requests for comment about the Saudi plans.
Bab al-Mandab is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that's assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed by the Iran conflict.

The American-Ukrainian investment fund has concluded its first deal in the field of &quot;critical minerals&quot; — media

The American-Ukrainian investment fund has concluded its first deal in the field of "critical minerals" — media
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukraine Reconstruction Fund has concluded its first deal with BGV Group and launched four more projects. The total value of the investments reached $70 million.
The joint U.S.-Ukrainian investment fund established to rebuild the country has concluded its first deal in the critical minerals sector and launched four other new projects. A senior U.S. official told Reuters, reports UNN.
Details
The fund, established under the minerals agreement (signed by both countries in April last year at the initiative of U.S. President Donald Trump), focuses on five strategic sectors, ranging from mineral extraction and defense to energy and infrastructure.
Conor Coleman, head of the investment division at the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), said that the total value of the fund’s projects currently stands at around $70 million, demonstrating Washington’s support for Kyiv in its prolonged war with Russia.
"It is extremely important for the Ukrainian people that we are investing right now," Coleman said in an interview, referring to the ongoing destruction Ukraine is suffering ahead of another winter.
The first, long-awaited minerals deal involves an investment of around $30 million in a "joint investment platform" with BGV Group, a company founded by Hennadiy Butkevych, a billionaire and co-owner of Ukraine’s largest supermarket chain, "ATB."
According to Coleman, at the initial stage, the activity will focus on early-stage mining projects across Ukraine, specifically deposits of rare-earth metals, uranium, beryllium, and zirconium.
"All of these resources are included on the U.S. list of critical minerals, so this aligns very well with the priorities of the American administration," Coleman said.
In addition
The two other new projects announced on Friday are aimed at strengthening Ukraine’s electricity and heating networks in response to the increasing frequency of Russian attacks on critical infrastructure ahead of winter.
Coleman said that one of these projects will complement a nearly $100 million loan that the DFC has just agreed to provide to Ukraine’s largest private energy company, DTEK. The funds will be used to create a new battery system capable of providing backup power to approximately 600,000 Ukrainian households for two hours.
The project also provides for "access to capital in the event of damage." The fund will also acquire a stake in a cogeneration platform (a system for the combined production of thermal and electrical energy) intended to create and operate a number of "energy hubs" whose purpose is to restore damaged electricity and heat supplies for households.
Coleman also noted that the fund is seeking additional capital to expand its capacity.

41 Ukrainians Return From Russian Occupation via Volyn, Including 9 children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:33:38 UTC
04:33:38 KST

Forty-one Ukrainian citizens, including four children and five teenagers, have successfully returned from Russian-occupied territories through the Mokrany-Domanove checkpoint in the Volyn region.
The returns, carried out through the crossing on Ukraine’s border with Belarus in August and September, were organized with the help of partner organizations and the office of Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, Dmytro Lubinets.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In a statement on Friday, Oct. 2, Lubinets described the experiences of several citizens who returned, while also pointing to civilians who remain trapped in occupied areas.
“For each of them, this is not just a border crossing. It marks the end of months or years of life under occupation – with fear, pressure, persecution and constant uncertainty,” Lubinets said.
He singled out the town of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, which he previously called a “death trap” and where Ukrainian authorities say a man-made humanitarian catastrophe is unfolding.
Detentions, mobilization threats and forced treatment
Volyn, bordering Poland and Belarus, remains one of few routes home for Ukrainians leaving Russian-occupied territories, as there is no safe way to cross the front line directly. Those who seek to escape often have to leave through Russia and travel via third countries before re-entering Ukraine.
One family was able to leave after the father was released from captivity. According to Lubinets, their eldest son had also been held captive since April 17, 2022. The mother and her younger son had been under constant monitoring by occupational law enforcement and medical services.
Putin’s Pantsir Problem: Why Russia’s Air Defense Is Failing
According to the family, they were previously placed in a detention facility under the pretext of receiving medical care, where they were held against their will and subjected to forced treatment.
A young medic was also brought out of the occupied territories moments before she would have effectively been mobilized into Russia’s armed forces. “A little longer, and her life could have followed a path that was decided for her under occupation,” Lubinets wrote in the statement.
A man who had been detained several times in the occupied territories managed to return as well. According to Lubinets, he has been held in a basement, with his Ukrainian passport confiscated.
“Occupation is not just territory on a map,” Lubinets said. “Its the loss of freedom, documents, housing, work, connection with loved ones and a sense of safety.”
Support continues after return
Under a joint project with the charitable foundation Caritas Ukraine, returnees receive help restoring documents, temporary housing, financial support, as well as psychological and social assistance, and tickets for onward travel.
The project assisted 1,140 Ukrainian nationals through August and September, including those evacuated with the help of the ombudsman’s office.
Kyiv Post could not independently verify these figures.
According to Lubinets, the office receives daily requests from people seeking to leave the occupied territories. His team reviews each case, subsequently searching for possible routes while working with international partners and third countries.
Oleshky remains cut off
The ombudsman warned that the situation remains particularly severe in Oleshky and nearby settlements, where elderly people, people with disabilities and families continue to live under constant danger.
The city is located in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region on the left bank of the Dnipro River, about 5 km (3 miles) southeast of the city of Kherson, and has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Residents have limited access to food, water, medicine, medical care and communications, and leaving safely remains extremely difficult, with people frequently walking through mined fields just to escape.
On July 16, Lubinets said Russian authorities had failed to uphold previously agreed arrangements for a humanitarian evacuation from the occupied town.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) was prepared to take part in the evacuation within its mandate, while Ukrainian security and defense forces made arrangements for a ceasefire during the proposed operation.
At the time, his office had received 176 appeals about the situation in Oleshky and verified at least 358 people in urgent need of help to leave.
Lubinets estimated that more than 6,000 people, including around 200 children, could still be in the town and surrounding area, though the figures could not be independently verified due to tight Russian restrictions on information.
“They see no other way to escape this hell,” he said, adding that “they risk stepping on mines or being hit by drones, yet they go because remaining in Oleshky is even worse for them.”
Ukrainian officials said on Monday, Sept. 28 that remaining residents have been forced to eat dogs and weeds as Russian forces prevent them from leaving and block supplies from entering the city. Ukrainian forces have resolved to use drones to drop food because ground convoys cannot safely enter the city, although the deliveries cannot replace regular humanitarian access.
On Wednesday, Sept. 30, Ukraine initiated an urgent meeting of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) over the worsening situation in the city.
Around the same time, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned that the Kremlin is preparing to stage dozens of videos featuring residents of occupied Oleshky, forcing them to claim they are “well-fed and happy.”
Meanwhile, the Kremlin continues denying that it targets civilians in its fifth year of war and has also sought to shift the blame for the crisis in Oleshky onto Kyiv.
