On the run for 20 years, Ugandan warlord Kony still 'active' within the Lord's Resistance Army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:31:27 UTC
04:31:27 KST

On the run for 20 years, Ugandan warlord Kony still 'active' within the Lord's Resistance Army
In recent months, the eastern Central African Republic has been hit by several attacks attributed to the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA), a Ugandan militia infamous for its massacres and mass abductions of children in the 1990s and 2000s. The group's leader, Joseph Kony, wanted by the International Criminal Court for more than 20 years, remains at large. FRANCE 24 spoke to Leonie von Braun, the ICC’s lead investigator on the Kony case, about the group's resurgence.
Joseph Kony, the fugitive rebel leader of the Lord's Resistance Army, has been wanted by the ICC for more than 20 years.
A former altar boy and self-proclaimed messiah, prophet and messenger of God, Kony founded the rebel group in 1987 with the aim of overthrowing Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni and establishing a theocratic regime based on the ten commandments in the Bible.
The LRA's bloody insurgency is one of Africa's longest and most brutal conflicts.
It has claimed more than 100,000 lives and displaced more than two million people, mainly in northern Uganda, according to the UN.
The group carried out numerous massacres and kidnappings of children, who were recruited by the thousands to fight or to satisfy LRA commanders' sexual appetites.
Resurgence in the Central African Republic
Driven out of the country in 2006 by the national army, the group gradually faded from the public eye, although it remains active in isolated border areas of Central Africa.
But in recent months, the LRA has once again made headlines. Central African authorities are concerned about a resurgence of attacks in the east and southeast of the country. At least 25 children have been abducted there during several raids on villages in attacks attributed to Kony’s notorious militia.
FRANCE 24 spoke to Leonie von Braun, Senior Trial Lawyer at the ICC and lead investigator in the Joseph Kony case, about the group's resurgence.
The Lord’s Resistance Army seemed to have virtually disappeared in recent years. How do you interpret these new attacks?
Leonie von Braun: The LRA is much less powerful than it was in the 2000s. The organisation used to be highly hierarchical, with four brigades, each estimated to have several hundred fighters. Today, they operate on a much smaller scale.
However, they remain active, employing a survival strategy very similar to the one used in northern Uganda and, later, when they were driven out of their country, in South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
In the Central African Republic, we are seeing attacks on villages located in the region where they have set up their camps. Civilians are being abducted and enslaved.
This information shows that they are still armed and ready to commit acts of violence. The more people they abduct, the stronger they become. They have always acted this way. They kidnap children because they are easy to indoctrinate, and they turn them into fighters. Within a few years, they have soldiers capable of handling rifles and throwing grenades.
Even though the LRA has been weakened, the risk remains very high for local populations due to these kinds of organisations, which are willing to commit the worst atrocities to ensure their survival.
Read moreVideo: Ugandan city still scarred by Lord's Resistance Army atrocities
You mention the recruitment of children, yet this movement defines itself as Christian. Is this recruitment based on religious grounds?
The LRA has its origins in another Ugandan rebel movement, the “Holy Spirit Movement", founded in the 1980s by a woman named Alice Auma. She called herself Lakwena, after the “spirit” from whom she claimed to receive orders. This group had already attempted – and failed – to overthrow the government.
Joseph Kony subsequently took control of it. The LRA is not a Christian movement in the strict sense but a syncretic movement that blends Christianity with local beliefs. Its leader uses belief in spirits to instill fear among his troops. But indoctrination is carried out primarily through violence.
Children are subjected to initiation rites – extremely violent acts that literally break them – and then the rules are explained to them. For example, dropping a pot of food is punished with severe beatings, just as is refusing to have sex with a commander. An escape attempt is tantamount to death or a near-death experience. Children are subjected to a system of the most severe disciplinary measures, with numerous rules designed to extract total obedience from them.
Read moreFormer Ugandan child soldier-turned-rebel commander sentenced to 25 years at ICC
The ICC issued an arrest warrant for Joseph Kony in 2005. He has been the subject of an intense manhunt, including by the United States, which offered a $5 million reward for any information leading to his capture. How can we explain the fact that he is still on the run?
There have been massive media campaigns on social media calling for his arrest, particularly around 2012 and when the United States deployed US special forces to Central Africa to track him down.
His ability to stay under the radar can be attributed to several factors. On the one hand, his knowledge of the terrain and his in-depth understanding of the region’s geography; on the other hand, his ability to endure hardship.
This is not, of course, meant to praise him, but it must be acknowledged that Joseph Kony has demonstrated extreme physical and psychological resilience. He has taught the members of his group how to survive in the bush under extremely difficult conditions, how to anticipate changes in the area, and has managed to set up an intelligence network – technologically unsophisticated but highly effective – to evade surveillance and, above all, continue carrying out criminal operations.
Furthermore, the very nature of this group poses a major problem because it includes a large number of children. Any planning for an operation must take into account the risk faced by those who are unarmed, who are not combatants, and who are in no way responsible for their situation. It is therefore essential to find the right moment to act. The situation is made all the more complicated by the fact that it is difficult to obtain reliable and up-to-date information about this group.
Read moreOvercoming the trauma: Singing lessons help former child soldiers in Uganda
What do we know today about Joseph Kony? He is reportedly 65 years old. Are you certain he is still alive?
We are monitoring the Lord’s Resistance Army very closely and are doing everything in our power to secure the surrender and arrest of its leader. The latest information we have indicates that he is still alive. He is not the only leader within this group. There is a hierarchy. And given his age, we might infer that he is not on the front lines in terms of operations. But he is still active and very much present within the LRA.
After 20 years of investigation, do you think it is still possible that Joseph Kony will one day be brought to justice? What does this case mean for the ICC’s credibility?
This case is particularly significant because of the gravity of the crimes committed against the most vulnerable members of society. The evidence shows that thousands of children and women were abducted during the period falling within our jurisdiction alone – from July 1, 2002, to December 31, 2005. This is a case of considerable magnitude – the largest we have ever handled involving crimes against children.
In a sense, this case tests the limits of the ICC, as we do not have our own police force. We issue arrest warrants, the recognition and execution of which depend on the cooperation of States. But it is extremely important for us to finally bring him to justice, and we are convinced that this is still possible. No one could have imagined that Milosevic, Charles Taylor, and many others would be held accountable for their actions before international justice. We are therefore continuing our efforts.

Russia 'tearing Kyiv apart', mayor says, as strikes paralyse traffic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:30:32 UTC
04:30:32 KST

Russian attacks on key infrastructure were "tearing Kyiv apart", the city's mayor said Friday, as strikes on a bridge linking the capital's east and west brought traffic to a standstill.
President Volodymyr Zelensky accused his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, of ripping up the rulebook of armed conflict by sanctioning massive attacks on civilian areas, an accusation the Kremlin has rejected.
The grinding conflict, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, has largely focused on ground fighting in the east, with Kyiv mostly spared from the devastation wrought near the frontline.
But Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city should now be on a war footing.
"The capital is in a very dramatic situation," he posted on Telegram. "It's no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we lived in peacetime."
"The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart."
His message came as the authorities shut one of Kyiv's main bridges and restricted movement on a second after another wave of deadly strikes by fast-moving, jet-powered drones.
Traffic heavily disturbed
Long lines of stationary cars and buses were gridlocked on main roads as commuters sought alternative routes — or even made their way on foot.
"I've been travelling for three hours... to get to work," said Tetiana Osypenko, a 49-year-old seamstress whose bus was stuck in a traffic jam.
"There's just no way to get there. Nothing. It's impossible to cross the bridges today," she said.
Traffic built up due to the complete closure to all vehicles going in both directions on the Southern Bridge, one of eight bridges connecting the east and west of Kyiv over the Dnipro river.
The cable-stayed bridge has been hit several times since Thursday, with new strikes confirmed by Klitschko on Friday afternoon.
The Paton Bridge, further north, was open in one direction only, though there were no reports that it had been struck.
On X, Zelensky accused Putin of last month declaring there were "no rules now", citing unnamed intelligence and people around Putin.
"The Russians couldn't occupy us. So now they are doing massive attacks and massive killings," Zelensky said in remarks first made in a Financial Times interview.
The Kremlin made no immediate public response to the claim.
Daily bombing fear
Kyiv has been increasingly under aerial bombardment in recent months, putting the city on near-constant alert and disrupting daily life.
Air raid sirens warning of approaching threats in the skies sound almost round the clock, urging the city's estimated three million people to seek shelter.
Repeated strikes on trains and petrol stations have already hit the rail and road networks while attacks on energy facilities threaten power and heating as winter approaches.
Osypenko, the seamstress, said previous disruptions to subway services during air raids have forced her to spend the night in a metro station near the Southern Bridge.
Loss of earnings compounds the financial pressures caused by the war, she added. "You just spend the whole day feeling completely beaten down."
The latest Russian attacks killed one person and wounded at least two other people when a 25-storey residential building was hit in southeast Kyiv.
Two people were killed and dozens more injured when Russian shelling hit residential areas in the eastern city of Kharkiv, city mayor Igor Terekhov said on Telegram.
'Political will'
Zelensky urged tougher sanctions to prevent Russia from manufacturing jet-powered drones, which are harder to intercept.
Russia's production of the weapons was "critically dependent" on foreign components, he wrote on social media on Friday.
"Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line. What is needed is the political will of these countries," he added.
Zelensky has repeatedly called on Ukraine's Western allies for more military support, particularly for US-made Patriot missile interceptors.
On Thursday, he said Ukraine had used its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, without disclosing where or what it had been used against.
He also said Ukraine was testing five of its own interceptors against drones.
Ukraine's military on Friday said it struck an oil refinery in Volgograd and another facility in Samara, both in southwest Russia, for allegedly supplying fuel to Russian forces.
Kyiv also dismissed reports that its F-16 fighter jets — another key tool used against jet-powered drones — could be grounded due to delays in maintenance inspections and the supply of parts.
But Zelensky told the Financial Times that around half of Ukraine's fleet was spending lengthy maintenance periods in Europe.

Tedesco and Ponga went through different worlds to meet in NRL grand final
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:27:50 UTC
04:27:50 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
analysis
James Tedesco and Kalyn Ponga came from different worlds to meet in NRL grand final
Sunday's NRL grand final between the Roosters and Newcastle is a land of contrasts and nowhere is more apparent than the difference between the two fullbacks and captains, James Tedesco and Kalyn Ponga.
Their position, status and ability is about all the two have in common and right from the start the two have walked very different paths to Stadium Australia.
Ponga has been in the papers since he was 15, his first highlights went viral when he was only 17, his first NRL game was a sudden-death semi-final and his first touch was a scorching linebreak that announced a new prince was born.
Once he joined Newcastle in 2018 and finished as the Dally M runner up in his first full season in first grade, his talent was so blinding he never had to prove himself — belief was in his ability was assured.
The world was his, because everyone in rugby league was so eager to give it to him.
For the 33-year old Tedesco, things were different. The Camden product was a good junior, but far from a great one. Just making first grade was far from a guarantee.
Eventually, he didn't just run down those who were ahead of him, he raced right past them and by the time he made his NRL debut for Wests Tigers in Round 1 of the 2012 season he'd shown himself to be a player of the future.
But that future would have to wait. Where Ponga's debut was covered in chrome, Tedesco's became the hardest day of his young life when he blew his knee out 30 minutes in and was stretchered off Leichhardt Oval in tears.
It kicked off a series of injury troubles and it wasn't until three seasons later that Tedesco managed to shrug them off and become an every-week first grader.
During those years, the naysayers rose up and once again Tedesco outlasted them. He is a player of enormous internal motivation — for him, improvement is less of a journey to be better than a compulsion that defines him and he has put a saddle on that beast and ridden it to greatness.
The doubt of others is the whip he uses to flog it, like he did when time seemed to come for him as he lost his New South Wales and Australian spots two years ago.
He was old enough to go quietly into that good night without shame, and after a career of magnificent achievement the game was prepared to move on only Tedesco would not let it.
"In 2024 and 2025 when I wasn't playing Origin or Test footy, people were doubting me a bit and I got some drive from that," said Tedesco.
"I've been used to that — growing up I was told I wasn't going to make it when I wasn't picked in teams, when I had injuries at the start of my career people told me my body wouldn't last.
"Those external things do motivate me, but the internal one is still the biggest. That'll always be there for me and when it isn't I'll realise it's time to finish."
It had been so long since he was counted out but Tedesco still fought like a demon to prove himself one more time as he claimed last year's Dally M medal and returned to Origin this season.
It has given him a second life but it's still not enough. He is not satisfied and doubts he ever will be.
"I'll never be happy with my game. I always want to improve and learn and get better," said Tedesco.
"That's a part of me, that's been ingrained in me since I was a kid. It's got me to where I am today."
Tedesco has been in that place for many years and that is where Ponga now strides towards.
Right from those first days in Newcastle his raw star power, through no fault of his own, quickly made him bigger than the club he played for.
The adulation continued to flow like a river as the highlights and the Fox League spots stacked up as personal success came naturally to Ponga, but in terms of team success there were many lean winters.
The 29-year old didn't play in a final until 2020, didn't win one until 2023 and in the last three weeks the Knights have more finals victories than the rest of Ponga's time with the club combined.
What seemed like a pre-destined journey to the top has not always been smooth. But if Ponga could speak to his younger self he wouldn't ask him to change because if he did it might not have brought him to where he is right now.
"He'd have wanted it earlier, he was impatient. But it makes it sweeter, to go through those tough times — the adversity, injuries, bad years," said Ponga.
"All the emotion came out when Sandon (Smith) took that intercept. But I wouldn't trade any of it because I'm grateful to be here now.
"There was a lot of tension. I think everyone was riding that last minute with us. The relief — nine years I've been here and I've always dreamt of being in this position and it came true with that intercept."
Ponga's uncontainable passion as a leader has been vibrant and bustling and it's come through in his football, which has perhaps been better but has never been tougher.
He has not scored a try or set one up in this finals series even as he's been outstanding in all three matches, with his running game, defence and leadership coming to the fore.
"When you grow up, you mature — or you'd hope so. The environment I'm in has changed, it allows me to be the best version of myself and it allows me to be myself," said Ponga.
"There's no pressure on me to be someone I'm not, as a player or a person. Justin (Holbrook) has done that and this playing group has done that."
The raw and bleeding edge Ponga has showed is a far cry from his younger days, when sometimes he could be a little too relaxed for his own good.
It helped him carry the weight of a city, a club and a game that expected so much of him, but other times it came to the surface in ways that did not befit a player of his stature — most notably when he said a strawberry thickshake lifted his spirits after coach Nathan Brown was sacked in 2019.
"Off the field, early in his career, he'd probably admit he was a bit lackadaisical. He was cruisy, he'd kick back," said Bradman Best, who first played alongside him that season.
"Now he holds everyone accountable, he drives standards. He's having an impact on other people.
"He's found that balance between staying calm and firing up."
Young prop Cody Hopwood, who was just 11 years old when Ponga first came to town and knows him only as he is now, puts it best.
"He doesn't try and overdo the role, he doesn't try to be someone he's not," said Hopwood.
"He's Kalyn Ponga and that's enough."
The Roosters always expect to be in grand finals so on some level they knew they could be here but the Knights have known it as well, as long ago as the old days of about three weeks ago.
Plenty said they'd never get anywhere, but now we know that they knew better and while Ponga has envisioned lifting the premiership trophy plenty of times before it's only in the last two weeks that it's come into sharper focus.
"You do it nearly every day because it gives you a purpose. It's why you wake up and train so hard, it's why you dedicate yourself to this, it's why you put your body through things you shouldn't," said Ponga.
"But it didn't become a reality until after the Warriors, before that it was just a thought."
Ponga's love for his club and his town is palpable and that's important because it hasn't always been so.
Over the years there have been whispers of moves to Sydney — the Roosters were always meant to be in the mix, even with Tedesco — or of a possible move to rugby, plus a serious flirtation with the Dolphins when they were entering the competition.
But earlier this season he signed for another four years on a watertight contract with none of the clauses or flexibility he's had in the past.
It was a show of faith that has been rewarded and since his transformation from a great player who plays for the Knights into a great Knight and now he is Newcastle, forever and always, no matter what.
"We're in it and to see it, to feel it, it's inspiring. It's everything you ever dreamt of," said Ponga.
"I'm proud to be a part of this club. I'm proud to lead these boys. I'm proud to be a part of this community."
A grand final win will be a moment for ascension for Ponga's nine years with the club and he has moved to the edge of paradise because he has been able to fuse the internal and external motivations as Tedesco has long done.
For Tedesco and his Roosters it's a bit simpler. Having slayed the latest demons, he wants to take the feelings out of the grand final as best he can.
Their key is to keep this as a football game rather than a holy war, to be as calm in the face of overwhelming passion as Ponga once was.
"Just the other night I found myself thinking about the game almost too much, thinking about moments and what could happen," said Tedesco.
"I had to get away from that, because I didn't want to play too early. But it's not about the result, it's about the performance and the process.
"It's easier to say that than it is to do it, but that's something I have to instil into the boys.
"Be proud of where we are, but know the job isn't finished."

Air Force and Space Force Shooting for Historic Recruiting Goals in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:26:19 UTC
04:26:19 KST

The Air Force adjusted its fiscal 2026 recruiting goal down by a few hundred enlisted Airmen due to higher-than-expected retention and the number of available training slots—but it is aiming high in fiscal 2027 with its biggest goal for the Active-Duty Air Force in nearly 25 years, and the Space Force has set its largest recruitment target ever.
In an Oct. 1 release touting its successes in fiscal 2026, the Air Force Recruiting Service said it “met its recruiting goals” and enlisted 31,950 Airmen into the Air Force and 730 Guardians into the Space Force.
That Air Force number is 800 fewer than the 32,750 recruits the service cited in April when it announced it had accomplished its goal five months ahead of schedule. Headquarters Air Force shifted the goal this summer, a spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine, as it adjusted to the “realities” of retention and the number of slots available at Basic Military Training. Every military service has an end strength authorized every year by Congress, and if retention is higher than expected, the service can only add so many recruits. BMT also can be limited by resources or available training dates.
The Air Force spokesperson said recruits were not cut but rather added to the Delayed Entry Program where they await their turn to start Basic Military Training. There are currently 15,799 recruits in the DEP, giving the Air Force Recruiting Service a healthy backlog to draw upon to start the new fiscal year.
That could prove crucial as AFRS attempts to pull off a massive 2027. Another spokesperson confirmed its goals for next year are 36,300 non-prior service enlisted Airmen for the Active-Duty force, and 1,402 enlisted Guardians for the Space Force.
The Air Force’s recruiting goal hasn’t exceeded 35,000 since 2003, according to data compiled by Air & Space Forces Magazine. And the Space Force has never aimed for more than 900 new Guardians in its brief history.
Those big totals come as officials across the military say they are seeing historically high interest among potential recruits—and as the Pentagon pursues a major increase in resources and overall end strength.
“In [fiscal 2027], we will grow the force again by an additional 44,000 service members,” Pentagon comptroller Jules “Jay” W. Hurst III said in April. “This growth will provide the manpower needed to employ new capabilities, and it will improve readiness and quality of life by ensuring units are properly staffed for the missions we task them with.”
The Air Force in particular wants to increase its Active-Duty end strength by nearly 9,000, from 321,500 Airmen to 330,400, and the Space Force wants to add 2,800 Guardians, going from 10,400 to 13,200.
In its release, the Air Force Recruiting Service said it will adjust its strategies for 2027 “based on labor market trends, propensity-to-serve data, and career field demand signals.”
In a panel discussion last month at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Air Force Deputy Chief of Staff for manpower, personnel, and services Lt. Gen. Jefferson O’Donnell said much of the service’s growth would be more “restorative” than “additive,” reversing declines in manning for key career fields.
“We are focused on making sure that we are prioritizing those things like maintenance and logistics and security forces to fill in those spots where we have been taking significant risk across our service,” O’Donnell said.

Russian billionaires 'volunteer' to fund state budget after closed-door meeting with Putin, Reuters reports

Russian billionaires 'volunteer' to fund state budget after closed-door meeting with Putin, Reuters reports
Russia's wealthiest citizens have funded over 1% of Moscow's state budget in 2026, "voluntarily" donating hundreds of billions of rubles to the government, Reuters reported on Oct. 2, citing state budget documents.
The donations followed a closed-door meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in March.
Wealthy Russians have already contributed a total of 471 billion rubles (over $5.6 billion) to the state budget in 2026, according to Reuters. The payments are listed as "voluntary receipts" in budget documents.
Western sanctions, wartime expenditures, and Ukrainian strikes have squeezed Russia's economy over the past five years, leading to stagnant growth, inflation, high interest rates, and low wages.
Yet Moscow continues to ramp up military spending, forcing the state to raise taxes and find new sources of revenue to fund its full-scale invasion.
Putin's meeting in March 2026 gathered elite Russian businessmen, many under Western sanctions. The list of attendees has not been disclosed.
According to the Kremlin, one participant voluntarily offered to donate a "very large sum of money" to the government, arguing that wealthy Russians who amassed large fortunes in the 1990s due to state ties now had an obligation to support the budget.
Putin reportedly agreed. Private contributions from Russian billionaires increased substantially after March.
Russia nonetheless faces a budget deficit of $87 billion for 2026, or 3.2% of the gross domestic product (GDP). The deficit is twice the state goal of 1.6%. Without the "donations" from Russian elites, the deficit would reach 3.4% of the GDP.

Canadian who moved his family to Russia for ‘traditional values’ says he no longer recommends it: permanent residency would require signing a Defense Ministry contract
Canadian farmer Arend Feenstra, who moved to Russia through a streamlined immigration program for citizens of “unfriendly” countries who share “traditional values,” has complained that he cannot get a permanent residence permit. The news outlet Nizhny Novgorod Onlain drew attention to his YouTube video.
Feenstra received a three-year temporary residence permit in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region in early 2025. He then brought his wife and eight children to Russia and began farming.
But Feenstra has now learned that to replace his temporary residence permit with a permanent one, he must sign a contract with Russia’s Defense Ministry.
We’ve already […] grown attached to this place. I didn’t come here to sign a contract. I understand what it’s for and why [the authorities] want you to sign it. But I have eight young children at home and a farm. […] In that case, I’d rather take my chances in Canada, though I think living there is risky too.
Feenstra said that once his current temporary residence permit expires, he will be able to apply for temporary residence again without signing a contract. He also said his family no longer recommends that other foreigners move to Russia because the authorities keep changing the rules and “there’s no way forward.”
The program, launched in August 2024, encourages foreigners from “unfriendly” countries who share “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values” to immigrate to Russia. Participants receive temporary residence permits through a simplified application process that, among other things, does not require them to take Russian-language exams.
Since November 2025, foreign men ages 18 to 65 who are deemed fit for military service have been required to sign a contract with the Defense Ministry to obtain a permanent residence permit in Russia. People who moved to Russia through the “traditional values” program are not exempt from this requirement.

FAA says Boeing 737 Max software glitch not a flight-safety issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:19:15 UTC
04:19:15 KST

The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday that it has determined a new software glitch on some Boeing 737 Max aircraft isn't a flight-safety issue.
The determination paves the way to certification for the last model in the company's best-selling family of airplanes, the 737 Max 10, just as Boeing seeking to sell and deliver more aircraft after years of safety and manufacturing crises.
Boeing flagged the software issue, which could affect certain landing procedures, last month and the FAA on Monday said it was reviewing to determine if it poses a safety of flight issue.
"Following a thorough review, a panel of FAA safety experts on Friday determined a software issue in certain Boeing 737 MAX flight computers is not a safety concern," the FAA said. "The FAA's Corrective Action Review Board made that determination because pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous."
Boeing said the issue could arise after a missed approach when pilots alter a preprogrammed flight path, and that pilots must take additional steps to use automated tools on subsequent approaches.
The FAA said on Friday that it will issue a special bulletin to airlines on how to recognize and respond to the issue if it arises.
The agency convened a review board on Friday to assess the issue. Participants included FAA experts on airframes, flight controls, propulsion, flight testing and others.
"As with any situation, the FAA will consider appropriate action if it receives new information about this issue," the agency said.
U.S. airlines said they're not affected by the issue since they could revert to older versions of the software, but the problem raised questions about certification of the Boeing 737 Max 10, which Boeing and airlines expected to come in early fall.
The Max 10 is the largest in the family of airplanes and would be the last of the Max lineup to win government certification to fly. The FAA approved the Max 7, the smallest in the Max family, in August.
Chief executives of 737 Max 10 customers, Alaska Airlines and Ryanair, earlier this week brushed off concerns about the aircraft's certification delays.

The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has been charged with engaging in conduct in preparation of acts of terrorism including against Nigel Farage.
Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts. The charge relates to activity alleged to have taken place between 31 May 2024 and 8 July this year, counter-terrorism police said.
Vicki Evans, the head of counter-terrorism policing, said: “We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time. The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the counter-terrorism policing network.
“This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge.”
Kerry was due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on Wednesday, police said.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the charge raised “serious questions” about the security of MPs.
She wrote on X: “I know the new charges made today will be extremely concerning. My profound sympathies are with Nigel Farage and his family.
“Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all.
“This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve.”
Widdecombe, 78, a spokesperson for Farage’s Reform UK party and a former Conservative minister, died in July after being hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, a court previously heard.
She was found lying face down on her kitchen floor by her gardener on the morning of 9 July and declared dead by emergency services shortly afterwards.
Kerry is accused of her murder. The suspect spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address during a hearing at Westminster magistrates court in July. He was not asked to indicate a plea.
Olivia Field, the chief executive of the Jo Cox Foundation, which was set up in honour of the Labour MP who was murdered in 2016 in West Yorkshire, said: “No one in public life should have to fear for their safety.
“Violence, abuse and intimidation not only endanger individuals and their families, but threaten our democracy and have no place in public life.
“We must do more to prevent the rising levels of abuse and intimidation in politics. That means looking across society – from education and political literacy to the safety of online environments – alongside ensuring that appropriate security and support are in place for politicians, their staff and families.”
In August, CTP reopened a year-long investigation into an alleged firebomb attack at Farage’s home in south London.
The Metropolitan police and CTP London said they investigated the incident as an “attempted burglary” but made no arrests before the case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.
After its reopening, CTP London identified a line of inquiry that it said “may have been relevant” but had not been “identified and pursued by them at the time”.

Poll shows China a more positive influence than US in Latin America

Poll shows China a more positive influence than US in Latin America
- A 2026 Latinobarometro poll shows 65% of Latin Americans view China as a positive influence, surpassing the US at 57%, marking a shift since 1995.
- US popularity has declined from 73% in 2024 to 63%, influenced by Trump's aggressive policy termed the "Donroe Doctrine" aiming for regional dominance.
- Despite US forces capturing Venezuelan leader Maduro being approved in most countries, only 35% believe it benefited Venezuela, highlighting mixed views on US actions in the region.
AI generated
BOGOTA - China is viewed as a more positive influence on the world than the United States, a major poll of citizens in 17 Latin American countries published on Oct 2 showed.
The 2026 Latinobarometro survey showed that for the first time since the annual survey began in 1995, China is seen as a more benign force than the United States.
It showed 57% of people in Latin America considering the United States to be a positive influence, down from 60% in 2020.
China, meanwhile, was considered a positive influence by 65% of respondents, a jump from the 48% it scored six years ago.
Based on the data, “China has more influence in Latin America than the United States,” the report concluded.
Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic were the only countries in the region where US influence was deemed more positive than that of China.
The growing disaffection towards the US comes nearly halfway through Trump’s second term, during which he has openly asserted his desire for hegemony over Latin America as part of what he calls the “Donroe Doctrine”.
The United States as a country remained more popular than China, with 63% saying they had a favourable view of the world’s top economy, compared to 58% for its arch-rival.
But US popularity was markedly down compared to 2024, when Democratic president Joe Biden was still in the White House.
Two years ago, 73% of people surveyed by Latinobarometro had a favourable view of the United States.
The “Donroe Doctrine” blends Trump’s first name with that of James Monroe, the fifth US president, who more than two centuries ago declared Latin America the United States’ exclusive sphere of influence.
Trump’s push to restore US dominance in what Washington calls “our hemisphere” was in evidence in January when the United States overthrew Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro.
The Latinobarometro poll showed a majority of people in all but one country – Argentina – approving of Maduro’s capture by US special forces.
But only 35% considered it benefited Venezuela, compared to 28% who said it harmed the Caribbean country.
Citizens of Venezuela itself were, however, among those who viewed US influence most positively.
Chile-based Latinobarometro is a non-profit organisation that surveys opinions on a range of issues, from democracy to the economy, security and migration.
The 2026 survey was based on some 19,200 face-to-face interviews carried out in 17 countries between May 7 and June 17, with a margin of error of 1%. AFP

• Rivera, a Republican who represented southern Florida in the US House of Representatives from 2011 to 2013, was convicted at trial in May of lobbying US officials on Venezuela's behalf in 2017 without registering as a foreign lobbyist as required by the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA).
• The sentence was handed down by US District Judge Melissa Damian at a hearing in federal court in Miami.

Russian businessman accuses Biden of stealing his money
Russian businessman Konstantin Malofeev has accused former US President Joe Biden’s administration of stealing his money and using some of it to support Ukraine’s armed forces.
Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a criminal case on Friday at Malofeev’s request over the seizure of his US assets. Investigators said they are trying to identify American officials involved in what the agency described as illegal decisions.
Malofeev, the owner of Russian TV channel Tsargrad, said the US seized $10 million from him, including $5.4 million that was later transferred to Ukraine.
“Former US president [Joe Biden] and Attorney General Merrick Garland stole my money, legally invested in the United States – even before any sanctions,” Malofeev wrote on Telegram.
He accused Biden and Garland of creating an “organized criminal group” between 2021 and 2024 to seize Russian state assets and property belonging to Russian citizens.
“Biden financed terrorists who kill Russian people,” Malofeev said, referring to Ukrainian forces.
The businessman described the case as “unprecedented,” saying “$10 million is only the first step” and predicting that other alleged victims would file similar complaints. He said any money recovered through legal proceedings would be used to support Russian troops.
“A thief belongs in prison. Even if he sat in the White House,” he concluded.
Malofeev has been under US sanctions since 2014. The American authorities said the $10 million had been invested in a Texas-based bank holding company before the restrictions were imposed, but accused him of later trying to transfer the investment to a business associate in violation of the sanctions.
A US court ordered the forfeiture of about $5.4 million linked to the investment in 2023. Garland subsequently authorized its transfer to the State Department to support Ukraine. The US Justice Department later said the money was used to assist Ukrainian veterans.
Malofeev has denied violating US sanctions and previously said he held no money or property in the West after 2014.
The Biden administration provided $65.9 billion in military assistance to Ukraine following the escalation of the conflict in February 2022, while imposing successive rounds of sanctions on Russia.
US President Donald Trump has criticized his predecessor’s support for Kiev, saying Washington was “getting fleeced” and claiming the US had committed $350 billion to Ukraine.
Moscow has repeatedly condemned Western arms deliveries to Kiev, arguing that they prolong the conflict, and has denounced sanctions and the seizure of Russian assets as “theft.”

New York governor condemns handling of Cornell rape case

New York Governor Kathy Hochul said the accuser of the six Cornell University students of gang rape was "failed" by those whose obligation was protecting her.
This includes both campus police and the county prosecutor, Hochul said.
At a press conference on Friday, she also announced the appointment of Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to take over the investigation due to the fact she had lost faith in the local district attorney's ability to handle the case.
This came after she learned the "troubling" details of the authorities' handling of the accuser's case so far.
"In what world does the district attorney not even interview her, or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?" Hochul asked.
"This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable. And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her."
According to Hochul, the woman, identified only by the placeholder name Jane Doe, told police "exactly what happened to her," including her firm belief that she had been raped.
"Yet, shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors."
Investigation to take time
Attorney General Letitia James said she did not know how long her investigation might take.
"I know that you want answers. I do too. A comprehensive investigation of this nature takes time, but my office is committed to seeing it through," James said, adding that evidence gathering and interviews will be carried out.
The original investigation into the case was closed without any charges in 2024.
According to Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who was responsible for the decision, the woman's sworn statement did not include her allegation of being drugged against her will without any ability to consent and forced into sex.
Van Houten reopened the investigation after the accuser filed a new lawsuit in September, 2026, against seven fraternity members, as well as against Cornell.
The lawsuit has since made national headlines and sparked protests at Cornell and across the United States.
Cornell said it launched a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity involved in the allegations, while also imposing a range of disciplinary measures.
The school also said it supports James' appointment and is "committed to an independent external review of all aspects" of its handling of the case.

Life on the edge of Israel’s occupation in southern Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:06:35 UTC
04:06:35 KST

Ihsan Yaghi sweeps the porch of her home in Zawtar al-Gharbiyah in southern Lebanon while her retired husband smokes a cigarette in the shade. It is a sweltering, humid day in the South, but Ihsan works tirelessly to clear away the dust and debris from the only part of their home that remains usable: the porch.
The couple have made do with what they have: a few chairs, a plastic table, a camping gas stove for making coffee and a small container of drinking water. Both of their faces bear the marks of time and exhaustion. Ihsan’s husband takes out his phone and shows us photographs of their home as it once was, before the war and Israeli incursions erased a lifetime of sacrifice and memories. On the screen is a family dinner, the table laid out in the middle of what, until March 2, 2026, was their garden. Today, in that same space, an excavator is clearing the rubble.
“This was our home before the Israelis tried to take it away from us,” he said. “It was habitual for us to eat and spend time together in the garden. We were happy.”
Like roughly one in five Lebanese people, Ihsan was forced to leave her village when Israel resumed attacks on South Lebanon in March 2026, issuing evacuation orders for residents. In the two months that followed, Israel killed over 4,200 Lebanese citizens and invaded the country’s southern border. A partial ceasefire was negotiated in early June that cemented an Israeli military presence and necessitated the withdrawal of Hezbollah from the so-called “Yellow Line” — an Israeli-controlled security zone that now occupies between 55 and 62 villages in South Lebanon, from the Israeli border to Zawtar Al-Gharbiyah. The village was singled out as a “pilot zone” for a U.S.-brokered arrangement involving a partial Israeli withdrawal and the deployment of the Lebanese Army, allowing displaced residents to begin returning.
Zawtar al-Gharbiyah was among the first villages to be included in the so-called “pilot zone.” On July 21, 2026, the Lebanese army began deploying in the village following the withdrawal of Israeli forces. In the days that followed, once clearance operations and checks for mines and unexploded ordnance were under way, residents gradually began returning to their homes. What they found was a village deeply scarred by destruction. Houses still bear the marks of bombardment and fighting: blackened walls, shattered sections of buildings and concrete perforated by gunfire and shelling.
The return to Zawtar is also taking place through small, practical gestures. Residents who have chosen to return are trying to salvage what remains of their homes, clearing away dust, rubble and debris. It is what Ihsan does every day on her porch, because before rebuilding can even begin, returning means trying to make what the war has left behind livable again.
While Zawtar al-Gharbiyah was not under continuous occupation throughout the war, it was subjected to incursions by Israeli forces, accompanied by demolitions and heavy shelling. Traces of the Israeli army remain visible inside and outside homes: Hebrew graffiti on walls and rubbish left behind by soldiers. For those who have returned, these traces are a painful reminder of what happened, and an imminent threat that it could happen again.
Ihsan’s family was among the first to return to Zawtar after the Israeli withdrawal and the cautious arrival of the Lebanese Army. She has since returned to what remains of her home every day. “We belong to the South,” Ihsan said. “It is this land that gives us strength. We belong to this land, and this land gives us the strength to resist.”
She repeats several times that her house was destroyed by the Israelis, speaking with a mixture of anger and resignation: the anger of someone who has seen part of her life destroyed, and the knowledge that it will take a long time before anything resembling normal life can return. She describes herself as a daughter of this village, where her family has lived for generations, tending to their large olive grove, which has now been destroyed by Israeli forces. Ihsan echoes what many of her neighbors in the South have expressed: that they have been left alone.
“We feel that we are still under occupation. There is no sovereignty. They promised us sovereignty, those who talk about sovereignty, but there is no sovereignty. What they told us was not true,” Ihsan says.
The situation in Zawtar al-Gharbiyah differs from that of the towns, villages and agricultural areas that remain inside the “Yellow Line.” Within the Israeli-occupied zone, which extends up to 6 miles into Lebanese territory, many villages have been entirely razed to the ground and restricted from entry, leaving hundreds of thousands of people still unable to return.
Just a few kilometers away, Zawtar al-Sharqiyah, the eastern part of Zawtar, was not included in the pilot zone and remains under Israeli control. Bombardments are a daily occurrence, as are the demolitions of homes by explosives and bulldozers. The constant hum of drones is a reminder that the occupying forces have not disappeared; they have merely moved a few kilometres away. Smoke rising after artillery strikes lays bare the gulf between the ceasefire proclaimed on paper and what continues to happen on the ground.
The proximity of the two areas makes the fragmentation of the territory particularly stark. While residents have begun returning to Zawtar al-Gharbiyah under Lebanese army control, Zawtar al-Sharqiyah remains on the other side of the line, under the control of Israeli forces.
According to the village mayor, by September around 100 families had returned to live in Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, out of roughly 500 who lived there before the war. But the destruction of homes is not the only obstacle to their return. As the pilot-zone agreement was taking shape, Israeli forces entered the village, demolishing and setting fire to additional homes and targeting what remained of essential infrastructure.
The mayor explained that the electricity network was destroyed, the water network severely damaged and the village well filled in, leaving Zawtar without running water or electricity. These conditions make the return of residents even more difficult and place tangible obstacles in the way of any meaningful reconstruction.
For the people of Zawtar, all of this has become part of a new normal: living with fear of what is to come and a continuous grief over what has been lost. It is a daily reality that sits uneasily alongside the language of diplomacy: while officials speak of a truce, southern Lebanon continues to come under attack.
Ihsan looks to the future with resignation.
“You can’t think about the future anymore,” she says. “We have to live day by day.”

Explainer-What do we know about flydubai flight 1073?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:03:37 UTC
04:03:37 KST

Explainer-What do we know about flydubai flight 1073?
LONDON, Oct 2 - Here is what we know, and don't know, about the reported attempt by the copilot of flydubai flight 1073 to crash the plane on September 30 before it landed safely in Saudi Arabia.
WHAT HAPPENED TO THE PLANE?
The flight, carrying more than 170 mostly Israeli passengers and crew, departed Dubai at 0305 GMT, according to flight data reviewed by Reuters.
At 0521 GMT in Saudi airspace it made a sudden, sharp turn and plunged towards the ground twice, before stabilising. The plane fell more than 16,000 feet in just over 30 seconds during its most dramatic dive.
It then put out distress signals indicating an emergency and unlawful interference. It changed course over Jordanian airspace and diverted to land in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
At one point the transponder was turned off for nearly half an hour, according to an Israeli official.
WHAT HAPPENED IN THE COCKPIT?
The copilot attacked and wounded the captain during the flight, the captain, Israeli and Saudi officials say.
During one of the plane's plunges, the wounded captain who was lying on the floor managed to open the door, he said, allowing passengers to enter the cockpit and overpower the copilot.
Israeli officials cite witnesses saying that the copilot was "bashing" the control panel, without elaborating. They say the copilot appeared to be trying to crash the plane.
One of the passengers managed to steady the plane after the copilot was subdued, which he knew how to do after watching an air-crash TV show, according to his own account.
A second pair of off-duty pilots on board then took the controls and landed, according to witnesses and Israeli officials.
Both the copilot and the captain suffered injuries, Saudi officials said. Videos from inside the cabin verified by Reuters show a wounded captain and copilot and blood apparently smeared on walls, and the copilot restrained by the passengers.
WHAT ISN'T CLEAR?
We don't know the exact timings of events on board, how the copilot overpowered the captain or what weapon he used. One passenger is heard in a video asking about a knife, and another talking about a stabbing.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has raised the possibility that a crash axe kept on board was used.
HOW CLOSE DID THE PLANE COME TO CRASHING?
At its steepest point, the plane was losing altitude at about 544 feet (166 metres) per second. Similar trajectories have resulted in several major crashes.
WHAT ROLE DID PASSENGERS PLAY?
One woman noticed a commotion in the cockpit when the captain opened the door and alerted the rest of the plane. At least four passengers rushed towards the cockpit, attacking and restraining the copilot.
The passenger who then steadied the plane before the off-duty pilots could take over said he first pulled the copilot away from the controls with the help of the other passengers.
Two other passengers attacked the copilot and tied him up using earphone cables, one of them said. A doctor on board treated the wounded captain.
WHY WERE THERE OTHER TRAINED PILOTS ON THE FLIGHT?
The two off-duty flydubai pilots were likely on board as backup for tired crew, a pilot interviewed by Reuters said. Middle East flights are often having to reroute because of the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran, the pilot said.
Flydubai said on Friday a full investigation was underway.
WHAT DO WE KNOW ABOUT THE COPILOT?
Israeli officials say the copilot is an Omani national and that he was trying to crash the plane.
Little else is known about his motives or identity. Omani authorities have not commented and there has been no comment from him or a representative.
After being treated for his injuries he was taken to Abu Dhabi, according to the Saudi interior ministry.
Netanyahu told Fox News that the copilot had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination", without providing details, and that he was suicidal. Israeli security officials have said he was likely acting alone, though investigation is ongoing.
Israel's ambassador to the United Arab Emirates has said no motive has been determined.
WAS IRAN OR ANOTHER COUNTRY INVOLVED?
Israeli security officials say Israel had not identified any Iranian involvement so far. Iran has not commented.
WHO IS HANDLING THE INVESTIGATION?
The United Arab Emirates has ordered an investigation. UAE judicial authorities have jurisdiction because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and flies under its flag.
Netanyahu said Israel, which has a close diplomatic and security relationship with the UAE, will be "possibly participating" in the investigation.
Saudi Arabia said it had conducted the preliminary investigation with security teams from the UAE.
HOW WAS THIS ALLOWED TO HAPPEN?
Pilots undergo background checks and regular psychological assessments, part of stringent measures in place since the 9/11 attacks in the United States in 2001.
Israel has strict screening for anyone travelling there. That includes not normally allowing in pilots from countries without diplomatic relationships with Israel, such as Oman. Netanyahu has said Israel will look at the "loophole" that allowed the copilot on board.
Israel is set to ramp up security checks on pilots flying into the country, Netanyahu's office said. REUTERS

2026 has been a record hot year for the U.S.—it can only get worse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:03:20 UTC
04:03:20 KST

It’s been a blistering year for the U.S. The first eight months of 2026 were the hottest such period ever recorded in the contiguous U.S. since at least 1895. That puts 2026 on track to being among the hottest years the country has ever seen—if not the hottest.
Whether or not this year takes the top slot in that bleak ranking is still unclear. But the outlook isn’t good, climate scientists say.
Right now where 2026 will clock in is a matter of probability. The hottest year the contiguous U.S. has ever recorded was in 2024, at 55.48 degrees Fahrenheit (about 13 degrees Celsius) on average, explains Zeke Hausfather, a climatologist and a lead author of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Seventh Assessment Report.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
We’re likely set to break that record, he says: January–August 2026 clocked in at 57.98 degrees F (14.43 degrees C) on average, 0.08 degrees F (about 0.04 degrees C) above the previous record of 57.90 degrees F (14.39 degrees C) for that period, which was set in 2012, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
If the U.S.’s temperature averages above around 50.5 degrees F (about 10.3 degrees C) this September through December, the country will break the record for its hottest year, Hausfather says. “That is a warm autumn but not an unusual one anymore,” he says.
In the last 10 years, the final four months of the year have averaged about 2.6 degrees F (about 1.4 degrees C) above the historical 20th-century average, Hausfather says. By his calculations, this fall only needs to hit 2.2 degrees F (about 1.2 degrees C) above average to be our hottest year. Data suggest September was anomalously warm.
“In other words, 2026 only needs a fairly typical recent-era finish to set the record,” Hausfather says, putting the odds at about 80 percent.
“It would take a cooler-than-normal autumn to keep it from happening," he says.
Other scientists are more cautious. When asked for comment by Scientific American, a NOAA spokesperson shared an early look at September’s temperatures and pointed to data showing that the agency expects above-normal temperatures across much of the continental U.S. from October through December. But neither source absolutely predicts whether 2026 will be a record-warm year, the spokesperson said, citing NOAA physical scientist Russell Vose.
Climate Central scientist Zachary Labe notes that forecasting the weather is complex and variable, which makes such predictions tricky. At this point in 2024, for instance, the year ranked as the second warmest, not the warmest, Labe says. Things could change.
What scientists do agree on, however, is that 2026 has been extremely—and concerningly—hot. “Average temperatures across the country continue to reach new record levels, which is consistent with the long-term warming driven by human-caused climate change,” Labe says.
“Whether 2026 ultimately ranks as number one or number three doesn’t distract from the bigger story that temperatures are rising across the country and leading to major impacts for communities,” he adds.
It seems “more than likely” that 2026 may turn out to be a record hot year for the U.S., says Kim Cobb, a climate scientist and a professor at Brown University. But even if it doesn’t, the country remains at high risk of “fossil-fueled extremes” such as heat waves and extraordinary rainfall.
“We do not need a record-breaking year for U.S. temperatures to know that fossil-fueled climate change is threatening our economy, our critical infrastructure, our health and our national security,” she says.
Then there’s next year. A brewing “Super El Niño” in the Pacific threatens to make 2027 even more destructive for the planet.
“Most climate scientists are looking at the projections for record-shattering global temperatures next year with a profound sense of dread—as hot as 2026 has been, and as horrific in terms of weather and climate extremes, 2027 looks like it could be a lot worse, according to our best projections,” Cobb says.

Charles, 77, who is still receiving treatment for cancer, will visit former colonies that are now independent from Britain and are members of the British Commonwealth.
He remains head of state in the archipelago nations of the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, a role that is largely ceremonial.
The palace spokesperson told reporters the king’s visit, from 27 October to 4 November, would not “shy away from the ‘darkest days of our past’, as His Majesty has described them”.
Charles used the phrase in a speech in Barbados when he attended the ceremony in which it became a republic in 2021, removing his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, as head of state.
He also said then that the “appalling atrocity of slavery” stains Britain’s history.
The palace said Charles had worked to acknowledge “the wrongs of the past” and “right inequalities that endure”, and on this trip would “renew his personal, wholehearted and continuing commitment to that process”.
The UK government reiterated last month its rejection of calls for the payment of slavery reparations after a Jamaican delegation filed a petition addressed to Charles on the issue.
It called on the monarch to refer three questions on the legality of the transatlantic slave trade to the Caribbean island’s highest court of appeal based in London.
Modern British royals have expressed remorse for the brutal slave trade that enriched their ancestors but like the UK government have not issued an official apology for the slave trade.
The palace said discussions about the colonial legacy and the slave trade were “important” but “primarily matters for governments to address”.
On a 2022 Caribbean tour, Charles’s son Prince William and his wife, Catherine, were met with anti-monarchy protests and calls for slavery reparations. Charles’s younger brother, Prince Edward, later that year cancelled a visit to Grenada after pro-republican protests there.
In Antigua and Barbuda, the royals will attend a parade to mark 45 years of independence.
Guyana, the only English-speaking country in South America, is a republic and Charles will make a state visit on the 60th anniversary of its independence from Britain.
The trip will feature plenty of meetings with local people and will focus on “the vibrant present and promising future of each country”, the palace said.
The programme includes meetings with cricketing legends in Antigua and Barbuda, where the West Indies team is based, and meeting conservationists responsible for Guyana’s rainforest.

'This is how we win': US counterterrorism chief on Iran, Hamas and Trump’s 'will to act'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
19:01:16 UTC
04:01:16 KST

Dr. Sebastian Gorka begins the conversation with a story he says illustrates US President Donald Trump’s approach to fighting terrorism.
“We were only eight days into the administration, and there was a very bad guy, a leader of ISIS, who was roaming free in a terrorist camp in northern Somalia,” says Gorka, the White House deputy assistant to the president and senior director for counterterrorism at the National Security Council.
“And the president is a very, very visual individual, like me. He likes pictures. And we created what we call in the community a ‘place mat,’ which is a large one-sheet diagram showing who this individual was, his role in killing Americans, where he was, and our capacity to strike and remove him.”
Gorka describes how he and other officials went into the Oval Office, placed the “place mat” in front of the president, and told him: “Sir, this ISIS leader has been tracked by our intelligence community for 18 months.
“He immediately looked up from the Resolute Desk and said to us, ‘What do you mean we’ve been tracking him? Kill him. Kill him now.’”
Since then, Gorka says, the United States has targeted 1,082 terrorists.
'Iran will imminently be resolved'
For Gorka, the common denominator in the fight against ISIS, the Muslim Brotherhood, Iran, and other terrorist hot spots around the world is simple: ideology, intelligence, and, above all, political will.
“Iran will imminently be resolved,” Gorka said in an interview with The Jerusalem Post, while declining to disclose details of the Trump administration’s plans.
He argued that understanding Trump’s intentions does not require access to classified intelligence.
“If you want to understand the president’s intent, you don’t need a top-secret clearance,” Gorka said. “All you have to do is get a Truth Social account and listen to what he puts on Truth Social. Listen to his press events.”
According to Gorka, the administration’s objectives toward Iran remain consistent with the demands Trump articulated in his correspondence with Iran’s leadership.
“What we wish to achieve in Iran is shaped by the president’s first letter a year ago to the then-ayatollah,” he said. “It was very explicit, and it was about nuclear weapons. It was about funding proxies. It was about everything they do in the region to destabilize that part of the world.
“Nothing has changed with regard to the president,” he added. “Now the decision lies with the mullah in Iran.”
For Israelis watching the possibility of another US-Iran confrontation – or another nuclear agreement – Gorka has a message: Do not underestimate Trump.
Asked about concerns that the president could eventually agree to a deal that falls short of his original demands, Gorka appeared almost incredulous.
“When I have Jewish conservative friends worrying that this president will somehow bring a watered-down deal that doesn’t comport with his demands from the beginning, it’s like, do you know who this man is?” Gorka said.
He pointed to Greenland as an example of what he considers the danger of assuming that Trump’s stated objectives are impossible to achieve.
“Everybody said, ‘Oh my gosh, outrageous or impossible,’” Gorka said. “Well, neither was it outrageous, nor was it impossible.
“So look, just watch the man and see what he has done,” Gorka said. “People need to calm down and look at the man who is behind the Resolute Desk and look at what he’s achieved.”
Gorka's responsibilities have also brought him into the effort to counter Iranian attempts to conduct operations on American soil.
Asked specifically about the attempt to target Yair Netanyahu, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s son, in the United States, Gorka declined to discuss the operation.
He described spending the first months of the administration visiting different agencies involved in counterterrorism, including the Joint Special Operations Command, the CIA, and the NSA.
According to Gorka, one message repeatedly emerged from those conversations: Officials wanted political leadership to demonstrate that it was prepared to act.
“All we want is to have will to act demonstrated by our leadership,” he recalled being told. “Will to act.”
If Iran represents one of the major strategic challenges Gorka sees facing the United States and its allies, the Muslim Brotherhood represents a deeper ideological battle.
Gorka has made the organization a central focus of his work, arguing that the Brotherhood is not simply another Islamist organization but the intellectual and ideological source from which numerous modern jihadist movements emerged.
“I think the reason I was propelled into the first Trump administration was in large part because of my first book, Defeating Jihad,” he said.
“I made it very clear in that book that every modern terrorist jihadi group, even the Shia, has a genetic code that goes back to the Muslim Brotherhood.
“The thinkers of the Muslim Brotherhood said that the only way to be a good Muslim is to be engaged in martial jihad, and that a new caliphate must engulf the Earth,” he said.
'I understood the cost of fascism'
Gorka’s worldview is also deeply personal.
He described how his father, Paul, was arrested and tortured by Hungary’s communist regime after being betrayed while studying at university. He was eventually given a life sentence before being liberated during the 1956 Hungarian Revolution and escaping to the West.
“My father was an anti-communist student,” Gorka said. “As a result, at the age of 20, my father, Paul, was arrested, tortured, and given a life sentence in a communist prison in Budapest.
“I understood the cost of fascism,” he said. “I understood the reality of the totalitarian communist ideology.”
Gorka said that experience eventually shaped his understanding of terrorism.
“It very quickly dawned on me that there is a connective tissue that binds Nazis to communists and to jihadists,” he said.
“In President Trump’s second term, we [began] designating the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist organization, starting with the Egyptian chapter, the Jordanian chapter, the Lebanese chapter, and since then we’ve designated numerous other chapters.”
“This is how we win,” he said.
“You cannot defeat the jihadi organizations like Hamas unless we destroy the progenitor, the grandfather of them all, which is the Muslim Brotherhood.”
The Trump administration subsequently issued an executive order initiating the process of designating certain Muslim Brotherhood chapters as Foreign Terrorist Organizations and Specially Designated Global Terrorists.
But the policy raises a difficult question for Israel: If Washington considers Brotherhood-linked organizations a security threat, what does that mean for countries such as Turkey and Qatar, which maintain close relationships with the United States while also maintaining relationships with the Brotherhood?
Gorka said the answer is not to designate countries.
“You can’t designate a country as a terrorist organization,” he said. “We have to do what is legal in US law.”
Gorka said he traveled to Ankara and described Qatar as an important partner in hostage negotiations and other sensitive cases.
“Qatar has multiple relationships with us on various issues,” he said. “They have been very helpful to me because counterterrorism, the directorate, includes hostages.”
He also stressed that Washington can simultaneously cooperate with a country on one issue while pressing it on another.
“It’s a constant discussion,” Gorka said. “There are issues that have to be resolved.
“But we are very clear-sighted, and we will continue to provide evidence where evidence is needed for whatever nation needs to help us to take the right decision.”
According to Gorka, Israel itself has provided valuable intelligence to the campaign.
“There are parts of the Israeli government, especially with regard to some materials that were discovered in the last three years, that have been incredibly helpful to us in providing primary evidence of organizations across the world that are part of the Brotherhood enterprise,” he said.
Next week, Israel will mark three years since the October 7 massacre. Asked what he, as an expert on terrorism, had learned from October 7, Gorka’s answer was not about Hamas’s operational capabilities. The shock, he said, was that Israeli decision-makers had adopted what he considers a flawed counterterrorism framework.
“The thing that shocked me is the decision-makers in Israel, or several of them, had, as we say, drunk the Kool-Aid of the Obama years’ counterterrorism analysis,” he said.
Gorka specifically attacked the theory that terrorism is fundamentally caused by poverty, lack of education, or political disenfranchisement.
“If poverty and political disenfranchisement were the root cause of terrorism, there’d be billions of terrorists around the world because of the poverty we have in various regions,” he said.
For Gorka, ideology comes first.
“You cannot have terrorism unless you have an ideologue that comes with an argument and says, ‘You are being oppressed for these reasons,’” he said.
He argued that Israel made a strategic mistake by treating Gaza and Hamas as essentially political problems.
“There was this decision somewhere inside Jerusalem that Hamas, Gaza, the West Bank isn’t a national security terrorist issue,” Gorka said.
They called it a political problem, to be solved by political issues, by money.
“No, you can’t,” he said. “If the person has an ideology, you have to address the ideology.”
Gorka argued that military action can remove individuals who pose an immediate threat, but that defeating terrorism requires a broader ideological campaign.
“You have to delegitimize the ideology,” he added, comparing that process to the ideological battles against Nazism and communism.
Throughout the conversation, Gorka repeatedly returned to his admiration for Trump’s personal style of leadership.
He recalled the assassination attempt against Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania, and said the president’s reaction illustrated what he calls “will to act.”
“Once there’s a threat to the president, by protocol the president, whoever he is, loses control of his body,” Gorka said.
But Trump, he recalled, pushed his security detail away.
“He knows somebody just tried to kill him. He doesn’t know who, but he knows the world is watching live. He needs to send a message right now to the world that everything’s okay.”
The conversation ended on another subject Gorka considers central to the current political moment: the revival of conservative intellectual movements.
Next week, Gorka will participate in the National Conservatism Conference (NatCon), held in Israel in cooperation with the Herzl Institute and the Edmund Burke Foundation in the United States. The conference is titled “National Conservatism as the Main Alternative to Liberalism.”
“What does the word conservative come from?” he asked. “It comes from the word ‘to conserve.’”
But, in Gorka’s interpretation, conservatives today face a paradox: They are attempting to preserve institutions and values they believe have already been weakened.
“That which they wish to conserve has been systematically dismantled,” he said. “So our job is not to conserve. Ours is to rediscover and rebirth those ancient values.”
This, he said, is why conferences such as NatCon have become important.
Gorka compared the current moment with the Reagan era, when conservative institutions developed an intellectual framework that eventually influenced American policy.
“That needs to be done now in a new context,” he said.
His argument is that the Trump movement is not simply a political phenomenon but part of a broader ideological realignment that requires its own intellectual infrastructure.
And that same philosophy runs through Gorka’s approach to counterterrorism.
Whether discussing Iran, the Muslim Brotherhood, October 7, or the future of conservatism, he returns to the same principle: Identify the ideology, understand the threat, and then demonstrate the political will to confront it.
