The New York Times obtains a purported Russian plan to cripple Ukraine’s power grid, including by cutting electricity and heat supplies to three major cities by 90%
Russia plans to disable Ukraine’s entire energy system. Ukrainian authorities have obtained a Russian Defense Ministry document outlining the plan, The New York Times reported. Ukrainian Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal showed it to two European politicians in late September, sources told the newspaper. The Times also obtained a copy of the Russian-language document but said its authenticity could not be verified.
The plan calls for a large-scale campaign using various types of missiles, guided aerial bombs, and drones, including jet-powered models. According to the document, Russia plans to carry out the campaign in three stages:
- First stage: Strikes on substations along Ukraine’s western border to prevent the country from importing electricity from Europe.
- Second stage: Strikes on hydroelectric power plants.
- Third stage: Strikes on substations that supply electricity to the three nuclear power plants still under Ukrainian control. Russian troops occupy Ukraine’s fourth nuclear power plant, the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant.
The campaign’s ultimate goal is to cut off electricity, heat, and water to major Ukrainian cities to provoke a humanitarian crisis.
The plan identifies Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa as the main targets. It calls for reducing electricity and heat supplies to these cities by 90% and disabling a substantial portion of their sewage systems.
The document indicates that Russia plans to eliminate nearly 15 gigawatts of generating capacity — almost as much as Ukraine had at the end of summer 2026, the Times reported.
In August, Shmyhal told Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, that the country would have 21 gigawatts of generating capacity by the end of the year. That would be enough to meet peak demand, which reached 18 gigawatts last winter. But Russia continues to strike Ukraine’s energy facilities, which could undo the country’s efforts to increase capacity ahead of winter, experts told the Times.
The war in photographs
On October 1, Russian forces deliberately struck a bridge across the Dnipro River in Kyiv for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russian drones attacked the bridge three times that day. On the morning of October 2, the Southern Bridge was closed to traffic, and traffic was restricted on the Paton Bridge and the Metro Bridge. Kyiv saw massive traffic jams.

Ukraine to Speed Up Identification of Fallen Soldiers as Over 26,000 Bodies Returned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:16:43 UTC
03:16:43 KST

Ukraine will set up an interagency group to speed up the identification of fallen soldiers, as a significant share of more than 26,000 repatriated bodies and remains returned to the country are still unidentified.
Head of the Presidential Office Kyrylo Budanov announced the plan on Friday, Oct. 2, after chairing a meeting of the Coordination Council on protecting the rights of war veterans and their families, as well as families of fallen defenders, prisoners of war (POWs) and missing persons.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Under the plan, authorities will review the work of forensic medical examination bureaus, particularly in the regions, and bring in additional international capacity for DNA testing.
“Why is identification proceeding so slowly, while families are forced to live in uncertainty for months and years?” Budanov said, adding that “bureaucratic delays and violations of regulations in the forensic examination system are unacceptable.”
‘A matter of state responsibility’
Budanov said the name of every soldier killed defending Ukraine must be established, calling it a matter of state responsibility.
The new interagency group will handle problematic cases related to the identification of the dead, he said. The government is expected to adopt all necessary regulatory decisions in the near future.
“Families must receive information about the fate of their loved ones as quickly as possible. Every fallen Hero will be found and honored with dignity,” Budanov said.
G7 Members Agree to Release Up to 100M Barrels of Oil Reserves to Curb Fuel Prices
He, however, did not specify how many of the repatriated bodies remain unidentified.
Explosives frequently found in repatriated bodies
The identification process is further slowed by safety and forensic challenges, stretching an already lengthy procedure even longer.
Explosive devices have been discovered several times in the bodies of Ukrainian soldiers repatriated from Russia, forcing investigators to carry out mandatory safety checks long before any identification work can start.
“We have found explosive objects, grenades and other things, so we work as carefully as possible,” Taras Tarasenko, a senior police investigator in the Kirovohrad region – where a large share of repatriated bodies are examined – told Ukrinform in June.
Once a body is cleared, specialists search for documents, phones, dog tags and bank cards, and photograph identifying features such as tattoos and clothing before forensic examination begins.
Tarasenko said batches of 200 to 250 bodies can arrive at once, while his team aims to examine about 10 a day to maintain the quality of its work.
The remains of several people are often found mixed in a single bag, requiring forensic experts to separate them before DNA analysis can match each person to their family.
Years of waiting
The Kirovohrad center for the search for missing persons and identification of unidentified servicemen was set up within the regional police in 2024 and employs 32 people, bringing together investigators, criminologists and cyber police.
According to Tarasenko, about 90% of the team’s time is centered on identification work.
A DNA match is possible only once both a family’s sample and the returned body’s profile are entered into the database, and years can pass between the two, according to Tarasenko.
He cited a soldier who went missing in 2023 and was identified only three years later, adding that some cases have remained unresolved since 2014.
Repatriation of bodies has continued alongside prisoner exchanges. Budanov has previously described the process as one of the few remaining areas where Kyiv and Moscow continue to cooperate as broader peace efforts stall – even with US mediation efforts in the recent weeks.
On Sept. 27, Budanov said a major prisoner exchange with Russia could take place as early as this current week, though he did not disclose its date or scale.
The last known return took place on Aug. 24, when Ukraine brought home 10 servicemen who had been listed as missing, according to RBC-Ukraine.
Several days earlier, on Aug. 19, Ukraine and Russia swapped 103 prisoners of war each.
Those returning to Ukraine included members of the Armed Forces, the State Border Guard Service and the National Guard, among them defenders of Mariupol and soldiers captured in several other regions.

Israel’s Supreme Court overturns election panel ban on Arab parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:11:37 UTC
03:11:37 KST

Israel’s Supreme Court overturns election panel ban on Arab parties
Court reinstates two Arab lists and Jewish Knesset member Ofer Cassif as Balad leader withdraws after pressure.
Israel’s top court has overturned an election panel’s ban on Arab parties contesting parliamentary elections this month, saying the decision had not met the legal requirements for excluding them, according to Israeli media.
The Supreme Court justices ruled unanimously on Friday to undo the Central Elections Committee’s disqualification of the country’s two main Arab-majority political lists – Ra’am, also called the United Arab List, and the Joint List, which is an alliance of Hadash, Ta’al and Balad.
The decision keeps Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population, in the race after critics accused the committee of double standards ahead of the October 27 Knesset vote.
The court also voted 7-2 to reinstate Ofer Cassif, a sitting Jewish member of the Knesset from the Arab-Jewish Hadash party and an outspoken critic of Israel’s treatment of Palestinians, media reports said.
The two dissenting justices said Cassif backs “armed struggle against the state of Israel”, which is grounds for his disqualification.
In September, the elections committee voted to disqualify the Joint List and Ra’am as parties, as well as Cassif and Sami Abu Shehadeh, head of the Balad party, as individuals.
Balad leader withdraws
The Supreme Court has nearly always overruled the committee when it votes to ban candidates.
However, at a hearing on Thursday, Supreme Court President Yitzhak Amit told Abu Shehadeh that a majority of the nine justices favoured disqualifying him from the election.
They gave him until Friday to withdraw, saying that if he did not, he would be disqualified, according to the Israeli Public Broadcasting Corporation.
Abu Shehadeh withdrew from the election after that.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right ally of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, led the push to bar him over an article written after the Hamas attacks on October 7, 2023. Abu Shehadeh described the attack as “an important historical event” in the piece, but denies supporting it.
Balad said in a statement that a court-ordered removal, rather than a voluntary one, would have had “grave consequences for the country’s political and parliamentary life” as it would set a precedent around the removal of Arab candidates.
Double standards
The Ra’am party made history after the 2021 election, becoming the first Arab party to join an Israeli government when it took part in a disparate coalition that briefly removed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from power. Most Palestinian citizens of Israel had stayed out of coalition politics until then.
In this election, Ra’am is also fielding a Jewish Zionist candidate for the first time, Yoav Segalovitz, who won popularity in Arab communities for his work to curb crime as deputy minister for internal security.
The election committee’s September vote drew accusations of a double standard, as Palestinian-led parties faced exclusion while parties led by far-right ministers, some of whom have been sanctioned internationally, stayed on the ballot.
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Friday, Abu Shehadeh said he withdrew because he “didn’t have any other choices”.
Although the Supreme Court has restored the Arab parties to the ballot, Abu Shehadeh said the reversal did not make the original disqualifications acceptable.
“In the end, what happened yesterday was a historical catastrophe for democracy, or the very narrow margins of democracy in the State of Israel,” he said. “I was disqualified because I think differently, because I have a different narrative on how to read history, the present, and the future in the place that we live today.”

LOEWE’s paris runway occupies an ethereal arena by casper mueller kneer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:10:07 UTC
03:10:07 KST

LOEWE’s paris runway occupies an ethereal arena by casper mueller kneer
guests watch the SS27 collection from above and across a circular runway built from white scaffold and sheer fabric.
architecture for looking
For Loewe’s Spring Summer 2027 show, the runway rises off the usual single plane. Inside a temporary white volume in the courtyard of Paris’ Château de Vincennes, Casper Mueller Kneer Architects has built a circular, two-story arena where guests look across, down, and through the space at one another. Models move along a runway that snakes between angular benches at ground level, while another band of viewers occupies the balcony above. Fashion becomes something seen from several heights at once.
The architecture borrows its basic geometry from places where an audience traditionally surrounds an event. The design team looked at the Anatomical Theatre in Padua and London’s Globe Theatre, among other historic references, before stripping the idea down to white scaffolding and translucent fabric. Detroit’s industrial gasometers also entered the reference pool, visible in the exposed framework that circles the room. The temporary construction feels almost diagrammatic: structure, audience, runway. Everything can be read at once.
the runway moves between the audience
In general, much of runway design depends on length. Loewe’s arena compresses the distance of a typical catwalk. The ground-floor benches zigzag across the center rather than forming long parallel rows, and leaves narrow routes for models to pass between them. From certain seats, the clothes move only a few feet away. From above, those same paths become part of a larger pattern.
Architect Casper Mueller Kneer describes proximity as central to the design. The circular plan gathers a large audience inside a relatively contained footprint, while the upper gallery introduces another line of sight into an event usually organized horizontally. A person watching from below may have another guest directly opposite and a second tier overhead. Faces, bodies, clothes, and bits of scaffold keep slipping into the same frame.
white scaffold forms the room
The material language for the SS27 runway stays deliberately spare. White scaffold forms the skeleton, with sheer white fabric drawn around it to establish the enclosure. There is little attempt to disguise how the temporary room stands up. Rails, posts, platforms, and stairs remain legible, giving the interior some of the directness of a studio theater assembled around a production.
The architecture itself takes on a prominent role here. The room establishes how the collection is encountered before the first model reaches the runway.
While runway audiences are usually given a privileged frontal view, the architecture here complicates that front. Other spectators become a part of your view, and looking becomes visible as an activity shared by the whole room. Instead of placing everyone along the edge of one line, the designers build an entire room around the act of watching.
project info:
name: Loewe SS27
architect: Casper Mueller Kneer Architects | @caspermuellerkneer
fashion house: Loewe | @loewe
creative directors: Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez
location: Château de Vincennes, Paris, France
year: 2026

21:08:44 EEST
03:08:44 KST

On September 29-30, the fifth Wild Drones military sports competition was held in Bukovina among the best unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) combat crews of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
Twenty teams participated in the competition: 17 teams from combat units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces and three teams from training centers that train UAV operators. Participants included representatives of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the National Guard of Ukraine, and the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine. Most of the service members arrived at the competition directly from combat zones. The training centers competed for the championship in a separate category.
This time, Wild Drones was held under strict secrecy with enhanced security measures.
Over the course of two days, participants competed in piloting Shrike FPV drones, Vampire (Baba Yaha) heavy bombers, and DJI Mavic quadcopters. The disciplines were based on the real combat experience of Ukrainian UAV operators and simulated the tasks that service members perform daily on the front lines.
The general partner of Wild Drones is the technology and defense company "SkyFall." To ensure fair competition, participants used identical unmanned systems manufactured by SkyFall – Shrike FPV drones and Vampire (Baba Yaha) heavy bombers. At the event, the partners unveiled the "Thor Hammer" middle-strike drone for the first time. The title partner of the competition is the Ukrainian unmanned systems manufacturer Vyriy Industries.
According to the organizers, one of the highlights of the fifth anniversary competition was the presentation of Wild Family – an ecosystem of military-sports projects that brings together the Wild Drones UAV operator competition, the Wild Race military-sports competition, as well as a new upcoming category – Wild Ground Robotic Systems – dedicated to ground-based robotic systems.
The competition is organized by the 93rd Separate Mechanized Brigade "Kholodny Yar," NGO Wild Race, the Dovzhyk training center, and Creative Agro Service LLC.
These competitions served as the second qualifying round of the 2026 Wild Drones season. Based on the results, ten more top teams of the season were selected. Next, the strongest participants from the qualifying rounds will face off in the finals, where the winners of the 2026 season will be determined.
In the FPV discipline, first place went to the 421st Separate Unmanned Systems Battalion of the Airborne Assault Forces, "Sapsan." The winners received three Vampire systems. Second place went to the Combat Hawks Unmanned Systems Battalion of the 25th Airborne Brigade. The team received two Vampire systems. Third place went to the 429th Separate "Achilles" Unmanned Systems Brigade. Their prize was one Vampire system.
First place in the team standings went to the 429th Separate "Achilles" Unmanned Systems Brigade. The team received a mobile UAV command post from Thor's Haven, as well as a UAH 800,000 grant from Chernivtsi Regional State Administration. Second place went to the fifth Border Guard Detachment "Prime." The team received a certificate for UAH 500,000 from Vyriy and a UAH 500,000 grant from the local military administration. Third place went to the 36th Separate Marine Brigade's "Vartovi" UAV Unit. The team received a certificate worth UAH 500,000 from one of the competition's partners, as well as a UAH 300,000 grant from the regional state administration.

Parliamentary government and political competition are the oldest traditions in Russian politics. Where did they come from, and why did they disappear? Writer Mikhail Zygar explains in a new film.
It’s hard to believe today, but Rus’ had a parliament before Britain did and a woman with the political stature of a prime minister five centuries before Margaret Thatcher. The Novgorod Republic was a state in which the prince was a hired manager, major decisions were made by the veche or popular assembly, and political culture resembled that of Western Europe in many ways. In his new film, Mikhail Zygar explains how this system emerged, why it lost out to Moscow, and why Vladimir Putin is so fond of Alexander Nevsky.

Amazon vows US$1 billion for data centre towns, decries ‘myths’
- Amazon pledges over US$1 billion for US communities hosting its data centres, funding education and energy-efficiency projects to gain local support amid AI-driven construction growth.
- The company commits to not raising local electricity bills, publishing annual energy and water use, and ending nondisclosure agreements with governments on data centre projects.
- Amazon warns that local moratoriums on data centres threaten US AI competitiveness, disputes myths about environmental harm, and accuses foreign misinformation campaigns of slowing construction.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO - Amazon on Oct 2 pledged more than US$1 billion (S$1.3 billion) over five years for US communities that host its data centres, the latest tech giant seeking to win over residents increasingly hostile to the AI-fuelled construction boom.
The “Built Together” programme, unveiled by Amazon Web Services chief Matt Garman in a 3,000-word blog post, will fund free community college degrees and trades training as well as energy-efficiency upgrades for schools and homes.
The company also announced a “Data Centre Commitment,” promising that its facilities will not drive up local electricity bills and that it will publish annual figures on energy and water use.
Garman said AWS would stop using nondisclosure agreements with government agencies on its projects, a practice that has become a major flashpoint for the movement opposing data centres.
Microsoft made a similar move in March, the first major tech firm to do so.
Garman cast the buildout as a national security imperative on par with the 1950s interstate highway system.
He warned that with more than 100 local moratoriums under consideration nationwide, the United States “could be writing its own losing ticket” in the AI race and that “the consequences would last generations.”
He also took aim at what he called myths about data centres, disputing as false arguments that they drive up power costs, deplete water supply and cause pollution from diesel fumes.
Citing “widespread reports,” Garman said some countries were deliberately seeding misinformation in the United States to slow construction – an argument also made by the Trump administration.
Disinformation researchers and fact-checkers say such claims overstate the role of foreign influence campaigns in a grassroots movement that spans the political spectrum and nearly every US state.
President Donald Trump, a vocal champion of the buildout, has warned that communities rejecting the facilities would “end up being backwards and poor.”
Amazon’s rivals have made similar overtures.
In January, Microsoft pledged to fully cover its data centres’ power costs and stop requesting local tax breaks, and OpenAI promised that its Stargate data centres would not raise local electricity prices.
In March, Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI signed a White House pledge to provide their own power for new data centres and pay for any grid upgrades they require. AFP

In Kuznets’s view, the proposed 17.1 trillion-ruble allocation for 2027 is an attempt to budget for war spending below the 2026 level.

Longitudinal study highlights the enduring toll of childhood loneliness and social isolation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:00:57 UTC
03:00:57 KST

A new study published in Development and Psychopathology indicates that experiencing loneliness during childhood does not help socially isolated youth reconnect with others later on. Instead, childhood loneliness and social isolation independently predict a range of mental health and socioeconomic difficulties in young adulthood. The findings challenge the idea that feeling lonely serves as a helpful biological alarm bell that pushes young people to repair their social bonds.
To understand the study, it helps to distinguish between two related concepts: social isolation and loneliness. Social isolation is the objective, physical reality of lacking positive social relationships and a support network. In childhood and adolescence, this often looks like social withdrawal and peer rejection. Loneliness, on the other hand, is the subjective, internal feeling of being dissatisfied with the quality or quantity of one’s relationships.
A person can be surrounded by peers but still feel lonely, or they can spend a lot of time by themselves without feeling lonely at all. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 found that teenagers who spend more time in physical solitude are not necessarily lonelier overall, highlighting the difference between temporary alone time and structural social isolation.
Past research has debated how these two social deficits influence one another. A 2013 paper proposed an evolutionary theory suggesting that loneliness acts as an adaptive warning signal, motivating individuals to seek out companionship and escape the dangers of isolation. At the same time, a 2018 study of middle-aged and older adults in Germany found that loneliness and social isolation interacted to predict mortality, with each amplifying the other’s effect.
The research team, led by Bridget T. Bryan and Louise Arseneault of King’s College London, wanted to directly test these competing ideas during the transition from childhood to adulthood.
“Although there is a large body of evidence that loneliness has negative consequences for health and wellbeing, some influential theories suggest that loneliness also serves a useful purpose by motivating socially isolated people to rebuild their social connections,” Bryan, a research fellow at King’s College London’s Social, Genetic & Developmental Psychiatry Centre, told PsyPost. “They argue that loneliness is a bit like hunger: an uncomfortable experience that signals to us that a basic need isn’t being met and motivates us to act on it. In this case, loneliness signals that we have unmet social needs, and pushes us to connect with others.”
“But few studies have tested whether this plays out in the long term, partly because loneliness and social isolation are rarely measured together,” Bryan said. To address this gap, the researchers designed a study to track whether loneliness actually helps isolated children reconnect over time, and whether facing both loneliness and isolation simultaneously creates a magnified penalty for a person’s future well-being. “We also wanted to better understand how loneliness and isolation work together and separately to shape a young person’s health, wellbeing, education and employment as they grow up,” she added.
To do this, the researchers used data from the Environmental Risk Longitudinal Twin Study, which follows 2,232 twins born in England and Wales in 1994 and 1995. The sample is nationally representative, covering a wide range of socioeconomic backgrounds, and consists of 49% male and 90% White participants. The team collected data on the participants at two key developmental stages: age 12 and age 18.
At age 12, the researchers gathered data on social isolation by asking mothers and teachers to rate the children’s social withdrawal and the extent to which they were rejected by peers. The 12-year-olds also filled out a questionnaire to self-report their own feelings of loneliness. At age 18, the participants self-reported both their loneliness and their level of social isolation, which was measured by asking about their access to supportive relationships with family and friends.
The team also assessed a wide array of life outcomes when the participants reached age 18. These included mental health indicators, such as depression and anxiety symptoms. They also measured general well-being, like life satisfaction and sleep quality, along with health behaviors such as smoking and alcohol use. Finally, they evaluated socioeconomic outcomes, tracking the participants’ educational achievements, employability, and whether they were currently out of school and out of work.
The researchers found that loneliness and social isolation feed into each other over time, rather than correcting one another. Children who felt lonely at age 12 tended to be more socially isolated at age 18, and this effect was about twice as strong as the reverse, where children who were socially isolated at age 12 reported higher levels of loneliness as young adults.
This does not support the evolutionary theory that loneliness acts as a helpful alarm bell. Isolated children who experienced high loneliness went on to experience high levels of social isolation as young adults, just like their peers who were isolated but not lonely. The distress of loneliness did not seem to help these youths successfully build or rebuild social connections over the six-year period. “Rather than assuming these children will find their own way through it, our findings suggest loneliness and social isolation may need to be tackled directly,” Bryan noted.
The study also evaluated how these two social deficits impact later life outcomes. Both loneliness and isolation at age 12 independently predicted poorer mental health, worse well-being, and lower socioeconomic standing at age 18. While most mental health links held even after accounting for childhood mental health and personality, childhood isolation’s link to depression and loneliness’s link to anxiety disappeared when these earlier factors were considered. However, childhood social isolation remained linked to every future socioeconomic outcome. “Each mattered in its own right, not just because they tend to occur together,” Bryan explained.
The impact on a participant’s future career prospects proved especially dramatic. “Social isolation was particularly important for education and employment outcomes – more socially isolated secondary school students went on to have fewer qualifications and be less employable in young adulthood than their less isolated peers,” the researcher continued. “The risk of becoming NEET (not in education, employment or training) was particularly striking: the most isolated children had around 2.4 times the odds of being NEET at 18, compared with their peers.”
Interestingly, the researchers did not find evidence of a compounded penalty. Young people who were both highly lonely and highly isolated struggled with similar levels of mental health and socioeconomic difficulties as those who experienced only one of the issues. For well-being and socioeconomic outcomes, the authors described this as a potential ceiling effect. For children who reported the highest levels of loneliness, being socially isolated did not add much extra damage to their well-being or socioeconomic outcomes, possibly because those outcomes were already heavily affected, or because loneliness and isolation work through similar pathways.
Despite this ceiling effect, the sheer impact of isolation alone stood out to the research team. “What surprised us most was the strength of the association between social isolation and poor education and employment outcomes,” Bryan said. “We didn’t expect it to be quite this strong – two to three times stronger than for other well-established risk factors, like childhood depression or anxiety.”
This finding highlights a potential blind spot in how society addresses youth employment. “Given how much public and policy attention youth employment is getting right now, it was striking to find social isolation playing such a large role, when most current strategies focus on skills and job opportunities instead,” she added.
These long-term impacts on mental health are in line with research covered by PsyPost previously. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 tracked youth into adulthood and found that adolescent loneliness predicted a higher risk for depression and stress-related conditions. In a similar vein, a meta-analysis covered by PsyPost in 2022 highlighted a steady link between youth loneliness and depressive symptoms across different ages and genders. However, while that review measured depressive symptoms at a single point in time, the new study tracked broader mental health longitudinally into young adulthood.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study measured loneliness and social isolation only at two points in time, separated by six years. This large gap makes it impossible to know if short, temporary bursts of loneliness might act differently than long-term, persistent loneliness. The evolutionary theory suggests that mild, fleeting loneliness might prompt social connection, but this study could not track daily or weekly fluctuations.
The researchers also used different measurement tools at age 12 compared to age 18. This was done to ensure the questions were appropriate for the participants’ changing developmental stages, but it makes it slightly harder to compare their social experiences directly across time.
There are a few things to keep in mind regarding the study sample. Because all participants are twins, their social experiences might look slightly different from those of single children. Twins grow up with a sibling of the exact same age, which could influence how they interact with peers and experience feelings of isolation or companionship.
Going forward, the team hopes to identify the mechanisms that prevent lonely youth from rebuilding their networks. “We’d like to better understand why loneliness doesn’t seem to help isolated children reconnect – for example, whether this is because they withdraw rather than reach out, or because other difficulties that often go along with loneliness (like social difficulties or anxiety) make attempts to reconnect less successful,” Bryan said.
The researchers also want to expand their timeline. “It would also be important to look at how loneliness and isolation relate to each other across different stages of life,” Bryan noted. “Our study focused on childhood and adolescence, but loneliness and social isolation matter at all stages of life.”
The study, “Investigating the interplay of loneliness and social isolation across adolescence: Findings from a nationally representative longitudinal study,” was authored by Bridget T. Bryan, Katherine N. Thompson, Helen L. Fisher, Timothy Matthews, Barry Milne, and Louise Arseneault.

Ukrainian Grandmother Flew to Kazakhstan to Bring Her Grandson Home—And Was Detained on Russia’s Request
Kazakh authorities detained Ukrainian citizen Liubov Rozhanska after she flew to Astana expecting to collect her grandson and bring him back to his family in Ukraine—only to discover at passport control that Russia wanted her detained over an alleged attempt to abduct the same child.
Rozhanska was taken into custody at Astana airport on October 1 after arriving from Istanbul, her attorneys told Deutsche Welle on October 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
She is currently being held in a detention center in the Kazakh capital, with a court hearing expected within days.
The case stems from a years-long custody dispute involving Rozhanska’s grandson.
In 2021, the boy’s mother, Alla Andreeva, took him from Odesa to Russia’s Kaliningrad region, where relatives of her second husband live. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Andreeva applied in March 2022 to renounce Ukrainian citizenship for herself and her son and later obtained Russian citizenship for both.
Meanwhile, the boy’s Ukrainian father challenged the situation in court. In March 2025, Ukraine’s Supreme Court ruled that the child should live with his father in Odesa.
More than a year later, in July 2026, Andreeva’s current husband, Vitaly Andreev, and his father, Vyacheslav Andreev, contacted Rozhanska and offered to hand the child over to her and his Ukrainian father, according to her attorney, with Astana supposed to be the meeting point.
But by then, Russian authorities had already been pursuing Rozhanska.
A criminal case had been opened against her in Russia in 2023 over an alleged attempted kidnapping of the child.
In late August 2026, a Kaliningrad court ordered her pretrial detention, while Russian authorities prepared paperwork to have her placed on a wanted list and extradited through the Collective Security Treaty Organization, according to documents reviewed by DW.
Rozhanska’s attorneys say she knew nothing about the Russian criminal case or detention order. One of her Kazakh lawyers told DW that she had never even entered Russia.
When Rozhanska arrived in Astana on October 1, Kazakh border authorities detained her on the basis of the Russian request.
Her attorney, Alexei Pryanishnikov, believes the circumstances raise questions over whether the planned transfer of the child and Rozhanska’s subsequent trip to Kazakhstan were used to draw her into a jurisdiction where Russia could seek her detention.
He described the arrest as “a fairly clearly planned operation” by Russia’s FSB and suggested it may have been driven by a “desire to curry favor and improve clearance statistics.”
Earlier, the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed more than 20,000 cases of the unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children done by Russia.

Debt-laden Argentina puts citizenship up for sale to wealthy foreigners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:00:40 UTC
03:00:40 KST

Argentina has announced plans to offer citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for cash contributions or investments in government bonds, as libertarian President Javier Milei seeks new sources of dollars for the debt-burdened nation.
Economy Minister Luis Caputo unveiled the so-called "golden passport" scheme at an investor event in Paris, saying applications are expected to open before the end of the year.
Applicants have two options: make a nonrefundable $350,000 contribution to the Argentine Treasury or invest $800,000 in a new government bond that must be held for seven years.
Contributions would increase depending on family size, with a family of four expected to pay $500,000, officials said.
Securing dollars is critical for Milei as he prepares to seek reelection next year. Argentina’s Treasury faces nearly $25 billion in foreign-currency debt payments coming due in 2027.
But having narrowed its financing options by holding off on a return to international bond markets, the government is searching for alternative sources of revenue.
A consortium of investment firms advising the government estimated that the paid-citizenship programme could raise up to $2.5 billion for Argentina if it receives the expected number of applicants.
US President Donald Trump launched his own "gold card" programme for the US last year.
Citizenship-for-investment programs go further, offering more rights and a passport that opens doors abroad. Only about a dozen countries have active programs, including small Caribbean island states.
Argentina, a G-20 nation of 46 million people home to a vast Patagonian wilderness and culturally vibrant capital, is set to become the first South American country to join their ranks.
"The Argentine passport is highly valued, accepted in more than 140 countries," Caputo said, referring to destinations Argentines can visit without obtaining a visa in advance — from China and Russia to Europe’s Schengen area and most of Latin America.
For wealthy people from countries that face visa restrictions, Argentine citizenship could make it easier to travel and do business internationally, said Kristin Surak, a professor at the London School of Economics and author of "The Golden Passport: Global Mobility for Millionaires."
"It’s not only the benefits that you get within Argentina," she said. "You also get benefits globally in terms of where you can go."
A second passport as a Plan B
The clientele of such programmes has shifted since the Covid-19 pandemic, industry experts say, with more Americans and Europeans — whose passports already offer extensive visa-free travel — seeking a foothold abroad as an escape hatch at a time of mounting geopolitical uncertainty.
"The Southern Cone of South America is the ultimate Plan B destination. It’s not on the way to anywhere strategically important. It’s a region that’s always staying out of global armed conflict," said Christian Nesheim, editor of Investment Migration Insider, a trade journal. "It’s self-sufficient when it comes to food, to energy."
Argentina, with a history of military coups, debt defaults and runaway inflation that long sent its own business elite seeking opportunities abroad might seem an unlikely refuge for investors chasing stability.
But Milei is trying to recast Argentina as a destination for foreign wealth, slashing public spending, dismantling regulations and courting investment in the country’s vast oil and mineral resources.
Caputo said the idea for the citizenship-for-investment programme emerged during Milei’s July 2024 visit to Sun Valley, Idaho, when tech executives expressed interest in obtaining Argentine citizenship.
A self-proclaimed "anarcho-capitalist," Milei has cultivated close ties with libertarian-minded tech billionaires such as Elon Musk, a vocal supporter of Milei's drive to shrink government.
Last year, he brandished a chainsaw gifted by the Argentine leader as a symbol of his own campaign to slash US government spending.
Vulnerability to corruption
Another ideological ally is Peter Thiel, a co-founder of software firm Palantir who temporarily moved his family to Buenos Aires in April.
Corporate records obtained by The Associated Press show that a company linked to his investment firm, Thiel Capital, owns a $13.5 million mansion in the city’s upscale Barrio Parque neighbourhood.
Thiel also secured New Zealand citizenship in 2011, receiving a special exemption from the usual residency requirements.
"I think that this 'Peter Thiel in Argentina' story is maybe a bit of a proof of concept (for the citizenship programme)," said Philippe Amarante, managing partner and head of government advisory at Henley & Partners, a consultancy that helps clients obtain passports around the globe.
"He stands for this idea that independent, wealthy, successful people do have choices around the world. And if you provide the right environments and right habitats, the right ecosystem, they might choose you."
Caputo vowed to prevent pitfalls, with intelligence and financial oversight agencies helping to vet applicants’ identities, criminal records and sources of funds.
The aim, he said, is to protect "the international standing of Argentine citizenship."

Orbán Could Face Charges Over Seizure of Ukraine’s €70 Million Cash and Gold Shipment
Hungarian authorities are investigating whether former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán personally ordered the seizure of a vehicle carrying €70 million in cash and gold belonging to Ukraine’s state-owned Oschadbank, a case that could potentially lead to formal charges against him, Financial Times reported on October 2.
The investigation comes after Hungary’s new government secured a constitutional majority in April’s elections and launched a campaign dubbed “Operation Cleansing Fire,” aimed at dismantling the political and corruption system it says developed during Orbán’s 16 years in power.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The case centers on a March operation in which Hungary’s counter-terrorism unit seized a vehicle transporting cash and gold worth approximately €70 million. The shipment was part of a regular transfer from Vienna carried out by cash couriers working for Oschadbank.
At the time, Orbán accused Kyiv of secretly financing the Hungarian opposition. The Ukrainian couriers were detained and reportedly kept handcuffed and blindfolded for several hours, including during questioning, before being released the following day. The seized funds were subsequently returned to Ukraine.
Investigators are now examining suspicions that Orbán personally ordered the vehicle to be seized in an attempt to use the incident for his own interests.
Lóránt Horváth, a lawyer representing the Ukrainian nationals, said the investigation was approaching completion and could become the first case to result in formal charges against Orbán. He noted that other corruption investigations involving the former prime minister remain at considerably earlier stages, according to the Financial Times.
Horváth also represents former prosecutor Pál Fürcht, who was assigned in March to handle the case against the Ukrainians. Fürcht alleged that Orbán personally instructed the security services to detain the Ukrainian cash couriers. According to Fürcht, he informed his superiors of this in the spring but was reprimanded and later became the subject of an internal investigation.
His account is supported by a June prosecution report reviewed by the Financial Times. The document cited János Hajdú, head of Hungary’s Counter Terrorism Centre (TEK), as indicating that those involved understood the arrests had been ordered by an individual who could not be implicated in the case. According to the report, the person in question was Orbán.
Hajdú now faces charges related to the alleged unlawful detention and mistreatment of Oschadbank employees.
Orbán also visited TEK on the day of the arrests, where he spoke about an increased terrorist threat. Official photographs from the visit showed him alongside some of the officials who later participated in the operation against the Ukrainian couriers.
Hungary’s tax authority opened a case against the Ukrainians while Orbán was still in office, but the investigation was subsequently closed due to a lack of evidence. Horváth said the absence of evidence against the couriers meant prosecutors should now focus on determining who ultimately ordered the operation, pointing to Orbán as the person investigators should scrutinize.
The case is unfolding amid a broader series of investigations involving former members of Orbán’s government and associates. In recent weeks, authorities arrested two former ministers and members of his Fidesz party after parliament stripped them of parliamentary immunity. Several business figures close to the former prime minister have also been detained.
Former central bank governor and economy minister György Matolcsy, whom Orbán had described as his right-hand man, has been questioned in an investigation into alleged abuse of office. Matolcsy’s son is separately under investigation in connection with alleged corruption at the central bank.
According to the Financial Times, Eurasia Group analyst Orsolya Ráczová said the accumulation of corruption scandals and investigations had reached a point where scrutiny of Orbán’s personal responsibility was becoming increasingly difficult to avoid.
The investigation follows heightened tensions with Brussels over Hungary’s detention of the Ukrainian couriers, who were transporting funds from Austria’s Raiffeisen Bank to Ukraine. The incident also prompted banking lobbyists to call for Orbán’s government to be barred from cooperating with key EU financial institutions.

Kyiv's other main bridges across the Dnipro River, the Darnytskyi Bridge, Metro Bridge, and Podilskyi Bridge, have been changed to single direction traffic, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMDA).
Kostiantyn Kryvolap, an aviation expert and former Antonov test engineer, told the Kyiv Independent that destruction of the bridge is most likely not the intent behind Russia's strikes.
"Destroying a bridge with a 50-kilogram explosive charge, even with a highly effective warhead designed to destroy steel bridge structures, is a major exaggeration. It is practically impossible. For a bridge like this, these strikes are more like mosquito bites," he said.
Instead, the idea behind the Russian strikes may rather be to halt traffic, interrupt logistics, and exert psychological pressure on Kyiv's population, according to him.
The Southern Bridge is one of the capital's main traffic arteries and connects important transport routes like the the M-05 Kyiv-Odesa, M-06 Kyiv-Chop, and M-03 Kyiv-Kharkiv-Izyum-Sloviansk highways. Every day, between 100,000 and 110,000 cars use the bridge, according to information from the Darnytskyi District administration from 2019.
Head of the Desnyanskyi district of Kyiv, Maksym Bakhmatov, told The Village in a 2020 interview that about 90% of transit traffic between the two banks passes through the Southern Bridge.
Hlib Vyshlinsky, executive director of the Center for Economic Strategy told the Kyiv Independent that the Southern Bridge is also crucial for the daily commute of the Pozniaky-Osokorky-Kharkivsky districts conglomeration that houses up to 500,000 people.

Why Lilly and Novo are betting on amylin to power a new wave of obesity drugs after GLP-1s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
17:55:26 UTC
02:55:26 KST

The next generation of blockbuster obesity drugs isn't trying to replace GLP-1 medicines.
Instead, drugmakers are developing treatments that can complement existing drugs and push weight loss further, or offer new options for potentially millions of people who may not get enough benefit from GLP-1s.
That's the early potential of a new slate of injections, pills, and combination regimens targeting the amylin pathway, which involves a hormone released in the pancreas alongside insulin that helps regulate hunger and fullness. Amylin gives Eli Lilly, Novo and several other companies another biological lever to pull in treating obesity and Type 2 diabetes, either as an independent treatment or layered on top of existing drugs.
Lilly offered a promising glimpse of that strategy this week.
The company's experimental amylin-targeting drug, eloralintide, helped produce substantially more weight loss when combined with tirzepatide – the active ingredient in its blockbuster Zepbound and Mounjaro shots – in a Phase 2 trial on patients with obesity and Type 2 diabetes.
At 48 weeks, people receiving the highest-dose combination lost an average of 23.3% of their body weight, compared with 14.8% among those only taking a high dose of tirzepatide. Those figures are based on efficacy analysis that assumes patients remained on treatment in the trial.
"These are encouraging results," said Benjamin Bikman, a professor at Brigham Young University and leading expert on metabolic health and insulin resistance. "Adults with type 2 diabetes typically lose less weight on these therapies than those without diabetes."
Lilly is developing eloralintide both as a standalone treatment and as part of that combo therapy. The two components make up what some analysts view as a major future franchise for the company.
Leerink Partners analyst David Risinger forecasts $23.2 billion in annual sales for Lilly's eloralintide products by the end of 2035. He said he expects the standalone drug to launch first in 2029, followed by the combo in 2030.
"There are millions of individuals, potentially over 10 million people, who have tried GLP-1s and failed due to efficacy reasons, tolerability issues, or genetic issues where they simply do not respond to one," Risinger told CNBC. "We think this novel mechanism, this amylin analog … will offer a major new treatment alternative for patients, both as a monotherapy and as a combination therapy. "
Risinger said he sees greater potential for standalone eloralintide given the "huge independent patient pool" that hasn't seen success on existing GLP-1s. Lilly still sees a clear opportunity for pairing the medications.
"Patients may not get what they need from a drug like tirzepatide," Ken Custer, president of Lilly Cardiometabolic Health, said in an interview. "They may not get what they need from a drug like a eloralintide on its own."
Bikman also said he sees the combo as an opportunity for patients who started on tirzepatide alone but saw their weight loss plateau.
But Lilly still has a lot to prove. The data comes from a relatively small Phase 2 study that the company will need to confirm in Phase 3 trials, which will begin later this year.
Lilly also aims to improve how well patients tolerate the combo regimen in later studies. More patients taking both drugs — 10.8% to 27%, depending on the dose — discontinued treatment due to side effects, compared with the 2.9% of people on tirzepatide alone in the trial.
"A therapy is only effective if patients can remain on it, so tolerability in Phase 3 will be as important as efficacy," Bikman said.
Dr. Caroline Apovian, co-director of the Center for Weight Management and Wellness at Brigham and Women's Hospital, added that "27% is not a good number."
Still, the results add to a growing body of evidence that amylin could become an important tool against obesity and diabetes.
Lilly isn't alone in betting that amylin can become a building block for the next generation of obesity drugs. Novo has spent years pursuing a similar strategy.
Novo's experimental amylin-based drug, cagrilintide, has shown meaningful weight loss as a standalone treatment in a late-stage trial. Combining it with semaglutide – together dubbed CagriSema – has produced even greater weight loss in clinical studies. CagriSema is expected to launch early next year, followed by standalone cagrilintide and a higher-dose version of CagriSema in 2028.
Novo is also developing another treatment called amycretin, or zenagamtide, which is a single molecule that would target both GLP-1 and amylin to treat obesity and Type 2 diabetes. The Danish drugmaker is testing it as a once-weekly injection and a daily oral tablet, and the drug showed promising Phase 2 results earlier this year.
Several companies, including Pfizer, AstraZeneca and Viking Therapeutics, are developing their own amylin products, as well.
Amylin vs. GLP-1
The first – and so far only – amylin therapy was approved in the U.S. more than two decades ago as an add-on mealtime injection for people with diabetes who use insulin. But adoption was limited in part because it required multiple injections a day.
New therapies in development are long-acting, meaning they are designed to mimic the hormone in a sustained way and can be taken once a week, Bikman said.
Amylin helps signal fullness, suppress appetite and slow the movement of food through the stomach, similar to what GLP-1 does. But amylin achieves that by acting on an entirely different biological pathway.
"It's the same outcome, but a different approach," Bikman told CNBC.
The idea is that targeting multiple pathways could produce more weight loss or other metabolic benefits than any single pathway can achieve on its own, and without relying entirely on higher doses of a single drug.
New data from Novo this week suggests that the benefits could go beyond physical changes.
CagriSema reduced "food noise" — persistent thoughts about food — and showed improvements to organ and bone health in a yearlong functional magnetic resonance imaging study, which is a noninvasive method to measure brain activity during specific tasks. Novo said CagriSema changed how the brain reacted to tempting, high-calorie foods in areas linked to cravings, pleasure and self-control in people with obesity or who were overweight.
"The signal in the brain changes in a way that actually is associated with improved quality of life," Martin Holst Lange, Novo's chief scientific officer, said in an interview.
Developing treatments that target several hormone pathways rather than one is part of a broader shift in the obesity drug race, even beyond amylin.
Tirzepatide already pairs GLP-1 with GIP, while Lilly's experimental drug retatrutide also adds glucagon to the mix. Retatrutide has produced some of the largest weight loss results reported in obesity drug trials to date, and Bikman said published data on the drug demonstrate substantial reductions in liver fat, triglycerides and fasting insulin.
It's too early to definitively say whether combination amylin drugs could be superior to tirzepatide or other next-generation treatments. They'll have to clear more clinical trials and regulatory reviews first.
But all the medicines in development are working toward a broader goal shared by several drugmakers: giving patients a variety of obesity and diabetes treatment options to meet their individualized needs.

Russian political researcher Alexander Finiarel has lived in Spain without papers for two years. But soon he (and half a million other refugees) will be able to get documents. This is his story.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
17:54:01 UTC
02:54:01 KST

Russian political researcher Alexander Finiarel has lived in Spain without papers for two years. But soon he (and half a million other refugees) will be able to get documents. This is his story.
In 2026, Spain is granting legal status to large numbers of undocumented migrants. The authorities initially planned to grant status to about 500,000 people, but nearly 1.2 million applied. Russian political researcher and journalist Alexander Finiarel is among those seeking legal status in Spain. He has lived there without it for two years and closely follows migration policy in Europe’s most attractive destination for migrants. At Meduza’s request, Finiarel explains how undocumented migrants live in Spain, what Spaniards think about migration, and how the mass legalization process works from the inside.
How I became an undocumented immigrant
When I moved to Spain, I had no intention of becoming an undocumented immigrant. Two years ago, they brought me and 64 other Russian journalists, activists, and human rights defenders here from Georgia, which was getting more and more dangerous. The plan was for 206 people to come here, and we were supposed to receive humanitarian residence permits on arrival.
But after the first group arrived, the agreement with Spain’s Foreign Ministry fell apart. More than a hundred people awaiting evacuation were stranded in Georgia, while those who had made it to Spain were left without papers or a clear legal status.
My boyfriend and I also had the option of applying for asylum. Since the Russian authorities declared the “LGBT movement” “extremist,” Spain has been accepting Russian LGBTQ refugees fairly readily, judging by the experiences of people I know and members of local refugee group chats. So Spain is probably one of the best options for this group. Applying for asylum on the grounds of political persecution was also fairly straightforward, and many people in our group ended up doing just that.
For the first six months, though, we kept hoping the negotiations with the Foreign Ministry would get somewhere. Besides, Spain’s asylum system is severely overloaded, both by the influx of refugees and by “appointment scalpers.”
Who are “appointment scalpers”?
A cita, Spanish for “meeting,” is an appointment. Because appointment slots are limited, they’re booked online or by phone (almost everything here gets done over the phone). Demand is high, especially in big cities, so a black market has emerged in Spain.
Companies have sprung up that build bots to monitor appointment calendars, grab slots as soon as they become available, and then sell them for hundreds of euros. As a result, getting an asylum appointment on your own is practically impossible, especially in Madrid, which accounts for 30% of all applications. You either have to spend whole days calling the immigration service or try to get an appointment in a less populated region. But then you’ll have to travel there for every step of the asylum application process.
Finally, my work requires me to travel within the EU to meet European officials and other Russian human rights advocates. As an applicant for international protection, however, you cannot leave the country where you’ve requested protection. In Spain, it usually takes about two and a half years to get approval.
Without applying for asylum, I can travel around Europe.
How does that work?
The organization that brought me from Georgia helped me get a five-year tourist visa to enter Spain. Although I’m technically violating the rules governing my stay, the visa allows me to travel around Europe without trouble. Legally, this type of visa allows you to spend no more than 90 days in the EU in any six-month period. But in my experience, no one checks how many days you’ve spent there.
A colleague of mine, also a human rights advocate, had a short-term visa instead. So when we encountered a spot check at Brussels Airport during a work trip in February 2025, I was allowed through, but he was detained because his visa had expired. The organization that brought us to Spain had to negotiate with the border guards to prevent his deportation. He’s been stuck in Spain ever since that trip. Still, that was the only time I’ve encountered checks when crossing borders.
Although refugees can obtain citizenship after just five years in Spain, many of us who moved from Georgia chose a different route to legal status: a residence permit based on our ties to Spain. That meant becoming undocumented immigrants.
In Spain, migrants can obtain a residence permit on this basis after two years of continuous residence, provided they haven’t applied for asylum during that period and have no criminal convictions. Applicants simply have to show that they’re already trying to integrate into Spanish society — for example, by working, studying, taking Spanish classes, having family ties, or volunteering with local nonprofits.
We got lucky: a year and a half after we arrived, the Spanish authorities announced an extraordinary legalization program. It doesn’t even require proof of integration.
The challenges undocumented migrants face in Spain — and the advantages of having no legal status
Living without legal status does, of course, come with restrictions and difficulties. The biggest is finding housing. Spain’s population has grown in recent decades because of a large influx of migrants, but all those newcomers head for Madrid and the coasts. These areas also draw people from the rest of the country. Those other parts of Spain have even acquired the nickname “España vaciada” (“emptied Spain”).
As a result, demand has overwhelmed the housing markets in Madrid and on the coasts, and landlords have become extremely selective. In most cases, they choose from several applicants and naturally prefer people whose papers are in order.
Making matters worse, Spanish law protects tenants so strongly that evicting them is practically impossible, even if they stop paying rent. This has given rise to “okupas” — people who either squat in someone else’s home while it’s empty or stop paying rent and refuse to move out.
Landlords, in turn, have started buying insurance to protect themselves against okupas. Companies offering this insurance check prospective tenants’ income. But without legal status, you can’t earn income on the books or pay taxes, so we had nothing to show them.
The easiest way to avoid these checks is to sublet a room. But that wouldn’t work for my boyfriend and me: we both work from home and are constantly on work calls. We didn’t want our calls to disturb anyone, or anyone to disturb us.
So we took the more difficult route: we looked for apartments listed by their owners on Spain’s main property website, contacted them directly, and tried to charm them during apartment showings. Like everyone who moved here at the same time as us, we found housing largely because we managed to win over our landlords. But the search took several months.
I studied Spanish in college, and although I hadn’t practiced for many years, I could speak it reasonably well. That helped. Without knowing the language, we would have had to pay a real estate agent extra to act as an interpreter.
We gave the landlords our work contracts and bank statements. Through friends, we found someone with officially declared income in Spain who agreed to be our guarantor and cover the rent if we couldn’t.
A lease lets you register your address immediately, giving you access to most public services. In Spain, for example, even migrants without residence permits have the right to use the public healthcare system and send their children to school. Unlike people living here legally, though, we don’t pay taxes or social security contributions for these services, because we’re simply off the tax authorities’ radar.
After finding housing, the next problem is opening a bank account. Of course, you can have money paid into foreign bank accounts. But without a Spanish card, you can’t make recurring payments for utilities, internet, phone service, private health insurance, or a gym membership.
I solved this problem by opening an account with the online bank Nickel, which lets you sign up using a passport. But the EU’s 19th sanctions package against Russia closed off that option. Under the new requirements, European banks must restrict services to Russian and Belarusian citizens who don’t have residence permits in the European Economic Area or Switzerland.
Russian refugees with legal status have also been affected. Local banks have become wary of opening accounts for them, and Nickel now requires Russians to have an EU residence permit. Still, people who opened accounts earlier continue to use them, promising to provide their papers once they’ve obtained legal status.
Finding work is another difficulty. Migrants without legal status have no right to work in Spain. Even so, employers hiring for low-skilled jobs in food service or cleaning are often willing to turn a blind eye. But they frequently exploit workers’ precarious status, for example by making them work 11 hours a day, six days a week, for less than the legal minimum wage.
How Spanish society views undocumented migrants
Spain’s laws give people without legal status a fair amount of leeway. Having worked for Russian opposition media and organizations under various legal statuses for a long time, I’m used to operating in a legal gray area, and Spain feels like one of the easiest countries to live in this way.
During my time here, I’ve never encountered hostility because of my undocumented status, even in government offices. Most local services apparently don’t consider it their job to track down undocumented migrants.
Even so, migration is one of the most contentious issues in Spanish politics. The far-right party Vox (“Voice”), which is gaining support, makes fighting illegal immigration a central part of its platform. Polls suggest that it will win next year’s parliamentary election in a coalition with the center-right People’s Party (Partido Popular). But as often happens, they could make both legal and illegal immigration harder: the People’s Party is already proposing new barriers to immigrating to Spain and obtaining permanent residency.
That’s why I don’t share many Russian immigrants’ enthusiasm for these parties, although I do think Spain may need to limit migration until it resolves its housing crisis. For me and for Russians living here legally, a right-wing government would mean more bureaucratic red tape.
Spanish society as a whole is clearly growing tired of newcomers, whether they’re undocumented immigrants, tourists, digital nomads, or British and German retirees. Tourism sparks frequent protests across the country. My Spanish acquaintances also complain about tourists, and especially about expats who don’t learn the language and expect everyone to speak English with them. The main reason for this growing resentment is simple: soaring housing costs.
Migration drives economic growth and has made Spain’s economy the fastest-growing among the major EU countries in recent years. It also reduces the country’s extremely high unemployment. But many Spaniards don’t feel these benefits.
The number of homeless people on the streets is growing. Real incomes here have stagnated for decades, largely because of rising housing costs. Young Spaniards usually live with their parents because they can’t afford to move out. This is partly responsible for the low birth rate, which in turn increases the country’s need for migrants: an aging population is becoming less able to do strenuous physical work.
In summer and at Christmas, the centers of major Spanish cities are packed with tourists. Renting apartments to them, wealthy digital nomads, or foreign retirees is usually more profitable than renting to Spaniards, because foreigners are willing to pay more.
Population growth is overwhelming the healthcare system and social services. Waits to see specialists can sometimes last months. Unions representing doctors, teachers, railway workers, and others regularly strike over excessive workloads and low pay.
Interestingly, opponents of migration mention almost none of these problems. The exception is the far left, which says wealthy tourists, digital nomads, and retirees have made it harder for Spaniards themselves to find housing (“they can afford it, but locals can’t”). Anti-tourism movements have already emerged in many cities, particularly Barcelona.
The right, meanwhile, sees the legalization program as a threat to itself. For example, Vox representatives have said the program is intended to keep the left in power by supposedly giving it new voters — migrants who have obtained legal status. That’s a fairly bold assumption: at least 10 years will pass between obtaining a residence permit and becoming a citizen.
Migrants themselves are often conservative and support the right, especially if they come from a left-wing dictatorship. Venezuelans in Spain, for example, vote for the right much more often than locals do.
Another myth common on the right is that the government gives undocumented migrants free apartments and pays them benefits. There are several counterarguments to this.
First, undocumented migrants are off the state’s radar precisely because they don’t have papers, so it provides them with no assistance. To start receiving help, they need to obtain legal status by applying for asylum.
Spain’s refugee programs aren’t exactly generous. Refugees either live in overcrowded centers or receive a few hundred euros toward rent and another few hundred for everyday expenses. Together, those amounts would barely cover renting a room in a major city. The payments last no more than two years.
Many refugees I know don’t even use these assistance programs and support themselves entirely. They often continue working for Russian companies.
Opponents of migration also often say that migrants take jobs from locals while simultaneously calling them all “layabouts living on government handouts.” In fact, migration has reduced unemployment in Spain, including among locals. Migrants themselves create demand for goods and services, and they take low-skilled jobs while Spaniards take management positions.
In the public imagination, undocumented migrants are often reduced to crowds of Africans storming ashore from boats or forcing their way across Spain’s borders, as happened recently in Ceuta. Yet statistics show that of those who applied for the extraordinary legalization program, 67% are from Latin America, almost 23% from Africa, about 8% from Asia (which includes the Philippines, a former Spanish colony), and less than 1% from Europe. Europe accounted for only about 13,000 of Spain’s undocumented migrants.
The origins of undocumented migrants largely mirror those of migrants to Spain overall, apart from Europeans. EU citizens don’t fall into this category because they can move freely within the Schengen Area. So a significant share of the nearly 13,000 undocumented Europeans are most likely Russians and Belarusians.
People from Belarus, Russia, and Ukraine have been one of the fastest-growing groups of migrants in recent years. There are already about half a million of them here, so Spain is gradually filling up with places serving raf coffee, syrniki, and borscht, as well as stores catering to Slavic communities — especially on the eastern coast.
In Torrevieja, a small resort town near Alicante, the combined number of Belarusian, Russian, and Ukrainian citizens has grown from 8,000 to 17,000 during the war, reaching 15% of the town’s population. Ukrainians have become Torrevieja’s largest group of foreign residents, while Russians rank third.
How legalization works — and why it’s happening
Critics of mass legalization believe it will, by itself, encourage more undocumented migrants to come to Spain. But such programs are fairly rare. They’re extraordinary events that no one can count on in advance. Spain last ran one in 2005, Belgium in 2000, Portugal in 2004, the U.S. in 2012, and Italy in 2013. Russia also ran one in 2024.
These programs don’t drive illegal immigration; they become necessary because of it. Illegal immigration, in turn, results both from fairly relaxed immigration rules and from local demand for workers.
The extraordinary legalization program had been under discussion since the COVID pandemic. The pandemic drew attention to the fact that many undocumented migrants worked in sectors essential to the country but lacked full access to legal employment and social protections.
Since 2021, civil society groups have collected more than 700,000 signatures in support of mass legalization. More than 900 nonprofits joined the campaign, along with unions, private businesses, and even the church. But the bill stalled in parliament. The governing Socialist Party did not want mass legalization, preferring to expand and simplify existing pathways.
In the end, the far-left party Podemos (“We Can”) pushed the initiative through. To bypass parliament, where every party wanted to add its own conditions to the legalization bill, Podemos secured legalization through a royal decree. The decree was adopted on April 16, 2026.
Under the decree, all undocumented migrants who arrived in Spain before January 1, 2026, and have no criminal convictions are eligible. Between 500,000 and 800,000 people were expected to qualify. But more than a million ended up applying.
My boyfriend and I applied through an organization for LGBTQ migrants where I take language classes. There are quite a few organizations helping migrants across the country, and they often receive state funding. They helped us gather the necessary documents and provided a certificate of “vulnerability,” which the government had added to the requirements at the last minute. It confirms that a migrant is vulnerable because they lack papers. The certificate doesn’t entitle you to anything else.
We submitted our documents in late May. Our lawyer said a letter confirming that our applications had been accepted should arrive from the immigration service a month later, after which we would have to pay a fee of 38 euros per person.
With that letter, we were also meant to receive an identification number for foreigners — a basic form of ID in Spain that makes it much easier to access services.
Without it, for example, I couldn’t sign contracts with half the internet and utility providers or book appointments with government offices online. I had to call or go in person. We were also meant to receive permission to work immediately.
But the process dragged on, as often happens with Spain’s overloaded social services. The unexpectedly large number of applications and the vacation season added to the delays. We received the letter only after three months. Now we’re half a step closer to legal status.
That opens up a much wider range of jobs. We can now start applying for more stable jobs with better labor protections.
Once we pay the fee, the immigration service should start reviewing our applications, and by law a decision should come within three months. Other migrants’ experiences suggest, though, that the process will most likely take at least six months. That’s what happened to people I know who were in Spain on student visas or were trying to obtain residency based on their ties to the country.
If approved, we’ll receive residence permits valid for one year. We’ll be able to renew them if we find work in Spain or register as self-employed to declare our foreign income.
* * *
Spain interests me as a country that lost its empire, went through a civil war and a nationalist dictatorship, and became a fairly stable, open democracy. I think understanding that experience, especially its experience of reconciliation, will be useful for Russia.
That’s why I’m always looking for information here about the civil war. But over the past half-century, Spaniards preferred not to discuss it, adopting the “Pact of Forgetting” to preserve peace after Franco’s death. Only in 2022 did Spain adopt the Democratic Memory Law, which condemns the crimes of Francoism.
The law also gave descendants of people who left during the dictatorship the right to obtain citizenship through a simplified process. More than half a million applications have been approved under this program over the past three years. The law also prompted a wave of discussion about the conflict the country had endured and inspired creative works about it.
I’ve moved many times since leaving my hometown of Lipetsk. And even more since leaving Russia: I’ve lived in Georgia, Turkey, Armenia, and India. I don’t think Spain is the end of my odyssey.
My boyfriend is waiting for legal status, hoping to find work here. I, on the other hand, feel more comfortable in the gray area where I don’t pay taxes, because Russian journalists and human rights advocates don’t earn much, and the pay is extremely unreliable. Paradoxically, I need legal status so I can leave Spain without trouble. I want to enroll in a doctoral program in another country.
So I’ll most likely resume my wanderings after a while. But I still hope to return to Russia one day.
