Spanish right wing votes down housing crisis plans as protest movement grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:27:47 UTC
01:27:47 KST

Rightwing lawmakers in Spain have rejected emergency measures put forward to tackle the country’s housing crisis, pitting a fractured parliament against the widespread protest movement that has swelled in recent days.
On Friday Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
As hundreds of protesters outside the parliament building in Madrid held up homemade signs bearing images of vultures, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees.
The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo.
News of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted.
The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was evicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years. The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Tens of thousands of people heeded the call by housing campaigners to take to the streets, while encampments protesting against the housing crisis sprung up in cities across Spain.
The demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life into Sánchez’s beleaguered government and shifting attention away from the lingering impact of recent events in Ceuta.
On Friday, as a poll suggested that two-thirds of people in Spain supported the idea of government intervention in the housing market to limit prices, sources told the news site Eldiario.es that the Socialists were mulling whether to bring forward next year’s elections, potentially to this November.
After news broke that several rightwing parties were planning to vote against the proposed measures, Sánchez said the parliamentary vote would go ahead as planned. “You’re with the social majority or with speculators,” the Spanish prime minister said on social media, adding that the vote would reveal the “true colours” of the rightwing parties.
Following five hours of parliamentary debate on Friday, Sánchez made a last ditch appeal to lawmakers to back the measures. “What is behind these decrees is the desire to instil order and a sense of humanity in a market that – if we do not rein it in – will destroy our society,” he said. “Do the right thing, or history will judge you, and sooner than you think.”
Across Spain, where rents have surged 80% within a decade and the cost of homes climbed by 63%, the issue of housing has long ranked as one of people’s biggest concerns.
Earlier this year, the Youth Council of Spain said the average rent in Spain had climbed to €1,176 ($1,323) a month – an amount equivalent to 98.7% of the average salary for under-30s.
The figures help to explain why the protests that began with Abascal’s eviction have continued even after the investment firm that bought her apartment said it had struck a deal that would allow her to return to her home, with her rent returning to a level closer to that she had paid in the past.
The government decrees presented in parliament on Friday were intended to quell some of this public uproar. As they were rejected, campaigners vowed to continue their push to improve access to housing.
“They’re not going to stop us,” the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions said in a statement, as it called on people across the country to take to the streets this weekend. “In the face of a parliament that is out of touch, the answer is more organisation and mobilisation. The next step: a general strike.”
Saturday will mark one week since a small group of protesters, intent on making their demands heard, set up 10 tents in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol plaza, a short walk from parliament. Since then, the encampment had swelled to more than 1,200 tents – a peaceful settlement in the heart of the capital with its own street names, a medical centre and even a co-working space.
As news of the vote reached the camp on Friday, some said it was not what they had expected. “People here are disappointed,” said Marta García. “We had thought that at least one of the decrees would be approved.”

====================================================================================================

First-ever ‘microbe for Mars’ targets terraforming the Red Planet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:26:37 UTC
01:26:37 KST

Last month Erika DeBenedictis, CEO of the nonprofit start-up Pioneer Labs, delighted or shocked many space nerds with some big news: she and her colleagues had engineered “the first microbe for Mars.”
In a post on X that has garnered more than two million views, DeBenedictis claimed that her bacterium, a tweaked version of Cupriavidus necator, represents “the first step towards terraforming” the Red Planet. By seeding Mars with microbial life, she has argued, we can make the world more Earthlike from the ground up.
“Everything life needs to thrive is given to us by nature,” observed DeBenedictis, a synthetic biologist with a Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in a slick promotional video that was included with the post. “When humanity goes to space, we have to bring nature with us.” The clip teased a future Mars with green valleys and self-sufficient, see-through, domed habitats, all constructed with locally sourced materials, some of them courtesy of the microbe, which DeBenedictis and Pioneer Labs call “sPL.001.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
It’s certainly a compelling story. And it’s backed up with a few recent preprint papers detailing Pioneer Labs’ research. But how much of it is fantasy?
Scientific American put that question to several researchers working at the intersection of planetary science, astrobiology, microbial ecology and bioengineering—and their responses are, on the whole, fairly positive. The most critical assessment comes from Chris McKay, a planetary scientist at NASA’s Ames Research Center, who has studied terraforming for decades. McKay is senior author of “The Case for Mars Terraforming Research,” a paper led by DeBenedictis that was published last year in Nature Astronomy. The engineered bacterium is “not very interesting, not very new yet,” he says. “I hope better is coming soon.” Paul Race, who studies industrial biotechnology at Newcastle University in England, offers the same impression, calling the announcement “rather over the top.”
Their core qualm is that this microbe alone can’t bring a dead planet to life. “This microorganism, sPL.001, is not for terraforming Mars—it’s for making feedstock for 3D-printed houses,” McKay says. “It can only be grown in a bioreactor,” an apparatus for incubating microbes, such as yeast, to yield useful by-products. DeBenedictis’s microbe would pump out a form of bioplastic by consuming Martian dirt, water and compressed carbon dioxide delivered to the bioreactor with autonomous machinery. To her credit, DeBenedictis has been clear on this point: sPL.001 “is the first of five organisms we will need to make Mars green,” she wrote in a post on Pioneer Labs’ Substack.
“Hopefully,” McKay says, “some of the other four are green and can actually grow on Mars!”
DeBenedictis founded Pioneer Labs in 2024, when she was a resident at the San Francisco Bay Area–based Astera Institute, a billionaire-backed nonprofit focused on incubating science and technology projects with ambitious long-term visions (and correspondingly ambitious needs for sustained funding). The company’s name, DeBenedictis says, comes from the ecological idea of “pioneer species” that colonize barren territory as a first step for the creation of complex ecosystems. And its stated goal is no small thing: to make the universe more friendly to life.
On Earth, pioneer species are usually organisms we think of as weeds or pests that can tolerate the harshest environments: molds that feast on decaying organic matter, lichens that thrive almost anywhere or dandelions that grow in and break up rock to make and enrich soil. They’re not glamorous, but they allow “fancier organisms and shrubs and trees and stuff to grow, and that’s exactly what we’re trying to do” for Mars, DeBenedictis tells Scientific American.
Bootstrapping a biosphere there isn’t easy, however. Biology is bedeviled on the planet, exposed as it is to unrelenting harmful radiation and given its paltry atmosphere, 1 percent as thick as Earth’s, and temperatures that, in a single Martian day, can swing violently by 100 degrees Celsius. The low levels of nitrogen in the atmosphere and in the ground add insult to injury—a 2025 review paper in Communications Biology noted that a lack of nitrogen is “a major limiting factor for establishing Earth-like organisms or supporting human agriculture, and limits our capacity to terraform the planet.” Plus, some samples of Martian soil contain high levels of perchlorates, toxic chemical compounds, also found in rocket fuel, that could potentially poison the planet’s supplies of water and food.
“We need to choose carefully” when we devise bioengineered microbes to overcome these immense challenges, DeBenedictis says.
Neveda Naz, an astrobiologist at Tufts University, who has grown microbes in material from Martian meteors, says Pioneer Labs had done just that with its focus on the bioplastic-producing version of C. necator. “They have picked an organism, adapted it to a defined Mars-relevant chemical environment and demonstrated improved production of a useful material,” Naz says. “If the goal is eventually to manufacture materials off-Earth using predominantly local resources rather than transporting everything from Earth, that’s a very worthwhile and smart direction to explore.”
Alexandre Rosado, a microbiologist who has studied terraforming and focuses on ultrahardy microbes called extremophiles, agrees. “I think the work is interesting, and there is certainly good science there,” he says. “I would not dismiss it. My view is that microbes will almost certainly be part of any serious attempt to use local Martian resources or, much further down the road, modify Martian environments.”
Both Naz and Rosado, however, quibble with Pioneer Labs’ declaration that this makes the modified C. necator a “microbe for Mars.” For Rosado, the company’s language around terraforming “goes quite a bit beyond what they have actually demonstrated.” And, Naz says, “there is an important distinction between showing that Martian regolith can provide biologically useful nutrients and showing that an organism can grow in the Martian environment.”
DeBenedictis is aware of the distinction—it’s the centerpiece of Pioneer Labs’ safety strategy for avoiding potentially ruinous interplanetary contamination, PRIM (Propagation Restricted, Inert on Mars). In her team’s experiments, the researchers found that C. necator failed to reproduce if it was starved of water and carbon. So, she says, if the microbe somehow escaped a bioreactor on Mars, its chances of survival and reproduction would be infinitesimal. “Even a full, catastrophic leak of an industrial-scale Mars bioreactor would still clear the planetary protection threshold by a factor of several hundred,” DeBenedictis says. “I’m genuinely not worried about it.”
Whether policymakers who set international standards for “planetary protection” protocols won’t worry about it, either, is another hazy aspect of Pioneer Labs’ hopeful aspirations. Without regulatory approval, DeBenedictis’s best-laid plans for helping to terraform Mars may literally fail to launch. As NASA administrator Jared Isaacman noted on X, however, his team has been working to revise the space agency’s protection policies to align them with what he calls the “common-sense principles” originally established in the “early days of planetary exploration and later reflected in Article IX of the Outer Space Treaty.” He thinks current protection policies needlessly add “extreme cost and time to robotic missions to Mars when the overarching goal is to send astronauts there as quickly and safely as possible.”
Ricard Solé, a biologist who heads the Complex Systems Lab at Pompeu Fabra University in Barcelona and studies, among other things, terraforming via bioengineered ecosystems, thinks PRIM is on point. “It separates useful biotechnology from uncontrolled ecological spread,” he says. “Pioneer Labs’ proposal is a very interesting and important step, but if the goal is eventually to build a stable, closed ecology on Mars, then a systems-level perspective will be essential.” Mars will need more than “a single engineered strain,” Solé says, envisioning a larger assemblage of multispecies communities that collectively recycle matter, turn one organism’s waste into another’s resource, regulate environmental conditions, and so on. “In that sense,” he says, “the challenge is not only to engineer organisms but to engineer the ecological interactions that allow the whole system to sustain itself.”
This is where DeBenedictis’s as-yet-unannounced four other microbes come in. They have yet to be revealed, she says, because Pioneer Labs hasn’t entirely settled on which organisms could do the job. Whichever ones win the day will have to offer “transparent building materials, perchlorate reduction, making fertile soil, and then food and oxygen,” she says. The transparent material, crucial for making windows, will be the hardest to find, she speculates. “We don’t have very many examples of biomaterials that are transparent when they’re dry, which is what you need on Mars because the atmosphere outside will dry anything out, so we’ll see what we come up with.”
If all goes to plan, she thinks, the effect will be to transform the night sky by a significant smidge. “You can see Mars outside with your naked eye, and it’s noticeably a little red relative to other stars in the background,” she says. “And I think, before I die, I’ll get to see it be a little bit green.”

Ramla Ali's In the Shadows: From Somali refugee to Olympic boxer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:25:57 UTC
01:25:57 KST

Breadcrumb
She fled war, found boxing and made Olympic history: Ramla Ali's In the Shadows
Ramla Ali is known for making firsts — she is the first Somali woman to become a professional boxer, and the first Somali to not only compete for a world title but also represent her home country at the 2020 Olympic Games.
Millions of people around the world watched Ramla make history, giving them hope that one day they could follow in her footsteps.
"Being the first only means that you can set a trend for others to watch you, look up to you, and think that I can do it too," the professional boxer tells The New Arab.
"I hope that me being the first in those things has shown young kids, boys and girls, who have come from similar backgrounds to me, that if she can do it, I can do it too, and I hope that it's something that they can look to achieve in the future," Ramla adds.
But her successes did not come with ease, as the boxer grew up amid fleeing war, being bullied for being overweight and navigating a culture that looks down upon women taking part in sports.
As she continues to fight matches, Ramla shares her story in her new movie In the Shadows, directed by BAFTA-winning and Oscar-nominated director Anthony Wonke, with Ramla and her husband, Richard Moore, serving as the film’s executive producers.
"It tells a migrant story, and then it also tells a love story, and there are messages of hope, showing migrants as human beings, and showing the different cultures, falling in love in a nutshell," Ramla shares.
Starring Top Boy’s Jasmine Jobson, who plays the boxer, and Peaky Blinders’ Finn Cole, the biopic follows the boxer from fleeing Somalia after her brother's death to finding refuge in the UK and discovering her love for boxing, much to her mother’s dismay.
"I think, being a migrant, when I came to the UK, it's not as bad, I believe, as it is now. I think being a migrant, always having that culture at home, has shaped me to be the person that I am," Ramla says.
The boxer was only a baby when her brother Abdi was killed by a mortar in Mogadishu during the Somali Civil War.
While the film shows Ramla as seven, her mother says she was still breastfeeding when she came to the UK.
"I actually don't know my age," Ramla reveals. "I don't know when I was born. I was obviously born during the Civil War. I don't have a birth certificate, and so my age and date of birth are guessed."
The biopic constantly shifts from Ramla shadowboxing and training for upcoming fights to scenes of her brother being killed and life in Mogadishu amid war, as if she’s constantly thinking about Abdi while fighting and reminding viewers where she is from.
The film also parallels the joy Ramla feels when she’s boxing with the mundane life of a corporate lawyer trying to keep her secret training sessions, knowing the culture she grew up in wouldn't allow it.
Growing up with a strict mother, Ramla never smoked, drank, or went out partying, but she trained in secret. Her family eventually finds out after she becomes Britain’s first Somali boxing champion, and viewers get to see the dreaded moment they learn their daughter is a boxer.
Viewers see her mother’s disgust, but also a sort of betrayal.
"I'm so scared of my mum, so I never did anything naughty apart from boxing," Ramla says.
"I think she was just mostly annoyed by the deception, the lies, but I couldn't tell her. How can I tell my mum who took us out from Somalia, we're fleeing danger, and I'm essentially putting myself back into danger? How can I tell my mum? So, I just kept it a secret."
Amidst fighting for her life and trying to maintain the image of an "ideal Muslim Somali girl," the movie is also a love story.
The biopic also shows Ramla meeting and falling in love with Richard, played by Finn Cole, a white British man who converted for the boxer and is now her full-time trainer and manager.
The film shows her family’s disapproval of her wanting to marry a white man, believing he was not a suitable match for her.
"It was two different cultures, a clash of culture, [Richard] wasn't very welcomed at the beginning by my family, but now they love him; he's like now my mum's fourth son," Ramla says.
Together, the couple founded 786 Films, a production company aimed at championing minority-led, female-driven and underrepresented narratives.
"For me, boxing is not going to be forever. You don't want to be 40-50, still competing. You need another thing that you can slowly go into," Ramla explains.
With Richard’s background in filmmaking, it felt like a natural progression for Ramla to take part, having co-written and co-directed their first short film, How to Hide It, starring the boxer herself and about a young Muslim woman who faces a moral dilemma after winning the lottery.
"I'm really enjoying this new chapter in my life, filmmaking, and for me, it just seems like a natural progression," Ramla shares.
The boxer also draws on her experience as part of an intercultural couple in her debut feature, Not Like Us, which finished production in July.
The film shows not only Ramla and Richard falling in love, but also Richard supporting Ramla in her endeavours when her family wanted him to end it in the name of "protecting his wife."
It portrays the couple taking matters into their own hands by working to represent Somalia in the Olympics after being rejected by Team GB, with Ramla always wondering why she was never selected to represent Britain in the international ring.
"I remember thinking that I'm not going to wait around and have my dreams in your hands; I'm going to go out and pursue myself," she tells The New Arab.
"It was just me and Richard representing Somalia all over the world. I think for me it's been the best decision."
As Somalia did not have its own boxing federation, Ramla had to create one after a friend suggested she represent her home country.
Despite having no national funding and working three jobs while competing against athletes training full time, the boxer says she wouldn't change it for the world, and that she became an inspiration to many.
"I got to do everything that I wanted to do. I got to go to any competition I wanted to go to. There was no politics around it," Ramla says.
"At the beginning, it was very selfish that me wanting to compete for Somalia was just about me, what can it do for me, what competitions can I do. But then receiving these comments from people just showed me that it's bigger than me and it's about inspiring the next generation, and it was great when I was doing it."
The boxer also shared that she wanted to put her country in a positive light.
"Too often, Somalia, it's all about war, it's about famine, if not, it's about corruption, it's about piracy, it's about Al-Shabaab," the boxer says.
"I wanted to paint Somalia in a positive light. I wanted to show Somalia that we're more than just that. We're actually people; we can actually do incredible things in this world."
The film shows Ramla finally achieving her dream of playing in the Olympics, along with the many achievements she reached along the way, but also remembering her brother whose death shaped the trajectory of her family’s lives.
Looking back on her film, Ramla's core message is that migrants, like her, are just regular folk.
"With the current migrant crisis, and all these anti-migrant groups, I hope this film just shows that migrants are human beings, and we're not evil people; we're just fleeing danger to pursue safety. I hope people go and watch this film with an open mind and an open heart."
In the Shadows releases in UK cinemas on 30 October

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) is working on a large-scale road construction project in Ukraine to address logistical problems and support exports, EBRD President Odile Renaud-Basso said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine.
"The other one is indeed that we have some broad project: we are working on a road project. We are discussing the priorities in this area," the institution's president said in response to a question about possible mechanisms for overcoming logistical challenges facing Ukrainian exports.
According to her, the bank is actively investing in the transportation and logistics sectors. In particular, an agreement on financing Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) was signed earlier, and a EUR 300 million project is being implemented to purchase new locomotives to replace damaged ones.

They were expected to be integrated into Ukraine's Unified Project Portfolio.

Saudi Arabia plans 100,000-troop Yemen offensive to retake Bab el-Mandeb from Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:22:51 UTC
01:22:51 KST

Saudi Arabia is preparing a new military offensive against Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen, with plans under consideration ranging from a focused coastal assault to a broader attack on several fronts, regional and Western officials told Reuters.
The operation, expected to begin in the coming weeks, would be led on the ground by Yemeni forces overseen by Riyadh and backed by Saudi airstrikes, according to six people familiar with the preparations.
More than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilized depending on the scale of the operation, the officials said.
A central objective is to reverse the Houthis’ rapid gains last month, when they pushed down Yemen’s coast and seized control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints.
Bab el-Mandeb connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and serves as the southern gateway for shipping between Asia and the Mediterranean. Its importance has increased sharply this year as the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed by the conflict with Iran.
Saudi officials are considering two main options, according to Gulf and Yemeni officials. One would concentrate the offensive around Bab el-Mandeb. The other would combine that coastal operation with simultaneous attacks in Al-Bayda, Marib, Taiz and Al-Jawf.
Riyadh has concluded that renewed peace negotiations with the Houthis are not viable while the group controls Bab el-Mandeb and the strategic leverage that comes with it, Western diplomats and a Gulf official said.
The precise timing remains unclear. Sources gave estimates ranging from within a week to after the US midterm elections in early November.
Michael Ratney, a former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia, said he expected any operation to be considerably narrower than the Saudi-led intervention launched in 2015.
“As much they want to vanquish the Houthis completely, they also need to get back to status quo ante before Houthis controlled territory along Bab el-Mandeb,” Ratney said. “Ideally, it would be a fairly limited operation to retake coastal areas and get back to normal maritime traffic.”
US intelligence, Turkish drones and Pakistani support
Washington is already providing military advisers and intelligence, including targeting information, to support Saudi air operations in Yemen, according to a Western diplomat.
Direct U.S. combat involvement, however, is not expected. Reuters previously reported that President Donald Trump rejected requests from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for direct military support including U.S. airstrikes.
Turkey and Pakistan have also supplied military equipment used by Saudi Arabia in Yemen, Pakistani and regional officials said.
Pakistan last month sent four cargo aircraft carrying equipment including air-defense systems, light artillery, drones and counter-drone systems to Aden, the seat of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, according to a Pakistani official.
Pakistani military advisers are also operating alongside Saudi counterparts in support of Yemeni forces, while Turkish drones previously purchased by Riyadh have been deployed over Yemen, officials said.
Saudi Arabia is particularly concerned about protecting its oil infrastructure and other strategic sites from Houthi missile and drone attacks during the campaign and has sought defensive support from several allies.
Pakistan has deployed between 30,000 and 40,000 troops to Saudi Arabia to help protect the kingdom’s borders and assist with missile and drone interceptions, according to a Pakistani official. Islamabad has not decided to send troops into Yemen for combat operations, the official said.
France has meanwhile announced plans to deploy defensive systems and troops to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.
Fractured anti-Houthi forces
Any ground offensive would depend heavily on the disparate Yemeni factions armed and trained by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates during earlier stages of the civil war.
Analysts say those forces remain divided and may struggle to sustain a major campaign against the Houthis.
“Many anti-Houthi forces are still not organised or prepared for the kind of sustained offensive required to push back a disciplined Houthi military force,” Yemen analyst Mohammed Albasha said.
Yemeni factions were further weakened by clashes last winter after UAE-backed southern forces attempted to seize territory in eastern Yemen and pursue secession, only to be defeated by Saudi-backed forces.
Ali Shihabi, a Saudi political analyst close to government thinking, said Riyadh’s forces had so far focused on stabilizing the front but were preparing to shift to the offensive.
“The priority so far has been to defend the positions on the ground and stabilize the front, but certainly they will be going on the offensive,” he said. “Success greatly depends on the quality of the performance of the local forces.”

Russian glide bombs strike Kharkiv, kill women, injure children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

01:21:59 KST

At least two people were killed and 36 injured after Russian glide bombs struck two areas of the city of Kharkiv on the afternoon of Oct. 2.
"Three glide bombs were recorded hitting the Slobidskyi and Nemyshlyansky districts of the city," Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional State Administration, said in a statement on Telegram.
"Two women aged 66 and 80 died as a result of the strike by the Russian army. 32 people were injured," Syniehubov said.
The State Emergency Service (DSNS) in Kharkiv later raised the number of injured to 36. Three of the injured were children, according to DSNS.
One of the Russian glide bombs "completely destroyed" a residential building, Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said in a statement.
Russian guided aerial bombs, often called KABs (Kerovana Aviabomba) in Ukraine, are repurposed aerial bombs equipped with wings and precision guidance systems such as GPS, laser, or infrared targeting.
Unlike traditional free-fall bombs, KABs can glide tens of kilometers before impact, allowing Russian aircraft — typically the Su-34 — to release them from a distance, safe from the operating range of Ukrainian air defense missiles or fighters.
Warhead sizes vary by model, ranging from about 300 kilograms to 3 metric tons, enough to destroy multistory buildings with a direct hit.
Russian forces use glide bombs against important, hardened, or entrenched targets, such as bridges, command posts, or drone teams spotted by reconnaissance assets.

Everyone can talk but only a few people get heard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:21:05 UTC
01:21:05 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Hello everybody,
This week we’re looking at who gets heard, with Francis Fukuyama.
I block people on social media quite a lot.
I’ve wrestled with this for a long time. I’ve debated it with friends and dithered for months, but I’ve decided I’m happy with blocking people. But some cases are easier to decide than others.
The easy cases are with trolls and personal abuse. If you see hurling vitriol as a sadistic playground game, fine. Please find a playground with others just like you. Mini Philosophy is not that kind of place. And if your contribution to a discussion is to call me an idiot, mock my accent, or make some snide comment about my age, gender, or upbringing, save it for in-person. It’s hard to banter over the internet affectionately, and so I’ll just have to assume you’re being an arse.
The difficult cases, though, are about those people who aren’t necessarily rude. It’s just that they simply want to borrow my megaphone.
It is an undoubtedly privileged position to own such a large following on social media as Mini Philosophy does. It has taken seven years of near-constant work, but here I am, with a few million people enjoying my stuff. And so, occasionally, someone sees that audience and decides they would like to speak to it too. Yes, there’s the usual political stuff, but you also get the self-promotional things: “Check out my video on this topic,” “I wrote a blog post last week over here,” or “Follow @mypage to learn about Y.”
None of these people are being abusive, and they are perfectly entitled to say those things. But are they entitled to say it to my audience from my page?
And so, the question I want to ask this week is: Does everyone deserve an equal right to speak — or an equal right to be heard?
Go well,
Jonny
Who holds the megaphone?
Last week, I interviewed Francis Fukuyama. Paid members can watch the full thing at the end.
Fukuyama is famous for his idea that liberalism is the “end of history” because no other political philosophy can ever hope to beat its particular blend of freedom, security, and affluence. For Fukuyama, liberalism is defined by many things, like equality before the law and individual autonomy, but one essential, indispensable element of liberalism is freedom of speech.
We could debate for weeks about what “freedom of speech” means. And the first thing to point out is that there is no such thing as total, unrestrained freedom of speech anywhere in the world. You cannot post how to make a bomb on the internet. You cannot tell a child they should hurt themselves and how to do it. You cannot invent job qualifications while interviewing to become a doctor. You cannot stand outside my front garden shouting four-letter insults for hours at a time.
Freedom of speech is a spectrum, and the job of philosophers, politicians, and judges is to put a pin along that spectrum to say, “Anything up to here is acceptable. Anything after here is a crime.” And it’s no easy job. Fukuyama, for example, argues that the American First Amendment “is a better system” than the European one because it’s “much more expansive and … more tolerant of a broader range of speech.”
For Fukuyama, the real problem isn’t really about free speech, because that’s a known problem and the demos can decide on that any way they want. The less discussed problem is amplification.
Some people have always been able to be heard more than others. On a basic physiological level, some people just have loud, clear, authoritative voices. A classically trained Shakespearean actor doesn’t need a microphone to be heard at the back. One step up from here, you have charisma and presence. I’m sure you know a few people in your life who speak with a kind of gravity that just makes you want to listen. There are some philosophers like G. A. Cohen who call this a kind of injustice. It’s not fair that Ian McKellen can speak louder and better than me. It’s not right that good-looking, funny, and personable people get the job ahead of others. We’ll have to park that one for another day.
The issue becomes more explicitly political when we talk about amplification technologies. Historians will often tell you how so much of what we know about the past comes from the literate, educated classes. We know less about life for poor, outcast, marginalized demographics because they couldn’t pass that information along. Up until the 20th century, publishing houses, printers, and the literati had a huge impact on what was said and what was heard. Everyone can speak, but only a few get to write books. Then came press barons like Hearst, followed by radio, TV, and media moguls like Murdoch who have always made sure a few voices are the loudest.
Today, we have the internet. The internet was originally seen as the great democratization of speech. Anyone can write a blog. Anyone can start a Twitter account. Say what you want, when you want, how you want, you long-silent masses.
For a time in the 2000s, it was thought that 12 million Americans were blogging — more than half had never published anywhere before. But being able to speak is one thing; having an audience to hear you is another. Over time, the internet did what markets tend to do: consolidate. Today, two companies — Alphabet (Google and YouTube) and Meta (Facebook and Instagram) — oversee a huge chunk of our online consumption. If you throw in TikTok, WeChat, X, LinkedIn, and Snapchat, you have only a few gatekeepers facilitating who the world hears and sees. So, while you might live in a free-speech country, how loud your speech is depends on the mercurial algorithms and rules of a handful of companies.
A lot has been made of why Elon Musk bought Twitter (and then rebranded it to X). But I suspect a large part of it was that it bought him a megaphone. It gave him a way not only to control speech but to amplify his own. You can still be the world’s richest man and get ignored. You can still be worth $200 billion and have to sit by the phone for the BBC, CNN, or Fox to call. That must have been hard. And so his money bought him amplification.
This is what Fukuyama said:
“Certain individuals control big media platforms, and their speech is much more impactful than the speech of ordinary people that don’t own a media platform. And I don’t think we’ve really worked out the limits of the kind of influence in speech that you can have if you’re, say, Elon Musk, or now we have this David Ellison that’s accumulating this gigantic media empire.
“Do his speech rights have any limitations? I think in a democracy, there probably ought to be some limits.”
There is a difference between naming a problem and offering a solution. And there’s no easy or obvious one here. Fukuyama himself has proposed that governments could require dominant platforms to allow “middleware” — independent services that sit between you and the platform and let you choose who ranks, filters, and recommends what you see. Instead of Musk or Zuckerberg deciding what gets amplified, users could choose different systems of curation. The legal scholar Tim Wu offers a more structural answer centered on antitrust law. For Wu, the problem is the consolidation: If a tiny number of companies have acquired extraordinary control over information, then reduce their power by breaking dominant companies apart and preventing them from swallowing up-and-coming competitors. Wu has specifically argued for breaking up Meta — separating Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and so on.
But neither answer is painless. Middleware sounds like a slippery slope toward constructing our own echo chambers. And breaking up companies creates more owners of megaphones without necessarily answering the deeper question of how powerful any one megaphone should be.
So what do you think? Is it unfair that some voices are heard louder than others? And if so, is there anything we can actually do about it?
Sign up for a paid membership to watch my full interview with Fukuyama below.
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.

US job growth slows as unemployment rises before midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:20:46 UTC
01:20:46 KST

US adds just 29,000 jobs as unemployment rises before midterm elections
The US economy added 29,000 jobs in September, with unemployment rising to 4.2 percent, according to Labor Department data.
Job growth in the United States slowed in September, falling short of economists’ expectations as the unemployment rate rose in the final jobs report before the consequential midterm elections.
The US economy added 29,000 jobs in September, according to the Labor Department’s report released on Friday, far below economists’ expectations. Dow Jones had forecast 84,000 jobs, while economists polled by Reuters said they expected 90,000 job additions.
The unemployment rate also rose by 0.1 percentage point, from 4.1 percent to 4.2 percent.
The healthcare sector led the gains, accounting for the majority of new jobs. The industry added 17,000 jobs, marking a slowdown from an average of 33,000 jobs per month over the past year. Construction added 11,000 jobs, while manufacturing added 9,000.
Financial activities, which include sectors such as commercial banking and insurance, shed 7,000 jobs.
Most other sectors were largely unchanged, including retail, oil and gas extraction, and leisure and hospitality.
“Today’s disappointing report shows the labour market is grinding to a halt, marked by slow hiring and declining real wages that leave workers with very little leverage,” Kyle Moore, chief economist at the think tank The Century Foundation, said in remarks provided to Al Jazeera.
Previous jobs reports were also revised downward. July was revised from an initial gain of 21,000 jobs to a loss of 10,000 jobs. August was revised down by 29,000 jobs, from 162,000 to 133,000.
Wages grew by 3 percent, marking the slowest annual wage increase in five years.
Friday’s jobs report caps a week of weakening economic data before the consequential midterm election on November 3.
According to an AP-NORC poll released on Thursday, 61 percent of Americans polled said the US economy is worse off now than when Trump took office in January 2025.
“When businesses are barely hiring and raises aren’t keeping up with rising prices, it’s a stalled economy – and working families are stuck in it,” Breyon Williams, chief economist for Groundwork Collaborative, an economic policy think tank, said in a statement.
Trump has been trying to change the narrative on the slumping economy. On Monday, he said in a Truth Social post that “The United States has the BEST Employment Numbers in HISTORY.”
Stalling growth
On Tuesday, the US Labor Department released the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, or JOLTS report, which showed little change, suggesting what economists call a low-hire, low-fire environment. That means those who have jobs are generally not leaving for new ones, while employers are maintaining the status quo rather than expanding.
On the other hand, ADP’s private payroll report, released on Wednesday, showed that 90,000 jobs were created across the private sector. The sheer number of layoffs fell, too, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. The report, released Thursday, showed that employers cut more than 43,000 jobs in September, marking an 18 percent decline in layoffs from August.
Friday’s jobs report comes before the Federal Reserve’s final policy decision before the midterm election. During its two-day policy meeting on October 27-28, the central bank will decide whether to raise, cut or maintain interest rates.
The odds increasingly suggest the Fed will hold rates steady in the 3.75-4.00 percent range, according to CME FedWatch, a tool that tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions. The FedWatch tool indicates there is currently a 77.3 percent chance that rates will hold steady, up from 35.8 percent this time last week.
US markets are trending upward on the heels of the report. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is up 1.5 percent, the Dow Jones Industrial Average is up 0.6 percent and the S&P 500 is up 1.1 percent in midday trading.
The price of gold, which is largely considered a safe investment during times of economic uncertainty, rose 1.1 percent to $4,223.49 amid the jobs report.

Speakers at TIME Impact Dinner Discuss Empowering and Supporting Survivors of Domestic Violence

01:20:15 KST

TIME held an Impact Dinner in Chicago on Thursday that featured reflections from four people who are working to support survivors of domestic violence.
The four speakers at the event, which was presented by The Allstate Foundation, were Donna Ferrato, a photojournalist and activist whose photographs of survivors helped raise awareness of domestic violence in the U.S.; Tommi Vincent, an author and speaker who is also president of the family lifestyle brand Vincent Country, and her husband, Troy Vincent, executive vice president of football operations at the NFL; and Ashley Judd, a humanitarian, activist, and actor who was one of the “Silence Breakers” recognized as TIME Person of the Year in 2017.
Here are highlights from each of the remarks.
Donna Ferrato
Ferrato opened her remarks by honoring her mother, who she said was a survivor and “will be forever the inspiration for my work.”
“I pledge allegiance to survivors of domestic abuse and sex trafficking,” Ferrato said. “Survivors are the ones who lead this movement.”
She also shared the story of the woman she said was “the person that I owe everything in my arsenal to.” One of Ferrato’s most well-known photographs, “Behind Closed Doors,” documented an act of domestic violence, focusing on a couple known at the time under the pseudonyms “Garth” and “Lisa.” Lisa’s real name was later revealed to be Elisabeth Lindberg—who today, Ferrato said, is “on top of the world.”
“She empowered herself,” Ferrato said. “Even as her life was unraveling, she allowed me to be with her. She’s not just a hero in my eyes … [but also] in the eyes of countless others who have followed her journey from being abused to becoming unbeatable.”
Ferrato called TIME “the midwife that brought Elisabeth’s rebirth to light,” recalling how Lindberg had shared her story in emotional interviews.
“She gave up her privacy for the good of other women,” Ferrato said. “She represents courage and love. And she proves why women must believe in their own inner voice.”
Ferrato also reflected on her decades-long career photographing the lives and experiences of survivors of domestic violence. When she began her focus on the topic more than 40 years ago, she said, victim blaming was pervasive in society. Ferrato set out to raise awareness about domestic violence through her photographs, and she praised the women who entrusted her with their stories.
She ended her remarks by emphasizing that such courage is needed now as much as ever. “Let’s break the silence,” she said. ”Let’s be outspoken. Praise these survivors.”
Tommi Vincent and Troy Vincent
The Vincents began their remarks by sharing how their own personal experiences drove them to become advocates.
“I am a thriving domestic violence survivor on a mission to normalize the conversation, not the behavior,” Tommi Vincent, who has been outspoken about her experience with past abuse, said. “I am compelled to use my voice, my experience, my resources, and my relationships to be part of the solution for victims and survivors.”
Her husband said that he also experienced “the devastation and the impact of domestic violence,” sharing how he and his younger brother witnessed their mother being abused while they were growing up.
“There were times when that abuse left her unable to work for extended periods,” Troy Vincent said. When “the shame of abuse finally lost its battle to the threat of eviction,” he said, his mother sought help from family members—underlining the link between domestic violence and financial instability. “That experience taught me something that still I believe in today—that people closest to the problem often are the ones equipped to help find solutions,” he continued.
The Vincents expressed their commitment to use their own experiences to help others. Tommi Vincent said that she and her husband, working with organizations including the National Domestic Violence Hotline, are “building a new house for survivors.”
“A house where survivors are centered. A house where their voices are heard. A house where their experiences help shape solutions,” she said. “And a house where we teach a new definition of love—one where love does not hurt, intentionally. That is the house we are committed to helping build.”
Ashley Judd
During her remarks, Judd said that, while not all men are violent, many are silent about the violence that other men perpetrate. She spoke about her own experiences with sexual violence and abuse, as well as stories of abuse that have made national headlines recently, and the common thread of “entitlement to female bodies.” Those who foster that attitude, or who see abuse and remain silent, are “all complicit,” she argued.
“I am resilient,” she said. “But why do we have to be strong? I am a survivor—of what are we surviving? Male demand to female bodies—and other men and some women and their families who are silent, do not confront and break their own denial, who minimize, trivialize, and dismiss what men do and say about women and to each other."
She urged anyone who witnesses abuse to speak up.
“There’s no such thing as a non-complicit bystander because if you really want to support survivors, you become an upstander,” Judd said. “You heal the village, you heal yourself, and you hold men accountable.”
If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic violence, the National Domestic Violence Hotline is available 24/7. Call 1-800-799-SAFE or visit TheHotline.org.
TIME Impact Dinner: Empowering Survivors: Building Strong Futures Together was presented by The Allstate Foundation.

Brazil’s Lula gears up for ‘last dance’ with run for fourth presidential term
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:20:06 UTC
01:20:06 KST

Brazil’s Lula gears up for ‘last dance’ with run for fourth presidential term
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will stand for re-election in Brazil on Sunday. At 80, the former steelworker hopes to capitalise on his popularity and economic successes to win a fourth term in office but is neck-and-neck in the polls with far-right rival Flavio Bolsonaro.
Nearly four decades after Lula’s first run for the Brazilian presidency, his name will appear on the ballot for a seventh time on October 4 as he aims to win a fourth term at the helm of Latin America’s largest economy.
This is despite a promise that his third tenure would be his last. “If I’m elected, I will only serve one term as president,” he said in the days leading up to his 2022 victory over former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Although Lula vowed to step aside and allow for “the emergence of new leaders” on the left, he now looks like the only presidential candidate who might beat far-right rival Flavio Bolsonaro – the eldest son of Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup.
Polls show Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro neck-and-neck in a race that has seen other candidates sidelined.
Read moreLula and Bolsonaro’s mudslinging heats up ahead of weekend vote
Throughout his campaign Lula, who will turn 81 on October 27, has tried to reassure voters that his age should not count against him.
“I’m in great health,” he said when he announced his candidacy in August, praising the benefits of his exercise routine.
But he has also promised – and this time “for real” – that if Brazilians elect him on Sunday it will be his last term.
‘Working-class roots’
On the campaign trail Lula has relied on a previous successful tactic: showing solidarity with Brazil’s working class.
Born into a poor family in Brazil’s northeastern Pernambuco state, Lula spent his childhood working as a shoe-shiner and courier in Sao Paulo before training as a lathe operator.
He rose through the ranks of the factory workers’ labour unions and became one of the faces of the largescale metalworkers strikes in Sao Paulo in the late 70s during the final years of Brazil’s military dictatorship.
In Brazil, “politics goes beyond a partisan framework,” said Marcia Dias, director of the school of political science at Rio de Janeiro’s Federal University of the State. “In terms of social policies, it's clear that Lula has a deep understanding of the daily lives and struggles of ordinary people.”
“His backstory of moving from the northeast, being raised by a single mother and trying to survive in a big city like Sao Paulo means he symbolises the Brazilian spirit for a lot of people.”
It is no coincidence that Lula launched his 2026 presidential campaign in the state of Sao Paulo at the football stadium in the Vila Euclides neighbourhood in Sao Bernardo do Campo district – an area known for its deep ties to the 1970s labour movement.
In his first campaign speech he leaned heavily on his “working-class roots”, paying tribute to his mother and speaking at length about his years as a trade unionist.
President ‘Little Lula peace and love’
In front of the crowd there to support him, Lula also referenced his 2026 treatment for early-stage skin cancer on his scalp. “I will risk my health, and I will take my hat off to all of you,” he said, before launching into a run-down of his previous administration’s successes.
The perennial leader of the Brazilian left has an unusually long record to draw on: few Latin American leaders have spent so long at the heart of government.
His career in politics began in 1980 as one of the founders of the Workers’ Party. He first stood for the presidency in 1989, then 1994 and 1998, but failed to win. At the time, the former union leader was viewed with suspicion by employers and some of the middle class.
He knew he had to build broader alliances and change his image to succeed, which led to him adopting the nickname "Lulinha Paz e Amor" (“Little Lula peace and love”) in a bid to soften his reputation.
The combative and radical trade unionist with a bushy beard soon started appearing in elegant suits and courting the private sector – and the strategy worked.
Lula won the presidency in 2002 with more than 60 percent of second-round votes becoming the country’s first labourer elected to the Planalto palace. He was re-elected four years later.
These two terms brought economic growth and social policies that transformed the lives of millions of people in Brazil.
Alongside measures such as a rise in minimum wages, Lula’s “Bolsa Familia” programme for low-income families was credited with raising 20 million people out of poverty.
Corruption accusations
As Lula’s popularity soared among the working class, Lula was also embroiled in corruption scandals that destroyed his reputation so badly that he dropped out of political life.
These included an alleged vote-buying ring in Congress orchestrated by the left-wing party between 2002 and 2005 which became the largest scandal involving the embezzlement of public funds ever uncovered in Brazil.
Lula was found guilty of corruption and money laundering in 2017. He spent 580 days in prison and was barred from running in the 2018 election.
But the ruling was revoked in 2021 by Brazil’s Federal Supreme Court which found that the trial lacked jurisdiction and that judge Sergio Moro had shown bias in certain proceedings.
After 12 years on the political sidelines, Lula returned to centre stage in 2022 with a successful presidential run against Jair Bolsonaro.
Despite the scandals, the leader of the left had maintained a powerful hold over the electorate.
“At least 30 percent of people who voted for Lula never believed the corruption accusations against him and never stopped supporting him,” said Dias.
“And when his conviction was overturned some of those who had been disappointed started to believe in him again.”
Read moreFlavio Bolsonaro probed for corruption as Brazil election tightens
A mixed economic record
When Lula returned to power in 2022 found a country that was very different from the one he governed from 2003-2010.
Even so, he has come to the end of his third term with some notable wins: unemployment rates are at a historic low, inflation has slowed, poverty rates are declining and the government voted in May to reduce the maximum workweek and ensure all workers get at least two rest days.
At the same time, growth has slowed, public debt has increased and household debt remains high. In other words, a large number of Brazilians are not feeling economic improvements in their pockets.
And, as Lula seeks re-election, his popularity levels are significantly lower than the first time he left office.
Some 34 percent of Brazilians think that he has managed the country well or excellently compared with 40 percent who think he has done a bad or very bad job, according to a September 24 poll published by Datafolha.
Security and scandals
Concerns over the cost of living and the balance of public finances have weighed on the octogenarian’s campaign. And there is another cloud on the horizon: the difficult issue of security, which persists despite Lula’s anti-crime policies.
Recent months have also seen the presidential race dominated by controversies and scandals.
Most recently there was a national outcry over fears that evangelical Christian Flavio Bolsonaro would strip the country’s patron saint Our Lady of Aparecida of her status if he was elected.
A denial from Bolsonaro did not stop Lula seizing the opportunity to be photographed with statuettes and images of the saint, who is a symbol of Brazil’s multicultural heritage.
But, even if Lula does not inspire the same levels of support as he used to, the Workers’ Party has been unable to find a better candidate.
In 46 years, the party has produced governors, ministers, mayors, and other presidential candidates – but no one who can replace Lula, despite him saying in 2022 that he wanted to use his term to foster new leadership.
"Lula’s leadership is very important for the party," said Dias. “He is one of the founding members that links Workers Party to the social movements of the 1970s. It remains the largest party not just in Brazil but also in Latin America.”
“The last time Lula was able to pass the baton was to Dilma Rousseff [who served as Brazil's president from 2011 to 2016],” Dias added. "Admittedly, we probably need new leaders right now. But today, no one is better equipped than Lula to confront the threat of the Bolsonaros’ radical neoliberalism.”
Read more'Banking on a national brand': Bolsonaro sons Carlos, Jair Renan run for power in Brazil's south
‘Meddling’ Trump
Beyond Brazil’s borders there is another major factor that could swing the election: the influence of US President Donald Trump who is fuelling the rise of the far right throughout South America.
While the US president has not publicly endorsed Flavio Bolsonaro, he has been accused of “meddling” in the Presidential campaign by imposing high tariffs in July that Lula’s government said were “illegal".
This leaves Lula walking a tightrope between maintaining good relations with Washington and presenting himself as a bulwark against North American imperialism.
Representatives from Brazil and the United States had a “constructive” discussion on trade relations in Brasilia on Wednesday, according to Brazilian authorities.
Meanwhile, Lula insisted at the UN last week that his country would never be “anyone’s backyard”.
He has signalled his intention to “deepen” Brazil’s ties with China and the other BRICS members and advocated for the use of strategic resources such as rare earth elements to boost the country’s industrial development.
On a national level, Lula’s manifesto is tried and tested – boosting the minimum wage, Bolsa Família and public investment, reducing inequality and expanding social rights – with the addition of improving security and the fight against organised crime.
After nearly four decades of public life, three presidential losses and three wins, 580 days in prison, and a return to power that few believed possible, Lula heads into Sunday’s election without the favourable poll numbers of the past and with a deeply polarised country.
He maintains that this will be his last run at the presidency. Brazil’s voters will decide on October 4 whether Lula will have one last dance.

Carney plans to visit Turkey this month, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:18:32 UTC
01:18:32 KST

Carney plans to visit Turkey this month, sources say
OTTAWA, Oct 2 - Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney plans to visit Turkey this month to meet President Tayyip Erdogan in what would be the first dedicated bilateral visit to the country by a Canadian leader, four sources with knowledge of the visit said.
One of the sources said Carney and Erdogan could discuss the free-trade talks they launched on the sidelines of a NATO summit in Ankara in July, as well as potential energy and defense cooperation. Canadian and Turkish trade ministers agreed this week to accelerate the talks ahead of the leaders' meeting, two sources said.
The visit would mark Carney's latest break with Canadian diplomatic convention as he seeks to reduce the country's reliance on the United States, by far its biggest trading partner, after a collapse in trade talks in August.
TRADE WAR
Carney has vowed to double Canada's non-US trade over the next decade and has rushed to establish ties with a host of countries, including China and India, with which it had past strains.
He has focused less on human rights than his predecessors to forge ahead, backed by polls showing strong support among Canadians for his efforts to reinforce the economy in the face of US tariffs.
Erdogan, Turkey's leader of 23 years — whom rights groups have criticized for a crackdown on the political opposition since 2024 — seeks new markets and collaboration for the regional military power's burgeoning defense industry. Erdogan says an independent judiciary is probing the opposition and rejects claims it is politically motivated.
Turkey, an emerging market economy whose biggest trading partner is the European Union, also seeks partnerships and investment in energy, infrastructure and mining.
The sources did not share the dates or agenda of the visit planned later this month.
Carney's office and Erdogan's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
LESS FOCUS ON RIGHTS
Western powers have grown relatively silent on Turkey's rights record as it has become a leading defense-industrial power and a bulwark against Russian aggression.
Since last month, a wave of arrests and restrictions has targeted Turkey's LGBTQ+ community in a probe the government says aims to protect children and family values, but which has drawn sharp criticism from rights groups and some European officials.
No Canadian prime minister is known to have made a standalone bilateral visit to Turkey in recent decades, though they have met Erdogan and other Turkish leaders on the sidelines of multilateral gatherings, including NATO and G20 summits hosted by Turkey.
MODEST BILATERAL TRADE
At the NATO leaders' summit in July, Carney and Erdogan formally launched negotiations for a free-trade agreement.
That month, Turkey agreed to join Canada's Defence Security and Resilience Bank as one of 10 founding member nations of Carney's multilateral "middle powers" bank.
The two countries' trade ministers met in June and planned to expand cooperation on renewable and nuclear energy, a Canadian government statement said, listing aerospace, defense and security as areas of potential new partnerships.
Turkey has held talks with Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis as well as South Korea's Korea Electric Power Corporation and China's State Power Investment Corporation about potentially building its second and third nuclear power plants, and Russia's Rosatom is building its first.
An executive at AtkinsRealis, which holds the exclusive license for Canadian-designed CANDU reactors, told Reuters this year that it anticipates Turkey will complete an early review of its CANDU reactors following an information exchange, which may lead to concrete talks for a plant bid.
In a step that helped thaw bilateral ties in 2024, Canada removed weapons-export controls on Turkey, including on optical technology used in drones that Turkey exports to dozens of nations.
Yet bilateral trade is small.
Turkey accounted for less than 0.3% of Canada's total merchandise trade in 2025, or C$4.34 billion ($3.05 billion), compared with C$1 trillion with the US, Statistics Canada data shows.
Canada mainly exports lentils, aircraft and electronics to Turkey, and imports medical devices, fishing vessels, aircraft engines and jewelry. REUTERS

Spain housing protesters vow new rallies after parliament vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:16:00 UTC
01:16:00 KST

Housing protesters in Spain vowed to return to the streets and continue their encampment in central Madrid after parliament on Friday rejected the government's proposed response to the country's deepening housing crisis.
Crowds gathered outside the assembly chanted "your profits, our misery" as lawmakers voted down the minority government's decree that had been drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman.
Protesters expressed exasperation as the debate in parliament over the measures highlighted bitter divisions about how to address the crisis. Earlier on Friday, Spanish media said Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez might call a snap election for November if the legislation failed to pass.
Sanchez's office declined to comment on the reports.
The legislation had sought to ban evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, impose a two-year rent freeze extension for existing leases and introduce tighter rules for short-term rentals.
The decrees failed after lawmakers from Catalan separatist party Junts - a sometime ally of the left-wing government - joined the opposition in voting it down, arguing that the proposals would exacerbate matters by reducing housing supply. A second decree proposing automatic and indefinite renewal of rental contracts also failed.
The Tenants' Union, which had driven the protests, said it would press on with plans for more mass rallies for Saturday, piling pressure on the coalition.
The eviction of pensioner Maricarmen Abascal last week triggered protests across Spain. Young people pitched tents in Madrid's central square and other cities for almost a week, reviving memories of anti-austerity sit-ins sparked by the global financial crisis in 2008-12.
"The encampment will continue and will continue expanding to other neighbourhoods. We're aiming for a general strike," Tenants' Union spokesperson Alicia del Rio said after the decrees were struck down.
Abascal's eviction unleashed anger over the cost of housing, with many young people living with parents past 30 years of age.
Rents have doubled over the last decade with average prices reaching €1,176 ($1,323) a month, equivalent to 98.7% of the average salary for a young person, according to the Youth Council of Spain.
Sanchez's coalition government has 147 seats in the 350-seat chamber and relies on smaller parties, including Junts, to pass legislation.
Junts parliamentary spokesperson Miriam Nogueras said the decrees would have the opposite effect of their intended aims. "Finding housing will become more difficult every day. Our responsibility is to provide certainty, not uncertainty."
She urged the government to work on a new decree.
The opposition People's Party also voted against the measures.
"Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building more homes. We’re not going to lie to you - it’s not going to be easy, and it’s not going to happen quickly," said PP lawmaker Juan Bravo.
Sanchez, who in recent months has faced pressure over the government's handling of a migrant crisis in Ceuta and accusations of corruption in his party, could decide that calling an election would be a good way to change the narrative, said Alejandro Quiroga, a political scientist at the Complutense University of Madrid.
"This could be Sanchez’s last big chance to become prime minister again," Quiroga said. "By swapping Ceuta for Maricarmen, you’re setting up a new framework for the conversation."
PP leader Alberto Nuñez Feijoo said he would welcome a snap election.
"If the prime minister needed a story to call an election and thus try to cover up corruption we still don't know about, then so be it. He has the alibi - just set a date," Feijoo said in a press conference after the vote.

Russian-Linked Saboteurs Tried to Blow Up Ukrainian An-124 at Leipzig Airport, Investigation Finds

2026-10-02

01:14:48 KST

- Category

Russian-Linked Saboteurs Tried to Blow Up Ukrainian An-124 at Leipzig Airport, Investigation Finds
A Russian national with alleged ties to a senior Russian military intelligence figure is suspected of masterminding a failed sabotage attack targeting Germany’s Leipzig-Halle Airport, according to a joint investigation by The Telegraph and Welt am Sonntag.
The investigation identified Oleg Levushkin, a Russian passport holder, as the suspected organizer of the operation, which involved a drone carrying a container packed with explosives. The drone struck the wing of a parked Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo aircraft at the airport but failed to detonate.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Citing classified intelligence documents from Germany, Lithuania, and Poland, as well as interviews with senior Western intelligence officials, the outlets reported that Levushkin traveled to Germany with a proxy agent to prepare the attack. German investigators suspect he planned the operation before instructing Belarusian national Andrei Karshakou, described by officials as a “disposable agent,” to carry it out.
Levushkin has maintained contact for years with Denis Smolyaninov, whom Lithuanian intelligence identified in a December 2025 report as the head of the Ukraine department within Russia’s GRU military intelligence service, according to The Telegraph. The report described Smolyaninov as specializing in psychological operations and linked him to covert sabotage campaigns in Europe organized through Telegram.
The Leipzig operation has been linked to GRU unit 29155, which German intelligence officials regard as a key force behind Russian sabotage operations in Europe. A senior German intelligence official told the outlets that Germany was increasingly becoming an “operational theatre” for Russian intelligence services, with activities previously considered isolated now occurring on a broader scale.
According to the investigation, Levushkin traveled to Germany via Türkiye and rented a vehicle at Berlin Airport about a week before the attack. Investigators said location data from the rental car indicated that he traveled to several suspected weapons caches and conducted reconnaissance near the terminals at Leipzig-Halle Airport on July 31.
Investigators suspect that 1.8 kilograms of Semtex used in the operation was smuggled into Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia, hidden in compartments inside trucks. Five days after Levushkin allegedly surveyed the airport, a drone carrying the explosives hit the wing of the Ukrainian An-124 and fell onto the runway without exploding.
The aircraft was carrying approximately 25,000 liters of jet fuel at the time. Investigators assessed that an explosion could have caused severe damage at the airport. Police subsequently recovered debris from two additional drones and discovered an improvised antenna array attached to a nearby tree, which investigators believe was used as a control relay, The Telegraph reported.
DNA matching Karshakou was later recovered from a fragment of a glove attached to the antenna. His DNA profile had previously been registered in Finnish and Lithuanian criminal databases, and Polish authorities subsequently linked him to a 2024 arson attack at a home improvement store in Łódź that prosecutors classified as state-sponsored sabotage.
The investigation also found similarities between the explosive device recovered in Leipzig and devices discovered in other suspected Russian sabotage operations across Europe. Lithuanian forensic reports found that metal components from homemade bombs recovered at several locations had been manufactured using the same equipment.
The Russian Embassy in Berlin rejected allegations of Russian involvement, describing them as “baseless accusations” and accusing European governments of using such claims to justify increased military spending.
“The purpose of this is obvious. Arguments are needed to maintain a persistently high level of anti-Russian paranoia that would justify the European elites’ immense military expenditure, as well as their misguided political and economic decisions. Since no such arguments exist and Russia does not in fact pose a threat to Europe, they have to be invented and disseminated to the public,” the embassy stated, according to The Telegraph.
The incident has also drawn a response from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who described the attempted attack at Leipzig-Halle Airport as an operation carried out by Russian intelligence operatives using military-grade materials on European Union territory.
Von der Leyen said that if Moscow had intended the incident to weaken European support for Ukraine, it had instead strengthened European countries’ determination to continue backing Kyiv.

AI Is Now Watching NATO’s Border With Belarus—And Poland Is Adding Robots Too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:14:34 UTC
01:14:34 KST

- Category
- World
AI Is Now Watching NATO’s Border With Belarus—And Poland Is Adding Robots Too
Poland has begun using artificial intelligence to monitor its border with Belarus, combining feeds from cameras, drones, and other sensors into a single system that automatically flags suspicious activity for soldiers and Border Guard officers.
The platform, known as Inteligentna Granica, or Intelligent Border, is already operating as part of Poland’s Operation Safe Podlasie, according to Defence Blog on October 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The military operation supports Poland’s Border Guard along one of NATO’s most closely watched eastern frontiers.
Instead of requiring personnel to continuously monitor dozens of individual camera feeds, Intelligent Border analyzes incoming data, recognizes objects, assesses their behavior and directs operators toward incidents that may require intervention.
According to Defence Blog, Poland is currently testing the system across a section of the Belarusian border several dozen kilometers long.
The trials extend beyond artificial intelligence. Poland’s Operational Command said robotics and autonomous systems are also being tested, though officials have not disclosed which platforms are involved, how many are deployed or the precise location of the test zone.
The system was developed jointly by Poland’s Artificial Intelligence Implementation Center—part of the country’s Cyberspace Defense Forces—and the Border Guard.
Its purpose is not to remove humans from border security decisions, but to dramatically reduce the amount of time personnel spend manually staring at surveillance footage.
The AI instead acts as a filter, identifying potentially significant movement and giving human operators a much narrower set of events to examine.
Defence Blog noted that data from cameras, observation equipment and other sensors can be fused into the same operational picture.
The Border Guard is responsible for installing and maintaining the surveillance infrastructure and providing its data, while the military handles much of the analysis.
At the center of that military component is AIRON TACTIC, an artificial intelligence platform developed by Poland’s cyber forces.
Information generated by the system can then be fed into TAK and JAŚMIN tactical command systems already used by Polish troops and Border Guard personnel.
That means a suspicious movement detected by a camera or drone can potentially move rapidly from automated recognition to the tactical networks used by forces operating on the ground.
Polish officials have described the project as part of a wider effort to automate surveillance along the country’s eastern frontier.
Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said earlier this year that Intelligent Border was expected to move into operational use in August.
Defence Blog reported that Brig. Gen. Jarosław Chojnacki, chief of staff of Poland’s Operational Command, recently reviewed the system’s progress during a visit to Task Group Podlasie, receiving a briefing on both its deployment and day-to-day performance.
The technology is arriving on a border already guarded by a substantial military presence.
Operation Safe Podlasie began on August 1, 2024, replacing two previous Polish military missions along the eastern frontier.
More than 10,000 troops participated in one recent rotation, with around 5,000 soldiers supporting the Border Guard along the Belarusian border each day.
Polish forces have supported border officers there since 2021, when Warsaw accused the government in Minsk of deliberately channeling migrants toward the Polish frontier as part of a hybrid pressure campaign.
Since then, Poland has steadily hardened the border with physical barriers, observation towers, thermal cameras, drone-detection equipment and additional military infrastructure.
Earlier, Belarus moved troops and military equipment to its borders with Poland and Lithuania for four-day command-staff exercises, with part of the maneuvers occurring right near the Suwałki Gap—a strategically vital section of the Polish-Lithuanian border for NATO.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) currently sees more risks of further downward revision to its forecast for Ukraine's gross domestic product than opportunities for growth, EBRD President Odile Renaud-Basso said.
"We see the economic slowing, really clearly, since August, with the intensification of the strikes on economic infrastructure. So it used to be mostly energy, but now it’s also ports, the port blockage plus the Black Sea blockage plus the attacks on logistics, on warehouses, on manufacturing capacities and so on," she said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine, commenting on assessments by the Ukrainian government, the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) and independent analysts regarding the slowdown in economic growth.
Commenting on the forecasts, Renaud-Basso said that the central bank had developed several different scenarios, but at this point the EBRD sees risks of further deterioration outweighing the risks of an improvement in the indicators.
As reported, the EBRD downgraded its forecast for Ukraine's GDP growth in 2026 to 1.5% and in 2027 to 2.5%.
Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said he allows for a downward revision of the 2027 GDP growth forecast by 0.3-0.5 percentage points from the already incorporated pessimistic plan, from 1.3% to 0.8-1%, and for 2026 to 0.5% from the current forecast of 1.6%.
In addition, the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) lowered its estimate for real GDP growth this year to 1.1-1.2%, compared with its estimate of 1.8% at the end of July this year.
