G7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:57:13 UTC
00:57:13 KST

Leaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel.
The French President, Emmanuel Macron, said ministers from some of world’s largest economies had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks on Friday.
Macron convened the leaders’ video call to discuss the global surge in diesel prices, and Trump’s threat to cut off US diesel exports unless Europe tapped their own stockpiles to help cool global markets.
Under proposals reportedly drawn up by Macron, the current G7 chair, members will release 50m barrels of diesel and 50m of crude oil into the global market to ease prices.
The agreement suggests European countries will avoid being cut off from vital supplies of US diesel after coming under pressure from the White House in recent days to release their emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban.
Trump said he was considering a ban on diesel exports after the surge in sales to overseas buyers pushed US diesel prices to record highs in a blow to the economy before the US midterm elections in November.
Macron said G7 nations – which also includes the US, UK, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan – wanted to “work in a coordinated manner to help bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”.
He added that the G7 members and partners would front-load a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days and that ministers would discuss the “possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary” in the coming days.
“We have all committed together to releasing these strategic reserves in the proportions I mentioned, with a focus on diesel, and we are all committed to ensuring there are no export bans, and President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point,” Macron said.
Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Europe had “agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil” and that the process would start “immediately”.
The threat of a US export ban presented a considerable challenge for Europe, which produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries but relies on imports to make up the shortfall.
The ongoing disruption to fossil fuel exports from the Middle East has limited output from the region’s refineries as well as those in China, which is a leading buyer of Gulf crude. Meanwhile, Russian refineries have come under attack from Ukraine, causing its fuel output to fall to 20-year lows.
In response, the US exported a record high of 1.9m barrels a week to overseas buyers in early August as the slump in global refining squeezed supplies across Europe and Asia.
The record exports caused the US’s own distillate stockpiles to fall to their lowest seasonal levels since 1996, causing diesel pump prices to climb above $5.85 a gallon (£1.18 a litre) for the first time in early September.
The proposed ban on US exports was expected to fuel greater competition for cargoes on the global market which would push prices in the UK and Europe well beyond current record levels.
In the UK, the average price of diesel at the pumps climbed to a record high of £2 a litre on forecourts on Friday, putting more pressure on motorists and the wider economy.
The cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, according to the RAC motoring group, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war. UK lorries, vans and farming vehicles are also typically diesel-fuelled, meaning the price rises will be felt in the higher cost of goods across the economy.
Brent crude oil was trading at just above $100 (£76) a barrel on Friday, compared with about $72 before the Iran war started. It fell to about $98 a barrel after news of the emergency stockpile release before returning to more than $102 a barrel by the end of the day.
Macquarie Group’s Walt Chancellor said Europe’s decision to rely more on its own emergency reserves than US imports would not address the underlying problem in the US or the global market.
“The core issue the US faces is not a diesel problem. Nor is it a refined product problem. It may not even be a petroleum problem. It is a global energy problem,” he said, according to CNBC.
“So what is the solution then? In short, more oil through the strait of Hormuz and out of the Middle East. Anything short of that is really just shuffling deck chairs,” he added.
The IEA, the world’s energy watchdog, ordered the largest release of government oil reserves in its history in March when it agreed to release 400m barrels of emergency crude, to help calm the oil price shock sparked by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
The intervention represented a third of the group’s total government stockpiles and was more than double the release of 182m barrels of oil made in 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

When the crew became the crisis: Air India’s 2009 mid-air brawl
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:54:21 UTC
00:54:21 KST

A brawl 17 years ago brought into question flight safety
The flight carrying 106 passengers from Sharjah to Delhi via Lucknow witnessed a mid-air confrontation that raised questions about cockpit discipline and flight safetyThe recent flydubai incident has highlighted an unusual aviation danger: what happens when those responsible for flying an aircraft become part of the crisis themselves.Captain Smit Machchhar was reportedly attacked by his co-pilot during a flight, triggering a dangerous descent before the injured captain managed to open the cockpit door and allow others to intervene. The aircraft eventually landed safely.Seventeen years earlier, an Indian Airlines (then a subsidiary of Air India) flight witnessed a mid-air confrontation that raised similar questions about cockpit discipline and flight safety.
A fight at 30,000 feetOn October 3, 2009, Indian Airlines flight IC-884 was carrying 106 passengers from Sharjah to Delhi via Lucknow. While cruising at around 30,000 feet over Pakistan, Captain Ranbir Arora and co-pilot Aditya Chopra became embroiled in a dispute with flight purser Amit Khanna and flight attendant Komal Singh.Reports said the confrontation spilled between the cockpit and galley while the Airbus A320 was airborne.The dispute had begun before take-off from Sharjah.From argument to violenceIn Sharjah, the cabin crew met Captain Ranbir Arora and co-pilot Aditya Chopra for a pre-flight briefing, during which the two sides were believed to have had an altercation.“The cabin crew lobby said that after the initial tension on the ground in Sharjah, when the woman crew member [Komal Singh] went into the cockpit, one of the pilots held her hand and then pushed her out of the cockpit,” according to a TOI report.
She reportedly hit the cockpit door and began bleeding.Khanna then intervened, according to a cabin crew representative, who alleged that the pilots became abusive and fought with him.The pilots denied the allegation. They instead accused Khanna of misconduct that they claimed had compromised flight safety. Bosses of three firms that supply trains to UK railways made £3.5m last year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:54:18 UTC
00:54:18 KST

The chief executives of three firms that rent out trains to Britain’s railways were paid a combined £3.5m last year as they passed on almost £400m to shareholders in dividends.
Rail unions accused the rolling stock companies (Roscos) of raking in profits at passengers’ expense.
The figures emerged in accounts published this week after ministers announced a new rolling stock strategy for Britain’s railways.
The government is considering direct ownership of trains through the public body Great British Railways rather than leasing them from the private sector.
The latest figures show Porterbrook Holdings paid £80m in dividends and increased the pay of its chief executive, Mary Grant, by more than 10% to £1.44m.
Eversholt Rail paid out £200m in 2025 shortly before it was sold by CK Hutchison to Beacon Rail, with its departing CEO, Mary Kenny, paid £1.33m.
Angel Trains paid £111m in dividends and a relatively modest £700,000 to its boss, Malcolm Brown.
Their pay far outstrips the highest salaries elsewhere on the railway, including the bosses of Network Rail and HS2.
The RMT union called for a levy on Roscos after highlighting the dividend payments and salaries. It said the three biggest Roscos had paid out £2.4bn over the last 10 years in dividends.
The general secretary of the RMT, Eddie Dempsey, said: “The government’s commitment to explore publicly owned rolling stock for the new trains in the future is welcome but in a cost of living crisis we need action now.
“We are calling on the government to use this month’s budget to introduce a ‘cost of travel’ levy on profits to fund a 3.4% fare cut, rather than watching the cash being salted away.”
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, told the Labour conference on Monday that if Great British Railways owning trains would best serve taxpayers and passengers, then we should do it”.
According to the rail regulator, operators last year spent more than £4bn leasing trains from the Roscos, whose net profit margin was 18.5%.
A spokesperson for Porterbrook said it had “deployed over £1bn of capital in new trains, fleet upgrades, traction innovation and rail infrastructure since 2020, and we are actively looking to invest a further £1bn in the years ahead”.
They said the group’s companies were UK tax resident, and had paid £82m in the past three years, adding: “It is because of the funding that our shareholders provide that we can make substantial investments in the railway.”
Angel Trains is incorporated in Jersey and within the realm of UK taxes. A spokesperson said: “We believe decisions on future fleets should be focused on securing the best outcomes for passengers, while maintaining the conditions and opportunities needed to attract future investment into the railway. We look forward to continuing to work constructively with government and Great British Railways.”
Eversholt and its new owner, Beacon Rail, were approached for comment.

G7 to release 100 million barrels from oil reserves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:52:34 UTC
00:52:34 KST

The Group of Seven (G7) agreed on Oct. 2 to release 100 million barrels of crude oil and fuel from emergency reserves over four months to ease rising energy prices.
French President Emmanuel Macron announced the agreement following a virtual meeting of G7 leaders.
The release will begin immediately under International Energy Agency (IEA) coordination, with substantial diesel supplies to reach the market within the first 20 days.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that Europe had agreed to release a “massive amount” of diesel from its stocks.
“The process will begin immediately,” he wrote.
The agreement followed pressure from Washington on European countries to release reserves, with Trump raising the prospect of restrictions on U.S. diesel exports to help lower domestic fuel prices.
Before the announcement, European Commission spokeswoman Anna-Kaisa Itkonen warned that an export ban would damage relations with Washington.
“A ban would not be beneficial to anyone. It would undermine our trust in the United States as a reliable partner,” she told reporters in Brussels.
Itkonen said the EU was ready to coordinate action through the IEA, which would organize any release of reserves.
In their joint statement, G7 leaders reaffirmed their commitment to avoid restrictions on energy exports between member countries and urged other producers to refrain from bans that could worsen market pressures.
They also agreed to coordinate refinery maintenance to prevent simultaneous shutdowns and temporarily increase production where possible.
The group will discuss possible additional diesel releases through the IEA in the coming days.

In Kyiv, the "operating mode" of the bridges has been determined: where traffic is blocked during air raids and where it is not
Kyiv • UNN
The Southern Bridge is completely closed, while partial restrictions are in place on the other crossings. The Darnytskyi Bridge is operating without restrictions.
The capital authorities have disclosed the “operating mode” of Kyiv’s bridges—where traffic is fully restricted during air-raid alerts, where it is partially restricted, and where it is not restricted, reports UNN.
Details
According to Petro Panteleiev, acting first deputy head of the Kyiv City State Administration, the current situation with traffic on the capital’s bridges across the Dnipro is as follows:
-  The Southern Bridge is currently completely closed to vehicular traffic in both directions. Today, expert conclusions from specialized research institutes are expected in response to a request from the Ministry for Infrastructure concerning the bridge’s further operation and the resumption of metro traffic across it;  
-  traffic across the Metro Bridge from the left bank to the right bank is partially restricted during an air-raid alert;  
-  traffic across Paton Bridge is permitted; however, during an air-raid alert, traffic from the right bank to the left bank is restricted; 
-  The Northern Bridge operates without restrictions; however, during an air-raid alert, traffic from the right bank to the left bank is also restricted;  
-  on the Podilskyi Bridge crossing, traffic from the right bank to the left bank is restricted during an air-raid alert, while the bridge continues to operate in a reversible-traffic mode;  
-  The Darnytskyi Bridge operates without restrictions. 
We would add
According to Panteleiev, city services, together with the military, law enforcement agencies, and other authorities, continue to work on optimal traffic schemes and routes for city residents, municipal services, and other services. A meeting of the Kyiv Defense Council was held, following which the city sent its proposals to the central authorities.
“The city is currently taking measures to adapt traffic and related processes of the city’s vital activities in view of the existing threats. The enemy is deliberately shelling the capital’s bridges connecting the left and right banks. We are taking into account private vehicle traffic volumes and the movement of public surface transport across the bridges,” he said.
What does the police say?
Later, Oleksii Biloshytskyi, head of the Patrol Police Department, adjusted the capital authorities’ information on temporary traffic restrictions during an air-raid alert:
🔹On the Southern Bridge — vehicular traffic is completely blocked from both banks;
🔹On the Darnytskyi Bridge — vehicular traffic will proceed in one lane from the right bank to the left bank;
🔹On the Metro Bridge — vehicular traffic is blocked from the left bank to the right bank;
🔹On the Podilskyi–Voskresenskyi Bridge — vehicular traffic will be blocked from the left bank to the right bank.
Please treat the implemented changes to the organization of traffic with understanding and take this information into account when planning your travel route
We would remind you
As Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko reported earlier, military personnel, law enforcement officers, the State Emergency Service, and municipal services were heard during a meeting of the city’s Defense Council. They submitted proposals to ensure security while taking into account the need to preserve logistical transport connections between the left and right banks. The operation of the “green” metro line was also discussed. The Kyiv Metro is ready to resume traffic across the Southern Bridge during a yellow-level air-raid alert after receiving an expert opinion on the condition of the structure.

UK diesel prices reach record level amid Middle East conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:50:30 UTC
00:50:30 KST

Aysu Bicer
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Britain’s Transport Minister Keir Mather said on Friday the country’s diesel supply remains “robust” and “resilient” despite record prices and growing concerns over global fuel supplies.
The average price of diesel in the UK reached £2 (nearly $2.7) per liter on Wednesday amid rising pressure on global energy markets linked to the conflict between the US, Israel and Iran.
“I want to reassure people this morning that the UK has got a diverse range of supply when it comes to diesel,” Mather told Sky News.
“We have resilience built into our system for that reason,” he added, saying Britain was working with the US, the International Energy Agency and European partners to sustain diesel flows.
Mather also pointed to the government’s decision to keep fuel duty frozen, saying people “shouldn’t be concerned about shortages because of the inherent resilience that is built into that system.”
The RAC motoring organization said diesel prices reached a record 199.33 pence per liter earlier this week, surpassing the previous record of 199.09 pence set in June 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Diesel prices have risen by 59 pence per litre, or nearly 40%, since the US-Israel conflict with Iran began at the end of February.
More than half of the UK’s diesel is imported, with 31% of those imports coming from the US.
Separately, G7 leaders have agreed to work “in a coordinated manner” to ease diesel prices. Measures include making production more flexible, releasing strategic reserves of up to 100 million barrels within four months, and avoiding energy restrictions among partner countries.
The developments come after US President Donald Trump said he could ask European countries to release diesel reserves while considering restrictions on US fuel exports.

Taliban Mounted BM-27 Uragan MLRS Launcher on BMP Chassis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:49:22 UTC
00:49:22 KST

Taliban militants have created an improvised multiple rocket launcher by mounting the artillery unit from 220 mm BM-27 Uragan multiple rocket launcher onto the tracked chassis of a BMP-1 or BMP-2 infantry fighting vehicle.
A video published by the Ministry of Defense of Afghanistan shows the homemade combat vehicle being transported on a wheeled semi-trailer towed by a tractor.
Judging by the footage, the standard turret with its armament has been completely removed from the BMP’s tracked chassis, and in its place, a rotating platform has been installed with the MLRS artillery unit, which includes a cluster of 16 launch tubes.
To ensure the vehicle’s stability while firing, two retractable jacks are installed at the rear of the hull; these rest on the ground and relieve the load on the running gear.
Historically, the Soviet Union actively supplied armored vehicles and artillery to Afghanistan in the 1970s and 1980s. In total, the Afghan army received over 1,000 BMP-1 and BMP-2 units, as well as approximately 50 BM-27 Uragan launchers.
A significant portion of this equipment was lost or rendered inoperable during years of combat, but the remaining vehicles fell into the hands of the Taliban after they seized power in the country in 2021.
The BM-27 Uragan multiple rocket launcher is a Soviet 220 mm multiple rocket launcher system developed in the 1970s to engage enemy personnel, armored vehicles, command posts, and fortifications.
The standard chassis for the BM-27 is the ZIL-135LM wheeled vehicle with an 8×8 wheel configuration.
The primary ammunition for the Uragan consists of 9M27F rockets with a 100-kg high-explosive fragmentation warhead, as well as 9M27K cluster rockets containing fragmentation, anti-personnel, and anti-tank mines.
The maximum firing range of the Uragan MLRS is 35 km, and a full salvo of 16 rockets is fired in 20 seconds.
By mounting the launcher on a tracked chassis, the Taliban sought to improve the system’s mobility in the mountainous and off-road terrain of Afghanistan.
At the same time, this modification significantly increases the load on the BMP’s running gear and suspension, which could negatively affect its reliability and firing accuracy.

Historic canals turn green in Belgium’s Ghent amid autumn warmth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

00:48:48 KST

Historic canals turn green in Belgium’s Ghent amid autumn warmth
- Historic canals in Ghent, Belgium, are covered with bright green duckweed due to record-breaking heat and lack of rain, creating an unusual autumn scene.
- The duckweed bloom is unprecedented in scale, affecting the Lys river and canals, thriving in warm temperatures over 20°C and stagnant water.
- While harmless to humans, the duckweed threatens aquatic life and disrupts boat tours, causing engine problems and raising concerns over climate change impacts.
AI generated
GHENT, Belgium – A bright green film carpets the historic canals in the medieval Belgian town of Ghent, as tourists and students relax along its edge in the unseasonable autumn warmth.
The blanket of duckweed covering the water has proliferated dramatically due to a lack of rain and record-breaking temperatures.
Like much of Europe, Belgium in recent months experienced an exceptional series of heatwaves, with the summer of 2026 being declared the hottest in its history.
“We’ve never seen anything like this here in Ghent,” Davide Siddi, who captains a boat giving tours of the canal, told AFP.
“It’s been like this for three weeks to a month.”
The lack of rainfall coupled with the unusually warm weather – with temperatures in September still regularly exceeding 20 deg C – provide the ideal conditions for the duckweed to flourish.
“Normally, the plant is found where water is stagnant, but at the moment it is spreading everywhere,” Geert Weymeis, head of Flanders Waterways, told AFP.
“This is the first time we have seen it grow on such a massive scale here.”
Weymeis said the phenomenon mainly affects the Lys, a river that flows from the north of France and empties into the Scheldt river which runs through Ghent’s centuries-old canals.
“It could last for a few more weeks if the temperature does not drop significantly,” Weymeis said.
Duckweed deprives the flora and fauna in the water of sunlight, but the plant is harmless for humans.
Tourists can still safely board the boats that wind their way past the churches and historic buildings in the city centre.
Against the blue sky, the pea green coating creates a striking image that passersby stop to photograph.
But there is also a sense of worry over the impact that man-made climate change is having on the environment around them.
“It’s both beautiful to look at and a cause for concern,” Ramzi Salhi said, after capturing the image.
For boat owners like Siddi, the problem is most practical.
The duckweed can clog up the engines of the tourist boats plying the canals and cause them to overheat.
“Over the past month, a few boats have already broken down,” he said. AFP

Roderick Moore has become the new president and chief executive officer of the America for Bulgaria Foundation, taking over from Nancy Schiller, who is retiring.
Moore assumed the position on October 1, 2026, after previously serving on the Foundation’s Board of Directors since 2019. He was chosen through a recruitment process in the United States conducted by the Board of Directors.
Schiller is stepping down after more than 10 years as president and 15 years as a member of the Foundation’s Board of Directors. She will remain on the Board following her retirement. She had led the organization since 2016 and had been associated with its activities since its establishment in 2008–2009.
Moore is a career diplomat with the U.S. Department of State and extensive experience in the Balkans. He earned a bachelor’s degree in International Relations and Russian Studies from Brown University and a master’s degree in Slavic Languages.
He worked at the U.S. Embassy in Sofia from 1990 to 1992, served as Chargé d’Affaires in 2015 and was Deputy Chief of Mission in Sofia from 2000 to 2003. From 2004 to 2007, he served as Deputy Chief of Mission in Belgrade, while from 2007 to 2010 he was U.S. Ambassador to Montenegro.
"I am returning to Bulgaria for the fourth time, and I feel as though I am coming home. I have a deep affection for the country and look forward to working with the Foundation’s team to continue finding meaningful ways to contribute to Bulgaria’s prosperity," Moore said.
The Foundation’s mission and working approach remain unchanged, its press office said. The U.S. nonprofit charitable foundation primarily supports cultural projects connecting the United States and Bulgaria.
America for Bulgaria has backed more than 1,500 projects in Bulgaria, the organization said.

‘Stand on the right side of history’: Starbucks urged to close stores in China’s Xinjiang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:44:48 UTC
00:44:48 KST

US lawmakers have urged Starbucks to close newly opened outlets in China’s Xinjiang, saying it was a “morally bankrupt decision” to operate in a region where Beijing has been accused of widespread human rights abuses against Muslim minorities.
The coffeehouse chain, which last year sold a controlling stake in its China retail business to the Hong Kong-based investment firm Boyu Capital, opened two stores in the region on Tuesday.
Videos on Chinese social media showed long queues for the flagship store in Urumqi’s Grand Bazaar tourist area, with influencers showing off special edition drinks including “milk-skin-flavoured salty milk tea”.
But John Moolenaar, the chair of the US House of Representatives’ select committee on China, called the move “morally bankrupt”.
“There is no justifiable reason for an American company to do business in a region where the Chinese Communist party has detained more than a million Uyghurs and is stripping them of their faith, language and culture,” he said. “Every cup sold in these stores ties an iconic American brand to the CCP’s brutal campaign against the Uyghurs.”
Washington is among several governments and rights groups that have accused China of genocide in Xinjiang, which Beijing has categorically denied.
The United Nations has warned of possible crimes against humanity, including the detention of more than a million Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities in camps.
China says these were “education” camps and that crackdowns were necessary to combat terrorism.
The World Uyghur Congress advocacy group called on Starbucks to “stand on the right side of history”.
“The presence of Starbucks in Xinjiang’s streets … fits in the party state’s narrative, that there’s nothing wrong about the region,” said Human Rights Watch’s deputy Asia director, Maya Wang.
Responding to the US comments, the Chinese foreign ministry told Reuters that allegations of repression were “naked lies” and that Xinjiang enjoyed a “stable society, economic growth, racial unity and religious harmony”.
The Guardian has contacted Starbucks and Boyu Capital for comment.
China has poured resources into developing Xinjiang as a tourism destination in recent years.
Starbucks is far from alone in seeing the commercial appeal there: other major western brands such as Hilton and InterContinental Hotels Group have been criticised for their operations too.
Critics have characterised Xinjiang’s development as “Disneyfication” – commodifying the region’s heritage even as its inhabitants’ ability to practise their culture on their own terms has been restricted.
On Chinese social media, excited visitors posted pictures of Starbucks-branded merchandise, including patterned flasks and teddy bears in outfits based on local ethnic dress.
When the deal with Boyu Capital was announced, Starbucks said it would bring “deep local expertise”, with analysts noting the US behemoth had been losing ground to domestic competitors for some time.
The move by Starbucks makes “commercial sense”, said Yaling Jiang, the founder of the research and strategy consultancy ApertureChina.
“What is politically correct in China is not necessarily politically correct in the rest of the world, and this is a prime example,” she said. “Starbucks in China is now operating from a Chinese perspective rather than a US perspective, and that is ultimately how they can win in China.”

Deepening global bond crisis fuels inflation amid record debt, surging AI investments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:41:16 UTC
00:41:16 KST

Bahattin Gonultas and Emir Yildirim
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Global bond markets have been seeing a sweeping selloff amid high inflation, rate hike expectations, and chronic debt burdens, pressuring households and companies while threatening to affect public finances.
The US economy grew above expectations in the second quarter, while the personal income and consumer spending indexes showed inflation remained well above the Fed’s 2% target.
The macroeconomic data released in the US showed that the economy and consumer appetite remain strong, pushing up the US 10-Year Treasury yield amid concerns of further monetary policy tightening, leading to a sharp selloff in stocks across the globe.
The key global borrowing cost indicator reached a level unseen since 2002 at 5.34%, while all US Treasury bond yields rose around 90 basis points in the third quarter, the largest quarterly surge of the century.
Investors continue to sell more and more bonds amid expectations that the Fed will continue raising its policy rate at the end of October, while economists point to signs of overheating in the US economy.
All eyes turned to the September labor report set to be released on Friday, as markets expect the US unemployment rate to remain at 4.1%.
The interest rate on the most common 30-year mortgage exceeded 7% for the first time since early 2025 as bond yields surged.
Interest payments in major economies outpaced global artificial intelligence (AI), defense, and clean energy investments, according to the Institute of International Finance (IIF).
The US-Iran tensions continue to drive up oil prices, fueling inflation and driving interest rates, which in turn exacerbate chronic debt concerns.
The US posted a total debt burden of over $40 trillion, while the debt-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio among G7 countries excluding Germany remains at or above 100%.
Surging AI investments are also playing a structural role in the mounting debt.
The five largest AI tech firms issued $220 billion in bonds this year to finance data center investments, while the rise in borrowing needs continues to push interest rates even higher.
The surge in government bonds is not exclusive to the US, as the yield on the UK’s 30-year bond exceeded 6% for the first time since 1998, while France’s 10-year bond hit its highest since 2002, and Japan’s yields also saw multi-decade highs.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says these issues should not overshadow the overall strength of the American economy.
The Treasury Department’s decision to at least double the size of its long-term bond buyback operations supported market liquidity, but ultimately this decision was not enough to ease the pressure on the bond market.
Experts advise investors demanding higher interest rates to adopt fiscal discipline and reduce their excessive spending.
Analysts say a potential drop in oil prices could bring some short-term relief but long-term borrowing costs can be reduced for good if governments take steps to reduce their debt.
The situation in the bond markets is pressuring the eurozone and foreign exchange markets.
Tim Waterer, a global chief market analyst at KCM Trade, stated that bond yields will remain high unless oil prices significantly drop or the US and Iran reach a resolution, while the macroeconomic pressure is worsening Europe’s fragility.
Francesco Pesole, foreign exchange strategist at the ING Group, stated that the French-German 10-year bond yield spread reached 130 basis points after Paris’ budget announcement fell short of resolving structural deficits, while the spread is threatening to widen as much as 150 basis points.
The volatility in the bond market is putting downward pressure on the euro, as the currency is expected to grow more sensitive to these developments despite the resilience of the euro/US dollar exchange rate.
Pesole said the exchange rate could retreat to 1.110 if yield spreads continue to widen.

Russian Mi-8 helicopter reportedly shot down in friendly-fire incident over Voronezh Oblast
A Russian Su-35 fighter jet reportedly shot down a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter in a friendly-fire incident in Russia's Voronezh Oblast on Oct. 1, killing all three crew members, according to several Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels.

Introduced in the 1960s, it remains one of the most widely operated helicopters globally, valued for its versatility, durability, and ability to operate in challenging environments.
The Su-35 is a Russian multirole fighter aircraft derived from the Su-27.

====================================================================================================

Aviation security back in spotlight after nightmare on flydubai flight to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:40:05 UTC
00:40:05 KST

At about 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her six-year-old daughter, Nina, to the toilet on the regular flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when she heard a series of heavy blows against the cockpit door.
Manes, an Israeli bank executive, immediately told a flight attendant seated nearby that something was wrong. When he did not react, she shouted at him: “Something is happening in there!” Seconds later, the man “simply went to the [cockpit] door and opened it”, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12 TV.
Inside, the scene was the stuff of travellers’ nightmares: blood spattered over the cockpit walls and a brutal struggle in progress between the badly injured pilot and the co-pilot, who was armed with some kind of sharp weapon. There was no one at the controls of the Boeing 737.
Manes shouted again: “He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!”
Many of the details of what happened on flight FZ 1073 are still unclear, but what happened next is well documented by witness testimony and videos.
As the plane went into a steep dive, losing 16,000ft of altitude in about a minute, most of the 182 passengers screamed, prayed and tried desperately to reassure panicking children. But a small group rushed to the cockpit and overpowered the co-pilot. One, a plumber, copied an action seen on TV documentaries about plane crashes to pull the aircraft out of its dive.
Two off-duty pilots on the flight, both among the handful of non-Israeli passengers, then took over the controls of the now almost rudderless aircraft to guide it eventually to a landing 90 minutes later in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. In the meantime, Manes had helped truss the co-pilot with a telephone cord while a dentist treated the injured Indian pilot, Smit Machchhar. It was a “great miracle”, Manes said on eventually reaching Tel Aviv on an emergency flight 10 hours later.
In a video call with Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, broadcast live by TV networks, Machchhar, who is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, said he had been “fighting for my life”.
The pilot successfully sent an alarm to air traffic control signalling the attack and then, as his strength ebbed, managed to unlock the cockpit security door.
“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” Machhchar said. “At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
For the moment, the identity of the co-pilot who attacked Machchhar is unknown, though regional sources said he was an Omani national who had joined flydubai – which is owned by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) government – between five and nine months ago.
The co-pilot was barred from flying in Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, the Associated Press quoted a source as saying on Saturday, and was subsequently hired by flydubai.
In Israel, there is little doubt about the co-pilot’s intentions. “The co-pilot is a terrorist who tried either to hijack the plane or bring it down as a suicide. The worst scenario is he was trying to get into Israel,” said Arik Arad, the chair of the aviation cybersecurity consultancy Cyviation and El Al’s former head of security at Ben Gurion airport
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, has claimed the co-pilot was exposed to “Islamist radical indoctrination”, saying Israeli investigators had found evidence on social media accounts that he wanted to “kill Jews”.
“The attacker, he calls out to the aircrew: ‘Kill me, kill me,’” Netanyahu told Fox News, adding it was “clear he was suicidal”.
Experts said there have been only a handful of instances of suicide by plane – cases where the pilot’s motivation is primarily to kill him or herself by crashing the plane, rather than using the plane as a weapon, as in the 9/11 attacks.
In 2015, the co-pilot of a low-cost German airline flight who had hidden evidence of psychiatric illness from his employers deliberately crashed, killing himself and 150 others. Suggestions that the crash of an AirIndia 787 in Ahmedabad last year was the result of a pilot deliberately cutting fuel to engines have been fiercely disputed.
Terrorism experts are sceptical that the flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life. “The odds that a pilot would decide to commit suicide and just happen to be flying a plane full of Israelis are pretty low,” said Colin Clarke, a terrorism expert at the respected Soufan Center in New York.
“Netanyahu has a big interest in this being terrorism, but the best explanation is probably the most obvious one [ie terrorism],” he said. “The question … is: was [the co-pilot] recruited by a group or an organisation … or was he radicalised alone? In which case, what was hyping him up, given he was flying a planeload of Israelis? Could that be Gaza?”
Security services have been warning of a wave of radicalisation across the Middle East prompted by the war in Gaza, which came to an inconclusive halt with a fragile ceasefire a year ago. But there has been limited evidence as yet that any violent Islamist extremist groups have gained support as a consequence of the conflict.
Terrorism experts said the most obvious group that might be involved in such an attack would be al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which is based in Yemen and has a history of efforts to bring down planes. They said AQAP had recently sought to launch or inspire violence internationally.
“Aviation remains the classic propaganda by deed,” Clarke said. “It’s been said that terrorism is theatre, and nothing is more theatrical than taking down an airplane. You get a body count, media coverage, you get your message across, and this makes a plane the ultimate spectacular terrorist attack.”
There are now many questions for aviation security. Changes made to plane design after 9/11, which allowed pilots to lock cockpit doors from the inside, have long been controversial among experts. If Machchhar’s desperate efforts to allow access to the flight deck had been unsuccessful, there is little doubt all onboard FZ 1073 would have died.
There are also questions about screening of pilots. This can be expensive for airlines and could deprive them of valuable crew if too many fail more rigorous efforts to expose psychiatric illness or extremist views. Pilots may be reluctant to fly routes where they undergo greater screening, and some may hide physical or psychological problems for fear of being grounded.
Arad said: “The important issue … is that obviously pilots are not being screened enough. Lots needs to be done.”
Dubai international airport, the world’s busiest airport for international passenger traffic, has built some of its appeal on a reputation for safety in a volatile region, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.
“They are very conscious of the fact – a little bit like Israel in many respects – that they cannot afford to have a terrorist attack happening on a flight out of there,” he said.
The UAE has ordered investigators to “collect information and evidence to determine the truth of the incident, its circumstances, details and motives, and to verify the extent of its connection to any terrorist activity or purpose, or the existence of prior planning or direction for it,” its attorney general, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, said on Thursday.
Arad foresees growing threats to civilian aviation from cyber-attacks and the malevolent use of AI, which could allow the targeting multiple planes simultaneously. But other experts pointed out there was no need for such sophistication to pose a threat.
Clarke said: “Whether or not it involves an attacker who was self-radicalised or part of a group, keeping things simple is always the best way to carry out an attack, and this came pretty damn close.”

Pentagon moves to accelerate counter-drone systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:38:25 UTC
00:38:25 KST

Diyar Guldogan
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
The Pentagon issued a memorandum Friday to accelerate the “lawful, safe, and effective” employment of counter-unmanned aircraft systems across the department.
The memorandum, titled Accelerating Employment of Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems to Protect American Airspace Sovereignty, directs the Defense Department to eliminate “unnecessary” administrative and procedural barriers that can delay counter-drone capabilities for military forces, installations and other assets.
Under the new policy, approval authorities are instructed to treat delays in deploying c-UAS capabilities as an “operational risk.”
“This memorandum directs the Department to accept prudent risks, identify approval paths early, staff them fast, standardize them across the Department, and elevate them when they stall,” Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote in the memorandum.
Officials are also directed to use relevant previous approvals, testing data and established risk mitigations when making comparable decisions.
Where testing demonstrates that risks are low or manageable, authorities may use interim, conditional or time-limited approvals to accelerate deployment.
The memorandum also establishes additional accountability measures. Any denial of a request to employ a c-UAS capability must include a documented rationale and be submitted to Joint Interagency Task Force-401, or JIATF-401.

Latvia votes with Russia threat looming large
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:37:36 UTC
00:37:36 KST

Latvia votes with Russia threat looming large
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, leader of the United List party, is seen on an election advertising banner before the upcoming election on Sept. 30, 2026 in Riga, Latvia. (Gints Ivuskans / AFP via Getty Images)
Latvia will elect a new parliament this weekend, in an election dominated by security concerns over the now emboldened Russia next door and a cost-of-living crisis shaping the domestic agenda.
The Oct. 3 vote for the 100-member unicameral parliament — the Saeima — will be the second since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a war in which Latvia threw its full support behind Kyiv.
It also comes as Western officials raise alarm over Moscow's escalating hybrid threat — a particularly pressing concern for Latvia, which borders both Russia and Belarus and where roughly a third of the 1.8 million population speaks Russian as their mother tongue.
Seven of the 14 running parties are expected to enter the parliament, with polling stations set to open at 8 a.m. local time and close at 8 p.m.
Surveys indicate a likely victory for the United List (AS) alliance of pro-Ukraine Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, but he will still need coalition partners to put together a majority.
Kulbergs has vowed "unwavering support to Ukraine" if reelected, and Riga is broadly expected to maintain a pro-Kyiv, pro-European course after the elections.
Nevertheless, roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of the votes are expected to go to parties fishing for support among Russian speakers, including the Latvia First party, led by a Trumpian tycoon, and the Moscow-friendly Sovereign Power.
A crowded election field
Seen as a relative newcomer to high-level politics, the former race car driver Kulbergs has led the Latvian government since May, when the mishandling of a Ukrainian drone crash led to the collapse of then-Prime Minister Evika Silina's cabinet.
Kulbergs' relatively short tenure saw his United List — an electoral alliance of regionalist and green conservative parties — surge in support.
With the backing of 22.7% of decided voters, according to a September poll by SKDS/LSM, the center-right alliance will almost certainly be the leading force in the next coalition.
Who else will land in it remains unclear.
Kulbergs currently sits in a cabinet with the nationalist National Alliance, the agrarian Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS), and the liberal-conservative New Unity (JV), led by Silina.
But recent surveys make it uncertain whether the latter two will cross the 5% threshold required to enter the parliament.
The pro-European, social-democratic Progressives — polling around 10% — could help Kulbergs cobble together a pro-Western bloc, but an ideological divide might complicate an alliance with center-right and right-wing parties.
The Progressives left Silina's cabinet in May along with their defense minister, Andris Spruds, whom the prime minister blamed for failing to protect Latvian airspace from Ukrainian drones diverted there by Russian jamming.
Latvia First (LPV), a right-wing populist party polling third at 13.3%, is led by businessman Ainars Slesers, whose political style has often been compared to that of U.S. President Donald Trump.
A populist who leans heavily on anti-establishment talking points and dabbles in disinformation, the "Latvian Trump" could be a wild card if several incumbent parties fail to enter parliament.
Slesers, who has had ties to Russian oligarchs, is courting both Latvian-speaking and Russian-speaking voters, criticizing the government's policies that prioritize Latvian over Russian in public spaces.
His record on Ukraine has been inconsistent. Before the full-scale invasion, he had mocked sanctions against Russia and dismissed warnings of the war.
But the populist leader changed his tune after 2022, naming Russia the aggressor and even booting those members of his party who failed to condemn Moscow.
While saying that Latvia's support for Kyiv should continue, his party also argues that Riga should restore economic ties with Russia after the war ends.
The politicians expelled from Latvia First in 2022 went on to found Sovereign Power, the other major party seeking support among Russian speakers and the only relevant political force opposing aid to Ukraine.
Running as Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance (SV/AJ), it polls second at 14.1%. But its stances make it an unlikely coalition partner in a country where popular support for Ukraine remains strong.
Kulbergs has ruled out a coalition with Sovereign Power, calling it a threat to Latvia's security and democracy.
For now, he has also rejected cooperation with Latvia First — but observers do not rule out that Slesers may eventually join the government, especially if Kulbergs is left with few other potential partners.
Security takes center stage
Security concerns and the Russian threat have loomed large over the election campaign.
Latvian intelligence warned in June that Moscow may be preparing to test Poland and the Baltic countries with hybrid attacks or drone and missile incursions.
Other Western officials have raised similar concerns as Russia's hybrid campaign — ranging from cyberattacks and disinformation to arson and sabotage — continues to grow increasingly brazen.
Mere days before the elections, Latvia's northern neighbor Estonia accused Russia of orchestrating an arson attack against a defense company in Tallinn.
A month earlier, Germany named Moscow as the culprit behind an attempted drone attack against Leipzig Airport.
And while Latvia has said it sees no sign of an imminent conventional Russian attack, the Russia-Ukraine war has already spilled over into Latvian airspace, with several stray drones shot down by NATO planes.
With elections approaching, governing politicians have sought to reinforce their image as Russia hawks.
Latvia was the only country to briefly block a Slovak and French request, ultimately successful, to delist two Russian oligarchs from EU sanctions.
National diplomats previously told the Kyiv Independent that Riga sought to postpone the EU decision until after the Latvian elections, as the delisting would be politically toxic.
Latvia eventually imposed unilateral sanctions on the oligarchs after they were removed from the EU sanctions list.
But Riga's hawkish posture is likely to outlast the election season. As Moscow's shadow war escalates, the next government will have little room to soften its stance on Russia.

What to Know About the Dengue Outbreak in the U.S.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:30:28 UTC
00:30:28 KST

This week, Hillsborough County in Florida, which includes Tampa, declared a state of emergency linked to a growing number of dengue cases. So far this year, around 485 cases have been reported in the state, according to the CDC. The disease, which is transmitted by mosquitoes, can cause serious flu-like illness, and one person in Florida has died in the outbreak so far this year, the state’s department of health told media outlets in September.
Seasonal outbreaks of the disease, which affects up to 400 million people worldwide annually, are not unusual in Florida, and they’re often linked to travelers. But this time is a little different, says Michael Johansson, an epidemiologist at Northeastern University. “This is the most locally acquired cases that we've seen in the state,” he says.
What is dengue?
Dengue, sometimes called dengue fever, is caused by a collection of viruses carried by mosquitoes, primarily Aedes aegypti. Dengue is endemic in a wide swath of the tropics, and usually, most Americans who have the infection acquire it outside of the U.S. during travel. Dengue symptoms can occur 5-7 days after being bitten and range from mild to severe. They may include painful body aches as well as fever and can last up to 10 days.
However, in parts of the U.S. where Aedes aegypti mosquitoes live, they can bite infected people and start to spread the disease locally. “The general pattern that we see—and we've seen this for more than a decade now—is that there are frequent travel-associated cases” in Florida, says Johansson. “We know we have the right vectors there, especially in southern Florida, where there's lots of Aedes aegypti, and there is some local transmission that occurs. Usually that looks like just one or two cases, but sometimes there are small outbreaks.”
In 2009, when two locally acquired infections were identified in Key West, public-health surveillance revealed that a substantial share of people in the town had markers in their blood showing a recent encounter with dengue, even if they hadn’t had symptoms. That suggests that in an outbreak, dengue is likely to be infecting more people than might immediately be clear from case counts.
One distinctive feature of dengue, however, is that the second time someone is infected is likely to be much worse than the first. Sometimes a second infection can progress to dengue hemorrhagic fever, which can involve bleeding and a drop in blood pressure, and is sometimes fatal.
This pattern, where the second exposure is more dangerous than the first, has complicated attempts to vaccinate people against the disease. In 2017, Sanofi Pasteur, the manufacturer of the dengue vaccine Dengvaxia, alerted the government of the Philippines that serious dengue infections might occur in people who had received the vaccine as their first exposure to the disease. No dengue vaccine is currently available in the U.S.; Dengvaxia was available starting in 2019 but in 2025 was discontinued by the manufacturer, which cited low demand.
Will dengue become endemic in the U.S.?
So far, dengue has not established a permanent foothold in the continental U.S., says Johansson. There are a few reasons why that might be: large numbers of people in Florida, where Aedes aegypti thrive, stay within air-conditioned spaces when they’re most active, which means chains of transmission tend to be short.
And the mosquitoes themselves are not particularly adventurous. They tend to stay close to home, within about a 100-meter range, so “it takes people to move the virus around,” says Johansson. If someone who’s infected doesn’t travel, the virus doesn’t either.
How can you protect yourself from dengue?
There is no cure for dengue; the only treatments are for symptoms. If you are in an area with mosquitoes that can carry dengue, the best way to protect yourself is to avoid mosquito bites. Keep windows closed or use screens, cover as much of your skin as possible with clothing when outdoors, and use mosquito repellent, says Johansson.
Keep yards free of containers that could fill with water and serve as breeding zones for mosquitoes. You’ll have to be vigilant: “These mosquitoes in particular, they can breed in a plastic bag that's collected a little bit of rainwater,” says Johansson.
Cooler weather brings relief. “We're getting to the time of year when things are cooling down, so we should expect a decrease in transmission,” says Johansson. “However, it's still hot in Florida right now”—so it’s not time to drop your guard yet.

Akhilesh Yadav's Rajya Sabha picks: Samajwadi Party's master strategy or 'PDA' contradiction?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:27:53 UTC
00:27:53 KST

SP chief Akhilesh Yadav has nominated Ram Gopal Yadav and Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani for the Rajya Sabha polls.
A 'family' man, a corporate executive, a possible third candidate and a high-stakes numbers game: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav's Rajya Sabha strategy has a bit of a test run for the 2027 UP assembly polls?His two picks have an element of continuity and also surprise. But then there is also an element of contradiction vis-à-vis the strong PDA pitch which has been the backbone of his 2027 poll strategy. Little wonder, then, that talk of a third nominee has begun even without the numbers, raising the stakes from a routine Rajya Sabha contest to an early test of Akhilesh's 2027 strategy.For the two sure-shot Rajya Sabha seats in Uttar Pradesh, Akhilesh Yadav has paired a familiar Samajwadi Party face with a distinctly unfamiliar political profile. Alongside his uncle Ram Gopal Yadav, the SP has nominated Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani, a senior Reliance Industries executive whose father, Parimal Nathwani, is a four-time Rajya Sabha MP backed by the BJP-led NDA. The choice immediately puts two very different images of the SP on the same ticket: its established family name and a corporate, professional profile from outside its traditional ecosystem.Nathwani's nomination also raises a larger question about the SP's direction as it prepares for the 2027 assembly election.
Is Nathwani's nomination an attempt to expand the SP's political appeal beyond its traditional social base, or does bringing a senior corporate executive into Parliament sit uneasily with a party increasingly building its politics for the 2027 polls around PDA, Pichhda, Dalit and Alpsankhyak? The question matters beyond the Rajya Sabha because the SP is simultaneously trying to project itself as the principal challenger to the BJP in Uttar Pradesh ahead of the 2027 assembly election.
Why Nathwani?
Akhilesh's second nomination is more than a surprise name on a candidate list. His corporate background gives the SP an opportunity to make a political argument it has not traditionally foregrounded. The party can present his candidature as evidence that its appeal is extending beyond its conventional political base and that people from the corporate and professional world now see the party as a credible political force.For a party preparing for 2027, that can also help reinforce a broader pitch around investment, jobs, industry and development alongside its social-justice agenda, which could become a significant part of the BJP and Yogi government's election campaign next year.Akhilesh, in fact, responded to queries over criticism of Nathwani's nomination by invoking Ram Manohar Lohia. "I think you should read about socialism again. I will give you a book by (Ram Manohar) Lohia," he said. He argued that socialist thought also talks about prosperity and equality and said governments across the country seek investment to generate economic growth."This time, it will be Lodhi vs Yogi (Adityanath)," he said on September 30.However, the same choice also produces a very different political reading.
Akhilesh's electoral strategy for the 2027 polls has been heavily identified with PDA, and Nathwani is not an obvious representative of the social coalition that phrase describes. That gives the opposition an opening to question why a party seeking votes in the name of backward classes, Dalits and minorities has chosen a senior corporate executive for one of its two Rajya Sabha seats.Mayawati, in fact, used the same charge against the SP. "SP wants votes in the name of PDA, but makes mostly its own family members and big capitalists MPs and MLAs," she said in a post on X.
State minister and Suheldev Bharatiya Samaj Party (SBSP) president Om Prakash Rajbhar also targeted Akhilesh, accusing him of repeatedly changing the framework for PDA. "Akhilesh Yadav keeps changing the PDA formula from time to time. Yesterday, he came up with the formula of a PDA family. 'P' now stands for 'Parivaar'," Rajbhar said, referring to Ram Gopal Yadav. "‘D’ stands for the 'Daulat', referring to Dhani Ram, who is affluent," Rajbhar said."Now, only 'A' remains, and he will bring in some criminal to represent it. The new PDA formula stands for 'Parivaar', 'Daulat' and 'Apradhi'," he added.The BJP, meanwhile, is watching Nathwani's nomination closely but has not mounted a similarly strong direct attack on the choice.
The third nomination suspense
The Uttar Pradesh assembly currently has 396 effective members after seven vacancies, putting the winning quota for a Rajya Sabha seat at 37 first-preference votes. The BJP has 255 MLAs, while the SP has 101 and Congress has two. The BJP's alliance partners include Apna Dal (S), RLD, SBSP and Nishad Party, giving the ruling camp a substantial numerical advantage. Broadly, the BJP-led camp is positioned to take the larger share of the 10 seats, while the SP-Congress combination has enough strength for two.The problem begins with the third candidate. The SP would need roughly nine additional first-preference votes to reach the quota for a third seat. That means Akhilesh cannot rely only on his existing alliance strength. He would have to attract support from outside it, potentially through smaller parties, independents or legislators willing to cross-vote.The suspense over that third candidate has now become central to the contest. SP MP Virendra Singh has said the party will field a third candidate, with the name to be decided and the nomination filed by October 5. Singh has also claimed that several BJP MLAs seeking SP tickets for the 2027 elections are in touch with the party.Akhilesh, meanwhile, has continued to leave room for political manoeuvring. Earlier in the day he described the Rajya Sabha election as "the time for coming together" and said it offered an opportunity to forget past mistakes and stand united with others on matters of principle.A day earlier, when asked whether the SP would field a third candidate, he declined to confirm the party's plans and said: "The BJP can do anything. They can field nine or even 10 candidates."The BJP, meanwhile, has made its own claims about SP legislators. Deputy CM Keshav Prasad Maurya has said that 25 SP MLAs are in contact with the BJP and warned that the party would "surprise" the SP.
A rehearsal for 2027
This Rajya Sabha election, along with the immediate parliamentary tally, will ultimately be about a strategic stress-test for 2027.In fielding Nathwani, Akhilesh Yadav is executing a high-stakes balancing act: attempting to reposition the Samajwadi Party as a pragmatic, investment-friendly government-in-waiting, without alienating the core PDA base that forms its electoral backbone. It is a gamble that risks handing opponents cheap ideological ammunition in exchange for broader institutional credibility and expanded corporate outreach.
Whether this move is remembered as a masterstroke of political expansion or a self-inflicted ideological contradiction will not be decided in the corridors of the Rajya Sabha. It will be decided by how effectively Akhilesh manages the cross-currents - maintaining the confidence of his grassroots voters while proving that his vision for Uttar Pradesh can accommodate both social justice and corporate capital. The upcoming floor vote, and the potential fight for a third seat, will offer the first real glimpse of whether that strategy can hold.

North Macedonia Seeks Bulgaria’s Help to Unblock EU Accession
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:26:23 UTC
00:26:23 KST

North Macedonia Seeks Bulgaria’s Help to Unblock EU Accession
North Macedonia will formally ask Bulgaria for a bilateral meeting next week in an effort to unblock its European Union accession process, Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski said after talks with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Skopje.
Mickoski said he had instructed Foreign Minister Timho Mucunski to send a diplomatic note requesting a meeting with his Bulgarian counterpart, Velislava Petrova, during his visit to Sofia for the Corridor 8 forum on Thursday, October 8.
The move follows von der Leyen’s call for Skopje to take a key step toward opening the first EU negotiation cluster, “Fundamentals.” She did not explicitly mention the constitutional amendments envisaged under the so-called French proposal, which would include Bulgarians in North Macedonia’s Constitution.
At a joint press conference with Mickoski, von der Leyen said the accession negotiations had started in 2022 after substantial work and dedication, but further progress depended on a new step by North Macedonia.
“North Macedonia has a place at the European table. I am aware of the sensitivities surrounding this, but I also want to be very clear: I want to state unequivocally the values Europe stands for. We welcome North Macedonia with its identity and language,” she said.
Von der Leyen added that Macedonian culture and language could enrich the EU, whose motto is “United in diversity.” She said the bloc took that principle seriously.
She also cited the Prespa Agreement as an example of political courage, saying North Macedonia had shown it could make bold decisions about its future. The agreement, reached by two countries that chose to turn the page and begin a new chapter together, paved the way for North Macedonia’s NATO membership, she said, describing the country as a valued ally.
At the beginning of her visit, von der Leyen said North Macedonia belonged in the EU and urged the country to act while the enlargement process was gaining momentum.
Mickoski said he and von der Leyen had discussed the challenges in North Macedonia’s relations with Bulgaria. He said Skopje wanted to address them through dialogue, goodwill and mutual respect, and expected EU institutions to help establish conditions for a sustainable solution without taking sides.
The prime minister said agreements and obligations should be clear and apply to everyone, while the accession process should not be reopened to new bilateral conditions, interpretations or demands. He said North Macedonia was not seeking to prolong the process but wanted it to proceed on a stable basis.
Mickoski also called for stronger political support from European institutions, saying his country wanted to join the EU and was working toward that goal. He said North Macedonia honored its obligations and carried out reforms, sometimes on time and sometimes with delays, but completed them.
Von der Leyen confirmed that the two sides had agreed on an initial step for the following week. She said a “pre-enlargement policy review” would also be presented during that week. The EU has roadmaps for countries that are already well advanced in accession talks and are opening and closing chapters, she said.
In her view, once the current impasse involving North Macedonia is resolved, the country could make rapid progress, although further work would remain.
BGNES reported that von der Leyen had told Skopje the country needed to take one key step to move forward and open the “Fundamentals” cluster. The agency also recalled that North Macedonia accepted the so-called French proposal in 2022, which was approved by all EU member states.
Under the negotiating framework, the inclusion of Bulgarians in North Macedonia’s Constitution is required for the country’s negotiations with the EU to begin. BGNES said the framework also requires Skopje to comply with the 2017 Treaty of Friendship, Good-Neighborliness, and Cooperation with Bulgaria and the two protocols attached to it.
The protocol from the second meeting of the Joint Intergovernmental Conference, signed three years ago by ministers Teodora Genchovska and Bujar Osmani, states that Skopje agreed to hold the next intergovernmental conference with the EU only after Bulgarians are included among the constituent peoples in the Constitution’s preamble and in two of its articles.
The same protocol records the North Macedonian government’s commitment that nothing in its Constitution may be interpreted as grounds to interfere in Bulgaria’s internal affairs in order to protect the status and rights of people who are not citizens of North Macedonia. BGNES said this provision means, both de facto and de jure, that Skopje will not seek recognition of a “Macedonian minority” in Bulgaria.
The protocol also covers measures against hate speech targeting Bulgarians and Bulgaria, the rehabilitation of victims of the communist regime in Macedonia, and the opening of the archives of the Yugoslav security services.

USA Imposes Sanctions on A7 Network, Which Supplied Components and Equipment to Russia’s Military-Industrial Complex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:26:00 UTC
00:26:00 KST

The U.S. Department of the Treasury has imposed sanctions against the A7 shadow banking network, which is linked to Russia and Iran.
This was reported on the department’s website.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) added the A7 network to its sanctions list as a transnational criminal organization.
According to the department, the network is headed by Ilan Shor, a Moldovan-Israeli oligarch who is already under sanctions and has been convicted, and the system itself was used to circumvent sanctions and launder money.
The A7 network was used to finance the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Hamas group, as well as to conduct transactions related to the sale of Iranian oil and the purchase of weapons.
The network used intermediaries in third countries, fictitious trade documents, and hidden VPN networks to funnel money through the international financial system.
All assets and property of the A7 network in the United States or under the control of U.S. citizens have been frozen, and any transactions involving them are prohibited under penalty of civil and criminal sanctions.
As a reminder, A7 developed a large-scale network of front companies that allows Russia to circumvent Western sanctions and purchase goods for its military-industrial complex
According to Western intelligence reports, Shor oversees these activities under the direct supervision of the Russian president’s administration.
Kyrgyzstan has long served as the main financial hub for the A7 schemes. Over $100 million in U.S. dollars and Chinese yuan passed through the bank accounts of local front companies.
To throw international oversight off track, the network created a special AI-based program that automatically forged invoices and customs documents. Instead of dual-use electronics, the documents listed civilian goods, such as car mats or light boxes.
Among the purchased goods, investigators discovered steel production equipment from the Chinese company Xi’an Heavy Equipment, which is used in the manufacture of ammunition and armor. Payments were also made for Nvidia servers for AI development and video components for Walksnail drones.

Trans-Caspian Corridor sea freight exceeds 4.5 mln metric tons in seven months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:25:27 UTC
00:25:27 KST

MINSK, October 2. /TASS/. The growth in sea freight along the Trans-Caspian Corridor has been impressive, with volumes exceeding 4.5 mln metric tons in the first seven months of this year, 60% more than in all of last year, Chairman of the Board of the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) Bakytzhan Sagintayev told reporters following a meeting of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council.
According to him, the heads of government discussed the development of transport infrastructure along the east-west and north-south routes, including in conjunction with China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Sagintayev noted that a common transport space is being actively developed within the EAEU, with the development of Eurasian transport corridors, including rail, road, and port infrastructure, among the key areas of this work. The EEC Board chairman noted that these corridors account for around 70% of transit freight traffic, making it crucial to synchronize the development of national sections of transport infrastructure in each country.
"In 2025, freight traffic increased in virtually all [EAEU] member states. In particular, 21.5 mln metric tons were transported along the North-South Corridor. The growth in sea freight along the Trans-Caspian route is impressive. In the first seven months of 2026, its volume exceeded 4.5 mln metric tons. For comparison, that is 60% more than in all of 2025. According to expert estimates, infrastructure modernization will increase the capacity of the eastern route of this corridor to 20 mln metric tons by 2030. This route has significant potential given our cooperation with China, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, and Mongolia," he said.
In addition, the second stage of introducing electronic document management at Russian and Kazakh seaports has been completed, with paper documents becoming a thing of the past, Sagintayev said. The EEC head noted that the introduction of digital tools simplifies procedures and reduces costs for businesses, while accelerating the movement of goods as much as possible.
The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor, runs through China, Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and onward to European countries. Container shipments along the route use both rail and maritime transport.

Damage to refineries decreasing — Novak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:21:44 UTC
00:21:44 KST

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Challenges arising in individual economic sectors, including oil refining, transport and logistics and agriculture, are in the sphere of higher attention and control by the government, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said when speaking in the Federation Council, the upper house of the Russian legislative assembly.
TASS put together key statements of the deputy prime minister.
Russian economy
The slowdown of national economy’s growth rates after high figures in 2023-2024 is an expectable phase. "Following high growth rates in 2023-2024, the economy moved to more moderate dynamic. This is an anticipated normalization phase after overheating and a condition for inflation decline at the same time," Novak said.
The current investment situation in Russia is the correction after the large-scale increase by almost 40% in 2021-2024. "Investments are definitely a factor of long-term growth. We forecast their decline this year, a minor increase by 0.2% next year, and growth by 2.5% and 3% in 2028-2029. This is the correction after the rise by almost 40% during the period by 2024," the official said.
The economy continues to be supported by revenues of households and the consumer demand. "In August, the GDP increased by 0.8%, and by 0.6% year-on-year during eight months of this year. According to the updated outlook, we expect approximately the same GDP level by the end of this year," Novak noted.
Requirements to efficiency of implemented projects have become more stringent currently. "The recent stage goes from a high base and increases efficiency requirements exactly for the new projects," said the deputy prime minister.
The unemployment rate in Russia remains historically low and equals 2.2%.
Government tasks
The task at present is "to restore sustainable growth rates of the economy and ensure further growth of citizens’ well-being," Novak said. "We plan to this end to expand domestic production, increase efficiency of resources utilization and create conditions for new investments," he added.
Difficulties arising in individual economic sectors are in the sphere of higher attention and control by the government. "Current objective difficulties are present in individual sectors," Novak said. "This refers to oil refining, transport and logistical sphere, and agriculture," the official said.
Fuel market situation
The government promptly took a wide range of measures to saturate the domestic market with fuel. "The temporary ban on gasoline and diesel fuel exports, organized imported fuel supplies, revised rules of exchange trading to restrain wholesale prices, and decision made on fiscal stimulation of extra production and import of fuel," Novak said.
The gasoline import measure is temporary as national fuel production is usually 10-15% higher than the demand. The diesel fuel market is now balanced.
Russia covered fuel needs of its northern region in full scope. "We supported fall field work of agricultural producers and fully supported northern import requirements of regions," said Novak.
Export fuel situation
Russia will partly authorize diesel fuel exports in case of overproduction. |Although we have just recently renewed the export ban for October, we will monitor the situation and in case of diesel overproduction, we will consider partial opening of exports," Novak said.
Russia will not accumulate too much fuel because it will lead to a decline in refining and output of other products. "It is a normal situation because since we produce 80% more diesel than consume in the domestic market, we support the domestic market and cannot accumulate more surplus than available tankage. Otherwise refining volumes have to be lowered, and this may adversely affect the output of other products enjoying demand," he added.
The country may return to gasoline exports when the domestic market situation stabilizes.
Operations of refineries
Authorities are currently exploring measures to support oil refineries and postpone their upgrade deadlines. "[Proposals] of the Russian Energy Ministry in cooperation with other federal executive authorities to are now being explored to support oil refineries that cannot currently meet the schedule and upgrade agreements signed with the Ministry of Energy, with the Federal Antimonopoly Service, due to objective reasons," Novak said.
Government agencies and oil companies completed a huge amount of work to protect oil refineries, which already led to a significant decline in damage. "We have seen lately that damage from continuous raids against refineries is much more mitigated. Passive protection was established, corresponding to threat models. Active protection by air defense assets was strengthened," the official said.
Oil companies managed to quicker put refineries into operation again after attacks. Four Russian refineries were attacked this night and only one refinery is currently estimating damage there. "We actually thwarted all the attacks against our plants," Novak noted.
Forecast
Inflation in Russia may total 6.8% as of the end of this year, the deputy prime minister noted. "Concerning inflation, it totaled 4.93% year-to-date. In annual terms, growth is 6.26% as of the end of September, we forecast 6.8% by the end of the year," Novak said.
The national GDP growth rate is expected to be 1.4% this year with gradual achievement of 2.4% in 2029.
Fuel prices and global demand
Non-oil and gas exports is expected to grow from $220 bln to $260 bln.
Global markets currently experience diesel fuel shortage. "Prices are exorbitantly high in global markets, exactly for diesel. We see diesel prices in Europe, in the United States of America break records," Novak said. Such situation has occurred due to sanction restrictions, attacks against the refining infrastructure and closing of logistical transport routes.
OPEC+ countries continue assessing maximal production capabilities of the states participating in the agreement. "This effort is still underway, as far as I know," Novak noted.

India: Authorities trampling on human rights in crackdown on electoral roll protests
