Trump’s Crazy AI Rebrand Was a Loyalty Test for Tech Execs—and It Worked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Seventy years ago last summer, a group of scientists met at Dartmouth College to discuss a wild idea—that machines might one day be capable of humanlike thought processes. One of those scientists, John McCarthy, had suggested a name for the new field: artificial intelligence. It stuck. When you search Google Scholar for “artificial intelligence,” approximately 7,420,000 results appear. The term is utterly ubiquitous. Everyone understands it. Even for people who despise AI, the least of their worries is what we call it.
Well, not everyone. Somehow, President Donald J. Trump developed a distaste for the term, and when he doesn’t like something, he feels free to issue an edict against it. In a September 23 speech at the United Nations, he hinted that he might want to do away with the term “artificial intelligence.” His rant seemed like bluster, even for someone with a penchant for renaming gulfs, lakes, and centers for the arts. Renaming an entire field of study and America’s most pivotal industry? This week, at a White House lunch with top AI leaders, he actually pulled the trigger with an executive order declaring that “artificial intelligence” was now a verboten coinage. Instead, the government will call it “Super Intelligence.” Clearly the president expects the private sector to follow suit.
To their shame, the lords of AI meekly acquiesced. From this point on, they will presumably be known as the lords of SI.
One can’t help but see this as the ultimate presidential flex—for all the executives’ trillions of dollars and all their actual intelligence, the alpha in the room was the guy with the orange skin. Changing a name might seem like a minor matter compared to the enormity of constraining a potentially catastrophic technology. But to this crowd, artificial intelligence is much more than a bunch of letters strung together. It’s their foundation. Their identity. When they were kids reading science fiction books under the covers, the term ignited their imaginations. They built or transformed their companies in service of AI, and it's just about all they’ve talked about for the past four years.
Yet when the president used his lunch soiree to win their approval for his wacky idea to undo 70 years of history, apparently not a single person in the room expressed an objection. Not Jeff Bezos, Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Greg Brockman, Alex Karp, or Elon Musk.
Jacob Weisberg, author of the recent book Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era, views the episode as a classic Trump loyalty test, meant to assess if otherwise powerful people will demean themselves to curry the president’s favor and avoid his wrath. If you pass the loyalty test, you fail the backbone test. “The only way to resist this kind of thing is by acting collectively,” says Weisberg. “If all of those guys had just said, ‘We'll agree to the terms of the self-regulation, but we don't accept [the name change], what would he have done?”
Instead, because of the lamblike silence of the billionaires, Trump could claim that those leaders actively blessed his idea. When a reporter in the post-lunch press gaggle mentioned AI agents, he corrected her, saying, “The name has been changed by the biggest, the smartest, the greatest people anywhere in the world.” Really?
Even using the magic of, uh, superintelligent systems like ChatGPT or Gemini, I could not find a single instance of any one of those great people previously politicking that the term artificial intelligence should be put to rest. Satya Nadella did once say that he would have preferred that AI had been called “different intelligence,” but that hasn’t dissuaded him from repeatedly using the term. And while it’s true that Mark Zuckerberg recently established a Superintelligence Lab, his company persistently pushes a product called Meta AI to its billions of users and sells what it calls AI glasses.
I asked Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI, and xAI whether they were going to change instances of AI in their product names, research papers, and communications. My query to the latter two was whether they were going to change their company names to get in sync with the presidential order. As I write this, none of them have gotten back to me.
My bet is that they will do the minimum to avoid presidential ire while trying to run out the clock until the next administration puts this bizarre idea out of its misery. It’s been suggested that the executives actually welcome a rebranding of what has become a toxic term. I’m skeptical of that, especially since the president’s mandated replacement, “super intelligence,” is a hell of a lot scarier than the original term.
From a scientific perspective the change also makes no sense. No less an expert than Nick Bostrom, the philosopher who popularized the term superintelligence in an eponymous book, seems baffled by the idea. Superintelligence, he explained to me in an email, “refers specifically to systems that greatly surpass all the best human brains. ‘AI’ has referred to a much broader category of systems, which includes, for example, email spam filters, spell checkers, simple navigation systems, early LLMs, and the chess engines of the ’70s that didn’t yet match the best human chess players. It seems awkward to refer to these as ‘superintelligent.’”
So what is the president’s reason for demanding the change, besides because he can? In his UN speech, he said he didn’t like the term because “the word ‘artificial’ makes intelligence fake. And it is not fake.” What is fake, he said after the White House lunch, is the term “artificial intelligence.” “It’s a fake word, it’s not good, an inappropriate term.” You don’t need to be a psychologist to see how this impulse might be associated with his decision to bounce CNN, Politico, and MSNow from the White House, because he perceives their news as “fake.”
Still, the leap that equates artificial with fake doesn’t track. In 1956, McCarthy used it to distinguish between human intelligence and the machine version of intelligence. The problem isn’t that the term leads people to regard AI’s output as fake—in fact, it’s so real that we human beings often can’t tell whether we’re dealing with an AI model or a human. Mandating that the distinction be explicit, with watermarks and labels, should be one element of the AI regulation that the White House seems allergic to.
As Weisberg notes, it’s very much in character for Trump to make a crazy edict like this one. What’s disturbing is the glaring lack of character from the executives who didn’t push back. They left with the prize of self-regulation instead of strict oversight, but not with their dignity.
But failure to defend the freedom to refer to artificial intelligence as artificial intelligence (as California governor Gavin Newsom decreed in his own Trump-trolling executive order) casts doubt on even that agreement. Making voluntary standards effective requires considerable fortitude, as prioritizing safety can be at odds with financial and competitive factors. Yet we are being asked to trust these supposedly independent corporate giants who nodded like bobbleheads while a technologically unschooled crank-in-chief demanded they abandon the term at the center of their lives and livelihoods. Inappropriate, and fake.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

On Friday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko warned that keeping the Ukrainian capital functioning under repeated Russian attacks had become a matter of “safety and survival.”
“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. We can no longer pretend that we can live as we would in peacetime,” Klitschko said following a meeting of Kyiv’s Defense Council on Oct. 2.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
His warning came as Russian strikes disrupted crossings over the Dnipro River. City authorities reported another hit on the Southern Bridge early on Friday and announced a full closure to road traffic that morning, alongside restrictions on two other bridges.
Klitschko said the council discussed how to protect bridge users while maintaining essential transport connections between Kyiv’s left and right banks. Military officials, law enforcement officers, emergency responders, and municipal services submitted proposals that would be forwarded to central authorities.
The mayor also outlined a condition for restoring Green Line metro services across the Southern Bridge during yellow-level air alerts: an expert assessment of the structure following Thursday’s attacks.
The metro operator is ready to resume those services, he said, but must first receive a conclusion from research institutes approached by the infrastructure ministry.
Beyond the immediate transport disruption, Klitschko described mounting pressure on the capital’s ability to function. Russian attacks were damaging infrastructure, logistics, homes, and public facilities, he said, while renewed strikes on the energy sector added to the strain.
Kremlin Urges US-Russia Deals Before Ukraine Settlement
“We are doing everything we can to keep the city functioning under constant destructive attacks, when the issue is no longer everyday comfort, but safety and survival,” he said.
Klitschko urged the agencies represented on the Defense Council to coordinate their actions, make carefully considered decisions and communicate honestly with residents.
“Now is not the time for populism,” he said.
He called for the same public unity shown at the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, arguing that Kyiv’s resilience depended on a shared understanding of the danger.
“Kyiv will withstand this,” he said. “But only through joint efforts.”
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia is targeting Kyiv’s civilian infrastructure and schools to pressure residents into leaving the capital.
The president said Moscow was using tactics similar to those seen at the start of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, when Russia sought to seize or paralyze Kyiv and undermine Ukraine’s government.

Military Police Officers Hospitalized In Poland After Opening a Letter From Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:58:48 UTC
23:58:48 KST

In the Polish town of Nowa Dęba, two military police officers and a civilian employee were hospitalized after opening a letter from Germany.
RMF24 reported on the incident.
The package arrived on September 30 at a local unit of the Military Gendarmerie in the Podkarpackie Voivodeship. According to the prosecutor’s office, a civilian employee accepted the envelope and handed it to the deputy head of the unit, who opened it.
Inside was a postcard with the inscription ‘Hello, Zlota.’ Investigators determined that there were no visible liquids or other substances in the envelope, and nothing spilled out when it was opened.
Shortly thereafter, the gendarme who opened the letter began to experience shortness of breath. Another military officer and a civilian employee complained of throat irritation. Skin irritation on the face and hands was also reported.
Four other gendarmes who showed no symptoms were placed in isolation. A total of 133 people were evacuated from a neighboring building. A specialized chemical and environmental rescue team responded to the scene. The Internal Security Agency and the Military Counterintelligence Service were notified of the incident.
According to an eyewitness account cited by Tygodnik Nadwiślański and reported by Onet, after the ambulances arrived, the hospital temporarily blocked the entrance to the emergency room. People were told the restrictions were due to possible quarantine measures.
On the evening of September 30, a spokesperson for the Polish Military Gendarmerie reported that an analysis of the letter ruled out the presence of chemical, biological, or radiological agents. Medical examinations revealed no signs of poisoning, after which all three were discharged from the hospital.
According to an update from the prosecutor’s office on October 1, the case is being investigated by the District Prosecutor’s Office in Lublin in cooperation with the Polish Military Gendarmerie and the Military Counterintelligence Service. The investigation concerns the possible exposure of individuals to an immediate risk of death or serious harm to their health.
Investigators are identifying the sender and the exact location from which the letter was mailed. The postcard is to be examined for fingerprints and genetic material. The prosecutor’s office is also verifying whether the employees’ symptoms were related to the envelope: spokesperson Marcin Kozak noted that they could have had another cause.
Poland has previously investigated the use of mail to carry out sabotage operations. In October 2025, it was reported that a group, acting on orders from Russian intelligence services, attempted to send packages containing explosive and incendiary materials to Ukraine. The packages were intended to explode or catch fire during transport, but they were intercepted by Romanian authorities.
At the same time, in the case of the letter in Nowa Dęba, Poland has not yet reported any established connection to Russian intelligence services or previous sabotage operations.

Russia’s latest propaganda? AI-generated war songs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:58:00 UTC
23:58:00 KST

Russia’s latest propaganda? AI-generated war songs
- Russia uses AI to create hundreds of pro-war songs glorifying its soldiers and dehumanising Ukrainians, spreading propaganda on major music platforms like Spotify and YouTube.
- These AI-generated songs surged after 2024, as new AI music tools made production faster, cheaper, and easier, with unclear direct Kremlin involvement.
- Streaming services struggle to moderate such content, often missing propaganda and hate speech in foreign languages despite some policies, allowing widespread dissemination of these songs.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Russia has a new weapon in its propaganda war against Ukraine: songs generated by artificial intelligence.
Hundreds of them – from maudlin ballads to grinding thrash metal – have sprouted on the world’s most popular music streaming platforms, created using a growing number of AI music generators, many based in the United States.
The songs glorify Russian soldiers and dehumanise Ukrainians, sometimes with ethnic slurs. They depict the front lines as a hellscape but generally portray President Vladimir Putin’s invasion in 2022 as a necessary defence.
One of the most popular songs, Power Of Artillery, is a churning rock paean in Russian to artillery systems with names like Krasnopol and Carnation.
Power of Artillery
She will catch you off guard night and day
The goddess of war, and God will not help you
You won’t be able to escape her wrath
You’ll have to remember your prayers quickly
The songs have been posted and played millions of times on the world’s most popular streaming platforms, including Spotify, Apple, YouTube and Deezer, according to research published by Terrecon, a non-profit organisation focused on threat intelligence in Ukraine that supports the government there.
The technological advances that have reshaped warfare are also reshaping wartime propaganda.
“They have found new ways to create cheaper drones and use them on a massive scale,” Daria Verbytska, a founder of Terrecon, said in a telephone interview, referring to the Russians. “It’s like that with music – creating massive propaganda with the help of AI.”
The extent of the Russian government’s role in propagating the songs is not clear, but the Kremlin has gone to great lengths to cultivate social and cultural support for the war.
Last week, a director of the Internet Development Institute, an organisation in Moscow that works closely with the Kremlin to promote patriotic values, cited in a presentation more than 350 artistic projects about the war the institute has promoted, according to news reports in Russia.
In all, Terrecon catalogued 981 songs generated by AI that contained what the group defined as pro-Russian war propaganda. Among those whose release date could be established, a vast majority appeared after 2024, when AI song generators including Suno and Udio entered the market.
“It takes a lot of resources to create a real song with songwriters, production,” Verbytska said. “It’s easier and faster and cheaper to make it through these AI generators.”
The surge in songs has also been enabled partly because of inconsistent rules by music generators and popular streaming services that have grappled with the increasing use of AI in music. Only some services, including Deezer and YouTube, require labelling that identifies AI content.
Spotify enacted a policy in September to label songs generated by AI and not to recommend them to users, the company said in response to questions. The company added labels to songs The New York Times shared as examples.
The major streaming sites have policies against hate speech and violent content, but few explicitly restrict propaganda. The sites also do not always capture idiomatic expressions or slurs in foreign languages.
Even when the platforms ban specific words and phrases as harmful, they do not necessarily restrict the martial themes that characterise many of the songs, Terrecon’s researchers argued.
The researchers also tested AI music generators – Suno, Udio and Google Flow Music in the United States, and Mureka, based in Singapore – by writing prompts in Russian and English for songs promoting Russian propaganda, including dehumanising content and calls for violence.
The generators refused to carry out some of the prompts, but the researchers were able to create songs similar to the ones they had catalogued and to upload them on YouTube Music and SoundCloud.
“The moderation systems mainly responded to specific banned words rather than the overall meaning of the prompts,” Terrecon’s report found.
Deezer’s spokesperson, Jesper Wendel, said the platform reviewed potentially violative content case by case. A spokesperson for SoundCloud, Sade Ayodele, said the company reviewed reported content, adding that “there is no place on SoundCloud for content that incites or glorifies violence”.
YouTube, which is owned by Google, said in a statement that it required creators to disclose the use of AI and required all content to comply with policies against hate speech. YouTube also labelled several songs identified by Terrecon and removed one that Terrecon had created as part of its test after the Times’ inquiry.
Apple, Suno, Udio and Mureka did not respond to requests for comment. Nor did the Internet Development Institute in Moscow, which is subject to economic sanctions imposed by governments in Europe and elsewhere for its propaganda.
It is unclear how popular the songs are. The song about artillery weapons, posted on YouTube accompanied by a video montage, has amassed more than two million views in two years.
The song, created on Suno, was posted by a user called Sergei Vaseykin, whose biography on a Russian poetry site says he was born in a Siberian village near Tyumen. Vaseykin, who has posted numerous odes to the Russian war effort (and one to hockey star Alex Ovechkin), did not respond to a request for comment.
The songs reflect a growing militarisation in Russian politics and culture since Russia invaded Ukraine, said Nina L. Khrushcheva, a professor of international affairs at the New School in New York City who has long studied Russian propaganda efforts.
They also tap into the Soviet Union’s tradition of promoting patriotism through music, especially during and after World War II, known as the Great Patriotic War in Russia.
Khrushcheva noted that those songs – many of them still familiar to most Russians – might have been used as propaganda by the Soviet government but reflected genuine experiences of soldiers fighting an existential war that touched virtually everyone in the country.
By contrast, these AI creations are “a simulacrum upon simulacrum upon simulacrum,” she said.
“It’s easy to chew on – you don’t have to feel anything,” she added. “It’s sort of couch patriotism.” NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Unknown

‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:50:59 UTC
23:50:59 KST

Valeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded. Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son.
“I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work.
A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.”
Across the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi, or Southern, Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing.
He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro.
On Saturday morning, Russia targeted a second major bridge connecting Kyiv, damaging the road surface on the Northern Bridge and temporarily halting traffic.
Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, as intensifying Russian attacks reshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.
For weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plunge Ukraine into darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.
“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”
This week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in an interview with the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.
“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.
Until recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.
The city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.
Kyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.
At the same time, Russia’s advances on the battlefield remain relatively slow and are coming at enormous cost.
Moscow captured about 361 sq km in September, according to the military analyst Konrad Muzyka, an increase on recent months but still far short of the pace needed to seize the rest of the Donbas before winter, when offensive operations typically become more difficult.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has clawed back about 126 sq km in a series of counteroffensives in the east, being conducted under the codename Vivaldi. That slower-moving battle on the ground is increasingly at odds with what is happening far behind the front. The contrast reflects a broader shift in the war, as Ukraine’s major cities come under growing pressure.
“You can be quite successful in the land domain, but if you are vulnerable in the air, especially in the rear, that is the vulnerability your opponent is going to exploit,” said Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies.
Ukrainian officials have been warning their European counterparts about the scale of the looming threat. According to the New York Times, Ukraine’s energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, recently briefed European counterparts on an intercepted Russian plan to use as many as 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs against the country’s energy system. The targets included electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants and boiler houses, in what appeared to be an effort to plunge Ukrainian cities into darkness and cold and create a humanitarian crisis.
“Russia plans to freeze Kyiv out, to throw it back into the stone age,” said one senior western diplomat in Kyiv, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Western diplomats say publicly that they intend to remain in Kyiv, mindful that leaving would hand Moscow a propaganda victory and risk creating the impression that Ukraine was being abandoned. However, privately two senior diplomats said contingency plans were being drawn up to relocate embassies to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign missions.
“The situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” the diplomat said.

The solar system will fall apart far sooner than anyone thought, scientists say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:50:31 UTC
23:50:31 KST

Earth will be long gone by then, but new research shows the outer planets will be thrown out too, and a billion times earlier than expected, according to astrophysics research.
The outer planets of the solar system will be thrown into chaos roughly a billion years after the Sun dies, a new study has found, cutting their expected life span a billion-fold.
Previous estimates put the stability of the giant planets' orbits at around a quintillion years, far longer than the current age of the universe.
Researchers at California’s Institute of Technology (Caltech) were investigating how the sun’s slow death would impact the outer planets including Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
It was also previously believed by many scientists, including Isaac Newton, that the sun would shed its mass smoothly as it slowly died, transitioning first into a Red Giant and later a White Dwarf.
Earth, Venus and Mercury would be the first to go, consumed by the Sun as it expanded into a Red Giant, with Mars the lone survivor, sitting far enough away to escape the engulfment.
Earlier studies found the outer planets would survive this process, with their orbits widening to about twice their current size as the Sun lost mass. Their eventual break-up was expected to come only from passing stars, over 30 to 100 billion years.
The new findings suggest this picture is wrong. Instead, the outer planets will be thrown into disorder roughly one billion years after the Sun becomes a white dwarf, which is still billions of years away.
When the Sun becomes a white dwarf, it rapidly cools and shrinks to half its current size, but this will not be a smooth process and previously thought.
The research argues the star will lose its mass in violent, random ejections known as “stochastic kicks,” rather than a calm, consistent release.
The new findings suggest this picture is wrong. Instead, the outer planets will be thrown into disorder roughly one billion years after the Sun becomes a white dwarf, which is still billions of years away.
The solar system is 4.57 billion years old, and the Sun has around five billion years left before it swells into a red giant. Scientists had long assumed the giant planets would outlast it by an almost unimaginable stretch of time.
The research was carried out using high-performance supercomputers and hundreds of advanced N-body numeral simulations, with no AI tools involved whatsoever.
The researchers programmed a virtual model of the solar system containing the Sun, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which the supercomputers then calculated and simulated the velocity and position over billions of years.
What made this year analysis different from previous research was the scripting of the sun losing its mass as it died via random, violent, episodic bursts, with hundreds of different model iterations tested in order to come to a consensus conclusion.
The findings were reported in a study called ‘Terminal Instability of the Solar System Triggered by Stochastic Solar Mass Loss’, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Israel needs a thin constitution to bridge its political divide - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:50:29 UTC
23:50:29 KST

In a political first, Israel’s opposition leaders have presented a common set of principles for the government they intend to form. Four issues top the agenda: equal sharing of the national burden, establishing a state commission of inquiry into the failures of October 7, instituting term limits for prime ministers, and adopting a constitution.
Resolving these issues is a matter of paramount national interest. Without equal sharing of the burden, Israel will struggle to function militarily, economically, and socially; without a state commission of inquiry, we will neither learn how to prevent similar failures in the future nor fulfill our most basic obligation to those who paid a heavy price as a result; term limits are needed to inject fresh thinking into national leadership and reduce the risk of government corruption; and a constitution is an indispensable social and legal framework for safeguarding the stability of Israeli democracy.
These issues are not all alike. The first three can be implemented swiftly through legislation and raise no especially complex professional questions. Adopting a constitution, by contrast, is a complex legal, cultural, and social undertaking – perhaps the greatest challenge a legislature can face – and will therefore take considerable time.
The first three measures also enjoy relatively broad public support in Israel. In-depth surveys indicate that even some supporters of the coalition back the opposition’s positions on these issues. Opinions differ over how equal sharing of the burden should be achieved and how far it should go, but the general direction is supported by a large majority.
The idea of a constitution also enjoys broad support – but only in the abstract. Once the Knesset seeks to translate it into concrete provisions, disagreements among the identity groups that make up Israeli society will erupt in full force. The record is clear: Israel has seen many serious attempts, both inside and outside the Knesset, to propose a constitution, and all have failed. Israel is more polarized today than it was then; the challenge has only grown.
There is another important difference. Arrangements governing the first three issues can be enacted by an ordinary coalition majority, however narrow. By contrast, constitutional arrangements require broader public support.
A constitution provides stability
A constitution has a stabilizing effect only if it is entrenched, so that it cannot later be amended by an ordinary coalition majority. But if the present generation is to constrain the legislative freedom of future coalition majorities, the constitution itself must be adopted by broad support. Without such support, the constitution’s legitimacy is called into question, and instability may actually deepen.
Even so, the opposition leaders are entirely right to put the constitutional challenge on the national agenda. The question is how, in practice, to advance a constitution after the election – and what, in principle, the proper path should be.
A full constitution addresses three fundamental questions: the state’s core identity (who are we?); a bill of rights (what do we believe in?); and the institutions of government (how do we manage our shared life?).
Given Israel’s polarization, broad agreement on the first two questions is unattainable. Even if the “reform parties,” as they call themselves, reach agreement on these matters, they would lack the professional and public legitimacy needed to entrench those arrangements so that future changes would require a larger majority than the one that enacted them.
Would opposition leaders accept constitutional provisions adopted by the current coalition requiring a supermajority – say, 80 MKs – for any future amendment? Hillel the Elder and Immanuel Kant taught us not to impose on others what we would not accept for ourselves.
There is, however, a way to stabilize Israel through a partial constitutional settlement – a “thin constitution” focused on the third question: relations among the branches of government. The fierce struggle over judicial reform shows that disagreement is intense here as well, but the prospects for broad agreement are comparatively greater because these are not questions of identity.
Most Israelis – including supporters of the opposition parties and members of the liberal camp – favor measured changes in the relationship among the branches. A thin constitution that sets rules all sides would regard as fair and effective when viewed from “behind a veil of ignorance” – without knowing whether they will find themselves in the coalition or the opposition in the future – could command broad support.
That is how Israel can achieve the reform it needs.
The writer is president of JPPI – the Jewish People Policy Institute – and professor emeritus of law at Bar-Ilan University.

A former senior UN food agency official has said he has launched an appeal against his dismissal, alleging it was motivated by his stance on hunger in Gaza, in a case that has exposed tensions within the Rome-based organization.
Benjamin Davis, 62, a Spanish American director at the Food and Agriculture Organization, was informed his employment would end on September 30 at the request of Director-General Qu Dongyu, according to documents seen by Reuters.
The papers cited breaches of international civil service standards which require staff to act with impartiality. Davis rejected the allegation.
Joined moments of silence for Gaza
"I feel it’s a terrible injustice. I’ve been disciplined without due process for speaking up about a subject at the core of FAO’s mandate about the right to food, which is the most basic of human rights," he told Reuters. He said he had filed an appeal.
The FAO did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Davis' allegations or on the grounds for his dismissal.
Davis said he had worked at the FAO for 26 years on a renewable contract, and that his dismissal was linked to staff activism over the Gaza war.
He was one of hundreds of employees who have joined moments of silence for hunger victims in Gaza, where an international hunger-monitoring system used by UN agencies determined famine in August 2025.
He also authored a report on food availability in the Palestinian enclave in May 2025.
The dispute burst into public view this week when Qu, speaking at a FAO conference, defended the dismissal of an unnamed staff member whom he accused of having "played the political game."
"We will not allow you to play the game here of human rights," Qu said.
Debate over staff activism
The remarks prompted fresh debate about whether UN employees are able to express views on humanitarian crises without jeopardizing their careers.
A large crowd of staff gathered at FAO headquarters in Rome on Wednesday to applaud Davis as he departed, according to UN officials and video seen by Reuters.
Under UN rules, staff are allowed to express political opinions but must ensure these do not adversely affect their official duties or UN interests.
Davis, who was head of the Rural Transformation and Gender Equality Division, said he was concerned that other employees would face retaliation over their participation in the Gaza moments of silence.
The case, now with the FAO's internal justice process, could later be escalated to a UN tribunal which has the authority to award damages in employment disputes.
Food entering Gaza 'significantly exceeds' number UN identified as necessary
A Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) report from earlier thia year stated that the amount of food and other humanitarian supplies entering the Gaza Strip between October 2025 and June 2026 had “significantly exceeded” the amounts that the United Nations had identified as necessary for the population.
According to COGAT, approximately 1.78 million tons of food entered the Gaza Strip during that time period, which is over three times more than the requirements set by the World Food Programme.

Vote your conscience: Five reasons why Israelis should forget the electoral threshold - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:49:50 UTC
23:49:50 KST

Every Israeli election season, the same warning shows up on schedule: don’t waste your vote. Don’t throw it away on a small party. Stick with the names the polls say are safe.
With five weeks left before we go to the ballot box on October 27, I want to make the opposite case: vote for the party you actually believe in, and let the electoral threshold take care of itself. Here are five reasons why.
1: Polls are wrong
In 2006, Gil, the Pensioners Party led by former Mossad legend Rafi Eitan, spent nearly the entire campaign looking like it would never enter the Knesset. Only the very last published poll gave it two seats.
On election night, it won seven, powered largely by young protest voters in Tel Aviv, and went straight into Ehud Olmert’s coalition.
Fifteen years later, the polls missed in the other direction. In January 2021, Naftali Bennett’s Yamina was polling at 14 seats, with some surveys giving it 16. It won seven, and Bennett was sworn in as prime minister.
If the polls could see neither of those outcomes coming, and have made plenty of other mistakes in between, why should they decide your ballot today?
2: Polls are political instruments used to manipulate you
Someone commissions every one of these polls, whether a news channel with an editorial line or a party trying to manufacture momentum, and the results tend to reflect who paid for the poll.
Two weeks ago, Channel 12 showed the two main blocs tied at 52 seats apiece. Channel 14 released its own numbers, giving Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc a commanding 63-to-44 lead.
Both claimed to be measuring the same electorate in the same week. When the “science” swings by 11 seats depending on who is asking, treat it as campaign material, because that is often exactly what it is.
2.5: The slant begins before a single question is asked
Some 38 parties submitted slates for this election, yet almost no poll asks about all of them. Most offer respondents a dozen or so familiar names and fold everyone else into “other,” so the majority of lists on the ballot never receive a number at all.
A party that is never listed can never be seen to grow.
Then comes the second move: pollsters and the channels that air their results announce that this or that new party won’t cross the threshold, which is a polite way of telling voters to stay away.
Debate organizers take the cue and leave those parties off the stage, and editors point to the same numbers to justify ignoring them.
The effect is a closed loop that protects the traditional parties, the ones most resistant to change, from any real competition, and shrinks the national conversation down to the familiar faces who brought us to where we are.
3: Large segments of the population never make it into the sample for the poll
Soldiers on active duty, about 165,000 people, are off limits to pollsters. That alone is enough votes to carry a party over the threshold.
Then come the voters pollsters struggle to reach: more than 66,000 new olim (immigrants) casting their first Israeli ballot; parts of the Arab community, where over 118,000 young people will vote for the first time; and the largest wave of first-time voters in the history of the state.
One recent analysis from The Jerusalem Post puts that group at close to 600,000 people, mostly between 18 and 22.
Many are in uniform. Many have just finished their service or are in national service. None of them has ever voted for a traditional party, and they carry no old loyalties to break.
4: Remember what so many of us said after October 7?
On social media and around kitchen tables came the demand to send all 120 MKs home. That anger was earned.
Yet a vote for the established parties that pollsters rate safely above the threshold is, for the most part, a vote to return those same people to the Knesset. Some lists have added fresh faces, but most sitting MKs are running again.
Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar now leads the polls, resigned his seat in July 2025. He was still an MK before and during October 7, and he sat in the war cabinet afterward.
If you want genuine renewal, look at the new parties built without any former Knesset members, such as People of Israel, Haredi Public, and others.
5: Look at what most of these parties are selling
The outgoing Knesset is organized by sector: Haredi against secular, religious-Zionist against liberal, Jew against Arab, Left against Right. Pro-Netanyahu vs anti-Netanyahu. Stop me if you’ve heard this before.
Parties raise money and turnout by convincing their base that the other side is the enemy. Very few are doing the harder work of building bridges or repairing the rifts that opened so dangerously before the war and have only deepened since.
They double down on their own voters and leave the country as a whole to fend for itself. Every vote that keeps that model profitable guarantees four more years of it.
Where I stand
So here is where I stand: I will not be voting for any party that sat in the outgoing Knesset and helped create the schisms, the divisiveness, and the hatred aimed at one sector of Israeli society or another.
I will be voting for one of the new parties that is looking to take responsibility for Israel’s shortcomings, working to build connections throughout our society, and wants to bridge the gaps between us rather than entrench them further.
I want a party that will work to heal a nation still suffering from the trauma of October 7 and everything that followed.
I haven’t yet decided exactly which party gets my vote. I have narrowed the field to those that meet that standard.
I’d urge you to learn about the parties and their platforms, set your own standard, and then vote for the party that you believe in, regardless of what any polls say.

He has an MA in Jewish history, is a volunteer first responder, and has served in the IDF. While originally from Canada, he has lived in Israel since 1999 and is a concerned citizen who loves Israel and its people.

G7 agrees 100 million-barrel emergency oil release amid US pressure over diesel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:48:11 UTC
23:48:11 KST

The G7, led by France, announced the release of 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil after Trump threatened a ban of diesel exports.
G7 countries have agreed to release up to 100 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves over four months in a coordinated effort to bring down soaring energy prices, with a particular focus on diesel.
The release will be coordinated by the International Energy Agency (IEA), with a substantial amount of diesel to be made available within the first 20 days, according to a G7 statement.
French President Emmanuel Macron, who currently holds the G7 presidency, said the countries had agreed to act together to ease pressure on energy prices.
"We will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months," the statement said.
The move comes after growing pressure from Washington for countries to release strategic reserves as diesel prices rise and supplies tighten.
Earlier on Friday, the European Commission pushed back against what it described as US "threats" to force European countries to act.
But an overnight call between Macron and US President Donald Trump appears to have helped push Paris towards action, amid concerns over the impact of a possible US diesel export ban.
The G7 package also includes measures to increase refinery output and a pledge not to restrict trade in energy and oil products between partner countries.
The 100 million barrels would amount to roughly 830,000 barrels a day if released evenly over four months.
But the impact will depend on how quickly countries release their stocks and how much of the oil can ultimately be turned into diesel.
Strategic crude releases do not immediately translate into extra diesel supplies. Refineries must first process the crude, with capacity, logistics and the type of crude available all affecting how much fuel reaches consumers.
The release could provide some relief ahead of winter, when demand for diesel and other refined products typically increases.

Asian Games | Day 13 roundup: China's Wang Xiyu wins tennis gold, virtual sports make debut
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:45:31 CST
23:45:31 KST

by sportswriter Li Jia
NAGOYA, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's tennis player Wang Xiyu claimed the women's singles title on Friday while virtual sports made its debut at the Aichi-Nagoya Games.
Virtual taekwondo opened a new chapter at the Asian Games on the day. The discipline brought together 16 athletes from 15 teams in a mixed-gender elimination tournament. Taekwondo specialists, equipped with virtual reality headsets and sensors, took to the stage at the Continental Games for the first time.
Jeus Gabriel Derick Yape from the Philippines grabbed the historical gold medal.
"I believe it's equal for both men and women. I've lost to a lot of women players in my training," said Yape.
"We're just really happy to contribute to the Philippines. It's our first ever taekwondo gold medal in the Asian Games. We're making history. He's making history, because this is also the first ever virtual taekwondo at the Asian Games," said Rani Ann Ortega, the winner's coach.
China's Ma Jingyue won the gold medal in the women's 49kg taekwondo event. In the same event, Talah Alhassan Alhindh competed as the first athlete from the Asian Refugee Team (ART). She lost to Ma in the round of 16.
"I was very excited. It was amazing to participate. It's the first time I've traveled from the refugee camp to another country. I've been trying to do my best these past few days," said Alhindh.
On the tennis court, Wang Xiyu claimed China's sixth straight women's singles Games gold, defeating teammate Zhang Shuai 6-2, 6-1 in a one-sided affair at Higashiyama Park Tennis Center.
Over 66 minutes, Zhang and Wang put their friendship aside as they dueled for gold in what was also the third consecutive all-Chinese final in this event.
For Wang, the result marked a return to form after struggling with injuries and inconsistency in recent seasons. The victory also gave her an automatic berth at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.
"She is someone I really respect," Wang said of Zhang. "Everything that she's been through is also a form of encouragement to me."
"Still, on the court, the biggest form of respect I can show is to give my best to play her," Wang added. "This is what sport, what elite competition is like. Your actions speak for you."
Wang reached the final on Thursday by defeating pre-tournament favorite Alexandra Eala of the Philippines 3-6, 6-3, 6-2. Eala, ranked No. 18 on the WTA Tour, picked up a bronze medal.
China's Wu Yibing, 2018 Asian Games runner-up, advanced to the men's singles final after defeating Japan's Hayato Matsuoka 6-3, 6-2. Wu will meet Coleman Wong from Hong Kong, China in the final.
In the men's doubles final, a pair of amateurs who juggle tennis with their day jobs at a local bank clinched Japan's first gold in this event since Tehran 1974. Yusuke Kusuhara and Shunsuke Nakagawa beat a South Korean pair 2-0 to win the gold.
China failed to defend its women's hockey title after losing 1-0 to India, while China's men's volleyball team was eliminated in the semifinals after a 3-2 defeat to Japan.
China's women's football team ended the tournament empty-handed after a 1-0 defeat to South Korea in the bronze medal match. Noh Jin-young's fourth-minute header proved decisive, earning the Taegeuk Ladies a bronze medal.
South Korea had not defeated China for 11 years before Friday's victory, ending a run of five draws and six losses against China.
On a day of fast and furious action at Yahagigawa Canoe Slalom Course, China grabbed a gold and a bronze in the women's kayak cross, while home favorite Kurumi Ito, winner of the women's kayak single, was knocked out in the quarterfinals. Chen Lin claimed the gold while 16-year-old Xu Linxi settled for bronze. Chang Chu-han of Chinese Taipei took silver.
In the men's kayak cross, Japan's Yuuki Tanaka, who claimed silver in the kayak single, powered past Chinese rival Quan Xin after the first gate to take the gold medal. Quan took the silver while Hu Zhaoshan, who won the gold in the men's kayak single, had to settle for bronze this time.
In archery, India won its first Asian Games gold medal in the recurve women's team event, ending South Korea's run of seven consecutive titles, which had stretched back to Bangkok 1998. China took bronze with a 6-2 win over Indonesia. China claimed the recurve mixed team title, edging India to second place. South Korea also captured a gold, its second straight Asian Games gold medal in the recurve men's team event after defeating India 5-1 on sets.
China also secured gold medals in judo and boxing, with Niu Xinran winning the women's over-78kg title and Paris Olympic champion Wu Yu taking gold in the women's 51kg division.
Moreover, host Japan claimed two gold medals as track cycling concluded, while China and Malaysia took one gold each on the final day.
In water polo, China's men failed to make the final after losing to Kazakhstan 11-10. Kazakhstan will meet Japan in the final.
In golf, four-time PGA Tour winner Kim Joo-hyung of South Korea is taking a one-stroke lead into the final round of the men's golf tournament. South Korea is also leading the men's team standings while China leads the women's team.
Elsewhere, two more athletes failed doping tests at the Games and have been provisionally suspended, according to the International Testing Agency (ITA). The two athletes are Kazakhstan's track and field athlete Aiana Bolatbekkyz and Tajikistan's tennis player Issamjon Sharifov. The number of doping cases at these Asian Games has risen to six. ■

Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery group to adopt Skydance name
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:45:13 UTC
23:45:13 KST

Dilara Hamit
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
The company formed through the merger of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery will be named Skydance Corporation when the transaction closes next week.
The deal is expected to be completed on Oct. 6, subject to customary closing conditions, according to company filings. It values Warner Bros. Discovery at an enterprise value of about $110 billion.
The Skydance name comes from the film and television production company founded by David Ellison, who will serve as chairman and chief executive of the combined group.
The corporate identity is intended to sit above Paramount and Warner Bros., allowing the two studios to retain their individual names and established brands.
Skydance also plans to transfer its Class B common stock from the Nasdaq exchange to the New York Stock Exchange. Trading on the NYSE is expected to begin Oct. 6 under the ticker symbol SKYD, replacing the current PSKY symbol.
The merger will bring together Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros., as well as the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming platforms. Its television operations will include CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central and Food Network.
The combined catalogue will encompass franchises and properties including Harry Potter, The Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones, the DC Universe, Yellowstone, Mission: Impossible, Top Gun and Nickelodeon’s children’s programming.
Former Mattel chief Ynon Kreiz will join the company as co-chief executive, while Ellison will remain chairman and CEO. Kreiz is scheduled to begin his role on Oct. 5, a day before the planned completion of the merger.
The transaction concludes a prolonged contest for Warner Bros. Discovery. Paramount prevailed after outbidding Netflix, which had reached an agreement to acquire Warner Bros.’ studio and streaming operations.
A federal judge cleared one of the final obstacles on Sept. 30 by approving a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sought to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.
The acquisition is being financed through a combination of shares, loans, bonds and outside investment. Paramount has arranged more than $41 billion in dollar-denominated bonds, €885 million ($993 million) in euro-denominated notes and new term loans worth $8.5 billion and €850 million ($954 million).
Affiliates of Oracle founder Larry Ellison have committed up to $46.7 billion in equity financing. Investment vehicles linked to the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are also participating in the transaction alongside RedBird Capital Partners.
Control of the company will rest with David Ellison, Larry Ellison and RedBird founder Gerry Cardinale. Skydance will begin operations with one of the entertainment industry’s largest collections of studios, networks and intellectual property, but it will also face the challenge of integrating two sprawling businesses while also managing substantial debt.

The forum was established as an African business forum to convene biennially in Egypt. ■

Last working engine of Japan's Hayabusa2 asteroid probe fails
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:44:49 CST
23:44:49 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Japan's Hayabusa2 space probe, which has been operating far beyond its design life, has suffered a malfunction in its last working ion engine, local media reported Friday.
According to Kyodo News, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) aims to keep the probe operating by combining the remaining functional components of its ion engines.
Hayabusa2 is equipped with four ion engines. Three had previously malfunctioned, leaving only one operational. The remaining engine B also failed in mid-August. Although JAXA attempted to restore it, the engine could not be restarted, the report said, citing JAXA sources.
Each of the probe's four ion engines normally uses its own ion source to eject ions and a neutralizer to emit electrons, with both components needed for an engine to operate.
According to Jiji Press, a detailed examination by JAXA found that the ion source of engine B has failed while its neutralizer still works. In the previously malfunctioning engines C and D, however, the problem lies in the neutralizers, and their ion sources still function normally.
JAXA therefore plans to use a "cross operation" method, switching the probe's circuitry to pair engine B's neutralizer with engine D's ion source so that the probe can continue its mission.
The same technique was used on the original Hayabusa probe and enabled it to return to Earth despite engine problems.
Nearly 12 years after its December 2014 launch, Hayabusa2 has greatly exceeded its design life, and many of its parts and systems have deteriorated or malfunctioned.
Whether the method will enable the probe to reach its new asteroid target, 1998 KY26, in 2031 remains unclear. ■

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.
The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.
Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.
Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.
The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.
“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”
Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.
The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.
Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try to stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.
Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.
Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election commission office in Delhi next week.

17 countries join forces to oppose EU budget cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:39:01 UTC
23:39:01 KST

BRUSSELS — Seventeen EU governments have publicly warned against cuts to agriculture and regional payouts in the next seven-year budget, in a rebuke of Germany's stance in the negotiations.
The letter — signed on Friday by Italy, Spain and Poland among others — heaps pressure on the Irish rotating presidency of the Council of the EU to leave untouched almost €900 billion of spending in the upcoming draft budget, which is expected to be presented next week.
This sets up tensions with a rival camp of six countries led by Germany, which renewed calls for cuts of several hundred billion euros across the board in a joint letter earlier this week.
Advertisement
"We therefore believe that the overall funding for Cohesion Policy and the CAP must be preserved in the next MFF," the seventeen countries wrote in the letter to Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin seen by POLITICO.
The signatories include Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Romanian President Nicușor Dan coordinated the initiative and will host an informal meeting of those countries in the margins of the next European Council on Oct. 15 and 16.
The Multiannual Financial Framework, or MFF, finances everything from farmers’ subsidies to development aid, and is among the toughest negotiations in Brussels. In 2025, the European Commission proposed a budget of nearly €2 trillion for the 2028-2034 period and shifted hundreds of billions from agriculture and regional payouts, known as cohesion policy, to new priorities such as defense and competitiveness.
The so-called Friends of Cohesion group warned that further reductions to agricultural and cohesion "would only weaken it [budget] and risk undermining public support for the European project."
Ireland’s negotiating document, or negobox, will set the scene for discussions among the EU’s 27 leaders during the summit in Brussels in October.
Advertisement
EU governments are rushing to secure a final agreement among themselves by the end of the year, before national elections in France, Poland and Italy threaten to derail the negotiations.
One of the most sensitive issues involves introducing new EU-wide taxes, known as own resources, to finance the budget. The Commission proposed five new levies that are estimated to generate €66 billion per year.
The tax package is strongly supported by France, but individual proposals have been opposed by several national governments who fear that they will be disproportionately affected by the levies.
The 17 countries wrote in the letter that new own resources"should be genuine, fair, simple and non-regressive."
To create more leeway, they also renewed calls to delay repayments of post-Covid debt that is expected to cost €25 billion per year and opposed budget discounts to wealthier countries, known as rebates.

The United Arab Emirates has warned the UK government that sanctions facing Manchester City could affect its interest in future major investments in Britain, Bloomberg reported Friday.

Warring out, Pargat Singh in: Has Congress solved Punjab crisis or created more confusion?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:37:33 UTC
23:37:33 KST

NEW DELHI: The churn in Punjab Congress is now complete. Or is it?Amarinder Singh Raja Warring is out and Pargat Singh is the new Punjab Congress president. The change came hours after Warring resigned from the post, ending his more than four-year stint as state party chief. Warring met Rahul Gandhi on Friday and formally submitted his resignation. A day earlier, he had changed his X bio to “Former PPCC President”, signalling the leadership change."He (Rahul Gandhi) gave me a lot of love. He sought information about the current political situation in Punjab, on what is happening with the government and what we should be doing there," Warring said after his meeting.Hours later, the Congress announced the appointment of Pargat Singh as the new Punjab Congress president with immediate effect. The party also appreciated the contribution of outgoing president Warring.The change in Punjab Congress comes after months of infighting over who should lead the Congress into the 2027 assembly election. The crisis was triggered by Congress’s decision to retain Warring as state unit president in July, ignoring the claims of former chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi. So, Warring’s exit marks a victory for Channi and his supporters, but the entry of Pargat Singh means he does not gain from Warring's loss.
Warring is out, but not down
Warring may be out of his post, but has dropped strong hints that his fight may be far from over. Hours after formally stepping down, Warring targeted his detractors, signalling he is not leaving the field yet. If Warring’s remarks against party incharge Sachin Pilot are an indication to go by, we could well see a reversal of roles in Punjab Congress infighting.In an interaction with news agency ANI, Warring said, “I feel that Sachin Pilot must have decided it was time to remove ‘Raja’ from the post.” Warring, though, added that he had “no concrete proof” of this.
Amarinder Singh Raja Warring hints that Sachin Pilot may have played a role in his exit.
Warring added he had not spoken to Pilot about his exit, but had heard that the state Congress incharge may have recommended a change. “Perhaps the in-charge mentioned that Raja Warring would have to be replaced,” he said when asked about the reasons for his resignation.Taking digs at those responsible for his exit, Warring said nobody had formally asked him to resign. Instead, he had simply read the “direction of the wind”."Just like elder women who could tell by reading the direction of the wind whether it was going to rain... I observed the situation closely, and it never reached the point where someone had to ask me to resign," Warring told IANS.That, he said, was why he changed his X bio to “Former PPCC President” even before formally submitting his resignation to Rahul Gandhi.
Amarinder Singh Raja Warring said he stepped down as Punjab Congress chief after reading the 'direction of the wind'
The timing and the turn of events are hard to miss. Nearly a month ago, Congress removed former Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhupesh Baghel as Punjab in-charge after the Channi faction openly rebelled against him. Baghel was accused of favouring Warring and was eventually replaced by Sachin Pilot.But now, Warring appears ready to open a front against Pilot and, of course, also Channi.That also raises questions about whether replacing Baghel with Pilot has actually helped Congress settle the Punjab crisis. Sugata Srinivasaraju, senior political analyst and author, believes that the leadership change appears to have created more confusion rather than resolving the crisis at hand."What is it that the Congress saw in Pilot that they did not see in Baghel? If you thought Baghel was part of the problem, now Pilot has also become part of the problem. He’s not part of the solution," he said.According to him, Congress may now have ended up with an even bigger problem. "All of them were against Warring. Now Warring goes out and Channi has not been catered to. So we don't know what's going to happen."Both Baghel and Warring are now out of their roles in Punjab Congress. For the Channi camp, it means one of their biggest demands has been met. But with Pargat Singh in the chair, will today's change end weeks of internal feud and bickering in Punjab Congress? Perhaps not.To understand why Warring’s exit and Pargat's entry may not be the end of the crisis, it helps to go back to where the tussle began.
How the Channi-Warring tussle began
The crisis began on July 1, when the Congress leadership announced that Warring would continue as Punjab Congress president and Channi would head the campaign committee. Senior leaders Sukhjinder Singh Randhawa and Vijay Inder Singla were also given specific roles for the 2027 assembly election.On paper, it looked like an attempt to balance competing camps. In practice, it did the opposite.Channi’s supporters questioned why Warring was being retained as state chief and began pushing for a larger role for the former chief minister. What was meant to settle the leadership question instead reopened old faultlines within the party.Warring had been appointed Punjab Congress president after the party’s crushing defeat to AAP in the 2022 assembly election. Channi had been the party’s chief ministerial face in that campaign but lost both seats he contested.Warring was then brought in by the Congress high command (read Rahul Gandhi) to rebuild the organisation and prepare it for the next election. For nearly four years, however, the Congress did not clearly announce who would lead its 2027 campaign.When it finally tried to do that in July, the compromise pleased no one.Bhupesh Baghel, who was then Punjab in-charge, tried to defuse the tussle between the Channi and Warring camps but was also caught in the crossfire and forced out of the state.His replacement, Sachin Pilot, initially managed to bring the rival factions onto the same stage during the Congress protest over the Gulzar Singh suicide case. But that show of unity did not last long.What followed was another round of meetings, complaints and feedback to the high command and, eventually, Warring's exit and Pargat's entry.
Warring out, but Channi not in
The Congress high command acted swiftly after Warring's exit and handed over the baton to Pargat Singh. The three-time Congress MLA from Jalandhar Cantt and former Indian hockey captain who has served as Punjab cabinet minister in Charanjit Singh Channi cabinet, has his task cut out.Pargat's name was doing the rounds along with other key contenders which included, former MLA Rana KP Singh, Raja Sansi MLA Sukhbinder Singh Sarkaria, former chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi and Gurdaspur MP Sukhjinder Singh Randhawa. But the frontrunner before today's appointment was former PWD minister and MP Vijay Inder Singla, who was appointed chairperson of the Congress Election Management and Coordination Committee in the July reshuffle."I am a loyal soldier of the party, and at all times, as a worker of the party, whatever responsibility I have been given, I have always fulfilled my duties. And in the coming times as well, we will work together with everyone in the same manner," Singla had said earlier reacting to speculations that he could replace Warring.However that did not happen.And this is where the leadership change in Punjab Congress becomes more interesting.The Channi camp had openly demanded that the former CM should lead the party into the next elections. In fact, their contention all along was that Warring should be replaced by Channi. But today's announcement would leave them disappointed much like the other contenders including Singla.
2022 rerun in Punjab
With the Congress picking up Pargat Singh as the compromise candidate, it is a rerun of what happened in the run up to the 2022 elections.And that brings Punjab Congress back to a very familiar problem of bitter power tussle between state leaders. A problem that played a key role in the party’s defeat in 2022.Ahead of the 2022 assembly election, then chief minister Captain Amarinder Singh and Navjot Singh Sidhu were locked in a bitter leadership battle. Sidhu wanted a bigger role in leading the party into the election, while Amarinder resisted attempts to cut into his authority.The Congress leadership allowed the dispute to drag on until the crisis became impossible to contain. Eventually, Amarinder Singh was removed as chief minister. Charanjit Singh Channi emerged as the compromise candidate of Congress high command and was made the chief minister.But the compromise did not end the factional war. Congress went into the election divided and suffered a historic defeat, with AAP sweeping into power.Four years later, the names have changed, but the problem looks strikingly similar.Srinivasaraju sees a larger pattern in Punjab Congress's repeated leadership tussles."Punjab Congress has not been able to resolve it at all. They've had five long years after Amarinder Singh’s exit and they have still not got it right," he said.
His argument is that every time Congress begins to see a chance of returning to power in Punjab, competing factions become more active and start weakening the organisation from within."We have seen that with Navjot Singh Sidhu and Amarinder Singh," he said, adding that similar mistakes "seem to be getting repeated".Once again, both the rival leaders - Channi and Warring - are out. But the battle for Channi is still half won. And with Warring all set for a rebel role, the road ahead for the former Punjab chief minister may not be easy.With Warring’s loss not translating into Channi's gain, it will be interesting to see if the Congress's compromise candidate ends this leadership fight once and for all without starting another power tussle?

Iran, Armenia stress removing border obstacles, increasing transit capacity
TEHRAN- A joint meeting was held between Iran’s Deputy Minister of Transport and Urban Development and Head of the Road Maintenance and Transportation Organization, and a delegation from the Republic of Armenia, with the presence of Armenia’s Deputy Minister of Infrastructure and Territorial Management, at the Nordooz border terminal.
According to IRNA, citing the Road Maintenance and Transportation Organization, in line with expanding trade and logistical relations between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Republic of Armenia and making maximum use of the two countries’ transport, transit, and infrastructure capacities, a joint meeting was held between Reza Akbari, Deputy Minister of Transport and Urban Development and Head of the Road Maintenance and Transportation Organization, and a delegation from the Republic of Armenia, with the presence of Armenia’s Deputy Minister of Infrastructure and Territorial Management, at the Nordooz border terminal.
The meeting focused on developing transport and transit cooperation, strengthening the two countries’ role in regional transit routes, and identifying and removing existing obstacles. During the meeting, increasing border exchange capacity, improving the level of services at official crossings, facilitating the movement of commercial fleets, and strengthening logistical infrastructure and border hinterlands were reviewed and discussed.
In continuation of their cooperation, the two sides will pursue the removal of existing obstacles, reducing the time required for border and customs procedures, improving the efficiency of border terminals, and increasing regional transit capacity.
It is worth noting that the Nordooz border terminal, as one of the important communication crossings between Iran and Armenia, has considerable capacity for developing trade exchanges and regional transit.
In late September, the Director General of the Central Asia, Caucasus and Russia Office of the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran announced a 7.5% increase in Iran’s exports to Armenia during the seven months of 2026, putting the value of goods exported from Iran to Armenia in that period at $385 million.
According to IRNA, citing the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran, Mehdi Babaei said, referring to the joint Iranian-Armenian border and customs meeting held on September 12, in Jolfa, that at the meeting the two sides stressed the development of customs cooperation and the facilitation of trade between the two countries.
He described one of the most important agreements of the meeting as the signing of a customs green corridor memorandum of understanding between Iran and Armenia, and said: “The necessary measures for the electronic exchange of customs documents and data, as well as identifying and introducing authorized operators, will be pursued more rapidly.”
Babaei, emphasizing that the implementation of these measures can provide the basis for facilitating and accelerating customs and transit processes at the two countries’ border, added: “Based on the agreements reached, if the desired requirements are met, the truck reception capacity at the Norduz border can increase to 300 trucks per day.”
The Director General of the Central Asia, Caucasus and Russia Office of the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran considered the development of customs infrastructure, electronic exchange of information, and increased truck traffic capacity at the Norduz border as paving the way for trade facilitation and strengthening Iran-Armenia economic and transit relations.
The joint Iranian-Armenian border and customs meeting was held with the presence of the heads and directors of the customs administrations of the two countries, the Armenian ambassador in Tehran, the embassy’s commercial attaché, and representatives of relevant bodies of both countries.

Spanish Congress rejects both of government's housing decrees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

23:36:31 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Spain's Congress of Deputies on Friday rejected two housing decrees approved by the government earlier this week, dealing a double defeat to its efforts to introduce new tenant protections and address housing affordability.
The first decree was defeated by 178 votes to 172, with the conservative People's Party, far-right Vox and Catalan separatist Junts voting against it.
The measure included protections against certain evictions, regulation of seasonal and room rentals, measures aimed at expanding affordable housing and restrictions on certain property purchases by investment funds.
A second decree was rejected by a wider margin, with 184 lawmakers voting against it and 166 in favor.
That measure included the automatic renewal of primary-residence rental contracts in cases where landlords could not provide legally recognized grounds for ending them.
Junts opposed both decrees and had called on the government to withdraw the measures before the votes and negotiate new legislation instead.
The two decrees had been approved by the Council of Ministers on Tuesday as part of the government's response to concerns over housing affordability and protections for tenants.
The votes came amid protests over Spain's housing crisis, with demonstrators who had been camping in Madrid's Puerta del Sol marching toward Congress on Friday to demand approval of the measures.
The protests followed the Sept. 23 eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than 70 years.
She was removed on a stretcher and taken to a hospital, with the case becoming a symbol of the country's housing crisis.
Abascal has since reached an agreement with the company that owns the apartment, allowing her to return to her home after leaving the hospital with a similar rent under a new contract, averting a significant price hike.
