UK sanctions seven Russians over deportation of Ukrainian children
The United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on seven people involved in Russia's programme of forced deportation and "re-education" of Ukrainian children.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life)
Details: The list includes the chairman of the board of Russia's Movement of the First, heads of its branches in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, and the chair of the board of trustees of Russia's National Centre for Assistance to Missing and Affected Children.
Bring Kids Back UA, a Ukrainian government-led effort to bring Ukrainian children home from temporarily Russian-occupied territories, told Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia about the people included on the sanctions list.
Who has been sanctioned?
The list includes Artur Orlov, chairman of the board of the Movement of the First, a Russian state-backed social movement for children and young people. Orlov is a Russian officer, tank battalion commander and combatant in the war against Ukraine. Russian ruler Vladimir Putin appointed him to head the movement in 2024.
Five heads of the movement's regional branches in the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts and Crimea have also been sanctioned:
- Denis Chernobai
- Riyal Aliyev
- Aleksei Lavrentyev
- Viktoria Kostromina
- Yekaterina Kozyr.
Russia established the Movement of the First in 2022 on Putin's initiative as one of the tools for militarising children. According to a report by the OSCE Moscow Mechanism expert mission, it has more than 344,000 members in the occupied territories alone.
The list also includes Yelena Milskaya, chair of the board of trustees of Russia's National Centre for Assistance to Missing and Affected Children.
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine has information that in October 2022 she used the centre's volunteers as cover for the mass abduction and illegal deportation of Ukrainian children, including orphans, from the occupied territories of Ukraine to Krasnodar Krai via Crimea.
At least three of the seven people – Orlov, Chernobai and Milskaya – have been sanctioned by Canada, while Milskaya has also been sanctioned by the EU.
"The Movement of the First in the occupied territories is not about children's clubs. It is a conveyor belt through which Russia turns Ukrainian children into Russian soldiers for a war against their own homeland. Britain has named those who run this conveyor belt from Crimea to Luhansk. We thank the United Kingdom: everyone who commits crimes against Ukrainian children must know that they will be held personally accountable," said Maksym Maksymov, head of Bring Kids Back UA.
The UK government said millions of Ukrainian children in the occupied territories are subjected to Kremlin propaganda programmes, including weapons training and drone operation. Their aim is to strip children of their Ukrainian identity and prepare them to serve the state attacking their homeland.
Those on the sanctions list have had their assets frozen, been banned from entering the UK, faced restrictions on trust services and been prohibited from serving as directors of companies.
Background:
- Defence Intelligence of Ukraine previously named 10 people involved in the militarisation of Ukrainian children in the occupied territories. They included Artur Orlov, Aleksei Lavrentyev, Riyal Aliyev, Yekaterina Kozyr and Viktoria Kostromina.
- The Russian curriculum is being imposed on almost 2,000 schools in Ukraine's temporarily occupied territories, shaping the education of over 582,000 children. Schools are introducing new subjects that emphasise "patriotic" indoctrination and cultivate loyalty to the Russian state ideology.
- Russian forces are actively militarising children in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, including through Yunarmiya and cadet classes. Another tool is the Movement of the First, which regularly holds military-style games and public ceremonies for handing out Russian IDs. More than 340,000 children and young people from the occupied territories are among its participants.

Beyond K-pop and cinema: Major Korean exhibition brings centuries of art and belief to London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:12:56 UTC
23:12:56 KST

The exhibition includes 10 national treasures and official Korean designations recognising their cultural importance, with most exhibits drawn from the collection of late Samsung billionaire Lee Kun-Hee.
Long before K-pop filled stadiums and Korean films won global acclaim, the peninsula’s artists were casting temple bells, shaping delicate ceramics and capturing mountains in ink.
That older cultural world takes centre stage in ‘Korea’, the British Museum’s first major exhibition on Korean art and history in more than 40 years.
Spanning from 300 BC to the present, its 100 exhibits explore the beliefs and traditions that shaped Korean art.
The display includes 10 national treasures and 13 other treasures, official Korean designations recognising their cultural and historical importance, according to Samsung, the exhibition’s corporate partner.
Among the objects on display are a 900-year-old incense burner crowned with a mythical creature and a huge Buddhist temple bell around 1,000 years old.
The exhibition moves from the luminous blue-green ceramics of the Goryeo dynasty to the restrained porcelain of Joseon, shaped by Confucian ideals, according to the British Museum and Samsung.
Together, they show how Buddhism and Confucian ideas shaped Korean art over the centuries.
For the exhibition’s curator, Yoojin Kwak Choi, the “absolute star exhibit” is Jeong Seon’s Clearing After Rain on Mount Inwang.
Jeong Seon is an 18th-century Korean painter of the Joseon dynasty who helped shift landscape painting from idealised Chinese-style scenes towards Korea’s actual scenery, Choi explains.
But there are modern examples of Korean craftsmanship too.
Yeesookyung’s 2018 vase combines ceramic shards from North and South Korea. In Korean artisanal tradition, imperfect work is destroyed, so the artist has taken broken shards from that destruction and glued them together with gold leaf.
Most exhibits come from the collection of the late Samsung chairman Lee Kun-Hee.
The billionaire amassed a vast collection over his lifetime, and after his death in 2020, his family donated more than 23,000 works to South Korean national museums.
“Some people might think that Korean culture is new, but it is thousands upon thousands of years old,” said Benjamin Braun, Samsung Europe’s chief marketing officer.
For visitors drawn to Korea through its music and cinema, the exhibition opens a door onto that longer history.
‘Korea’ runs at the British Museum until 31 January 2027.

Sofia Adds New Direct Connection to Egypt
Wizz Air launched its new scheduled direct service between Sofia and Sharm El Sheikh, Egypt, on October 1, the airline said in a statement dated October 2, 2026.
The new route will operate twice a week, on Thursdays and Sundays, through October 22, before switching to three weekly flights on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays in the following months.
With the Sofia-Sharm El Sheikh service, Wizz Air becomes the only low-cost airline in Bulgaria offering a scheduled direct connection between the country and Egypt. The carrier will add another direct route to Egypt, from Sofia to Hurghada, starting October 27, as demand for winter sun holidays grows.
Tickets for the new flights are already available through wizzair.com and Wizz Air’s mobile app, with fares starting at €45.99.
Sharm El Sheikh, on the Red Sea coast, is among Egypt’s most popular resorts. Its beaches and clear waters attract more tourists each year, while visitors can choose from luxury accommodation and activities including diving and snorkeling around the coral reefs of Ras Mohammed National Park, sunset sand dune safaris, camel rides and dinners under the stars at a Bedouin camp.
The resort also combines opportunities for relaxation with nightlife, with Naama Bay offering a waterfront promenade, restaurants and shops, while the Old Market is known for its busy streets, Oriental atmosphere and Al Sahaba Mosque.
"We launched a number of new routes from Bulgaria last summer, and today we are delighted to kick off our winter schedule with the launch of direct flights from Sofia to Egypt! With this new direct connection, we reinforce our commitment to Bulgarian travelers to offer increasingly convenient and affordable travel options within Europe and beyond. Bulgarian travelers deserve the chance to enjoy sunny vacations in winter, too, and starting October 27, we will make Hurghada an even more accessible destination from Bulgaria. We look forward to welcoming Bulgarian passengers on board WIZZ this winter! Let's WIZZ, Bulgaria!" said Salvatore Gabriele Imperiale, Corporate Communications Manager at Wizz Air.
Wizz Air has operated in Bulgaria for more than two decades and has carried over 34 million passengers to and from the country during that period. The airline has 11 Airbus A321neo aircraft based in Bulgaria, with eight in Sofia and three in Varna, and holds a 33% share of the Bulgarian airline market.
Demand across Wizz Air’s network is also continuing to increase as the winter season approaches. The airline carried more than 7.7 million passengers in September 2026, up 24.5% from a year earlier, while its flight completion rate reached 99.65%.
The Sofia-Sharm El Sheikh service will operate on Thursdays and Sundays until October 22 and on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays from October 26, with fares starting at €45.99.
The Sofia-Hurghada route will begin on October 27, with flights scheduled for Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, also with fares starting at €45.99.
The one-way fare includes the administrative fee and a small cabin bag measuring no more than 40x30x20 cm. Wheeled luggage and other checked baggage incur additional fees. The stated fares are available for bookings through wizzair.com and the Wizz Air mobile app, with a limited number of seats offered at those prices.

Hungarian alliances in Ukraine express satisfaction with draft law on education
The Cultural Alliance of Hungarians in Sub-Carpathia and the Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Ukraine have welcomed the draft law on the educational rights of national minorities and called on the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament) to adopt it as soon as possible.
Source: European Pravda, citing a joint statement by the organisations on Facebook
Details: Both organisations noted that they welcome the draft law introduced on 1 October for consideration by Ukraine's Verkhovna Rada, which was developed following bilateral consultations between the governments of Hungary and Ukraine, as well as with the involvement of related European institutions.
They emphasised that the presented draft law resolves the issue in the field of education. The joint statement reads that the draft law comprehensively and fundamentally regulates the issue of implementing the educational rights of national minorities, ensuring the preservation of the nation's network of educational institutions and the free use of the native language in the educational process.
Read more in the article by European Pravda: Hungary lifts its veto: what the deal means for Ukraine's EU accession
The statement stresses that the proposed legislative solutions meet the interests not only of the Hungarian national minority in Zakarpattia, but also of all national minorities and indigenous peoples of Ukraine.
Both organisations advocated for the prompt and full adoption of the draft law by the Verkhovna Rada.
The statement says that this step is necessary to guarantee the rights of national minorities, establish good-neighborly relations between Hungary and Ukraine and support the process of Ukraine's European integration.
The statement was signed by the heads of both organisations. At the same time, it is worth noting that Vasyl (László) Brenzovych, head of the Cultural Alliance of Hungarians in Sub-Carpathia, is considered close to former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, whereas László Zubánics, leader of the Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Ukraine, holds a skeptical view toward the former Hungarian government.
Background:
- On 1 October, a bill on education in the languages of national minorities was registered in the Verkhovna Rada. Its adoption is expected to help lift Hungary's veto and clear the way for two of the negotiating clusters.
- Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán welcomed the submission of the draft law on the educational rights of national minorities to the Verkhovna Rada, stating that she expects it to be passed this month.

Türkiye and Georgia have signed a cooperation agreement to strengthen ties in education, Türkiye’s education minister Yusuf Tekin said on Friday.
Tekin, who was in the Georgian capital Tbilisi for official talks, met his Georgian counterpart Givi Mikanadze at the education ministry.
The two ministers discussed bilateral cooperation in education and other areas before signing the agreement following their roughly hour-long meeting.
“The stronger we and our neighbour are, and the better our cooperation with our neighbour is, the stronger peace, human rights and democracy will be in our region,” Tekin said after the ceremony.
Mikanadze said Tekin’s visit would help advance ties between the two countries, describing their relationship as one of “extremely positive cooperation, strategic partnership and friendship”.
Under the agreement, Türkiye and Georgia will seek to strengthen cooperation in education and open educational institutions on the basis of reciprocity.
The two sides will also work towards recognising diplomas and other educational documents, promote the teaching of Turkish and Georgian, and increase exchanges of information and expertise in education.

Šefčovič: Verhandlung mit China noch ohne  Ergebnisse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:04:26 UTC
23:04:26 KST

Šefčovič: Verhandlung mit China noch ohne Ergebnisse
Der EU-Handelskommissar erklärt gegenüber POLITICO, China habe verstanden, dass eine Einigung dringend notwendig ist. Er hofft auf Ergebnisse zu drei Hauptthemen.
MILWAUKEE - China und die EU seien in Bezug auf ein mögliches Handelsabkommen „noch lange nicht am Ziel“, sagte EU-Handelskommissar Maroš Šefčovič am Donnerstag (Ortszeit) im Gespräch mit POLITICO. Die Gespräche seien „konstruktiv, aber schwierig“.
„Ich spüre großes politisches Interesse und natürlich sehr hohe Erwartungen seitens der Staats- und Regierungschefs in der gesamten Europäischen Union“, sagte Šefčovič am Rande eines Treffens der G20-Handelsminister in Milwaukee. „Ich weiß, wie politisch ungeduldig die europäische Führung ist.“
Šefčovič reist am 8. Oktober nach Peking für ein, wie er es nannte, „äußerst wichtiges Treffen“ mit dem chinesischen Handelsminister Wang Wentao. Er sei optimistisch, dass die Reise Früchte tragen werde. „Man muss daran glauben, dass man etwas erreichen kann, sonst sollte man besser gar nicht erst hinfahren.“
Advertisement
Über die Ergebnisse der Reise sprechen die EU-Staats- und Regierungschefs am 15. und 16. Oktober bei ihrem EU-Gipfel in Brüssel. Die EU droht damit, den Zugang chinesischer Unternehmen zum Binnenmarkt einzuschränken, sollten die Gespräche scheitern.
Die EU und China verhandeln seit Juni. Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU haben erklärt, sie wollten die große Menge chinesischer Importe und das hohe Handelsdefizit mit China, nicht länger hinnehmen.
„Ich glaube, unsere chinesischen Partner haben verstanden, dass dies direkte Auswirkungen auf die Zukunft bedeutender europäischer Unternehmen hat – buchstäblich Tausende von Arbeitsplätzen“, berichtete Šefčovič. „Und auch auf das soziale Gefüge und das Sozialmodell, das in Europa über viele, viele Jahrzehnte hinweg entwickelt wurde.“
Im Mittelpunkt der Gespräche steht das wachsende Handelsdefizit der Union mit China von einer Milliarde Euro pro Tag. Um dieses Defizit zu verringern, müssen die Importe aus China reduziert und/oder die EU-Exporte nach China gesteigert werden.
Šefčovič erklärte, er hoffe, aus Peking Ergebnisse zu drei Hauptthemen mitbringen zu können: plötzliche Exportanstiege Chinas in wichtigen Industriezweigen, Maßnahmen zur Steigerung europäischer Warenexporte nach China, Klarheit hinsichtlich chinesischer Exportbeschränkungen für Rohstoffe, insbesondere für Seltene Erden.
In Milwaukee traf sich Šefčovič mit dem chinesischen Vizeminister Li Chenggang. Der slowakische Kommissar erklärte, China habe Verständnis für die Bedenken Europas: „Alle von uns angesprochenen Themen liegen auf dem Tisch. Ich sage nicht, dass wir Zusicherungen haben, dass wir sie lösen werden, aber sie liegen auf dem Tisch.“
Advertisement
In der Vergangenheit hätten sich einige dieser Themen nur schwer auf die Tagesordnung setzen lassen. Dass dies nun möglich ist, „spiegelt das Bewusstsein dafür wider, wie wichtig dies politisch für uns beide ist“, sagte der Kommissar.
Die Gespräche der EU mit China wurden bisher in vier Arbeitsbereiche unterteilt: Handels- und Investitionsgleichgewicht, Exportkontrollen, geistiges Eigentum und die Reform der Welthandelsorganisation WTO.
Eine mit den Verhandlungen vertraute Person erklärte, die Kommission strebe eine Einigung mit China an, die eine Mischung aus bilateralen Abkommen für bestimmte Produktgruppen und einseitigen Beschränkungen für andere Kategorien vorsehe.
Dieser Text erschien zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO.

====================================================================================================

The right side of the brain shows more signs of aging than the left, new study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:00:52 UTC
23:00:52 KST

A recent study published in PNAS introduces a new artificial intelligence approach to map how different regions of the human brain age. By analyzing MRI scans in fine detail, the research provides evidence that aging does not happen evenly across the brain, with certain areas showing more advanced biological age in individuals with Alzheimer’s disease.
Doctors and scientists use Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), a technique that uses strong magnetic fields to create detailed images of the body’s internal structures, to estimate a person’s “brain age.” This metric tells us whether a person’s brain looks older or younger than their actual chronological age. An older-looking brain is often a risk factor for cognitive decline and neurodegenerative conditions.
Usually, researchers calculate a single, global brain age. But the human brain is a complex organ made of distinct regions, each handling different tasks. For instance, the frontal lobe is involved in complex decision-making, and the hippocampus plays a role in memory. Because these regions perform differently, they also tend to age at different rates. A single brain age score can hide these regional differences, making it harder to detect early signs of localized damage.
“Our earlier work focused on global brain age, where AI estimates how old a person’s brain appears from an MRI,” study author Andrei Irimia, an associate professor of gerontology at the USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology, told PsyPost. “That provides a useful summary, but it reduces the entire brain to a single number, making the result difficult to interpret biologically.”
“We therefore developed local brain age, which asks not only ‘How old does this brain look?’ but ‘How old does each part of this brain look?'” Irimia explained. “The resulting model transforms a structural MRI into a spatial map of local brain age.”
The research, led by Nikhil N. Chaudhari with Irimia and colleagues at the Irimia Lab, aimed to create a more detailed map of brain aging. The authors wanted to measure biological aging at a fine-grained level, breaking the brain down into tiny three-dimensional pixels called voxels. By doing this, they hoped to pinpoint exactly where the brain is aging the fastest and how these specific regional changes relate to cognitive decline.
To build their localized map of brain aging, the scientists trained a deep learning computer model using MRI scans from 14,748 cognitively healthy adults ranging in age from 19 to 100. “Scale and interpretability were important aspects of the project,” Irimia noted. “We trained the model using 14,748 cognitively normal participants from multiple imaging cohorts, exposing it to substantial variation in age, anatomy, and imaging data.”
“Our goal was not simply to produce an AI model with good predictive accuracy, but to generate an output that neuroscientists can map directly back onto brain anatomy,” he said. “In that sense, local brain age is intended to provide a bridge between AI-based prediction and questions about the biology of human aging.”
After training the system, the research team tested it on a separate group of 1,985 individuals from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. This testing group included 1,102 adults with normal cognitive function, 354 with mild cognitive impairment, and 529 with Alzheimer’s disease.
When observing the cognitively healthy adults, the model’s estimates were off by about 5.9 years on average. It identified a distinct pattern of aging across the brain. The frontal and temporal lobes, which are heavily involved in higher-level thinking and memory, exhibited a more advanced biological age compared to regions at the back of the brain, such as the visual processing centers in the occipital lobe.
The researchers also looked closely at the brain’s folded outer layer, the cerebral cortex. They found that the sulci, which are the deep grooves between the folds, appeared biologically older than the gyri, the outward-facing ridges of the folds. On average, the local brain age gap (the difference between the estimated biological age and the person’s actual chronological age) was 0.40 years higher in the sulci. The team also observed that the right hemisphere of the brain generally showed an older biological age than the left hemisphere, a pattern that persisted when the researchers retrained the model on a sample balanced between left- and right-handed people.
“The left–right asymmetry was particularly interesting,” Irimia told PsyPost. “The model estimated systematically higher local brain ages in the right hemisphere than in the left, and this difference remained when we investigated whether handedness in the training data could account for it. We do not yet know what produces this asymmetry, but it raises an interesting question about whether structural aging may differ between the two hemispheres.”
When comparing the groups, the researchers found that patients with Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment had older local brain ages in specific regions known to be affected early in neurodegeneration. In Alzheimer’s patients, subcortical structures like the pallidum and putamen, which help regulate movement and some types of learning, showed brain age gaps about 3.5 to 3.6 years larger than those of cognitively healthy adults. The hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure important for forming new memories, appeared more than three years older on average in the Alzheimer’s group compared to the healthy adults.
“The main message is that the brain does not appear to age uniformly,” Irimia said. “Different regions can exhibit different aging patterns within the same person, and these regional differences become more pronounced in cognitive impairment. This gives us a way to move beyond a single estimate of overall brain age and investigate where aging-related structural differences occur.”
The team also analyzed how these localized aging gaps related to performance on cognitive tests. In patients with Alzheimer’s disease, having an older local brain age in regions like the right pallidum strongly correlated with worse scores on general cognitive screening tests and a measure of everyday functioning. These associations were much weaker in people with mild cognitive impairment and largely absent in healthy adults.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in May 2026, which demonstrated that mapping regional structural changes across the brain with MRI can track neurodegeneration across the progression from healthy aging to Alzheimer’s disease. The new study differs slightly in its approach. The previous research compared scans to an established Alzheimer’s structural vulnerability blueprint, whereas the current model estimates localized biological brain aging at the voxel level without relying on a pre-existing disease map.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The artificial intelligence model was trained using research-grade MRI scans, which are typically much higher quality than the standard scans taken in everyday clinical settings. It is unknown if the system would perform as accurately on the lower-resolution images typically produced by hospital equipment.
Because of this and other factors, the tool is not yet ready for everyday medical use. “I would view local brain age primarily as a research tool at this stage rather than a clinical test,” Irimia noted. “Its importance is that it provides spatial information that is lost when brain aging is summarized with a single number. The next question is whether these regional patterns can eventually help us understand differences in cognitive aging or predict clinically meaningful trajectories, which will require further longitudinal validation.”
Additionally, the model was trained exclusively on the brains of cognitively healthy adults. The researchers suggest that future versions of the software might benefit from training on the brains of individuals diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. Including those cases could help the system become more sensitive to specific disease-related changes.
Finally, the study analyzed images captured at a single point in time, with limited follow-up data. Because of this, it is not possible to say whether having an older local brain age directly predicts that a healthy individual will eventually develop cognitive impairment. Tracking individuals over many years with repeated scans is a necessary next step to determine if these local age gaps can serve as an early warning system for dementia.
Irimia echoed this caution against overinterpreting a single scan. “An ‘older’ local brain age does not by itself mean that someone has Alzheimer’s disease or will develop it,” he clarified. “The method identifies structural MRI patterns associated with aging; determining whether it can predict an individual’s future disease trajectory will require longitudinal validation. The longitudinal examples in this study are encouraging, but we regard them as supportive rather than definitive validation.”
Looking forward, the team hopes to uncover the root causes of these regional differences. “A major next step is understanding what local brain age represents biologically,” Irimia told PsyPost. “We want to relate these spatial aging patterns to vascular and cardiovascular health, metabolic factors, lifestyle, and other biomarkers to understand why some regions appear to age faster than others. Longitudinal studies will be particularly important for determining whether changes in local brain age can track aging trajectories and identify factors associated with healthier brain aging.”
The study, “Deep learning maps local brain aging in relation to cognition across human adulthood,” was authored by Nikhil N. Chaudhari, Owen M. Vega Huerta, Samayan Bhattacharya, Nahian F. Chowdhury, Andrei Irimia, and the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

What’s in a name? Why Trump wants to rebrand AI as ‘super intelligence’
The US president’s insistence on using the term ‘super intelligence’ reflects a wider debate over the technology’s future, analysts say
US President Donald Trump wants to retire one of the technology sector’s most recognisable acronyms, arguing that the term “artificial intelligence”, or AI, is no longer fit for purpose.
On Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order directing US federal agencies to replace “artificial intelligence” and “AI” with “super intelligence” and “SI” in official communications and non-statutory documents. He also instructed the White House science adviser to draft a new federal definition.
The change has sparked debate and put US tech leaders in an awkward position. SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk caught himself using the old term during a recent appearance with Trump, before correcting himself: “SI, pardon me.”

Palestine Action crowdfunder for UK supreme court challenge blocked due to US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:00:10 UTC
23:00:10 KST

An online crowdfunder to raise money for the UK supreme court challenge to the ban on Palestine Action has been blocked as a result of US sanctions against the direct action group.
CrowdJustice, a UK company, has declined to host a fundraiser for legal fees to fight proscription because the platform uses the US company Stripe as its payment processor.
In an email seen by the Guardian, CrowdJustice said Stripe had confirmed “that it cannot support accounts or transactions linked to, or for the benefit of, Palestine Action. This includes circumstances where funds are being raised for legal proceedings.”
The US sanctions were imposed last month by Donald Trump, using powers introduced by President George W Bush in 2001 shortly after the 9/11 attacks by al-Qaida on the twin towers in New York.
Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action, who has brought the legal challenge against the UK ban, said: “Due to CrowdJustice’s and other platforms’ reliance on US services, we are unable to fundraise for legal fees needed for our supreme court challenge.
“On the other hand, the state continues to spend millions of pounds to cover their legal costs to defend the disproportionate and draconian ban, which has led to more than 3,700 arrests for holding signs [allegedly supporting a proscribed organisation]. The British government and the US are putting every possible obstacle in our way, in order to stack the odds against us.”
The Home Office has spent £700,000 defending proscription in the high court, according to the Independent. The total amount spent by the government will be far higher as the case has since been heard by the court of appeal, which overturned the high court’s decision that the ban was unlawful, and moves to the UK’s highest court in November.
When the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, announced her intention to ban Palestine Action under UK law in June last year, placing the group alongside the likes of Islamic State and Boko Haram, a CrowdJustice fundraiser for legal fees to fund a high court challenge raised more than £300,000 within days.
Ammori said: “Clearly, the powerful have banded together against citizens acting on their conscience against the Israeli war machine and ethnic cleansing of Palestine. It is extremely clear that Palestine Action faces harsher sanctions than Israel.
“The supreme court case is extremely important for our rights to free speech in Britain, but also for the people of Palestine. If we are successful, all prosecutions of protesters who held signs will be rightfully quashed. If not, we will witness thousands of people facing jail for holding placards.”
The former British diplomat Craig Murray, who is separately challenging the legality of the ban on Palestine Action in Scotland, had his own CrowdJustice fundraiser for legal fees taken down after the US designated the group as a global terrorist organisation.
“It’s really disgraceful,” Murray said. “Not only do you have draconian legislation with the proscription of Palestine Action affecting freedom of speech but you’ve then got moves to cripple our ability to fight it legally through the courts, which is just adding injustice to injustice.”
Stripe said it did not comment on individual users. CrowdJustice was also approached for comment.

The simple secrets behind great ramen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:00:09 UTC
23:00:09 KST

At its simplest, ramen is the balance of five elements: broth, tare (secret seasoning sauce), noodles, fat and toppings. If you understand that, this seemingly cryptic and complex corner of Japanese food culture opens right up. The first four take time, but if you pick up a shop-bought stock and some decent noodles, I won’t tell anyone. But the toppings are where the real payoff is: the fastest way to turn a midweek nothing into something worth showing off.
A universal note
Spring onions should be used to top every bowl (finely diced white onion will work as a backup). Where there’s a broth, aim for 300ml, and where dashi is mentioned, instant is fine – unless you’re vegan, in which case steep 20g each of kombu and dried shiitake in one litre of cold water overnight, and keep the mushrooms for the soboro. Noodle portions are 130g unless stated otherwise, and any specialist items should be available online or at your local Asian supermarket.
None of these toppings belong to one bowl, so swap them about – and they’re all good beyond ramen: chashu in a cheese toastie, say, soboro on rice, or ajitama in a caesar salad. The tares are multiuse, too: the tantanmen tare is great in scrambled eggs; the miso tare on corn on the cob, and the shio tare will improve pretty much anything.
Tokyo shoyu
Ramen’s platonic ideal, and one piece of pork gives you the topping, tare and fat.
Broth 50:50 chicken stock and dashi
Tare 3-4 tbsp chashu braising liquid
Fat 1 tbsp, skimmed from chilled braising liquid
Noodles medium classic
Toppings pork belly chashu, shop-bought menma (seasoned bamboo), ajitama
For the chashu (serves 6-8)
Roll and tie 500g pork belly and brown it all over in a pan. Deglaze the pan with 150ml sake, add 300ml each of shoyu, mirin and water, 30g demerara sugar, six sliced garlic cloves and a sliced 4cm piece of ginger, and simmer gently, turning, for two hours,. Cool in the liquid to room temperature, then chill overnight. Cut into 1cm-thick slices and torch or pan-fry to serve.
Tantanmen
Sichuan dan dan noodles, but make it ramen. Sesame, spice, and a soboro that works like a ragu.
Broth 50:50 kombu-shiitake dashi and unsweetened soy milk
Tare 2 tbsp tahini, 1½ tbsp shoyu, 2 tsp black vinegar, 1 tsp sugar, a pinch each of MSG and ground Sichuan pepper
Fat 1 tbsp rayu chilli oil
Noodles medium classic
Toppings spicy mince soboro, pak choi
Spicy mince soboro (serves 6-7)
Soften a small diced onion and 2cm piece grated ginger in oil for five minutes. Add five grated garlic cloves followed by 500g fatty pork mince – although any mince works, but vegan mince will need more water - and fry until it’s in grains, not lumps. Add three tablespoons of doubanjiang (chilli bean sauce), one and a half tablespoons each of shoyu and mirin, plus a splash of water. Cook for 15 minutes until glossy.
Hakata tonkotsu
Japan’s most famous ramen export. Thin, straight noodles in a creamy pork bone broth, eaten fast by design.
Broth tonkotsu
Tare 30ml shio (30g salt, 10g sugar and 10g MSG dissolved in 70ml sake, 20ml mirin and 110ml water – makes 230ml/about 7 bowls)
Fat 1 tsp sesame oil
Noodles thin, straight
Toppings ajitama, pork belly chashu, shop-bought kikurage (wood-ear fungus), beni-shoga
Ajitama (serves 6)
Warm 100ml water, dissolve 10g brown sugar in it, then add 100ml each shoyu and mirin and chill. Pierce six fridge-cold large eggs at the wide end and boil for seven minutes, stirring for the first 30 seconds to centre the yolks. Plunge into iced water, peel, and submerge in the cold marinade for 12-72 hours.
Chippy Lane mazesoba
A late-night Cardiff cult classic – chicken, curry sauce and chips – our version of nagoya mazesoba. Sauce in the bowl, hot noodles on top, toss hard.
Broth none – rules are meant for breaking
Tare 100ml shop-bought Japanese curry roux, made thick and salty
Fat 1 tbsp each butter and chicken fat (from the thighs)
Noodles thick (200g)
Toppings shio koji chicken, crispy onions, beni-shoga, and grated cheese, if you’re feeling cheeky
Shio koji chicken thighs (serves 4-5) 
Coat 500g skinless and boneless chicken thighs in 50g shio koji, 20g mirin, half a tablespoon of shoyu and one teaspoon each of grated ginger and garlic. Leave up to three hours. Add 100ml water, cover and cook over a low heat for 45 minutes. Uncover and reduce until it crisps. Shred the meat and toss through the glaze.
Sapporo yasai miso
Usually built on pork broth and lard for Hokkaido winters, this version is plant-based, but stands up.
Broth kombu-shiitake dashi
Tare 60g a bowl – 100g each white and red miso with 2 tbsp sake, 1 tbsp each mirin and shoyu, 1 tsp each grated raw garlic and ginger
Fat 2 tbsp vegetable oil, fried with grated garlic and ginger
Noodles thick, wavy, yellow
Toppings stir-fried cabbage and beansprouts, sweetcorn, toasted sesame seeds, and butter, if you’re not vegan
Stir-fried cabbage and beansprouts (serves 4)
Get a wok very hot with a little neutral oil. Add 200g shredded cabbage and 150g beansprouts, and toss hard for two minutes – you want char, not steam. Season with a tablespoon of shoyu, a teaspoon of sesame oil and a pinch each of salt, sugar and shichimi togarashi.
- James Chant is the owner of Matsudai Ramen in Cardiff. Watch him make ramen in Feed with Jimi Famurewa

Tesco is first supermarket to offer paid ‘safe leave’ for victims of domestic abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:00:08 UTC
23:00:08 KST

Tesco has become the first supermarket to introduce paid “safe leave” for victims of domestic abuse, giving staff dedicated time to access support, secure their safety and take steps to move on with their lives.
The UK’s largest private-sector employer is offering up to three days of paid leave which can be taken flexibly for activities such as attending court hearings, arranging emergency accommodation, changing locks, securing childcare or separating finances.
Managers across the business, which employs 300,000 people, have also been trained to spot the signs of domestic abuse, support those affected and flag them to specialist services.
Under the new policy, which was developed in partnership with the shopworkers’ union Usdaw, Tesco will not ask those suffering abuse to provide formal evidence to gain access to the special leave.
Tesco is thought to be the first big British retailer to introduce safe leave, but similar policies, such as protected paid leave, emergency accommodation and training staff to spot the signs of domestic abuse, have been enacted at other UK companies, including BP and Vodafone, as well as some local councils.
Daniel Adams, an Usdaw national officer, said domestic violence and abuse affected the lives of at least one in five women, and he urged other employers to introduce similar support.
“Usdaw has long campaigned for support at work for survivors of domestic abuse and we are pleased to have successfully negotiated this new policy with Tesco. Domestic abuse often has an impact on the working lives of survivors, and it is important that employers understand this and the actions they can take to support and protect them,” he said.
“Historically violence against women, and domestic violence in particular, has been hidden, excused and ignored. That needs to change.”
Emma Taylor, the chief people officer at Tesco, said: “We believe we have a responsibility to support colleagues in what are likely to be some of the most challenging moments in their lives.
“That’s why we’re introducing guaranteed safe leave, ensuring colleagues can access practical support and the time they need without worrying about taking unpaid leave or explaining deeply personal circumstances.
“We’re proud to be taking this step and want it to help drive wider action from employers across the UK. No one should have to choose between their job and their safety.”
More than 3 million people suffered some form of domestic abuse in England and Wales last year, most of whom were women, according to the campaign group SafeLives. It says eight women a month are killed by a current or former partner in England and Wales, based on 2023 data.
There was a sharp increase in abuse incidents during the pandemic lockdowns as victims were trapped at home with perpetrators. The permanent shift to working from home since then is seen to have made some people more vulnerable.
The Domestic Abuse Act, which became law in April 2021, includes workplace protection for domestic abuse victims, who can see their place of work as somewhere to seek help and support.
A private member’s bill currently before parliament proposes granting 10 days of paid leave for domestic abuse victims in England and Wales to give them time to deal with the practical and emotional steps.
In 2020, Northern Ireland passed legislation guaranteeing domestic abuse victims 10 days’ paid leave, and similar laws exist in Australia, New Zealand and the Philippines.

Are hypernovas real?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Chemical traces in some oddball stars hinted at the existence of hypernovas — a type of hyper-energetic supernova. But new mathematical models are questioning the hype on hypernovas.
Models of how elements mix across generations of stars suggests the parentage of stars attributed to hypernova events might have been standard supernovas and other relatively common cataclysmic stellar events instead, researchers report in the September Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.
“The evidence for [hypernovas] is now very seriously challenged,” says astrophysicist Ralph Schönrich of University College London.
Not everyone is fully convinced of the change in the stars’ proposed origins, including astronomer Anna Frebel of Massachusetts Institute of Technology, who thinks both supernovas and hypernovas remain plausible candidates as the stars’ parents. Frebel notes, however, that the findings are a good reminder for astronomers to be careful about claiming uniqueness.
Astronomers look for clues to a star’s origins in the elements it contains. When an earlier star dies, it releases elements into space, sometimes in a supernova explosion. That material mixes with gas that may eventually form new stars. Different kinds of explosions leave different chemical patterns, so the relative amounts of elements in a star can help astronomers work out what happened before it formed.
But tracing a star’s origins this way depends on knowing how elements from an earlier explosion spread through space. Models have often treated a supernova’s expelled material as though it mixes evenly with the gas that forms new stars. The new research accounts for observations and computer models that have shown that these explosions can spread elements asymmetrically. For example, a clump of a supernova’s oxygen might go preferentially in one direction and nickel another. While the ejected elements get mixed with other dust and gases in interstellar space, the overabundance in some areas isn’t likely to average out, especially in the earliest generations of stars, which have fewer heavy elements, Schönrich says. As a result, two stars forming on opposite sides of a supernova site could have different compositions.
This isn’t surprising for astrophysicist Adam Burrows of Princeton University, who studies supernovas and was not involved in the research. Burrows says that the idea of irregular mixing from these events is well known among supernova researchers but not well shared with astronomers who study the evolution of galaxies and generations of stars. “They’re taking seriously what we have seen for a long time,” Burrows says.
Accounting for this uneven spread of materials, the researchers created a mathematical model to see if the element ratios produced from lopsided explosions could match the mix seen in some unusual stars in the Milky Way’s halo, the galaxy’s outer sphere of stars that contains a lot of old stars that are low in heavy elements. Previously, researchers thought the ratios of elements in these stars couldn’t have formed by regular events alone and proposed hypernovas as their source. But the researchers found their model matched the observed element ratios as well as or better than the hypernova model.
“A good fit tells us that a particular enrichment scenario is possible, but it does not necessarily tell us that it is the only scenario,” Frebel says. While ordinary supernovas may explain these stars’ chemistry, she says, the new models don’t rule out hypernovas.
Regardless of where these oddball stars came from, astronomers agree the results show that more studies on supernovas and gas mixing are needed.

Spanish Congress rejects housing laws despite Sánchez's warning: 'They'll be judged sooner than they think'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:59:37 UTC
22:59:37 KST

Spanish Congress rejects two key housing measures aimed at quelling public uproar over housing affordability. The bills' rejection after last-minute talks leaves Pedro Sánchez's government without two key housing measures and exposes its struggle to win support in Congress.
Spain's parliament on Friday rejected two housing decree-laws promoted by the government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, aimed at tackling a housing crisis that has spurred nationwide protests.
The two votes are a heavy political blow to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and went ahead as hundreds of protesters gathered outside parliament.
These rejections, delivered in a voice vote, represent a parliamentary setback for the executive and came after a sitting marked by last-minute negotiations and uncertainty over the support of its parliamentary partners. Sánchez spoke for a few minutes before the vote to urge MPs to "do the right thing or history will judge you sooner than you think and more harshly than you can imagine."
After the first of the decrees was rejected by 172 votes in favour and 178 against, a demonstration marched to Madrid's central Puerta del Sol square, chanting "General strike!" The second decree was then also voted down.
Housing affordability crisis
The government decrees were intended to quell a public uproar following the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman last week in Madrid that sparked protests and a camp-in that has occupied Madrid’s most important square ever since. Barring a surprise, the progressive coalition of Sánchez will suffer a costly legislative defeat that will likely fan the flames of the protests.
The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the past 10 years. The average price per square meter has risen from €8.20 in 2016 to €15.1 this year, according to the real estate website Idealista.
The elderly woman whose eviction sparked the protests, Maricarmen Abascal, has become a symbol for the fight for lower housing costs in the southern European country, where many people are priced out of buying a home and are being squeezed by a small rental market.
The company that evicted her finally caved under immense public and political pressure this week and said that she can return to the apartment. Abascal is currently in a hospital since being removed from her home on a stretcher, but her lawyer said she is happy to know she will be going home.
Crushing votes
The vote came after a morning of speeches in which the housing minister, Isabel Rodríguez, urged the different groups to back the measures, having explicitly asked Junts per Catalunya to vote in favour or abstain, after the pro-independence party announced on Thursday night that it would oppose both texts and submit its own proposal to the government. In the end, Sánchez's PSOE, Spain's social democratic party, refused to withdraw the two decrees, as the Catalan party had demanded.
Rodríguez told the chamber that one of the two decrees incorporated many of the proposals (source in Spanish) put forward by Junts. "Ninety per cent of what they handed to the prime minister is now set out in the Official State Gazette," said the housing minister, who pledged to process the decrees as a bill so that "clarifications or technical corrections" requested by the groups could be incorporated later.
The minister also warned in her speech about the consequences of the vote and appealed to MPs' sense of responsibility. "With this vote, we are deciding whether we do not want another eviction or are willing to face the next one," Rodríguez said, while hundreds of people gathered outside the Congress of Deputies, Spain's lower house of parliament, to demand a solution to the housing crisis gripping the country.
Diverging positions
The sitting began at 11:00, after Sánchez was greeted with an ovation from the socialist benches on his arrival at Congress. During the debate, the groups stuck to the positions they had set out in the preceding hours, albeit with different nuances.
The PNV, the Basque Nationalist Party, announced that it would support one of the decrees "with many doubts". Its spokesperson, Maribel Vaquero, lamented that it had not been possible to reach the minimum agreement her party had called for.
The Canarian Coalition party, a regionalist centre to centre-right party, for its part, confirmed its favourable vote on the first decree because it sees it as "a starting point."
Spain's far-left party Podemos confirmed its four votes in favour of both texts, although its secretary-general, Ione Belarra, criticised the government for having "chopped up" the measures. "It's just another excuse. People don't want excuses; they want solutions," she argued during the sitting.
EH Bildu, another Basque nationalist party leaning left, also expressed its displeasure during the debate. Its MP Oskar Matute said he was "deeply angry" at the prospect of particular interests prevailing over the measures proposed to tackle the housing problem, brought into sharp focus by Maricarmen's eviction and which culminated last weekend in a protest camp in the central Puerta del Sol square.
Opposition from conservative parties PP and Vox, together with Junts' rejection, had left the government facing particularly tight parliamentary arithmetic. The coalition executive needed to win support from different parties to get the initiatives through a chamber in which socialist parties PSOE and Sumar do not have an absolute majority.
Possible early election
The vote on the housing decrees had also sparked, within the PSOE and the government, a debate about the possibility of bringing the elections forward if Congress rejected the initiatives.
Sánchez's office insists that no decision has been taken, although government and PSOE figures had floated the possibility of Sánchez calling elections if the decrees were voted down. At the same time, other socialist leaders have urged caution and argued that the consequences of any eventual call need to be carefully weighed.
The issue is therefore tied to the outcome of a vote the government has presented as a test of the chamber's ability to reach agreements on one of the main problems facing Spanish society. Sánchez had already urged the parliamentary groups to show "a sense of perspective" in backing the measures and argued that housing should be kept out of "partisan confrontations."
While the sitting was underway, around a hundred people gathered outside Congress, mobilised by the Tenants' Union. Protesters chanted slogans against PP, Vox, and Junts and also held a banner critical of PSOE and Sumar. Police had deployed a large security operation around the chamber.

UK sanctions 7 Russians over deportation, indoctrination of Ukrainian children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:58:41 UTC
22:58:41 KST

The U.K. sanctioned seven Russian individuals involved in the forced deportation and re-education of Ukrainian children from occupied territories on Oct. 1, the Ukrainian President's initiative, Bring Kids Back, said on Oct. 2.
Russia is militarizing Ukrainian children and youth in the occupied territories, removing their Ukrainian identity to "raise future soldiers" and involve them in the fight against their own people.
Russia has abducted tens of thousands of Ukrainian children since the start of the full-scale invasion. As of September 2026, Ukraine's Justice Ministry has officially confirmed 20,610 cases of deportation, though Ukrainian officials estimate the real total could number in the hundreds of thousands.
According to Bring Kids Back's press release, the sanctions target Artur Orlov, head of Russia's Movement of the First, a state-backed organization for children and young people, as well as five heads of its regional branches in occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts and Crimea.
The Movement of the First was established in 2022 at the initiative of Russian President Vladimir Putin and has more than 344,600 members in occupied Ukrainian territories, according to a report from an Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) expert mission.
The sanctioned officials are Denis Chernobay, Ruyal Aliyev, Aleksey Lavrentyev, Viktoriya Kostromina, and Ekaterina Kozyr.
The list also includes Elena Milskaya, chair of the board of trustees of Russia's National Center for Assistance to Missing and Injured Children. Ukraine's military intelligence agency said Milskaya used the organization's volunteers in October 2022 to facilitate the mass abduction and unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children, including orphans, from occupied territories to Russia's Krasnodar Krai via occupied Crimea.
The sanctioned individuals face asset freezes and travel bans, as well as restrictions on trust services and director disqualification. At least three of the seven — Orlov, Chernobay, and Milskaya — have previously been sanctioned by Canada, while Milskaya has also been sanctioned by the European Union.
"These people are already under Canadian sanctions, and now British ones as well. When the same names appear on the lists of different countries, they have fewer places to hide their money or to hide themselves. We call on other partners to align their decisions: there must be no safe jurisdiction left for those who deport and militarize Ukrainian children," Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Commissioner of the President of Ukraine for Sanctions Policy, said.
Russia's abduction of Ukrainian children could constitute an act of genocide, according to the U.N.'s Genocide Convention, which lists "forcibly transferring children of the group to another group" as one of the five acts that fall under the definition
In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia's Commissioner for Children's Rights, for their role in state-sanctioned child abductions.
The U.K. announced the sanctions on Oct. 1 as part of a wider package targeting 31 individuals over Russia's war against Ukraine. The package also includes eight people accused of involvement in arbitrary detention, torture, and ill-treatment of civilians in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories, including Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.
"We are targeting both the revenues that help sustain Russia's aggression and the perpetrators of horrendous crimes against Ukrainian civilians, including children. The UK will not flinch in our support for Ukraine," UK Minister for Europe Lord Wood of Anfield said.

22:56:13 KST

Three Israeli creators have released a documentary designed to directly counter and discredit NAZA, the controversial, Venice Film Festival award-winning film that alleges systematic Israeli military misconduct in Gaza.
The counter-project, titled NAZA: The Real Story, dropped this week with English subtitles in an effort to immediately shape the global narrative.
Directed by Lt. Col. Roi Danino, Hagai Gutman, and Ariel Averbuch, the documentary positions itself as an explicit rebuttal of the original film’s anonymous whistleblower claims.
The filmmakers go on the offensive, using declassified IDF recordings, combat footage, and captured intelligence to mount a sharp counter-narrative focusing on the battlefield tactics of Hamas.
The core of NAZA: The Real Story tackles the primary accusations made by NAZA regarding civilian casualties. It centers on three main fronts: the systematic exploitation of civilian areas by terrorists, the severe operational limitations imposed on troops by the presence of hostages, and the immense security risks involved in facilitating humanitarian aid deliveries.
'An offensive film, not a defensive one'
Unlike the original anti-IDF film, which relied heavily on hidden-identity testimonies from junior personnel, this project features open interviews with active intelligence officers and frontline military commanders.
The creators present captured enemy manuals and operational videos to visually document their thesis: that civilian clothing, weapon stockpiles in family homes, and tactical hubs in residential areas are part of a calculated defensive strategy deployed against the IDF.
“This is an offensive film, not a defensive one,” the directors said, making it clear they intend to shift Israel out of the traditional position of the defendant on the world stage.
The urgency behind the project underscores how high the stakes are in the digital arena. Parts of the documentary were filmed under tight operational security and the cover of night on Tel Aviv rooftops. Key personnel involved in compiling the sensitive declassified materials still have their identities withheld for safety reasons.
With the original NAZA film gaining heavy distribution and visibility across Europe and the United States, the creators of this rebuttal are utilizing digital influencers and grassroots international networks to push their footage directly to global policymakers and journalists. For the production team, the ongoing clash is no longer just a debate over military strategy but a definitive, high-stakes war over who dictates the historical record to the international community.

Hunger increasing in Yemen, record number of people unable to meet food needs, WFP warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:55:54 UTC
22:55:54 KST

Three-in-four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the "absolutely devastating" impact of a surge in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said on Friday.
Yemen is experiencing the most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthi group since a UN-brokered truce largely halted cross-border attacks in 2022. The renewed conflict could reshape control in Yemen, with implications for Red Sea shipping lanes.
Within just a few weeks, the fighting has driven the share of households without sufficient food to 74% in government-controlled areas accessible to WFP, the UN hunger body's Assistant Executive Director for Programme Operations told reporters in Geneva. The total population of government-held areas is estimated at around 10 million people.
“The effect of this latest flare-up of insecurity on the food security situation threatens to be absolutely devastating,” Hollingworth told reporters in Geneva via video link from Rome.
The Houthis, who already control most of northern Yemen including the capital Sanaa, seized the country's entire Red Sea coast last month from Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognized government, based in the southern port of Aden.
Displaced families are arriving outside Aden and around the mountain city of Taiz without any water or food, as many had to leave everything behind, WFP said.
Prices of basic food staples such as wheat flour and vegetable oil are rising in a country that imports around 90% of its food.
Hunger crisis 'going to grow,' Hollingworth says
“We are looking at a hunger crisis that is going to grow as it persists,” Hollingworth said, adding that frontline areas like Taiz were increasingly hard to access due to the fighting.
WFP said it was scaling up its response, but unless it gets around $109 million in funding within a few weeks, it will run out of food stocks and money to help the 152,000 newly displaced persons inside the country, as well as the 1.4 million people it is already supporting.
Hollingworth also pointed to the potential ripple effects of disruption to two major chokepoints in the Middle East: the Bab el-Mandeb Strait near Yemen at the mouth of the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula.
That, as well as disruption in the Black Sea due to the Ukraine-Russia conflict, risks driving up food and fuel prices and deepening food insecurity globally.
A new analysis published by UN Women on Friday said an additional 11.7 million women and girls across 28 countries, including Yemen, Sudan and Lebanon, could face food insecurity by the end of the year, due to escalation in the Middle East and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz.

Swedish Corvette HMS Helsingborg Transferred to Finnish Command for Border Security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:54:31 UTC
22:54:31 KST

The Swedish Visby-class corvette HMS Helsingborg entered the Gulf of Finland as part of a naval operation to secure Finland’s borders.
For the first time in history, the Swedish corvette has been placed under Finnish military command, according to the SVT television channel.
The decision to involve Swedish forces was made in August following a request from Finland due to ongoing incidents involving drones and airspace violations.
As part of the mission, which will last throughout the fall, Sweden is deploying not only ships but also JAS 39 Gripen fighter jets for joint patrols.
The corvette HMS Helsingborg is one of five Visby-class ships designed by the Swedish company Kockums for the Swedish Armed Forces.
The corvette class was designed using stealth technology, which significantly reduces the ship’s radar and infrared signature.
The ship’s 73-meter-long hull is constructed of carbon-fiber-based composite materials to reduce weight and magnetic signature.
The corvette has a displacement of 640 metric tons, and thanks to its gas turbine propulsion system the ship is capable of reaching a maximum speed of over 35 knots.
The corvette is armed with a 57 mm Bofors Mk3 artillery system, RBS-15 anti-ship missiles, torpedoes, and anti-submarine depth charge launchers.
As a reminder, on September 24, Finnish and Swedish fighter jets conducted their first joint operational mission to intercept and identify Russian military aircraft over the Gulf of Finland.
Finnish F/A-18 Hornets and Swedish JAS 39 Gripens from the Quick Reaction Alert (QRA) force were deployed for the mission. They operated under the command of the Finnish Air Force Command’s Air Operations Centre.
Finland has also completed the construction of a 200-kilometer fence along its eastern border with Russia in three years.

Ethiopia, Eritrea break ties: Does the conflict risk becoming regional war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:53:24 UTC
22:53:24 KST

Ethiopia, Eritrea break ties: Does the conflict risk becoming regional war?
Analysts warn unrest is likely to spill into neighbouring states and could further destabilise war-torn Sudan.
Eritrea has cut off diplomatic relations with neighbouring Ethiopia, escalating a long-simmering conflict between the two states rooted in territorial disputes and mutual accusations of interference.
The move comes as fighting flares in northern Ethiopia between Ethiopian federal troops and an opposition alliance that Addis Ababa accuses Eritrea of backing.
The clashes are the most severe in Ethiopia since its 2020-2022 civil war that killed hundreds of thousands of people.
But this time, the ripple effects could go further, potentially fuelling broader unrest in a region already plagued by numerous interrelated conflicts, analysts warn.
Here’s what we know about the Ethiopia-Eritrea conflict, the latest fighting in northern Ethiopia and what it could mean for the region at large:
Why did Eritrea break off ties with Ethiopia?
Eritrea announced it was severing ties with Ethiopia on Thursday, after Addis Ababa announced it would close its embassy in Asmara and expel 10 Eritrean diplomats.
In a statement, Eritrea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Ethiopia’s actions had left it with “no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia”.
The Eritrean ministry accused Ethiopia of pursuing a years-long “agenda of incessant hostility”, including by infringing on its coastal areas and arming fighters opposed to Ethiopia’s government.
Ethiopia has likewise accused Eritrea of backing armed groups opposed to its government. Both sides have rejected the other’s accusations.
The diplomatic breakdown follows months of worsening relations, driven largely by disputes over landlocked Ethiopia’s push for access to the Red Sea and allegations that Eritrea is backing the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which leads the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, a rebel alliance fighting for control of parts of northern Ethiopia.
Have Ethiopia’s ties with Egypt and Sudan been hit, too?
Yes. Ethiopia accuses Egypt and Sudan of joining Eritrea in backing Tigrayan rebel forces, worsening already strained ties with both countries.
Ethiopia has long been at odds with Egypt over the status of Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) project, which Cairo views as a risk to its water security and share of the Nile.
Ethiopia and Egypt have also expelled diplomats. Cairo ordered an Ethiopian diplomat to leave the country on Thursday, after Addis Ababa earlier kicked out an Egyptian diplomat, Egyptian state-linked media reported.
Egyptian state-linked broadcaster Al-Qahera News quoted an Egyptian official as calling Ethiopia’s move to expel the Egyptian diplomat as “regrettable and unjustified” and saying that Cairo responded in line with “the principle of reciprocity”.
The latest conflict also has implications for Sudan, whose military-backed government accuses Ethiopia of backing rebel forces it is fighting in its own civil conflict. Ethiopia rejects those allegations.
“The conflicts in Ethiopia and Sudan have become more interconnected, with the Ethiopian government and Sudanese Armed Forces accusing each other of harbouring and equipping respective opposition forces from inside their own borders,” Ahmed Soliman, senior research fellow at the Chatham House think tank’s Africa programme, told Al Jazeera. “Egypt has also been drawn into the escalation with its long-running enmity with Ethiopia over the Nile.”
What is happening in northern Ethiopia?
Tigrayan-led rebel forces have engaged in clashes with Ethiopian government-backed forces in the country’s north since last week. Fighting is concentrated in three regions: Tigray, Amhara and Afar.
Al Jazeera’s bureau chief in Ethiopia, Mohammed Taha Tawakel, reported that forces loyal to the federal government have made significant gains in the Tigray region, taking control of several towns and closing in on the regional capital, Mekelle.
Further east in Afar, a pro-government armed group claimed on Thursday to have recaptured the town of Erebti, which rebel forces had taken control of earlier in the week. The pro-government group thanked the Ethiopian military for its “magnificent air support” and said it would pursue further advances.
Despite the pro-government advances, Tawakel reported that rebel forces still maintain what he described as a “strong rear link with Eritrea” along the countries’ border.
He also reported growing fears that fighting could move into major urban centres of Tigray, such as Adwa, Axum, Shire and Mekelle. Some people have already begun fleeing to Amhara and Afar, he added.
Outside northern Ethiopia, the conflict appeared to spill into the capital, Addis Ababa, for the first time early on Thursday, as an explosion was reported at the Ministry of Defence.
AFP quoted a diplomatic source as saying small drones were the most probable cause of the blast.
While Ethiopia’s army has a much larger arsenal of drones, rebel forces have previously used them to target airbases and airports in various parts of the country, reported conflict monitor ACLED.
What are the roots of the Ethiopia-Eritrea dispute?
Ties between the neighbours have been historically fragile. In 1962, Ethiopia annexed Eritrea. An armed independence struggle, led by Eritrea’s current President Isaias Afwerki, secured independence in 1993. The countries fought another border war from 1998 to 2000.
When Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power in 2018, he moved to end the tensions and normalise diplomatic relations with Eritrea. During Ethiopia’s last civil war in 2020-2022, Eritrea even backed Ethiopia’s government against the TPLF.
But Abiy’s ambitions to seek direct sea access for landlocked Ethiopia have contributed to recent tensions, say analysts. Abiy has repeated that Ethiopia has a right to sea access, words that officials in Asmara take as a declaration of territorial conflict with Eritrea.
Could the current conflict spread in the region?
Many analysts fear it could.
Laura Hammond, professor in development studies at SOAS University of London, told Al Jazeera this scenario is already under way.
“The risks that conflict will spread to other countries, or that neighbours in the region will be brought into the present conflict are already playing out in terms of Eritrea’s support for the TPLF and the Alliance for Survival,” said Hammond.
“There is a strong possibility that Eritrea will become more involved in the conflict on the ground inside Tigray if it continues much longer,” she continued. “There is also a risk that the conflict could inflame relations with and inside Sudan.”
Martin Plaut, an analyst specialising in the Horn of Africa, also said there was a “real danger” of the conflict spreading.
“The situation is extremely tense and it would only require a spark to ignite a conflagration that could engulf [Ethiopia and Eritrea], as well as neighbouring Sudan,” he told Al Jazeera.

Asian Games | China, Japan split golds on Asian Games kayak cross debut
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:52:31 CST
22:52:31 KST

Gold medalist Chen Lin (C) of China, silver medalist Chang Chu-han (L) of Chinese Taipei and bronze medalist Xu Linxi of China pose during the awarding ceremony for the women's kayak cross final of canoe slalom at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Toyota of Aichi Prefecture, Japan, Oct. 2, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Haobo)
NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- China's Chen Lin and Japan's Yuuki Tanaka won the inaugural Asian Games kayak cross titles on Friday as the canoe slalom program concluded at the Aichi-Nagoya Games.
Chen led from the start of the women's final and held off her rivals to take gold. Chang Chu-han of Chinese Taipei claimed silver, while China's Xu Linxi took bronze.
The victory gave Chen her second medal in two days after winning silver in the women's kayak single on Thursday, as she topped the morning time trial and won both her quarterfinal and semifinal heats before securing the title.
"I stayed calm through all the races today and I'm quite satisfied with my performance," Chen said. "After yesterday's race, I reviewed things and made adjustments. Today I felt more confident."
Japan's Yuuki Tanaka won the men's final ahead of China's Quan Xin and Hu Zhaoshan, who took silver and bronze respectively.
Tanaka added gold to the silver he won in Wednesday's men's kayak single, when the Japanese paddler finished behind China's Hu.
China's Quan led early in Friday's final but lost momentum when his paddle collided with a Japanese competitor's boat at a gate. Quan and his Chinese teammate Hu had advanced together through the quarterfinals and semifinals, finishing in the top two of their heats.
"Kayak cross is a contact event, so contact is normal," Quan said. "But if I had been even half a second faster today, perhaps I could have avoided it and won on speed alone."
China finished with four golds, two silvers and two bronzes, winning medals in all six canoe slalom events. The addition of men's and women's kayak cross expanded the program from four medal events to six. ■

Ukrainian Grandmother Detained in Alleged FSB Trap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:50:36 UTC
22:50:36 KST

Kazakh authorities detained Ukrainian citizen Liubov Rozhanska at Astana airport at Russia’s request after she traveled there to collect her grandson, in what her lawyer described as a possible operation organized by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).
Rozhanska was detained while passing through border control after arriving from Istanbul to Kazakhstan on Thursday, Oct. 1, her lawyers Alexei Pryanishnikov and Riza Nurbayeva told Deutsche Welle (DW).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Russian request was reportedly transmitted through the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), a Moscow-led security alliance that includes Kazakhstan.
Rozhanska is being held in a detention center in Astana. Her lawyers said a court hearing was expected within three days and warned that she could be sent to Russia despite being a Ukrainian citizen.
Neither Kazakhstan’s authorities nor Ukraine’s foreign ministry had publicly commented on the case at the time of publication.
Grandmother traveled to collect child
According to the lawyers’ account, Rozhanska traveled to Kazakhstan to collect her grandson, who was supposed to be brought there from Russia and returned to his father in Odesa.
The boy was born in Odesa in 2018 to a Ukrainian family. His parents later separated, and in 2021 his mother moved with him to Russia’s Kaliningrad region, where her new Russian husband lived.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the mother applied to renounce Ukrainian citizenship for herself and the child, both receiving Russian citizenship in 2022, according to DW.
Kremlin Urges US-Russia Deals Before Ukraine Settlement
The child’s father began legal proceedings in Ukraine and in March 2025, Ukraine’s Supreme Court determined that the boy should live in Odesa with his father.
Russian case opened before proposed handover
Pryanishnikov said that the mother’s new husband, Vitaly Andreyev, and Andreyev’s father contacted Rozhanska in July and proposed handing over the boy to his Ukrainian father and grandmother.
Negotiations over the transfer intensified in late August.
At the same time, however, Russian authorities were pursuing a criminal case against Rozhanska over the alleged attempted abduction of the child.
Nurbayeva said the case had been opened in Russia in 2023, even though Rozhanska had never entered Russian territory and was allegedly unaware of either the investigation or an arrest order.
“When she arrived in Kazakhstan, she was detained under a ruling by a Kaliningrad court,” Nurbayeva told DW.
Documents sent by Russia reportedly show that investigators from the FSB’s Kaliningrad regional branch were preparing to place Rozhanska on a wanted list and seek her extradition while negotiations over the child’s transfer were continuing.
Lawyer alleges FSB provocation
Pryanishnikov described the arrest as a “rather clearly planned operation” and an FSB provocation, arguing that the invitation to collect the child may have been used to lure Rozhanska to a country where Russia could seek her detention.
“Despite the seemingly family nature of this case, I clearly see a political context connected with the war between Russia and Ukraine,” he said.
Pryanishnikov’s allegation has not been independently confirmed, and neither the FSB nor the relatives involved in the proposed handover have publicly responded.
Kazakhstan has previously transferred people wanted by Moscow to Russia. In February, Kazakh authorities deported IT specialist Oleksandr Kachkurkin, who was detained upon arrival in Russia, and charged with treason over alleged financial transfers to Ukraine.
