GUIYANG, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- When foreign players marched past the stands at the Village Super League (VSL) football field, it drove home for many in Rongjiang County that the "World Cup" they had long dreamed of was finally happening.
The grassroots VSL, known in Chinese as "Cun Chao," originated in Rongjiang County, Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Guizhou Province, and has been running for more than three years.
The opening ceremony of the 2026 VSL International Football Cup was held at the VSL field in the county on Thursday evening, attracting a total of 371 players from 16 teams representing more than 30 countries and regions, including 199 foreign players, who took part in the parade.
Yang Bing, the evening's commentator, said excitedly, "The 2026 Mini Cun Chao World Cup opened today. Rongjiang has truly turned a county-level village tournament into a global one."
Since going viral from May to July 2023, the VSL has pursued the goal of "attracting people from all over the world to play together." It plans to hold the Mini Cun Chao World Cup in 2026 and the Cun Chao World Cup in 2028. The 2026 international tournament is the so-called Mini Cun Chao World Cup.
Yang, a native of Kouzhai Village in Rongjiang County and a lifelong football fan, has commented on hundreds of VSL matches, including many international friendlies. He said that this international football cup is different. It is the first time the VSL has hosted an international cup, making his dream of a Mini Cun Chao World Cup a reality.
When 14-year-old Yang Zheng, a football fan from Rongjiang, saw foreign teams from Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia and elsewhere at the field, he could not help exclaiming, "A Mini Cun Chao World Cup is really being held in my hometown!"
"The Brazil team also came to Rongjiang during last year's National Day holiday. They were unbeaten in all their matches, so I am very curious about their performance this year," said Yang Zheng, who has played football for four years. He added that he was delighted and inspired to see players from around the world compete in his hometown and hoped to play on the VSL international stage himself one day.
"Since the VSL went viral, I have played in the first two international tournaments, but this is the one with the most foreign teams and players I have ever seen," said Lu Jinfu. He played for the Rongjiang County team against Malaysia South Tigers that evening and felt the same sense of excitement.
Lu was once an energetic teenager on the pitch and has now grown into a calm veteran. "Walking along the sideline, I heard different languages. It really felt like walking into a World Cup stadium. I was very excited," Lu said.
"This is the Mini Cun Chao World Cup!" said Jiang Zuoxian, a VSL ambassador, noting that the seven-day competition began on September 30. She has been at the pitch since the first day to watch and cheer for the teams.
On the morning of October 1, when Jiang saw Mateus Pereira, a Brazilian player who had visited Rongjiang before, she taught him to sing a Miao folk song. She hummed slowly, line by line, and Pereira imitated her with gestures.
"Language barriers do not matter. Players come to the VSL not just for matches, but also for fun," Jiang said, adding that football has no borders and sincerity is the most touching. "We admire their skills, and they love our way of life. This mutual affinity has made us good friends."
As old friends of the VSL, the Brazilian players enjoy the football and cultural atmosphere each time. Off the pitch, they took photos with tourists and cheered for other teams. On the pitch, they won applause with their samba style.
"The VSL international tournament has the best atmosphere of any amateur international football match I have ever seen," said Akonjom Great Nek, a Brazilian player whose Chinese name is Kang Wei.
"Many players from different countries came to this tournament," said Nek, adding that the international football cup really feels like a Mini World Cup, through which he has made many friends and had pleasant conversations with them.
"This is the charm of football," said Nek, emphasizing that it brings people from all over the world together to understand each other, share joy and build consensus.
It also made Nek look forward to the 2028 Cun Chao World Cup, and he hoped to participate and experience an even more enthusiastic football atmosphere.
Yang added that more and more foreign teams have come to Rongjiang to play in recent years, gradually turning the VSL pitch into a major platform for people-to-people exchanges between China and the rest of the world. ■

====================================================================================================

There is a way to look after people, the planet – and Britain’s growth. It’s what we call the ‘wellbeing economy’ | Jamie Driscoll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:01:29 UTC
22:01:29 KST

You’ve just left school. What’s your future?
I know a physics graduate making flat whites; a 30-year-old living in his childhood bedroom who feels like a failure; a lad in Blyth who turned down a job 15 miles away because there’s no bus, and for young people his age car insurance is almost £2,000 a year. Britain’s young people are our greatest resource, and we are failing them because capital markets won’t allocate investment where it is needed. Saying “hope” in a conference speech sounds warm. But people need a plan.
The first priority of any government is the security of its people. Financial markets are sending price signals that AI booms and share buybacks are more important than clean energy or warm homes. We fund aircraft carriers and artillery shells. But wind turbines and council houses are part of our national security, too. Imagine a country with a 20-year investment plan, with retrofitted homes and fast transport connections that leave nowhere behind. That’s a future filled with the potential of proud work for young people.
But four words run Britain: “We can’t afford it.” Governments call this mindset “prudence”. My response to it is Hostage Nation, my plan to fix Britain. This is a report that lays out how to source the finance, shows what we need to build – and tracks why it would make us more prosperous and resilient. I joined the Green party to achieve this vision. As we approach the party conference, I hope this will become official Green policy that we’ll fight the next election on.
Nine sets of fiscal rules have been broken and abandoned since the financial crash. Andy Haldane, a former chief economist of the Bank of England, said current fiscal rules were “far from optimal; in fact I’d go as far as to say silly”. The Institute for Fiscal Studies said in 2024 that changing policy based on fiscal headroom projections was “almost literally mad”. What if we’re not really hostages to the bond market? What if politicians have got Stockholm syndrome instead?
Bond markets are just complex betting shops. That’s their business model: guess the future, and price accordingly. That price changes when the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates or the strait of Hormuz closes. Why do we let bookies decide whether we build railway lines? Give a country nothing to build and struggling people will find someone to blame.
Businesses want customers more than they want tax cuts or light-touch regulation. I once asked the chief executive of a global engineering firm if he would invest in green hydrogen. “I’m not investing half a billion in a plant and staff unless I can sell it for 20 years,” he said. No government gave that signal.
Provide demand, and supply chains will organise themselves. When I was mayor of the North of Tyne combined authority, I moved our adult training providers from one-year to rolling three-year contracts. Employment training places rose from 22,000 to 35,000 a year on the same real-terms budget. That’s what certainty brings.
Markets are great at providing barber shops and burger vans, but markets don’t build reservoirs. The only organisation that can guarantee orders for infrastructure 20 years from now is the state. Public ownership is a must for public planning. We’re not short of need: 100,000 council homes a year; fully renewable energy with a storage grid; clean transport; insulating every home; buses and trains that run as one network and are cheaper and more convenient than cars; regenerated high streets with sports centres and warm youth clubs. What George Monbiot calls public luxury.
We can fund it with off-market finance. The government savings bank National Savings and Investments (originally the Post Office Savings Bank) has been going for more than 160 years, and 24 million of us use it. The government could offer savers national infrastructure Isas – a fair, safe return for investment in public works. The gilt market carries on; this is a separate channel insulated from tariff antics and international conflicts. No hedge fund has ever shorted a premium bond.
We invest £70bn a year in cash Isas. Our pension pools hold more than £2tn, yet less than 5% is invested in British firms. There is tax relief on both. If you want to speculate on Silicon Valley, that’s your right. But tax subsidies should be reserved for savings that build Britain.
As for infrastructure, the state can outcompete private capital. For a business, wages are an expense. For a country, wages lower the welfare bill. The state collects 40p in every pound back in tax. Money flows through high streets and pays business rates. A 2014 pilot in Sunderland showed that a £5,000 investment in insulation and energy-efficient boilers for people with COPD lowered bills and reduced hospital admissions by 25% and GP appointments by 60%. Combine retrofit and clean energy at cost and energy bills fall by 67%. It turns out the cheapest way to heat a home is also the quickest way to decarbonise a country.
This is what a wellbeing economy looks like. In the North of Tyne we judged projects on mental health, environmental impact and community wealth before a penny was released.
What about inflation? Train the workers, build the supply chains, then release the money. This creates real capacity and builds assets on the public balance sheet. We have the powers. We don’t need new treaties or quangos. We need to wake up the state machinery we already have.
In 1946 Britain was so poor we started rationing bread. The national debt was two-and-a-half times the size of the economy. That generation built the NHS. Then an average of 126,000 council homes every year for 35 years. Eight prime ministers and two parties kept building. Today our relative debt is under half that. We have machines they could only dream of. They weren’t richer than us. They were braver.
I don’t have a crystal ball, but I’ll wager the upcoming budget will tinker around the edges of these issues. Voters already know the Greens care, and with a plan to really fix Britain – and fund it – support will keep growing. Hostage Nation is backed by 134 endnotes that are there to be checked. We can start this plan tomorrow. Values win sympathy, but answers win seats.
- Jamie Driscoll is a Green party councillor on Newcastle city council and former North of Tyne mayor

I opened the door, and everyone else came immediately afterward.” He added: “I realized that if I did not show courage, 170 passengers would lose their lives.” Modi praised his courage and composure, while Machchhar, visibly emotional, told him: “You are my idol. I never thought I would have the opportunity to speak with you.”

Inside Soitec, the French tech company powering the global semiconductor industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:00:57 UTC
22:00:57 KST

From smartphones to data centres, the French company’s advanced silicon substrates underpin technologies used around the world. Valérie Gauriat went inside its production site in the French Alps.
In the Grésivaudan Valley near Grenoble, sometimes dubbed the “Silicon Valley of the Alps”, millions of highly sophisticated silicon wafers are produced every year.
They come from Soitec, a French company little known to the general public, but a world leader in advanced substrates for the semiconductor industry.
Founded 33 years ago around an invention developed at French technological research institute CEA-Leti, Soitec started with just a dozen or so people. Today, it employs more than 2,000 and holds more than 4,700 active patents worldwide, with production facilities in France and Singapore.
“Our roots are French, our reach is global. Our job is to run faster than the competition,” says Christophe Maleville, Soitec’s Chief Technology Officer.
The company produces advanced substrates: a high-tech silicon wafer used as the base material to build the world's most powerful microchips. Its technology can be found in mobile phones, connected devices, cars and household appliances, as well as data centres.
“Today, we are the world leader in advanced substrates for semiconductors,” says Chief Operations Officer Cyril Menon. He points to Grenoble’s combination of research laboratories, universities and industrial companies as one reason for that success.
Inside Soitec’s highly controlled clean rooms, wafers pass through between 30 and 50 processing stages, involving the transfer of extremely thin layers of material from one substrate to another at atomic scale.
Several million advanced substrates leave Soitec’s factories each year. Around 60% of its revenue is generated in Asia, 30% in Europe and 10% in the United States.
Maintaining a technological lead requires heavy investment: SOITEC devotes 20% of its revenue to research and development.
“The speed of innovation becomes absolutely key, because we have to maintain the distance with the competition,” Maleville says.
Artificial intelligence is creating another opportunity, and another challenge. Its rapid development is driving demand for increasingly powerful data centres, while raising concerns about their energy and resource consumption.
SOITEC’s photonics products are designed to transfer information faster while reducing energy use.
They could also help fuel the highly controversial growth of artificial intelligence.
“How this AI is used is a debate that is worth having,” acknowledges Cyril Menon. “How we regulate it, how we make the best use of this AI, is an important issue for society. And this AI consumes a lot of energy, a lot of resources. So it is also important to provide products that help address this issue.”
For SOITEC’s executives, mastering these technologies is also about Europe’s place in the global industry.
“It is also by having these advanced technologies that we can have an impact on Europe’s future,” concludes Cyril Menon. “And have a seat at the table.”

French government forecasts 1% growth in 2027: what do experts think?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:00:43 UTC
22:00:43 KST

France's High Council for Public Finance calls the government's 1.0% growth forecast for the 2027 budget "optimistic", as economists warn of a possible "slippage" and the executive still has to secure approval.
The budget battle is only just beginning, and the growth figure chosen by the government for 2027 is already prompting reservations.
In an opinion published on Thursday, the High Council for Public Finance (HCFP) judged that the draft budget and social security financing bills, presented the same day to the Council of Ministers, were based in particular on a 1.0% growth forecast it considers "optimistic".
The institution chaired by Amélie de Montchalin, currently First President of the Court of Audit and formerly minister for Public Action and Accounts under Emmanuel Macron, also highlights the "significant uncertainty" surrounding the domestic situation, notably regarding "the very adoption of the budget for 2027".
According to the first draft unveiled, the executive aims to bring the public deficit down to 5.0% of GDP in 2027, from 5.4% this year, at the cost of an "effort" totalling €54 billion.
"That would make it the fifth consecutive year with a deficit equal to or above 5%," notes Hadrien Camatte, senior economist for France, Belgium and the eurozone at Natixis CIB, in a commentary to Euronews.
"Risk of budget slippage"
To reach this target, the government is planning €43 billion in new measures, including €25 billion in spending cuts and €18 billion in additional revenue. On top of that would come €12 billion already decided this year.
In detail, the deficit of central government would widen to 5.0% of GDP in 2027, from 4.8% in 2026, mainly "under the impact of higher debt-servicing costs (€10.3 billion), defence spending (€6.5 billion) and the contribution to the EU budget (€2.8 billion)," observes Hadrien Camatte.
Most of the measures would focus on the social security system, the expert continues, "with a target surplus of 0.2% of GDP, compared with a deficit of 0.1% in 2026". This would notably involve a partial freeze on pensions, expected to generate around €4 billion in savings, and on family benefits, for €500 million, according to the government.
As for the deficit of local authorities, it "would improve slightly", the economist says, narrowing to 0.1% of GDP from 0.2% in 2026.
On the revenue side, the plan provides for €17.2 billion in new compulsory levies, notably through an overhaul of cuts to social contributions (€6.6 billion), higher local taxes and shaving down a tax allowance currently enjoyed by retirees.
This trajectory rests on several assumptions judged "optimistic", Hadrien Camatte recalls. The government is banking on GDP growth of 1% in 2027, compared with 0.8% for Natixis, the corporate and investment bank of the BPCE group (Caisses d'Épargne and Banques Populaires).
The economist also points to "an average rate of 4.3% for 10-year government bonds, a level already far exceeded in recent days, at 4.9%."
"Weaker economic growth, the high sensitivity of debt-servicing costs to interest rates – a 100 basis-point increase would mean an additional €3.4 billion in 2027 – and the insufficiently documented nature of certain measures all create a risk of budget slippage in 2027," warns the Natixis expert.
For Jérôme Mathis, professor of economics at Paris-Dauphine University, the government is adopting "a stance of deliberate confidence."
"By basing its forecasts on the assumption that energy costs will stabilise and household consumption will gradually recover, the executive is seeking to maintain a positive signal for investment and economic activity," he told Euronews.
The challenge of the upcoming parliamentary debates, the researcher added, is precisely to "find that point of balance: a responsible budget that credibly reduces the deficit without stalling the engine of growth."
Mathis stressed that the review of the 2027 draft budget "highlights a fundamental consensus: the absolute imperative to restore France's public finances in order to preserve our financial sovereignty and our credibility within the eurozone."
"The current discussions are not about that objective, which everyone shares, but about the most appropriate calibration for achieving it," he noted.
"Tomorrow the overseas territories, universities, the health sector"
It is "very difficult" to predict what growth will be in 2027, says François Facchini, professor of economics at the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. He points in particular to the uncertainty surrounding the outcome of the war in the Middle East, which is driving the surge in fuel prices in France, but also stresses political instability.
The new government, which will take office after the 2027 presidential election, "will probably pass an amending finance bill that will affect growth", he believes.
According to the researcher, it is also "likely" that the election year will be marked by strikes and social movements, with each group seeking to "weigh on candidates' promises". He mentions civil servants and students, but also, potentially, "tomorrow the overseas territories, universities, the health sector, all the sectors that are highly dependent on political choices".
"It is likely, moreover, that food prices will rise after the heatwaves and drought of 2026," he adds.
François Facchini considers that, between geopolitical and political uncertainty, likely inflationary pressures and the risk of a debt crisis, "the High Council is right: 1% [growth] is optimistic". He does, however, qualify this: "That is generally the rule for budget scenarios."
A parliamentary wall
But the current government must first get this budget passed, in a National Assembly that is becoming ever more fragmented as the presidential election approaches.
Hadrien Camatte identifies two scenarios for Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu: resorting to article 49.3, which allows adoption without a vote but automatically triggers no-confidence motions, or using ordinances.
The first option would, however, mean reducing the planned savings effort in the budget and would require "abstention either by the Socialist Party – an unlikely prospect in light of its recent statements – or by the National Rally, whose stated positions are more open to this possibility but with red lines that could shift, particularly on pensions", according to the Natixis CIB expert.
As for ordinances, they would give France a budget "matching the version adopted by the government" in the event of deadlock at the end of the 70 days of debate in the National Assembly.
France would then be entering uncharted territory under the Fifth Republic.

Andy Burnham urged by Lib Dems to reveal all meetings with owners of Manchester City
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

22:00:13 KST

Andy Burnham is facing calls from the Liberal Democrats to publish details of all his meetings with Manchester City’s owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group (Adug), and declare all hospitality he has accepted at the Etihad Stadium.
The prime minister was widely criticised this week for saying he would be “really concerned” if Adug were forced to sell City after being found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial regulations, which led to Downing Street issuing two clarifications of his position on Thursday.
Burnham also praised Adug’s investment in Manchester, having had close relations with the company, through which Sheikh Mansour bought City in 2008, during nine years as the mayor of Greater Manchester which ended when he returned to parliament this summer.
In a strongly-worded letter to Burnham the Lib Dems’ spokesperson for culture, media and sport, Anna Sabine, criticised his apparent defence of City as “extraordinary” and invoked Gianni Infantino’s aborted World Cup sell-off scheme in what she described as a difficult year for football.
“As you will know, an independent commission has found Manchester City guilty of 114 charges of breaching financial rules over a timeframe of nearly a decade, including the use of ‘sham contracts’ and schemes to disguise more than £830m of funding,” Sabine writes in a letter seen by the Guardian.
“Despite this, your response was to thank the club’s owners for their work and describe the findings as ‘contested’ and that it was ‘wrong to jump to a conclusion’. It is extraordinary that a prime minister would use his position to call into question the findings of the independent investigation, and risk undermining trust in the Premier League’s processes.
“This has been a difficult year for football’s reputation. Fifa’s conduct around the World Cup has already raised serious questions about integrity in the game we love. At a moment like this, fans expect their prime minister to stand up for the rules in place, not to appear to side with a club found guilty of breaking them.”
Sabine also told the Guardian that Burnham’s ties to Adug should be scrutinised and is planning to write to Downing Street and the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to demand details of their meetings.
“Football fans up and down the country deserve to know that the rules apply to everyone, however rich and powerful they are,” Sabine said. “When the prime minister leaps to the defence of a club’s owners within hours of a verdict, people are entitled to ask what their relationship is.
“Andy Burnham must come clean and publish details of every meeting and conversation he has had with City Football Group, Abu Dhabi United Group or UAE government representatives, going back to his time as mayor – and that includes any hospitality freebies received.”
Burnham, an Everton fan, has been pictured attending City games at the Etihad Stadium in hospitality areas.
The extent of that hospitality is unclear because under GMCA regulations the public disclosure of gifts is available for current office holders without the submission of a freedom of information request.
A Downing Street spokesperson said Burnham had not met City’s owners since becoming prime minister in July and that his quarterly list of engagements would be published before the end of the year.
City’s chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, visited Downing Street last month for a meeting with the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, but Burnham did not attend.
Burnham has not been to a City game since he became prime minister but has attended two Everton matches at Hill Dickinson Stadium, where he was accommodated in the directors’ box despite having a season ticket in the South Stand.
City confirmed on Friday that they had appealed against an independent commission’s verdict. They repeated their assessment that the verdict “contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe”.

China’s C919 jet faces further delivery delays amid US export chill: analysts
Washington has reportedly restricted exports of aircraft parts to China to gain leverage over Beijing, adding to Comac’s supply pressures
A reported move by the United States to restrict exports of aircraft parts to China would place another speed bump on production of the C919 – a Chinese passenger jet designed to compete with Airbus and Boeing – as alternative sources of critical components for the plane are not readily available, according to analysts.
The US Commerce Department has slowed export licensing for civilian aeroplane parts to China in recent weeks to strengthen Washington’s position in trade talks with Beijing, Reuters reported on Thursday, citing unnamed sources.
The move was designed to prevent the state-owned Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (Comac) – the maker of the C919 – from stockpiling parts, Reuters said. US officials have also reportedly expressed interest in regulations that would make it easier to restrict shipments of aviation hydraulic fluid.

From ocean waste to fabric: inside Spain’s sustainable fashion revolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:00:08 UTC
22:00:08 KST

Every year, more than 12 million tonnes of plastic ends up in our oceans. Spanish fashion company Ecoalf transforms marine waste and discarded materials into fabrics and clothing through a circular supply chain. But can sustainable fashion transform an industry built on overproduction?
There are almost 5,000 fishermen and one not-for-profit foundation behind Spanish sustainable fashion brand Ecoalf. Every day, the fishermen recover waste caught in their nets, while the Ecoalf Foundation has developed a system to give that waste a second life, turning it into raw material, ultimately, fabric.
"Plastic alone now accounts for around 80% of everything we bring up. This is our daily reality,” says fisherman Tony Beltrán, while showing the waste that got caught in his nets off the coast of Gandía, south of Valencia. **“**Even before recycling became popular, we were already collecting it, the only difference was that we didn't separate it."
Since 2015, the Upcycling the Oceans project, launched alongside the creation of the Ecoalf Foundation, has recovered more than 2,000 tonnes of marine waste, the equivalent of around 100 truckloads of rubbish. Today, the initiative involves around 80 ports and has expanded to France, Italy, Greece, Egypt and Thailand. Yet, it’s still a drop in the ocean: the Foundation points out that every minute, the equivalent of a truckload of plastic ends up in the world's oceans.
“Our goal has always been to bring together 10,000 fishermen across the Mediterranean so that, together, we can help clean up the Mediterranean Sea,” explains Andrea Ruzo, director of the Ecoalf Foundation.
Of all the materials recovered from the sea, most of them, like glass and metals, follow conventional recycling routes. But around 5% of this waste are plastic bottles, which are transformed into what Ecoalf calls Ocean Yarn.
“The first step, once the waste has been collected, is to shred it and turn it into flakes and then pellets, that’s the stage before spinning,” explains Ángela Pérez, Ecoalf’s expert in textile innovation and sustainability.
The beating heart of this supply chain is Ecoalf’s headquarters in Madrid, where ocean yarn and other recycled materials are turned into fabrics.
Since its creation in 2009, the company continues to source raw materials from a range of waste well beyond plastic bottles. Some fibres come from discarded fishing nets, others from tyres or recycled natural textiles, such as cotton and wool. The goal, the company says, is to reduce the environmental impact of both production and the finished garment, while maintaining its look and quality.
Circularity influences the decisions a fashion designer makes throughout the design process says Julie Sohn, Ecoalf’s creative director.
“It changes everything from the very beginning. Everything is designed so that the garment can be completely disassembled, without any additional processing, and re-enter the circular economy,” she says.
Among the pioneers of sustainable fashion, Ecoalf was founded with a clear ambition: to prove that a business can succeed while helping transform one of the world’s most polluting industries. 17 years later, the company has grown into a global brand, with annual revenues of around €65 million, 300 employees and dozens of stores worldwide.
“The problem we’ve been facing in recent years is mass overconsumption and overproduction. Brands need to move beyond sustainable capsules or focusing on a single material. We need to learn to design with eco-design principles from the very beginning,” explains Carolina Álvarez-Ossorio, Ecoalf’s chief marketing officer.
But could sustainable fashion eventually replace fast fashion? There is still a long way to go according to Álvarez-Ossorio, who is also convinced designers have a role to play in finding new ways to work with purpose and ultimately help protect our planet.
Ecoalf is a striking example of the circular economy, but it also raises a bigger question: can recycling the waste we already produce ever compensate for new waste we continue to create?

U.S. in mega deal to build more long-range anti-air missiles
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:00:07 BST
22:00:07 KST

The U.S. Navy has awarded Raytheon a five-year contract worth up to $24.4 billion to accelerate production of the Standard Missile-6, its principal long-range anti-air and anti-surface weapon.
Announced on 1 October by Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao, the multi-year procurement agreement includes two additional option years. The U.S. Navy says the long-term commitment is intended to give the RTX business the stability and predictability needed to expand production capacity, while delivering cost savings through a negotiated deal rather than year-by-year buys.
“Maritime strength demands weapons at speed and scale,” Cao said in the release. “This investment expands production and delivers the firepower our warfighters need to fight, win, and come home safe.”
The SM-6 has become one of the most versatile weapons in the surface fleet’s inventory. Fired from the Mk 41 Vertical Launch System aboard Arleigh Burke-class destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers, it can engage aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles in their terminal phase, and can also be used against surface ships. Its active radar seeker allows it to engage targets beyond the horizon of the launching ship when cued by other sensors, a key element of the U.S. Navy’s Cooperative Engagement Capability. U.S. warships have fired SM-6s in combat during operations in the Red Sea and Middle East since late 2023, including against Houthi anti-ship missiles, drawing down stocks of a weapon that costs several million dollars per round.
Adm. Daryl Caudle, Chief of Naval Operations, linked the contract directly to the size of the fleet’s magazines. “Combat credibility depends on having enough weapons, produced at the speed and scale the Fleet requires,” he said. “This SM-6 award gives industry the demand signal and stability to expand production, strengthen the munitions industrial base, and build the magazine depth our Fleet needs. That is the Foundry delivering for the Fleet – and ensuring our Sailors have the combat power to fight and win.”
The award is being managed by the U.S. Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive (PAE) Munitions, an organisation responsible for the development, procurement and delivery of naval munitions and strike capabilities. It follows a recent Tomahawk contract, which the service describes as part of the same effort to speed up weapons production across the portfolio.
“This award demonstrates what is possible when the Department leverages innovative acquisition approaches to deliver capability at the speed of relevance,” said Van Hendrey, Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Munitions. “Through PAE Munitions, we are bringing together the authorities, resources, and partnerships needed to accelerate production, reduce costs, and strengthen the industrial base that supports our warfighters.”
Raytheon produces the SM-6 at its facilities in Tucson, Arizona, with final assembly at Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Alabama. The missile has also been cleared for export to a number of U.S. allies, with Japan and Australia among the nations to have pursued it for their own air defence destroyers.
According to the U.S. Navy, the agreement will support a larger workforce, higher manufacturing throughput and stronger supply chains for the missile, as part of a wider push to rebuild the defence industrial base and keep Navy and Marine Corps forces supplied with advanced weapons.

Trump is disappearing refugees into the hands of torturers – and rewarding them handsomely | Tutu Alicante and Uzra Zeya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:00:07 UTC
22:00:07 KST

For nearly a year, the Hotel Bamy in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea, has been Adam’s prison. He is confined alone to a hotel room, under constant watch by the security officers and soldiers of a notoriously oppressive regime who control his movements. Not long ago, they barged into his room, handcuffed and beat him, and warned him not to tell anyone. There is no cell to point to, no charges or formal sentence, and nothing on paper to document his plight.
Adam, 26, has chosen not to share his real name or even his country of origin out of fear for his safety. He fled indefinite, forced military conscription in his home country after enduring abuse during his military service.
Adam sought safety in the United States. A US immigration judge heard his case, found that he would probably face persecution if forced to return to his country of origin, and issued a formal order shielding him from removal there. Then, in November 2025, the United States sent him to Equatorial Guinea, a country he had never set foot in and where torture reportedly occurs in every prison nationwide, according to the most recent state department human rights report. Adam, and the other men onboard the flight, were told they were being transferred to another US detention facility. It was only midway through the 13 hour and 10 minute flight that they found out – while shackled – that they were headed toward Equatorial Guinea.
None of this is happening in a vacuum. In November, the Trump administration repurposed $7.5m to pay the government of Equatorial Guinea to accept third country nationals from the United States, a 275% foreign assistance increase and departure from longstanding US policy against direct provision of aid to a deeply corrupt and abusive regime. Congress appropriated these taxpayer funds for humanitarian assistance for refugees in dire need – money that is now used to detain, shackle and eventually send refugees back to the countries they fled. Since then, the US government has forcibly transferred at least 65 third country nationals to Equatorial Guinea. US immigration judges had granted protection to nearly all of these individuals due to the high risk of persecution or torture they face in their countries of origin. Yet one by one, Equatorial Guinea has been sending them back to harm in the very places from which they fled.
In the past few weeks, in retaliation for speaking out against the detention conditions and police violence, police in Equatorial Guinea violently assaulted and arrested two of the refugees, witnesses and lawyers say, including Ahmed Soliman, an Egyptian man from Arizona who has lived in the United States since he was three years old, and Samson Birhane. Today, they remain in police custody, detained incommunicado.
This is part of an escalating scheme by the Trump administration to send immigrants and refugees to countries around the world where they have no connection and often face grave harm. In Equatorial Guinea, it is also fueling the corruption and impunity our organizations have spent decades documenting and countering.
Equatorial Guinea’s government and ruling family are, by any measure, among the most corrupt on earth. About a decade ago, the US justice department settled a civil forfeiture case against the country’s vice-president, Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue, or “Teodorín”. He forfeited a $30m Malibu mansion, a Ferrari and Michael Jackson memorabilia.
Some governments have rightly taken serious action to restrain Teodorín’s corruption, such as the sanctions the UK government imposed on him in 2021. Yet last September, the Trump administration did the opposite, and quietly paused corruption-related visa restrictions that had prevented Teodorín from traveling to the United States, clearing the way for him to meet with Christopher Landau, the US deputy secretary of state, before the deal to accept non-Equatoguineans removed from the United States.
In addition to these funds, the deal affords Teodorin something he has long sought: legitimacy and access in Washington DC.
We are seeing that access to US policymakers deepening in real time. Last week, Teodorín was back in New York, meeting with Landau again, this time at the United Nations, where they celebrated what the government of Equatorial Guinea referred to as a positive evolution of the bilateral relationship. They discussed expanding cooperation beyond energy to banking, trade investment, security and diplomacy.
Our organizations have worked for years to demand accountability for rampant corruption in Equatorial Guinea, and now, to fight for the refugees and torture victims being unlawfully sent there. After building the evidentiary dossier that led to UK sanctions, EG Justice is now challenging Equatorial Guinea’s participation in the US deportation scheme before the African Commission on People’s and Human Rights, while working with local attorneys to offer legal and humanitarian aid. In July, the African Commission on Human and People’s rights issued an emergency ruling, ordering the government of Equatorial Guinea not to send people back to danger in their home country – a ruling that the government has ignored since, sending four people back to the very places from which they had sought, and received, protection.
Human Rights First (HRF), for its part, together with partner organizations, successfully challenged the third-country deportation policy in federal court, but the US supreme court has since intervened to allow these rapid third-country deportations to resume while it rules on the case. HRF also leads the ICE Flight Monitor platform, uncovering in real time hidden deportation flights to Equatorial Guinea and beyond, while partnering with Refugees International to shed light on proliferating and often opaque US third-country forced transfer agreements with 35 countries.
Time is of the essence, as Adam has been sick with malaria and typhoid fever since November. His second asylum claim, filed with Equatoguinean authorities in January, remains in indefinite limbo. The judge in the case told local counsel that he does not have authority to hear it, as the vice-president is in charge of these cases. The habeas corpus petition his lawyer filed also remains unanswered. Guards tell him repeatedly to “go back to your country,” the very outcome a US judge already ruled would put him at high risk of persecution.
There is a clearcut, fair, and humane path forward. We are pressing for coordinated Magnitsky-style sanctions against senior Equatoguinean officials, including Teodorín, in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the European Union simultaneously, building on the evidentiary dossier the UK relied on in 2021. In the United States, Congress must exercise fully its oversight authority to end misappropriation of migration and refugee resettlement funds to finance arbitrary detention and chain refoulement – and, in effect, to reward torturers.
Adam and everyone held at Hotel Bamy should be released and given the chance to have their asylum claims heard in a country capable of hearing them, or returned to live safely in the United States. They deserve the protection that was promised to them and is enshrined in US and international law.
- Tutu Alicante is founder and executive director of EG Justice
- Uzra Zeya is president and CEO of Human Rights First

The occupiers beat the 46-year-old Palestinian man in the town of Beita, south of Nablus, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.
Witnesses told Anadolu that a group of Israeli occupiers fired stun grenades and tear gas at farmers in the Jabal al-Arma area, forcing them to leave.
“The olive harvest, traditionally an important source of income for Palestinian families, has become a dangerous season because of occupier attacks and restrictions on access to farmland,” a farmer, Ismail Abu al-Sheikh, told Anadolu.
“We used to celebrate the arrival of the season and eagerly wait for it. Today, we fear for our lives and the lives of our families and children,” he said.
Another farmer, Saqr al-Jabali, said: “Olive oil production this year could fall to around 20% because farmers are repeatedly prevented from reaching their land.”
Similar incidents were reported in Salfit province, where occupiers, backed by Israeli forces, prevented farmers from harvesting olives in the Deir Istiya area and forced others from their land in Farkha and Haris areas, according to the Palestinian official news agency Wafa.
Israeli forces also detained three farmers from Haris while they were harvesting olives, it added.
The olive harvest begins in early October and continues through the end of November, making it one of the most important agricultural and economic seasons for Palestinian towns and villages.
With the start of the season, attacks by occupiers and Israeli restrictions on farmers’ access to their land have intensified, including beatings, blocking access to fields, theft of crops and the uprooting or damaging of trees.
The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said more than 45,000 trees were cut down or damaged across the West Bank in the first half of 2026, including more than 26,000 olive trees.
Nablus province recorded 900 occupier attacks during the same period, the highest number among West Bank provinces, according to Palestinian data.
6 Palestinians arrested
Elsewhere in the West Bank, the Israeli army arrested six Palestinians during raids, according to the Palestinian Prisoners' Media Office.
Israeli forces stormed Burqa, northwest of Nablus, raided and searched several homes, damaged their contents and arrested three Palestinians, the office said.
A young man was arrested in Zababdeh, south of Jenin, another in Jayyus in Qalqilya province and a sixth Palestinian in Hebron province.
Israeli forces also carried out raids in parts of Ramallah and Al-Bireh province, with no arrests reported there.
More than 9,300 Palestinian prisoners are held in Israeli prisons, including 350 children and 90 women, according to Palestinian organizations concerned with prisoners’ affairs.
Those organizations say detainees face torture, starvation and medical neglect, which have resulted in the deaths of dozens since the start of the war.
2,051 attacks in September
Palestine's Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said Friday Israeli forces and occupiers carried out 2,051 attacks against Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in September.
Of these, 1,404 were carried out by the Israeli army and 647 by occupiers, according to the commission.
Ramallah and Al-Bireh recorded the highest number with 506 attacks, followed by Nablus with 342, Hebron with 272, Jenin with 202, Bethlehem with 187, Tulkarem with 152 and Jerusalem with 149.
The attacks included assaults on Palestinians, damage to property and crops, restrictions on access to land, and the demolition of homes and agricultural structures.
The commission said occupier attacks alone killed three Palestinians and injured 88 others, including seven children and six women.
Attacks on agricultural land affected 14,600 trees during September, including 9,334 olive trees.
Occupiers also attempted to establish 21 new outposts during the month, including 10 in Ramallah and Al-Bireh, five in Nablus, two each in Jerusalem and Bethlehem, and one each in Hebron and Jenin.
Israeli authorities issued two military seizure orders affecting 9.1 dunams (2.25 acres) of Palestinian land, as well as seven orders to remove trees and vegetation covering a declared total of 560.6 dunams (138.5 acres), according to the commission.
Israeli forces also carried out 62 demolition operations during September, affecting 254 structures, including houses.
The commission said occupiers carried out 5,561 attacks against Palestinians, their land and property from the beginning of 2026 through the end of September.
Around 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in illegal settlements and outposts across the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem.
Since October 2023, Israeli forces and occupiers have intensified attacks across the occupied West Bank, killing 1,206 Palestinians, injuring around 13,350 others and arresting more than 24,600, according to Palestinian figures.

Can releasing more of Europe’s emergency reserves bring diesel prices down?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:59:32 UTC
21:59:32 KST

The EU says it is ready for collective action with the IEA on a fresh emergency release. Analysts say releasing diesel reserves could lower pump prices within days, but would offer only short-term relief.
Historically high diesel prices in the EU and growing concerns about a potential US diesel export ban have prompted calls for action in the bloc.
European Commission spokeswoman Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said on Friday that the bloc was ready to work with the International Energy Agency on the possible release of fuel reserves to bring down energy prices.
On Wednesday, the International Energy Agency confirmed that it could consider releasing more emergency oil stocks if supply disruptions worsen.
At the time of writing, the size of a potential release has not been confirmed, although France suggested releasing 50 million barrels of diesel — approximately 6.7 million tonnes — alongside 50 million barrels of crude oil from the International Energy Agency’s emergency stocks on Friday morning, according to EU diplomats.
George Shaw, senior insight analyst for distillate markets at Kpler, sees the proposed 50-million-barrel diesel release as substantial.
According to Kpler, the EU and UK imported 24.25 million barrels of diesel from outside the region in September, meaning the proposed release would amount to roughly twice that monthly volume.
Analysts agree that the impact on prices would depend on both the volume released and how quickly it reaches the market.
Alan Gelder, senior vice-president for refining, chemicals and oil markets at Wood Mackenzie, said: "A major release of diesel reserves could lower wholesale prices by US$20–30/bbl, which equates to about €0.10–0.15 per litre at the pump," adding that motorists could see prices fall within a few days. Shaw said significant market price changes typically take one to two weeks to reach the pump.
However, this is a short-term remedy, Gelder added. "Any further release only buys time, as global diesel supply is still below global diesel demand, so we continue to draw on inventories and are vulnerable to the export policies of others (such as the US)," Gelder said.
The chart below shows overall emergency oil stocks by country, including diesel reserves.
Diesel supply in Europe has been severely affected, partly because Russian refineries are not fully operational following drone strikes. This is compounded by reduced exports of refined products from the Middle East and lower exports from Asia in response to the US-Iran conflict, which is restricting crude exports from the Middle East.
On the size of European countries’ strategic reserves, Gelder said that "major countries have 70 to 100 days of cover", adding that the requirement is to hold stocks equivalent to approximately 60 days of inland consumption or 90 days of imports, whichever is greater. "We hence have at least two months of cover if there is no supply and European refineries continue to operate."
Petrol and diesel have remained particularly expensive in Europe not only because of rising international crude oil prices but also because of the soaring cost and limited availability of refining capacity.
European refineries have been running close to full capacity, and there is little room to increase production.
According to Gelder, refinery capacity in use across European OECD members "is at over 80% (measured by crude intake against nameplate capacity), processing about 11 million b/d of crude," meaning that production is close to maximum levels.
These constraints leave Europe reliant on diesel imports. Releasing refined products from EU countries’ strategic reserves could therefore be the fastest way to affect prices.
However, replenishing those reserves would take time. “Releasing strategic stocks would mean that you are eroding an important buffer,” Shaw said, warning that the duration of the crisis remained uncertain. He said rebuilding stocks would depend on increased production and exports from the Middle East.
The EU has been under pressure from the United States to release some of its strategic oil reserves “immediately” to help lower global diesel prices.
On Friday, Brussels criticised the threatened US ban on diesel exports, warning that it would undermine trust in Washington as a reliable partner. "We fully reject any ban on diesel."
A fresh release would follow the agreement reached by IEA member countries in March to make 400 million barrels of emergency oil stocks available to the market, with each country following its own release timetable.
Shaw said Middle Eastern diesel exports in September were still more than 50% below their level a year earlier.
According to Gelder, "for diesel prices to fall sustainably, the global refining system needs to ease, which requires a resolution of the US-Iran conflict to enable higher production from Middle East exporting countries, along with greater exports from other suppliers, such as Russia".
Pressure on diesel supplies could also ease if high energy prices and high government bond yields trigger a global economic slowdown, reducing demand for the fuel.

Argentina announces citizenship-by-investment program

Argentina announces citizenship-by-investment program
BUENOS AIRES, Oct 2 - Argentina will launch South America's first citizenship-by-investment program, Economy Minister Luis Caputo said on X on Friday.
Applications will open in the fourth quarter of 2026 and will offer citizenship through a non-refundable contribution of $350,000 or the purchase of an $800,000 public bond, the Economy Ministry said in a statement.
The plan accompanies other measures to strengthen Argentina's investment climate, the ministry said. President Javier Milei has sought to stabilize the country's macroeconomy and increase its dollar reserves through deep austerity measures and foreign investment stimulated by an incentive program known as RIGI.
"The announcement is part of Argentina's ongoing process of opening up and international integration," the ministry added.
Officials hope the program will inject much-needed financing into Argentina's economy. Monthly inflation dropped from 25.5% when Milei took office in December 2023 to 1.7% in August, but the government faces a debt payment crunch next year that will coincide with Milei's likely reelection bid. Investors are watching for signs Milei may struggle to sustain his fiscal tightening, which could pressure the peso and unsettle markets.
Under the announced program, an applicant's spouse, as well as their children between 18 and 25 who are single and without children of their own, may also apply for citizenship by contributing $100,000 to Argentina's treasury. Children under 18 may apply by contributing $25,000.
Jeremy Savory, the United Arab Emirates-based CEO of consultancy Millionaire Migrant, which focuses on citizenship- and residency-by-investment programs, recently launched a waiting list for people interested in applying for Argentina's anticipated program. Some are clients who already have a second passport that lacks the benefits of Argentina's, such as the ability to travel visa-free to countries in the Mercosur trade bloc, he said.
"There's a lot of people interested, including people who have already been through this process before," he said.
Other countries have unveiled programs that provide an expedited path for wealthy people to live or work there. In December, US President Donald Trump, an ally of Milei, launched the "Trump Gold Card" visa program, which allows applicants to pay a $15,000 fee to the Department of Homeland Security for speedy processing. After a background check or vetting process, applicants must make a $1 million contribution to obtain the visa, which allows them to live and work in the United States.
Promoters of Argentina's new program have highlighted American billionaire Peter Thiel's activities in Argentina. While it is unknown whether he will participate, Thiel created international buzz when local media reported he had temporarily relocated his family to Buenos Aires. A regulatory filing showed his fund bought a 1% stake in Vista Energy, an oil producer operating in Patagonia. REUTERS

Casa de México in Madrid unveils 2026 Day of the Dead altar inspired by Michoacán and Agustín Lara
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:57:54 UTC
21:57:54 KST

Casa de México in Madrid unveils "Viva la vida!", its 2026 Day of the Dead altar honouring Agustín Lara, inspired by Michoacán and the monarch butterfly, with a musical tour. Free entry from 2 October to 8 November.
The Casa de México in Spain Foundation is unveiling the ninth edition of its Day of the Dead altar, the institution's most visited exhibition of the year. Under the title "Viva la vida!", the 2026 installation has been designed by Mexican artist Beatriz Redo and pays homage to composer Agustín Lara, with a set design inspired by the cemeteries and mountains of Michoacán.
The set recreates a mountain cemetery in Michoacán on the night of Day of the Dead, when, according to tradition, families gather to symbolically reunite with their deceased loved ones.
Beatriz Redo, the designer of this year's installation, explains that she wanted to pay tribute to the monarch butterfly, one of the region's great symbols: "Michoacán is an area of Mexico that receives the migration of the monarch butterfly, a massive migration that comes from Canada and coincides with the days at the end of October and the beginning of November. Tradition also links it to Day of the Dead," she notes.
Among the Purépecha and Mazahua communities of Michoacán, the arrival of these insects in the region's forests is interpreted as the return of the souls of the departed.
Agustín Lara, the musical protagonist of the tour and a great lover of Madrid
The altar is dedicated to Mexican singer and composer Agustín Lara (1897–1970), who was married to film star María Félix. Lara, known as 'El Flaco de Oro', was a prolific composer and author of classics such as 'Granada', 'Solamente una vez', 'María Bonita' and the emblematic chotis 'Madrid', which reflects his close relationship with Spain.
The artist is depicted at the top of the altar as a papier-mâché skull next to his piano, created by artisans Raimundo Amezcua and Marta Linares. New this edition, the entire tour will be accompanied by his most emblematic songs, something unprecedented in this exhibition and which will guide visitors on a visual and sonic journey through one of the most colourful traditions in the world.
Papel picado, a tradition rich in symbolism, and an altar for pets
One of the most representative craft elements on the tour is papel picado, a traditional technique created with hammer and chisel that is also used for patron-saint festivities and birthday parties.
Its role on Day of the Dead goes beyond decoration: "When it is hung up and begins to move, it represents the moment when the souls arrive at the altar to consume everything we have placed in the offering for the deceased," explains Citlali Pérez from Casa de México's Communications Department.
In addition to the main altar, the experience includes a tour with pieces of Mexican folk art and other complementary altars. New for 2026, an altar dedicated to pets has been added to remember the animals that bring so much companionship and happiness to households. On the second floor, visitors can also leave a message for their deceased loved ones; once Casa de México removes the exhibition, these messages are burned in a ceremony.
Beyond Casa de México: altars in Madrid and Santander
The foundation is extending the celebration beyond its headquarters on Calle Alberto Aguilera. In collaboration with Madrid City Council, three other altars will be open to visitors from 23 October to 2 November at:
- CentroCentro, designed by Guillermo González
- La Montaña de los Gatos, in El Retiro park, designed by Fer Ferez
- Arganzuela Greenhouse, designed by the studio Señoritos Creativos
The newly opened Faro Santander cultural centre will also host an altar designed by set designer Cristina Faesler, in collaboration with Casa de México.
A heritage recognised by Unesco
The Day of the Dead celebration in Mexico was declared Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by Unesco on 7 November 2003.
Of pre-Hispanic origin, the tradition understands death as the beginning of a journey to Mictlán and sees the altar not as a reason for sorrow, but as a celebration of memory and the bond between generations, through photographs, candles, cempasúchil flowers and objects that were meaningful to the deceased.
Dates, opening hours and free entry to the 2026 Day of the Dead altar
The altar can be visited from 2 October to 8 November, Monday to Sunday, including the public holidays on 12 October and 2 November. Admission is free.
Monday: 10:00 – 18:45
Tuesday to Friday: 10:00 – 13:45
Saturday and Sunday: 10:00 – 12:30
Guided visit (around 20 minutes, covering the building's three floors): Tuesday to Friday from 14:00 to 20:30, Saturdays from 13:00 to 20:30 and Sundays from 13:00 to 18:30.
Access without a booking is via a queue and is subject to capacity; for the guided visit with booking, you must subscribe to Casa de México's newsletter at casademexico.es.

‘We just want to be listened to’: student protests shut schools across France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:57:16 UTC
21:57:16 KST

As dozens of school pupils sat on top of a pile of wheelie bins blocking a high school entrance in north-eastern Paris, Sophia, 17, was on the frontline of the barricade, when she would normally have been attending Spanish class.
“We hope this grows into a massive youth protest movement,” said the final year baccalaureate student at Paris’s Lycée Voltaire, who did not want her real name published. She was on her second day of blocking the school entrance along with hundreds of others, ensuring all lessons were cancelled. “We just want to be listened to by the government. We’d rather stand here doing this than have to learn in poor conditions. It’s the only way to make ourselves heard.”
“School is a right, not a privilege,” read a cardboard sign as Sophia listed the grievances of teenagers across France: a lack of state investment in education, overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other reasons for the protest included the opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the unbearable temperatures in classrooms during the heatwaves in May and June.
“The education budget is being cut to shreds while so much extra funding is being put into the army,” said Sophia, who wanted to go on to study art and work in animation. She said she hoped the demonstrations and blockades would continue into next week. Several teachers stood by the barricades in support.
The French government is struggling to deal with its worst crisis in months after it was taken by surprise by the thousands of teenagers demonstrating outside schools across the country this week. Students’ unions say the education system is underfunded and neglected. Hundreds of high schools were closed or barricaded on Friday, and hundreds of young people have been arrested as the movement threatens to roll on into next week.
Many school students protesting have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education, describing difficult conditions in classrooms with ceilings partially collapsing during class, leaks, cockroaches and buildings in disrepair. Others have spoken of excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff.
The government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing teargas canisters to disperse the protests. In Paris on Friday morning, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools – Léonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the south-east.
Several students have been injured in the protests, while the education ministry said 65 education staff were injured, including 40 school principals. An investigation is under way after a 14-year-old boy in Val d’Oise suffered serious injuries to his mouth and jaw after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher. The family’s lawyer said the boy had thought he was “going to die”.
Outside Lycée Voltaire, riot police stood guard on Friday amid the quiet demonstration by hundreds of children. “We’re totally pacifist,” said Yves, a 17-year-old final year pupil who did not want his name published. He would normally have been in history class but said he had the full support of his parents to be on the barricade. He wanted to study catering next year.
“The atmosphere on this barricade is generally very calm,” he said. “But there have been other people from outside school who have come past and tried to set fire to things, so we’ve tried to move the bins to stop that.”
On Friday morning, loud bangs rang out as some people further away from the school let off firework mortars. Yves said: “Yesterday I heard bangs going off every two minutes, it’s loud and scary when things are being fired horizontally and not up into the air. There were people provoking running battles with police but it wasn’t pupils from our school.”
Camille, 18, who said he wanted to become a teacher, said pupils were also protesting over the French government’s lack of engagement over poor results in international education rankings. “France has disastrous results and yet we’re one of the countries with the longest school days,” she said. “The government refuses to see that it’s about quality, not the number of teaching hours.”
Farther east, on the barricade outside the Lycée Hélène Boucher, students were singing and holding cardboard signs of support for people in Gaza, as well as banners against the far-right presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, who is riding high in the polls.
Sofiane, 19, who was studying literature, said students feared the government would scrap its special €1 meals for struggling students and reduce welfare aid for housing. “We’re also protesting about the conditions in the heatwave,” he said. “It was unbearable sitting exams in 35C-40C heat, even the teachers said those were impossible conditions.”
He said the demonstrations were likely to continue. “Young people just want to study and learn in decent conditions. The French state seems surprised about worsening school results, but they’re doing nothing to remedy that.”

Ukraine joins European Defence Fund — Zelensky signs law
According to Ukrinform, this was reported with reference to the bill record on the Ukrainian parliament's website.
The purpose of the law is to complete the domestic procedures required for the Agreement between Ukraine and the European Union on Ukraine's participation in the EDF to enter into force. The agreement was concluded on July 13, 2026, in Kyiv.
The law will establish the legal basis for Ukraine's participation in the Fund, an EU instrument designed to support joint defence research and development and strengthen Europe's defence technological and industrial base.
Ukraine's participation in the Fund is expected to:
- deepen defence-industrial cooperation between Ukraine and the European Union;
- enable Ukrainian legal entities to participate in joint projects with European partners involving defence research, development and production of defence products and technologies;
- increase the technological, innovative and production capabilities of Ukraine's defence industry.
The initiative is expected to contribute to the development of defence-industrial cooperation with the European Union, attract partner funding for defence research and development, and strengthen Ukraine's defence capabilities.
As Ukrinform reported, on September 16, the Verkhovna Rada adopted the law ratifying the Agreement between Ukraine and the European Union on Ukraine's participation in the European Defence Fund. The legislative initiative was supported by 312 lawmakers.

The US plans to increase the number of unmanned &quot;canoes&quot; for border protection — what Ukraine&apos;s experience has to do with it
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:56:57 EEST
21:56:57 KST

The US plans to increase the number of unmanned "canoes" for border protection — what Ukraine's experience has to do with it
Kyiv • UNN
Autonomous Lightfish boats help detect trespassers and contraband on the Rio Grande. The Pentagon is considering deploying them in the Gulf.
The Pentagon may expand its use of autonomous surveillance boats on the Rio Grande River and in the Gulf of Mexico after the canoe-sized vessels helped authorities detect and prevent instances of illegal border crossings and drug smuggling as part of a pilot program launched in January. A U.S. government official said this, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The publication notes that these unmanned surface vessels, created by San Diego-based startup Seasats, patrol the river for extended periods without a crew. They are part of a broader initiative by the military and law enforcement agencies to use relatively inexpensive autonomous systems for surveillance and security missions.
The use of these vessels along the border also demonstrates how a new generation of venture-backed defense startups is gaining the opportunity to win contracts previously handled primarily by traditional contractors. The Pentagon is seeking faster and cheaper ways to deploy cutting-edge technologies capable of operating around the clock.
Defense officials are considering broader use of these solar-powered boats to monitor remote sections of the Rio Grande. In addition to Seasats, similar maritime drones are supplied by Saronic, Saildrone, and Splash.
Military officials plan to increase the number of robotic vessels—10 are currently being tested—by another 50 units. This is intended to reduce the workload of Coast Guard boats and manned aircraft patrolling the border with Mexico as part of President Donald Trump's administration's efforts to combat illegal immigration.
Maritime drones are "cost-effective solutions for intercepting violators and maintaining a presence in areas where drug traffickers are now moving," said M. Roosevelt Ditlevson, Assistant Secretary of Defense for Homeland Defense and Hemispheric Affairs.
In recent years, small drones and other unmanned platforms have become widespread in the U.S. military after repeatedly proving their effectiveness during the war in Ukraine.
In addition
According to media reports, Lightfish— a low-profile autonomous vessel made by Seasats—is approximately 3.3 meters (11 feet) long and weighs 154 kilograms (340 pounds). It costs approximately $240,000 and can be launched from a boat ramp or from the bed of a pickup truck. The drone is capable of operating for months, even in challenging maritime conditions. These vessels are equipped with various sensors—including electro-optical, infrared, and hydroacoustic (sonar) systems—that transmit tracking data in real time directly to military software networks, such as Palantir Technologies' Maven Smart System and Anduril Industries' Fortress platform, alerting Customs and Border Protection and Coast Guard units.
The Pentagon said that, on average each month, Lightfish drones help detect 452 violations, carry out 350 apprehensions, and prompt 100 turnarounds (when a group of people abandons an attempt to cross the border after realizing that they have been detected).
"They see that the vessel is waiting for them and realize that they have effectively been exposed," Ditlevson said.
The drone manufacturer attracted global attention in July, when Reuters reported that the commercial Lightfish vessel, operating in the Philippines' exclusive economic zone, came close enough to a People's Liberation Army Navy destroyer equipped with guided missiles. This made it possible to record detailed close-range video and demonstrate how inexpensive autonomous vessels can monitor military assets worth billions of dollars.
According to Ditlevson, if the project continues to succeed, the number of Lightfish vessel orders could increase by 50 units; their use in the Gulf of Mexico to create a radar barrier between Texas and Key West is also being considered. At the same time, he noted that the expansion of their application would take place gradually, alongside the testing of various technologies.
"We are not tied to a specific manufacturer. We need the best technology," he said in an interview with Reuters.
Seasats CEO Mike Flanigan said that unmanned systems provide continuous monitoring that traditional means, which require large amounts of fuel, cannot match.
"An aircraft or ship can cover vast distances quickly, but if you wanted, say, to keep a Boeing 737 over a certain area of the ocean for an entire day, that would simply be impossible," Flanigan explained. "Our vessel does not cover such a large area in a short time, but it can remain in a designated area for months, which is a key advantage for security and monitoring missions."
As intensified border controls and targeted military operations have closed off a number of drug-smuggling routes, cartels are increasingly shifting their activities to coastal waters and areas near the shore. The expanded use of these unmanned vessels in the Gulf of Mexico precedes their testing in more challenging conditions in the Pacific Ocean, near San Diego.

Ebola death toll surpasses 4,000 as DR Congo struggles to suppress outbreak
Burning of a Ebola-hit transit camp sends 19,000 fleeing, illustrating the difficulties of controlling epidemic.
The Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak has now killed more than 4,000 people, according to government data, making it the worst epidemic in the country’s history.
Figures released on Friday showed that the death toll has risen to 4,018, and confirmed cases had reached 8,300 across seven provinces, as the government continues to struggle to contain the outbreak.
Weak infrastructure, the remoteness of the region in eastern DRC, and ongoing conflict with armed groups near the borders with South Sudan, Uganda, and Rwanda have hindered efforts to respond to cases quickly and effectively.
The United Nations reported on Friday that an Ebola-hit camp housing a transit centre for infected patients was burned by soldiers earlier this week as they were looking for weapons on the outskirts of Bunia, capital city of Ituri Province, which is at the epicentre of the outbreak.
The incident forced 19,000 people to flee the camp.
“The enormous challenge of halting the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) just became even harder after a key transit centre for patients requiring treatment burned down in Ituri province,” the UN said.
People’s mistrust and anger towards health workers and authorities have also contributed to the obstacles the government faces in its efforts to contain the outbreak.
A senior member of DRC’s governing Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party was beaten to death days ago after taking part in a radio programme to raise awareness about the epidemic.
The attack on Marie-Celestin Karondwa, a local official with UDPS, took place last Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterwards, and he died at hospital from his injuries.
The World Health Organization has warned that the epidemic is “far from over” and on track to surpass the regional 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone.
Caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, the current epidemic became the largest and deadliest in the DRC after surpassing the 2018-2020 epidemic.
Several treatments and vaccines are being trialled against Bundibugyo, but currently, there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
The current outbreak, which is the DRC’s 17th, has spread rapidly since it was officially declared on May 15.
More than 2,000 patients have recovered from the Ebola epidemic so far. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, although that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.

Taiwan Indigenous Atayal weaving techniques revived from textiles held in Austria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:55:28 UTC
21:55:28 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Indigenous Atayal textiles recreated from 19th-century pieces held in an Austrian museum are now on display in New Taipei, offering a closer look at traditional weaving techniques that have gradually disappeared.
Five pieces, recreated by Atayal weavers who studied the techniques used to make them, are featured in an exhibition at Wulai Atayal Museum. The display is the result of a research project carried out in Austria last year by New Taipei’s Indigenous Peoples Department and a weaving team, according to the Indigenous Peoples Department.
The group visited the Weltmuseum Wien to study Atayal textiles in its collection, examining their weaving patterns, materials, colors and techniques to understand how the originals were made.
Among the exhibits is a sleeveless jacket featuring white vertical and horizontal stripes and shell beads. Traditionally worn by Atayal men on ceremonial occasions, it represented bravery, achievement, and social status.
One sleeveless garment reaches the thighs and retains the rectangular shape and diamond patterns commonly found in traditional Atayal clothing. A shoulder cloth, meanwhile, combines three sections of plain and patterned weaving. It can be worn over the shoulders, across the chest or on the back, demonstrating the versatility of traditional Atayal dress.
Another sleeveless garment stands out for its pink and varying shades of indigo. The deeper blue resulted from repeated dyeing and oxidation, producing different shades over time.
The reconstruction also examined the knowledge and techniques behind the textiles, including how different dye materials were combined, how mordants were used, and how the sequence and timing of dyeing affected the final colors. The research and reconstruction process is presented through interactive AI installations alongside video documentation and contemporary creative works.
Weaving and facial tattooing have traditionally been important parts of Atayal culture. The Atayal are distributed across mountainous areas of northern and central Taiwan and have the widest geographic distribution among the country's Indigenous peoples, according to the Council of Indigenous Peoples.
Traditionally, weaving was used to reflect women’s skills and social standing, with girls learning the craft from a young age. Atayal textiles were mainly made from hemp and featured striped patterns in colors including red, yellow, black and blue, as well as commonly seen brown-striped white fabric.

Austria estimates nearly 1,000 heat-related deaths during record-hot summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:53:39 UTC
21:53:39 KST

Timo Kirez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
An estimated 995 people died from heat-related causes in Austria between June and August 2026, the highest figure since such records began in 2017, according to an analysis released Friday by the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety (AGES).
The estimate was significantly higher than in recent years. AGES estimated 948 heat-related deaths during the same three-month period in 2024 and 428 in 2025.
Since 2017, estimates for June through August have ranged from 324 heat-related deaths in 2020 to the previous high of 948 in 2024.
AGES stressed that the figures are statistical estimates for the entire period rather than a running count of individual deaths directly attributed to heat.
The methodology also takes into account that the effects of extreme heat on mortality can extend into subsequent days. Because of delays in the underlying data, estimates for particular periods can later be revised, the agency said.
The elevated mortality estimate coincided with Austria's hottest summer in 260 years of temperature records, with new record highs registered at more than 100 GeoSphere Austria monitoring stations.
Temperatures exceeded 41C (105.8F) for the first time since records began, reaching 41.2C (106.2F) at Bad Deutsch-Altenburg in the state of Lower Austria on Aug. 5.
Temperatures exceeded 40C on three days during the summer, while Austria also recorded its highest-ever number of heat days.
