Hungary lifts its veto: what the deal means for Ukraine’s EU accession
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:51:00 EEST
21:51:00 KST

Hungary lifts its veto: what the deal means for Ukraine’s EU accession
The crisis in relations between Ukraine and Hungary is nearing its end. Following a public confrontation, Kyiv and Budapest have quietly shifted to constructive negotiations.
The solution they’ve arrived at is a win-win for everyone concerned – Ukraine, the Hungarian government, the Hungarian minority and the European Union.
Ukraine has taken the first step under the agreement: introducing a draft amendment, agreed on with the Hungarians and key political players, to the legislation on education in parliament. Even MPs known for their caution on minority issues, such as Volodymyr Viatrovych of the European Solidarity party, are prepared to vote in favour of these changes.
Once the law is passed, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar will be able to claim that he has won and has helped the Hungarian minority in Ukraine – an outcome his predecessor Viktor Orbán was unable to achieve.
And Ukraine will gain something no less important. Budapest is set to unblock two clusters in Ukraine’s EU accession negotiations on 13 October. Kyiv, Brussels and Budapest will have to stick to a fairly demanding schedule to meet that deadline.
This agreement does not resolve all the problems in the countries’ bilateral relations.
There is very little trust between Ukraine and Hungary, and the agreement underscores this.
It’s hoped that the current plan, if successful, will mark the beginning of a long-term solution to the crisis. Kyiv has stated that it expects to conclude further agreements with Hungary and wants EU accession negotiations to be fully open by the end of 2026.
However, this agreement leaves Orbán’s pro-Russian party on the losing side, so it cannot be ruled out that attempts may be made to derail the agreement between the Ukrainian and Hungarian governments.
How the Hungarian government changed its stance on Ukraine
Just two weeks ago the conflict was at its peak. In mid-September, Hungary refused to attend the Carpathian Eight summit. Instead, it began escalating the diplomatic conflict, openly demonstrating its disrespect for Ukraine.
The prime minister personally contributed to the bridge-burning.
And the summit wasn't the only issue. Péter Magyar announced that he was terminating an agreement between Ukraine's Naftogaz and Hungary's MOL to build oil storage facilities, a business deal that would have provided a new source of revenue for Hungary and greater fuel supply stability for Ukraine. Magyar gave no reason for terminating the agreement.
Why did Magyar do this? The context is important.
The Hungarian prime minister's anti-Ukraine remarks were made during a parliamentary session in response to renewed accusations from Orbán's party that the government had become "too pro-Ukrainian". It wasn’t the first time Magyar has been thrown off balance by such unfounded allegations.
But it wasn’t long before the Hungarian authorities realised they had gone too far.
Not all of Magyar's voters support his attacks on Ukraine, and Western countries are also becoming increasingly concerned about them. So just a few days later, Budapest began looking for ways to reopen dialogue with Kyiv.
The turning point came on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, sources say.
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán met with her Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, and the two ministers agreed to keep the negotiations quiet for a while. Only now, as the implementation of the Kyiv-Budapest agreement has entered its final stages, has Sybiha acknowledged those talks.
Meanwhile, despite the public crisis, Anita Orbán suddenly gave an interview to Index, a Hungarian opposition outlet sympathetic to Viktor Orbán, in which she spoke of positive developments on the national minorities issue, without going into detail.
Behind-the-scenes negotiations were also taking place between Anita Orbán and Ukraine's Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration, Vsevolod Chentsov.
"Chentsov is talking to Anita so much these days that he's probably fluent in Hungarian by now," one of European Pravda's sources joked.
In a comment to European Pravda, Chentsov acknowledged the negotiations and spoke of the ongoing efforts to rebuild relations.
"We seek to build trust with Hungary. To achieve this, concrete practical steps are needed from both sides," he explained.
An action plan without a shred of trust
The details of the agreement, which has been obtained by European Pravda, clearly demonstrate the lack of trust between the two countries.
Each side is expected to fulfil an existing commitment and, in return, secure a diplomatic victory.
Ukraine has committed to adopting amendments to the Law On Education, which is nothing new – it’s one of the official benchmarks in the EU accession process. Hungary has committed to the opening of two more clusters in Ukraine's EU accession negotiations. This, too, is not a new commitment on Hungary's part: it promised to lift its veto back in June but did not do so.
Because of the lack of trust, however, Hungary and Ukraine have devised a framework in which the commitments are fulfilled in parallel, leaving each side the option of halting the process if the other breaks its promise.
Ukraine has taken the first public step under the agreement: a draft bill has been submitted to parliament. It was jointly drafted by the government and MPs and agreed on with minority communities.
Hungary is expected to take the next step.
On 6 October, at a meeting of COELA (the EU's Working Party on Enlargement) in Brussels, Hungary will agree to the Irish presidency sending Ukraine a letter requesting it to submit its negotiating positions to the EU for Clusters 2 and 3 (Internal Market and Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth).
This may sound like a highly technical decision, but it is this bureaucratic step that Hungary has been vetoing until now, blocking Ukraine's accession progress.
The subsequent technical procedures will then follow step by step, with the process expected to conclude on the afternoon of 13 October, when an Intergovernmental Conference will take place in Luxembourg.
Ukraine's Verkhovna Rada will have to convene an extraordinary session on 12 October to meet this deadline and fast-track the adoption of the amendments to the Law On Education.
"This will make it possible to open the second and third clusters ahead of the EU Summit on 15 October," Chentsov said. "Among other things, the summit will focus on enlargement. So opening the clusters for Ukraine and Moldova will send a strong signal that both the EU and the candidate countries take their commitments seriously."
For this to happen, the process will need to go ahead without a hitch. Parliamentary sources say this is achievable.
Amendments with no detriment to Ukraine
The substance of the draft bill is not new. Even under Orbán the discussions had focused on targeted amendments to Ukraine’s education legislation to address concerns raised by representatives of the Hungarian and Romanian minorities.
The Foreign Ministry emphasises that this cannot be called a "Hungarian law".
"It will apply not only to the Hungarian minority, but to all minorities living in Ukraine," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha stresses. There is one exception: the Russian language will not be covered.
Since Hungary has advocated for these provisions more vigorously than other EU member states, the negotiations have been conducted primarily with Budapest.
The main amendment is the introduction of national minority school status. Mykyta Poturaiev, co-author of the bill and chair of the Verkhovna Rada's Committee on Humanitarian and Information Policy, says there were discussions with Hungarian representatives over specific provisions during the drafting process, and compromises were reached on all of them.
The key question was at what point a school would qualify for national minority school status. "We reached an agreement with our Hungarian partners that the threshold would be 50% plus one student. However, if the number of students receiving Hungarian-medium education subsequently goes down, that won’t mean the school's status will be automatically revoked," the MP explains.
Another important provision for Hungarians, to which there have been no objections from the outset, is the explicit legal right of children to speak their own language at break time and during extracurricular activities.
There is also a fundamental innovation unrelated to Hungary.
There are separate provisions on the possibility of establishing schools for indigenous peoples – namely Crimean Tatar schools. The requirements here are considerably more flexible: just one class taught in an indigenous language is sufficient.
Poturaiev is confident the bill will receive enough votes.
"The bill will pass in the plenary chamber," he assured European Pravda.
The willingness of other parliamentary groups to support the bill is an encouraging sign. This is confirmed by Volodymyr Viatrovych, who has been a consistent advocate for legislative protection for the Ukrainian language and was involved in revising the draft.
"We’ve eliminated the main risks. The bill in its current form poses no danger, so I plan to vote in favour of it," he said.
There are also discussions about adopting, in the first reading, previously registered bills aimed at strengthening protection for the Ukrainian language alongside the amendments to the Law On Education. However, no decision has been made on this yet.
What’s next?
Officials in Kyiv believe that successfully implementing the agreement will make it possible to emerge from the prolonged crisis in Ukrainian-Hungarian relations and change the approach to bilateral ties.
Budapest’s official position has indeed shifted over the past couple of weeks. The Hungarian government has publicly thanked Kyiv for submitting the draft bill.
It’s hoped that this will pave the way for a meeting between the leaders of the two countries, which Magyar has been avoiding. Now the Hungarian prime minister will be able to tell his voters that he has achieved something in relations with Ukraine that Orbán failed to deliver.
Resolving the most urgent issue for national minorities will also allow the leaders to focus on other, less contentious matters in bilateral relations.
It’s hoped that a Zelenskyy-Magyar meeting will also lead to Hungary lifting its veto on the final two clusters in Ukraine's EU accession negotiations.
"We are fulfilling our commitments, and this should also be reflected in progress in the accession negotiations," said Chentsov, adding: "We expect the remaining clusters to be opened by the end of the year."
Sergiy Sydorenko
Editor, European Pravda

They claimed that troops had resorted to eating nettles, tree bark, and wild animals, and to collecting rainwater to drink. One Russian officer reported cases of soldiers dying from exhaustion and hunger.
Biletskyi attributed the growing number of prisoners partly to deteriorating command structures in several Russian regiments. He noted that Ukrainian forces were increasingly capturing specialists rather than only infantry, including drone operators, mortar crews, and electronic warfare personnel.
"Captivity is the best thing that could have happened to you," Biletskyi told the Russian prisoners, warning that their forces would soon face even heavier fighting.
Russian officers also claimed that conditions in the sector had deteriorated sharply about eight months earlier. According to their accounts, Russian advances stalled while carrying out commanders’ orders became increasingly difficult.
The expansion of Operation Vivaldi into phases focused on breaking Russian supply chains and logistics has weakened Russian command effectiveness across the northern Donetsk region. The Third Army Corps has consistently targeted fuel pipelines and rear-area infrastructure, forcing Russian forces to scatter supply bases and extend their logistical reach across the border into Russia.
Ground robots deployed during earlier phases of the operation have also degraded Russian defensive capabilities. The unmanned systems, air-deployed more than 10 kilometers behind enemy lines, have cleared routes, carried out demining operations, and identified vulnerabilities in fortified positions that infantry assault groups exploited.

AI decodes 217-year-old Napoleonic letter in 6 hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:49:49 UTC
21:49:49 KST

An engineer used artificial intelligence to decode a military cypher from the Napoleonic era that had gone unsolved for more than two centuries.
Artificial intelligence has decoded a letter written on Napoleon Bonaparte’s orders for the first time in more than 200 years.
The document was not a letter written directly by Napoleon. It originated at the headquarters of Eugène de Beauharnais, Viceroy of Italy, and was an encrypted troop briefing passed to Marmont on Napoleon's orders.
An engineer at cybersecurity company SentinelOne, Carter Church, wrote on social media that OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model deciphered an encrypted 1809 letter sent to French General Auguste de Marmont.
The AI model transcribed the image to break the cypher in roughly six hours, Church said.
“Astra cut the 1,202 by 1,836 plate into rows, read the signs, decided which of 175 hand–drawn marks were the same sign written twice, and only then began breaking the cypher,” Church wrote in a blog post.
Several researchers had tried over the decades to reconstruct the document's contents, but none had published a full decipherment.
Astra handled the work end to end, including transcribing the image, analysing the homophonic substitution cypher, writing code and cross-referencing historical records.
The text revealed the positions of Bavarian, Polish and French forces.
In 1809, Europe was edging toward war. Austria was preparing to fight France, while a large share of French forces remained tied down in Spain. Marmont, commanding French troops in Dalmatia, risked being isolated if Austria attacked.
On March 16, Napoleon ordered Eugène to inform Marmont of the positions of the main French and allied forces, specifying that the message be "written in cypher" and carried by a reliable officer.
“The Russians are marching against Austria, and the army [of] Friuli today numbers eighty thousand men,” the document reads.
“Add the Dalmatian corps, without counting the reserves being organised everywhere in the rear, and you see that Austria will be attacked at once on every side.
“She is consequently hastening toward her ruin. When you receive the order to march, you must not allow yourself to be intimidated by a few troops or a gathering of rabble.”
Using the decoded troop numbers, officers' titles and unit positions, Church re-dated the document to late March 1809, about two weeks before Austrian forces launched the offensive.
Church published his complete research record on September 18, including the transcription, cypher tables and scripts that allow others to reproduce the result.
According to Church, Satoshi Tomokiyo, the Tokyo-based researcher who maintains Cryptiana, reviewed the solution and marked the entry as "solved."

The number of unemployed people changed little last month, holding at 7.1 million as the jobless rate remained in a narrow range since March.

Among major worker groups, the unemployment rate for Black Americans increased to 7% in September, while the rates for adult men and adult women showed little change at 3.9% and 3.6%, respectively.

Over the past five years, applications for residence permits submitted by Brazilians in Paraguay have more than doubled. Many of them are Bolsonaro supporters who are afraid October's presidential election will be won by incumbent leader Lula – whom they accuse of plunging the Latin American giant into an unprecedented economic crisis. FRANCE 24's Fanny Lothaire, Valeria Saccone and Mélanie Blondeau report, with Jan Onoszko.
Brazil is holding presidential elections on October 4 and 25, but some voters have already decided to go into exile, convinced that the country will go from bad to worse if President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is re-elected.
These Brazilians support Bolsonaro: the father Jair, sentenced to 27 years in prison for an atttempted coup and his son Flavio, the far-right presidential candidate. A small country wedged between Argentina and Brazil, Paraguay is now seen as a tax haven by Brazilians who say they can no longer tolerate the rising taxes under Lula’s government.
In 2025, Paraguay issued a record 40,600 residence permits to foreign nationals, 23,500 of them Brazilians. In 2026, this figure is expected to rise further. In the first three months of the year alone, 9,200 residence permits were issued to Brazilians.
In the far south of Brazil, the border is a hive of activity. Day and night, hundreds of cars and lorries cross the Friendship Bridge linking Brazil and Paraguay, with one objective in mind: staying for good.

Swiss president Guy Parmelin to quit government
- Swiss President Guy Parmelin announced he will quit the government at the end of 2026 after 11 years of service, citing weariness and the need for new energy.
- Parmelin played a key role in negotiating a tariff reduction with the US, lowering duties on Swiss goods from 39% to 15% and securing a US$200 billion Swiss investment pledge.
- He has served as defence and economy minister, was president in 2021, and his successor from the Swiss People’s Party will be chosen by Parliament in December 2026.
AI generated
GENEVA – Swiss President Guy Parmelin announced on Oct 2 that he will quit the government at the end of 2026, in a sudden move after more than a decade of ministerial service.
Switzerland’s presidency rotates annually among the seven members of the government, called the Federal Council, of which Parmelin, 66, was the longest-serving minister.
Parmelin told a press conference in Bern that he had informed ministerial colleagues of his decision to step down on Dec 31.
“By then, it will have been 11 years since I was elected to this role, and the time has come for me to make way for new energy in these times of great uncertainty,” he said, admitting to feeling “a certain weariness”, while insisting he was not stepping down for medical reasons.
Tariff tussle with Trump
A pragmatist, Parmelin seemed to make more headway with US President Donald Trump than his predecessor Karin Keller-Sutter.
Trump shocked Switzerland in Aug 2025 when he announced 39% duties on imports of Swiss goods, among the highest in his global tariff blitz.
Parmelin, the economy minister, went to Washington three times in a bid to reduce the rate.
Eventually, Switzerland and the United States announced a declaration of intent to cut tariffs to 15%, with the Swiss vowing to invest US$200 billion (S$256 billion) in the United States.
A wine-grower by trade, Parmelin is from the French-speaking western canton of Vaud. He is from the hard-right Swiss People’s Party (SVP), which is the biggest in the country.
Parmelin was previously president in 2021 and took centre stage as Switzerland hosted a summit in Geneva between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Joe Biden.
The president of the Swiss Confederation is first among equals on the Federal Council, chairs its meetings and typically represents the country in major domestic and international matters.
The position goes to whoever has had the longest run on the council without being president.
Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis will become president in 2027.
Parmelin joined the Federal Council in 2016 as defence minister and has held the economy brief since 2019.
The Federal Council seven seats are shared 2-2-2-1 among the four main political parties under a decades-old tacit agreement known as “the magic formula”.
Parmelin’s successor will come from the SVP. Candidates have until Oct 23 to come forward, and Parliament will choose on Dec 9.
Parmelin will visit India for a three-day state visit from Oct 5. AFP

Ukraine calls for tighter sanctions as Russian attacks spark Kyiv gridlock
Closure of bridges struck by drones in Ukrainian capital causes traffic chaos.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on allies to tighten sanctions against Russia after a wave of strikes triggered gridlock across Kyiv.
Traffic chaos gripped the Ukrainian capital on Friday after Russian drone attacks overnight closed key bridges. Zelenskyy called for allies to act to prevent Moscow from sourcing components for its arsenal as Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine face attacks around the clock.
Kyiv’s Southern Bridge and Paton Bridge, key routes for cars and public transport across the Dnipro River, were closed in both directions after the attacks. The Metro Bridge was closed in the direction of Kyiv’s right bank, the city administration said.
Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post that Iranian-type Shahed kamikaze drones struck the Southern Bridge “several times”. One person was killed as Russia launched more than 100 drones across the country.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko later said Russian aerial attacks forced the partial closure of three bridges over the Dnipro River.
He said Russia was “tearing Kyiv apart” and that the city should now be on a war footing.
“The capital is in a very dramatic situation,” Klitschko posted on Telegram. “It’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we lived in peacetime.”
Long lines of stationary cars and buses were gridlocked on main roads as commuters sought alternative routes or made their way on foot.
“I’ve been travelling for three hours … to get to work,” Tetiana Osypenko, a 49-year-old seamstress whose bus was stuck in a traffic jam, told the AFP news agency. “There’s just no way to get there. Nothing. It’s impossible to cross the bridges today.”
Zelenskyy, who has persistently called for additional help to boost Ukraine’s air defences during Moscow’s concentrated air campaign, noted that supply chains for such weapons trail through Europe, the United States, China and Japan.
“No matter how hard Moscow tries to fully localise the production of its drones and missiles, its ability to escalate remains critically dependent on foreign components,” Zelenskyy wrote. “Most of these companies are well-known manufacturers, but their components still make their way to Russia.”
“Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line. What is needed is the political will of these countries,” he continued. “If the Kremlin has chosen more strikes, sanctions must work and must be strengthened.”
Last month, European Union foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc was “working on new proposals to tighten sanctions enforcement” and implement new measures.
US President Donald Trump separately signed a sweeping Russian sanctions package into law, taking aim at Russian President Vladimir Putin, banks, other financial institutions, and the energy and defence sectors.
Elsewhere in Ukraine on Friday, Russian strikes targeted a kindergarten in Kherson, a grocery store in Kharkiv and apartment buildings in Kramatorsk and Sumy, Zelenskyy said.
The Dnipro, Odesa, Kharkiv, Kyiv, Poltava and Rivne regions also came under attack with at least four people reported wounded.
The Russian Ministry of Defence said on Telegram that its drones hit a bridge over the Dnipro River in Kyiv, a power station in the surrounding region, the Izmail port near Odesa and a cargo vessel. It claimed all the sites were used for Ukrainian military purposes.
Ukraine’s military carried out its own overnight attacks on Russia and said they hit a Lukoil facility in the city of Volgograd as well as an oil dispatch station in the Samara region with fires breaking out at both sites.
Ukrainian forces also carried out missions in several other Russian regions that targeted airfields, industrial sites and other facilities, including in the Black Sea, Zelenskyy said.
Russian authorities in the Black Sea port town of Tuapse said an enterprise was damaged by drone debris, but they did not provide details.

France's Le Pen pledges to hardwire deficit cuts with 'golden rule'
PARIS, Oct 2 - French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen set out on Friday plans for a binding budget rule she said would put France's public finances back on track, seeking to ease investor concerns about her fiscal credibility.
Le Pen leads the polls for both rounds of the April 18-May 2 election, but investors have cut exposure to French assets, doubting that whoever wins the presidency next year can bring the deficit under control.
The premium investors demand to hold French 10-year bonds over their German equivalent rose above 150 basis points on Friday, its highest since late 2011, after the government's budget bill for 2027 offered little relief.
Writing in French newspaper L'Opinion, Le Pen said a "golden rule" she has proposed would be put to referendum, binding lawmakers in annual budget legislation, with exceptions tightly limited, similar to the way Germany's debt brake works.
The rule would require the deficit to fall by at least half a percentage point of economic output each year, which she said would cut it from 5.4% this year to 2.9% in 2032, the end of the next presidential term.
It would keep falling and stay near balance until debt - currently at 119% of GDP - reaches 60%, she said.
She did not spell out when the referendum might happen or how the government would achieve that level of cuts.
But Le Pen called the figures she had outlined a minimum and said that her fiscal programme, to be outlined on Tuesday, would cut spending even faster.
She reiterated a pledge to carry out €125 billion ($140.35 billion) in savings over five years, which she said would be net of tax cuts. Neither growth nor tax rises could repair the finances, she said.
Lawmakers could allow a larger deficit only with a three-fifths majority, she said. A second consecutive exception would require a referendum.
The High Council of Public Finances would validate the assumptions behind the annual deficit ceiling, and the Constitutional Council would reject "insincere" budgets, she added. REUTERS

School protests send shivers down French government's spine
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:43:02 BST
21:43:02 KST

School protests send shivers down French government's spine
- Published
It is a piece of wisdom that all French leaders take care to heed: young people on the street equals trouble.
Since the student protests of May 1968 – memorably described by President De Gaulle as chienlit (bed defecation, in other words chaos) – every government has run scared of angry French youth.
Why? Because youth movements are unpredictable and shapeless, often with no clear structure to negotiate with. Because when they protest, other groups join in.
Also: because as they're young, the public tends to sympathise. And because if the police mess up and cause injury or worse, then the consequences are incalculable. And presidential elections are only months away.
For all these reasons, when la jeunesse en colère (angry youth) is at the barricades governments tread very carefully indeed.
Right now, French teenagers are at the barricades and if they are not visibly angry (the mood is more excitement), they certainly have the government of President Emmanuel Macron in what Le Monde called on Friday "the cold sweats".
A movement that started nearly two weeks ago in the low-income Seine-Saint-Denis area of northern Paris has in the last few days spread across the country.
On Thursday – the high point so far – hundreds of lycées (where 15-18 year-olds finish their schooling) were being blockaded. On Friday, the situation had improved but around 400 lycées were closed in order to protect staff and students. Universities are beginning to join in.
Violence has erupted. On Thursday the main hall of a lycée in Nantes was destroyed by fire. Smaller fires too numerable to mention were lit at school entrance gates around the country. The cost of the damage is millions of euros.
According to Education Minister Édouard Geffray, 65 teaching staff including 40 school heads have been injured. "Most of the staff who were hurt said that the people they were facing… were not their own pupils," he said.
In addition, the government says that around 300 police and firefighters have been treated for injuries, and some 2,000 people – mainly minors – taken into custody. For their part, student groups say they have a long list of people injured by police. Two teenagers have serious eye injuries and one has lost many of his teeth.
The problem would be hard enough if it was just a question of meeting the protesters' demands. But there is another dimension – a political and social one – which makes this student crisis far more dangerous than in the past.
The demands do exist, even if they remain vague. They are about money – the lack of it – and the need for more teachers, smaller classes and better buildings.
On such matters, many in France would agree with the teenagers. Certainly using protest to demand money from government is such a national habit that even governments agree it's legitimate. And of course, things are indeed getting worse in the education system – because money is so tight.
This week Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu published his draft for next year's budget. The motif is "More cuts – and this time we're serious!"
Whether or not he manages to remove €54bn (£46bn) from state spending, as he promises, remains open to question.
But it is surely obvious that the era of public largesse to defuse social unrest in France is now in its twilight. Students demanding an extra school nurse or insulation in the dining-block are likely to be disappointed.
But that is the lesser of the worries.
The far greater fear is that these student protests are being manipulated by the hard left – and that the violence of recent days is a foretaste of what awaits a dangerously polarised society in the year of elections that is coming.
For the right and centre, there is no doubt that behind the student trouble lies the cunning hand of the France Unbowed party (LFI) and its popular presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
LFI leaders have regularly appeared next to the students – notably in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis whose mayor Bally Bagayoko was criticised for saying that "violence can sometimes be legitimate."
An internal report prepared for the Paris police department which was leaked to the media analysed the opening of the movement in Seine-Saint-Denis. It concluded that students were being "egged on by far-left elements from students unions… and political groups such as… LFI."
It said the tensions "could be part of a flame-kindling strategy… aimed at imposing their ideas ahead of the national elections".
In support of its conclusion, the report's writers cited the presence of protesters who are not themselves lycéens, the vagueness of the demands, the flying of Palestinian and Algerian flags, and the use of tactics – like calling for supplementary protests at police-stations - that come from the radical-left playbook.
The LFI strongly denies doing anything more than lending its natural support to a movement it regards as legitimate. On Thursday Mélenchon called on students to avoid violence "which only serves our enemies' interests".
But his opponents believe that the 75-year-old veteran – who stands a good chance of making it to the second round of the presidential elections in May, probably against the hard-right's Marine Le Pen – knows exactly what he is doing.
Polls show he has massive support – some 40% -- among 18-24 year-olds in France, and that this is concentrated in the populous, high-immigration city suburbs where his talk of a "new France" and "creolisation", to reflect France's changing language and population, are highly appreciated.
But young people are also the biggest abstainers in French elections, so the strategy – as the elections approach – will be to give constant reminders to this part of the population that the LFI is at their side, and that their vote can count.
Whether this will be enough to ensure victory for Mélenchon is another matter. He must surely take seriously the polls which all show him losing massively in a run-off against Le Pen.
If that happens, France will be in very unstable territory - for which the young people's protests of recent days will indeed have been a harbinger.

Shahed- and Geran-type drones heading toward western regions of Ukraine and the border area with Poland receive additional signal support from Belarusian territory. Andrii Demchenko, spokesperson for Ukraine's State Border Guard Service, said this in a television interview.
"The repeater is switched on when Russia launches the drones and is subsequently switched off. We can see that they are activated, and the locations where they operate also change, because Belarus is apparently concerned that Ukraine could fully determine the steps being taken to operate such repeaters on Belarusian territory," the spokesperson emphasized.
He added that the operation of these systems is clearly coordinated with Russia and is activated specifically when attack drones are launched toward western Ukrainian regions, including Volyn region.
Ukraine is working to ensure that the repeaters operating on Belarusian territory cease functioning. According to Demchenko, this is likely being handled through non-public efforts involving other services and units.
As Ukrinform reported, a Russian attack drone recently struck several hundred meters from the border with the Republic of Poland, in the village of Starovoitove in Kovel district, Volyn region, near the Yahodyn border crossing.

Andy Burnham is rethinking the UK’s ties with the EU. What are his options?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:37:55 UTC
21:37:55 KST

Burnham’s decision to put the prospect of EU membership back on the table has caught attention in Brussels. But any attempt to unpick Brexit could come with conditions and difficult trade-offs.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will set out “options” for a new relationship with the European Union – including the possibility of Britain rejoining the bloc – arguing that Brexit has done “more harm than good”.
His government is now expected to flesh out those options ahead of a EU-UK summit in Brussels in November.
“We have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each,” Burnham said earlier this week.
In Brussels, Burnham was initially seen as less focused on international issues than his predecessor, Keir Starmer.
But his willingness to raise the prospect of the UK rejoining the EU – despite the political risks in reopening the issue – has raised the stakes in Brussels and shifted expectations for the reset.
“This was a politically bold move,” one EU official said. “It now opens up the possibility of a far more ambitious approach.”
But officials privately acknowledge that much greater clarity is needed over what Britain is actually prepared to pursue, while stressing that the principles established during the hard-fought Brexit negotiations still stand.
“Burnham now needs to clarify what he means,” Sandro Gozi, a leading Member of the European Parliament (MEP) on relations with the UK, told Euronews. “And on our side, we should show openness to engage in a new sort of partnership.”
‘All the way’: Rejoining the EU
Burnham said that the most ambitious option would be to go “all the way” and rejoin the EU, but has also suggested the time is not yet right to re-run the Brexit referendum.
UK officials say Burnham could use the next general election in 2029 to gauge support for the move, making Brexit a major dividing line in the campaign. Recent polling suggests a majority of UK voters would back rejoining the EU if given the choice.
A pledge to rejoin the EU could alienate traditional Labour voters who backed Brexit, pushing some towards the Conservatives or Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, while drawing more pro-European voters to Labour from the Left.
Burnham came into 10 Downing Street earlier this year as Labour sought to curb Reform UK’s sharp rise in the polls. His predecessor, Keir Starmer, had faced criticism for his cautious and often ambiguous approach to Brexit, seeking closer ties with Brussels while ruling out a return to the EU.
Burnham’s pivot has sent a positive signal to Europe at a time when traditionally Eurosceptic parties are polling strongly ahead of major elections next year in countries including France and Italy.
It also comes as the EU accelerates efforts to enlarge eastwards and into the Western Balkans, and looks to negotiate a special ‘associate membership’ for Canada.
But UK re-entry is widely seen as a long-term prospect that would require a clear national mandate. Officials are all too wary that a shift in government could quickly unravel the plans.
In the meantime, Brussels wants London to clarify its shorter-term objectives.
“This will have come as a moral boost for leaders,” Charles Grant, Director at the Centre for European Reform, told Euronews. “But EU officials will be thinking about the work that needs to be done now, and I think many of them will be quite hostile to what the British are saying.”
Halfway House: Single Market or Customs Union
Burnham also floated the prospect of rejoining the EU’s customs union – which would remove internal tariffs on goods – or the Single Market, a much bolder proposal that would restore the free movement of goods, services, capital, and people.
Former Conservative Chancellor George Osborne, who served under David Cameron during the Brexit campaign, recently said that rejoining the customs union would be a “simple” and “straightforward” solution that could restore free trade and bolster the UK’s economic outlook.
But research suggests that most of the decline in UK exports linked to Brexit stems from leaving the Single Market, and that an arrangement to enter the customs union would only undo a fraction of the damage.
Rejoining the Single Market would however carry a greater political cost. The UK would be obliged to reintroduce free movement, accept European Court of Justice (ECJ) jurisdiction and “dynamically” align its rules to EU standards – conditions Brussels considers non-negotiable.
An attempt by Keir Starmer to sidestep those constraints by creating a Single Market just for goods with the EU was quickly struck down by EU officials earlier this year. Starmer had been constrained by the red lines set out in Labour’s 2024 electoral manifesto, which ruled out a return to the single market, customs union or free movement.
Talks between Brussels and London are now expected to proceed with greater freedom. “I’m glad Burnham has swept away the red lines that we saw as obsolete,” MEP Sandro Gozi said.
Sticking with status quo
The final option proposed by Burnham is to maintain the current arrangement. “That's definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay,” he said.
Under this scenario, the UK would continue pursuing a series of smaller, sector-specific deals to improve the post-Brexit relationship.
Deals to boost agrifood trade by aligning sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) rules, bring the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market and grant special visas to young Europeans and Brits under a youth experience scheme were close to completion when Starmer abruptly stepped down in June.
His departure forced both sides to postpone an EU-UK summit planned for the following month.
Burnham has now moved the goalposts by urging the EU not to shut the UK out of its “Made in Europe” public procurement scheme, designed to boost domestic production and shield European companies from unfair competition, notably from China.
He has warned of the risk of “collateral damage” to UK industries unless the EU allows a carve-out that would see UK companies treated as European ones, telling the bloc: “We are not your enemies”.
But European negotiators have tied the request to lower university tuition fees for EU students, EU sources have told Euronews.
Brussels wants tuition fees for European students, which can exceed £30,000 (€35,000) a year, to be cut to the same rate paid by British students, typically £9,790 (€11,500) annually.
It remains unclear whether the two sides can reach a deal in time for the November summit.

12 minutes of madness: How Flydubai pilot, passengers saved plane midfall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:37:20 UTC
21:37:20 KST

12 minutes of madness: How Flydubai pilot, passengers saved plane midfall
As it plunged 17,000ft in under two minutes, a quick-thinking captain and passengers saved the plane from crashing.
The “hero” Indian captain of Flydubai Flight FZ1073 has described how he fought to open the door to the cockpit of his plane as he was being stabbed by his copilot on Wednesday.
In a video call from his hospital bed in Saudi Arabia on Friday, Captain Smit Machchhar told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi: “When I was down, I could feel that the aircraft was plummeting, and I knew this is a last chance to do something. I knew the door was just there.”
As a result of his action and as the plane was hurtling towards the ground, passengers and crew were able to storm the cockpit, subdue his attacker and regain control of the aircraft, ultimately preventing it from crashing.
Meanwhile, United States President Donald Trump praised the actions of an “Israeli plumber” on board whose quick actions in the cockpit helped prevent a major tragedy.
“An Israeli plumber saw what was happening – he’s strong; you know, when you lift pipe all day, you’re strong – and he saw what was going on and he heard the screaming,” Trump told reporters.
As the plane plummeted about 17,000ft (5,180 metres) in just a matter of minutes, the US president said, “with the G-forces as they were, he ripped the guy out of his seat, threw him back – the crowd got him – and, having never flown a plane, he took the stick and lifted it up and levelled out the plane before it crashed.”
In the days since the incident, more accounts from passengers have come out.
At 7:05am (03:05 GMT) on Wednesday, Flight FZ1073 departed Dubai for Tel Aviv, climbing to 34,000ft (more than 10,000 metres), according to Flightradar24. A little more than two hours later, it suddenly began to descend, plunging before rising and then descending again.
By 05:33 GMT, 12 minutes after the plane started to plummet, it was flying at roughly 15,000ft (4,570 metres) when it started to level out.
Here’s what we know about what happened in those terrifying minutes in between.
05:21 GMT: Flydubai plane begins steep descent
Flightradar24 data show that the aircraft started with a deep descent, followed by a sharp climb and a second steep descent.
Passenger Adam Polo, who was on the plane with his wife and two young children, told CNN that for a moment, the initial fall felt “like a normal air pocket”. “But after one second, you felt that the decrease and the acceleration of the downfall is not normal.”
“The electricity, all of the multimedia system and the air conditioning in the airplane stopped working,” he said. “People that were standing in the aisle or just going to the toilet, they fell. Anyone that wasn’t sitting fell. So it was like the craziest roller coaster that you ever did but multiplied by a thousand.”
In two minutes, the plane had descended more than 17,000ft. Passengers who have spoken to the media since returning safely home have described “chaos” in the cabin with people screaming and multiple waves of turbulence.
“The plane was going sharply down at an unbelievable angle, so sharp that the rudder ripped off the back of the plane,” Trump told reporters on Thursday. “The plane wasn’t designed to go at a speed anywhere near that, so it was well beyond its limits.”
‘Fighting for my life’: Captain stabbed
In the meantime, a fight had begun in the cockpit between the two pilots. The copilot had attacked the Indian captain of the plane, Smit Machchhar, by stabbing him.
On Friday, Machchhar described how he suddenly found himself on the floor of the cockpit, grievously wounded.
“I was lying on the floor injured, but I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside,” he told Modi in a video call.
All cockpit doors are kept locked during flights, and only the pilots are able to open them. But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s spokesperson Doron Spielman told the media that despite being bloodied and lying on the floor, Machchhar had drawn on “the last moments of his energy” to click open the release on the cockpit door.
“Others came in and also played a role. I was, of course, fighting for my own life, but at the same time, I knew I was not going to let others die,” Machchhar told Modi.
Netanyahu has since praised Machchhar as a “true hero”, saying he demonstrated “extraordinary bravery” and saved the lives of the 174 people on the plane with that one act.
“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker – preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster,” he said on X.
The captain told Modi he had been flying planes for 17 years and “can tell what is happening to the plane even with my eyes closed”.
The prime minister told him “his courage, patience and quick decision-making saved the lives of so many people” and all of India was proud of him.
On Thursday, the Indian embassy in the United Arab Emirates reported that Machchhar was “in good health and recovering well” in Abu Dhabi, where he was airlifted after receiving initial treatment in Saudi Arabia.
The Indian embassy in Riyadh said the “brave Indian pilot” had initially been admitted to hospital in Tabuk, a city in northwestern Saudi Arabia where the plane landed.
“A full update on his health is awaited but he is reported to be in stable condition. We hope that he recovers from his injuries at the earliest,” it wrote on X.
‘Like in the movies’: Passengers storm the cockpit
As soon as the captain opened the door, according to passenger Tzvika Manes, his wife, who was taking their young daughter to the toilet at the front of the plane, heard screams and a struggle in the cockpit.
As she alerted a flight attendant, the pilot fell through the cockpit door as his copilot was stabbing him, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12. Manes said he pulled his daughter out of the toilet before heading to engage the attacker.
At that point, “some of the passengers who realised something was happening raced forward, entered the pilot’s cabin. They saw the injured pilot on the ground, and the other, … the attacking pilot, was standing over the control panel, bashing the control panel,” Spielman said.
Asaf Rajuan, one of the Israeli passengers who restrained the copilot, told Channel 12 that the incident “was just [like] in the movies. I didn’t think something like this could happen in real life.”
Rajuan said he and other passengers heard shouting from the cockpit as they felt the plane plummeting.
Passenger Yaniv Hayun, the Israeli plumber Trump referred to, later said in a TV interview how he, Manes and Rajuan forced their way into the cockpit, where they found the wounded captain lying by the door.
“When I went in, I saw the terrorist on the controls, between the two seats. There were no pilots in the seats. I grabbed the terrorist, put him in a hold and first of all pulled him outside,” he said, adding that the copilot appeared to be trying to destroy the controls on the flight deck.
Once the copilot was in the cabin, passengers, including a dentist who was tending to the captain’s injuries, spent several minutes restraining him, using corded headphones to tie him up. Some have reported that he was shouting, “Kill me!”
‘Jumped back in’: Passenger seizes controls of plane
After pulling the copilot into the cabin, Hayun rushed back into the cockpit.
“I jumped back in there, grabbed the controls, started pulling the controls,” he said. “I watch Mayday,” he added, referring to a Canadian TV series about air crashes.
At that point, another pilot who had been travelling farther back in the plane arrived at the cockpit.
“The plane started levelling out a little more, and then the pilot told me he was taking over from there,” Hayun said.
At 05:28 GMT – it is unclear if this was before or after the new pilot reached the cockpit – the aircraft began transmitting the transponder code 7700, the international code for a general emergency. The plane was, at this point, flying near the Saudi Arabia-Jordan border.
‘Real bad shape’: Passenger tends to captain
The dentist, who was travelling home to Israel from China, rushed to help the wounded captain amid the chaos.
Shota Musayev told The Times of Israel: “When I heard screaming, after 10 seconds I ran – I didn’t wait. When I came into the cockpit, the pilot was in real bad shape with heavy bleeding, particularly from his head.”
“I was the only doctor on the plane, and eventually, I managed to stop the bleeding and stabilise his blood pressure,” he said.
Musayev said he believes the emergency medical treatment he provided to the 39-year-old pilot helped save Machchhar’s life.
“These were very hard moments, but together with a few brave people on the plane, we managed to avert a situation that was very close to a disaster,” Musayev said. He also told Channel 12 how he tied the copilot’s hands and legs multiple times to secure him.
05:33 GMT: Flydubai plane is flying at 15,000ft
Flightradar24 recorded the plane levelled out at 15,000ft. Two minutes later at 05:35 GMT, its transponder code changed to 7500, signalling unlawful interference. Then, the aircraft turned west, briefly entered Jordanian airspace and then turned back towards Saudi Arabia.
05:44 GMT: Alert seeking an emergency landing
Air traffic controllers in Tabuk received a distress call from FZ1073 asking for an emergency landing.
As the aircraft approached Tabuk, its transponder switched back to code 7700, indicating a general emergency.
06:58 GMT: FZ1073 lands
Nearly four hours after it took off, the Flydubai plane landed in Tabuk, where emergency medical staff and security officials waited for the 174 people on board, including the wounded attacker, the bleeding pilot and the “plumber” who temporarily took charge of the plane’s control panel.

Kickbacks through charitable foundations: the ESBU is investigating a scheme involving the purchase of medical equipment, in which Bogomolets National Medical University figures
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
15:36:18 EEST
21:36:18 KST

Kickbacks through charitable foundations: the ESBU is investigating a scheme involving the purchase of medical equipment, in which Bogomolets National Medical University figures
Kyiv • UNN
The ESBU is investigating possible overpricing of medical equipment for the National Medical University and hospitals. According to the investigation, losses to the budget amounted to UAH 5.6 million.
The embezzlement of budget funds in the procurement of medical equipment involving Bogomolets National Medical University is being investigated by the Territorial Office of the Economic Security Bureau in Vinnytsia region, reports UNN.
The investigation began at the beginning of 2025. It concerns the procurement of medical equipment manufactured by Karl Storz. According to the investigators, the prices specified in the tender documentation were artificially inflated. Bogomolets National Medical University is among the customers of the equipment.
Criminal proceedings were initiated under Parts 4 and 5 of Article 191 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — misappropriation, embezzlement, or seizure of property through abuse of official position, including on an especially large scale.
According to the detectives, the scheme was organized by officials of Karl Storz Ukraine LLC — the official and sole distributor in Ukraine of products manufactured by the German company KARL STORZ SE & Co. KG. The aim, investigators allege, was to embezzle budget funds allocated for expensive medical equipment and consumables.
Apparently, the first episode in the case was the investigation into embezzlement at the Podilsk Oncology Center. Subsequently, investigators uncovered an entire network of dealers who, according to law enforcement officials, acted under the control of Karl Storz Ukraine. These included Livin, Medprovider, Ksenko, and Yasmed. In addition to the Podilsk Oncology Center, they entered into agreements with the Sumy Regional Oncology Center, the Zhytomyr Regional Hospital, the Ladyzhyn City Hospital, and Bogomolets National Medical University.
The investigation established that between June and December 2024, the budget suffered losses totaling UAH 5.6 million as a result of artificially inflating equipment prices and creating discriminatory conditions for participation in tenders.
According to a court ruling, in April 2024 the medical university signed a contract worth more than UAH 4 million with Ksenko LLC. According to the investigators, before the procurement was announced, the head of NMU (the surname is not given in the publicly available court ruling, but it likely refers to the university's rector, Yuriy Kuchyn) allegedly discussed its specifications with a representative of Karl Storz Ukraine. Among the items seized from the distributor during the investigation were four Ksenko payment instructions from 2024.
Apparently, this concerns a tender for the procurement of equipment for operating units (a set for ENT surgical procedures, not containing medicinal products and intended for repeated use), in which the aforementioned company Ksenko was the sole participant.
The court rulings contain information about the mechanism used by the participants in the scheme: first, representatives of Karl Storz Ukraine and representatives of the customer institutions coordinated the tender and the specifications of the procurement item. The procurement customers then “tailored” the technical requirements to a specific manufacturer, narrowing the range of participants and making it possible to artificially inflate the price. Under such conditions, victory in the tender for “their participants” became guaranteed. Subsequently, according to the investigators, a “kickback” amounting to 5–10% was transferred to controlled charitable foundations. The detectives believe that the participants in the scheme withdrew the remaining unlawfully obtained funds in cash from bank tellers and handed them over to representatives of Karl Storz Ukraine and the customers during personal meetings.
Interestingly, after the aforementioned tender worth more than UAH 4 million, NMU concluded four more agreements with Ksenko worth a total of more than UAH 2 million. Also, in April 2024, the university signed an agreement with another company from among the dealers listed above — Livin LLC — to procure a steam sterilizer and operating lights worth more than UAH 2.5 million. Livin was the sole participant in the tender. According to our information, these agreements do not appear in the Eсonomic Security Bureau's criminal proceedings.
We remind you
The State Audit Service began monitoring two procurements by Bogomolets National Medical University due to possible violations.
It concerns the renovation of two university dormitories in the capital. Journalists’ investigation indicates a possible overpricing of construction materials.

Ex-UN director who protested Gaza famine challenges his dismissal
A former senior UN food agency official has said he has launched an appeal against his dismissal, alleging it was motivated by his stance on Israel imposing hunger on Gaza, in a case that has exposed tensions within the Rome-based organisation.
Benjamin Davis, 62, a Spanish American director at the Food and Agriculture Organisation, was informed his employment would end on 30 September at the request of Director-General Qu Dongyu, according to documents seen by Reuters.
The papers cited breaches of international civil service standards which require staff to act with impartiality. Davis rejected the allegation.
"I feel it’s a terrible injustice. I’ve been disciplined without due process for speaking up about a subject at the core of FAO’s mandate about the right to food which is the most basic of human rights," he told Reuters. He said he had filed an appeal.
The FAO did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Davis' allegations or on the grounds for his dismissal.
Davis, said he had worked at the FAO for 26 years on a renewable contract, and that his dismissal was linked to staff activism against Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
He was one of hundreds of employees who have joined moments of silence for hunger victims in Gaza where an international hunger-monitoring system used by UN agencies determined famine in August 2025.
He also authored a report on food availability in the Palestinian enclave in May 2025.
The dispute burst into public view this week when Qu, speaking at a FAO conference, defended the dismissal of an unnamed staff member whom he accused of having "played the political game".
"We will not allow you to play the game here of human rights," Qu said.
Debate over staff activism
The remarks prompted fresh debate about whether UN employees are able to express views on humanitarian crises without jeopardising their careers.
A large crowd of staff gathered at FAO headquarters in Rome on Wednesday to applaud Davis as he departed, according to UN officials and video seen by Reuters.
Under UN rules, staff are allowed to express political opinions but must ensure these do not adversely affect their official duties or UN interests.
Davis, who was head of the Rural Transformation and Gender Equality Division, said he was concerned that other employees would face retaliation over their participation in the Gaza moments of silence.
The case, now with the FAO's internal justice process, could later be escalated to a UN tribunal which has the authority to award damages in employment disputes.

Ukraine aims to produce up to 400 interceptor drones as Russian jet-powered drone use grows, Zelensky says

Ukraine aims to produce up to 400 interceptor drones as Russian jet-powered drone use grows, Zelensky says
Ukraine will be able to produce up to 400 interceptor drones by the end of October to counter Russia's growing use of jet-powered attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2.
As Russia scales up production of its jet-powered drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5 — Ukraine is struggling to shoot them down amid the hours-long attacks.
Russia launched around 500 drones against Ukraine over the past day, about half of which were jet-powered and significantly harder to intercept, Zelensky said.
Only 57% of jet-powered versions of Shahed-type drones are currently shot down by Ukraine, Zelensky said in his evening address on Sept. 28, a figure he described as "much less than necessary."
According to Zelensky, Ukraine is testing five types of high-speed interceptor drones designed to counter Russian weapons. One of the models is expected to reach production of around 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remain in the testing stage.
The development of the interceptors is being slowed by a shortage of engines. Ukraine imports most of the engines used for the drones, while domestic production remains insufficient, Zelensky said.
Russia's jet-powered drones target civilian infrastructure such as supermarkets, schools, shopping malls, telecommunications infrastructure, data centers, gas stations, and medical facilities.
Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones while launching attacks on Kyiv in recent months. The onslaught began last month but has intensified over the past week.
Zelensky also said in the interview that Ukraine is unable to use all of its F-16 fighter jets during Russian attacks because around half of the aircraft are undergoing scheduled maintenance and repairs in Europe.
F-16s, which Ukraine first received in the summer of 2024, are used in both offensive and defensive operations. The aircraft have been used to intercept Russian missiles and drones during aerial attacks on Ukraine. They could also be deployed to launch missiles and bombs against Russian positions along the front line.
The lengthy maintenance periods leave some aircraft unavailable when they are particularly needed for air defense. Kyiv wants to move some F-16 maintenance work to Ukraine to allow the jets to return to service faster.
Zelensky also said Ukraine faces a budget shortfall that is limiting the development and mass production of critical defensive weapons.

Barry the St Bernard, the national animal of Switzerland?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Barry the St Bernard, the national animal of Switzerland?
Switzerland hasn’t got a national animal, but if it did, there’s a good case to be made for Barry, a much-loved barrel-wearing St Bernard who died more than 200 years ago and is stuffed and on display in Bern.
Barry saved 40 lives as a mountain rescue dog on the border with Italy in southwestern Switzerland, including a half-frozen boy whom he flipped onto his back and carried to safety. Barry was eventually bayonetted to death by one of Napoleon’s soldiers who mistook him for a wolf.
Well, he might have saved 40 lives – the rest is a shaggy dog story. “The truth is that not even the cleverest or strongest of dogs would be capable of such a feat,” admits Bern’s Natural History Museum, which has a permanent exhibitionExternal link devoted to Barry, regarding the child-saving. And as for his dramatic death, “while it’s true that a few isolated wolves lived on the pass at this time, and that Napoleon crossed it in May 1800 with around 46,000 soldiers, Barry wasn’t actually born until that same year”.
“When you’re a saint or someone very famous, your death has to be something special too – you can’t just die in your bed!” Marc Nussbaumer, an archaeozoologist and scientific advisor at Bern Natural History Museum, told Swissinfo at the exhibition’s opening in 2014.
Which, in reality, is what Barry did in Bern in 1814, having been brought down – old and tired – from the Great St Bernard HospiceExternal link on the Swiss-Italian border two years earlier.
Quite why a monastery servant brought the 12-year-old dog to Bern is a mystery. Possibly he was to have an educational role, advertising the work of the Augustinian canons up at the hospice.
Indeed, when Barry died, it seems he was already well known. In 1816, Friedrich Meisner, a professor of natural history in Bern, wrote: “I find it pleasant and also comforting to think that this faithful dog, who saved the lives of so many people, will not be quickly forgotten after his death!”
Barry’s first appearance on the big screen was in the French melodrama Barry in 1949 (producers might have noted that Lassie had recently appeared in several Hollywood hits). According to this summaryExternal link, “a young woman is rescued at the St Bernard Pass. As a result, she is reunited with the man to whom she was once engaged. Now she must choose between two men. Barry, the avalanche dog, plays a fateful role in this regional romance”. Sure enough, Barry saves a child.
In 1977, Disney produced a two-part television film, Barry of the Great St. BernardExternal link. Shot largely on location in the Swiss Alps, the film follows an orphan at the hospice who trains a St Bernard pup to become a rescue dog. The film goes big on monastic life in the hospice, but dog fans won’t be disappointed – Barry saves a child.
In January 2026, Mein Freund BarryExternal link (Barry & Me) reached Swiss and German cinemas. If you liked Heidi and Schellen-Ursli, you’ll probably like this: gloriously shot Alpine landscapes and cute orphans (and puppies). I haven’t seen it, so I can’t say whether Barry saves a child, but I wouldn’t bet against it.
‘Ambassador for Switzerland’
The Great St Bernard Hospice is located at nearly 2,500 metres above sea level on the treacherous Great St Bernard Pass, which connects Martigny in canton Valais, southwestern Switzerland, to Aosta in Italy. It has provided food and shelter for travellers for almost 1,000 years.
While the canons would spend their days and nights praying and looking after guests, local guides would patrol the paths helping anyone who had got into trouble. In the mid-17th century, these guides started taking strong farm dogs of all breeds with them – including a young Barry. The hospice and its dogs are estimated to have saved more than 2,000 lives over the years.
“The canons’ rescue dogs were not like modern avalanche dogs,” the Natural History Museum explains. “Their main role was to find the way back to the hospice in heavy blizzards. Barry was almost certainly an extraordinary dog, or he wouldn’t have been famous even before his death. However, many of the legends which surround Barry are not based in fact.”
This was not a problem for Michael Keller, in 2014 the vice-director of Bern Tourism. “His story is still great – running around the mountains saving people. He’s giving hope to everybody, and I think it’s this combination that makes Barry, even today, a good ambassador for Switzerland,” he told Swissinfo.
Keller said Barry remained very popular, especially in Asia. “A lot of Japanese people come to Bern. They don’t know much about Bern, but they know about the bears and Barry – they always ask where they can find Barry.”
Noble and heroic
The answer is in Bern’s Natural History Museum, where a multimedia, interactive exhibition includes Barry himself – or at least his fur.
“Barry – the legendary St Bernard” is a permanent exhibition at Bern Natural History Museum which opened in June 2014, 200 years after his death.
Previously Barry had been squeezed between the men’s and ladies’ lavatories near the museum entrance.
The multimedia, interactive exhibition not only explains the story of Barry but also looks at the Great St Bernard Hospice and the monks who lived there and compares mountain rescue of 200 years ago with that of today.
It is aimed at an international audience of all ages. Information signs are in German and English.
You don’t have to be a Crufts judge to notice that Barry bears little resemblance to the hulking St Bernards that we know today. Looking at him in his golden shrine-like display, you can’t help noticing that he looks more like an athletic Labrador.
The canons in the hospice didn’t care what the dogs looked like, as long as they could do the job. But when pedigree breeding took off at the end of the 19th century, appearance was everything and, when it came to St Bernards, bigger was better.
As a result, in 1923 Barry’s stuffed body was modified because it no longer conformed to the public’s expectation of the breed (Barry weighed 40-45kg whereas modern St Bernards can be double that). His head was made bigger – the original skull is shown in a separate case – and his legs were stretched by about 10cm (look closely and you can see the difference in fur colour and texture). In addition, his head was raised, to “correct” the previously submissive stance and make him appear more noble and heroic.
More
The Swiss dog that conquers hearts
A dedicated theme park
The exhibition is well worth a look, but there’s one place that Barryphiles really can’t miss: Barryland!
The Barryland Theme ParkExternal link in Martigny, funded by the Barry FoundationExternal link, offers “an immersive experience entirely dedicated to St Bernard dogs”. For example, what would happen if you became a St Bernard? The “Sensorama” lets you see, hear and sniff like a dog. You can also watch the dogs have their daily meal (and learn about their diet) and see them enjoy grooming and hydrotherapy sessions. Summer hikesExternal link or winter strolls, accompanied by two or three dogs, are also available.
The Barry Foundation, the organisation responsible for breeding the dogs from the Great St Bernard Pass, currently has 32 St Bernards (one of whom is always called Barry). An average of 20 puppies are born a year at the Barry Foundation and most are sold – at CHF2,800 ($3,500) a pop/pup (if certain conditions are met).
If you weren’t planning on returning home with a puppy, the Barry Shop has something for all tastes and budgets: how about some Barry schnapps glasses? Or a Barry biscuit set? Or a Barry reversible neck warmer?
Barryland opened in August 2025 in the presence of Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter, who held the rotating Swiss presidency at the time and is godmother to a St Bernard, Zeus.
Keller-Sutter was visibly moved. “Even today, the name Barry stands for courage and heroic deeds,” she said. “Through this, Barryland honours an entire Swiss tradition.”

Inglourious subtitlers and the art of cinematic transcreators
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

Inglourious subtitlers and the art of cinematic transcreators
Often criticised but rarely appreciated, subtitles have been essential to global cinema for nearly a century. The head of the Swiss Film Archives, Vinzenz Hediger, explains why, in multilingual Switzerland, they are also a vital part of film history.
When Sony Pictures distributed Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon in theatres in the United States in 2000, they came up with a clever trick in order to get people into cinemas to watch a foreign film in a foreign language. The trailer External linkportrayed no scenes with Mandarin dialogue, relying instead on an English voice-over to narrate the synopsis.
Subtitled films represent between 1.1% and 2% of the box office in the US; in the European Union, roughly 53% of theatrical releases are shown exclusively dubbed, 29% in both dubbed and subtitled formats, and a smaller minority rely strictly on original-language subtitles. Yet Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon remains the highest-grossing non-English film in the US.
The film’s success proves that translation can redefine a movie’s global reach, making subtitles essential – if often overlooked – components of the cinematic experience. Today, in this extremely globalised era in which we can access films from every corner of the world thanks to subtitling, subtitles become increasingly crucial yet remain largely invisible.
But the translator is “also doing a creative act”, Vinzenz Hediger, head of the Swiss Film Archives (Cinémathèque Suisse) tells Swissinfo. He discusses how translation plays a role in the archival world, specifically in the Swiss context. For him, “the concept of transcreation” demands a lot of creativity from the translator to make possible for a film “to live in a different linguistic environment”.
Subtitles or dubbing, that is the question
Up until the talkies – from the late 19th century until the late 1920s – films provided our world with the promise of a universal language. In the silent film era, intertitles (a piece of printed or hand-lettered text edited into the middle of a silent film to show dialogue, narration or story details) were easily swapped for other versions and the moving image allowed for common ground across languages.
However, when sound appeared at the end of the 1920s, so came the subtitles: although it still used intertitles for dialogue, The Jazz Singer (1929) was the first film to be subtitled. Meanwhile, Hollywood poured funds into what they called multiple-language versions of the same film. This involved using the same set and crew, but different actors in order to film simultaneously various versions. During the 1930s, both subtitling and dubbing were developed simultaneously.
Meanwhile in Europe, countries generally split into two camps: subtitling foreign films or dubbing them into the local language. Switzerland, considering its linguistic diversity, opted for subtitling, both for “historical reasons that date back to the 1930s, but also for simply economic reasons”, Hediger says.
According to him, subtitled versions remain the preferred choice for moviegoers in Zurich and Lausanne, even for commercial releases, reflecting a continuity with the policies adopted nearly a century ago when talkies first emerged. Interestingly, research shows External linkthat prioritising subtitled content has contributed to higher English proficiency in countries like Switzerland, Portugal, and Norway.
More
Schiff ahoy! Why dubbed films are making waves
The figure of the translator has always been rendered invisible. This plight is now being accelerated by the rise of streaming platforms and artificial intelligence (AI). Yet these ghosts still haunt our film prints and digital streams as much as they do our books.
Since the early days of cinema, credit has rarely gone to those who enabled international audiences to understand one another; studios simply bought translations outright without granting copyright or screen credits. To this day, many countries still refuse copyright protections to subtitlers. Streaming giants and VOD platforms External linkhave pushed this dynamic even further by bringing subtitling entirely in-house and leaning heavily into machine translation and AI automation, the human author is being erased faster than ever.
Compare that to dubbing, where recognition is built into the craft: specific voice actors become tied to Hollywood legends. Rosa Guiñón became the definitive voice of Meryl Streep in Spain and Philippe Peythieu plays the iconic French Homer Simpson. Subtitlers, meanwhile, remain cinema’s ghostwriters.
As Hediger puts it, “translation work is the most thankless intellectual endeavour that you can think of”. There are no notorious subtitlers. While some actors know the names of their foreign dubbers, most filmmakers don’t bother to know the names of those who subtitle their films.
Swiss Babel on the screen
Navigating film distribution in Switzerland means tackling a uniquely complex, multilingual terrain. Here, every film must cater to distinct French- and German-speaking audiences, while carefully balancing separate strategies for the smaller Italian-speaking market: translation isn’t just an afterthought; it’s a non-negotiable commercial necessity.
This intricate balancing act is preserved in the archives of the Cinémathèque Suisse, home to one of the richest film collections in the world. As Hediger explains, “that has everything to do with the fact that the people who ran the Cinémathèque early on struck a deal with distributor in Switzerland: once a film had run its commercial course, the distributors would deposit all prints in the Cinémathèque, which would keep the best five or eight”.
As a result, virtually everything screened in Switzerland since 1952 has been safeguarded alongside its corresponding French and German subtitles. For the Italian-speaking market, distributors often imported Italian prints that were already either dubbed or subtitled.
Yet localising cinema across Switzerland goes far beyond standard language barriers. Hediger emphasises that language is deeply situated: “dialects are always regionally specific, but in Switzerland, if you grow up as a Swiss German native speaker, you will be able to place people by about 30 kilometres if you hear them speak”. Capturing these accents and social nuances on screen is a delicate task for any translator, and virtually impossible to fully convey within the constraints of a subtitle line.
What actually gets found in translation?
When people talk about subtitles, the feedback is usually limited to whether they are “bad”. The audience tends to dwell on what’s lost in translation rather than seeing subtitling as a key part of the creative process, even if that connection seems obvious once we think about it.
Digging deeper into the conversation surrounding translation, Hediger refers to transcreation, which is when translation doesn’t choose the literal path but, rather, a more tonal and emotional approach. As such, we can acknowledge not what is “lost” in the meaning through the process of translation, but actually what is transformed.
Perhaps what does fall short in subtitling films are the nuances found in each language or dialect that is spoken. Films are situated, so are the languages we speak. Hediger shares a recent experience where they screened a Nigerian film in the Hausa language which will soon be restored by the Cinémathèque Suisse “in the presence of a room full of Hausa native speakers”. He describes the experience as “totally unfair because they were laughing through half of the film while I sat there, wondering what the hell was going on? What are we missing?”
In this way, subtitles can oftentimes feel like a “crutch” simply allowing us to follow along the best we can. On the other hand, we’re unable to grasp the nuances of the spoken dialogue when we are reading a text on the screen, especially if we are completely foreign to that culture.
When visiting Cairo and watching local films without translation, Hediger and his wife found themselves piecing together the plot like solving a riddle, an experience he found deeply “intellectually stimulating”. This exercise echoes Henri Langlois’ provocative belief that it’s best to watch foreign films without any subtitles at all.
Subtitles are often treated as invisible bridges, but theoretically, they also function as unique historical markers. Looking at archived prints, a subtitle track offers tangible proof of how a work crossed borders at a particular time. It reflects the linguistic nuances, ideological choices and technical standards of its era, making the translation inseparable from the film’s archival identity.
This theoretical dimension comes into sharp relief when looking at specialised collections like the Arsenal Filminstitut in Berlin. Originally founded to spotlight alternative and emerging cinema, the institute has maintained a practice since the 1970s of retaining every film screened in its Forum programme as a subtitled print.
In discussion with Hediger about international archival practices, he points out a striking reality: for many of these works, the Arsenal’s subtitled copy is the only surviving print in existence. The act of translation, initially meant just for a local screening, ultimately doubled as an act of absolute preservation.
