Media reveal information about Russian who may have organised sabotage at Leipzig airport
Russian biker Oleg Lyovushkin, who is linked to a Russian military intelligence officer, may have organised an attempted sabotage at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany.
Source: a joint investigation by The Telegraph and Welt am Sonntag, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to the investigation, Lyovushkin presumably organised the attempt to plant explosives at the airport. German investigators believe that Belarusian intermediary agent Andrei Karshakov was supposed to carry out the plan.
Journalists analysed intelligence documents from Germany, Lithuania, and Poland, and also spoke with representatives of Western secret services. According to their data, Lyovushkin and Karshakov arrived in Germany to carry out the sabotage operation.
German investigators suspect that Lyovushkin conducted reconnaissance of the airport shortly before the attack, after which he instructed Karshakov to execute the plan.
Investigators also found similarities between the incident in Leipzig and other attempted Russian sabotage operations in Poland, Lithuania, and Germany.
Specifically, the explosive device seized in Leipzig was reportedly similar to devices used in other sabotage operations in Europe.
Lyovushkin, who holds a Russian passport and is an avid motorcyclist, is also linked to Denis Smolyaninov, a man Western secret services consider to be one of the coordinators of Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
According to Lithuanian intelligence, Smolyaninov headed the Ukrainian desk in Russian military intelligence and specialised in psychological operations, among other things. Documents also link him to secret sabotage campaigns in Europe.
It is noted that Lyovushkin and Smolyaninov met back in 2007. Reportedly, they have kin repeated contact over the many years.
German security agencies link the Leipzig attack to GRU Unit 29155, which, according to German intelligence assessments, plays a key role in Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
German security agencies assess that the goal of such operations could be to create a sense of insecurity among European society due to its support for Ukraine and to influence the debate on further assistance to Kyiv.
Lyovushkin himself publicly leads an inconspicuous life. He takes part in motorcycle races, travels around Europe, fishes, and skis with his family.
At the same time, journalists claim that this lifestyle may conceal his involvement in Russian sabotage operations in Central Europe.
According to German intelligence, he travelled to Germany via Türkiye this summer to prepare an attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. Investigators stated that Lyovushkin rented a car at Berlin airport a week before the attack and over the next few days drove it to several locations where weapons were suspected of being stored.
They believe that the explosives used in the operation were transported to Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia, hidden in the cavities of trucks, and were likely temporarily stored along the route.
The journalists say that Lyovushkin's links to the GRU were known at the time he entered the country. However, he was not placed under surveillance upon his arrival.
Background:
- On 1 September, Germany directly accused Russia of a hybrid attack at Leipzig airport in early August and announced countermeasures.
- On 6 September, it was reported that German Interior Minister Nancy Faeser was planning a set of measures to cover protection against drones, sabotage of critical infrastructure, and cyberattacks, as well as the detection of spies and potential terrorists.

Ethiopian forces near Tigray capital, fears grow of wider conflict
Oct 2 - Ethiopian government forces closed in on the capital of the northern rebel stronghold of Tigray on Friday, residents and a diplomat said, as fears grew that fighting could spill into a wider war after Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties.
Banks and shops in the city, Mekelle, were closed with the Ethiopian National Defence Force and allied militiamen reported to be within striking distance, two residents, who asked not to be named for security reasons, told Reuters.
Pro-government forces have made quick advances into Tigray since combat erupted last week with a rebel alliance led by the region's ruling party, the Tigray People's Liberation Front, in the worst escalation of violence since a 2020-2022 civil war.
But suspected drone attacks on the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, earlier this week suggested the TPLF and its allies might have better striking capability than previously thought.
Spokespeople for Ethiopia's military and government did not respond to requests for comment on the reported advance or suspected attacks on Addis Ababa.
ETHIOPIA CLOSES EMBASSY IN ERITREA
Analysts fear the current conflict could spread beyond Ethiopia's borders in an increasingly fragile territory where regional powers are competing for influence. Tigray has Ethiopia's longtime foe Eritrea to its north, and Sudan — caught up in a more than three-year-old civil war — to its west.
Ethiopia's government has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting the opposition alliance - an allegation they have all denied.
On Thursday, Ethiopia said it was closing its embassy in Eritrea "in response to Eritrea's direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence" and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave Ethiopia within 48 hours.
Eritrea responded by severing all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia. The two countries fought a border war from 1998-2000 and only restored diplomatic relations in 2018.
Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopia's federal government against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war, in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed. Relations have since soured, in part over landlocked Ethiopia's public insistence that sea access is vital for its security and economy.
Eritrea says it fears Ethiopia will try to take its Assab port by force. Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has said Ethiopia intends to secure sea access through peaceful means.
TPLF THREATENS COUNTER-ATTACK
The federal forces and allied militiamen captured a town about 75 km (50 miles) south of Mekelle, the pro-government Tigray Peace Forces militia said on Thursday. One of the Mekelle residents said they were now within 30 km.
TPLF chairperson Debretsion Gebremichael acknowledged on Thursday that federal forces had occupied some parts of the region but said his forces would counter-attack "in due course".
"We should ensure that Tigray is their graveyard, not their playground," he said in a statement.
On Thursday, Ethiopia's foreign ministry also expelled an Egyptian diplomat, prompting Cairo to respond in kind by expelling an Ethiopian embassy counsellor.
In a statement, the African Union Commission urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise "maximum restraint".
EXPLOSIONS HEARD IN ETHIOPIAN CAPITAL
Ahead of the latest fighting, the TPLF formed an alliance with six other Ethiopian armed groups that say they aim to overthrow Abiy's government.
While the TPLF and allied fighters made some initial gains in the neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions, pro-government forces say those have been largely reversed.
Explosions were heard late Wednesday night in Addis Ababa, in what a source linked to the opposition alliance said were drone attacks targeting the ENDF headquarters there and other sites.
Reuters could not independently verify this.
If confirmed, it would be the first known drone attack by anti-government forces on Addis Ababa, which is hundreds of kilometres from the northern front lines. REUTERS

Ethiopian forces near Tigray capital, fears grow of wider conflict
Oct 2 - Ethiopian government forces closed in on the capital of the northern rebel stronghold of Tigray on Friday, residents and a diplomat said, as fears grew that fighting could spill into a wider war after Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties.
Banks and shops in the city, Mekelle, were closed with the Ethiopian National Defence Force and allied militiamen reported to be within striking distance, two residents, who asked not to be named for security reasons, told Reuters.
Pro-government forces have made quick advances into Tigray since combat erupted last week with a rebel alliance led by the region's ruling party, the Tigray People's Liberation Front, in the worst escalation of violence since a 2020-2022 civil war.
But suspected drone attacks on the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, earlier this week suggested the TPLF and its allies might have better striking capability than previously thought.
Spokespeople for Ethiopia's military and government did not respond to requests for comment on the reported advance or suspected attacks on Addis Ababa.
ETHIOPIA CLOSES EMBASSY IN ERITREA
Analysts fear the current conflict could spread beyond Ethiopia's borders in an increasingly fragile territory where regional powers are competing for influence. Tigray has Ethiopia's longtime foe Eritrea to its north, and Sudan — caught up in a more than three-year-old civil war — to its west.
Ethiopia's government has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting the opposition alliance - an allegation they have all denied.
On Thursday, Ethiopia said it was closing its embassy in Eritrea "in response to Eritrea's direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence" and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave Ethiopia within 48 hours.
Eritrea responded by severing all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia. The two countries fought a border war from 1998-2000 and only restored diplomatic relations in 2018.
Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopia's federal government against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war, in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed. Relations have since soured, in part over landlocked Ethiopia's public insistence that sea access is vital for its security and economy.
Eritrea says it fears Ethiopia will try to take its Assab port by force. Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has said Ethiopia intends to secure sea access through peaceful means.
TPLF THREATENS COUNTER-ATTACK
The federal forces and allied militiamen captured a town about 75 km (50 miles) south of Mekelle, the pro-government Tigray Peace Forces militia said on Thursday. One of the Mekelle residents said they were now within 30 km.
TPLF chairperson Debretsion Gebremichael acknowledged on Thursday that federal forces had occupied some parts of the region but said his forces would counter-attack "in due course".
"We should ensure that Tigray is their graveyard, not their playground," he said in a statement.
On Thursday, Ethiopia's foreign ministry also expelled an Egyptian diplomat, prompting Cairo to respond in kind by expelling an Ethiopian embassy counsellor.
In a statement, the African Union Commission urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise "maximum restraint".
EXPLOSIONS HEARD IN ETHIOPIAN CAPITAL
Ahead of the latest fighting, the TPLF formed an alliance with six other Ethiopian armed groups that say they aim to overthrow Abiy's government.
While the TPLF and allied fighters made some initial gains in the neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions, pro-government forces say those have been largely reversed.
Explosions were heard late Wednesday night in Addis Ababa, in what a source linked to the opposition alliance said were drone attacks targeting the ENDF headquarters there and other sites.
Reuters could not independently verify this.
If confirmed, it would be the first known drone attack by anti-government forces on Addis Ababa, which is hundreds of kilometres from the northern front lines. REUTERS

Russian GDP to grow by 1.4% in 2027 — Novak

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Russian GDP is anticipated to grow by 1.4% next year and reach the growth rate of 2.4% in 2029, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said at the plenary session of the Federation Council, the upper house of the Russian legislative assembly.
"Concerning the forecast indicators, the gross domestic product is expected to grow by 1.4% in 2027 and subsequently reach 2.4% in 2029," Novak said.
Inflation in Russia may total 6.8% as of the end of this year, the deputy prime minister noted.
"Concerning inflation, it totaled 4.93% year-to-date. In annual terms, growth is 6.26% as of the end of September, we forecast 6.8% by the end of the year," Novak said.
The unemployment in Russia is at a historically low level and stands at 2.2%, the official stressed.

Taiwan franchise association calls for 5% migrant workers in service sector

21:08:05 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The government should allow businesses in the service sector to employ up to 5% migrant workers, the Taiwan Chain Stores and Franchise Association said Friday.
Since the sector is still struggling with personnel shortages, foreign nationals should be allowed to work in services, said the association chair and MedFirst Healthcare Services CEO Tsai Te-chung (蔡德忠). He also called for a relaxation of the two-year maximum limit on work without a work permit for overseas graduates, per Liberty Times.
A July-August survey of the chain store and franchising sector found that 98.8% of businesses are dealing with staffing shortages. For more than half the companies, the situation has been ongoing for at least a year, the association said.
Tsai said that while the hotel sector had been allowed to start recruiting overseas workers, there is still a ban in place for retail and restaurants. Change could start gradually, with at first a limit at 5% of total staff, he said.

My Word: The art of resilience - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:06:59 UTC
21:06:59 KST

If the proverbial picture is worth a thousand words, the Jerusalem Biennale 2026 has too many words to count – many of them prayers, pleas, and thanksgiving.
This is the seventh Jerusalem Biennale since it was founded in 2013, and like its predecessors, it is dedicated to a theme, but individual artists have been literally creative in the way they chose to interpret it.
Jerusalem Biennale founder Ram Ozeri told a press tour last week that he chose the theme “De Profundis,” “Out of the Depths,” or “Mima’amakim” in Hebrew, after the opening words of Psalm 130: “Out of the depths I call You, O Lord.”
It was the psalm many Jewish communities added to their prayers following the horrors of October 7, 2023, the war, and especially the fate of the hostages held in Gaza. Even now, a year after the last living captives returned home, the Hamas-led invasion and mega-atrocity of October 7, when 1,200 were murdered and 251 abducted, continues to haunt us.
Ozeri noted that choosing the Latin “De Profundis” was based on a large bank of works, including the letter by Oscar Wilde in Reading Gaol with the oh-so-quotable: “Where there is sorrow there is holy ground.” Ozeri sees art as a form of prayer, and also as a part of the recovery and healing process – a way of bringing the collective subconscious to the surface.
Displaying works of more than 250 Israeli and international artists in 42 exhibitions across 21 venues throughout the capital, JB2026, running through November 12, is the biggest yet, but was one of the most challenging to assemble.
The Jerusalem Biennale was created to give space to contemporary art, beyond Judaica, mixing with the Jewish and Israeli experience, although not all the artists are Jewish. Despite its starting point in the depths, there is also optimism in JB2026, which Ozeri sees as “creating a dialogue among different communities… celebrating Jewishness rather than hiding it.”
While some artists abroad were afraid of a possible backlash for participating in the event in Israel, others were delighted at the chance to push back against the cultural boycott.
The press tour took place at the Biennale’s main venue at the former National Library at the Hebrew University’s Givat Ram campus. It was a chance to remember the charm of the old building that has been overshadowed since the opening of the new National Library, a nearby architectural gem.
Undoubtedly, the outstanding feature of the building itself is the monumental stained-glass windows created by Mordecai Ardon, three immense panels reflecting Isaiah’s “Vision of Eternal Peace.” Dr. David Sperber and artist Porat Salomon, the curators of the Or Chozer (Reflected Light): An Active Vision exhibition, made good use of Ardon’s work as an impressive backdrop.
Art to bring us out of the depths
There was too much to relate to everything within the constraints of this column, but some sights and insights made a particular impact.
In a combination-confrontation between the old and the new, Isaiah’s Still Waiting, by Andi LaVine Arnovitz, is composed of mounted old-fashioned View-Masters, the black-and-white scenes of the wheel changing with every click of the device, using the light of the windows.
Close to Ardon’s panel depicting the swords turned into plowshares are powerful works by Swiss-born Jerusalem artist Ariane Littman. One component is an “incantation bowl,” reminiscent of the ancient amulets often buried under the entrance to a home as a form of magical protection.
Littman’s bowl is covered with the date 7.10.23, written in spiraling form in red ink. It was the first work she was able to produce, a month and a half after the attack, and she describes it as “a counter-curse of that horrific day.” Next to it, Littman, who works a lot with gauze, has “blood-soaked” (red ink) bandages hanging from meat hooks in a work called “Sanguine Fields.”
Richard McBee has completed 100 paintings in 35 years based on the biblical figures of Abraham and Isaac, and God’s command to the father to sacrifice his son. McBee told the journalists: “After the Holocaust, we Jews are all Isaac,” even more so after October 7, when “the modern world turned its back on Israel.”
The six paintings on display start with the question: “Where is the lamb?” and Abraham’s reply: “God will provide,” and ends with Isaac abandoned, alone, on the mountaintop after the intervention of the angel and the sacrifice of a ram instead. I was struck by the extent to which the “Akeida” was a test of Isaac no less than Abraham.
The One Who Dwells in This House, curated by Shoshana Gugenheim Kedem and Ahuva S. Zaslavsky, is described “as a visual commentary on what it means to grieve, to be marginalized, vulnerable, witnessed, and to return again.”
The curators told the press tour how their Portland, Oregon Jewish community – known for its progressive politics – suffered painful fissures following October 7, like many similar Diaspora communities. A group of local artists grappled with these issues through their Art Lab.
Zaslavsky’s To Move a Mountain II is a work in slow motion. Visitors are invited to scoop soil from a central pile into small linen bags in something that feels like a reverse burial service, while Gugenheim Kedem contemplates loss and grief through works based on burial shrouds.
Abraham’s Children, by artist Mel Brown and curator Ori Z. Soltes, broadens the dialogue even further. Brown described the dilemmas of being a Torah-observant Jew who started working as an artist at a relatively late stage in life. Acutely aware of the Second Commandment not to make a graven image, he produces abstract works on biblical themes.
Together with Soltes’s input, the exhibition extends to include, among others, Muslim artists – including a Turkish father and son in exile, and a painter from the United Arab Emirates. Unlike Christian art, which readily depicts human forms, Muslim and Jewish art have traditionally been non-representational. The result is a reminder of what we have in common.
Czech photographer David Tesinsky, who is not Jewish, said he wasn’t bothered by negative comments and the small number of followers who dropped from his Instagram account. He has seen it in other places he has visited, including Russia, Ukraine, Iran, and Pakistan.
Tesinsky captures street scenes with his camera, and Jerusalemite visitors will recognize places he visited in the capital – including Mahaneh Yehuda, Mea She’arim, and downtown Jerusalem –as part of his The Light Within series.
American artist Rina Nissel Shalhov provides a positive note in her acrylic work, A Sabra is Born. Shalhov, who is married to an Israeli, explained that the desert fruit has become “a symbol of the national pride and patriotism of the Jewish state. The sabra cactus faces tremendous challenges as it struggles to survive in a hostile environment…
“After years of dormancy, the cactus blooms, producing vibrant flowers that eventually transform into bright, vivid fruit. Upon closer inspection, the thick outer skin is covered in prickly bumps and more barbed needles. Only those patient enough to carefully peel back the tough layers will discover the sweetness and complexity hidden within.”
The metaphor is as clear as the blue desert sky above the “prickly fruit” in her painting.
Coming out of the depths, the sky is not the limit: Mexican artist Alejandro Glatt makes a truly uplifting contribution to this year’s Jerusalem Biennale in his Mezuzah to the Moon exhibition. Glatt is as colorful as his artwork and proud of both elements of his Mexican-Jewish identity.
In 2024, a representation of one of his papaya works landed on the moon as part of the Lunaprise mission. Now he aims to similarly elevate one of his striking mezuzot in some form. I can imagine a UN debate on “Jewish colonization” when news of a mezuzah landing on the moon gets out, but as this Biennale proves, the fear of antisemitism should not leave us grounded.
Navigating around Jerusalem at a time of massive construction can feel as challenging as space travel (although Mayor Moshe Lion is credited with helping make this year’s Biennale possible), but planning visits to the multiple venues is a reminder of Jerusalem’s special cultural map.
We have come out of the depths, bearing the scars both physical and emotional, but Glatt’s vision of Jewish art one day landing on the moon left me raising my eyes to the heavens with a sense of hope.

AI, fraud, and cyberattacks: What security threats face Israel’s 2026 election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:06:59 UTC
21:06:59 KST

Israel’s elections may increasingly be surrounded by artificial intelligence, deepfakes, and online disinformation, but the actual process of casting and counting a ballot remains strikingly old-fashioned.
That is intentional, according to attorney Dean Livne, acting director general of Israel’s Central Elections Committee.
As the country prepares for the 2026 election, the CEC is confronting technologies that were not part of the electoral landscape when Israelis last went to the polls in November 2022.
Generative AI has advanced rapidly since then, creating new opportunities for campaigners, as well as new ways for false information to reach voters.
“What we were doing in 2022... is different from what we’re doing in 2026,” Livne said. “The world is different, and in practice, technological advancement is amazing and surprising.”
But while the technology surrounding elections has changed dramatically, the system responsible for counting the votes remains deliberately physical.
The challenge, he said, is adapting to those technological changes without compromising the integrity of the actual vote.
Local voters still mark a physical paper ballot and place it in a ballot box. From there, the CEC builds multiple layers of verification around that slip of paper.
Livne also emphasized that the results are not simply transmitted from polling stations over the internet.
Instead, once voting ends, they are recorded in a protocol at the polling station. That protocol is then signed by representatives, with the process documented on video.
The physical materials are then transported to a regional election committee.
“And there it goes to a regional judge, who sits and checks whether what happened is really true,” Livne said.
The judge checks the numbers against each other, the number of voters and the number of votes, to ensure that they are consistent.
“It hasn’t happened that there were more votes than the number of voters there; it doesn’t happen, but he still checks it again,” Livne said. “Of course, it’s counted and checked several times.”
Only after those physical checks does the information enter the CEC’s central systems.
And even then, Livne said, the central systems themselves are not connected to the internet.
“It’s up to the security systems of the central polling station, which are secured with military-grade equipment,” he said. “The level of data security and cyber defense that the committee adheres to is unprecedented.”
The public-facing results are separate.
“The only thing that’s available over the internet is a view to the public that is completely separate from our systems, which are not connected to the internet,” Livne said.
The CEC also publishes images of the handwritten protocols alongside the results, allowing the public to compare the physical record with the electronic results.
“So the public can know that what is handwritten on the copy... is what’s in the computer,” Livne said.
The result is a system in which changing a digital number would not, by itself, change the underlying vote. That paper trail also gives the CEC a way to investigate allegations after the fact.
“The moment there is an allegation that, God forbid, there was fraud, the first thing we do is examine the claim,” Livne said. “We examine it on its merits.”
He said that the CEC deploys large teams after elections to examine allegations individually.
“I deploy teams of hundreds of legal professionals immediately after the election to examine every allegation individually,” he said.
The committee has the physical records required to conduct those investigations, he said.
“Because I have all the ballot boxes, all the protocols, and all the photographs, the examination will be very, very fast,” Livne said.
“And there will be an unequivocal answer: Yes or no.”
Livne is confident that most allegations will not withstand that examination.
“And I can already tell you that usually the answer will be no because it is almost impossible to rig elections on that level,” he added.
He then offered a more colorful assessment of the idea that Israel’s elections could be systematically rigged.
“Anyone who believes [these] elections can be rigged can also believe in flat Earth and that birds are CIA drones,” Livne said.
The confidence comes from the number of independent records produced during the voting and counting processes. A claim about a particular polling station can, in principle, be tested against the ballot box, protocol, photographs, signatures, and other documentation generated there.
The information environment around the physical voting process has changed
THE PHYSICAL voting process may have remained largely unchanged, but the information environment around it has not.
Livne said the CEC has been forced to adapt to the rapid development of artificial intelligence, notably generative AI, since the last election.
Israel has amended its election law to address campaign material created or altered using advanced technologies, including AI, and the CEC subsequently established rules for labeling such material.
The issue is particularly significant when artificial content looks real.
As Livne explained, there is a difference between a video that is obviously fictional and one that appears to show a real political figure saying something which that person never said.
The CEC’s response is therefore not limited to labeling requirements. It also wants to make voters more skeptical of what they encounter online.
“Today, whatever you see online or on WhatsApp or anywhere else, doubt if it is true,” Livne said. “Be confused, learn, and come to us.”
The CEC is also preparing for situations in which false information could directly interfere with the election process.
Asked about a hypothetical deepfake released shortly before Election Day showing a major candidate falsely announcing that they had withdrawn from the race, Livne said the CEC would act.
“We deal with the big platforms,” he said.
The committee works with security authorities and the Cyber Agency, he said, and can seek to have false material removed.
The CEC can also warn voters that the material is fake. Livne said that the committee would work to ensure such warnings reached the public.
The CEC’s role becomes more complicated, though, when the threat originates outside the electoral system itself.
Livne declined to discuss specific countries or intelligence assessments, saying that such information is classified. But he described extensive coordination between the CEC and Israel’s security establishment.
“The committee is working in full coordination with the security authorities,” he said, naming the Shin Bet (Israel Security Service), IDF, Israel Police, judiciary, and Prime Minister’s Office.
The CEC, therefore, is protecting a voting process that is deliberately difficult to manipulate electronically, while other government bodies work to identify threats to the broader electoral environment.
That distinction is crucial as technology changes what an election can look like.
Israel is hardly alone in retaining a physical component to elections. Livne noted that much of the world continues to use analog voting or maintains a paper trail because of cyberattack concerns. Even countries using electronic voting can maintain a physical record, which allows the electronic result to be checked.
Israel’s system is particularly suited to paper because voters select a single party list. “With us, you vote very simply,” Livne said. “You vote for one list.”
That makes it possible to keep the voting process relatively simple even as the technological environment surrounding the election becomes increasingly complicated.
The most consequential threats may not necessarily involve the ballot boxes at all
THE IRONY of Israel’s election security system is that the most consequential threats may not necessarily involve the ballot boxes at all.
The CEC has spent decades building layers of protection around the physical vote: paper ballots, signed protocols, photographs, multiple checks, judicial oversight, and an offline central system. But none of those safeguards can tell a voter whether the video they watched on WhatsApp that morning was real.
They cannot determine whether an apparently authentic recording of a candidate was AI-generated. Nor can they stop a voter from making a decision based on deliberately fabricated information before that person walks into a polling station.
That is the increasingly complicated part of election security.
“The world is different,” Livne said.
The ballot box may still look much the same as it did in previous elections, yet the information reaching the person carrying the ballot there is changing rapidly.
And while the CEC can check a ballot, a protocol, and a photograph against one another, the harder question may be what happens before the voter ever reaches the ballot box.

India continues efforts to secure the return of nationals serving in the Russian army (File photo)
NEW DELHI: Around 140 Indian nationals recruited into the Russian army have been discharged, while India is seeking information on the whereabouts of 55 others reportedly serving in the Russian armed forces, according to the details from India-Russia consultative committee meeting as cited by news agency ANI.New Delhi has engaged with Russian authorities for the early discharge of all such individuals."The government of India engaged with Russian authorities, including at the highest levels, for the early discharge of all such individuals. So far, around 140 Indian nationals have been discharged. Indian side is in touch with Russian authorities for the whereabouts of 55 Indian nationals who are reportedly in the Russian Army. Strong action being taken by the Indian law enforcement authorities against unscrupulous agents," the update from the meeting said.
The latest figures are broadly in line with those shared by foreign secretary Vikram Misri last month. At the time, Misri said 139 of the 227 Indian nationals recruited into the Russian armed forces had been discharged, while 51 had died.
Misri said the issue had been raised with Russia “at various levels on various occasions”.
“At last count, we had information about 227 Indian nationals who had been recruited into the Russian army,” Misri had said. “Out of that, we have information that 139 of our nationals have been discharged from the army. And unfortunately, of course, we have information also about 51 people who have perished so far.”Misri had said India remained in constant discussions with Moscow to secure the early discharge and repatriation of those still serving.
Aastha Jha is a writer at The Times of India, covering politics. She also writes on business, global affairs, social issues, with a focus on policy, governance and their impact on everyday lives. Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

Ukraine sends mixed signals on F-16 repair delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:06:47 UTC
21:06:47 KST

- Zelensky told the Financial Times that about half of Ukraine's F-16s have spent long periods in Europe for repairs and maintenance.
- Ukraine's Foreign Ministry later called reports of catastrophically low F-16 availability false, saying overhauled jets are returning at an increasing pace.
About half of Ukraine’s F-16 fighter jets have spent long stretches in Europe for repairs and maintenance, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, and some have taken so long to come back that Ukraine lost time when it needed them most to defend its skies.
Zelensky made the comments in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2. He said Kyiv wants Western partners to help move more of the maintenance work inside Ukraine, arguing that keeping the jets closer to the front would get them back into service faster. He did not say how many aircraft are affected, where in Europe the work is done, or how long the jets have been away.
Zelensky said the F-16s have been effective against Russia’s newer jet-powered drones, which fly faster than the propeller-driven Shahed-type drones Russia has used for most of the war. In the same interview, he said Ukrainian forces are shooting down about 57% of jet-powered drones and between 85% and 90% of conventional ones.
Hours later, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry pushed back on reports describing a readiness crisis in the F-16 fleet. Spokesperson Heorhiy Tykhyi said on X that claims of catastrophically low aircraft availability and excessively long maintenance turnaround times were false. He said Ukraine’s industrial partners are returning overhauled aircraft at an increasing pace and that maintenance times are getting shorter, not longer.
Tykhyi acknowledged that the fleet is hard to keep flying. Ukraine flies the jets intensively under demanding conditions, he said, and some components for its early-model F-16s are no longer produced and are getting harder to find. He warned that such reports should not undermine international funding for F-16 maintenance or cast doubt on the need for more jets from partner nations.
Ukraine’s F-16s are older jets from European air forces, mainly the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway and Belgium. The first ones arrived in the summer of 2024. They have been used to intercept Russian cruise missiles and drones and to strike ground targets, and Ukraine has lost several of them in combat and accidents.
Because the jets are Western-built, much of their deeper maintenance has been done outside Ukraine, where parts, tools and trained technicians are available and the aircraft are out of reach of Russian strikes on airfields. Moving that work into Ukraine would bring the jets closer to the fight but would also put repair sites within range of Russian missiles and drones.

UAE president's senior advisor calls flydubai plane hijacking 'dangerous terrorist attack'

The United Arab Emirate's president's diplomatic advisor, Anwar Gargash, said on Friday that the recent attempted hijacking of a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv was a "dangerous terrorist act."
Gargash said this while praising the Indian pilot of the flight, Capt. Smit Machchhar, who fought back against his Omani co-pilot and helped allow passengers into the cockpit and rescue the plane.
"He embodied the meaning of courage and responsibility in the face of a dangerous terrorist act and a potential disaster," Gargash wrote in a post on X/Twitter.
"His professionalism and moral sense in the darkest of circumstances make him a true hero."
Gargash also cautioned that vigilance was essential to confronting future possible acts of extremism and terrorism, and warned against promoting conspiracy theories about the attack.
Netanyahu says hijacking had potential to be a disaster on 'scale of 9/11'
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave an update on the incident on Friday, characterizing the attempted hijacking as a potential "disaster on the scale of 9/11."
Regarding the Omani hijacker-pilot, Netanyahu said he "underwent Islamist radicalization."
"He intended to crash the plane with all its passengers on board," Netanyahu said in a post on X. "We are now investigating whether he was sent, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price.”
Passengers return to Israel after attempted flydubai hijacking
One hundred and seventy-four Israeli passengers were returned to Ben-Gurion Airport Tuesday evening after multiple passengers helped restrain the Omani hijacker-pilot who attempted to crash the airplane earlier in the day.
The passengers were initially on a flydubai commercial passenger aircraft flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, but then the pilot-hijacker, who was the deputy pilot for the flight, stabbed the lead pilot and tried to crash the aircraft before as many as four passengers wounded him and tied him up.
An additional flight crew member on board was then able to handle landing the plane in Saudi Arabia, though the original pilot, Machchhar, was in critical condition, having been stabbed repeatedly by the Omani pilot.

OpenAI dismisses 3 researchers over alleged mishandling of sensitive information
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:06:28 UTC
21:06:28 KST

Dilara Hamit
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
OpenAI has dismissed three researchers after an internal investigation concluded that they mishandled sensitive company information, the ChatGPT developer told news outlets.
“We have parted ways with three individuals” for violating information-access and handling policies, an OpenAI spokesperson said.
The company said the researchers dealt with sensitive material outside its established procedures, violating internal rules and undermining the trust required for its work.
The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the dismissals late Thursday, identified the researchers as Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni. It said the alleged misconduct included sharing confidential information with an external AI-safety organization that was helping analyze OpenAI’s models.
Neither the outside organization nor the material allegedly shared was identified publicly. OpenAI has not confirmed the names reported by the newspaper.
The dismissals come amid heightened scrutiny of OpenAI’s safety procedures, as well as questions about the safety of AI for the industry as a whole, following several incidents in which experimental AI agents acted outside their intended boundaries during training or evaluation.
In July, OpenAI agents escaped a restricted testing environment and gained access to the internet before breaching systems operated by the open-source development platform Hugging Face.
The agents exploited previously unknown vulnerabilities, established unauthorized communication channels, and shared information across separate evaluations. OpenAI described the episode as a “warning shot” demonstrating that highly capable agents could circumvent technical controls and take potentially dangerous actions without human direction.
Company channel for reporting 'misalignment'
A subsequent company review found other instances in which its models affected external websites and services. OpenAI said it had notified third parties whose security controls may have been bypassed or whose services were affected, while stressing that notification did not necessarily mean private data had been accessed or a system fully compromised.
The company also acknowledged that in June, its experimental models accessed Australian government websites without authorization during internal testing. One model obtained non-public access to a Services Australia system and retrieved internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics, although OpenAI said no individual medical records were accessed.
OpenAI has since tightened network restrictions, expanded monitoring, and temporarily paused some training and evaluation involving tool use for its most capable models.
The company has also introduced a framework for publicly reporting examples of model “misalignment,” including unauthorized actions, efforts to evade oversight and communication between agents outside approved channels.
OpenAI has said the industry has not yet solved alignment and monitoring well enough to continue expanding the most advanced AI systems at maximum speed indefinitely.

Turkish modular building manufacturer Karmod has produced custom container buildings for the UN climate conference COP31, which will be held in Antalya, Türkiye, in November, the company said in a statement on Friday.
The specially designed structures, built using a hybrid construction system, will serve as rest areas for participants attending the COP31 summit in the Mediterranean resort city.
Karmod Container General Manager Ensar Cankaya said the buildings were designed in line with the summit’s sustainability goals, using environmentally friendly production methods and a zero-waste approach.
Cankaya said container structures, traditionally associated with construction-site facilities, are increasingly being used for purposes ranging from housing to offices.
“Container buildings are still widely known as a construction model used mainly for site mobilization,” he said.
“Today, however, they are preferred in many areas, from housing to offices. Their structural safety, compatibility with modern architectural designs and environmentally friendly production model make them a suitable building alternative for the resilient cities and buildings agenda.”
Cankaya said the units produced for COP31 feature a hybrid design developed specifically for the event.
He said Karmod reinforced the wall panels with steel frames beyond its standard specifications to improve the buildings’ structural performance.
“The buildings have been upgraded to the highest level in terms of insulation. On-site installation of the seven blocks is nearly complete, with each block covering 300 square meters. The container buildings, which will serve as lounges for international participants during the summit, include amenities such as accessible restrooms. All of the buildings were produced as demountable structures and will be reused at different locations after the summit,” Cankaya said.

Tunisia softens its ‘false news’ penalty. What really changed, and why now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:03:20 UTC
21:03:20 KST

Tunisia softens its ‘false news’ penalty. What really changed, and why now?
Fines replace jail terms for first-time ‘false news’ offences under a decree rights groups say is still repressive.
Tunisia has softened a cybercrime law that has landed journalists and activists in prison, letting first-time offenders pay fines instead of serving time.
The amendment to Decree 54, which went into effect on Wednesday, sets fines of 10,000 to 20,000 Tunisian dinars ($3,370 to $6,740) for a first offence of spreading “false news” and related violations.
The fines replace a five-year prison sentence. However, repeat offenders may still face jail.
Rights and media freedom advocates in Tunisia and abroad have long opposed the decree as repressive, saying it has been wielded against President Kais Saied’s opposition, activists and reporters.
The government, meanwhile, says the decree protects people and public order from attack, and is needed to tackle online crime and disinformation.
So what has changed, how has the decree been used, and why has Tunisia softened it now?
What does the amended law say?
Decree 54, issued by President Kais Saied in September 2022, made it an offence to spread falsehoods by electronic means.
Until this week, anyone convicted of circulating untrue information deemed threatening to public security, or to infringe on other people’s rights, risked up to five years in prison.
The penalties also applied when allegedly doctored content, personal data or untrue allegations were spread to stir up hatred, incite attacks, defame someone, damage their reputation or cause them material or moral harm.
Targeting a public official or a person of equivalent status raised the ceiling to a decade behind bars and a fine of 100,000 dinars (more than $32,000).
Anyone who reoffended faced six months behind bars on top of a 50,000-dinar fine (more than $16,000).
The penalties doubled when the offence was aimed at a public official or someone of equivalent status.
How has Decree 54 been used?
The decree has garnered widespread criticism from Tunisian and international organisations concerned with press freedom.
The law was “one of the potent tools of oppression used by the government to crush dissent, crack down on civic space and arbitrarily restrict the freedom of expression in the country,” Said Benarbia, Middle East and North Africa director of the International Commission of Jurists (ICJ), told Al Jazeera.
Rafik Abdessalem, Tunisia’s foreign minister from 2011 to 2013 and a senior figure in the Islamist Ennahdha party, said the decree had been used “to silence every voice critical of the regime”.
Ennahdha was a leading opposition party under Saied until he initiated a severe crackdown against it, sentencing its leadership, including Abdessalem, to long prison sentences, some in absentia.
The National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists (SNJT) documented that hundreds of journalists, bloggers, opposition politicians, lawyers and activists had been tried under the decree since it came into force in 2022, and declared the situation an “emergency”.
In its latest annual report, the SNJT recorded 14 prosecutions of journalists between April 2025 and April 2026 – six of them under the decree.
In one example, prominent Tunisian lawyer and columnist Sonia Dahmani was sentenced to two years for criticising conditions in Tunisian prisons in a radio interview this May.
She has been charged under the decree in five cases, each relating to remarks she made in media appearances, and had already been sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment after criticising Saied’s policies in 2024.
Another citizen, Saber Ben Chouchane, was sentenced to death after being charged under a number of censorship laws, including Decree 54, for Facebook posts. He was later granted a presidential pardon.
Among international critics of the decree are Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the European Parliament, which has described it as “a tool to interfere with fundamental freedoms” and called for its repeal.
Critics connect it to a larger trend of democratic backsliding in the country since Saied took office, undoing progress the country has made after its 2011 revolution.
In 2021, during his third year in office, Saied suspended parliament, dismissed the government and began ruling by presidential decree – steps his critics have denounced as an autocratic subversion of Tunisia’s democratising political system.
A new constitution, put to a referendum in 2022 that many Tunisians boycotted, later locked in those powers.
In 2024, amid political repression, Saied won a second five-year term with more than 90 percent of the vote. It was the lowest turnout of any election since 2011 at 28.8 percent.
Saied rejects accusations of autocratic rule, saying his actions are legal and are needed to end years of disorder and alleged corruption.
Why now?
Hours before Wednesday’s amendment came into effect, civil society groups spearheaded by Tunisia’s largest labour union unveiled plans for a nationwide march over what they regarded as restrictions on civil liberties.
Seven years after Tunisians elected Saied on promises he would address the country’s poor economic situation and tackle corruption, Tunisians have found themselves facing a cost-of-living crisis and restrictions to their political freedoms.
In the past year, the country has seen a rise in demonstrations by civil society against abuses of power, democratic backsliding and deteriorating living standards. In June, hundreds of protesters in Tunis called for press freedom and for detained critics to be freed. In July, thousands gathered on the fifth anniversary of Saied’s suspension of parliament, urging him to “leave”.
Abdessalem, the former foreign minister, credited popular mobilisation – in the form of marches and gatherings – for forcing the government to back down.
Saied also faced mounting pressure from abroad. In July, a member of the US House of Representatives, Joe Wilson, said he would keep pushing a bill that would impose sanctions on Saied and those closest to him for anti-democratic policies.
Is the amendment enough?
Critics say the amendment does little to address freedom of speech concerns under Saied’s government.
The reduction in penalties was a “positive development”, Benarbia of the International Commission of Jurists said, but what was required was an end to all abusive prosecutions and the release of those arbitrarily detained under the decree.
Even if repealed, a host of other legal measures have been used to harass, imprison and exile Saied’s opponents.
“In short, the punishment has been reduced, but its repressive and punitive character remains unchanged,” Abdessalem told Al Jazeera. The amendment aimed to make the image of Saied’s Tunisia “less bleak” after it has become associated with “trials, arrests and the use of arbitrary decrees,” he said.
Lotfi Hajji, head of Al Jazeera’s bureau in Tunisia, said civil society groups and the journalists’ union were demanding Decree 54 be scrapped altogether, so that journalists could be judged under the 2011 press freedom law instead.
That law was one of the main gains of the revolution, Hajji said, balancing freedom with responsibility. Proposals in parliament since 2024 for a wider overhaul have been ignored.

Ex-UN director who protested Gaza famine challenges his dismissal
GENEVA/ROME, Oct 2 - A former senior UN food agency official has said he has launched an appeal against his dismissal, alleging it was motivated by his stance on hunger in Gaza, in a case that has exposed tensions within the Rome-based organisation.
Benjamin Davis, 62, a Spanish American director at the Food and Agriculture Organization, was informed his employment would end on September 30 at the request of Director-General Qu Dongyu, according to documents seen by Reuters.
The papers cited breaches of international civil service standards which require staff to act with impartiality. Davis rejected the allegation.
JOINED MOMENTS OF SILENCE FOR GAZA
"I feel it’s a terrible injustice. I’ve been disciplined without due process for speaking up about a subject at the core of FAO’s mandate about the right to food which is the most basic of human rights," he told Reuters. He said he had filed an appeal.
The FAO did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Davis' allegations or on the grounds for his dismissal.
Davis, said he had worked at the FAO for 26 years on a renewable contract, and that his dismissal was linked to staff activism over the Gaza war.
He was one of hundreds of employees who have joined moments of silence for hunger victims in Gaza where an international hunger-monitoring system used by UN agencies determined famine in August 2025.
He also authored a report on food availability in the Palestinian enclave in May 2025.
The dispute burst into public view this week when Qu, speaking at a FAO conference, defended the dismissal of an unnamed staff member whom he accused of having "played the political game".
"We will not allow you to play the game here of human rights," Qu said.
DEBATE OVER STAFF ACTIVISM
The remarks prompted fresh debate about whether UN employees are able to express views on humanitarian crises without jeopardising their careers.
A large crowd of staff gathered at FAO headquarters in Rome on Wednesday to applaud Davis as he departed, according to U.N. officials and video seen by Reuters.
Under UN rules, staff are allowed to express political opinions but must ensure these do not adversely affect their official duties or UN interests.
Davis, who was head of the Rural Transformation and Gender Equality Division, said he was concerned that other employees would face retaliation over their participation in the Gaza moments of silence.
The case, now with the FAO's internal justice process, could later be escalated to a UN tribunal which has the authority to award damages in employment disputes. REUTERS

America orders 22 more upgraded F-15EX Eagle jets
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:00:54 BST
21:00:54 KST

The U.S. Department of the Air Force has awarded Boeing a contract for 22 F-15EX Eagle II fighters under Lot 7, keeping all planned aircraft in the batch within the funding Congress provided through budget reconciliation, the service stated.
The contract was finalised before the end of the fiscal year on 30 September, following negotiations between the F-15 Program Office and Boeing that the Air Force described as focused and complex. According to the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s Fighters and Advanced Aircraft Directorate, the agreement takes account of the effects of the 2025 production disruption and wider inflation across the defence industrial base. That disruption was the strike by around 3,200 International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers members at Boeing’s St. Louis-area plants, which began in August 2025 and halted work on the company’s military aircraft lines for around three months.
Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, portfolio acquisition executive for the directorate, said in the release: “Lot 7 reflects a disciplined approach to executing available resources while balancing the realities affecting defense production.” He added: “The team remained focused on affordability, production continuity and delivering the aircraft needed to modernize the U.S. Air Force’s fighter fleet for the threats we face today and into the future.”
The reconciliation funding referenced by the Air Force came through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed in July 2025, which included tens of billions of dollars for defence procurement on top of regular appropriations. The service said the negotiation team worked across programme management, contracting, pricing, engineering, financial management and logistics to assess the impact of changing production conditions and align the aircraft buy with the money available.
The F-15EX is a two-seat-capable development of the F-15 family, derived from the Advanced Eagle variants Boeing built for export customers such as Qatar and Saudi Arabia. It features a fly-by-wire flight control system, large-area cockpit displays, the Eagle Passive/Active Warning Survivability System electronic warfare suite and an open mission systems architecture. The Air Force intends the aircraft to replace its ageing F-15C and F-15D fleet, and the Oregon Air National Guard’s 142nd Wing at Portland became the first operational unit to receive the type. The service’s planned total has shifted over the life of the programme, falling from 144 to 98 aircraft in the fiscal 2025 budget request.
The Air Force also presented the award as an example of the Secretary of War’s acquisition transformation principles, saying an integrated negotiation team was empowered to elevate issues needing senior-level decisions while keeping accountability for cost, schedule and aircraft numbers.
Col. Jonathan Varoli, system program manager of the F-15 Program Office, was quoted in the release as saying: “The Lot 7 award demonstrates what is possible when the acquisition enterprise moves with purpose, remains accountable to the taxpayer and stays focused on delivering capability to the warfighter.” He continued: “This effort brought together the right expertise, at the right time, to achieve an outcome that strengthens the F-15EX program and supports the future fighter force.”
According to the service, the award sustains near-term production of the F-15EX while the Air Force continues to assess its future requirements and acquisition strategy for the aircraft.

Gut bacteria and digestive metabolites are linked to psychopathic traits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:49 UTC
21:00:49 KST

Specific bacteria in the gut and mouth, along with the chemical byproducts of digestion, are associated with traits like emotional detachment and impulsivity. These findings suggest that the microscopic organisms living inside the human body might play a role in shaping complex personality characteristics. The research was published in Translational Psychiatry.
The human body is home to trillions of microorganisms, collectively known as the microbiome. These bacteria, viruses, and fungi do a lot more than digest food and fight off infections. They communicate directly with the central nervous system through a network of chemical signals, hormones, and immune responses called the gut-brain axis.
Previous research links this biological pathway to mood disorders like depression and anxiety. More recently, researchers have started looking at how the microbiome relates to everyday personality traits and social behavior.
Psychopathy is a personality construct defined by emotional detachment, a lack of empathy, manipulative behavior, and a tendency toward impulsivity. In a clinical setting, it affects roughly one percent of the population. The exact biological mechanisms behind these traits remain poorly understood.
Carolina F.F.A. Costa, a researcher at the University of Porto and the University of Oxford, led a team to investigate this knowledge gap. The researchers wanted to see if the bacteria in the gut and mouth could be tied to subclinical psychopathic traits in the general public.
The researchers recruited 200 adult volunteers from the community in Portugal. The participants were screened to remove individuals who had taken antibiotics in the prior three months, as those medications drastically alter intestinal bacteria. The volunteers completed extensive self-report questionnaires designed to measure their levels of psychopathy, empathy, and anxiety.
These psychological assessments measured several distinct components of personality. The psychopathy survey looked at interpersonal manipulation, affective callousness, an erratic lifestyle, and antisocial behavior. Empathy was measured by testing how well participants could understand the perspectives of others and share their emotional states.
Alongside the psychological assessments, participants provided stool, saliva, and blood samples. The research team used a laboratory technique called DNA sequencing to identify the specific types of bacteria present in the gut and oral microbiomes. They also analyzed the samples for metabolites, which are the small molecules left behind when the body or bacteria break down food.
The researchers first grouped the participants based on their psychological survey scores. A computer algorithm separated the volunteers into four distinct groups characterized by varying levels of psychopathy and anxiety. As expected, participants who scored high in psychopathic traits tended to score lower in overall empathy.
Next, the team examined the bacterial makeup of the participants. They found that the overall richness of the microbiome, meaning the total number of different species present, did not vary among the four psychological groups. Any initial correlations between total diversity and psychopathy were not statistically significant after adjusting for the ages of the participants.
While overall diversity did not differ, the abundance of specific bacterial families did show a relationship with personality traits. In the gut, bacteria from the groups Allisonella and Prevotella, as well as a species called Cloacibacillus evryensis, were positively associated with higher psychopathy scores.
Participants with elevated levels of traits like an erratic lifestyle and emotional callousness had higher amounts of these specific intestinal bacteria. In the mouth, a bacterial species called Treponema vincentii showed a negative association, meaning it was less abundant in individuals with higher psychopathy scores.
Many of these specific bacteria have known biological roles that could influence the brain. Allisonella is known to produce histamine, a chemical that triggers immune responses and inflammation. Chronic inflammation in the body can send stress signals directly to the brain, which often influences mood and behavior.
Cloacibacillus evryensis has the genetic potential to produce gamma-aminobutyric acid in the gut. This specific chemical acts as an inhibitory signal in the central nervous system, helping to regulate impulsivity and self-control. Prevotella has been previously associated with differences in how the brain processes emotional and sensory stimuli.
After identifying the bacteria, the researchers looked at the metabolites in the stool and blood samples. Out of over 200 molecules analyzed, two stood out in the stool samples: glucose and taurine. Both molecules were found at elevated levels in the group of participants who scored high in both psychopathy and anxiety.
When looking at the scores on a sliding scale, higher levels of fecal glucose and taurine correlated positively with traits like antisociality and interpersonal manipulation. Glucose serves as the primary energy source for the body. The digestive tract contains specialized sensors that detect glucose and send metabolic updates to the brain.
Finding elevated glucose in feces suggests a disruption in how energy is extracted from food and absorbed into the bloodstream. Previous studies have noted abnormal glucose metabolism in the brains of individuals with high psychopathic traits, suggesting a potential link between energy use and behavior.
Taurine is an amino acid primarily produced by the liver, and it is involved in brain development and anxiety regulation. It normally binds to bile acids to help digest fats, and gut bacteria eventually separate the taurine from the bile. Finding excess free taurine in stool can indicate that the gut is struggling to absorb nutrients properly, or that specific bacterial populations are overgrown.
Finally, the team cross-referenced the bacterial data with the metabolite data. They found that higher levels of Allisonella in the gut predicted higher amounts of both glucose and taurine. This suggests that specific gut bacteria might be altering energy metabolism in ways that ultimately relate to personality expression.
The researchers note several caveats to their findings. The study relies on observations at a single point in time, meaning it cannot prove that gut bacteria cause psychopathic traits. It is equally possible that the behaviors associated with psychopathy, such as dietary choices or physiological stress responses, alter the microbiome.
The participants were volunteers from the general community rather than individuals with clinical diagnoses. The findings relate to subclinical personality traits, which may not fully represent the severe psychopathy seen in forensic settings.
The psychological data came from self-reported surveys. While these are standard tools in psychology, they are subject to personal bias, as individuals may lack self-awareness or alter their answers to appear more socially acceptable. Future research using animal models could help determine if altering gut bacteria directly changes behavior.
The study, “Gut and oral microbiota composition is associated with psychopathic personality: a cross-sectional study,” was authored by Carolina F.F.A. Costa, Daniel Radford-Smith, Alexandre R.T. Figueiredo, Rita C.M. Ribeiro, Sofia Pinto, Fay Probert, Renata Barros, Paula Serrão, Luisa Barreiros, Marcela A. Segundo, Daniel C. Anthony, Fernando Barbosa, Philip W.J. Burnet, and Benedita Sampaio-Maia.

Rare northern bald ibises take flight in human-led European migration project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:07 UTC
21:00:07 KST

Fifteen new birds have joined a growing flock of bald ibises in northern Spain, guided there by human migration guides in micro aircraft who helped them along the route.
The birds are part of the growing European flock of the northern bald ibis (Geronticus eremita), the charismatic and frankly extraordinary bird that had been extinct on the continent for 300 years.
By the end of the 20th century, the last major population in Morocco had fallen from 9,000 to 250 individuals in the wild. But then captive breeding and reintroduction plans were launched at various sites in Europe, initially in Austria and in Jerez, Andalucía. This most recent project, in Alt Empordà, Catalonia, has just welcomed the birds from Austria, to join an already established flock.
“They are such intelligent birds,” says Bernat Garrigós, a biologist who runs the Alt Empordà project, “very sociable, all with different personalities. They like to check everything that comes into the project with their beaks; your socks, the food, everything.”
There is no fear of humans because, as Garrigós explains, the birds do not really know any predators. They are still curious, and trusting.
“We started working on the project in 2024, and by 2025 we had a first generation flock of nearly 60 ibises,” he says. “They were released in March 26 here [at Torre d’en Mornau, a converted Spanish army stable]. Currently there are two full-time and two part-time staff on the team, plus 20 volunteers, to manage the flock and site.
“The Aiguamolls Park [a protected coastal wetland and nature reserve] is a close collaborator and with whom we maintain a very close, ongoing relationship. The goal is to mitigate risk to breeding, and mortality, until there is have a self-sustaining population.”
In a year or two, and with some luck, Garrigós’ project should have its first breeding pair. Ibises do not breed until they are at least three or four years old. The plan is to establish a breeding colony, with nests on the towers dotted around the stables. The team will help by partially building the nests. Like most teenagers, they need to be shown how to make their beds.
The Alt Empordà group is in constant contact with the projects in Austria and Jerez, and the birds migrate between the groups with the help of the human “foster parents” of the Waldrapp team (Waldrapp is another name for these birds) who guide their path with the help of an ultralight aircraft. With 20 years of experience, they have helped Garrigós’ group avoid many of the mistakes made early on. So far, as a result, the mortality rate has been much lower.
Over the next 10 years, Garrigós is aiming to release his ibises into the Alt Empordà, the plan being a minimum of 50 breeding pairs and about 300 individuals living wild. The comarca, or county, which is about halfway between Austria and Jerez, serves as an excellent stopover point in the migration route. The shared goal for the three projects is to establish colonies across Europe. These colonies will be connected by migrating birds, to form breeding pairs of different lineage and creating a robust gene pool to ensure survival.
The project in northern Spain is one more piece in a broader European effort to save a species that has been among the most threatened in the world. The charisma of the ibis and the passion of the team are essential for promoting environmental education, raising awareness in younger generations and driving the importance of active conservation.
And that charisma is a useful tool for winning over people. Recently, representatives from the Endesa, a large electric utility company, came to visit and were so bowled over by the project that they began retrofitting their pylons to be more visible and less dangerous for birds, with the ibis particularly in mind.
“It’s not enough to stop destroying our environment,” says Garrigós. “We need to make a positive, active effort to prevent extinctions and the destruction of habitats where this and many other species live. In the end, it all comes down to having diverse, resilient ecosystems that provide the ecosystem services necessary for the survival of the ecosystem and of humanity itself.”

Does Philadelphia’s ‘house of horrors’ hold the key to seven missing women?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:07 UTC
21:00:07 KST

A dilapidated house, burned out above the second story, may hold clues to dark tales and – potentially – the darkest of endings as the FBI and police in Philadelphia try to unpick what took place at 417 West Chew Avenue for more than three decades.
Last week, homicide investigators shifted their focus from examining an archive of a million photographs and film recovered from what is known locally as the “house of horrors” to excavating what is in or under the home of Raymond “RC” Horsch, a career criminal, local artist, author and snuff photographer who died last year aged 82, and his son Eugene, 44.
So far, at least seven missing women have been linked to the home in the Olney section of the city, originally a German American neighborhood but now largely African American, Hispanic and Asian. Investigators believe five are dead.
Fifty-eight women seen on film and in photographs recovered from the trash-strewn property have been identified. Of those, 25 have been located but not yet interviewed; 19 have spoken with detectives but declined to cooperate.
Investigators are faced with a difficult task: how to discern from images whether Horsch’s subjects are posing, and what is real and what is staged. Such is the grim nature of snuff photography and the murky exchanges that lie beneath. Investigators have said that the five women appear unconscious, lifeless or injured, but with no bodies the medical examiner cannot issue death certificates.
“We’re going slow and methodical,” a police source said. “Do we think people were killed in the house? Sure. It’s a tough investigation because the guy who had the house was a violent pornographer. Is it art or is it reality?”
Deputy police commissioner Frank Vanore said at a news conference on 10 September: “Some of this is play-acting. Some of it we believe could be real, but we’re not there yet.”
The five women who police believed to be dead are Blair Tonzelli, 35, missing since 2023; Nicole Fusaro and Maribel Fresses, both 27, who disappeared in 2018; Amy McHale, who disappeared in June 2016 and had been married to Horsch; and Gabrielle Amarando, 22, who disappeared in 2012.
Four miles from the Olney home lies Philadelphia’s Kensington neighborhood, an area notorious for its open-air drug use, prostitution and homelessness, and as a place where people simply disappear from life.
Many women in the community last week recalled some of those identified by investigators. One had connections to the Olney house – her driver’s license was registered there – but declined to discuss the case. Others said they recalled Horsch’s son, Eugene, currently in custody pending federal gun and drug charges, cruising the block in a black BMW. One remembered Fresses as an “Italian princess – sweet and kind”.
Ashley, making her way from a woman’s shelter with a plastic bag of candies, syringes, and a glass bowl for smoking fentanyl or meth, said bleakly: “A lot of girls go missing here. You get dope sick, it makes you crazy, and then you make bad decisions.”
Not all the women who passed through the Olney home were connected to Kensington. Media reports suggest that some met Horsch in Camden, New Jersey, 20 miles away. A woman from the area told ABC Philadelphia she had gone to the Olney home, blacked out from the drugs Raymond Horsch gave her, and woke up with him standing over her, taking pictures.
Police first raided the home in June after Eugene Horsch was stopped in a car in Philadelphia’s Old City neighborhood. Horsch was carrying fake ID indicating he was federal law enforcement and DEA agent. A female passenger was carrying Tonzelli’s identification.
Two handguns and approximately $8,000 worth of illegal drugs were found in the vehicle. According to court documents, Eugene Horsch allegedly said Tonzelli would “never be seen again”. A search of the home turned up an additional illegal firearm, a marijuana grow operation, a fake FBI badge and five urns containing cremated remains.
The arrest of the younger Horsch, who had not been charged in connection with the missing women, shone a spotlight on his father, who was never charged in connection with the disappearances of any of the five identified women. The city’s medical examiner’s office has advised that if images of at least three women recovered from the home “are authentic and have not been altered, the women depicted appear to be deceased”.
Court records show that Raymond Horsch was convicted in 2009 for attempting to lure a nine-year-old girl into his car in Kensington. “Come here, in my car, sexy girl,” Horsch said to her, according to an arrest report. Horsch was found guilty, sentenced to two and a half to five years in prison, and required to register as a sex offender.
But his lawyers sought a new trial and the case collapsed because the girl was too afraid to testify a second time, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer. Horsch’s conviction was expunged and the records placed under seal. A judge has ordered them to be preserved.
According to a 1985 psychological examination obtained by the Inquirer, Horsch was a manipulative criminal who was “consumed by anger … grandiose, mistrustful, suspicious, and excessively controlling”.
The profile was commissioned as part of a federal drug manufacturing case. Horsch fled the US with his second wife, Myroslawa Anna Ferkuniak. He was arrested in New Zealand, where he’d been living under the name of Stanley Stokowski, a real California chemist who had a Stanford doctorate.
According to the profile, he spoke in the third person, as if describing “events from someone else’s life”. Michael Yoder, a retired FBI special agent, told the outlet that, judging from the report, “I would say you have a potential serial killer on your hands.”
For a time, Horsch and his young son lived in Pennsylvania’s Berks county, where he opened a barbecue restaurant while also pursuing a career as a fetishistic or “snuff” photographer. In 2009, he was arrested after a marijuana grow operation was discovered in his basement, and he was sentenced to five years in prison.
Raymond Horsch had been offering cash and drugs to women in Kensington in exchange for participating in his violent pornographic films since the early 2000s. He also had access to to a crematorium connected to Kensington’s Garzone funeral home to photograph corpses. In 2007, the business was shut down for selling body parts on the black market.
Horsch wasn’t hiding his access to the morgue – a video exhibited at a “Transgressions” art show in 2014 featured a body being loaded into an incinerator. The exhibition asked visitors to consider if Horsch’s “often transgressive images can possibly be art? Or, as many critics and philosophers claim, are art and pornography completely and forever mutually exclusive?”
Horsch was not reticent about his obsession with women in addiction. He uploaded photos of his subjects to his website featuring women “imagining and acting their own deaths” juxtaposed with real photos of overdose victims. A handwritten note found in the home describes hurting people and makes reference to serial killer Ted Bundy.
Horsch’s films included a documentary, Whore!, and films including Deleted Scenes: A Serial Killer’s Video Journal and Slaves. He starred in and directed Lovers, which was produced by a feminist porn studio. He produced The Erotic Memoirs of a Male Chauvinist Pig, featuring Georgina Spelvin, the star of The Devil in Miss Jones.
He published a two-volume photo book called Eroto~ To the Prurient Interest, showing a woman he referred to as “Anna” in staged “deaths”. 2014’s Empathy included a chapter about dissolving a murdered woman’s body with chemicals.
The home is already a tourist attraction even as investigators still search for evidence. “It was creepy vibes. He’d be out front staring at women, or he’d be in his yard doing some kind of chemist stuff,” recalled Jessica Diaz, 37. A neighbor living opposite the home said he recalled young women coming and going from the home. On occasion, ambulances were called. “They need to tear that house down,” he opined.
With Raymond Horsch dead, and his son Eugene under investigation, it remains possible that no charges will be brought and the best the families of the missing can hope for is a police report. “We have a duty to those families who are all concerned about whether their loved one lost their lives in that house or maybe somewhere else,” said the Philadelphia police commissioner, Kevin Bethel.
But the story of Raymond Horsch is already entering the annals of Philadelphia horror lore. Edgar Allan Poe and Bram Stoker both wrote in the city, and it’s had serial murderers in the past. In the 1980s, Gary Heidnik, an inspiration for the fictional character Buffalo Bill in The Silence of the Lambs, imprisoned six vulnerable women in a pit in his basement with the goal of creating a “baby farm”.
Josh Hitchens, a writer and historian known locally as a prominent “purveyor of the macabre”, said that in each case, it was people preying on the vulnerable. “These are often not the people that law enforcement pays much attention to. That’s one of the horrifying things about what’s unfolding now – what Raymond Horsch was doing was apparently known and talked about within the community.”
Hitchens said Horsch is likely to become a point on the horror map of Philadelphia, achieving a measure of recognition in death that his films and writings failed to secure in his life.
“I hope that within that we’re not just talking about Raymond and Eugene Horsch, but the lives of the women are also remembered and given the respect they deserve.”
