Tip Toe Is a Harrowing Melodrama of Queerness and Masculinity in a World Gone Mad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:06 UTC
21:00:06 KST

Tip Toe refuses to be misunderstood. Premiering Oct. 2 on Starz, the British miniseries from Queer as Folk creator and Doctor Who reviver Russell T Davies set its stakes as high as the lamppost from which Alan Cumming’s character is seen hanging, dead, just outside his home, in the very first scene. Reminders of this awful outcome open each episode, preceding flashbacks that take us through the escalation of tensions between Cumming’s Leo Struthers and his next-door neighbor, Clive Goss (David Morrissey), over the course of just 10 days. Scripty speechifying and a finale that strains believability notwithstanding, Tip Toe is, in its unabashed melodrama, a harrowing cri de coeur about masculinity in crisis and queer liberation reversed.
Leo and Clive have a few things in common. Both pushing 60, the men have been sharing a wall in outwardly identical Manchester rowhouses for 14 years. They’ve also both, when we meet them, hit rough patches in life. Clive, an electrician, is having trouble finding enough work to support a family that includes touchy 16-year-old George (Jackson Connor) and 25-year-old Saul (Joseph Evans), who assists his dad on jobs but isn’t exactly earning the kind of money that would enable him to move out. As gossip swirls that he’s cheated on her, Clive’s wife, Marie (Pooky Quesnel), constantly berates him. Meanwhile, Leo’s longtime partner, Curtis (Charlie Condou), has left him for a woman. Not only is he unmoored in his personal life, overrelying on his indulgent best friend, Stephanie (Elizabeth Berrington); he’s also struggling to manage Spit & Polish, the bar in Manchester’s gay nightlife district that he and Curtis used to run together.
Early one morning, Leo chases after an anonymous hookup who has just absconded with his laptop—only to find himself locked out of his house in his underwear. Clive reluctantly lets him in to call Stephanie for a spare key, making clear all the while that Leo’s lifestyle disgusts him and that he’s uncomfortable having his neighbor around his sons, one underage and the other a musclebound Adonis. The thing is, Clive’s kids are nowhere near as innocent as he thinks. And he’s drawn further out of his comfort zone when Leo, against his better judgment, hires Clive and Saul to fix some wiring at Spit & Polish. The first sign of worlds perilously colliding is when a bar employee recognizes Saul from OnlyFans. An unsubtle but rhetorically effective montage of Leo and the Gosses, each in separate rooms, indulging in their preferred forms of pornography, reveals both the secrets they’re keeping from each other and the loneliness they share.
While Tip Toe spends time with all of these characters, Leo is its protagonist. And he’s an admirably imperfect one, charming and fundamentally kind but also pugnacious, prone to exaggeration, self-centered enough to earn Stephanie’s accusation that he doesn’t really value women. (She, in turn, shows glimpses of the J.K. Rowling-style transphobia that seems to afflict British feminists more than most.) His bar functions as a portal into the lives of less privileged members of the queer and trans communities, from his old, flamboyant, gender-nonconforming friend and unrequited admirer, Melba (Paul Rhys), to a 20-something trans bartender (Iz Hesketh), who’s calling herself Zee as she deliberates on a permanent female name—and who dodges transphobic violence daily. The question of whether the visibility Leo’s generation fought so hard to win has backfired, making them all easy targets, haunts the series.
Davies recently raged against the homophobia of the early AIDS crisis in the searing period piece It’s a Sin and looked queasily ahead to a dystopian future in the sci-fi family drama Years & Years. Tip Toe unites their themes to complete a sort of trilogy, combining the anxieties of LGBTQ people, intrafamilial alienation, economic strife, the social-media panopticon, and an overarching sense of doom into a fire sermon against our toxic present. That it shares its Manchester setting with the far breezier, Y2K-era Queer as Folk underlines just how much that community’s outlook has changed in a quarter-century. And the fact that Cumming’s phenomenal performance is airing concurrently in the U.S. with The Traitors: New Blood, which he hosts with high-camp aplomb and an androgynous glam wardrobe, highlights the cognitive dissonance of a society where queerness is embraced—by everyone except the sizable faction that actively hates it. More than just Leo’s antagonist, Clive is an avatar for straight masculinity in crisis, desperately vulnerable but too terrified of showing emotion to say so. Morrissey captures that tightness of that bind. Devalued at home and work, he dabbles in conspiracy theories and marinates in videos of “real deaths.” His story can feel like an adult Adolescence.
Tip Toe also calls to mind other recent series (BEEF, too many reality shows about feuding neighbors) and films (Eddington, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri) that translate current political and social fault lines into tête-à-tête conflicts. On both sides of the Atlantic, storytellers are trying to understand the hateful tenor of the contemporary public sphere by distilling it down to its simplest, me-against-you form. The difference here is that, although Leo and other characters are shown to have healthy senses of humor, Tip Toe itself doesn’t share those titles’ tone of black-comic absurdity. It isn’t a funny show. Sometimes its seriousness veers into stridency. I didn’t find the abrupt escalation to Leo’s death particularly convincing.
Yet, as in It’s a Sin and Years & Years, it’s the incandescent clarity of Davies’ anger and fear that make Tip Toe powerful. For all the dumbed-down dialogue we get from streamers worried they’ll lose distracted viewers unless someone on screen recaps the plot every five minutes, it’s rare to hear characters plainly state things like: “History tells us one thing—that blood and fire and retribution always happen. And right now it’s coming for us.” When Stephanie confesses her worry that she’ll die in 30 years without living to see the pendulum of progress swing society out of what she calls a “new Dark Age,” I suspect she’s speaking for a lot of people. Too often in fiction (which this is, despite ending title cards that purport to update us on the characters’ lives post-Leo), social commentary is inoculated with optimism or couched in irony. In its unblinking earnestness, Tip Toe’s melodrama accesses a truth that transcends any shortcomings of its plot.

Cocktail of the. week: Palé Hall’s Have your cake and drink it – recipe | The good mixer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:06 UTC
21:00:06 KST

The move into autumn proper leads our taste buds to crave warmth and comfort in equal measure. And what could be more warming and comforting than a spiced vodka and citrus cocktail spiced with nut liqueur? Slice of carrot cake optional.
Have your cake and drink it
Serves 1
For the vodka infusion (for 7-8 serves)
Peel of 1 unwaxed lemon, all white pith removed
375ml good vodka – we use Belvedere
For the drink
50ml lemon peel-infused vodka – see above and method
15ml hazelnut liqueur – we use Frangelico
15ml vanilla syrup – homemade or store-bought (Bristol Syrup Co make a good one)
15ml fresh lemon juice
15ml fresh orange juice
15ml fresh carrot juice
6 dashes foamer, or 1 egg white
4 dashes aromatic bitters (we use Angostura aromatic), or 1 pinch ground cinnamon
1 orange slice, to garnish (or 1 slice carrot cake, to accompany)
The night before, infuse the vodka: put the lemon peel and vodka in a jar, seal and leave to steep overnight. Next day, strain the vodka into a clean jar or bottle, seal and store in a cupboard out of direct light, where it’ll keep almost indefinitely.
To build the drink, measure all the liquids into a shaker filled with ice, shake hard, then double strain into a coupe. Garnish with an orange slice, or serve with carrot cake to nibble on alongside.
- Bruce Dorfling, bar manager, Palé Hall, Bala, Gwynedd, Wales

The True Story Behind Iraq War Reconciliation Drama Atonement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:05 UTC
21:00:05 KST

In April 2003, a family in Baghdad was driving home as U.S. Marines engaged in a firefight with Iraqi forces. The family was caught in the crossfire, and three men were killed. Nearly 10 years after the shattering incident, the two women who survived the attack, having immigrated to the U.S. and settled in Glendale, Calif., sat down with one of the Marines who opened fire on them.
Journalist Dexter Filkins told the story of this encounter in the 2012 New Yorker article “Atonement After Iraq.” The piece details the efforts of U.S. Marine Lu Lobello to speak to Margaret and her daughter Nora Kachadoorian and seek their forgiveness for the attack that killed Margaret’s husband James and their sons Nicolas and Edmund and left Nora with a wound to the shoulder. Lobello reached out to Filkins to help facilitate the meeting.
Lobello’s time with the Kachadoorians informs the climax of Atonement, written and directed by Reed Van Dyk and now in theaters. Their real names have been changed for the film: Filkins becomes Michael Reid (Kenneth Branagh), Margaret is Mariam Khachaturian (Hiam Abbass), and Lobello is Lou D’Alessandro (Boyd Holbrook).
“I cried through most of the article,” recalls Van Dyk, sitting down to discuss the film at a hotel in Toronto, where the film had its North American Premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival. He first read the New Yorker piece the year it was published. “I found it really touching to see and feel in a very detailed way the impact that this one incident in war had had on all of these characters' lives, and I did remember thinking, ‘Boy, this would be a really beautiful film story.’”
From concept to screenplay
At the time, however, Van Dyk was at the beginning of his career and in no position to make that film. Six years later, he won an Oscar for Best Live Action Short Film for DeKalb Elementary, inspired by a school-shooting incident in Atlanta. That brought attention his way, allowing his feature-film ambitions to begin to materialize. “After that,” says Van Dyk, “I immediately reached for my copy of that New Yorker issue, which I still have, and started trying to make this film.”
His first challenge was turning a 12-page article into a two-hour film. “You have this wonderful reportage to work with, and all of the texture and specificity that comes with that,” says Van Dyk. “Then there are all the rooms that Dexter wasn't in. That's where my job comes in. There were three people that the story is centered around, two of whom come to life in Dexter’s article. He’s not much of a character in his own piece, so I had to flesh out this character that Branagh plays.”
It’s a unique story that requires a unique take on a film about war. For one thing, there are hardly any actual scenes of war depicted on screen. Van Dyk’s film uses a single event from the Iraq War as an opportunity to explore the humanity in, and aftermath of, conflict. War movies often seek to enforce the lines of division, but Atonement is more interested in the unexpected ways in which people come together. Van Dyk was keen to explore the humanity in the story, not only from the American perspective, as we so often see in Hollywood films, but from the Iraqi one, too.
“I’m accustomed to seeing Iraqi characters in most Western films about war through sniper scopes. That wasn’t something I was interested in,” he says. Instead, the director wanted to centralize the voices and people that are typically marginalized in American films. “As a writer, I want to know my characters as deeply as I can, and I want to have love for them. The real pleasure of writing was getting to know this Iraqi family, who lived a very different life than I did, and I worked really hard behind the scenes to make that feel real.”
The real-life meeting
The real Lobello first reached out to Filkins in March 2012 on Facebook, saying that he had been trying to get in touch with him for a decade. “You could ease my PTSD,” he added. The two began communicating, and Filkins learned that Lu wanted him to help connect with the Kachadoorians so that he could atone and apologize for the tragedy that transpired that day.
Filkins had previously reported on the Kachadoorians in Iraq, but later lost touch with them. Thankfully, Lobello had already found them, via Facebook. He asked Filkins to facilitate the meeting, hoping he could bridge the gulf between them.
The Kachadoorians were not hesitant to meet Lobello. “If he is asking for forgiveness, then we will give him forgiveness. God ordered us to forgive. He forgives us, so we must forgive others. Even people who killed our dears,” Margaret said.
The meeting took place on a Saturday in July 2012. Lobello was deeply anxious going in, and immediately burst into tears upon meeting Margaret and Nora. Margaret comforted him with a pat on the back. The conversation that followed was tense. As Filkins describes it, the day ended with a sense that a true resolution would never be reached, though progress had been made. While forgiveness was granted, forgetting is impossible, and resentment lingers. There are no easy answers when it comes to grief and war. But something extraordinary did, in fact, happen in the room, just as Van Dyk recreates in Atonement.
Explains the filmmaker: “They begin to see themselves in each other.”
Several days after meeting, Lobello received a Facebook message from Nora. She said she felt happy when he came to visit, and that she felt she got “a third brother,” and “the third son to my mom.”
Holding conflicting truths
In order to capture the emotional depth and intensity of that encounter, Van Dyk conducted extensive research throughout his years writing Atonement. He spoke to as many people involved in the real events as he could, including Lobello and the Kachadoorian family. He spoke to countless marines and Iraqi civilians and traveled to Baghdad with his director of photography, Jon Peter. The visit challenged his perception of the country based on what he’d seen in cinema. “I found it rich with color and rich with spirit, when most films posit the country as something more apocalyptic,” he says. “It was important for us to highlight that richness when we were working on the design and how we were shooting.”
He drew further from books written by Iraqi authors, and marines who’d come back from war. Documentaries also played a key role. He credits the documentary Homeland: Iraq Year Zero by Abbas Fahdel as “the best document of the Iraq War, certainly from the civilian perspective. It became a reference point for all of us.” Restrepo was an important reference when it came to filming the war sequence, and Van Dyk notes that The Act of Killing influenced the way he thought about the psychological and spiritual effects of men who have killed, as well as the moral implications of that experience.
Van Dyk became close with the Kachadoorian family while making Atonement. He’s spent “too many hours to count” with them, and they regularly have dinner together. “Every visit is like a five-hour hang,” he says. It was during one of those visits that Van Dyk had a breakthrough moment that prompted him to revise the movie’s script. “In one of the conversations we had, Margaret said something about Lobello that ended up in the movie: ‘Sometimes I look at him and I see my son, and sometimes I look at him and I see the man who took my son.’ I thought it captured very poignantly the complexity of her experience on that day, and I think it was teaching me too that the film had to hold both visions she had of him.”
As Van Dyk puts it, Atonement “pushes back on the larger narrative we’re absorbing from the media about other countries.” The film’s ultimate aim, like so many great works of cinema, is to give the audience an opportunity to expand their empathy for people they might never encounter in their daily lives.
“It’s rare that there are opportunities to make amends,” says Van Dyk. “Thats what makes this story so different from other stories that unfold during a war. Everyone got to sit down together again. I think there’s something powerful about people willing to hold space with others who were on a completely different side of war, let alone forgive someone.”

Gaza: WHO appeals for massive aid influx ahead of winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Gaza: WHO appeals for massive aid influx ahead of winter
Repeated delays in bringing lifesaving medicines, prosthetics and more from Israel into Gaza risk having devastating consequences on Palestinians who urgently need them in the war-torn enclave, the UN World Health Organization (WHO) said on Friday.
“A truck full of non-priority supplies or the right supplies arriving too late, doesn't save lives. That's the question that actually matters," said Dr Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO Representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT).
Almost 12 months into a fragile ceasefire agreement between Hamas fighters and Israel marked by ongoing Israeli airstrikes and other military activity, Gaza’s humanitarian situation remains “overwhelming”, according to the UN aid coordination office, OCHA.
Approved aid can only be brought into the Strip via Kerem Shalom in the southern tip of the enclave, while Rafah (also in the south) is open for the limited movement of people including patients requiring medical treatment abroad. At least four other main entry points into Gaza for aid remain closed: Kissufim, Gate 96, Erez and Erez West.
'Dual use' denials
In a call to the Israeli authorities to “release the pressure on medical supplies”, Dr Van De Weerdt also stressed that essential medicines “should not be considered as dual use” – and therefore banned by Israel on the grounds that they could be used by Hamas fighters – “as they are globally accepted standards on medical items anybody needs anywhere to run a hospital or a clinic”.
In the last six months, one shipment of prosthetics and assistive devices was rejected four times. "Every rejection means another delay for someone who has already lost a limb and is simply waiting for the chance to walk again," stressed the WHO official, who noted that medicines "by contrast, move relatively well", with almost 87 per cent approved and just over 1 per cent rejected.
UN aid agencies operating in Gaza still provide critical assistance to families across the Strip in coordination with the Israeli authorities, but this lifesaving work is impeded by a lack of reliable and timely access.
“Our ask is simple and has not changed: we need the unimpeded and predictable entry of humanitarian and health supplies into Gaza at scale. We also need a multi-crossing model so that aid isn't forced to trickle down through a limited number of crossings,” the WHO senior official said.
Highlighting the “extraordinary health workers” still risking their lives to help others in Gaza, Dr Van De Weerdt said that too few supplies were reaching them and not enough patients were getting the care they needed and deserved. The already dire humanitarian situation risks getting even worse soon, once autumn ends.
Rodent threat
“As winter begins, this urgency to get supplies into Gaza only deepens. Almost two million people are in need of shelter to protect against the cold and the risk of flooding, exposing people to serious health and safety risks, let alone [their] dignity,” the WHO official explained.
As in previous winters in Gaza, the enclave’s residents are expected to face a heightened risk of preventable disease outbreaks, linked to the absence of safe shelter, a lack of clean water and the high number of rats, whose bites transmit infection. The destruction of public health laboratories has complicated the task of identifying potential epidemics, WHO explained.
The development follows a warning from OCHA on Thursday about serious public health risks linked to the accumulation of solid waste in the heart of Gaza City.
Recent gains in improving sanitation in Gaza remain fragile because of a lack of reliable access to heavy machinery and equipment, OCHA explained, “or to engine oil and spare parts required to keep them running. Sustained funding for fuel is also critical.”
Meanwhile, mine action partners reported that they still lack “permissions and equipment” to remove unexploded ordnance hazards identified in the rubble during 37 assessment missions.

Escalating fighting in Yemen deepens food security crisis

Unknown Publisher

21:00:00 KST

Escalating fighting in Yemen deepens food security crisis
Renewed conflict in Yemen has triggered a surge in hunger that could have consequences in the wider region and beyond, the World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Friday.
Fighting between Government forces and Houthi rebels along the southwestern coast has forced nearly 150,000 people from their homes, disrupted markets and restricted humanitarian access.
“What is beginning as a hunger crisis in Yemen could certainly compound a greater food security crisis far beyond its borders,” Matthew Hollingworth, WFP Assistant Executive Director for Programme Operations, told journalists in Geneva.
Families going hungry
Yemen was already among the world’s top humanitarian crises and “hunger hotspots” prior to the escalation. More than 18 million people nationwide face acute food security, and some 2.2 million children under five are acutely malnourished.
Speaking from Rome. Mr. Hollingworth said that today, nearly three out of four households in accessible areas are unable to meet their basic needs – “a record number for this year in just a few weeks.”
“People are finding it hard to put any food on the table, or if they indeed have a table if they're displaced,” he said.
“They're skipping meals, they are eating a much smaller diversity of food types, and they are facing hunger on a daily basis.”
Food prices are rising sharply, while traders report limited wheat flour stocks and disruption to vegetable oil supplies, which is making it difficult for families to afford these items.
Meanwhile, the influx of displaced people is putting pressure on urban areas and existing displacement sites. Many have arrived at these locations after walking for days without water or food.
Scaling up support
WFP is stepping up operations in Yemen and has assisted more than 70,000 people across two of the biggest “displacement hotspots” in Lahaj and Taiz, providing hot meals and other assistance.
The UN agency was already supporting more than 1.5 million people in Government-held areas prior to the escalation.
“We know we can reach that height of support with the pre-positioned stocks we have, but we are finding it increasingly hard to move food into frontline areas,” Mr. Hollingworth said.
The fighting has cut off access to parts of Taiz and Hudaydah, preventing WFP and partners from accessing some 350,000 people in areas where they used to assist.
Humanitarian teams cannot work in these areas, which are under the control of the Houthi de facto authorities, in line with an operational pause mandated by the UN Secretary-General.
Limited resources, bleak outlook
In the face of the food security crisis, WFP is drawing on its stocks already allocated for the broader response in Yemen.
“We're robbing Peter to feed Paul,” Mr. Hollingworth said, stressing the critical need for funding to support both newly displaced people and the millions who have depended on the agency’s support for years.
“If the world doesn't step up soon to help Yemen, the outlook is going to get bleaker,” he warned, because “the consequences of this conflict are stretching beyond Yemen.”
At least 3,700 Yemenis have crossed the Bab al-Mandab Strait to seek shelter in Djibouti, where WFP is working with the authorities to support the arrivals.
Maritime corridors under pressure
Mr. Hollingworth said the Strait is critical for the transport of food, fuel and commercial goods moving between Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Europe.
“Instability around this corridor risks driving food prices higher and deepening food insecurity across a much bigger region –the world.”
He noted that the Yemen crisis is happening at a time when Bab al-Mandab and two other “critical maritime choke points” – the Black Sea and the Strait of Hormuz - are under pressure.
“When all three of these are under pressure at the same time, you can add to that the impact of a super El Niño weather pattern. These consequences are going to ripple through food systems everywhere,” he said.
“We've said this before but let me be clear once again: today's humanitarian shock and supply chain disruptions can become tomorrow's global food crisis.”

World News in Brief: Cycle of violence continues in Haiti, seafarer deaths off Somalia, food insecurity in the Middle East

World News in Brief: Cycle of violence continues in Haiti, seafarer deaths off Somalia, food insecurity in the Middle East
Haitians remain in the grip of lethal gang violence as it continues to “adapt and expand”, the UN’s top rights official, Volker Türk, said on Friday.
In an update to the Human Rights Council, the High Commissioner welcomed the first Gang Suppression Force operations, mandated by the UN Security Council.
These will help boost security in Haiti “but the Force remains far below the strength needed”, Mr. Türk insisted, in support of its “full, accelerated deployment” with human rights safeguards embedded.
Grim toll
At least 5,700 people have been confirmed killed or injured by gangs – or during operations against them – since 1 January, according to the UN human rights office, OHCHR.
Gang members have also kidnapped more than 230 people and raped at least 1,000 women and girls. The real figures are likely much higher, Mr. Türk said.
In his update, the High Commissioner for Human Rights also warned that “extortion, looting and destruction of property” are crippling economic activity in Haiti.
The “constant danger” prevents people from reaching schools, hospitals, and essential services, Mr. Türk stressed.
Five seafarers killed as three hijacked ships are freed off Somalia
Three hijacked ships have been freed after months in captivity, but five seafarers died during the rescue of one of them, the head of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has said.
IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez offered his condolences after the operation to free the HONOUR 25 in Somali waters on 29 September, in which several other crew members were seriously injured.
Mr. Dominguez said seafarers “should not have to lose their lives for the service they provide for the world”, and called for renewed resolve, targeted cooperation and the resources needed to stop piracy in the region.
Repatriation effort underway
The HONOUR 25 was one of three vessels released this week, along with the SEAMULL (also known as SIBU 1) and the MT EUREKA, all seized between April and August by pirates and armed robbers.
In total, 44 seafarers were freed and their governments are working to arrange their repatriation. Mr. Dominguez thanked Somalia's Government for its efforts, but noted that 22 seafarers remain captive aboard the ASANA.
He urged Governments to bring new initiatives, such as the proposed Group of Friends of Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers, to the IMO, and stressed the importance of the EUNAVFOR Aspides and Atalanta operations for maritime security in the region.
Millions more women could go hungry as tensions escalate in the Middle East
An additional 11.7 million women and girls in 28 countries could face food insecurity by the end of the year due to the escalating conflict in the Middle East and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
These crises are driving up food prices and putting a strain on livelihoods and household resources, UN Women said in new analysis published on Friday.
Presenting the findings to journalists in Geneva, UN Women Deputy Executive Director Nyaradzayi Gumbonzvanda said the estimates are a potential scenario, not a forecast, and that the number is in addition to the 208 million women and girls who were already estimated to be food insecure or malnourished in these countries.
“Experience from past conflicts shows that when food is scarce, women often reduce the amount they eat or skip meals so that children and other family members can eat,” she said.
The greatest numbers of women and girls at risk are in populous countries, while South Sudan, Sudan, Haiti, Yemen and Palestine face the highest concentration of overlapping vulnerabilities.
Calls for urgent action
UN Women recommends linking food and cash assistance to nutrition, protection, employment and agricultural services. Women should also have access to land, credit and productive resources.
The agency also highlighted the need for better collection of data that shows where food insecurity is worsening and who is eating less, losing income and carrying the heaviest burden of unpaid care work.

Global life expectancy bounces back to near pre-pandemic levels, WHO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Global life expectancy bounces back to near pre-pandemic levels, WHO says
According to the UN health agency’s latest Global Health Estimates, life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2023, just shy of the 73.4 years recorded in 2019.
“Living longer is one of the great achievements of public health,” said Dr. Alain Labrique, Director of WHO’s Department of Data, Digital Health, Analytics and AI.
The estimates, which cover trends in death and disability worldwide by region and by country from 2000 to 2023, draw on various sources including national vital registration data and estimates from WHO technical programmes alongside UN partner organizations.
Healthy life expectancy – the years people live in good health – has recovered more slowly, reaching 62.8 years in 2023, still 0.4 years below its 2019 level.
“The next challenge is to ensure that those additional years are lived in good health, while health systems are equipped to respond to the changing needs of populations,” Dr. Labrique said.
Milestone for low-income countries
The estimates also point to a long-term shift in what people die from.
In 2023, for the first time, communicable diseases – one that spreads from one person or animal to another, or from a surface to a person – accounted for less than half of all deaths in low-income countries, a further step in what WHO calls the “global epidemiological transition”.
Worldwide, noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) caused 74 per cent of deaths in 2023, up from 58 per cent in 2000, and eight of the world’s 10 leading causes of death were NCDs.
Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of death and disease burden. Ischaemic heart disease alone caused approximately 9.5 million deaths in 2023 and the loss of 210 million years of healthy life.
Many parts of the world have made substantial progress in reducing that burden since 2000, though individual risk increased in Western Pacific and Southeast Asia regions, highlighting persistent inequalities.
Rising burden of dementia
Other chronic conditions are becoming more prominent. Dementia rose from the 19th leading cause of death globally in 2000 to the fifth in 2023, with deaths from the condition tripling over the period.
The risk of dying from diabetes has also risen substantially since 2000, particularly in South-East Asia.
Between 2019 and 2023, the global age-standardised rate of “healthy life” lost rose by about 20 per cent for depressive disorders and nearly 45 per cent for anxiety disorders.
For drug use disorders, the Americas recorded the largest increases in risk of death and healthy life lost between 2000 and 2023, while the Western Pacific saw substantial declines.
Diagnosis points to cure
“The value of these estimates is not only in the numbers themselves,” Dr. Labrique said. “By showing how causes of death and disease burden are changing over time and across populations, they give countries evidence to help shape health policies and priorities.”

Ukraine war ‘a human rights catastrophe’ that must end, says Türk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Ukraine war ‘a human rights catastrophe’ that must end, says Türk
The war in Ukraine is a human rights catastrophe that is “growing and intensifying by the week” and threatening an even greater disaster across the region, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said on Friday.
Addressing the Human Rights Council in Geneva, Mr. Türk said his office had verified some 15,280 civilians killed and injured in Ukraine during the first eight months of this year – on average more than 400 every week, and 55 per cent more than in the same period in 2025.
“The full-scale invasion unleashed by the Russian Federation is killing and injuring hundreds of people every week, as frontlines barely move,” he said, noting that apartment buildings, schools, medical centres, railways and shops had been hit in recent attacks.
Cruelty made manifest
The UN rights chief said a recent report by his office had found “shocking levels of sexual violence against civilians and prisoners of war”.
Of more than 1,000 cases documented, 89 per cent were attributed to Russian authorities and 11 per cent to Ukraine. Most victims were men, particularly in places of detention, but women and children were also affected, primarily in occupied territory.
“This is just one terrible manifestation of the cruelty that has come to define this war. Alongside peace, there must be accountability,” he said.
‘Laboratory for drone warfare’
Mr. Türk said people across Ukraine were living in constant dread, with air raid alerts in Kyiv active for 33 hours during one 48-hour period earlier this week.
Near the frontlines, the use of aerial glide bombs by the Russian Federation in the Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia regions killed and injured nearly 2,500 civilians in the first eight months of the year; 62 per cent more than in the same period last year.
“Ukraine is a laboratory for drone warfare,” he said, calling for urgent international action to deal with the carnage caused by these weapons around the world.
Attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial property have increased sharply, he said, and Russian strikes on supermarkets and food companies are already causing temporary shortages of vegetables and dairy products in some areas. “As winter approaches, Ukrainians fear the worst is yet to come.”
An estimated 2,000 people are trapped in Oleshky without running water, electricity or gas, he added.
Civilian casualties in the Russian Federation have also reportedly increased, Mr. Türk said, though his Office has been unable to fully verify reports as it has not been granted access.
He urged the Russian leadership to “consider what this war is doing to their own society”, which he said was sinking into fear, denial and a militarized economy “that puts death and destruction ahead of healthcare and education”.
Mr. Türk also said he was alarmed by human rights violations linked to the presence of fighters from third countries.
His staff have interviewed prisoners of war from 36 countries held by Ukraine, many of whom said they had been deceived into joining Russian forces.
Steps towards peace
Mr. Türk called for confidence-building measures based on human rights to rebuild momentum towards negotiations.
These could include an agreement to end attacks on economic targets and energy infrastructure, local ceasefires on the frontlines, enabling civilians to leave – and a full exchange of prisoners of war.
“To the international community, and particularly states with influence, I say: please take urgent action to push for a negotiated peace now, before this tragedy becomes even worse,” he said.

Collective action needed to tackle global information crisis, UN-led dialogue hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Collective action needed to tackle global information crisis, UN-led dialogue hears
Governments, UN entities, civil society, media, academia and the private sector have called for stronger cooperation and practical action to respond to a rapidly changing global information landscape.
The call came at the high-level Information Integrity Solutions Dialogue at UN Headquarters in New York during the high-level week of the 81st session of the General Assembly.
Co-hosted by Brazil, the UN Secretariat, the UN development Programme (UNDP) and the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), the event brought together practitioners and policymakers from across regions and sectors to examine how the UN Global Principles for Information Integrity and the Global Digital Compact can be put into practice.
Information integrity means ensuring reliable and accurate information is available to all, allowing people to make informed decisions, participate meaningfully in public life, and exercise their right to freedom of expression.
Participants warned that the rapid transformation of the information ecosystem, including the growing use of unregulated and untested artificial intelligence systems and other emerging technologies, is deepening existing risks.
“Today, a handful of companies still dominate and shape our global information architecture,” said Melissa Fleming, UN Under-Secretary-General for Global Communications.
“Their priorities remain the same: engagement, profit. Always placed above the public interest,” she said. “Today, information defenders – civil society, journalists, scientists and others – are still underfunded and under attack.”
“In short, we are deep into a global information crisis. The crisis has grown but so has our resolve.”
From principles to practical solutions
The Dialogue also showcased how governments, organizations and communities are responding, with an emphasis on turning shared principles into solutions at national and regional levels.
Climate information integrity was a central focus. Participants highlighted the Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change as a model for connecting global norms with national realities and placing the Global South at the centre of solutions.
Projects supported by the Initiative include efforts to improve public access to evidence-based research, strengthen information literacy and community communications, and advance platform accountability.
Participants said many of these approaches could also be applied to other priorities, including elections, peace and security, child online safety, the protection of human rights defenders and disaster response.
The private sector also came under scrutiny, including business models that can incentivize harmful practices online. Speakers highlighted work with advertisers to promote human-rights-responsible advertising and reduce the inadvertent funding of harmful content and practices.
Trust was another recurring theme, with participants highlighting the growing difficulty of determining what is real and identifying accurate, reliable information. Proposed solutions emphasized community outreach and direct human engagement.
“The solutions we have are as wide-ranging as the threats we face,” Ms. Fleming said. “From climate to health, to democratic governance. From prevention to response. Together, we’re pursuing those solutions.”
Building stronger networks
Participants reaffirmed information integrity and the UN Global Principles as a common framework for bringing diverse actors together in support of a safer, more humane information ecosystem.
They also called for greater exchanges of knowledge and experience across regions and sectors, as well as increased investment to sustain and expand solutions that are already working.
As a concrete next step, the UN is developing the Global Information Integrity Exchange (GIIEx), which will connect practitioners, researchers, policymakers and other stakeholders working on solutions to information threats.
It will facilitate the sharing of research, tools, training materials, and policy developments, while connecting people working towards common information-integrity goals. The UN Centres of Excellence for Information Integrity and related initiatives will feed into the Exchange.
Participants also called for a pan-African UN-African Union conference on information integrity, greater availability of research tools and stronger protections for information integrity defenders.
AI in the spotlight at UNGA81
The Dialogue was held during the Assembly’s high-level week in which artificial intelligence featured prominently in discussions on multilateralism, human rights, development, and global governance.
Opening the annual General Debate on 22 September, Secretary-General António Guterres highlighted the speed of AI development and called for reliable guardrails to limit potential harm while allowing innovation to continue. He also stressed the need to involve governments, businesses, scientists, civil society, and academia.
The impact of AI on children was also in focus. On 22 September, the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of Artificial Intelligence brought together global leaders to strengthen cooperation on protecting children’s rights and safety in the digital age.
That meeting launched a roadmap covering safety by design, protection of children’s data, action against AI-enabled sexual abuse material, age assurance, AI literacy and stronger evidence on how children use AI.
Against this backdrop, the Information Integrity Solutions Dialogue examined AI as part of the wider information ecosystem and how technological change is affecting trust, access to reliable information and people’s ability to participate meaningfully in public life.
Participants closed with a call for greater collaboration across sectors and regions, so that the principles underpinning information integrity can translate into measurable action ahead of COP31, the next edition of the UN climate conference, as well as the Internet Governance Forum and beyond.
Find the Chair's Summary of the event here.

‘Money alone won’t get us there’: UN steps up aid for 12 forgotten crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

‘Money alone won’t get us there’: UN steps up aid for 12 forgotten crises
Getting aid to people in the world’s most neglected emergencies takes more than money. It takes open roads, open borders and leaders willing to help it reach those in dire need.
That was the message from UN relief chief Tom Fletcher on Friday, as the aid coordination office he runs, OCHA, released $160 million to keep life-saving help flowing in 12 of the most underfunded crises on the planet.
“We have 87 million people to reach, and no time to waste,” said Mr. Fletcher, the Emergency Relief Coordinator.
“Today’s new funding will help us get aid to people who might otherwise be left behind. But money alone won’t get us there: leaders must exercise political will to open access, remove obstacles and help us reach people whose lives are on the line.”
The 87 million are the world’s needy facing the most severe crises this year.
Access the sticking point
Five of the 12 crises – Afghanistan, the Occupied Palestinian Territory, South Sudan, Sudan and Yemen – are among 10 contexts where Mr. Fletcher has called for urgent diplomatic action to secure access. Unlocking it would open the way to assistance for 11 million people.
The bulk of the allocation, $150 million, comes from the UN’s Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) and will be shared out as follows:
- Afghanistan, the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Yemen: $18 million each
- Somalia and Sudan: $16 million each
- South Sudan: $15 million
- Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger: $10 million each
- Chad: $9 million
- Cameroon: $6 million
- Cuba: $4 million
Including people with disabilities
A further $10 million is set aside for people with disabilities in the same 12 crises, so that aid reaches them and works for them.
CERF is teaming up with the UN Global Disability Fund, which will add up to $4 million in funding and technical support through its Inclusion Catalyst Hub.
Part of that will go towards strengthening local organizations of people with disabilities and their role in the response.
Fast-moving fund
CERF, managed by OCHA, is one of the fastest funding tools available. Allocations for underfunded emergencies rest on analysis of more than 100 humanitarian indicators and wide consultation with partners.
Friday’s release takes CERF allocations in 2026 to $483 million.
Since the General Assembly created it in 2005, the fund has channelled some $10.2 billion to hundreds of millions of people in more than 117 countries and territories, thanks to 135 Member States and observers, along with private donors and individuals. Its annual funding target is $1 billion.

MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. The Russian diesel fuel market is now balanced and Russia will authorize its exports in part in case of overproduction, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said.
"I can say we have the market balanced now for the diesel fuel; there is enough fuel. Although we have just recently renewed the export ban for October, we will monitor the situation and in case of diesel overproduction, we will consider partial opening of exports," he said.

UK scraps charges to seat children with parents on flights, and for simple name errors

20:58:35 KST

The new rules, announced by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, have now come into force.
The UK has just announced that airlines will no longer be able to charge parents to secure seats next to their children.
The new rules, which come into force today (2 October), apply to children under the age of 14 with a parent or accompanying adult.
Before the rule change, a parent and child could be charged up to £104 (€122) on a return ticket to book seats next to each other.
Passengers will also be able to correct simple name errors on bookings for free. Previously, some airlines were charging up to £40 (€47) to do so.
“Parents should not have to feel the pinch just to sit next to their child on a flight, or for amending a simple booking error,” UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said.
“That’s why we’re scrapping these unnecessary charges for all airlines – another everyday fix to help put money back in people’s pockets and give households more breathing room.
“These common-sense reforms will make flying safer for staff and passengers and protect people from unnecessary charges, whoever they fly with.”
Under the EU’s new air passenger rules, which are yet to come into effect, parents must be afforded a seat next to their child provided they are under the age of 14 free of charge. The same is also true for those accompanying a pregnant passenger, or a passenger with a disability or reduced mobility.
The proposed rules, which could come into effect next year, will also allow for free spelling correction or administrative name updates.
Further to this, the regulations would ban airlines from charging checked-in passengers for a printed boarding pass.
Ryanair CEO responds
Ryanair’s outspoken CEO Michael O’Leary has slammed the UK’s move, claiming that no such fees exist. According to Ryanair, passengers have a 24-hour grace period to correct minor spelling mistakes.
“There are no fees for children to sit with their parents on UK airlines, and no fees for making minor spelling changes to bookings,” he said.
“[Alexander’s] press release is designed to cover over the damage that this Labour Govt has inflicted on UK air travel by raising UK APD to £15 (€17.63) per ticket (£60 (€70.53) for a family of 4) in 2026, and her inexplicable failure to sack failing overpaid NATS CEO, Martin Rolfe, from his £1.4m (€1.65m) job despite ‘taking responsibility’ for 4 ATC system collapses in the UK over the last four years, when no other European ATC system has suffered any collapses.”
Unruly passengers to be added to list
At the same time, the UK government has announced it is working with airlines and trade unions to create a new system for sharing information on persistently disruptive passengers.
Last year, more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents were logged by airlines.
The move will allow airlines to see if other carriers have banned passengers in order to extend the ban to their own flights if it is deemed necessary.

Our tactics will remain unchanged: to be very flexible. We will continue to support Ukraine – EBRD President
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:58:15 EEST
20:58:15 KST

A сonversation with the President of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) Odile Renaud-Basso.
Text: Dmytro Koshovyy, Mariia Boltryk
— What do you think is the main result of your meetings this time in Kyiv? We read about your meetings with the head of NBU Pyshnyy, president Zelenskyy, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky, Minister of Energy Denys Shmyhal, Minister of Economy and Environment Oleksandr Kravchenko.
— Yes, we had a lot of meetings. I think for us, first of all, for the EBRD, Ukraine is very important. We have invested almost EUR11 billion since the beginning of the war. So it’s very important. We plan to invest around EUR 2.7 billion this year.
The core of the discussion was the priorities: to discuss the situation, where are the needs in the state on everything related to the state sector, key infrastructure and so forth, the priorities, implementation issues. When you invest such a large amount of money, how do you know how to accelerate implementation and be as efficient as possible?
We had a very good exchange. A lot of what we do is also in the private sector. This year, we expect that 80% of the financing will be in the private sector. We meet clients to understand the project, the situation, some banks and other partners.
For now, we see that many discussions are focused on winter preparation. Where do we stand on the preparation for winter? What can be done? What are the new risks emerging from the escalation of Russian pressure on Kyiv, those kinds of issues.
Also, the reform agenda, because we work a lot with state-owned enterprises and in a number of sectors we are supporting reform, for example, reform of the state governance of state enterprises, board composition, appointment, the role between the board and the government.
— Do you see some improvements in corporate governance after the last scandal?
— We see some. It sometimes has good progress and sometimes experiences some backtracking. It’s a bit uneven.
And in the last few years, it’s been uneven, but we see some progress. For example, the board composition in a number of companies is now built up in a professional manner with external advisers, recruitment specialist committees to decide on appointments and so forth.
We see some progress in Energoatom, which was one of the companies where the governance was probably the most problematic. There are still some important decisions that should be taken.
This is also important for Naftogaz, but the process seems to be well on track.
— You talked about this year, but what about next year, 2027? What is the financing planned for?
— So far, as we are demand-driven, we depend on the projects that we see. It depends on the demand for investment from private-sector clients and so forth, so it’s difficult to say. I think our capacity to invest will be of the same order of magnitude.
But we need to see whether our clients invest or need working capital and support.
What will be the bank appetite? We have a lot of activity that takes the form of portfolio risk-sharing, where we cover part of the risk of the banks.
Bank lending has been increasing quite significantly in the last few years. This was a driving factor for our portfolio risk-sharing.
What will be the behaviour of the banks in the new economic environment is uncertain, but more or less in the last few years our activity has been increasing. Now we are remaining around this level. We hope that this will be the case.
In the public sector, there is a lot of investment needed. But state enterprises face some limitations in how much they can borrow and how much they can pay back. So there is some investment in fact. We need some external guarantee and external donor support to be able to continue to invest.
— What change might be made to the strategy and tactics of the bank in this new stage of war escalation?
— Our tactics will remain unchanged: to be very agile.
Of course, as a bank, we also look at our own risk, how we can cover our risk, and what kind of risk. This will remain in the background in how we take our decisions.
But there is no big change of tactics that I see coming, maybe a change of priorities. What we’ve been very agile about, when you look at the past, is how we supported the energy sector when confronted with attacks in the last few years.
Now, I think, with the current situation in the Black Sea, there is renewed interest, for example, to focus on how to ensure that the railway, the roads connecting Ukraine and Europe, either to Poland or Moldova, function well.
So that could be a change of what kind of investment becomes priority investment, but I don’t see a change of tactics for the bank.
So it will remain supporting Ukraine, balancing our risks by taking risks that are palatable for us and that do not challenge our financial strengths, so working with donors in order to mitigate risk and support investment.
— Recently, the EBRD downgraded the forecast of GDP this year to 1.5%, but unfortunately the Ukrainian government and the National Bank (NBU) now see near 0.5%. Independent analysts, for example Dragon Capital, said it’s near 0% or maybe even negative. What’s your view? Do you see a new downgrade?
— I think that we see the economic slowing, really clearly, since August, with the intensification of the strikes on economic infrastructure.
So it used to be mostly energy, but now it’s also ports, the port blockage plus the Black Sea blockage plus the attacks on logistics, on warehouses, on manufacturing capacities and so on.
So this has a very negative impact on the economy. So I think the central bank, for example, has made some different scenarios.
What I could say is that we still see more downside risk than upside risk.
— Maybe a few words about new projects? Yesterday I read about a new one, the stabilization of the balancing electricity market. The total funding requirement is approximately EUR 600 million. What’s the part of the EBRD?
— So this is a big, important decision we are having with the Minister of energy and the government, because I think they are really willing to implement this very important reform, which would have a very strong impact on the market. It’s really a structural reform, which we would very much welcome. It’s a complex project.
I think our part of financing would be co-investing probably with other international financial institutions (IFIs).
It may still be very much in the making, but we could have something like a EUR150 million loan, another IFI doing another share, and then it would need some important funding on a concessional basis from the EU because part of the debt will never be recovered, so it can not be financed by debt.
— What other systems can the bank offer to address the challenges of the logistics of Ukrainian exports? Is there ane project of developing new roads?
— We are doing logistics. We have signed a project with financing to Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways - UZ), we had elocate targeting more energy generation projects. Now, because they have been under attack and need working capital, we reallocated EUR 130 million to give them working capital.
We also have a big project worth EUR300 million which is being implemented to buy locomotives. And it’s very much needed because a number of them have been damaged, so that’s one important way in terms of logistics.
The other one is indeed that we have some broad project: we are working on a road project. We are discussing the priorities in this area.
The third element is that we put in place, with local insurers a mechanism to guarantee war-risk logistics in the transport of goods in Ukraine. We have already covered the EUR500 million worth of goods. It’s working quite well, and this is a mechanism that we are working to extend a bit so as to be able, for example, to guarantee what is stored in the warehouse.
— But Ukrzaliznytsia is now in default, Ukrenergo is now in process of restructuring the eurobonds. Isn’t it a problem for you?
— It’s always a problem. It’s never very comfortable to lend to a company which is in default or in restructuring... But, on the other hand, they have always been paying us on time, which is very important because of our multilateral status. To provide money, they need to pay us.
It reflects the financial constraint. We were very supportive of two measures that have been taken by the government, which were really needed in order to help Ukrzaliznytsia to rebalance its situation, and this is the PSO. So the compensation by the government for the PSO. And the second is a freight tariff increase. It’s not a very popular decision, but it’s very important. At some point, you need to have the company able to have revenues to deliver the service.
— About the war risks. The business is calling for help with insurance issues but opposes tax increases. Could the EBRD help in this situation?
— As I was saying, we’ve already developed a targeted product because we believe it’s extremely challenging to cover it. So we really focused on transport because there was really no market at all. We have also developed some projects with our banking portfolio.
This was done on a pilot basis, but we are looking to scale it up to include the possibility, when the loan finances an investment and the investment, for example, a new facility, is destroyed, to reduce the debt repayment and take into account the fact that there has been a loss.
So this is an Enterprise Security Enhancement, what we call ESE, the name of the product. And this is a bit like war insurance, but because it reduces the debt that you have to pay back.
This is something we try to develop to adjust our tools, our toolbox, to the needs of the clients and the economy.
— The increasing of tax - is it a critical condition for you, for the EBRD, or other IFIs to take part in this new insurance fund? Because as for now, it’s a very difficult discussion is going on in business.
— I don’t think we are going to take part in the insurance fund as such, because we are a bank, so we cannot finance an insurance fund which is for compensation, because we have no money. We need to pay it back. As a bank, we need to be paying back.
So we have been having a discussions, and we continue to have discussions on what kind of scheme is the most effective, what the solutions are in view of the situation and so forth.
But I believe indeed they need to have a mechanism of compensation by the government. You need some funding and the resources are very scarce. But it’s not up to me to make a judgment or decision whether they need to increase tax or not.
— Another question about the attraction of strategic investor to the new infrastructure holding on the capital markets. Unfortunately, again, we have an internal discussion in Ukraine between the NBU, the Securities Commission, some PMs, and we have an alternative law. The head of the National Bank said he is asking for your help in this dialogue. For example, for our news agency, this is a very important project, because it’s hard to survive without capital markets and investors.
— We agree with you that it’s a very important project for the future because when the economy reconstructs and bank lending will not be enough. So companies will have to access capital markets and so forth. That’s why we initiated this work with the central bank and with the Securities Commission and all the players. Really to study what would be needed in terms of vertical integration. I think the idea is really to integrate the different infrastructure in order to make the system more efficient and then possibly to attract a strategic investor in this and to boost the market.
And so we were very much working hand in hand with the NBU to prepare a tripartite MOU with the NBU, the Securities Commission. It was on the Ukraine Recovery Conference (URC 2025) in Rome. So the MOU, designing the commitment, preparing them as a milestone to prepare the law. We are actively explaining it’s quite a technical issue to the Rada members who are interested in this project and who will participate in the decision-making: what is the whereabouts and what is what we expect as an impact.
— Because today the Commission wants at least two candidates of big strategic investors for this holding. As for me, if we have one strategic investor, it will be a big victory.
— At least. So it would be an open process. People, I think that we’ll see who comes.
— Are you ready to invest in the Ukrainian defense industry?
— As we are a development bank, we do not invest.
We do not invest in defense, because we have a lot of shareholders with very different positions. Sometimes they don’t get along too well together, so there are some tensions. We do not invest in military equity.
— We are talking about the dual-technology, because in the press release of Ukraine`s economy ministry there are a few terms, where are the red lines?
— We are doing a study on dual-use business, to have a picture of what it’s doing and so forth. There may be, for example, when you think about drones. There is a huge military use, but it also could be used for completely civilian things like agribusiness and others.
We need to figure out. We have the capacity to invest in dual-use, but it’s quite restricted. What is the share of military, what is the share of civilian?
But, I mean, that’s something we are exploring to see also what will be the role in the Ukrainian economy in the future, what is the structure of the business because it’s very new. And maybe there will be some opportunities, we will see. The study will be done in few months. We want to present the findings at the URC in Tallinn at the end of January.
— Is the winter URC is a good decision for you?
— And I think it’s too close to the previous one. I think it’s a bit because there have been a lot. The URC is helpful for coming up with a deadline. Now it’s very close.
— About new safety confinement. We are looking forward with great hope to the Donors’ Conference in Paris this November. I know that the need amounts to about EUR 500 million. How much does EBRD plan to raise at this conference?
— Hopefully, EUR500 million. Hopefully, that’s our target. We are ambitious and need to have the funds. We would like to be as close as possible to the EUR500 million, because it’s a question of safety.
And we already have some commitments which are around half of it. The U.S. has committed to providing $100 million. We already know that there will be additional.
The work needs to start in 2028. I think it’s very important.
— Do you have any actual information about the situation on the nuclear station?
— Because of the war there had been some fire, so the whole protection cover has been really damaged. So there had been a very temporary sort of protection system put in place, but it doesn’t protect against humidity and the risk of corrosion and so on. It’s not an immediate risk for radiation, but it’s more if nothing is done, then you have this nuclear reaction still going on under the shelter, I mean, under the confinement.
And everything has been built in order to be able to manage this reaction with equipment without human intervention, and all this system which has cost EUR 2 billion and has been built with a lot of international corporations.
Of course, if it becomes useless, we’ll have to build something completely new. It would be much more expensive than repairing it, even if repairing is already quite expensive. We should do it now. The whole structure will have to be reconstructed, and the whole equipment that is below the structure, within the structure, will have to be reconstructed.
— Maybe some thoughts about municipalities. You have signed a EUR150 million agreement with Kyiv regarding the metro. What are the municipality projects now in the bank’s portfolio? How important are the municipality projects for you?
— It’s important, and we’ve done projects with Lviv on transport resilience. And we have projects in Kharkiv, in Dnipro, in Ternopil and in Kyiv.
And so municipalities are very important players with important responsibilities in transport, energy, and water management. We have been focusing on this.
We also provided emergency liquidity support to Kyiv last year when the CHP were under attack in order to help them with repair, rebuild and so forth.
Overall, I think before this new loan, we financed EUR300 million of projects in the municipal sector. So now this one is EUR 150 million. It’s quite significant overall.
— I asked you about red lines, but now we have a blue line, Dnipro river, and unfortunately some companies said that we invest only on the right bank of Dnipro. Some companies are saying that they invest only in the 35 region near the west border. Do you have some geographic restrictions for your bank?
— We have a map which shows that we have projects very well spread across Ukraine.
Of course, a lot of business are here, in Kyiv. But also we have some renewable investment or business partners in different parts of the country, so it’s quite well balanced.
— But Dnipro is almost on a frontline?
— Dnipro and Kharkiv, yes. They are two of our best municipal clients, so we have large funding for them. We have private-sector projects on the front. We have all of our projects, municipal projects, quite spread out.

On the same day, RBC-Ukraine reported that Kyiv currently has four international proposals concerning possible ceasefire arrangements, with India presenting the broadest initiative.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We have four proposals. The broadest is India’s proposal. For the first time, India has offered to play a role,” Sybiha told journalists.
Türkiye and Egypt have proposed a grain and food-related ceasefire in the Black Sea. Sybiha noted that the issue is particularly important for Egypt, which depends on Ukrainian grain for roughly one-third of its needs.
The US proposal concerns an energy ceasefire previously discussed between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump. Ukraine has presented partners with its own approach and is prepared for both an energy and Black Sea ceasefire as part of a broader arrangement.

EasyJet cabin crew strike disrupts hundreds of flights in Portugal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:57:05 UTC
20:57:05 KST

Aysu Bicer
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
A strike by easyJet cabin crew in Portugal began Friday and is set to continue until Tuesday, with 443 flights from the airline’s bases in the capital Lisbon, Porto, and Faro already canceled, according to the National Union of Civil Aviation Flight Personnel.
Union leader Ana Dias said the canceled flights represent around 80% of scheduled services during the five-day strike, while warning that other flights could also face disruptions.
“Crews arrived in Porto from France, and will probably operate flights to replace the strikers, once again in an illegal manner,” Dias said Thursday, according to the union.
An easyJet official told the Lusa news agency that the airline expects to operate around 55% of its scheduled flights during the strike.
The company said minimum services account for around 22% of its Portugal-based operations, while additional flights to and from Portugal will be operated by aircraft and crews from other European bases.
EasyJet said the operation is being conducted “in full compliance with applicable legislation and regulations.”
The union disputes the use of crews from other bases to replace striking workers, calling the practice illegal and saying it may take the matter to court.
The strike follows disputes over flight schedule stability, pay progression based on length of service, and terms proposed during negotiations for a company agreement.
Another easyJet cabin crew strike is scheduled for Dec. 19-23, potentially affecting travel during the busy Christmas period.

Russia’s Offensive Goes Backward as Ukraine Regains Nearly 300 Square Kilometers Since March
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:57:02 UTC
20:57:02 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Offensive Goes Backward as Ukraine Regains Nearly 300 Square Kilometers Since March
Russia lost ground in September while suffering more than 46,000 casualties—its worst monthly toll of 2026—as Ukrainian counteroffensives erased months of Russian gains, according to ISW.
Russian forces have lost control of nearly 300 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory since March 2026, while suffering their highest monthly casualty rate of the year in September, according to the Institute for the Study of War’s (ISW) October 1 assessment.
ISW said Russia’s territorial gains have slowed dramatically since March, at times becoming negative as Ukrainian forces launched successful counterattacks across several sectors.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
After adjusting for the timing of Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi, analysts assessed that Russian forces have lost a net 293.59 square kilometers across the front since March. Even when areas of Russian infiltration are included, Moscow expanded its presence by only 174.44 square kilometers over the same period.
ISW assessed that Russia seized 175.54 square kilometers during the month but lost 256.35 square kilometers, leaving Moscow with a net territorial loss of 80.81 square kilometers.
When Russian infiltration zones are also counted, the picture becomes even worse: Russian forces entered or seized 143.2 square kilometers while losing 318.38 square kilometers, a net difference of 175.18 square kilometers in Ukraine’s favor.
At least 147 square kilometers liberated around Lyman during Operation Vivaldi became visible in ISW’s September mapping, although Ukrainian forces had actually conducted parts of the operation over several preceding months.
Ukraine deliberately kept much of Vivaldi concealed while the operation was underway, making exact month-to-month comparisons difficult. ISW therefore concluded that Russia likely achieved no net territorial gain at best in September—and probably lost ground overall.
Ukraine’s General Staff reported 46,320 Russian casualties in September, according to ISW—the highest monthly figure of 2026 and the third consecutive month in which Russian losses exceeded 40,000 personnel.
Operation Vivaldi played a major role in reversing Russian gains around Lyman. The Ukrainian counteroffensive eliminated a Russian salient that had threatened the northern approaches to Sloviansk and disrupted Moscow’s plans for a broader maneuver around Ukraine’s Donetsk region defensive belt.
ISW assesses that the consequences may extend beyond the territory already retaken, as Ukrainian positions around Lyman could complicate future Russian attempts to advance toward Sloviansk from the east.
Earlier, internal Russian military documents revealed battlefield losses, mass unauthorized absences, suicides, and serious disciplinary problems inside Russia’s 127th Motor Rifle Division.

Russia may have used new 40kg warhead to strike Southern Bridge in Kyiv – ISW
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:56:58 EEST
20:56:58 KST

Russian occupation forces may be using shaped charges on long-range drones to strike large, fortified targets such as the Southern Bridge in Kyiv, analysts from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) suggest.
“Russian forces may leverage shaped charges on their long-range drones to strike large, reinforced targets like the Southern Bridge, but such efforts would require repeated, precise strikes over a short period of time to cause significant damage,” ISW said in its report on the website.
As Russian milbloggers claim, Russian forces aim to disrupt traffic crossing the bridge and to use repeated strikes against the same area to cause compounding damage to the bridge. The Russian strike against the Southern Bridge is part of Russia’s wider strike campaign targeting civilian facilities and using both daytime and nighttime strikes to make life in Kyiv City difficult and to disrupt daily civilian functions in the city. The strike also aims to degrade the Ukrainian economy by disrupting the movement of people and cargo through the city.
Serhiy (Flash) Beskrestnov, an advisor on defense technology to the President of Ukraine, reported on September 30 that Russian forces had used a 40-kilogram shaped-charge warhead on Geran-type jet-powered drones. These were employed to destroy electricity pylons and steel bridge structures. “A shaped charge focuses its explosive energy to enhance penetration of hardened steel and concrete targets, causing more extensive damage to bridges, armored vehicles, fortifications, pylons, and other reinforced structures,” the ISW explained.
However, experts at the institute note that the type of drone warhead Russian forces used to strike the bridge remains unclear. “Some Russian milbloggers suggested that Russian forces used a Geran-type drone with a shaped-charge warhead to strike the Southern Bridge in Kyiv City, while others claimed Russian forces used the new warhead to strike power lines,” the think tank added.
“Such technological adaptations to the Geran strike drone could, however, allow Russian forces to repeatedly conduct precise strikes against structural vulnerabilities,” the ISW said.
As earlier reported, on the night of Friday, October 2, Russia once again struck the Southern Bridge in Kyiv.
The Southern Bridge was closed to traffic in both directions, while traffic on the Paton Bridge was halted in the direction from the right bank to the left bank.

Fire Erupts Near Major Volgograd Refinery After Drone Attack
A drone attack targeted industrial infrastructure in Russia’s Volgograd region overnight, with a large fire visible near major industrial facilities, OSINT channel ASTRA reported on October 2.
Volgograd region Governor Andrei Bocharov claimed the attack was carried out by Ukrainian drones and confirmed that a residential building caught fire in the city’s Krasnoarmeysky district. One person was hospitalized.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries, launched in retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure, have repeatedly disrupted fuel production and contributed to shortages nationwide. UNITED24 Media reported that the campaign had disabled more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity by September, increasing pressure on fuel supplies and refinery operations.
“Tonight, as a result of a massive UAV attack on the industrial infrastructure of the Volgograd region, a fire was recorded in an apartment building on Udmurtskaya Street,” Bocharov stated. “One injured person was hospitalized, the fire has been contained.”
Residents reported numerous explosions across Volgograd and published footage showing drones in flight and air defenses operating. ASTRA initially noted that its OSINT specialist had not independently verified the footage.
Further analysis of eyewitness footage placed the glow from a major fire in the area of the Volgograd oil refinery and the Kaustik chemical plant, which are located close to each other. ASTRA emphasized that the available footage did not make it possible to determine which facility was burning.
The Volgograd refinery, operated by Lukoil, is one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities, with an annual capacity of roughly 14.8–15.7 million tons of crude, or about 5% of Russia’s total refining capacity. It produces gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel, fuel oil, and bitumen, ASTRA noted.
Kaustik is a major chemical producer in southern Volgograd. According to ASTRA, the facility manufactures dual-use basic chemicals considered important to Russia’s military-industrial sector.
Russia’s aviation authority also imposed restrictions at Volgograd airport at around 1 a.m., disrupting flights to and from Moscow. One aircraft was diverted to Samara after several hours of delay, the outlet wrote.
The same Volgograd refinery was already struck on July 31, when drones also hit a major Wildberries logistics hub in the city, and fires broke out at both sites.
