Russia Stops Cyprus-Flagged Cargo Ship Heading to Estonia in Gulf of Finland
Russian border guards detained a Cyprus-flagged cargo vessel bound for the Estonian port of Sillamäe while it was passing through Russian territorial waters in the Gulf of Finland, ERR reported.
The vessel, Vasterbotten, was traveling through an area of Russian territorial waters where ships are permitted to transit under an agreement between Estonia, Finland, and Russia. Estonia’s Police and Border Guard Board confirmed that the vessel had been detained.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to vessel-tracking data cited by ERR, Westerbotten appeared to have entered Russian territorial waters before it was stopped. The ship was later allowed to resume its voyage, departing at around 5 p.m. and continuing toward Sillamäe.
The route through Russian waters is covered by an agreement between the three countries because it provides a safer passage for larger vessels than navigating shallower waters on the Estonian side.
Are Piel, head of the Vessel Traffic Management Department at the Estonian Transport Administration, said that while the incident was unwelcome, inspections of vessels within a country’s territorial waters were not unusual.
“Every country has the right to inspect vessels in its territorial sea, and apparently the Russian administration considered it necessary to inspect this vessel as it passed through their territorial sea,” Piel said.
He added that all vessels have the right to innocent passage through another country’s territorial sea, but stressed that this does not prevent the coastal state from inspecting them.
The Estonian Transport Administration said it had received no explanation from Russia regarding the reason for the vessel’s detention.
The incident comes amid growing scrutiny of Russian maritime activities in the region. Russia is working to expand a new “shadow fleet” of tankers in an effort to bypass British sanctions and preserve revenues from energy exports, The Telegraph reported on October 1, citing the UK Foreign Office.
The reported expansion involves a network of civilian vessels used to transport Russian fuel and generate revenue that supports Moscow’s war against Ukraine. The fleet reportedly includes at least two newly built tankers designed to carry liquefied natural gas (LNG) through Arctic waters.

Bulgaria has offered German defense group Rheinmetall a new site near Burgas for part of its planned investments in the country, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy, Investments and Industry Alexander Pulev said during a parliamentary “blitz control” session.
The proposed property belongs to the Ministry of Defense and already has the infrastructure needed for the investment. The government plans to classify it as a site of importance for national security and a project of national significance, allowing the project to move forward under simplified administrative procedures.
Pulev said the proposal had been discussed at a meeting with a Rheinmetall delegation on Wednesday, with the two sides examining the investment’s future and parameters.
"We discussed and proposed a new site located near Burgas. It is owned by the Ministry of Defense and has all the necessary supporting infrastructure, enabling us to establish this high-quality production facility there on an expedited basis," Pulev said.

After taking office, the current government said it would reassess elements of the investment, including its financing and location. Pulev nevertheless said work on the project was continuing.
"Rheinmetall is one of the key technological and industrial leaders and giants in the defense industry. Germany, on the other hand, is a major foreign trade partner for Bulgaria, regardless of the metric used - whether in terms of trade or foreign direct investment. Therefore, we are actively proceeding at full speed with structuring the investment proposal with Rheinmetall," Pulev said.
Bulgaria will seek full technology transfer and the creation of highly skilled jobs as key conditions for the investment. Pulev said part of the production would remain connected to VMZ-Sopot.
Satellite technologies are among the possibilities under consideration and could also be used by the surveillance center currently being built in the Dobroslavtsi area.
The sides have also discussed projects involving logistics and transport vehicles, with the aim of moving some Bulgarian specialists from the automotive sector into new positions and creating further career opportunities for them. Pulev said this area could provide jobs for Bulgarian professionals with automotive industry experience.
Talks with Rheinmetall are also set to continue in Germany, with Pulev announcing plans for a reciprocal visit to the country this month.

====================================================================================================

Burger King is betting on local franchisees to fuel its U.S. comeback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

When Jeremy Kline was 15, he started as a crew member at Taco Bell. In the decades since then, he worked his way up the restaurant industry to director of franchising for Burger King North America.
These days, he is on the other side of the aisle as one of the burger chain's newest franchisees, after buying 16 locations in the Salt Lake City area in February.
Kline is one of the new operators betting on Burger King as it embarks on a U.S. comeback. The burger chain is on track to sell about 200 company-operated restaurants to franchisees by the end of the year as part of a broader refranchising initiative, and buyers like Kline will be critical to the plan.
Since late 2022, Burger King has embarked on a turnaround strategy focused on revamping its marketing, improving food quality and renovating restaurants. The comeback has already started to pay off; Burger King recently overtook Wendy's as the number two burger chain in the U.S., based on system sales.
To accelerate the modernization of Burger King restaurants, its parent company Restaurant Brands International bought the chain's largest U.S. franchisee, Carrols Restaurant Group, in 2024 for roughly $1 billion. The Carrols deal added 1,023 company-owned locations to the 175 that Restaurant Brands already held at the time, largely acquired during franchisee bankruptcy sales as Burger King struggled before its turnaround.
Restaurant Brands always planned to sell most of those restaurants back to smaller, local franchisees. Ultimately, Burger King wants to end up with about 300 company-operated restaurants; franchisees will run the rest of its more than 6,000 locations in the U.S.
In other words, the future of Burger King rests on the shoulders of its franchisees at a time when slow traffic, elevated inflation and high interest rates make running a restaurant a challenging proposition.
"A franchising contract is 20 years. The average marriage in the U.S. is 8.2. So you got to get it right," Burger King U.S. President Tom Curtis told CNBC.
Regal returns
Over the last year, shares of Restaurant Brands have risen about 6%, lifted by strong international growth and green shoots for Burger King's U.S. comeback. For comparison, shares of rival McDonald's have tumbled 23% over the same period, although its market cap is still more than six times larger than Restaurant Brands'. In its latest quarter, Burger King reported domestic same-store sales growth of 8.5%, while McDonald's U.S. same-store sales rose just 0.8%.
Refranchising the Burger King restaurants could help send Restaurant Brands' shares even higher.
Selling off locations generates cash for the company. It also results in an asset-light model that typically means higher earnings for the chain and its parent company. And most importantly, franchisee-operated locations usually report better results than those run by a company because franchisees are personally invested in their success.
"Getting these stores in the hands of better operators is a key part of the turnaround," TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles said.
Higher sales also mean more cash to spend on investments back into restaurants.
To be sure, it could be a while before investors see the fruits of refranchising. As the chain starts selling off company-owned locations, it is prioritizing smaller operators, a shift in strategy from the days when larger, private equity-backed franchisees like Carrols received preferential treatment.
At the time that the Carrols deal closed in 2024, Restaurant Brands said it would refranchise those restaurants over the next seven years.
Burger King initially targeted refranchising about 300 locations this year, but Curtis now expects to sell only about 200 restaurants in 2026.
One bottleneck slowing down the process is Burger King's effort to make sure that a prospective franchisee is the right fit for the chain.
Community connections
When Kline was still a director of franchising for Burger King North America, his responsibilities included selling company-owned restaurants. That wasn't always an easy task.
"I was trying to sell these restaurants here in Salt Lake City for two years, and I couldn't really find anyone to buy them, but I saw the potential," Kline said.
In February, he bought those same 16 locations, which were once owned by Meridian Restaurants Unlimited. Meridian was at one time one of Burger King's biggest U.S. franchisees, with more than 120 locations across nine states before it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in 2023.
Kline isn't the only Burger King franchisee to originate from its own ranks. Even some corporate employees from sister chain Tim Hortons have signed term sheets, according to Curtis.
To run his new franchise, Kline relocated from Miami to Salt Lake City. Local operation is another part of Burger King's refranchising strategy.
"We want franchisees who live and work in the communities that they serve," Curtis said.
Proximity means that operators will visit their restaurants frequently. Plus, complaints are more likely to come from their neighbors and acquaintances, holding them accountable for any issues in their restaurants.
That franchise policy likely means that Burger King will have fewer operators with backing from private equity firms. For more than a decade, PE firms have been buying multi-location franchisees and adding more locations, typically by buying smaller operators' restaurants and then selling the business at a higher valuation.
"I would tell you that we have less of it today than we've had in many years, and we will most likely have less of that going forward," Curtis said. "... It really needs to be a great story of a company with a great operator who's significant equity in the business, who has a long-term outlook, not a five-year plan."
For other restaurant chains, private-equity franchisees are often attractive because of their access to capital, particularly in today's high-interest rate environment. But Burger King is more focused on ensuring that its franchisees are skilled operators and that it can help set them up for financial success, Curtis said. For example, its Crown Your Career program helps restaurant leaders and managers acquire funding and financing to buy their own Burger King restaurants.
The Domino's blueprint
Curtis would know what makes a good franchisee — he used to be one.
Years before he joined Burger King, he was a franchisee for about two decades with Domino's Pizza. Then he joined the pizza chain's management team, working alongside then-CEO Patrick Doyle to lead a comeback of Domino's that is still held up as one of the greatest corporate turnarounds. Doyle has been executive chair of Restaurant Brands since late 2022.
Under Doyle's leadership, Domino's revamped its pizza recipe and released an ad campaign comparing its previous crust to cardboard. Under the radar, executives were also focusing on franchisee profitability.
Burger King has taken a similar tactic, centering operators' earnings so franchisees feel comfortable reinvesting in their restaurants.
"Everything that we're doing is based around franchisee profitability," Kline said. "It's not just to drive top-line sales, it's not just to drive top-line traffic. It's not just to be able to report a huge number to the Street."
Todd Jackson, Thomas Crowson and Colby Kaminer were impressed by Burger King's management team and their vision for the chain. They acquired 20 Burger King locations in Florida in July 2025. As CKJ Management, they already had nearly two decades of experience as franchisees of Newk's Eatery, a Southern fast-casual chain.
The business partners were even more enthused after the sale closed, when they discovered from their Newk's employees how involved the franchisor's due diligence was.
"We found out that Burger King came to our restaurants and interviewed our general managers and wanted to know 'Are the owners in the restaurants? Do you know who they are, how involved they are?'" Crowson said.
Of course, not all of the refranchised locations are going to first-time Burger King franchisees.
Kevin Haas just celebrated his 40th anniversary as a Burger King franchisee in June. Several months later, Haas and his wife bought three more restaurants, formerly of Carrols, bringing K&JK Enterprises' total footprint up to 15 locations. Haas said Burger King's recent success gave him the financial means to make the acquisition.
From the ground up
Just as Burger King embarks on a turnaround for its U.S. business, the chain's newest franchisees have also been trying to improve their restaurants' own results.
First-time franchisee Brian Orlando, a former executive in the consumer packaged goods industry, said that he is focused on improving the culture within his recently acquired Delaware restaurants. For example, his younger employees are often reluctant to offer the chain's signature paper crowns to diners, but Orlando is enforcing Burger King's requirement to make the gesture and embrace "the performance of hospitality."
Orlando is also part of a franchisee pilot to take all of customers' complaint phone calls on his cell phone. (Earlier this year, Burger King promoted a phone number to text and call Curtis to share their feedback.)
For CKJ Management, a shift in culture meant rebuilding its restaurant teams, from the top down, and convincing employees to believe in the Burger King brand.
"We've been up 21% year over year for our market, which is really exciting," Crowson said. "But I think the most exciting thing is we're up 16% on traffic. That's the thing for us — you can raise prices and try to grow your average check, but you can't fake traffic."
In Salt Lake City, Kline has been investing in the restaurant facilities and making sure that employees feel "like they're part of something bigger and not just another fast-food job," he said. Kline added that since he took over the restaurants eight months ago, customer complaints have fallen sharply.
Franchisees are expecting to see further improvements in sales when they remodel their locations. CKJ will need to remodel seven out of its 20 restaurants to fit Burger King's modern design standards.
Orlando will soon break ground for his only remodel, although the rest of his restaurants have recently been outfitted with Burger King's current logo.
Those renovation plans are just a small part of Burger King's overall footprint. By the end of 2028, Restaurant Brands wants 85% to 90% of the chain's domestic restaurants to look "modern." The company has committed more than $1 billion to revamp its restaurants, primarily through remodels, but also with equipment, tech and building enhancements.

====================================================================================================

Israeli settlers target a Ramallah road, and the city’s future with it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

The urban area of Ramallah, the main commercial and economic hub of the occupied West Bank and the seat of the Palestinian Authority (PA), is now in the crosshairs of Israeli settler expansion. According to a report by Haaretz, an Israeli plan is underway to “allow” Israeli settlers to drive on a road in the northern part of Ramallah’s urban area, a main thoroughfare for Palestinians that connects Ramallah’s city center and its northern suburbs.
Haaretz reported that the Israeli army has begun preparations for settler access to the road, which are expected to include military outposts and checkpoints that would fragment the city and disrupt Palestinian movement within and around it. For Palestinians in Ramallah, this move is not a simple case of urban planning or rerouting of traffic, but yet another settler strangulation of Palestinian existence in the West Bank that is making daily life impossible.
The road in question, known in Israel as “Road 463,” is 10 kilometers long, running from the west Ramallah village of Ain Qinia to the Jalazon refugee camp in the east.
The road currently connects the heart of Ramallah to seven towns, a university, a school, a major hospital, and a sewage treatment plant on its northern edge. Today, under the jurisdiction of Ramallah’s municipality, the road is well-served with trees, side drains, new pavement, and roundabouts. The visual absence of Israeli settlers along the tree-lined road gives Palestinians a rare experience of normality, residents say.
“It is the only drive where I feel like I’m in a normal country,” Yousef Masalmeh, a taxi driver from Birzeit, north of Ramallah, tells Mondoweiss. “I use this road every day, and I drive from Birzeit to the Ramallah city center in just 15 minutes, which makes it so easy for people to live in Birzeit, al-Rihan, or Jifna, while working in Ramallah, and that’s a privilege.”
A privilege, because unlike elsewhere in the West Bank, Palestinians in the immediate surrounding metropolitan area of Ramallah, especially the residential areas north of the city, had been able to move between the city center and its suburbs without encountering Israeli checkpoints or settler attacks — that is, as long as they stayed within Ramallah. This freedom of movement does not apply to Palestinians who live a few kilometers outside of the city, including the majority of the governorate’s 80 villages, who have to deal with daily road closures, iron gates, Israeli military checkpoints, or threats of Israeli settler attacks on the road.
Cutting off a rare space for Palestinian urban development
The Palestinian areas served by the “Chinese Road,” as locals call it — due to partial funding of the road infrastructure by the Chinese government — are among the few spaces in the West Bank that have seen urban expansion, not in small part because of the road’s access.
Most major cities and towns in the West Bank are choked off by Israeli settlements, settler roads, military checkpoints, and other movement barriers imposed by the occupation. That reality has led to overcrowding in city hubs like Ramallah, driving up prices and making most cities unaffordable for Palestinians, particularly young professionals. The suburbs surrounding the Chinese Road have offered a small relief from sky-high prices in the city, offering a rare chance for Palestinians with the financial means to purchase property. 
Eyad Shoufani, a real estate agent, sells apartments to middle-class Palestinian families in the al-Rihan neighborhood, which sits just north of Ramallah along the road, just ten minutes from the city center by car. Al-Rihan was a pre-planned residential area built between 2009 and 2012 by a private Palestinian investment firm. Shoufani’s customers, he says, are mostly young Palestinian professionals working in Ramallah, many of whom are from other parts of the West Bank and need to live close to the city. Prices for apartments in the neighborhood range from $100,000 to $300,000, with long-term monthly payment plans available. For comparison, an average apartment in Ramallah can cost anywhere from $170,000 to $1 million. For Eyad, the Israeli plans for the road will kill the chances of many Palestinians to own a home there.
“Apartment prices are already high in Ramallah, and businesses like mine are meant to offer some kind of solution for middle-income Palestinians who want to live in Ramallah,” he told Mondoweiss. “If the road becomes closed, entirely or partially, the prices will at least double, because the space for more urban buildings will be drastically limited around the city…and buying an apartment here will become available only for the most wealthy Palestinians.”
“Today, I was speaking to an employee at a bank in Ramallah, who has been looking for an apartment, and he told me that the current prices are just too high for him,” Shoufani said. “He is thinking of leaving the country altogether, because he can’t afford a home here, and if settlers’ plans go ahead in Ramallah, this will be the case for many more people like him.”
‘Taking the road back to Jewish hands’
The push to open the road to Israeli settlers has been driven by settler groups, according to Haaretz, under the slogan of “Taking the road back to Jewish hands.” This is because the road was originally carved out by the Israeli settlement council of Benyamin in 1994, without the approval of Israeli planning authorities. As other roads opened after the signing of the Oslo accords in 1993, this one was meant to not only to shorten the distance for settlers travelling between the settlements of Dolev in the west, adjacent to the Palestinian village of An Qinia, and the settlement of Beit El in the east, adjacent to the Jalazaun refugee camp, but also to limit the size of land to be returned to the Palestinian Authority’s self-administration.
The Israeli army’s chief of staff at the time opposed allowing Israeli settlers to use the road, which was dubbed Road 463, but then-Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres approved it. Then, during the Second Intifada between 2000 and 2005, Israeli forces blocked the use of the road to both Israelis and Palestinians, before gradually allowing Palestinians to use it in the years following the Intifada, as urbanization north of Ramallah resumed and later experienced a boom.
As the road became a busy Palestinian thoroughfare, especially with its easternmost part — crossing through what became practically an extension of Ramallah’s urban expanse — Israeli settlers stopped using it, and the Israeli army closed it to Israeli circulation altogether.
In recent months, Israeli settler groups have staged several “visits” to the area along the road, placing Israeli flags on the roundabouts, later to be removed by Palestinians, and performing group dances at a city park near the road. Haaretz quoted an Israeli army source confirming that the army “is working to put in place special security arrangements for future travel on the route.” For Palestinians, opening up a road to Israeli settlers does not mean having to share a road. It means new checkpoints and iron gates will come first, and then settlers will follow.
The Ramallah municipality, which currently maintains the road, has announced steps to counter Israeli plans. These include, according to the municipality’s statement, organizing social and cultural activities in the area and increasing infrastructure and maintenance work there to strengthen the Palestinian presence.
But Palestinians’ limited options to protect their movement on the vital road seem to be an uphill battle against Israeli preparations. Haaretz reported that Israeli media quoted Israel Ganz, the head of the Yesha council, which groups settlement councils across the West Bank, confirming that opening the road to settler traffic had been approved in principle, that a budget had been allocated, and that the army had already begun preparing. The fact that part of the road runs through areas classified as Area C — the 60% of the West Bank that falls under Israeli military control as part of the 1993 Oslo Accords — provides the administrative grounds for the Israeli army to open the road for settlers. But the reality is that the majority of the road used by Palestinians falls within Areas A and B — the 18 percent and 22 percent of the territory falling, respectively, under full PA administrative and security control and joint Israeli-PA control.
A growing pattern
This is not the first time that Israeli control is planned inside a Palestinian city’s urban parts that fall within Area A. In fact, it is already a reality on the ground in other West Bank cities. In Hebron, the Old City has been under direct Israeli military control for decades, alongside the presence of 400 Israeli settlers, in the heart of the largest Palestinian city in the West Bank. Last May, in Jenin, the Israeli army established a military base in the Jabriyat neighborhood, inside Jenin city. In June, Israeli settler groups announced plans to establish 100 settler outposts in areas classified as Area A. These plans were endorsed by Israel’s hardline Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich.
But giving Israeli settlers access to this road in Ramallah would have much larger repercussions, as the city represents the center of the PA’s self-government regime, while serving as a work hub for countless humanitarian organizations, cultural institutions, and international diplomatic missions. Ramallah is also the center of finance and commerce in the West Bank, and has a mixed population of Palestinians from across the entire territory, in addition to Palestinian Jerusalemites and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship.
Despite the almost-daily Israeli army raids into Ramallah’s neighborhoods, the city has been considered a prosperous bubble of Palestinian stability by many Palestinians, although it has drawn considerable criticism for what some say is a normalization of the Israeli occupation.
The planned settler road would stand to shatter that normalcy, as any Israeli expansion into this major urban area would have significant symbolic and political implications for Palestinians and the perception of the PA’s efficacy.
Since October 2023, Israeli settlers have taken over 1 million dunums (1,000 square kilometers) of Palestinian land across the West Bank and established between 100 and 150 outposts, many of which have been recognized by the Israeli government. This takeover has displaced at least 107 Palestinian communities. In May, the Israeli anti-occupation group Peace Now reported that the Israeli government had allocated $270 million to build more roads to connect Israeli settlements and settlement outposts across the West Bank.

Traffic chaos in Kyiv after Russian strikes hit key bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:59:30 UTC
19:59:30 KST

A Russian drone struck the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River in Kyiv around 5:40 p.m. local time, as Russia takes aim at the bridge for two days straight.
At the time of the fourth drone strike, the bridge was still closed for traffic from an earlier attack in the morning, said Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Black smoke could be seen rising over the bridge, while the damage to the structure is not yet determined.
The Russian attack coincided with Kyiv's evening rush hour, adding further stress to the already congested city. Kyiv's other main bridges across the Dnipro River, the Darnytskyi Bridge, Metro Bridge, and Podilskyi Bridge, have been changed to single direction traffic, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMDA).
Kostiantyn Kryvolap, an aviation expert and former Antonov test engineer, told the Kyiv Independent that destruction of the bridge is most likely not the intent behind Russia's strikes.
"Destroying a bridge with a 50-kilogram explosive charge, even with a highly effective warhead designed to destroy steel bridge structures, is a major exaggeration. It is practically impossible. For a bridge like this, these strikes are more like mosquito bites," he said.
Instead, the idea behind the Russian strikes may rather be to halt traffic, interrupt logistics, and exert psychological pressure on Kyiv's population, according to him.
The Southern Bridge is one of the capital's main traffic arteries and connects important transport routes like the the M-05 Kyiv-Odesa, M-06 Kyiv-Chop, and M-03 Kyiv-Kharkiv-Izyum-Sloviansk highways. Every day, between 100,000 and 110,000 cars use the bridge, according to information from the Darnytskyi District administration from 2019.
Head of the Desnyanskyi district of Kyiv, Maksym Bakhmatov, told The Village in a 2020 interview that about 90% of transit traffic between the two banks passes through the Southern Bridge.
Hlib Vyshlinsky, executive director of the Center for Economic Strategy told the Kyiv Independent that the Southern Bridge is also crucial for the daily commute of the Pozniaky-Osokorky-Kharkivsky districts conglomeration that houses up to 500,000 people.
Serhii Fursa, deputy managing director at investment firm Dragon Capital, told the Kyiv Independent that these attacks are unlikely to affect the Ukrainian economy massively.
"I do not think there is significant economic effect by this attack. But there is moderate negative impact. But we would not see it on GDP level numbers. There are a number of bridges," he said.
The earlier closure of the bridge in Kyiv caused major traffic jams across the capital and disrupted public transport between the city's eastern and western banks, city authorities said on Oct. 2.
The KMDA said on Oct. 2 that the Southern Bridge was closed in both directions. Some public buses were rerouted via the Darnytskyi Bridge.
According to Klitschko, movement on the Metro Bridge is limited to one lane from the eastern bank toward the western bank, while traffic on the Paton Bridge is fully restricted from the western bank toward the eastern bank.
Amid the disruption, some Kyiv residents were crossing the Dnipro River bridges on foot as traffic remained heavily congested, social media footage showed.
The Southern Bridge, which carries both road traffic and the metro across the Dnipro, was struck multiple times on Oct. 1 and early Oct. 2. Its road surface, a bridge support, a guardrail, and a protective concrete structure around the metro line were damaged in the attacks.
Russian drones struck near the bridge's supports at around 11:30 a.m. on Oct. 1 while cars and a metro train were crossing, according to Klitschko. Traffic was temporarily halted, but city officials later said a preliminary inspection found no critical structural damage and reopened the bridge.
The bridge was hit again overnight on Oct. 2, with the latest strike damaging a bridge support, part of the road surface, a barrier and a protective concrete structure around the metro line, Klitschko said.
Emergency crews were sent to the site and the metro tracks were de-energized. Traffic, including metro and surface public transport, was subsequently suspended.
A Russian overnight attack on Kyiv killed one person and injured two others, local authorities reported early on Oct. 2.
Kyiv has faced repeated Russian attacks in recent days. A large-scale Russian missile and drone attack beginning on Sept. 30 killed four people and injured at least eight, while also damaging residential and energy infrastructure in the capital.
Tis week alone, the capital had 56 air raid sirens, lasting over 87 hours in total, KMDA said on Oct. 2.

An American found a diamond that could be worth more than $1 million during a TikTok livestream
Kyiv • UNN
A U.S. Navy reservist dug up a 6.03-carat diamond in Arkansas. The find was valued at more than $1 million.
A U.S. Navy Reserve serviceman who has been sifting through rocks in Arkansas for more than a decade found a 6.03-carat diamond that collectors believe could be worth more than $1 million. The Independent reports, UNN writes.
Details
Jack Pireidin openly admits that his hobby of searching for gemstones has never made him any money.
However, the stone he dug up with a friend in one of Arkansas’s fields earlier this year did not resemble anything he had found before. Collectors told him that the diamond could be worth more than $1 million.
One experienced appraiser said that a diamond of such size and quality could be worth a quarter of that amount.
The discovery took place during a livestream of Pireidin’s search on TikTok.
"Oh my God! Oh my God!" Pireidin exclaimed.
This is the largest diamond found this year at Crater of Diamonds State Park.
Since the former open-pit diamond mine became part of the state park in 1972, more than 37,000 diamonds have been found there.
For $15, park visitors can fill a five-gallon bucket with rocks, and they can keep any gemstones they find.
Most of these finds are small and may be worth a few hundred dollars.
The largest diamond ever found in the United States—a 40.23-carat stone called the Uncle Sam—was found in this park in 1924.
According to park employee Sarah Beavens, between 400 and 800 diamonds are found there each year, most of them weighing about a quarter of a carat.
However, larger stones are also found, said the park’s deputy manager, Waymon Cox.
In 2020, an Arkansas bank manager found a 9-carat diamond in the park. In 2024, a French tourist dug up a 7-carat diamond there.

Appeal court lengthens British man's sentence for attempted murder of Finnish woman
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
13:57:45 EEST
19:57:45 KST

The Eastern Finland Court of Appeal has increased the sentence handed down to a British man found guilty of trying to murder a Finnish woman in January 2025.
North Karelia District Court had previously sentenced 32-year-old Satinder Minhas to a five-and-a-half-year prison term on charges of attempted murder, two counts of attempted assault as well as an additional charge of aggravated endangerment of traffic safety.
The appeal court lengthened this sentence, ordering him to serve six and a half years behind bars, and also increased the amount of compensation he was ordered to pay to his intended victim.
A psychological assessment carried out during the first trial found that Minhas was of reduced responsibility at the time of the offence, but he understood the nature of his actions. This finding was taken into consideration by the district court when handing down the sentence.
In its own ruling, the Court of Appeal stated that Minhas should have been sentenced to eight years in prison — not seven years as decided by the district court — for his crimes, which could then be reduced on the basis of diminished responsibility.
Police: Motive was revenge
During the trial, the court heard that Minhas travelled from the UK to Joensuu in eastern Finland after refusing to accept the woman's wish to remain only friends. She had also ended their online friendship and informed him she was already in a relationship with someone else.
The woman told police during the pre-trial investigation that the man's arrival in Finland was a complete surprise to her, as they had never discussed meeting in person.
Investigators concluded that Minhas had developed feelings for the woman through their online conversations, and he came to Finland to seek revenge for what he saw as her rejection of him.
After arriving in Finland, Minhas followed the woman for a period of about five days before confronting her as she made her way home from a grocery store. He first tried to force the victim into his rental car, telling her he had a knife.
The woman fled, but Minhas made three separate attempts to knock her down with his rental car. He also rammed another vehicle after the woman jumped into its back seat to escape his attempts to run her down.
The woman fled again and Minhas began chasing her with a hammer, which he dropped after being wrestled to the ground by members of the public.
They then detained him until police arrived. When Minhas was searched, he was also found to be carrying a knife, while there were two ropes, cable ties, and a chainsaw in his rental car — all of which had been acquired in Joensuu.
The appeal court's verdict is also not yet final, meaning the ruling can be appealed further to Finland's Supreme Court.

Frankreich erwägt Freigabe von Öl- und Dieselreserven nach US-Druck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:57:29 UTC
19:57:29 KST

Frankreich erwägt Freigabe von Öl- und Dieselreserven nach US-Druck
Paris hat vorgeschlagen, 100 Millionen Barrel Rohöl und Diesel freizugeben. Eine offizielle Bestätigung gibt es noch nicht. Deutschland will den Forderungen Washingtons noch nicht nachgeben.
French President Emmanuel Macron (C) walks with France's Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noël Barrot (L) as they head to Trump Tower in New York City on Sept. 21, 2026, ahead of a meeting with US President Donald Trump. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
BRÜSSEL - Französische Regierungsvertreter haben am Freitag bei Krisengesprächen eine umfangreiche Freigabe strategischer Öl- und Dieselreserven vorgeschlagen, wie zwei mit den Einzelheiten des Treffens vertraute Personen POLITICO berichteten. Zuvor hatte Washington europäische Regierungen gedrängt, ihre Vorräte auszuschütten, andernfalls drohe ein Verbot von US-Dieselexporten.
Der Vorschlag aus Paris, der am Freitag bei einem Treffen hochrangiger europäischer Energiebeamter unterbreitet wurde, sieht laut Angaben der Informanten vor, dass die EU-Länder 50 Millionen Barrel Rohöl und 50 Millionen Barrel Diesel freigeben sollten. Der Vorschlag werde derzeit noch einer technischen Prüfung unterzogen, sagte einer der Informanten.
POLITICO hatte zuvor berichtet, dass US-Energieminister Chris Wright von mehreren EU-Staaten forderte, über einen Zeitraum von drei Monaten 120 Millionen Barrel aus ihren Vorräten freizugeben, um den steigenden Dieselpreisen entgegenzuwirken und damit Exportbeschränkungen abzuwenden. Den Informanten zufolge war das Kompromissangebot Frankreichs am Freitag eine Reaktion auf eine erneute Aufforderung der USA an den französischen Präsidenten Emmanuel Macron, 100 Millionen Barrel Kraftstoff freizugeben, wobei es sich ausschließlich um Diesel handeln sollte.
Advertisement
Berlin hingegen zögerte laut den Informanten, überhaupt Barrel freizugeben. „Deutschland und andere Länder wollen nicht instrumentalisiert werden; sie möchten ihre Vorräte nur aus echten Gründen der Versorgungssicherheit freigeben“, sagte einer von ihnen POLITICO unter der Bedingung der Anonymität, um – wie auch andere in diesem Artikel – offen sprechen zu können. Deutschland und Frankreich verfügen laut offiziellen EU-Statistiken über die größten Reserven an Öl und Erdölprodukten in Europa.
„Frankreich ist sehr daran interessiert, sich zu beteiligen und der Bitte nachzukommen … es ist klar, dass die EU etwas unternehmen wird, sofern sie sich auf etwas einigen kann“, sagte die zweite Person. Sie fügten hinzu, dass unklar sei, ob die Freigabe gemeinsam von der EU koordiniert oder auf bilateraler Basis erfolgen werde, angesichts des „chaotischen“ Vorgehens der USA, die unterschiedliche Anfragen an verschiedene Länder gerichtet hätten. „Das ist eine typische Anfrage der USA – sie nutzen nicht die üblichen offiziellen Kanäle.“
Ein Sprecher des französischen Wirtschaftsministers Roland Lescure wies den Vorschlag als „Gerüchte“ zurück und lehnte eine weitere Stellungnahme ab. In einer Erklärung teilte der Élysée-Palast mit, dass Emmanuel Macron „so bald wie möglich“ ein Treffen der G7-Staats- und Regierungschefs einberufen werde, „um die erforderlichen Maßnahmen zu koordinieren, die dazu beitragen sollen, den Preisdruck zu mildern und die Versorgung mit Rohöl und Raffinerieprodukten in den G7-Ländern sowie weltweit sicherzustellen“.
Macron führte am Donnerstagabend ein Telefongespräch mit US-Präsident Donald Trump, um „die weltweite Energiesituation zu erörtern“ und „die weltweite Verfügbarkeit von Raffinerieprodukten sicherzustellen“, teilte der Élysée-Palast mit.
Britische Regierungsvertreter erwarten die Einberufung eines G7-Treffens bereits am Freitag, doch seien unmittelbare Ergebnisse unwahrscheinlich, so eine mit der Angelegenheit vertraute Person, der Anonymität gewährt wurde, um über sensible Fragen der Treibstoffversorgung zu sprechen. Eine etwaige Freigabe von Reserven in Europa würde unter der Leitung der IEA erfolgen, so die Person.
Die USA sind zunehmend frustriert über EU-Länder, die ihre Zusagen zu der 400-Millionen-Barrel-Freigabe Anfang des Jahres nicht eingehalten haben. Diese hatte die Internationale Energieagentur (IEA) nach Ausbruch des Krieges im Iran und der Schließung der Straße von Hormus koordiniert. Bei der Sitzung der hochrangigen Energy Union Taskforce am Freitag kritisierten einige EU-Länder laut einer der informierten Personen auch Frankreich und Deutschland dafür, dass sie keine nennenswerten Ölreserven auf den Markt gebracht hätten.
POLITICO berichtete am Donnerstag, dass führende EU-Länder und Großbritannien auf den Druck der USA mit einer „entschlossenen“ Haltung reagieren wollten, gleichzeitig aber eine Deeskalation anstrebten.
Nicolas Camut und Charlie Cooper haben zu diesem Bericht beigetragen. Der Text erschien zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO.

Ukraine testing five models of jet drone interceptors – Zelensky

Ukraine testing five models of jet drone interceptors – Zelensky
According to Ukrinform, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in an interview with the Financial Times.
According to the Ukrainian leader, Ukraine will be able to produce about 400 of one of the interceptor drone models by the end of October. Four other models remain in the testing stage.
Zelensky said the race to counter the Russian drones faced hurdles, including a shortage of engines for their interceptors.
"Engines [are] the key, we really import a lot of engines. There are some engines of our production, but not enough," he said.
He noted that Ukraine also faced a budget hole that was preventing the development and mass production of crucial defensive arms.
According to Zelensky, U.S.-made F-16 jets were proving effective against Russia's new jet-powered drones, but that too many of the aircraft – around half – were spending lengthy periods in Europe for repairs and maintenance. Some jets, he said, were taking so long to return that Ukraine was losing valuable time when the fighters were most needed to defend its skies.
Zelensky stressed that Kyiv wanted its western partners' help to move more maintenance work inside Ukraine, arguing that keeping the aircraft closer to the battlefield would allow them to be returned to service faster.
He criticized the U.S. and European governments for what he described as insufficient political will to force Putin to end the war, arguing that Ukraine's partners had the economic and diplomatic leverage to exert greater pressure on Moscow.
When asked whether his partners were doing all they could to help Kyiv, Zelensky said: "Not enough, of course not enough."
As reported, the Ukrainian Armed Forces are already testing four promising models of interceptor drones on the front line to counter Russian forces' jet-powered UAVs, while about ten more manufacturers are testing their own designs.
Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine Kyrylo Budanov said that countries with existing agreements with Kyiv on cooperation in the drone sector could agree to gain access to Ukraine's latest technologies for countering Russia's new jet-powered drones.

FlyDubai pilot tells his survival story in emotional call with Indian leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

FlyDubai captain tells India's leader how he saved himself and 173 others while fighting for his own life
The FlyDubai captain attacked by his co-pilot on a Wednesday flight to Israel says his faith gave him the courage to seize what he believed to be a last chance to save himself and the 173 other people on board the plane.
Flight captain Smit Machchhar told India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi in an emotional video call from his hospital bed in Saudi Arabia on Thursday that, despite multiple stab wounds, he managed to open the cockpit door to let in passengers who subdued the attacking co-pilot, likely saving the 174 people on the Boeing 737.
"I was fighting for my life," said Machchhar, who is an Indian national. "When I was lying on the floor I could feel the aircraft was going down. I knew exactly that this would be the last push. I told myself that if I didn't get up, there would be a problem. I managed to open the door, and then everyone else came in."
Machchhar told Modi how, in his darkest moments, he repeated Hindu religious chants and clung to his faith, believing "God would save us."
He apologized for breaking down in tears as he told the Indian leader he had never really been "proud of myself, but today I am."
The first question Modi asked Machchhar was how he was feeling, to which Machchhar, wearing a bandage around his head and with an oxygen tube still in his nose, replied simply: "All good, sir."
"I am not thinking about the wounds that much," the captain said. "I look at this as a journey. I am confident of my recovery and return."
"Get better and healthy, the whole nation is with you," the Indian leader told him. "I don't want to bother you much. My best wishes are with you."
Co-pilot transferred to UAE for questioning
The co-pilot of FlyDubai flight 1073, who has not been identified by authorities, was transferred Thursday from Saudi Arabia to the United Arab Emirates for questioning by Israeli, UAE and Saudi officials, an Israeli official confirmed to CBS News on Friday.
"As time passes, the picture is becoming clearer; the attacker underwent Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane with its passengers," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday. "We are investigating whether he was dispatched, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price."
Saudi officials said Wednesday that the co-pilot was hospitalized after the incident and treated for unspecified injuries.
An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the copilot was born in Oman and currently holds Omani citizenship, but Oman's government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.
Netanyahu said Thursday that Israel knew he had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination" based on "personal information" gathered during initial questioning. He offered no further information on the alleged indoctrination Thursday or Friday, but told Fox News on Thursday that the alleged attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"
President Trump on Thursday suggested the co-pilot was linked to Iran, going further than Netanyahu, who had said it was still "too early to say" if Iran could have been involved.
"We're working on it right now," Mr. Trump said Thursday at the White House when a reporter asked if the co-pilot had links to Iran. "They're being very open with us. I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes. But we're working on it right now."
Asked if the co-pilot could have been working for or with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps or radicalized some other way, Mr. Trump replied that he "could've been, yeah."

Nepal plans to drain four glacial lakes after a deadly flood

Unknown Publisher

Nepal plans to drain four glacial lakes after a deadly flood
Kyiv • UNN
Nepal will launch a six-year, $50 million project to lower the levels of four glacial lakes. The goal is to prevent dam breaches and floods.
Nepal will launch a large-scale program this fiscal year to drain four glacial lakes located high in the mountains, in an effort to reduce flood risks. Officials made the announcement after a recent disaster that killed more than 1,400 people, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Rescuers are still searching for more than 5,000 people who went missing in the border region with China after a glacier collapse in August triggered landslides and a sudden flood that tore through the valley.
"Our goal is to reduce the risk of the lakes breaching natural dams and to lower the risk of flooding downstream," said Subash Tuladhar, an expert at the government research center tasked with overseeing the new project.
He said channels would divert water into nearby rivers in a controlled manner, adding that workers face health risks from prolonged periods of work at high altitude, as well as the danger of sudden floods.
Design work and detailed studies targeting the central and eastern lakes of Tula Gi, Lower Barun, Lumding Tsho and Hongu II will begin in the fiscal year that runs until mid-July 2027, authorities said.
The United Nations Development Programme and the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) said in a 2020 report that the lakes, located at elevations ranging from 4,050 to 5,483 meters, are among the most potentially dangerous in Nepal.
Nepal had the skills and experience needed for the $50 million project, which will be financed by the Green Climate Fund, UNDP and the government, added Tuladhar of the Nepal Center for Hydrology and Water Resources Research.
Work to divert water "through sluice structures" will begin after a detailed study and could take up to six years, said the Center's Executive Director Sanjib Baral.
They will include installing sensors, flood forecasting and warning systems, as well as efforts to improve resilience downstream and prepare communities for the risks.
In similar earlier efforts, Nepal lowered the level of the central Himalayan glacial lake Tsho Rolpa by 3 meters in 2000 and that of Imja Lake near Mount Everest, the world's highest peak, 10 years ago.
The disaster in Nepal served as a warning to the world, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said last month in a passionate speech before the United Nations, in which he blamed climate change against the backdrop of his country's negligible emissions.
The retreat of glaciers, unstable mountain slopes and increasingly unpredictable rivers showed that Nepal is paying a high price, he added.
In Nepal, where about 26 glacial lake outburst floods have been recorded over the past four decades, more than 300 people die on average each year from extreme weather events, while property damage runs into millions of dollars.
The latest floods destroyed a dozen hydropower plants, roads, bridges, farms and settlements. Officials said Nepal, which is in a difficult situation, will need nearly $5 billion for rapid recovery.
Climatologists say that as temperatures rise, glaciers in the Himalayas are retreating, leaving behind unstable glacial lakes held back by little more than rock and ice above valleys where millions of people live.
Lowering lake levels by 3 meters would significantly reduce the threat, said Samjwal Ratna Bajracharya, a retired ICIMOD expert on glaciers, glacial lakes and glacial lake outburst floods.

Digested week: My heart sank at seeing Labour’s ‘Hope Again’ conference slogan. But then came Andy Burnham | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:55:39 UTC
19:55:39 KST

Monday
Words I thought I’d never write. We owe a huge debt of gratitude to the Tory party. Look, I know we ended up with Theresa May and Boris Johnson in the Conservative party leadership contests of 2016 and 2019 – and they were shockers, both of them – but at least the Tory MPs twice ensured we dodged the bullet of Michael Gove. Last week, Sky broadcast The War Game, a reality show for superannuated politicians and former senior civil servants and military officers. The setup was that the Russians had engineered an attack on a British warship in the North Sea and over the course of four episodes set in the Cobra emergency situation room, the assembled cast had to figure how to respond. We were left hanging at the final credits, but a nuclear apocalypse felt like the most likely outcome. And for that we have The Govester to thank. He was playing the prime minister and – to be blunt – he had an absolute shocker. For the first two episodes he seemed to be in a coma. All he could manage was to repeat back what the last person had said to him and then shout “asap”. But that was far more preferable to the Gove that turned up for the last two episodes. Despite frequently being warned about the dangers of escalation and the inadequacy of the UK war machine, Mikey kept on taking the option that would get the most people killed. Why bomb one Russian city when you can bomb two? The game ended with what were almost certainly nuclear warheads minutes away from destroying a major city in the UK. Still, Gove wasn’t the only deadbeat. Nicola Sturgeon, acting the deputy prime minister, was as hopeless as you would expect of someone who failed to notice her kitchen filling up with new appliances. It was terrifying TV. Not so much in the premise. What was really scary was the knowledge that our politicians were even more clueless than the rest of us.
Tuesday
Pep Guardiola timed his departure well. Perhaps he had an inkling of what was coming down the road. The top bods at Manchester City have predictably responded to being found guilty of 114 charges of financial misconduct by insisting they will appeal and drag out proceedings. No doubt hoping that either the charges will go away or they can reduce the potential penalties. I wouldn’t bet against it. My main reaction when the news broke that City had been found guilty was surprise. Not that I thought they were innocent – there wasn’t a football fan who didn’t think they were bang to rights – but that the Premier League finally got round to doing something about it. The earliest charges date back 17 years and it just felt as if nothing was ever going to happen. What happens next is anyone’s guess. Obviously any fine would be more or less meaningless as the City owners have bottomless pockets. Removing titles is equally pointless. Who would turn up for an open-topped bus ride for a cup won years ago? The issue of compensation is more nuanced. Because where does it all end? Can I file a claim for mental distress, not to mention the travel and ticket costs, for having paid to see countless matches which had been financially rigged against Spurs that are now null and void? There again, I have had two of my best nights ever at the Etihad. When Spurs secured a Champions League place for the first time and when we won a Champions League quarter-final thanks to City having an injury time goal disallowed by VAR. There has also been talk of a 50-point deduction. Probably not enough to ensure they finish behind Spurs. We’re only five games into the season and already 13 points adrift.
Wednesday
By a very rough calculation, I reckon I’ve spent the best part of six months of my life at party conferences. And yes, I am a lucky man to be doing a job I love, but it is sometimes hard not to feel a wee bit jaded during the conference season. Living out of a suitcase and listening to a series of speeches from politicians who can often barely hold their own attention let alone an audience’s, can make the days feel very long. And I was prepared for more of the same when I arrived in Liverpool for this week’s Labour conference. My heart sank when I saw banners, mugs and T-shirts with the slogan “Hope Again” everywhere. There’s nothing more guaranteed to see me sliding into despair then people loudly instructing me to look on the bright side. To make it worse, I had to endure the chancellor, John Healey, lie through his teeth and say “I am an optimist”. You’re fooling no one, John. He had clearly been told to be upbeat and dropped the H-word about 20 times. But on every occasion he gasped “Hope” it looked like a dagger had been plunged into his heart. Come the end, the whole audience was signing up to Dignitas. But then, Andy Burnham. By far and away the most powerful, emotional and gamechanging leader’s speech of the century. I can’t tell you how rare it is for a politician to hold an audience in his hands for an hour and say exactly what he thinks, feels and believes. Only Nigel Farage comes close, though what he offers is only anger, grievance and division. Burnham was offering something else. I may not have agreed with the details of all of it and most of it may never happen, but this was a world of social care, closer ties to the EU and electoral reform to which most in the socially progressive world could sign up. It was as though the sun had come out.
Thursday
When I turned 50, friends used to assure me that 50 was the new 40. That felt almost true. I can remember my Dad’s 50th birthday and he looked ancient to me. For my 60th birthday, those same friends were confident that 60 was the new 50. There was the slight drawback that I had already had a knee replacement, but I still went to the gym four times a week and my career was in good shape. Next week I will be 70. No one has even tentatively suggested that 70 might be the new 60. Seventy is unequivocally old. Some might even say that 70 is the new 80. I am now undeniably at the business end of life. My children are both in their 30s and have gone on to live their best lives. Much of my work as a parent is done. I had a heart attack two and a half years ago and am doing my best to avoid another one. My wife is being treated for cancer. Yes, I still enjoy my work and go to the gym four times a week but, as the great Leonard Cohen so exquisitely put it, “I ache in the places where I used to play”. It’s been weird watching the series 70 Up. I’ve always felt a kinship with the men and women in the documentary because I’ve followed them since I was 14 when they were the same age and felt grateful that my own life had not been part of the social experiment. But now we hear that 70 is to be the end point of the series. As though the lives have come to a meaningful end. I’m not quite so ready to go quietly into the night. I plan to keep going for a while yet. And for those of you who would like to join me trying to make sense of the world, there are still tickets available for my shows at the Komedia in Brighton on 18 October and at the MAC in Birmingham on 31 October.
Friday
My happy place. The Celebrity Traitors is back and all is more or less well with the world. The first episode may not have quite lived up to the hype but as a scene setter it was more than good enough. The side missions increasingly feel pointless – we all know everyone is in it for their ego and career rather than the charity cash – and in any case the celebs always need time to bed in and show their true colours. Though not Ross Kemp, who was showing worrying levels of paranoia from the off. Who will be the Alan Carr, a true star of the series? Who will be the Stephen Fry, all affected diffidence? And who will be the David Olusoga, the one who tried to work things through with careful intelligence yet always comes to the wrong conclusion? The first to show his face was actor Michael Sheen who declared that he didn’t know what he was letting himself in for and then said “I’m a huge fan of the game”. Hmm. Maybe he’s been watching with his eyes closed. The rest of the celebs trooped in one by one and we were up and running. Things soon hotted up when Claudia nominated Maya – never heard of her – and Richard E Grant as traitors. Richard was so thrilled – he had been desperate to be a traitor – that he promptly blew the show wide open by telling all the other celebs that he was a traitor. A move that may prove to be utterly inspired or catastrophically dim. Given a night to sleep on it, Richard was inclined to believe it might have been the latter and spent the rest of the day trying to persuade everyone it was a bluff. Sit back and enjoy the next five weeks.

Ukrainian foreign minister discusses protection of Ukraine against Russian attacks with NATO representative
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has held a meeting with Geoffrey van Leeuwen, Chief of Staff of the NATO Secretary General.
Source: Andrii Sybiha on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Sybiha and van Leeuwen discussed further cooperation and assistance to help protect Ukrainian cities and put an end to Russia's drone and missile terror. Specifically, more than 230 air-raid warnings were issued in Kyiv in September.
Quote from Sybiha: "I briefed him on Russia's ongoing terror campaign, including the use of jet-powered Shahed drones, and on the steps needed to counter it. We appreciate his readiness to visit Ukraine and witness firsthand the conditions in which our people and cities live every day."

Feijóo: In Ceuta, it’s up to Europe to clean up the Spanish government’s mess
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:51:49 UTC
19:51:49 KST

Police officers keep watch over a group of migrants outside the entrance to the Loma del Colmenar reception centre in Ceuta on 1 September 2026. | Antonio Sempere/AFP via Getty Images
Alberto Núñez Feijóo is Spain’s leader of the opposition and the president of the People’s Party.
On July 30, at least 80,000 people crossed into Ceuta from Morocco, the largest violation of territorial integrity we have experienced in recent decades. That challenge tested the resilience of Spain’s southern border and, therefore, of Europe’s southern border. It continues 50 days later. With no clear prospect of when it might be resolved. It is therefore time to ask ourselves whether our response matches the scale of what is at stake.
A border is not just a line on a map. It is the expression of a political community that decides which values to protect and which responsibilities to share. When a European border is breached, Europe as a whole becomes weaker. When a border is not properly defended, Europe as a whole is left unprotected. That is what is happening.
Advertisement
The response of the current Spanish government, incapable of acknowledging the true nature of the problem and implementing the correct solution, obliges me to reiterate, first and foremost, the obvious, as the President of Ceuta did last week during his visit to Brussels. We are not witnessing a conventional migration crisis, but rather the consequences of an invasion originating from Morocco, which must therefore be held responsible for having condoned or instigated it.
Normality has disappeared from Ceuta for more than six weeks, and the scenes of chaos, overcrowding and insecurity should both shame us and compel us to act. To think that the prolongation of this situation will have no consequences is a mistake we cannot afford to make: it affects our sovereignty, our collective capacity to defend the rule of law, the safety of our citizens, and the credibility of the European project in ensuring its own stability.
Undoubtedly, the national authorities are the first to bear the responsibility for resolving this crisis, in accordance with a non-negotiable principle shared by all EU member states under the Pact on Migration and Asylum: those who have entered irregularly must be returned. All of them. The Spanish government’s obligation is not to find accommodation for them, but to expedite their departure.
That said, given the time that has elapsed and the escalation of violent incidents in Ceuta, Europe as a whole must recognize the failure of the Spanish government and exert the necessary pressure to prevent this crisis from becoming entrenched, spreading, or happening again. Just as Europe has responded when faced with other hybrid threats — on energy, trade or disinformation — the attack on our southern border now demands the same determination.
Firstly, the European Union must ensure that Spain implements, with due rigor and efficiency, all the European instruments available to facilitate returns. Secondly, it must clarify why the Kingdom of Morocco itself has reiterated in an official statement its willingness to take back all those who entered on July 30, while Spanish ministers maintain that no such cooperation exists.
Thirdly, it must make full use of all its diplomatic resources to ensure that the relationship with Morocco, a strategic partner for Spain and for the rest of Europe, continues to develop on the basis of transparency and mutual respect. While I advocate the need to establish a loyal and stable relationship with our neighboring country, I believe it is in the interests of the entire European Union to ensure that this relationship is not undermined by the exploitation of migration flows or by the questioning of the Spanish identity of Ceuta and Melilla, territories that are just as European as Berlin, Paris or Brussels.
Advertisement
Finally, I would like to stress that humanity cannot be used as an excuse for inaction in response to what has happened. It is true that the attack on Ceuta did not involve soldiers, that many of those who crossed Europe’s southern border were themselves victims and that, in fact, more than a hundred people died. But contrary to what some cynically claim, it is precisely humanity that compels us to discourage people from risking their lives at sea: this must cease to be a valid means of reaching Europe.
As many know, I aspire to become the next prime minister of Spain. Consequently, it is my duty to seek the support of the European Union and all of its member states for my country at this crucial moment. The first duty of a leader is to guarantee the safety of citizens, defend national sovereignty and uphold the credibility of institutions. But this also reflects a commitment to a certain way of understanding Europe, one that I personally share with all our allies: the responsibility to safeguard its territorial integrity and its values is a shared one. Now it is our turn to defend Ceuta, Spain and Europe.
POLITICO occasionally publishes opinion pieces from guest authors to offer our readers a range of perspectives on the intersection of power and politics. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of POLITICO.

we watched marina abramović die seven times in a shadowy cisterne beneath copenhagen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:50:40 UTC
19:50:40 KST

we watched marina abramović die seven times in a shadowy cisterne beneath copenhagen
inside a damp underground reservoir, viewers follow operatic deaths from screen to screen, accompanied by a soprano's haunting voice.
opera reaches us before the screen does
Beneath Copenhagen’s Søndermarken park, opera travels through the dark before we can locate its source. Water drips from overhead, and puddles catch what little light reaches the floor. A low rumble of music moves through the former reservoir at Cisternerne and spreads beyond the screen where it began. During our visit this spring, we could only make out portions of the dim space which sprawled into darkness before us. Small theater-like setups emerged from the shadows as we moved farther inside, each with seats facing a glowing screen.
Here, Marina Abramović’s Seven Deaths places the artist inside seven doomed female roles made famous by Maria Callas. The performance artist appears opposite actor Willem Dafoe in a series of short films, accompanied by recordings of the soprano’s voice. The installation takes about an hour to experience in full. Its subject is familiar to anyone who has sat through an opera: a woman dies, and an audience stays to watch. At Cisternerne, that audience has to keep moving and re-experiencing her death over again.
seven endings, one body
Here in Copenhagen, Marina Abramović draws from operas whose heroines meet very different ends. Violetta dies of tuberculosis in La traviata, while Tosca jumps to her death. Desdemona is killed by Otello; Carmen by Don José. Each has her own story, although Seven Deaths brings their fates together through a single body. Abramović dies onscreen, then returns in the next film to die again.
The films draw on these stories without reproducing their original staging. They give the deaths a cinematic scale, with the artist‘s body becoming the point around which each scene is constructed. The title has already told us where everything is headed. We watch for how it happens, and for how long the image allows it to happen. The slow pace gives us time to look, even when the action makes looking uncomfortable.
the audience moves together
Only one film plays at a time, which gives Marina Abramović’s scattered theaters a shared rhythm. We join a small group already watching and take the available seats. When the short film ends, everyone rises. Low, echoing murmurs and the shuffle of feet replace the singing as the group moves quietly through the dark toward the next screen. For a few moments, watching becomes a practical exercise in finding somewhere to sit.
This repeated migration is a substantial part of the work at Cisternerne. In an opera house, the audience generally occupies the same seat while the scenery changes around the performers. Here, we change position between deaths. The darkness prevents an overall view of the installation, so each theater has to be found along the way. Sound reaches beyond those individual viewing areas, while the damp air and dripping water remain present through every scene. In this way, the room keeps intruding on the film.
a dying heroine still has a voice
Opera has long devoted some of its most memorable music to women approaching death. The plot brings a life toward its end while the singing gives that woman an extraordinary presence in the theater. Tosca’s ‘Vissi d’arte,’ sung before her final act, looks back on a life devoted to art and love. Listening means remaining with her, even when her fate is already known. The duration of the aria allows an audience to stay inside that feeling.
Seven Deaths separates the singing voice from the body we see. Abramović performs the deaths; Callas supplies the voice through recordings made during her lifetime. That separation becomes especially palpable underground, where the sound seems to occupy more space than the screen. Callas died in 1977, yet her singing continues to reach new listeners. As Abramović returns for another filmed death, the voice gives the sequence a continuity that the images repeatedly interrupt.
‘you give me your time’
Abramović describes a direct exchange with her audience: ‘you give me your time, and I die for you seven times.‘ At Cisternerne, that time includes the solemn gaps between films. We wait for an ending, stand with the people beside us, and follow them toward another set of seats. The group gradually becomes familiar through this repeated movement, even with very little conversation. Everyone is working through the same sequence.
She observes: ‘you die many times in life, and yet you continue living.‘ This opens her work beyond the literal deaths of its characters. An ending can feel absolute while a life continues beyond it. The installation gives that thought a physical rhythm: after each death, there is still another stretch of the reservoir to cross. We get up again, with water dripping overhead, and find the next screen.
project info:
name: Seven Deaths
artist: Marina Abramović
onscreen performers: Marina Abramović, Willem Dafoe
recorded vocals: Maria Callas
venue: Cisternerne, Frederiksberg, Copenhagen, Denmark
dates: March 14th — November 30th, 2026

Israel’s Supreme Court on Friday overturned a Central Elections Committee decision barring two Arab electoral lists from running in the Oct. 27 Knesset (parliament) election.
The ruling came after the court heard appeals Thursday from the Joint List, led by Yusuf Jabareen, the United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, and Joint List lawmaker Ofer Cassif.
Israel’s Channel 12 said the court ruled by a majority that Cassif was eligible to run.
“In addition, the judges unanimously decided to allow both the United Arab List and the Joint List to participate in the election,” the channel reported.
The ruling by Israel’s highest judicial body clears the way for both Arab lists to contest the election.
Separately, Sami Abu Shehadeh, a candidate on the Joint List and leader of the National Democratic Assembly party, announced Thursday evening that he was withdrawing his candidacy after the Supreme Court advised him to do so as a majority of judges favored disqualifying him.
Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israel’s population of 10 million, while opinion polls project Arab lawmakers to win between 12 and 14 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party, far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party, and other right-wing groups had submitted requests to disqualify the Arab lists to the Central Elections Committee, which approved them in September.

Indian authorities clamp down as ‘cockroach’ movement launches new protests
Demonstrators gathering in Mumbai and New Delhi to demand the resignation of Election Commission chief meet stern police response.
Indian security forces have clamped down as the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), other student coalitions and opposition forces gathered for planned protests in New Delhi and Mumbai.
Hundreds of police and paramilitary personnel surrounded a barricaded protest site in the centre of the capital on Friday and bundled demonstrators into buses as they arrived. The CJP warned the government last week that it would launch nationwide protests unless the Election Commission chief resigned amid a voter roll controversy.
Authorities closed at least 11 metro stations around the Jantar Mantar observatory, where the protesters were assembling, and repeatedly issued warnings to disperse from loudspeakers.
Delhi Police earlier imposed Section 163, which bars gatherings of more than five people, the use of slogans, speechmaking and other protest activities, The Times of India reported.
Reports about 3pm (09:30 GMT) suggested that more than 500 people – including former Delhi Chief Minister Atishi Marlena, members of the Aam Aadmi opposition party and members of student organisations – had been arrested in New Delhi.
“The right to protest is our fundamental right, and we want answers from the government on vote theft,” demonstrator Rishabh Singh said as police shoved him into a bus, according to the Reuters news agency.
In Mumbai, where protests were planned to begin at 4pm (10:30 GMT), a crowd slowly grew in Shivaji Park. A heavy police presence patrolled the area, where they also declared a no-parking zone.
The CJP called the latest round of protests after the Indian Express newspaper reported that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s two deputies had formally raised concerns at least 14 times in the past 10 months over revisions to voter lists, registration procedures and digital systems.
Critics said a nationwide voter-verification exercise launched last year led to millions of eligible voters being removed from electoral rolls. They said the changes favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.
The commission has denied the allegations and said the changes removed duplicate, deceased or ineligible voters.
The CJP said it plans to expand demonstrations nationwide in the coming days.
“We will ultimately end it only when Gyanesh Kumar resigns. He has to go,” Saurav Das, CJP’s convener, said in remarks on Friday that were reported by The Times of India.
“We will ensure that he is removed from that position, all his crimes are undone and he pays for the crimes he has committed against the young generation and against the country.”
Opposition protests led by the Indian National Congress party are also set to demand Kumar’s resignation starting on Tuesday.
India’s “cockroach movement” began with online satire mocking the government before amassing millions of followers on social media. It has since brought thousands onto the streets, including during mass demonstrations in July that led to the resignation of India’s education minister.
Those protests also drew an outsized police response with Amnesty International reporting that authorities used lethal weapons to suppress crowds.
