Life on a hair trigger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
25 minute listen
The day before we spoke, King1, 26, had learned that his friend Lamont had been killed. He was at home when his cousin called to break the news and asked him to come over. ‘I’m on my way,’ King replied immediately, knowing what was being asked of him. He ran up to his room to retrieve his Glock, opened his box of bullets and, one by one, filled the clip.
Lamont was dead, though King couldn’t fully wrap his mind around the fact. He’d seen him only hours earlier, when Lamont and King’s cousin stopped by his house. They’d been shot at by their rivals the day before, and King had warned them to be careful: ‘Y’all need to keep y’alls’ heads up.’ Now the car Lamont died in sat empty on a nearby street, shot up and stained with his blood. King watched a video posted on Facebook of paramedics draping the body with a sheet and carrying it into an ambulance.
King knew what came next. He and his cousin would go out with their guns and ride through the neighbourhood until they found the men responsible. ‘I just wanted my get-back,’ he said. He wanted the people who killed Lamont to feel what he was feeling. And if he couldn’t find them, he’d find someone else he had beef with. King reasoned: ‘It could be a person who I don’t like or who I’m already into it with. I’m going to slide on them too and whoever else. That’s how I grew up with my feelings. That’s how I let off my rage.’
To King, retaliation felt less like a choice than an inevitability. ‘Whether I do it or not, somebody going to do it,’ he said. ‘If it ain’t me, I got other homies who feel the same way I feel. I got cousins, family members, they mommas. That’s how it be, and that’s how it’s going to always be. It’s a repeated cycle.’
His clip was full. Then King decided to do something that a year earlier he would not have done.
For King, and for many Americans like him, gun violence is not an exceptional event but a fact of life. In some parts of the United States, lethal violence has reached a scale exceeding recent wars and military occupations. Between 2020 and 2021, a young man in Chicago’s Garfield Park neighbourhood, where King is from, faced a higher risk of being killed than a US soldier deployed to Afghanistan or Iraq. By age 40, around half of the city’s Black and Hispanic residents will have witnessed someone being shot.
Violent crime has fallen steeply across the US since 2021, though not everywhere. According to Chicago’s crime dashboard, fatal shootings in Chicago were up 7 per cent this year as of late September. But even in cities where the decline has held, a citywide figure is a poor description of how violence is experienced. In US cities, most shootings concentrate in a few dozen blocks and among a few hundred people who account for less than 1 per cent of a city’s population. Thus, citywide numbers cannot capture what it is like to live inside that zone, where violence is not a discrete event but an experience that leaves stubborn traces on many lives.
In 2022, I was part of a research team that interviewed 99 men from Chicago’s highest-violence neighbourhoods. All were former or current participants in the Rapid Employment and Development Initiative, or READI Chicago, a community violence intervention run by a partnership of Heartland Alliance, the University of Chicago and seven nonprofit organisations on the city’s south and west sides. READI served adult men at greatest risk of shooting someone or being shot. By the time they entered the programme, 98 per cent had been arrested, averaging more than 17 times each, and 35 per cent had been shot. For 18 months, participants were paid to work and attend group cognitive behavioural intervention (CBI) sessions. Outreach workers helped them navigate housing, legal, safety and substance-use crises that might otherwise have made steady participation difficult.
The men had learned to anticipate danger in ordinary moments and to meet it by fighting back
We asked each person we spoke with to tell us the story of his life, then to reconstruct minor confrontations, conflicts averted, and those that escalated into violence. We asked what they had been thinking and feeling as these events unfolded, returning to a single question: ‘What was going through your mind when that happened?’ Our aim was to access a layer of cognition beneath the behaviour, and to understand how the men made sense of their own actions and those of others.
Our conversations revealed something important about what violence teaches the mind. Lives spent amid violence meant the men had learned to anticipate danger in ordinary moments and to meet it by fighting back. The premise of READI’s work, and our research, is that because this way of seeing was learned, it could also be unlearned.
The danger these men read into the world is real; recall that more than a third of them had been shot. The difficulty is that a mind shaped by real danger does not confine its lessons to dangerous situations. It brings them into ambiguous ones, where the reading is wrong often enough to produce the very danger it anticipates. The outer world and the inner one are not separate. A world of violence sustains itself not only through guns, poverty and other social ills, but also through the ways of seeing it produces. Our research asks where these patterns of seeing and responding come from, why they persist, and how they can change.
Again and again, three patterns surfaced that could make future violence more likely.
The first was misreading situations. A great deal of violence, the men told us, stems from misconstruing some aspect of an interpersonal interaction, such as the nature of the situation or the other person’s intent. Past experiences of violence had created threat-oriented frames that quickly registered ambiguous cues as dangerous. Nuke, 24, told us that even a stranger looking at him for too long could escalate into a confrontation: ‘Sometimes I’ll react. Like: “Man, what the fuck is you looking at?”’
Tim, now 30, traced this reactive impulse to being shot and nearly killed at 17. ‘I was young in the streets, so I was always an impulsive person,’ he recalled. ‘But it got really bad after [I was shot]. I felt like the world was against me … If you approach me a certain type of way and if you wasn’t a person I was with on a daily basis, I felt like you was my enemy.’ Even casual remarks became charged: ‘Before that incident, I’ll be like: “Man, whatever.” But now it’s like: “Man, what you mean by that?… You saying that you going to shoot me?”’ Like many others we spoke with, Tim had lost loved ones to gun violence and had been shot at himself. But a mind tuned to danger could also misread ordinary situations, reproducing the violence that had trained it.
The second pattern was a narrowing of perceived response options. When violence seemed possible, those we spoke with often saw only a narrow set of things they could do. Kobe, 24, described the months after his release from prison: ‘I was walking around like a ticking time bomb. Soon as somebody did anything, I’m whooping them like I’m they daddy.’ Similarly, when King learned that Lamont was dead, his thoughts narrowed to one response: revenge.
Such narrowing can be adaptive in dangerous situations, where hesitation can be costly. But when it is applied more generally, it can lead to serious problems. In these moments, people tend to bypass deliberate reflection and may feel that certain responses are inevitable, as King told us: ‘That’s how it be, and that’s how it’s going to always be. It’s a repeated cycle.’
Third, our interviews revealed that participants often read violent behaviour as proof of who someone was, rather than how that person had responded to a situation. Psychologists call this the fundamental attribution error, or our tendency to explain behaviour through features of a person’s character rather than circumstance. But the men turned this error most mercilessly on themselves.
Accepting violence as part of who they were made their future involvement in violence more likely
Take William, who had lost 11 close friends to gun violence by the age of 29. He came to see revenge not as something he did but as something he was. ‘I ain’t been a civilian since I was like eight…,’ he told us. ‘To sleep at night [with what I’ve done] you got to be a different type of monster.’ After his best friend was killed, he said: ‘I bought guns, a lot of them … I wasn’t going to feel safe until somebody was dead.’ Over time, the identity hardened: ‘To put that bet on somebody else, you got to be a cold-hearted motherfucker. Melatonin can’t even help you sleep after that.’
Terrel, 29, had endured a childhood of compounding losses. His mother was incarcerated, his little sister killed in a house fire, and he was shot – all before finishing the eighth grade. ‘I was an angry-ass little kid,’ he recalled. ‘I was angry because my momma was gone … My little sister dead … Everything I got is gone, so I’m angry.’ Terrel came to read his anger and the violent behaviour it spawned as a verdict on himself. Beneath the easy smile others saw, he felt he was ‘just covering up [what’s inside] with that smile’: ‘I been fucking up the community for years. How the fuck am I good?’
In sum, many we spoke to had come to see themselves not simply as people who had done bad things, but as bad people. By their own accounts, accepting violence as part of who they were made their future involvement in violence more likely.
Violence alters how people experience the world and read everyday encounters. These patterns are neither irrational nor pathological. They are adaptations to real danger, where quick responses can save a life. But carried into the wrong situation, the same shortcuts can be overgeneralised in ways that cause grave harm.
While the stakes of these cognitive patterns are exceptional, the mental machinery underpinning them is not. Say you’re driving and another car cuts you off. Before you’ve even thought about it, your mind has supplied a reason: This driver is reckless and has no regard for anyone else on the road. The interpretation arrives in a split second, built more out of your irritation than anything you know about the driver. Maybe she’s racing to a hospital for an emergency. The writer David Foster Wallace described such a scene in his commencement speech, ‘This Is Water’ (2005). His point was hopeful: we are free to choose how we read such a moment. The automatic, egocentric perspective is never the only one available.
Nuke’s mind did the same when a stranger held his gaze too long. The look may have meant nothing, yet he imagined a motive and a threat, drawn from his life, as most of us do, rather than anything the stranger had done. Nuke is working with the same machinery as the rest of us. What that machinery was trained on is different, and so is the price of getting it wrong. For the driver, a misreading ends in a muttered curse or a blown horn; for Nuke, it could end a life. As Nuke admitted: ‘I know what comes with it. It’s either death or jail.’
We tend to imagine that we take in the world and then respond to what we find. In fact, the mind guides what we see, filling gaps with expectations built from experience. The journalist Walter Lippmann in 1922 called these expectations ‘the pictures in our heads’ and explained that it is the pictures we respond to, not some objective environmental stimuli. Psychologists and sociologists call these shortcuts frames and scripts. Frames answer, in a fraction of a second, the question under every social encounter: What is going on here? Scripts suggest what to do next. Together they help us move through our days without deliberating over each interaction. Frames and scripts are tools that make daily life possible.
The vigilance that keeps someone alive at one point can generate danger at another
Among the men we spoke with, these shortcuts took their shape from a world that taught a brutal lesson early: people are dangerous, and hesitation can get you hurt. The lesson came from somewhere. The sociologist Elijah Anderson in 1994 called it the ‘code of the streets’. Where safety is not a given, a reputation for violence becomes the protection people can supply themselves. The frame comes first: this is a threat. The script that follows, I have to fight back, is learned from experience and reinforced by others.
But a shortcut is only as good as it is accurate. Threat-oriented frames and scripts may be adaptive in the specific situations that produced them, but the same reading carried into an uncertain moment can be destructive and self-defeating. The vigilance that keeps someone alive at one point can generate danger at another, converting an ambiguous situation into a hostile one and producing the very conflict it anticipated. The mind continues to guard against a world that is, in part, no longer there.
Of course, the milieu that trained these frames and scripts has not entirely disappeared for most. Recall that young men in these neighbourhoods faced a greater risk of being killed than a soldier deployed to Iraq or Afghanistan. A soldier, though, eventually returns home; these men have no such separation. What they must learn is more complex: how to hold on to vigilance without letting it dictate their reactions in the wrong place or at the wrong moment. The problem is not the impulse to fight back itself, but being unable to distinguish situations that call for it from those that don’t.
The idea that changing how we see can change how we respond is ancient. In the 2nd century, Epictetus said: ‘Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them.’ What is unusual is its application. Offering the opportunity to reframe a situation, as a serious answer to lethal violence, to a 26-year-old sitting in his room with a loaded clip is a novel proposition. It begins from an assumption too rarely extended to men like King with a history of violence: that despite what he has been through, his inner life is not fixed.
READI offered men a chance to discipline their inner worlds. The 18-month intervention paired a part-time job with cognitive behavioural sessions, held three to five mornings a week, that participants called ‘CAD’ (Control-Alt-Delete, the keystroke that reboots a computer). The lessons taught participants how to slow down to reconsider an automatic reaction and widen the range of responses in a tense moment. They learned that they did not have to be ruled by their first feeling or thought. In doing so, they began to loosen the identity that violence had formed
A randomised controlled trial of READI estimated that participants were arrested for shootings and homicides 65 per cent less often than comparable men who were not offered the programme. Findings from a related programme point in the same direction. Becoming a Man, a school-based programme run in Chicago by the nonprofit organisation Youth Guidance, cut violent-crime arrests among high-school-age participants by nearly half. Our interviews complement these trials by showing what the changes these programmes brought felt like from the inside.
What seemed to be a threat from the man across the street might be coming from somewhere much older
The first thing the men learned was to question their reading of a situation. In one CAD session, the group was given a scenario: somebody walks past and calls you a name. What do you do? For TY, 20, who had spent his adolescence surviving, the old answer would have arrived without thought. Instead, he worked through it. ‘I ain’t got no right to cause hurt to another person [if] this person ain’t do nothing to me,’ he said. ‘He probably having a bad day. He probably just got into it with his wife. You don’t know what’s wrong.’ Such exercises helped participants practise reframing a situation more charitably.
Questioning a reading also meant learning that a feeling of threat was not always about what was happening in the present; sometimes, it was a reaction to events in the past. The men practised noticing what fear was doing in their bodies, such as a racing pulse, tightened fists, pressure in the chest, and learning to treat those sensations as signals to investigate rather than signs of objective threats. Larry, 31, described it as learning to check in with his body: ‘Far as articulating the things that’s going on inside of my body and how I’m feeling, that’s what I’m really learning.’ What seemed to be a threat from the man across the street might, at times, be coming from somewhere much older.
Second, they learned to see more than one possible response to feeling threatened. Kobe described his old reflex as follows: ‘If you said something, I was going to touch you or tap you or get on your ass.’ Now, Kobe said: ‘I think before I act.’ Recalling a role-play in which he was bumped outside a store, he laid out what he could now see: ‘I could whoop one of they ass and one of them could shoot me… or I could just walk away. Or I could ask him, did he mean to do it?’ Three options emerged where there had previously been one.
To help them remember they had options in the moment, the men developed mantras simple enough to recall under pressure. Keith, 24, learned to: ‘Take 10 deep breaths, pace back and forth, and you might see things differently.’ Tune, 30, used: ‘It only takes three seconds to ruin your life.’ Larry, in a fight with his son’s mother, told himself: ‘It’s just words.’
Finally, participants learned to distinguish what they had done from who they were. Jaysean, 22, had taken the bad things he had done as proof that he was a bad person. Abandoned by kin while still a boy, he had sought out older robbers to teach him how to survive. He said: ‘A lot of things that I did bad, I did it for survival. Cause I didn’t really know no other way to get no money.’ Jaysean explained: ‘I was looking for the wrong help. I didn’t know no better. You a product of your environment to a certain extent.’ The reframing allowed him to imagine a self no longer defined by his past: ‘I’m a good person within… I’m still falling down but I’m picking myself back up.’ What Jaysean had once believed was a sign of his character, he could now see as a result of surviving tough circumstances.
Terrel reached the same realisation by naming the trauma he had long carried. ‘I never got through my first trauma,’ he said of his sister’s death; in the years since, he had lost a brother, a cousin, a nephew and friend after friend. ‘That shit just fucked me up to this day. I’m suffering with PTSD bad.’ Understanding his behaviour as a response to those losses, rather than as proof of who he was, made change imaginable. As Terrel said: ‘If you don’t deal with it… you can bring that baggage into your adult life.’ Naming the ways in which his past spilled into the present through his PTSD allowed Terrel to challenge his own narrative about himself and begin to heal.
These are ancient skills. READI’s contribution was not inventing them but building a place where men could practise them. These changes required certain conditions. READI’s wages gave the men enough stability to keep returning, and staff created a space safe enough for them to lower their guard, even around those participants they previously considered rivals. The pay check may have been what initially brought them in, but it was not how they ultimately understood the programme. In fact, 70 per cent described READI primarily as an opportunity for personal growth rather than just a job, and they spoke at length about how it reshaped their closest relationships, their daily habits, even their sense of who they were.
Which brings us back to King, in his room, with the clip full. Despite his initial instincts, he did not join his cousin to retaliate. He put the gun down and stayed put. ‘So I got high and I sat right there and just calmed myself down,’ he told us. ‘I shed a couple of tears for my boy and said: “Everything going to be all right.”’ It was the very mantra he had been practising in READI. King’s grief had not abated. What had changed was that revenge no longer felt inevitable. ‘Why I go try to waste my life for nothing?’ he asked. ‘That’s not me no more.’ In the space between feeling and action, King could see another response.
King did not arrive at that response alone. For months, he had practised slowing down and questioning his first reaction with other men. READI did not make the danger around him less real, nor did it ask him to abandon the vigilance that had sometimes kept him alive. Rather, it helped him more clearly discern the moments it threatened to reproduce the very violence he feared.
This is where I part with Wallace. He was right that we can choose how to read a situation, but he underestimated what such a choice requires. For the men we interviewed, seeing differently was not just a private act of will performed alone in traffic. It was something they practised repeatedly with others, under conditions of safety, enough time and skilled support.
‘I didn’t know that if you yelled at me, I was gonna break down. But now I [see]: it’s not you, it’s a past trigger’
I have seen the same skills taught in a classroom, on a corner by an outreach worker, and in a boxing gym in the Chicago neighbourhood of North Lawndale, where the former gang member Derek Brown* has been running a programme called Boxing Out Negativity since 2009. He teaches boys to box and, alongside it, to sit still and breathe, to notice what their bodies are doing before a fight and after one, to name what they are feeling and to wait. The boys come to Derek’s gym to learn how to fight. They are also learning how to handle the moments before a fight starts, which is the harder lesson and the one they need more often in life.
These skills are also useful to people who meet others in moments of crises. LaToya Baines* manages victim advocates on Chicago’s West Side who spend their days supporting people through the worst moments of their lives, and who bring their own histories to that work. She learned the same techniques through training and now teaches them to her staff. ‘Once you learn, you’re able to identify those triggers. I didn’t know that if you yelled at me, I was gonna break down. But now I’m able to [see]: it’s not you, it’s a past trigger. I just stepped back into the past, for something else that happened to me that has nothing to do with you.’ Chicago police officers are being taught to do the same thing, through a programme called Situational Decision-Making. Officers who went through it used less force and made fewer discretionary arrests.
None of this is particular to places where violence is the problem. When my husband and I started having conversations about merging our finances, I would respond by shutting down and becoming frustrated. He studies financial decision-making for a living, and talking about money was second-nature to him. For me it was physically painful. My chest would tighten, and I would go quiet, get anxious or find a reason to end the conversation.
It took me a long time to understand why. In the family in which I grew up, we didn’t talk about money. When we had it, nobody mentioned it. Then we lost our house, my parents divorced, and money was a more frequently discussed issue. It wasn’t until years later, while having conversations about finances with my husband that stirred negative responses in me, that I recognised how I automatically logged a conversation about money as the beginning of something going wrong. With help from a cognitive behavioural therapist and my very patient husband, I learned what the men in READI learned: to notice a reactive feeling in my body, to have compassion for myself about where it came from, and to recognise when it no longer served me.
Violence teaches the mind what to expect and how to answer. Because these are learned habits, they can be remade. A mind formed amid violence is not fixed by it. But few people revise their habits of mind on their own, sitting in traffic and deciding to see things differently. With proper training, people can learn to question their first reading of a situation, to see more than one response available to them, and to stop taking what they have done as proof of who they are. They learn, in other words, that their pasts need not define their present. The capacity is ordinary. What is not is the safety and ongoing support it takes to use it.
1 Names of READI Chicago participants have been changed to protect individuals’ privacy.
* Indicates real name used with permission.

News Analysis: Saudi Arabia once counted on U.S. protection. Now it's pivoting to new alliances

News Analysis: Saudi Arabia once counted on U.S. protection. Now it’s pivoting to new alliances
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- After Washington rebuffed calls to strike Houthi rebels, Saudi Arabia is pursuing new maritime and defense alliances.
- Houthi forces have seized territory on the Red Sea coast and threatened Saudi shipping, endangering an export route made more vital by Iran’s stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz.
BEIRUT — For decades, the relationship between Saudi Arabia and the U.S. has centered on an often-mentioned but rarely tested supposition: If the kingdom were attacked, America would come to its rescue.
But recent events have shown that much-vaunted security umbrella to be a leaky one.
Last month, Iran-aligned Yemeni rebels blitzed through Yemen’s coast and threatened to shut down Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea lifeline. But the Trump administration, reluctant to open a new front in its war with Iran, rebuffed Riyadh’s calls to come to its rescue.
That has left the kingdom searching for friends beyond Washington, for allies ready to put rockets where the rhetoric is and assist in a fight Saudi Arabia considers existential.
Over the last few months, as Persian Gulf nations contended with the fallout from the Israel-U.S. war on Iran, Saudi Arabia has supercharged its military-focused diplomacy. In July, it announced a 15-nation maritime alliance to safeguard shipping through the Red Sea, the Bab al Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden.
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which links the Mediterranean Sea with the Indian Ocean, is a new tinderbox in the Iran war.
Soon after came the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a NATO-inspired security pact where any attack on Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan would be regarded as an attack against all three.
And this week, Saudi Arabia’s race to rally allies spurred a detente of sorts with its frenemy the United Arab Emirates, with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman — the country’s de facto ruler — and defense minister brother receiving the Emirates’ vice president for the first high-level meeting since the two sides fell out over Yemen late last year.
There have even been reports of possible cooperation between Saudi Arabia and Israel against the Houthis, a notable development — if true — for two countries with no formal diplomatic relations.
The Saudi overtures come at a sensitive time for the kingdom. The standoff between the U.S. and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz has largely cut off Saudi Arabia’s main export channel, and attacks on its energy infrastructure are lowering its oil output.
As a result, the kingdom saw a 25% contraction in “oil activities,” according to official economic data, triggering an almost 5% decrease in the country’s gross domestic product between April and June, compared with the first quarter of the year.
That reduction forced painful cuts to Vision 2030, the prince’s signature policy aimed at remaking Saudi Arabia. So-called giga-projects, such as the Line and Trojena, have revised their ambitions downward amid the financial realities of a Saudi Arabia under fire.
Saudi Arabia is gambling on a gargantuan building boom to remake its image and economy, but history offers cautionary tales over such ambitions.
And all that was before the Houthis got involved.
The Houthis had been fighting the Saudis since 2015 in Yemen’s civil war that killed hundreds of thousands of people before settling into a stalemate and an uneasy ceasefire in 2022.
But in July, Saudi Arabia attacked the airport in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, to prevent the landing of an Iranian plane carrying high-ranking Houthi officials. That set off a flurry of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure, and the Houthis’ announcement of a blockade against Saudi shipping on the Red Sea — now the main corridor for Saudi energy exports.
Then in September, the Houthis overran Yemen’s coastal cities, snapping up materiel left behind by Saudi-backed government fighters and seizing control of territory near the Bab al Mandab strait.
A few days later, the Saudis accused an Iranian-backed militia in Iraq of coordinating with the Houthis to hit the East-West Pipeline, the vital infrastructure that had allowed Saudi Arabia to reorient its oil from Hormuz to the Red Sea.
All that pushed the Saudi crown prince to turn to the U.S. for help — and he had reason to think it would come: Late last year, the U.S. signed a strategic defense agreement with the kingdom, designated it a major non-NATO ally and agreed to sell it advanced F-35 fighter jets.
Mohammed also has something of a personal relationship with President Trump, who made Saudi Arabia the first stop of his first overseas tour in 2025 after being reelected and boasted that he had garnered almost $1 trillion in Saudi investments into the U.S. economy.
Trump initially seemed receptive to the prince’s entreaties but reportedly pulled back just as U.S. warplanes were set to take off for sorties on Houthi targets. Later, he told Fox News that Washington was “in constant communication with the Houthis and that they’ve agreed not to fight the United States.”
The Houthis have also assured European nations, which have been wary of provoking the rebels’ ire, that they won’t attack their shipping either. Last month, France and the U.K. said they would offer defensive assistance to Saudi Arabia, while Greece is operating U.S.-made Patriot missile batteries in the kingdom.
The Saudi deal stoked surprise and immediate concern across Washington, as well as in Israel, itself a nuclear power that has long feared an atomic arms race could grip the region.
With the U.S. hesitating, the expectation is that Saudi Arabia’s partners in the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement will form the international cavalry to help, but that has yet to manifest itself on the ground.
This week, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif said his country was “bound” by the pact to defend Saudi Arabia.
“That means whatever means are available at our disposal, they’ll be available to Saudi Arabia also,” he said.
Pakistan already has 8,000 troops in Saudi Arabia, along with 16 Chinese-made JF-17 Thunder fighter jets, combat drone squadrons and a surface-to-air missile battery. But it’s unclear whether they have participated in attacking the Houthis.
Turkish officials, meanwhile, say they have “no issues meeting” Saudi Arabia’s “military needs,” especially on technical matters.
The Houthis say any party attacking them will face retaliation.
“By God, if Turkey and Pakistan become involved, we will strike them with an iron fist,” said Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior member of the Houthis, in an interview on Iraqi television.
Observers say Saudi Arabia is gearing up for a ground offensive aimed at preventing the Houthis from consolidating their gains on the Red Sea coast and reversing the tide. The plan is for Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighters to lead the charge.
“It will be mostly an air campaign for the Saudis, with Yemenis and maybe Pakistanis on the ground, though I doubt the latter will get involved beyond being on the border,” said Bernard Haykel, a professor of Near Eastern Studies at Princeton University.
There is little chance the U.S. would contribute to such a fight with boots on the ground. But it could provide intelligence and logistical support, just as it did during Mohammed’s 2015 foray into Yemen. The U.S. Navy could also launch strikes, as it did when the Houthis blockaded the Red Sea in 2025, before Trump declared a ceasefire.
In any case, although Saudi leaders may not expect Washington to get involved, their fear is that the U.S. will forge another agreement with the Houthis to the exclusion of Riyadh’s concerns, Haykel said.
“The Saudis want a signal that the U.S. is in the background as support if something happens,” he said.
“They’d love to have it in the center of everything. But if they can’t, they want to make it seem like America is fully on board without necessarily being in the battle.”

Israeli opposition leader says young Israelis backed killing ‘everyone’ in Gaza

Abdel Ra'ouf Arnaout and Lina Altawell
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid said he met a group of young Israelis who expressed support for killing all Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, including babies.
Lapid made the remarks in a podcast interview, excerpts of which have circulated on social media platforms in recent days.
“I had a painful meeting with a group of very young people, and I heard from them all those statements calling for killing everyone and claiming that there are no innocents,” Lapid said.
He said he asked them: “Even babies?”
According to Lapid, they replied: “Babies too, because eventually they will grow up and become terrorists.”
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel, with US support, has carried out a genocide in the Gaza Strip that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, most of them women and children.
Since the start of the war on Gaza, Israeli officials and public figures have made statements calling for the use of overwhelming force against Palestinians and minimizing distinctions between civilians and combatants.
Criticism for government ministers
Lapid also criticized remarks by government ministers, saying Israel “will not recover” from allowing a minister to remain in office after calling for dropping a nuclear bomb on Gaza.
Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu called in November 2023 for using a nuclear weapon against Gaza.
Lapid also criticized statements by Israeli officials concerning starving civilians in Gaza, saying such remarks by ministers who remain in office damage Israel.
He also addressed the Israeli government’s policy toward countries that criticize it, arguing that cutting ties or closing embassies does not serve Israel’s interests.
“Anti-Israel rhetoric in Ireland and Spain was unacceptable, but questioned the usefulness of closing Israel’s embassy in Dublin or recalling its ambassador from Madrid,” Lapid said.
He said he would instead prefer to travel to those countries, appear in their media and engage with critics of Israel rather than boycott them.

Kinky dating app Feeld’s founders share in record £3.8m dividend after sales jump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:58:19 UTC
18:58:19 KST

Feeld, a UK-based dating app aimed at non-monogamous, queer and kinky users, has reported strong sales growth and paid its largest-ever dividend as it attracts users from more “vanilla” rivals.
Revenues jumped by 32% to £64m following a surge in interest from what it called “open-minded people exploring love, desire, and alternative relationships in a safe, inclusive space”.
Pre-tax profits grew from £9.3m to £11.4m, and the company’s shareholders – including the couple who founded it – shared in a dividend of £3.8m.
Ana Kirova and her partner, Dimo Trifonov, started the business under the name 3nder (pronounced Thrinder), initially targeting couples and singles looking for threesomes.
They were forced to change the company’s name to Feeld owing to a lawsuit from Tinder but it has since experienced rapid growth even as larger rivals have faltered.
Match Group, which owns Tinder and other dating apps such as Hinge and OK Cupid, reported a 5% decline in user numbers earlier this year, amid reports of fatigue with the experience of seeking romance or sex via an app.
But Feeld, which calls itself a dating app “for the curious”, appears to be scooping up some of those users. While this has prompted reports that its edgy image has been watered down by an influx of people with more conventional or monogamous sensibilities, Feeld’s president, Kyle Brennan, said it reflected changing tastes.
“These numbers speak to something bigger than the growth of our business,” said Brennan. “They reflect a broader shift in how people are thinking about connection, with greater openness, curiosity and agency to do things differently.”
Accounts filed at Companies House said rising sales reflected “strong global user growth”, particularly outside the UK, with the rest of the world accounting for £56m of its total £64m in revenues, nearly 90%. Mexico and Spain were Feeld’s fastest-growing regions, while New York, Toronto and Paris led the way among cities, each recording an uplift in user numbers of more than 20%, the company said.
Feeld makes money via the sale of its Majestic memberships, which give users features such as unlimited opportunities to “like” other members, the ability to see who has liked them, and advanced filters to tailor specifications for a potential partner.
It also sells members extra “pings”, a feature that allows members to express interest in someone and send them a message, without having matched with them first.
In 2024, it emerged that some of these features were temporarily vulnerable to manipulation due to security “vulnerabilities” exposed by cybersecurity experts.
Research by the London-based cybersecurity firm Fortbridge found that users could have had sensitive data including messages, private photos and details of their sexuality accessed or even edited.
At the time, Feeld said it had investigated the problems brought to its attention by Fortbridge on 3 March and fixed them by 28 May that year. It said there was no evidence that any customer data had been accessed. It has invested £10.5m in technological upgrades in the past year.
The largest dividend reported in Feeld’s previous accounts was £600,000 in 2024.
As well as its dating platform, Feeld runs in-person social events including a “kinky trivia” night and a “pitch your mate” event, at which guests take to the stage to wax lyrical about why people should date their friends.

UN allocates $160M to 12 of the world's most underfunded humanitarian crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:57:18 UTC
18:57:18 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
The UN on Friday allocated $160 million from its Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) to support life-saving assistance in 12 of the world's most underfunded humanitarian crises.
The allocation is part of a broader effort to reach 87 million people facing the most severe humanitarian needs this year, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
“We have 87 million people to reach, and no time to waste,” UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said in a statement.
Fletcher stressed that funding alone would not be enough, urging leaders to “exercise political will to open access, remove obstacles and help us reach people whose lives are on the line.”
Of the funding, $150 million will go to Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Chad, Cuba, Mali, Niger, the occupied Palestinian territory, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, and Yemen.
Afghanistan, the occupied Palestinian territory, South Sudan, Sudan, and Yemen are also among 10 crises where Fletcher has called for urgent diplomatic action to secure humanitarian access.
Another $10 million will address the needs of people with disabilities across the 12 crises.
The latest allocation brings total CERF funding provided so far in 2026 to $483 million.

charlotte perriand’s built-in interiors survive inside 1960 paris tower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:55:18 UTC
18:55:18 KST

charlotte perriand’s built-in interiors survive inside 1960 paris tower
the preserved rooms show how furniture, structure and everyday life were brought together within an early french residential high-rise.
CHARLOTTE PERRIAND’S APPROACH TO DOMESTIC SPACE
Designed by architect Édouard Albert in 1960, the Albert Tower in Paris’s 13th arrondissement contains a surviving apartment interior shaped by Charlotte Perriand, with built-in storage, a kitchen and furniture designed by the influential architect and designer. Now offered for sale, the property provides a rare glimpse into Perriand’s approach to domestic space within one of France’s early experiments in residential high-rise architecture.
The residence occupies a high floor of the tower, with 102.49 square meters of living space and extensive views across the French capital. Its interior includes an entrance hall with built-in closets attributed to Perriand, a separate kitchen, and a living and dining area. The apartment was once home to Swiss designer Ubald Klug and his wife Helena, a ceramicist. Their home was part of the creative circle around designers such as Jean Prouvé, reflecting the experimental spirit of postwar French design.
ÉDOUARD ALBERT’S FLEXIBLE STEEL STRUCTURE
The interior, listed for sale by the real estate agency Architecture de Collection, gains significance from its relationship to Albert’s construction. The Albert Tower uses a regular metal grid of steel tube columns filled with concrete, supporting reinforced concrete slabs and cross-shaped bracing. Designed to combine lightness and transparency, the structure leaves the facade to reveal its underlying construction. With the supporting elements concentrated in pillars, the plan can be reorganized with relative freedom, giving Perriand’s built-in elements a flexible architectural setting.
The kitchen and entrance storage are particularly revealing. Perriand’s designs are built into the rooms, making storage and other everyday functions part of the architecture. The space shows how architects and designers of the period brought furniture, interiors and structure together.
MODERNIST HIGH-RISE LIVING IN PARIS
Albert’s tower, now listed as a historical monument, was conceived as an experiment in bringing high-rise residential construction into the Parisian context. The metal structure of the building, developed through Albert’s research into steel tubes, reflects his interest in linking construction, economy and architectural expression.
The panoramic position of the apartment makes the relationship between structure and domestic life particularly apparent. Its many windows open toward landmarks including the Eiffel Tower, the Invalides, the Val-de-Grâce, the Sacré-Cœur, the Panthéon and Notre-Dame, while its western exposure brings changing light into the rooms.
Yet the more revealing aspect of the property is closer to eye level. The Perriand-designed elements show how the ambitions of postwar modern architecture could extend where things are stored, how a kitchen is organized and how furniture occupies a flexible plan.
project info:
name: Albert Tower apartment
architect: Édouard Albert
interior designer / furniture designer: Charlotte Perriand
location: Paris 13th arrondissement, France
year: 1960
living area: 102.49 square meters
total area: 106 square meters

SAO PAULO – Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his election rival Flavio Bolsonaro are leaving no controversy unturned in their last-ditch efforts to discredit each other and win over voters ahead of Oct 4’s nail-biter election.
A campaign dominated by scandals and insults has done little to ease the deep political polarisation in Latin America’s biggest economy, one of the last major leftist bastions in the region.
The tight race pits Lula, 80, against the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of Donald Trump who has backed a wave of victorious right-wing candidates in Latin America.
Trump said on Oct 1 that he was watching Brazil’s election “very closely”.
Opinion polls predict the vote will go to a run-off on Oct 25, with Lula and Flavio in a dead heat.
“The race is tied but not at a standstill: the final week will determine where the voters who can still be swayed will go,” Felipe Nunes, director of the Quaest polling institute, told AFP.
Many of the nation’s 160 million registered voters are disenchanted with their options and were deprived of a debate between the leading candidates when both declined to attend a televised programme on the evening of Oct 1.
Marcelo Vilanova, 32, a fish market manager in the southeastern city of Juiz de Fora, said he was voting for Lula as the “lesser of two evils”.
“He did good things for me, for my family,” he said, referring to Lula’s social welfare programmes. “I have criticisms of him too.”
Lucas Sales, 38, a cell phone shop owner in the city, is voting for Flavio Bolsonaro even if “he himself isn’t the best option”, citing his promise to be tough on crime, a key concern for many Brazilians in this election.
A saintly spat and gynaecological gaffe
The race for undecided voters has had both sides on alert for anything they can twist to their advantage.
In recent days, Brazil’s beloved patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, depicted as a black Madonna, became the focus as rumours erupted that Flavio Bolsonaro planned to strip her of her post if elected.
Flavio issued fierce denials as Lula took to the campaign trail clutching a statue of the saint, declaring that “messing” with her was “unacceptable”.
The electoral court ordered on Oct 1 that posts with the “untrue” claims be taken down.
Lula tends to have more support among Catholics while Bolsonaro has the backing of a booming Evangelical population.
Next, Flavio Bolsonaro and his supporters pounced when Lula said that men were “cowards” when it comes to getting their prostates examined, while “women learn to receive a touch from a young age”, referring to gynaecological exams.
Clips of his comment circulated widely on social media as if it were an allusion to abuse, and Flavio Bolsonaro accused Lula of being “sexist”.
“It’s really turned into a circus... My vote won’t go to any of them,” said Gisele Sousa, 45, a clothing shop employee.
In another jab during a podcast on Oct 1, Lula said he was sure he would win in the first round, over a rival he said was not even qualified “to serve as a building manager”.
Lula’s political clout
Veteran leftist Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, boasting he is fitter than ever despite his advanced age.
The former union leader has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment while massively curbing deforestation in the Amazon rainforest.
Nevertheless, voters complain about a high cost of living and are fed up with violence and crime.
Lula unveiled a flurry of measures in the run-up to the election to win over voters, increasing social welfare payments and banning sports betting that has ensnared many in gambling addiction.
“Only Lula has the political clout and credibility to carry out reforms,” Edinho Silva, president of Lula’s Workers’ Party, told AFP.
Lula made Brazilian sovereignty a central plank of his campaign, warning Trump not to “meddle” in his country’s elections.
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has remained a tough foe for Lula, even as it emerged he was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic Dark Horse about his father.
He was forced during the campaign to admit he had asked jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro, at the heart of one of Brazil’s largest financial fraud cases, to bankroll the film.
Bolsonaro was also confident of a first-round win, vowing that Lula would be “ousted from the presidency” on Oct 4. AFP

Meloni asks Brussels for fiscal leeway as energy shock squeezes Italy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:53:35 UTC
18:53:35 KST

Italian prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is urging the European Commission again to relax the EU's fiscal rules, saying that higher inflation due to soaring energy prices is squeezing households and businesses, according to a letter seen by Euronews.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is urging Brussels once again to give capitals more room to cushion households and companies from the latest energy-price shock, arguing that European Union fiscal rules are becoming increasingly restrictive as inflation drives up government spending.
In a letter addressed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, seen by Euronews, Meloni said the prolonged Middle East crisis has left European energy markets “extremely tight,” with oil prices up almost 80% and gas up to 156%.
"Against this backdrop, the agreed net expenditure paths under the European fiscal framework leave limited room to alleviate the impact on households and firms without resorting to tightening measures at a time of significant downside risks for the economy," Meloni added.
Italy, which is heading to polls next year, holds one of the highest debt-to-GDP ratios in the EU, trailing only Greece, which has recently sought a similar appeal to relax fiscal rules with the Commission.
The Italian leader argues that governments are collecting more tax revenue because prices are higher, but EU fiscal rules make it difficult to recycle that windfall into temporary energy support.
Higher inflation automatically increases indirect tax receipts such as VAT, but using that additional revenue to finance measures that reduce energy costs can count as discretionary fiscal action and run into limits imposed by agreed national spending paths, Meloni noted.
As a solution, the Italian leader is asking Brussels to recognise that some of the additional spending is not the result of governments choosing to spend more, but of inflation mechanically increasing existing obligations.
Meloni wants the Commission to find a way to allow at least part of those additional revenues to be used for "temporary and targeted measures" to reduce the impact of high energy prices — an approach that has been repeatedly recommended by EU officials.
EU budget rules put a limit on how much governments can increase spending, based on the amounts agreed in their budget plans. But when inflation rises more than expected, some government costs automatically go up — such as pensions linked to the cost of living — leaving governments with less room to absorb those extra costs.
The EU’s fiscal framework sets national spending limits in nominal terms, meaning governments cannot simply raise expenditure when inflation comes in significantly above initial forecasts. At the same time, some areas of public spending automatically increase as prices rise.
Meloni said that spending directly affected by inflation exceeding the assumptions underpinning Italy’s budget plan amounts to 20.4% of GDP, while a further 12% of GDP in other expenditure is also expected to come under pressure in 2027.
"We are mindful of the risk of amending newly introduced fiscal rules that pursue a goal we all share, debt sustainability. We are also fully mindful of Italy's commitments under the ongoing excessive deficit procedure and of the need to comply with the corrective net expenditure path," reads the letter.
Meloni called for the issue to be discussed at the upcoming meeting of finance ministers in Brussels on 9 October.

Claims about catastrophically low availability and excessively long maintenance of F-16s are false - Ministry of Foreign Affairs

Ukraine’s F-16 fighter fleet is being used intensively and under challenging conditions, but recent reports of catastrophically low aircraft readiness rates and excessively long maintenance periods are false. Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi made the statement on October 2 on X, UNN writes.
Ukraine operates its F-16 fleet intensively and under demanding conditions. We have always recognized that sustaining these aircraft would be challenging, particularly because certain components for this early F-16 variant are no longer in production and are becoming increasingly difficult to source. However, recent reports alleging catastrophically low aircraft availability rates and excessively long maintenance turnaround times are simply false
According to him, "contrary to these claims, our industrial sustainment partners are not only continuing to deliver overhauled aircraft, but are doing so at an increasing pace. Turnaround times are decreasing, not increasing."
"We have full confidence in our industry partners and their ability to further optimize sustainment processes, ensuring the highest possible levels of F-16 readiness and availability during the coming winter months, when these capabilities will be needed most," the Foreign Ministry spokesperson stated.
"Such reports should not undermine confidence in the international funding that supports F-16 sustainment efforts or question the continued need for additional F-16 aircraft from partner nations' inventories," Tykhyi noted.
He emphasized: "We should not allow misinformation to weaken this vital support. The modernization and sustainment of our F-16 fleet remain essential to Ukraine's ability to defend its airspace and protect its people."
Addendum
The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson’s statement followed a publication by the WSJ, which claimed that more than half of Ukraine’s F-16 fighter jets are in a state of uncertainty regarding maintenance.

Germany’s Army will establish a drone systems regiment in 2027, which will become part of the 10th Panzer Division.

The newly established formation will consolidate capabilities for operating unmanned systems with a range of up to 500 km.
The regiment will also include an electronic warfare company and units tasked with intercepting enemy drones.

Man City verdict puts UK-UAE diplomatic relations under strain
- A court found Manchester City guilty of nearly all 115 financial charges, risking penalties like points deduction or expulsion, straining UK-UAE diplomatic and investment relations.
- The UAE has invested over £30 billion in the UK, but the ruling has caused frustration and may affect future large-scale investments and defense cooperation.
- UK officials stress Premier League independence despite political tensions; Manchester City plans to appeal, while the case threatens football governance and bilateral ties ahead of an October summit.
AI generated
A historic legal ruling against Manchester City Football Club has placed diplomatic ties between the UK and the United Arab Emirates under significant strain, with billions of pounds in projected foreign investment at stake.
Over the past five years, the UAE has poured more than £30 billion (S$50.6 billion) into major UK sectors, including defence, life sciences and technology. The two nations are eager to maintain their financial partnership, and an investment summit is pencilled in for October, but frustration on both sides has escalated due to the fallout surrounding the Manchester City case.
In a seismic judgment late last week, Abu Dhabi-owned Manchester City was found guilty of all but one of 115 charges brought against it by England’s Premier League after a four-year investigation. The club artificially inflated its financial results by more than £900 million, according to the findings of an independent commission published on Sept 29.
Potential punishments include points deduction, heavy fines or even expulsion from the Premier League.
The ruling is a major blow for the 18-year soft power project, at the top of which is Manchester City’s ultimate owner, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the brother of the UAE’s president. The Emirati owners, with Khaldoon Al Mubarak as the club’s chairman, have delivered eight premier league titles and transformed the club into a footballing superpower.
Emirati officials have warned the UK government that the severity of the ruling could undermine their appetite for future grand-scale UK commitments, according to people familiar with the matter. They consider the Premier League’s actions to have an influence on the bilateral state relationship, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing undisclosed information.
UK government officials are equally frustrated by the conduct of their UAE counterparts in relation to the scandal, according to other people familiar with the matter. They believe some in the Gulf nation must have been aware of the extent of Manchester City’s wrongdoing, even while insisting there was nothing untoward, said the people, who asked not to be identified talking about private deliberations.
The scandal has also caused splits in the UK government. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s comments thanking Manchester City’s owners for their investment riled his own politicians who want to keep the process independent of government influence.
A spokesman for the UK government declined to comment. The UAE’s Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The frustration from both sides comes at a crucial time for UK-UAE relations. The current investment partnership is up for discussion ahead of an Abu Dhabi summit to be held in London later in October, with British officials eager to secure more commitments.
Man City ruling may test billion-dollar ties: Mideast money
Under the original five-year agreement, the UAE’s sovereign wealth fund Mubadala, led by Mubarak, committed £10 billion to British industries, though the total has reached nearly £30 billion. That has been a small part of a global commitment: Abu Dhabi, home to wealth funds holding more than $2 trillion (S$2.5 trillion) of assets, is planning to invest another $1.4 trillion in the US and has pledged $46 billion in Germany.
Defence is central to UK-UAE talks, with the need for cooperation heightening due to the ongoing US-Iranian war and wider unrest in the Middle East. The UK lent military support to the UAE after the US and Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic prompted Tehran to retaliate against Washington’s Gulf allies.
Despite both sides agreeing that talks on defence are far more important than football, the Premier League’s judgment has injected political tension into the negotiations. Longer standing issues remain contentious, including the UAE’s alleged role in the Sudanese civil war and the thwarted Emirates-backed takeover attempt of The Telegraph newspaper.
Officials are now trying to smooth over the issue. In a UK media interview on Sept 30, Burnham thanked City Football Group – the owners of Man City – for their investment in Manchester.
“I would be really concerned to lose them,” Burnham said. “They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester.”
The relationship is important to Burnham and fellow senior politicians. Shortly after becoming Prime Minister in July, Burnham spoke to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. They connected over Manchester, where Burnham was mayor before ascending to the top job. Massive Emirati capital injections into urban regeneration across the east of the city helped bolster Burnham’s political profile during his tenure.
UK government officials have privately suggested that Premier League investigations are outside their control, given sporting regulation and judicial matters are not subject to state influence.
“The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions,” Manchester City said on Sept 29. The club has until Oct 2 to appeal the decision.
Manchester City has been one of the UAE’s most successful outlets for projecting soft power. Under Sheikh Mansour’s ownership, the club came out of the shadow of crosstown competitor Manchester United and usurped its historically more successful rival as a perennial challenger for league titles. It has attracted a string of star players, notably Sergio Aguero, Kevin De Bruyne and current striker Erling Haaland.
The league has yet to set out sanctions, but the guilty verdict already threatens to upend the Premier League and football in England more widely. Manchester City’s haul of trophies during the period in question potentially opens the door to compensation claims from rival clubs and even fans.
While no prosecutor is known to be looking at criminal charges, false accounting is a crime in England and Wales that carries potential jail terms. Meanwhile, the club’s auditors could face a probe from the Financial Reporting Council. Neither regulator responded to requests for comment.
The UK has long touted its investment links with the UAE. A little over a week before the Manchester City verdict, Burnham posted a video to his almost one million TikTok followers showing him inside a McLaren sports car boasting “that is the sound of Britain making things again”.
Burnham’s comments came as McLaren Automotive announced plans to invest £500 million into the UK, part of a larger commitment from McLaren Automotive shareholder L’IMAD Holding, a sovereign investor of the Government of Abu Dhabi.
But the prime minister’s recent comments backing Manchester City’s owners have riled local lawmakers. They risk undermining legislation aimed at preserving the operational autonomy of the Independent Football Regulator, which is responsible for determining the outcome of the case against Manchester City, Bloomberg reported.
Downing Street later issued a statement saying Manchester City are not “above the rules”. BLOOMBERG

Large volumes of medical supplies for Gaza face wait times of 74 days for Israeli clearance: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:49:19 UTC
18:49:19 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Large volumes of medical supplies meant for Gaza wait a median of 74 days for clearance by Israeli authorities, the World Health Organization said Friday, urging “unimpeded and predictable” access for the much-needed aid.
“Not one hospital in Gaza is fully functional,” Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the occupied Palestinian territory, told reporters in Geneva.
Van De Weerdt said chronic shortages of medicines and medical supplies remain a major obstacle to restoring health services, despite a year having passed since the ceasefire was announced.
"Without those items, no hospital will ever be fully or even partially functional," she said.
According to the WHO's latest analysis, large volumes of medical supplies wait a median of 74 days, roughly 2 1/2 months, for Israeli clearance.
“If the shipment hasn't been approved, then we start that lengthy, cumbersome process all over again with no guarantees for a different outcome,” she said.
Medicines have an approval rate of nearly 87%, while medical equipment – including X-ray machines, sterilization equipment, and spare parts for CT scanners – is regularly rejected, she said, "often with no explanation given."
"Every extra day in storage or in transit brings medicines a day closer to expiry, an equipment closer to being damaged before it ever reaches the person who needs it," she warned.
She also described the security situation in Gaza as “very, very precarious,” saying collecting medical supplies from the Kerem Shalom crossing requires WHO teams to travel through an area controlled by the Israeli military using armored vehicles and personal protective equipment.
The process must be coordinated with Israeli authorities and teams often face delays in receiving the green light, she said, adding that logistical staff can leave early in the morning and return late in the evening with supplies that had been waiting at the crossing.
The WHO called for the “unimpeded and predictable” entry of humanitarian and health supplies into Gaza at scale and the use of multiple crossings.

A Flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac App Could Have Let Hackers Grab Sensitive Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

Hardly a day goes by lately without news of AI agents autonomously hacking websites or AI tools being used by cybercriminals and scammers. But a recently patched vulnerability in the macOS version of OpenAI’s ChatGPT underscores the potential value to attackers of compromising AI software itself as these apps proliferate more and more.
The bug could have been exploited to essentially take over ChatGPT on a victim’s computer, giving an attacker access to all the chat logs and other data stored by the app, as well as interconnections like browser sessions. Discovered by researchers at the Objective-See Foundation, the vulnerability illustrates the deep system access and trust that AI platforms are afforded in order to work—and the target that this puts on their backs.
“Agents need a lot of access to do their job,” says Objective-See Foundation software analyst and longtime macOS researcher Patrick Wardle. “They are like the building manager who has access to the keys to all the rooms. So if they can be corrupted or subverted, that’s super problematic. It can mean that unprivileged code could then potentially have access to all the things.”
OpenAI publicly acknowledged the security flaw and fix in its system change log on September 25. “We continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster,” OpenAI spokesperson Shane Bauer told WIRED in a statement.
The ChatGPT macOS app includes multiple components that communicate with each other securely by checking for digital signatures. The idea is to confirm with these validity checks that both processes are OpenAI components and not outside, potentially malicious software making a request. And the system design goes so far as to require these signature checks at three layers of remove from the request, to ensure that malicious software isn’t somehow directing an OpenAI component to be a proxy and make a seemingly trusted request.
Objective-See Foundation researchers found, though, that there is a trusted component, a script interpreter, that would accept an untrusted script (or list of commands to run) and could then be manipulated to deliver this script into the main ChatGPT process. “They also check the parent and grandparent of that process, but the malicious script just spawns the script interpreter three times and then makes the request so it will satisfy the requirements,” Wardle says. The flaw could only be exploited by an attacker who already had malware installed on a target machine.
The vulnerability was “insanely trivial” to exploit, he adds, and his proof of concept only required about a dozen lines of code. In addition to accessing ChatGPT chat logs, the vulnerability could also be used to get ChatGPT to run commands for the attacker, such as accessing a browser or other sensitive applications, with the requests appearing as legitimate instructions issued by the OpenAI software.
Wardle will present analysis of a number of AI macOS application bugs at Objective by the Sea, an Apple-focused security conference in November.
He recently found a flaw, now patched, in the dictation feature of Meta’s new Muse AI assistant that could have been exploited by a local attacker to grab a mishandled authentication token and gain access to user data. And he says that he has already submitted a new vulnerability finding to OpenAI related to the integration between ChatGPT and the company’s new always-on Dots AI assistant. OpenAI is currently reviewing his report.
“AI companies are fixated on adding features right now,” Wardle says. “But as always, the more features, the broader the attack surface. So all of these companies need to be fully focused on security, and from what I can see, it still often seems like an afterthought.”
Update: 10/2/2026, 2:07 pm EDT: WIRED has updated the story to elaborate on how the flaw could be exploited.

Overnight on October 2, units of Ukraine's Defense Forces struck the LUKOIL-Volgogradneftepererabotka oil refinery in Volgograd, Volgograd region. Explosions and a fire were recorded at the facility.
LUKOIL-Volgogradneftepererabotka is one of the largest oil refineries in the Russian Federation. Its refining capacity is about 15 million tonnes of oil per year. The facility produces motor gasoline, diesel fuel and aviation fuel. It is involved in meeting the needs of the Russian Armed Forces.
In addition, the Samara linear production and dispatch station (LPDS) in the area of the settlement of Prosvet, Samara region, was hit. A fire was recorded at the facility.
The Samara LPDS is a production facility and a major oil receiving, storage and blending hub. Oil reaches the station via trunk pipelines from Tatarstan, Western Siberia and other oil-producing regions of Russia. The facility blends high- and low-sulfur crude from different fields to produce Urals export-grade crude, which accounts for up to 50% of Russia's total oil exports. The facility is involved in meeting the needs of the Russian Armed Forces.
The results of the strike are being clarified.
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that, together with other components of the Defense Forces, it had carried out long-range strikes against four important oil infrastructure facilities in Russia's Samara and Volgograd regions.
Drones operated by the SBU's Alpha Special Operations Center, together with the Unmanned Systems Forces, Special Operations Forces and the Main Intelligence Directorate, struck the Samara linear production and dispatch station, as well as the Samara-1 and Samara-2 pumping stations near the settlement of Prosvet. Fires were recorded at the facilities following the strikes.
The Volgograd Oil Refinery was also hit in a joint operation with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate. A fire was recorded at the refinery.
NASA's FIRMS satellite service detected fire hotspots near the delayed coking unit and the ELOU-AVT-1 and ELOU-AVT-5 units, which are key processing facilities at the refinery.
As reported, the Transneft hub caught fire in Samara following explosions, while a fire broke out in the area of an oil refinery and chemical plant in Volgograd.

At the age of 100, Zenon Vrublevskyi, a veteran of the Galicia Division and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, has died
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
12:44:55 EEST
18:44:55 KST

At the age of 100, Zenon Vrublevskyi, a veteran of the Galicia Division and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, has died
Kyiv • UNN
In Lviv, OUN figure and veteran of the Galicia Division and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army Zenon Vrublevskyi has died. He survived captivity, Soviet camps, and arrest.
In the 100th year of his life, Zenon Vrublevsky, an OUN figure and veteran of the Galicia Division, died. This was reported by Maksym Kozytskyi, head of the Lviv Regional Military Administration, on Telegram on October 2, UNN writes.
Almost a century of life. And what a life! An OUN underground member, a soldier of the Galicia Division and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army. He experienced captivity and Soviet camps. He fought for Ukraine back when one could pay with freedom or life merely for thinking about its independence
More detailed information about the funeral will be announced later.
Supplement
Zenon Vrublevsky was born in Lviv on March 17, 1927. At the age of 16, he left the gymnasium and secretly, without his parents’ knowledge, volunteered for the Galicia Division. Later, he was the personal driver of Colonel of the Army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic Ivan Rembolovych. During the fighting in the "Brody cauldron," he was taken prisoner and transported to a concentration camp in the Urals. After spending two years there, he managed to escape. In Lviv, he established contacts with the OUN underground.
He was arrested in 1947 and sentenced to 25 years in prison and five years of deprivation of rights, with confiscation of property. He served his sentence in the prisons and camps of Sverdlovsk, Karaganda, Kemerovo, and Vorkuta. After his release, he was forced to live in Vorkuta for several more years. He returned to Lviv in 1960.

Bonds steady as French borrowing costs hit 24-year high and UK 30-year yields top 6%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:43:43 UTC
18:43:43 KST

Government bond markets steadied on Friday morning after a sell-off pushed France's 10-year borrowing costs to their highest since 2002, lifted UK 30-year yields above 6% for the first time since 1998 and drove the benchmark US 10-year yield to a 24-year high.
Global bond markets found their footing on Friday morning, with yields slipping back after a turbulent Thursday in which government borrowing costs in Europe and the US hit multi-decade highs.
Yields, which rise when bond prices fall, retreated as Brent crude slipped about 2% to around $99.95 a barrel, tempering fears that the energy shock would keep inflation high and force central banks into more rate hikes.
In the UK, the yield on 30-year government bonds, or gilts, fell to around 5.92% after climbing above 6% on Thursday for the first time since 1998. The 10-year yield dropped to about 5.37%, below the 19-year high reached earlier this week, while the two-year yield slid more than six basis points to around 4.77%.
Thursday's sell-off also hit British bank shares, with NatWest, Lloyds, HSBC and Barclays falling around 4% to 5%.
The losses deepened after Sky News reported that Chancellor John Healey had summoned bank bosses to a meeting ahead of his 28 October budget, fuelling speculation about new bank taxes.
France in the firing line
France's 10-year yield hit 4.96% on Thursday, its highest since July 2002, before easing to about 4.92% on Friday at about 11 am CEST. The extra yield investors demand to hold French rather than German debt reached over 140 basis points this week, the widest gap since 2012.
That gap jumped 13.9 basis points on Thursday, its biggest daily rise since March 2020, according to Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid.
"The daily moves were reminiscent of the Euro crisis in many respects, with sovereign contagion a big talking point," Reid told clients in a note.
The sell-off came as Paris unveiled a 2027 budget seeking €43 billion in new savings to cut the deficit from 5.4% of GDP this year to 5% next year. Public debt stands at a post-war record of 119% of GDP, and France plans to borrow a record €340 billion next year.
"Here and there, I hear the prophets of doom promising us worse times ahead. I would like to reiterate here that France's signature is solid," French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said.
France's fiscal watchdog, the High Council of Public Finances, was less upbeat, calling the government's 1% growth forecast for 2027 optimistic and a return below the EU's 3% deficit limit by 2029 very unlikely.
"With a difficult political process ahead, French bonds are likely to remain under pressure, while the threshold for ECB intervention remains high," ING analysts wrote.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen leads polls ahead of next spring's presidential election.
Fresh figuresadded to the inflation worries behind the sell-offas eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, its highest in three years, up from 3.2% in August, according to Eurostat's flash estimate published on Friday.
Economists had expected 3.6%, and Spain's annual rate hit 5%.
It was the seventh month in a row above the European Central Bank's 2% target as traders expect the ECB, which raised rates in June and September, to lift its deposit rate by another quarter point to 2.75% by year-end.
US Treasuries retreat from 24-year high
In the US, the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.34% on Thursday, its highest since 2002, before pulling back to around 5.26%.
Surging energy costs are stoking inflation, while the AI and data-centre boom competes for capital. After a rate hike in September, markets expect at least three more from the Federal Reserve by mid-2027.
"As yields have crept higher, that is going to tighten financial conditions and could increase the risk of a slowdown," said Danny Zaid, portfolio manager at TwentyFour Asset Management.
Overall, the bill is mounting.
Developed economies paid more than $3.3 trillion (€2.9tn) in interest on internationally traded government bonds over the past year, according to the Washington-based Institute of International Finance, which is more than the estimated global spending on defence or AI.

Sudan’s Bashir transferred to Khartoum, seeks treatment abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
09:40:34 UTC
18:40:34 KST

Ousted Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir has been moved to a military-run hospital in Khartoum for treatment and needs further medical care abroad, his lawyer said Thursday.
Bashir, 82, was ousted by Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in April 2019 after months of mass protests that brought an end to his nearly three-decade rule.
The army and RSF later turned against each other over plans to integrate the paramilitary force into the military as part of a planned transition to civilian rule. Their dispute erupted into war in April 2023, triggering a devastating conflict that has killed and displaced large numbers of people and left much of Sudan in ruins.
Bashir had been moved from prison to a hospital before the war broke out and was later transferred to the town of Merowe in northern Sudan, where he was placed under military guard.
Bashir was sent to Khartoum for medical tests after developing symptoms that required diagnosis and treatment outside Sudan, his lawyer, Mohamed Alhassan Alameen, told Reuters.
In a statement Wednesday, Bashir’s family said his need for medical treatment outside Sudan "has become critical and urgent, and cannot be delayed any longer," but said they had not received official permission to send him abroad.
It was unclear precisely what condition Bashir was suffering from. Sudan’s military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Several prominent Sudanese Islamist figures also called for his transfer out of the country on social media.
Any such move would likely cause discord within Sudan and could draw international condemnation, as Bashir is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges including genocide. He also faces open cases in Sudan.
During Bashir’s three decades in power, Sudan was listed by the U.S. as a state sponsor of terrorism and was subject to wide-ranging sanctions. Protesters during the popular uprising accused him and his Islamist National Congress Party of widespread corruption and repression.
After his ouster, Bashir was tried on various charges and convicted of corruption and illicit financing, for which he was serving a prison sentence when the war began.
